On 5 September 2007 the Acting President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theApplication at the same time. On 19 September 1995 the applicant was arrested and charged, inter alia, with aggravated debtor fraud. On the same day he was detained in solitary confinement, which was prolonged at regular intervals until he was released on 22 December 1995. On 25 June 1998, the indictment was submitted to the City Court according to which the applicant (and five co-accused: A, B, N, M and R) were charged of “tax asset stripping” committed jointly. The applicant was charged with fifteen counts out of a total of fifty-nine committed between March 1992 and May 1993. His responsibility related to an amount of DKK 9,890,000 out of the total amount of tax evaded in the case which came to approximately EUR 19,000,000. The applicant was sentenced to two years’ imprisonment. but on one count he was acquitted. The co-accused were also convicted. An amount of DKK 2,200,000 was seized, and he was deprived for an indefinite period of his right to establish a private limited company or a company or an association requiring public approval. The City Court dismissed the applicant’s claim that the length of the proceedings had been at variance with Article 6 of the Convention, stating the following: “The City Court finds no reason to criticise the prosecution’S decision to join the criminal proceedings against the [applicant and the five co‑accused].” The High Court upheld the City Court’s judgment on 28 September 2004. The applicant and the co‑defendants requested that the Leave to Appeal Board grant them leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) Three of the defendants stated in their petitions that they would submit supplementary comments, which were received on 17 December 2004. In January 2005 the cases were sent to the prosecution, which gave its opinion on 29 March 2005. Thereafter, due to an error, nothing happened in the case until 2 May 2006, when the police telephoned theleave to appeal board and drew attention to the case. The applicant and the co-defendant were informed on 21 June 2006 that their requests for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court had been refused. Subsequently, on his request, counsel for the relevant co-Defendant who had wanted to submit supplementary comments did so on 2 and 13 June 2006. the case. The applicant was found guilty on all charges and sentenced to 10 years in prison. The case was heard at the High Court in London and the sentence was upheld on appeal. The appeal was adjourned until after the 20th anniversary of the decision on July 19, 2006. The judge ruled that the appeal was not necessary and the case was dismissed.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the Assize Court of the Canton of Geneva had tried and convicted him in absentia, in breach of Article 6 of the Convention. The Court decided to dispense with a hearing of the merits of the case (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The Court declared the application partly admissible in a decision of 16 December 1999. The Swiss Government (“the Government”) was represented by their Agent, Mr P. Boillat, Head of the International Affairs Division, Federal Office of Justice. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court. The applicant was accused of causing Yugoslavia’s welfare institutions to sustain substantial losses with the complicity of an official at the consulate of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in Geneva. On 27 October 1982 he was arrested and charged with fraud, intimidation and forging documents. On 1 February 1984 the applicant paid the stipulated sum and was released. He then travelled to the United States of America, where he acquired American nationality and practised as a doctor specialising in the treatment of certain serious forms of cancer. On 15 March 1989 the President of the Assize Court made an order for the applicant to appear before the Assizing Court on 17 April 1989. At the hearing one of the lawyers for the defence indicated that he envisaged making an application for an adjournment of the trial. One of the applicant’s American patients, applied to the United States District Court for the District of South Carolina, Charleston Division, for orders requiring the applicant to continue to treat him until he could be replaced by another doctor. He maintained that his life would be in danger if there were any interruption in the treatment he was receiving from the applicant. The American court issued a restraining order prohibiting the applicant from leaving the territory of the U.S. and requiring him to surrender his passport. That decision was served on the Swiss authorities, including the Principal Public Prosecutor of the Canton of Geneva, who was given sixty days in which to respond. The applicant was requested to find replacement doctors for his patients. The President observed that the decision appeared very favourable to the applicant, who had not appealed against it, despite being entitled to do so. The applicant lodged an application with the United States District Court for the District of South Carolina to have the restraining order of 28 March 1989 set aside. In a judgment of 26 May 1989 the Canton of Geneva Assize Court convicted the applicant in absentia and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment, of which two years, eight months and twenty-five days remained to be served. It also made an order excluding him from Swiss territory for ten years. On the other hand, the applicant was acquitted by the jury on 672 counts of fraud. An application for the applicant’s immediate arrest made by the Principal Public Prosecutor after the delivery of the verdict was dismissed by the Assize Court. The offences to which the convictions related had been committed between 1973 and 1981. The applicant lodged an application with the Court of Justice of the Canton of Geneva for the conviction in absentia to be set aside, under Article 331 of the Geneva Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 42 below) He maintained that good cause had been shown for his absence at the hearing on 17 April 1989, as he had been compelled to comply with the enforceable decision of the American court – which clearly constituted a reason beyond his control. The applicant was also held to be at fault for having delayed in appealing against the decision of the American court. The appeal had been lodged on 26 April 1989, that is to say a week after his trial had actually begun, and his application for an adjournment had been dismissed. By that juncture, for reasons of time, he could no longer reverse the course of events he had helped set in motion. In a judgment of 27 June 1990 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal as unfounded, holding that he had brought about the situation that had prevented him from leaving his patients and appearing before the Assize Court by his own conduct. The applicant lodged a public-law appeal with the Federal Court, seeking to have set aside the Canton of Geneva Court of Cassation’s judgments of 27 June 1990 and 14 February 1991. He alleged, inter alia, a violation of his right to be heard and to attend his trial. The Federal Court dismissed his appeal. It held that Article 6 § 1 of the Convention did not preclude a trial being held in the defendant's absence if the defendant refused to attend or was unable to attend through his or her own fault. It considered that the applicant had misled the American court by making inaccurate statements, notably regarding Swiss procedure, in order to secure a judgment. The applicant was arrested at Munich Airport (Germany) on his way to a conference. He was extradited to Switzerland and transferred to Champ-Dollon Prison. An application he made for a pardon was refused in February 1996. He served the remainder of his sentence, spending part of it in a secure wing of Geneva Cantonal Hospital. On 20 December 1996 he returned to the United States and served his sentence in prison until he was released in May 2000. He died in July 2008 in the care of his family in Los Angeles, California. The application for clemency was denied in July 2009 and he died in August 2010.

It originated in an application (no. 10300/83) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of that State. The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6:2. The President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the Lutz and Englert cases should be considered by the same Chamber. The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mrs. Maier for the Government, by. Mr. Weitzel for the Commission and by Mr. Bergemann for the applicant. The Commission, the Government and the applicant filed a number of documents and written comments either at the Court’s request or of their own motion. The Government, the Delegate of the Commission, and the lawyer for the. applicant all appeared before the Court. The President granted the Government leave to speak in German (Rule 27 § 2) and granted the members of the Government’'s delegation leave to talk in German. The applicant's memorial was lodged with the registry on 1 July 1986. Martha Nölkenbockhoff, a German national, is the widow and heir of Mr. Theodor Nölbockhoff. She lives in Selm-Bork. Her husband was a senior manager in a holding company, Stumm AG, whose trading activities centred on iron, steel and fuel, including motor fuel. He was found guilty inter alia on several charges of breach of trust (Untreue), criminal bankruptcy (Bankrott) and fraud (Betrug) and given an aggregate sentence of eight years’ imprisonment. His four co-defendants were also sentenced to prison terms - two of them, for more or less identical offences and a few additional ones. Mr. Nölkenbockhoff entered an appeal on points of law on the same day that judgment was given. The Federal Court of Justice (Bundesgerichtshof) had not given a decision by the time he died on 13 November. Three of the co-defendants, who had likewise challenged the Regional Court’s judgment, later withdrew their appeals. The appeal lodged by the fourth person convicted, Mr. M, was dismissed by the Federal Court on 7 July 1982 as being manifestly ill-founded. The applicant sought orders that the Treasury should bear the necessary costs and expenses incurred by her late husband in connection with his conviction. On 5 March 1982, the Essen Regional Court found against Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff. The defendant had already been found guilty, in a judgment that had not become final, after lengthy court proceedings in a trial (Hauptverhandlung) lasting more than three and a half years. The defendants withdrew their appeals on points of law, thereby confirming the judgment against them. The judgment convicting the three co-defendants ..., who were likewise sentenced to several years’ imprisonment, has become final. The defence's submissions again provide nothing to support the hypothesis that the proceedings were moving towards an acquittal. The quotations from the trial court’s judgment are taken out of context. The court declines to award compensation for the time spent in detention on remand, pursuant to section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act. The court does not consider it necessary to defer judgment until a decision has been given on the co-defendant M’s appeal on points of law. In view of the reasons given for the judgment, it was much more likely, having regard to the adverse financial position of the Stumm holding company, that if the proceedings had continued, the defendant would have been convicted on the counts in question. The applicant appealed to the Hamm Court of Appeal against that decision on 11 March 1982. The Regional Court disregarded the presumption of innocence in stating that the grounds of appeal afforded no reason to suppose that the defendant would have been acquitted. It was as if it were sought to obtain a final (abschliessend) conviction of the deceased by a side wind in the form of a decision as to costs. The applicant had requested an adjournment to await the judgment of the Federal Court of Justice in the appeal proceedings brought by one of the co-defendants. Since criminal law was based on the principle of individual guilt, it was quite simply unacceptable - and, once again, contrary to Article 6 § 2 (art. 6-2) - to judge the deceased. On 28 December 1981, the Bochum public prosecutor submitted that, having regard to the state of the proceedings, there was every likelihood (hohe Wahrscheinlichkeit) that the conviction would have been upheld. The Hamm Court of Appeal dismissed the action on 14 July 1982. It left open the question whether, in the event of a defendant’s death before the final conclusion (rechtskräftiger Abschluss), a decision such as that sought by Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff could be taken, by analogy, under Article 467 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act. Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff then applied to the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) claiming a breach of the Basic Law. On 30 September 1982, a bench of three judges of the Constitutional Court refused to entertain the constitutional complaint. The reasons for its decision were as follows: “1. The presumption of innocence, which is founded on the principle of the rule of law, precludes treating as guilty a person who has not been finally (rechtskräftig) convicted’ 2. The refusal of the applications for an order that the Treasury should bear the deceased defendant’s necessary costs and expenses is based on Article 467 § 3, second sentence, sub-paragraph 2, of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The courts’ reference to the lack of success of the appeal proceedings instituted by the co-defendant M and to the withdrawal of the appeals on points of law entered by the other defendants is clearly to be regarded merely as an additional argument, and the impugned decisions are not based on it. Nor do the grounds advanced in support of the constitutional complaint show the unreasonableness of the Regional Court’s opinion that, had the proceedings been continued, a conviction would have been more likely than an acquittal. “Eine derartige Einschätzung enthält indessen nicht die Feststellung einer Schuld, sondern lediglich die FestStellung  einer fortbestehenden Verdachtslage.”

According to X’s submissions, he was the only person who had observed the crime and who dared to testify. It thus appeared comprehensible that X feared reprisals and did not even hesitate to kill somebody. The court considered that the measures taken were both necessary and sufficient to prevent identification of the witness X. The court had taken a number of measures to compensate the restrictions imposed on the rights of the defence. The witness had not been examined by the regional prosecutor (Bezirksanwalt), but by the president of the court. There was no indication that X had been in any way involved in the crime. It was further known that X spoke the Serbo-Croatian language. The principle of a public hearing had been safeguarded by allowing the press directly to follow the interrogation from the separate room in which the defence was seated. A conviction could not be exclusively based on testimony given by an anonymous witness. The jury court considered that the applicant’s own submissions, according to which he could not have been present at the crime scene as he first entered Swiss territory in January 2002, were contradictory and thus lacked credibility. Conversely, the court considered the testimony given by the anonymous witness, who submitted that he had seen the applicant shooting the victim, to be credible. Relying on all available evidence, the jury court concluded that there was no doubt that N. B. had been shot by the applicant. The applicant lodged a nullity appeal (Nichtigkeitsbeschwerde) with the Court of Cassation (Kassationsgericht) of the canton of Zurich. Court noted that the anonymous witness had been heard in camera and that the applicant’s counsel did not have the possibility directly to question the witness. Neither the applicant nor his counsel had ever seen the witness, whose personal details remained secret. Adequate compensation could only be conceivable if at least the defence had the right directly to take part in the interrogation of the witness and was given the opportunity to assess the witness’ credibility. As this had not been the case, the court considered that the criminal court could not rely on the testimony given by theAnonymous witness. The court did not call into question that the legal conditions for granting anonymity were fulfilled in the instant case. The Court of Cassation found that the. modalities of the witness’ interrogation did not comply with the standards set up by the Court and were thus contrary to Article 6. § 3 (d) of the Convention. The Federal Tribunal (Kassationshof) quashed the decision of 19 December 2005 and remitted the case to the Court of. Cassation. The senior public prosecutor (Oberstaatsanwalt) of. the canton of Zurich lodged a nullity appeal against the decision. of the Court. The Court of cassation upheld the lower court’s judgment and found that. the testimony given by the anonymous witness had to be regarded as the decisive evidence (“massgebliches Beweismittel”) The tribunal concluded that the anonymous testimony only served as one piece of a mosaic which enforced the conclusion drawn from the remaining evidence. It followed that the criminal courts were not prevented from taking this evidence into account. The jury court had considered that the testimony given by the witness X had been credible and that it was in line with the scientific conclusion that the victim had been killed by gunshot in the back of his neck on 15 October 2001. The Court of Cassation rejected the applicant’s nullity appeal on 12 February 2007. On 19 April 2007 the Federal Tribunal rejected the appeal. of guilt. The tribunal further reviewed the other evidence examined by the jury court and concluded that this evidence, taken separately, would have been sufficient ‘to establish a strong suspicion of a criminal offence, or even to establish his guilt’

eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the German Government on 10 August 1992 and by the European Commission of Human Rights on 11 September 1992. It originated in an application (no. 15473/89) against Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 on 11 July 1989. The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3 and 8 (art. 3, art. 8) of the Convention. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them (Rule 30). The President gave the lawyer leave to use the German language (Rule 27 para. 3). The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 March 1993. The Court heard addresses by Mr Meyer-Ladewig for the Government, by Mr Frowein for the Commission and by Mr Stüben for the applicants. It also heard replies to its questions and by two of its members individually. The case was brought by a mother who was accused of driving through a red traffic light and of trying to get away - an allegation denied by the applicant. The police officers claimed to have detected a strong smell of alcohol on her breath when they checked her driving licence. Despite having been shown what to do, she proved unable to provide a specimen of breath satisfactorily. Mrs Klaas was arrested. The precise course of the events is disputed by the applicants (see paragraph 7 below) and the police officers. She was driven to the hospital for the blood test, which showed the level of alcohol in her blood to be 0.82 per ml (milligrammes per millilitre) She was subsequently released. The first applicant underwent two medical examinations. On 11 February 1986, Dr Schwering certified that he had examined the applicant on 29 January and noticed bruises which were about 10cm long on her right arm, considerable problems in moving her left shoulder, and bruises on that shoulder. He also stated that she would suffer long-term problems. Police Constable Bolte had followed the applicants to the back door of the house. Mrs Klaas struggled, struck out and tried to free herself from the police officer’s grip. With great difficulty the officers managed to control the applicant, who was putting up a fight. They handcuffed her in order to avoid further criminal offences being committed, in particular injury to the person. In November 1986 the competent administrative authority imposed an administrative fine of DM 500 for having committed the “regulatory offence’ (Ordnungswidrigkeit) of driving with a blood. while under the influence of alcohol contrary to Article 316 of the said code. Mrs Klaas claimed police officers used a disproportionate amount of force, causing injuries to her head, left shoulder and upper right arm. She maintained that the blood test showed the level of alcohol to be 0.80 per ml. It was argued that the degree of force used against an unarmed woman was incomprehensible on an objective or subjective analysis. The Lemgo District Court (Amtsgericht) confirmed this decision. The first applicant’s subsequent appeal to the Hamm Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht), and to the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht, were dismissed. For confidential support call the Samaritans on 08457 90 90 90, visit a local Samaritans branch or click here for details. The first applicant instituted civil proceedings in April 1987 against the Land North-Rhine Westphalia and the police officers concerned. She claimed compensation for the injuries sustained on 28 January 1986. Her request to take her daughter to a neighbour’s first was granted. When the first applicant opened the door and tried to enter with her daughter, one of the officers held her right arm fast, whereupon she started to kick and to hit out with her left hand. She had to be handcuffed. It was not accepted that her head knocked against the window-ledge at any moment in the course of the arrest. On 10 July 1987 the Detmold Regional Court, in a partial judgment, dismissed her complaint. Police Constable Wildschut confirmed the general circumstances of the first applicant’s arrest as described by Police Constable Bolte. He could not remember who had kept hold of Mrs Klaas until they had put her into the police car, or whether she had bent forward suddenly owing, for instance, to a jerking on her handcuffs and the resulting pain. He confirmed that she had requested that the handcuffs be removed but did not remember her complaining about any pain - in particular pain in her left shoulder. He denied that he had pushed the first applicants head against the window-ledge. Finally, the second applicant, Monika, gave evidence. She stated that she remembered the incident. Monika's mother had rung the doorbell and opened the door using a key. Monika had then gone into the house and closed the door behind her. She said that she had managed to see through the plain glass door panel that one of the police officers had pushed her mother’s head against the wall. The officer concerned had blond hair. The plaintiff ended up with a graze on her temple, contusion of the left shoulder and probably also concussion, as was also confirmed in part by witnesses Bolte and Wildschut. These injuries were probably sustained by the plaintiff in the context of her arrest. It does not follow, however, that the defendant Land is liable in damages. The plaintiff was under suspicion of having committed a criminal offence. The arrest itself was not unlawful, says the court. It is for the plaintiff to prove that in this initially lawful exercise of their duty the police officers went further than was necessary, the court adds. The plaintiff, however, has not succeeded in providing such proof, it says. The Chamber is not convinced that the police. officers caused the plaintiff’s injuries by exceeding what was necessary when arresting. her. With respect to the origin of the graze, the. evidence of witness Monika Klaas, the plaintiff's daughter, conflicts with that of the plaintiff, the Court adds. Mrs Hildegard Klaas, the first applicant, submitted that, in the presence of her daughter, Monika, she had been subjected in the course of her arrest to inhuman and degrading treatment by the police. It is not clear to the Chamber which of the statements corresponds to what really happened. Neither the balance of probability nor general experience militate in favour of accepting the plaintiff’s version of events. The Chamber considers it by no means improbable that the plaintiff sustained all her injuries when she resisted being handcuffed. In the process her head could easily have knocked against the wall; the shoulder contusion could also have occurred when she struggled. For these reasons the claim must be dismissed. Monika Klaas, the second applicant, contended that the aforementioned treatment of her mother in her presence had violated her right to respect for her private and family life. The full text of the Commission’s opinion and of the various separate opinions contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to this judgment. The Government in their memorial of 12 November 1992 invited the Court to find “that the applicants did not suffer violations of their rights under Article 3 ( art. 3) or Article 8 (art. 8) of the Convention’’. The Court found that there had been a violation of Article 3 in respect of the first applicant.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 71893/01) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The domestic court also emphasised that there was a considerable and ever-changing number of parties to the proceedings. name: Metin Köksal

name: Aniela Leszczyńska
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47551/99) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 23 February 1998. eval_texts: Aniela Leszczyńska lodged an application against the Republic of Poland under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant and her neighbours were the co-owners of real estate located in Włocławek, Poland. On 19 September 1989 the District Court gave a decision. The neighbours appealed and the case was remitted. On 10 July 2001 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. It decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The application was lodged on 23 February 1998 and the court heard evidence from an expert on 3 August 1993. The court held a further hearing on 29 April 1994. The respondents appealed against the decision of the Włocławek District Court to dissolve the co-ownership. They lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) The Supreme Court dismissed the cassation case on 3 September 1997. On 21 September 1996 the applicant filed an action for repossession of part of the property. She claimed that the court in its decision of 27 April 1995 (given in the first set of proceedings) had not ordered the respondents to surrender part of. the property in question to her. The defendants appealed. On 28 January 1998 the trial court held a hearing. On 14 March 1998 an expert opinion was submitted to the court.

name: Jadwiga Hulewicz

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35302/08) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. name: Andrej Furman

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 16608/09) against the Republic of Slovenia lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been unable to enjoy family life with his daughter on account of the lack of diligence on the part of the Slovenian and Austrian authorities in regulating and enforcing contact between them. Tichy, Head of the International Law Department. M.P. sent a letter to the Centre informing them that she would be living abroad in the period between 1 July 1998 and 31 August 1999 for the purposes of her doctoral studies. She requested that the contact proceedings be suspended during that period. On 26 August 1998 the applicant sought an interim order granting him contact with P once a month and for a week during both the winter and summer holidays. The applicant was supposed to pick up his daughter at M.P’s permanent address in Maribor and bring her back to the same address in the following month. The hearing was adjourned at the request of M. P., who informed the Centre that she was taking holiday during the period in question. M.P. temporarily living in Graz, Austria. Centre rejected her appeal as out of time, whereupon she appealed to the Ministry of Labour, Family and Social Affairs (hereinafter ‘the Ministry’) The Ministry upheld M.P’s appeal against the interim order, quashed the order and remitted the issue of the provisional contact schedule for a fresh examination by the Centre. The case was remitted to the Maribor Administrative Unit and the enforcement proceedings were subsequently stayed as a result of the quashing of the interim Order. On 15 March 2000 M. p. informed the Centre of the address of her representative authorised to receive her official mail. On 12 June 2000 the applicant made a counter-proposal. The Centre issued an order granting the applicant contact with P. every Tuesday afternoon, every first weekend of the month and a few weeks during the winter and summer holiday periods. On 19 July 2000 M.P. sent a reply to the Centre, without, however, providing the requested information on P. On 29 September 2000 the Centre held a hearing in the applicant’s presence. The applicant reiterated his request for the setting up of a contact schedule between him and P. on 4 and 28 December 2001 and on 23 January 2002 the applicant requested that the contact schedule be enforced. On 7 May 2003 the Centre was informed that the Slovenian Ministry for Foreign Affairs had upheld the appeal against the order of 5 October 2000. On 1 May 2004 the courts acquired jurisdiction to decide on issues relating to rights of contact. In June 2004 the applicant instituted proceedings before the Maribor District Court. M.P. proposed that the Slovenian courts relinquish their jurisdiction in the matter in favour of the Austrian courts. The applicant sent a letter to the Graz Youth and Family Office asking them for help in re-establishing contact with P. He also attached a letter he had written to P., with photos of him and his family. The letter was handed over to M. P. by a social worker on 6 October 2005. The hearing was adjourned on 14 November 2005. Two attempts were made to serve a summons on M.P. at her home address. The social worker in charge of the case requested three times to meet with M.M. and P. in order to prepare the report, but without success. On 7 February 2007 the Maribor District Court held a hearing and on the same day issued an order setting out a contact schedule. M.p. did not attend the hearing; however, she informed the court that she did not wish to have contact with the applicant. The court ruled that the applicant could visit P. every two weeks by picking her up at M.B.’s home. M.P. was ordered to comply with the terms of the order, subject to a fine of 200 euros (EUR) for each breach. On 1 September 2007 the applicant saw P. for the first time in more than nine years. On the latter occasion, P. left after less than an hour, after which she refused to see the applicant again. The applicant lodged a supervisory appeal under the Right to Trial without Undue Delay Act (hereinaina) on 10 February 2009. On 11 September 2008, the Maribor District Court explained to the parties that the contact proceedings had been concluded by a final decision and the Maribu Local Court was competent to decide on the enforcement of the contact order. P. lodged a request with the Graz-West District Court seeking suspension of the applicant’s contact rights. On 3 March 2009, the Maribor Local Court imposed a fine in the amount of EUR 600 on M.P. for not complying with the contact order. On 23 April 2010, the applicant was invited to supplement his request for enforcement. On the basis of that request, a new enforcement order was issued on 2 November 2010, ordering M. P. to allow contact between the applicant and P., subject to a fine of EUR 500. On 4 September 2012, the Maribor Local Court quashed all the enforcement acts executed until that date. M.P. asked the Graz-West District Court to increase the monthly child maintenance from EUR 137 to EUR 250 on the grounds that P’s needs, as well as the general cost of living, had increased since 1997. On 12 February 2009 the court, taking into account the financial situation of both parents, allowed M.P.'s request. The Graz Regional Civil Court dismissed an appeal lodged by the applicant on 31 August 2009. The court found that P. had consistently expressed her wish not to have contact with the applicant and concluded that contact against her wishes would not be in her interest. The applicant sent a number of letters to the courts in Graz complaining that the court documents were in German, which he did not understand, and requesting that the issue be decided by Slovenian authorities.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 11564/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant, a gynaecologist, was born in 1956 and lives in İzmir. In the course of an investigation into the PKK (the Kurdistan Workers’ Party), an illegal armed organisation, the applicant’s name was mentioned by a few detainees suspected of membership of that organisation. The applicant claims that, while he was in police custody, he was ill‑treated. The applicant was heard first by the public prosecutor and later by a judge at the İzmir State Security Court. The latter ordered his release from custody. The applicant did not object to this decision. The criminal proceedings brought against the applicant before the    for aiding and abetting an illegal armed organisation ended on 23 May 2000 with his acquittal. The prosecution noted that none of the persons put forward as witnesses by the applicant were able to confirm the applicant’s version of events. None of the medical reports, dated 19 October 1999, 23 October 1999 and 25 October 1999 save for one dated 11 November 1999, i.e. fifteen days after the events, noted any physical findings of ill-treatment.

name: Robert Głowacki
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1608/08) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, a violation of Article 3 of the convention on account of the imposition of the “dangerous detainee” regime on him. He further complained about the length of criminal proceedings against him. The application was communicated to the Government on 17 November 2010. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The Polish Government were represented by their then Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was arrested on 18 May 2007 and placed in the Warsaw Białołęka Detention Centre. He was convicted of armed robbery, burglary and causing serious bodily harm and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment. The applicant lodged an appeal against the last of those decisions and was released on 10 April 2010, at the applicant’s request, the detention was lifted and he was released from custody. On 2 March 2011 the applicant began serving the prison sentence imposed on 22 September 2009. The application was not successful and he has since been released from prison. The case is being investigated by the Płock Regional Prosecutor (Prokurator Okregowy) The applicant was placed in the Warsaw Białołęka Remand Centre (Areszt Śledczy) on 21 May 2007. On 18 December 2008 the Płock Regional Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to seven years and six months’ imprisonment. On 1 September 2009 the applicant lodged a complaint with the Warsaw Court of Appeal under the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. The applicant sought a ruling that the length of the proceedings before the Warsaw Regional Court (see paragraphs 6-19 above) had been excessive, and also sought an award of just satisfaction. The applicant was placed in solitary confinement at Warsaw Mokotów Remand Centre. He was charged with numerous offences, including armed robbery. The commission also referred to his “serious lack of moral character” The applicant appealed to the penitentiary courts against most of those decisions. He argued that he was suffering from various health problems including hemiparesis and discopathy. He also stressed that he had never been charged with acting as part of an organised criminal group. The courts gave decisions on 26 May, 29 August and 17 October 2008, 15 April and 24 June 2009, and 4 March 2010. The authorities relied on the grounds given for the initial decision. In particular they stressed the risk posed by the seriousness of the offences. The applicant was detained in the following detention centres: Warsaw Białołeka Detention Centre, Lublin Remand Centre, Warsaw Mokotów Remand Center, and Płock Prison. The Government submitted that during the applicant’s detention in all four of the penal establishments listed above all standards of detention were respected. The applicant argued that the living conditions in the detention centres in which he was detained were inadequate. He failed to lodge a claim for compensation for damage to his health sustained as a result of inadequate conditions of detention. He was allowed to receive visits from his family. The majority of these visits lasted one hour. His sister and son visited him on average once a month.

name: Vedat Çetin
train_texts: The case originated in two applications (nos. 40153/98 and 40160/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. eval_texts: Case originated in two applications lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Object of the applications was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10 of the Convention. This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section of the Court. The Chamber declared them partly admissible in a decision of 6 November 2001. The applicants are Turkish nationals and live in Diyarbakir. At the material time, they worked as journalists on Ülkede Gündem, a Turkish-language daily newspaper based in Istanbul. Publication of the newspaper ceased on 24 October 1998 and it was replaced initially by Özgür Bakis. The main point at issue in the present case is a ban that was imposed on 1 December 1997 by the governor of the state of emergency region on the distribution of Ülkede Gündem. The Government have produced to the Court seventy-two warrants issued by judges of the Istanbul National Security Court for the seizure of various issues of the newspaper in the months of September, November and December 1997. On 13 November 1997 the proprietor of. Ülkeder Günderm sent a letter to the Ministry of the Interior informing it of the disruption. caused to the distribution and demanding an end to these unlawful acts. He also sought compensation. On 1 December 1997 the governor of the state of emergency region imposed a ban on the publication and distribution of Ülkede Gündem in that region. On 5 February 1998 the Diyarbakir Administrative Council held that there was no case to answer in view of the seizure warrants that had been issued by the Istanbul National Security Court. Its decision was upheld by the Supreme Administrative Court on 3 March 2000 and the ban was lifted on 1 February 2000. The ban was imposed in accordance with Directive no. 1344 of the governor's office of theState of Emergency region, issued on December 1, 1997. The daily newspaper was banned from being published in the provinces in which a state of Emergency has been declared. The applicants have produced a notice dated June 2000 which shows that at different times the governor of the state of emergency region imposed bans on the publication and distribution of seventeen periodicals, including Ülkede Gündem, Özgür Bakis and 2 Binde Yeni Guendem.” The applicants claim the bans were imposed under Article 11 (e) of Legislative Decree no. 285 of the State of Emergency Act. The applicants also claim that the bans have been imposed on the successor publications to Özgur Bakis, and on the weekly publication Yedinci Guevendem.

name: Sıddık Onay
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 31553/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 12 July 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 31553/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants, Sıddık Onay and Zinnet Onay, were born in 1985 and 1948 respectively and live in Diyarbakır. The second applicant is the mother of the former applicant. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 28 May 2002, the applicant was brought for a further medical examination. The medical report noted two bruises of 10 x 2 cm on his right upper arm and a bruise of 5 x 1cm on his left upper arm just below his shoulder, which were estimated to be two or three days old. The applicant was given a second medical examination at 4.15 p.m. on the same day. The second medical report confirmed the findings of the first report. These reports both stated that the medical examinations had been performed upon the request of the Peace and Order Department. In his statement to the public prosecutor, made in the presence of another duty lawyer,. the applicant denied the charges against him. He alleged that, after the police officers had apprehended him, they blindsided him. The applicant was beaten with truncheons and forced to admit to the charges. He showed the marks on his body to the judge. The judge noted a bruise of 7 cm about the thickness of a little finger on the applicant's right upper arm. The applicant's lawyer filed a complaint with the Diyarbakır Public Prosecutor's Office, requesting the public prosecutor to bring criminal proceedings against the police officers who had been on duty when the applicant was in their custody. The public prosecutor launched an investigation into the applicant’s complaint of ill-treatment. On 18 November 2004 the publicProsecutor decided not to prosecute the applicant. The applicant challenged this decision before the Siverek Assize Court. The court ruled that the lesions had occurred prior to the applicant's arrest and that the scars on his body and arms had been self-inflicted, as he admitted in his statement of 30 May 2002. the police officers concerned. On 19 January 2005 the Assize court rejected the applicant’s objection. The decision concluded briefly that the lesioning had occurred before the applicant was arrested and that he had self- inflicted the scars. The applicant was sentenced to a year in prison and a fine of £1,000. He was released from prison in April 2005 and is serving his sentence.

name: Ireneusz Lachowski
train_texts: The case was brought under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) The application was made on 8 August 2003. It was decided to consider the merits of the case at the same time as the application's introduction. The case was settled on 8 December 2005. The appeal was dismissed on 11 December 2005 after the appeal was heard by the Court of Appeal. The judge ruled in favour of the appeal on the basis that it had been presented in a fair and just way. He said that the case should have been heard as part of the legal proceedings against the Polish government.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 27556/03) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Mr Ireneusz Lachowski (‘the applicant’), was arrested on 20 September 1999 on suspicion of homicide. On 22 September 1999 the Chełm District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) ordered that the applicant be remanded in custody for a period of 3 months in view of a reasonable suspicion that he had committed homicide. It further held that the likelihood that he would be given a heavy sentence justified his detention on remand. On 19 December 2005 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application. The applicant was charged with two counts of homicide and armed robbery. There were four other defendants in the case. On 23 September 2002 the Lublin Regional Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to 25 years’ imprisonment. The applicant, who remained in detention, appealed against the first-instance judgment. The Lublin Court of Appeal quashed the judgment of the Regional Court and ordered a retrial. The trial court held 20 hearings in the period from 16 May 2001 to 19 September 2002. It appears that the applicant’s detention was prolonged on 28 November 2001 (until 15 March 2002) and on 24 April 2002 (until 30 September 2002) On 7 May 2004 the Regional Court ordered that the applicant be kept in custody until 31 December 2004. The applicant’s detention was subsequently prolonged on 3 December 2004 (until 31 March 2005) and on 29 March 2005 (until 30 September 2005) The Court of Appeal upheld the decision on 21 December 2004 to prolong his detention. It held that the continued detention served the public interest of protecting society, given the applicant had been charged with the homicide of two women, having first cruelly treated them. In those circumstances, it was not necessary to prolong further the applicant's detention. He was released on 6 October 2005 and banned from leaving the country. The Regional Court held 22 hearings in the period from 28 January 2004 to 11 April 2006. The proceedings are still pending. The hearings took place in the counties of Dorset, Somerset, Gloucestershire, Lincolnshire, Leicestershire and Northamptonshire. The Regional Court heard a total of 22 cases between January 2004 and April 2006, and the final proceedings were held on April 11, 2006. In total, there were 22 hearings and the proceedings were still pending in April 2006 when the case was finally dismissed. The case was heard in the Regional Court of the Dorset County Court of Appeal, Dorset. The hearing was held in the county court of the same name, which is now based in Leicester, Somerset.

name: Monica Fexler

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36801/06) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the administrative appellate courts had failed to hold an oral hearing in proceedings relating to her request for disability benefits. She claimed that, due to her health problems, she had incurred, and still incurred, extra costs for, inter alia, medication, doctors’ visits, treatment, travel expenses, special clothes and shoes, special soap and creams, and for supplementary vitamins and minerals. She had calculated that these extra costs amounted, in total, to SEK 75,314 (approximately EUR 8,150) per year. The applicant's extra costs per year amounted to no more than SEK 7,300 from September 1999, SEK 8,900 from January 2000 and SEK 6,800 from January 2001. The Office concluded that the applicant’s extra costs did not reach the minimum level established for each year to be granted disability benefits. The decision was based on Sections 5 and 6 of the Act on Disability Benefits and Care Allowance (Lagen om handikappersättning och vårdbidrag, Act no. 1998:703) The applicant appealed against the decision to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Blekinge, requesting that the decision be set aside. The applicant appealed to the Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten) in Jönköping, insisting that she was in need of assistance for one hour per day. She alleged that she had to buy custom-made clothes and special shoes due to her deformities caused by the lymphatic oedema and hip problems. All these extra costs should, in her view, be included in the calculation to grant her disability benefits. The court concluded, in an overall assessment of the applicant’s need of help and of her extra costs, that the conditions for granting disability benefits were not fulfilled and that the applicant was not eligible for a disability allowance. The applicant asked for an oral hearing to clarify certain unclear points of the case. The court, consisting of five judges including two lay judges, found it established that lymphatic drainage treatment of the kind the applicant needed was to be regarded as medical treatment. The County Council was responsible for costs of such treatment to the extent that it could be considered medically motivated. Accordingly, when. assessing the application for disability benefits, the applicant was not entitled to include extra costs for lymphatic. drainage treatment. In the light of this and as the court also shared the County Administrative Court’s assessment concerning the remainder of the subject‑matter, the case could be decided on the case file as it stood. In 2005 the applicant made a further appeal to the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten), requesting that the Administrative Court of Appeal’s judgment be repealed and the case returned for renewed examination. She referred to Article 6 of the Convention and claimed that an oral hearing was necessary in order to clarify the case. In the alternative, the applicant requested that the court grant her disability benefits. On 17 May 2006 the Supreme. Administrative Court refused leave to appeal. The judgment was unanimous and the. appeal was to be rejected. The appeal was settled in August 2006 and the application was dismissed. The case was decided in favour of the applicant.

The applicant alleged that his pre-trial detention exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the convention. The Ukrainian Government did not exercise their right to intervene. The Słubice District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) remanded him in custody, relying on the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offence in question. It considered that keeping the applicant in detention was necessary to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings, given the risk that he might tamper with evidence. The applicant was tried on the basis of the relevant provisions of the Criminal Code of 6 June 1997 (the so-called ‘New Criminal Code’) which entered into force on 1 September 1998. The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to 15 years’ imprisonment. The court noted, inter alia, that although the applicant pleaded guilty, his testimonies had not been fully coherent and contained a number of inconsistencies. It therefore considered that the conditions for the extraordinary mitigation of sentence had not be met in the case. However, the applicant's legal-aid counsel argued that the first-instance court had not mitigated the applicant’s sentence. The applicant was convicted and sentenced to 15 years’ imprisonment. The applicant, other co-accused and the District Prosecutor appealed. On 23 November 1999 the Poznań Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) heard the appeals. It quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case for retrial. The court repeated the grounds previously given for the applicant’s continued detention. It ordered that the applicant's detention should continue until 31 January 2001. On 14 March, 15 March and 27 April 2001 the trial court held hearings. On 18 April 2000 the Gorzów Wielkopolski Regional Court convicted the applicant as originally charged. The applicant was sentenced to 25 years' imprisonment in December 2001. The applicant's legal-aid counsel argued, inter alia, that the trial court had erred in that it had not mitigated the applicant’s sentence. On 16 May 2002 the Poznań Court of Appeal upheld the first‑instance judgment. Admittedly, the applicant had changed his pleadings after the judgment of 18 April 2000. That, however, should not have had any bearing on the outcome of the case. Since that date he has been committed to Międzyrzecz Remand Centre. Since 19 August 1998 the applicant has appealed against his. release and appealed, likewise unsuccessfully, against decisions extending his detention. The parties gave partly differing accounts of the conditions of the applicant’s detention. The applicant maintained that during most part of his detention he was held in overcrowded cells in conditions which did not comply with the basic standards of hygiene. On 10 December 2007 the applicant was transferred to Hrubieszów Prison where he is currently detained. The Government submitted that the applicant's detention in cells in which the statutory minimum requirement of 3 m² per person had not been respected amounted to some 979 days. This submission was not contested by the applicant. The application did not bring a civil action in tort to seek compensation for the infringement of his personal rights.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 15476/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Mr Artur Bystrowski, is a Polish national who was born in 1963 and lives in Strzelin. On 8 September 2000 the Wrocław District Court detained the applicant on remand on suspicion of having committed theft and forgery. On 9 February 2001 a bill of indictment was issued, charging the applicant with multiple theft, forgery, possession of a firearm without a licence and leadership of an organised criminal gang. In successive decisions, the court repeatedly relied on the strong probability that the applicant had committed the offences and that he would receive a severe sentence. The applicant challenged his detention on remand. He lodged appeals against the Wrocław Regional Court’s decisions of 15 February 2001, 4 September 2002 and 5 March 2003. The applicant did not lodge a complaint about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time with the domestic court, under the Law of 17 June 2004 (Ustawa o skardze na naruszenie prawa strony do rozpoznania sprawy w postępowaniu sąd) The applicant was found guilty as charged and sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment in 2004. The applicant’s requests for visits from his wife were rejected on 23 February, 2 March and 30 April 2001. He alleged in particular that he was detained with six other persons in a room measuring 16m2; he could only take walks in a closed area measuring 20m2 for 25 persons; there was no warm water available and the ventilation and sanitation were insufficient. He also claimed that if he were to complain to higher authorities he would run a risk of harassment by the guards, given that his correspondence had been censored. The relevant domestic law and practice concerning the imposition of pre‑trial detention (aresztowanie tymczasowe), the grounds for its extension, release from detention and rules governing other “preventive measures” (środki zapobiegawcze) are stated. Law and practice pertaining to conditions of detention and to civil law action for compensation against the State Treasury are laid out in the judgment in the case of Orchowski v. Poland. Detainees’ correspondence and contact with family are also covered. Remedies for the excessive length of judicial proceedings are stated in the Court’s decisions in the cases of Charzyński v Poland, no. 15212/03 (dec.), §§ 12-23, ECHR 2005-V. The relevant domestic law and practice concerning detainees’ right to receive visitors in remand centres are stated. in the Case of Gradek v Poland.

The applicants alleged that section 52 of the Offences against the State Act 1939 constituted a violation of the rights guaranteed by Articles 6, 8 and 10 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 21 September 1999, the Court declared the application admissible. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) and the parties replied in writing to each other's observations.
eval_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that section 52 of the Offences against the State Act 1939 constituted a violation of the rights guaranteed by Articles 6, 8 and 10 of the Convention. By a decision of 21 September 1999, the Court declared the application admissible. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required. The parties replied in writing to each other's observations on the merit of the case. The case was decided by the Court on 23 October 1999, and the decision is obtainable from the Registry. The Irish Government was represented successively by their Agents, Ms E. Kilcullen, Mr R. Siev and Mr A. Connolly. A. large explosion occurred at a British Army/Royal Ulster Constabulary checkpoint in County Derry. Five British soldiers and one civilian were killed and a number of other British army personnel were seriously injured. Irish police officers on surveillance duty noted a light in a house approximately four miles from the scene of the explosion. At approximately 6.05 a.m. on 24 October 1990 a warrant was obtained to search the house. The police entered the house and found an assortment of gloves (rubber and knitted), balaclavas, caps and other clothing. The seven men in the house, including the owner and the applicants, were arrested and detained. Both applicants were acquitted of the charge of membership of an unlawful organisation but each was convicted of failing to provide an account of their movements during a specified period contrary to section 52 of the 1939 Act. Both applicants were sentenced to six months' imprisonment. The applicants appealed against their conviction and sentence under section 52 to the Court of Criminal Appeal. In 1994, the High Court rejected their application. It based the applicants' right not to answer questions as regards their movements on Article 38 of the Constitution rather than on Article 40, noting that their case related to suspects in custody and not to accused persons on trial. The High Court also considered that the restriction did not excessively impair the right to silence. The Supreme Court rejected the applicants' appeal, finding that section 52 of the 1939 Act was not inconsistent with the Constitution. It was noted that the right to silence was a corollary to freedom of expression guaranteed by Article 40 of the Constitution and that the relevant assessment was to consider the proportionality of the restriction. The Supreme Court noted that an innocent person had nothing to fear from giving an account of his or her movements even though such a person may wish, nevertheless, to take a stand on grounds of principle. It considered that the entitlement of citizens to take such a stand must yield to the right of them to remain silent. The Court of Criminal Appeal had suggested that information lawfully obtained under section 52 might be later used in evidence. Supreme Court concluded that the restriction in section 52 was proportionate to the State's entitlement to protect itself. The applicants' appeal to the Court of Criminal Appeal in relation to their conviction under section 52 of the 1939 Act has been adjourned generally pending the outcome of the present application. The entitlement of those with something relevant to disclose concerning the commission of a crime to remain silent must be regarded as of an even lesser order, the court said. the State to protection itself. the Supreme Court concluded. The appeal to be heard by the court of criminal appeal is adjourned until after the end of this month. The application is expected to last for up to two weeks.

He contended that because he held a vocational high school diploma, the new selection system had put him at a disadvantage in relation to candidates from ordinary high schools. It was also decided that the Chamber would rule on the admissibility and the merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1 of the convention). The applicant was born in 1981 and lives in Antalya, Turkey. The applicant considered that applying a weighting to the average marks used for calculating the results of the entrance examination gave an advantage to students from ordinary high schools over those from vocational schools specialised in communication. He calculated that had it not been for the 0.2 weighting on his average high school marks, the marks which he had obtained in the examination would have been sufficient for him to enrol in the faculty of communication sciences of his choice. Relying on the principle of equality among holders of the different types of high school diplomas, he complained of the unforeseeable nature of the changes introduced under the reform carried out during his final year in secondary education. He applied to the Supreme Administrative Court for judicial review of the decision in question. New rules were introduced in 1998 to allow students to change schools. The rules did not include a transition period for students to switch schools. Students were allowed to stay at the school for a year before moving to another school. The new rules were approved by the Supreme Administrative Court in 2000. But the students were not allowed to leave the school until the transitional period was over. The students were then able to return to the school to complete their studies. The move was seen as a victory for the students, who had been waiting for the new rules to be implemented. The decision was overturned in 2002, when the students moved to the new school with a new set of rules.

The court decided to examine the merits of the applications at the same time as their admissibility. The applications were dismissed. The applicants were taken to the Forensic Medicine Institute for medical examinations both in the evening of 3 August 2001 and in the morning of 4 August 2001. The medical reports drafted on these dates concluded that there were no signs of blows on the applicants’ bodies. On 7 August 2001 the public prosecutor at the Istanbul State Security Court filed an indictment, charging the applicants with aiding and abetting the PKK under Article 169 of the Criminal Code. The applicants denied all the allegations made against them. They contended that they had been forced to sign police statements without reading their contents. The court ordered their detention on remand. The first applicant contended that, although there was no marks on her body, she had been tortured in police custody. The second applicant maintained that police officers had hit him, pulled his hair and insulted him. The applicants’ lawyer filed two separate petitions with the Fatih public prosecutor, complaining about the applicants' ill-treatment during their arrest and detention in police custody. November 2001 the first hearing was held before the Istanbul State Security Court. The court gave a decision of non-jurisdiction and transferred the case file to the Ümraniye Criminal Court of First Instance. On 16 February 2004 the  court acquitted the applicants on account of lack of evidence. The investigation against the police officers against the applicants was dropped in March 2002. The case is still pending in the Turkish High Court of Justice and Human Rights.

The applicants' parents owned a plot of land with a house in Warsaw prior to 1 May 1993. Pursuant to the provisions of the 1945 Decree on the Ownership and Use of Land in Warsaw they were expropriated and the ownership of the property passed to the Warsaw municipality. The President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time as the Government. Two‑thirds of the property was sold to a certain B.K. on 19 April 1985. The applicants requested that the property be restored to them. A right of perpetual use of one-third of the land and ownership of one‑third of a building situated on that property were awarded to them in 1987. In 1990 the authorities indicated that since two‑thirds had been sold to third parties before the entry into force of a certain statute in 1985, only one- third of the plot could be restored. In accordance with the 1985 law, any compensation claims had expired on the date of entry into Force of this law. The Supreme Administrative Court regarded the applicants' subsequent complaints as unfounded. The applicants made a complaint about the inactivity of the administrative authorities and the failure to issue an administrative decision. The court found that, when deciding on the return of the one‑third of the property, the authorities had failed to determine the remainder of the applicants' claim. By a judgment of 11 October 1991 the court obliged the District Mayor to issue a decision concerning the remaining two-thirds of the Property. The matter remained dormant between 1994 and 1996. The District Prosecutor intervened and filed a complaint with the Board of Appeal of the Local Government (Samorządowe Kolegium Odwoławcze) on 13 November 1996. On 23 October 1996 the District Office rendered a decision on the merits. The 1945 Decree on the Ownership and Use of Land in Warsaw expropriated owners of real property located in Warsaw and transferred the ownership of land to the municipality of Warsaw. The applicants filed an appeal with the Supreme Administrative Court. On 12 March 1999 the court dismissed their appeal and held that the two‑thirds of the property could not be restored to them as third parties had been vested with the right of perpetual use. On 7 June 1999 the applicants were served with this judgment. According to section 5. 1 of the Law of 10 May 1990 the. ownership of the land which had previously been held by the State Treasury and which was within the administrative. territory of municipalities was transferred to the latter. The right of perpetual use is defined in Articles 232 et seq. of the Civil Code (Kodeks Cywilny) It is an inheritable and transferable right in rem which, for ninety‑nine years, gives a person full benefit and enjoyment of property rights attaching to land owned by the State Treasury or municipality. It has to be registered in the court land register in the same way as ownership. Inactivity of the administrative authorities can lead to a fine or a ruling on the merits of the case. A party to administrative proceedings may make a complaint under Article 37 of the Code to urge the relevant administrative authority to issue a decision within the time-limits fixed in the Code.

On 19 July 1989, the applicant joined an anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia in which the applicants in the Chrysostomos and Papachrysostomou v. Turkey also took part. The applicant's properties were located in the area under the occupation and control of the Turkish military authorities, who prevented her from having access to and using them. Since the 1974 Turkish intervention, the. applicant has been deprived of her properties, which were located under the. occupation and. control of Turkish military. authorities. She claims that the demonstration was peaceful and was held on the fifteenth anniversary of the. Turkish intervention in Cyprus, in support of the missing persons. Injured woman claims she was hit with a bayonet by a Turkish soldier. She was taken by ambulance to Nicosia General Hospital. For the next six months, the applicant suffered considerable pain in her leg. She could not walk or even put weight on the leg and was forced to use crutches. She continued to have problems climbing stairs and the scar on her leg remained visible. The applicant produced a medical certificate issued on 27 March 2000 by Doctor Stelios Georgiou, a specialist orthopaedic surgeon practising inNicosia. The certificate reads: “The [applicant] was injured on 19.7.1989 by Turks following an attack on women near Ayios Kassianos in NicosIA in the Ayios Kasianos Primary School’’ The applicant was arrested by the Turkish-Cypriot police after crossing the UN buffer zone and entering the area under Turkish- Cypriot control. The Government alleged that the applicant had participated in a violent demonstration with the aim of inflaming anti-Turkish sentiment. The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 on the UN operations in Cyprus stated that no more force was used than was reasonably necessary in the circumstances in order to arrest and detain the persons concerned. No one was ill-treated. It was possible that some of the demonstrators had hurt themselves in the confusion or in attempting to scale barbed wire or other fencing. Had the Turkish police, or anyone else, assaulted or beaten any of the protesters, the UN would no doubt have referred to this in his report to the Security Council. Turkish-Cypriot police and security forces elements forced their way into the area and apprehended 111 persons, 101 of them women. The Ayios Kassianos school complex is situated in the UN buffer zone. Turkish forces claim it to be on their side of the cease-fire line. Some 300 Greek Cypriots gathered at the main entrance to the UN protected area in Nicosia, in which the UN headquarters is located, to protest the continuing detention of those apprehended. The demonstrators, whose number fluctuated between 200 and 2,000, blocked all UN traffic through this entrance until 30 July, when the Turkish- Cypriot authorities released the last two detainees.

The applicant is currently serving his prison sentence in Muğla Prison. The applicant was taken before the public prosecutor and the judge. He was placed in Fethiye Prison. The other co-accused, Y.A., who had allegedly killed İ.G. according to the applicant’s statement, was arrested. The applicant had previously told him that he knew of a person who was harassing high-school girls and that the applicant was looking for someone to murder this person. The doctor noted that the bruises had been caused by a blunt object 24 to 48 hours prior to the examination. She considered that the injuries rendered the applicant unfit for work for three days. She finally noted that he should therefore be examined by an ear, nose and throat specialist. Y.A. retracted the statements he had made during the preliminary investigation stage. He stated that he had been severely tortured while in police custody and had given those statements under duress. The applicant denied being involved in a money-related dispute with İ.G. He said he had never traded on the stock market on behalf of the applicant. On 30 June 2004 the Fethiye Assize Court convicted the applicant and Y.A of homicide and sentenced them to life imprisonment commuted to sixteen years and eight months’ imprisonment. The medical reports issued at the beginning and the end of the. applicant's detention did not reveal any sign of ill-treatment on the applicant's body. It is medically impossible to specify what type of blunt object had caused the injuries as they could have been caused by the applicant having been beaten, or by him hitting himself with a belt or against the metal frame of the bed or the walls. An objection by the applicant was dismissed by the Muğla Assize Court. The public prosecutor considered that the applicant could have caused these injuries by hitting himself on the walls or his bed while in prison. In this connection, the public prosecutor relied on the statements of the doctor who had examined the applicant on 19 January 2004. Not necessarily mean that he had been beaten, the prosecutor said. On 15 December 2004, the applicant's objection to the decision of the court was dismissed. The court said that the allegations against the applicant were without merit and that the decision was not to be appealed. The appeal was dismissed on 19 December 2004.

eval_texts: The case originated in three applications (nos. 71912/01 and 26968/02 and 36397/03) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Two Turkish nationals, Mr Rifat Böke and Mr Halil Kandemir (‘the applicants’), on 15 June 2001, 7 May 2002 and 28 October 2003 respectively. The applicants were brought before a single judge at the Aydın Magistrates’ Court, who ordered their detention on remand. According to the document, both applicants confessed to their involvement in a criminal organisation. Doctors noted in their reports that there were no signs of ill-treatment on the applicants’ persons. One of the weapons found in the car of the first applicant’s brother had been used in the shooting of 14 February 2001. The Court of Cassation upheld the decision of the İzmir State Security Court on 5 May 2003. The applicants were acquitted on 4 December 2006. The applicant complained about the ill-treatment he had allegedly suffered in police custody. He asked his representative to secure him a medical examination. A doctor examined the first applicant and drafted a report in which he noted that there was no sign of ill- treatment. The applicant further submitted that the doctor had noted in his report that he was suffering from cervical disk syndrome. The doctor sent the applicant’s x-ray to the Aydın prison. On 4 April 2001 a doctor at the Ayden State Hospital sent a letter to the prison administration, requesting the latter to send the applicants for medical examinations. He further asked the prisonadministration to provide him with the medical reports concerning the applicants’ bodies so that he could verify whether they had been subjected to ill- Treatment. On 10 May 2001 the applicant filed a complaint with the Aydın Public Prosecutor’s office against the police officers who had allegedly ill‑treated him. He also complained about the doctors who had not examined him in accordance with the regulations and had failed to note his injuries in their reports. On 23 October 2001 the public prosecutor issued a decision to discontinue the criminal proceedings against police officers since no sign of ill-treatment had been detected on the applicant's person. On 9 January 2002 Mr Böke filed an objection with the Nazilli Assize Court against this decision. He maintained that he had worn a cervical collar for three weeks. He further contended that the cervical X-ray, the medical report diagnosing him with cervical disk syndrome and the prescriptions had not been given to him.

He alleged that they had failed to perform their duties, to properly secure the place in which his brother had died. The officer in charge had already been disciplined. On 24 January 2006 the Cracow district prosecutor discontinued the investigation, finding that no offence had been committed. The prosecutor concluded that the police officers had not failed to properly perform their professional duties and that all the relevant procedural rules had been followed. On 27 February 2006 the applicant lodged an interlocutory appeal against this decision. He maintained that the detective had arrived at the scene six hours after the accident. In addition, he questioned the fact that he had been assisted by S.S., who was an employee of the company. The applicant appealed again. against this decision. The prosecutor concluded that no offence had been committed as regards the alleged breach of professional conduct on the part of the police officers and that there was not enough evidence to substantiate the allegations. The court found that (although this had not been not confirmed by any of the witnesses) the heater might have been moved before it was secured because several other persons had been in the room where the accident had happened before the arrival of police. However, even if it had been moved, there were no grounds to suspect that this had been done in order to deflect suspicion onto any particular person. The Cracow District Court upheld the prosecutor’s findings and considered that the circumstances of the case had been established sufficiently to make a decision on the merits. The court found that the procedures relied on by the applicant had to be followed only in a case where there was a suspicion that a crime had been committed. In the present case there had been no evidence that any third person might have been involved in the death of J.K. J.S. M., S.S., W.D. and A.M.
