At an unspecified time on the evening of 3 January 2003 they arrived at the Słubice border check-point. During a routine passport check the applicant was asked to get out of his car by the border guard officers. The applicant was arrested at 8.15 p.m. on the basis of the detention order and the wanted notice issued on 15 July 2002. He was questioned by the officers but could not understand anything they said and refused to sign any documents. In his submissions to the European Court, he said that various requests he made through his wife, such as to be allowed to contact the French Embassy or his family, were refused. Franck Ladent was detained on remand on the basis of a detention order issued by this court. On 6 January 2003 the applicant's wife engaged counsel to represent the applicant. The applicant's counsel filed an application with the Kraków–Śródmieście District Court for his release and requested that his detention be replaced by other, less restrictive, preventive measures. On the same date it quashed the detention order of 15 July 2002 and replaced it with a ban on leaving the country and ordered the applicant to surrender his passport. The District Court held that the evidence obtained in the case had not sufficiently justified the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed slander. In any event, the alleged offence only carried a fine or a penalty of restriction of liberty but not a custodial sentence. The applicant was released from detention in the morning of 13 January 2003 (a Monday) Upon his release he received copies of the three documents translated into French. The applicant submitted that it was only then that he learnt for the first time that he had been accused of slandering B.M. The court has found the arguments raised by counsel to be compelling. In these circumstances, in the court's view the detention on remand should be replaced with other measures, namely a ban on leaving the country together with seizure of his passport. That measure will adequately secure the proper conduct of the proceedings...”. The. Kraków–Śródmieście District Court granted that application. The MP sent a copy of the President of the Court of Appeal's reply to the applicant's wife. He advised the applicant and his wife that they could seek to institute disciplinary proceedings against the judge who had issued the detention order and criminal proceedings for abuse of power. On 5 October 2004 the Kraków–Śródmieście District Court delivered judgment and acquitted the applicant. On 10 January 2005 the Krakow Regional Court upheld the first-instance judgment. The President further noted that the orders to remand the applicant in custody and to issue a wanted notice had been based on that erroneous premise. Lastly, he stated that the lessons to be drawn from the case would be used for training purposes.

name: H. Rydz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 13167/02) against the Republic of Poland lodged on 1 March 2002 with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant alleged that the length of his detention was excessive. The President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility. The application was dismissed on the grounds that it was not supported by the evidence.
eval_texts: The applicant alleged that the length of his detention was excessive and that the criminal proceedings in his case exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of the Convention. The case originated in an application (no. 13167/02) against the Republic of Poland lodged on 1 March 2002. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of having committed multiple gang rape (including statutory rape), of inducing the victims to take intoxicants and of persuading the victims not to inform the police about those crimes. The court pointed to a serious risk that the applicant, if not detained, might attempt to influence the co-accused and the victims. The applicant was charged with seven offences, including participation in an organised criminal gang, gang rape (including statutory rape) and with threatening the victims. The court found that the grounds for detention on remand were still valid and owing to the fact that the crimes had been committed in co-operation with other persons. The courts also pointed to the necessity of separating the suspects. Seven other hearings scheduled in 2000 were cancelled or adjourned for reasons not attributable to the court, in particular the absence of the suspects' behaviour at the time of the offences. The applicant was acquitted of all the charges against him in February 2003. He was sentenced to a term of life in prison with a minimum term of 15 years. The case involved thirteen defendants and sixty-six witnesses. Hearing scheduled for 30 January 2001 was adjourned in order to have one of the victims heard with the assistance of a psychologist. On 28 June 2001 the Wrocław Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's detention until 15 November 2001. The court requested the police to determine the whereabouts of nine witnesses. Fines were imposed on eleven absent witnesses. Several witnesses had changed their testimonies and the reading out of their earlier statements had been justified. Almost thirty witnesses remained to be heard at that stage of the proceedings and there was a need to summon further witnesses. The applicant served a one-year prison sentence imposed in separate proceedings. The Wrocław Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's detention until 15 February 2002. The court noted that, since June 2000, the first-instance court had held seven hearings and examined ten witnesses. The absence of other witnesses was the major reason for the prolongation of the proceedings. The defendants made almost twenty applications for the examination and cross-examination of witnesses, the ordering of expert opinions and inspections of the crime scene. and to cross-examine them.From 10 April 2002 until 9 December 2002 the applicant was serving a prison sentence imposed on him in separate proceedings. One witness was examined at his place in court. Opole Regional Court found the applicant guilty as charged and sentenced him to nine years' imprisonment and a four-year period of deprivation of his civic rights. All the accused appealed. Wrocław Court of Appeal rejected the applicant's complaint of 25 January 2005 about the excessive length of the proceedings. Supreme Court dismissed applicant's cassation appeal on 11 March 2005. On 29 April 2005 the Court of appeal dismissed the complaint as ill-founded. The court examined solely the part of the. proceedings conducted before the Opole Regional. Court. The applicant appealed again on 14 February 2005, but the case was dismissed on 24 February 2005.

name: Maciej Ziembiński
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1799/07) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his conviction for insult had been in breach of his right to freedom of expression. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz, succeeded by Ms J. Chrzanowska, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was communicated to the Government on 8 March 2010. The case was heard by the Polish Supreme Court.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1799/07) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his conviction for insult had been in breach of his right to freedom of expression. In issue no. 33 of 18 August 2004 the applicant published an article entitled “Elegantly wrapped dung” (“Łajno – elegancko opakowane”). It read, in so far as relevant: “A poser is someone who does everything to produce external effects by his conduct, speech and, in particular, with the populism he preaches” The Radomsko District mayor and two other officials accused the writer of defamation. They accused him of using words such as ‘numbskull’, ‘dull boss’ and ‘dim-witted official’ The applicant went on to describe in general terms a local economic development programme. He finished his article with the following paragraph: ‘This is not a venture of the quail variety by some smart poser or populist who is able to sell his dull bosses dung nicely wrapped in words. And he actually sells it.’ He added: “No numbskull will convince me that I am wrong. ...” The Radomsko District Court ruled that it did not have jurisdiction in the case, and transmitted the private bill of indictment to the Piotrków Trybunalski District Court. Private prosecutors sought an order requiring the applicant to publish an apology in the weekly newspaper. They further sought reimbursement of their legal costs and payment by the applicant of 5,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) to a charity. The court held that the use of the words “numbskull”, “poser” and “dim‑witted official” in respect of K.H. had defamed them as local government officials. The trial court rejected the applicant’s argument that the impugned article had been a simple weekly column in which any similarity to actual persons had been purely coincidental. It found that the article in issue had been part of a campaign carried out by the newspaper against the private prosecutors. The court noted that a journalist had the right to criticise the actions of public officials, but was not entitled to use media in a manipulative way to wage private wars. The latter behaviour was not only unethical and unprofessional, but also incompatible with the role of the media, which was to serve the State and society. It is difficult not to agree with the position that the word “numbskull” (“palant”) in the analysed context is legally irrelevant. The court found no grounds to hold that the impugned words had the effect of lowering the private prosecutors in public esteem. The court imposed a fine of PLN 10,000, which it considered proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of the applicant’s guilt. By using insulting words in respect of the district officials, Maciej Ziembiński intended to derive satisfaction from doing them moral harm. By doing so in a newspaper, he fell within the scope of Article 216 § 2 of the Criminal Code, acting unlawfully, reprehensibly, and, in the absence of circumstances capable of precluding or mitigating his guilt. Piotrków Trybunalski Regional Court upheld the first-instance judgment. It ordered the applicant to pay PLN 1,000 (approx. EUR 256) in respect of the costs of the appeal proceedings. The Regional Court held that the lower court had correctly established the facts of the case. It endorsed the trial court’s findings that the words used in the article had been insulting and harmful to the private prosecutors’ dignity. It further held that, although fair criticism of public authorities and officials was socially desirable and legally accepted, the protection afforded by law did not extend to the use of insulting words which offended human dignity.

name: Arkadiusz Demski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 22695/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant alleged that his rights under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) were violated as he had no opportunity to examine the main witness in the criminal proceedings against him. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. It was also decided to examined the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3)
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 22695/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his rights under Article 6. 1 and 3 (d) were violated as he had no opportunity to examine the main. witness in the criminal proceedings against him. The case was decided on the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Ms B. Słupska-Uczkiewicz. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to four years’ imprisonment. The court established the following facts. On 10 June 2000 M.H., who was at that time 17 years old, met the applicant, J.K. and another man in a bar called “DIK”. They told her to come to the same bar the next day at 5 p.m., which she did. On 11 June 2000 the applicant and J.k. again threatened M.h. in the bar. The applicant then led M. h. out of the bar and together with J. k. they went to the latter’s house. They took turns to rape her in the basement of the house. The following day M. H. spoke about the incident to her grandmother. M.H. described in identical terms the course of events of 10 and 11 June 2000. It is no surprise that it was out of fear of the accused that she went [back] to the bar. As the explanations of both accused are contrary to the testimonies of M.H., [they have been considered untruthful]. ... The victim could not have counted on anybody’s help in such a place and she believed that putting up any resistance would have been pointless. ... It appears that M. H. is a girl of average intelligence, with a normally developed normally developed personality. ... The truthfulness of her testimonies is confirmed by the testimonies. of witnesses R.K. [bartender], M.Ł [grandmother], and P.N. [work colleagues] No injuries were established. The test excluded the presence of semen. A lack of abrasions ... cannot prove that sexual intercourse had not taken place. The circumstances examined above allowed the court to believe that the accused, acting together and in agreement, threatening to beat M.H. up and using force by holding her arms, had raped her on 11 June 2000. She has a strong feeling of injustice and feels guilty that she was not able to react differently in a threatening situation. Her statements were coherent and logically linked. According to the expert they do not have the characteristics of a lie or confabulation. M.Ł. - the victim’s grandmother - has been treating the victim since January 2001. A certificate from a psychological clinic in Germany constitutes proof of her continuing and permanent residence in Germany. M.Ł. wyższy complained that the victim has only been summoned to the hearing of 21 May 2000 once and that the summons had been sent to an address in Poland even though the trial court had known her new address in Germany. The applicant concluded that he had been deprived of the right to put questions to the witness and to confront her with other evidence, which he had repeatedly requested during the trial. On 11 March 2003 the Supreme Court dismissed the cassation appeal. The Supreme Court stated, in so far as relevant: “...[Article 391 § 1] does not mean that in every case when a witness is abroad an automatic application of an exception from the rule of principle of directness should apply” The victim was heard in the preparatory proceedings by a court according to the provision of Article 316 § 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The author of the cassation appeal ... failed to indicate what concrete, additional information he would have liked to obtain from M.H ...” said the judge in the case, who was himself in hiding at the time of the hearing. The court heard the victim in the presence of a psychologist, but the applicant had been in hiding. The victim did not participate in this important evidentiary stage of the proceedings and consequently deprived himself of the opportunity to put questions to the witness, the judge added.

name: Tibet Menteş
train_texts: The case originated in five applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, that the final judgment in their case, dismissing their claims for overtime pay, had run contrary to the prohibition of forced overtime. On 24 September 2015, the Vice-President of the Section decided, under Rule 54 § 2 (c), to invite the parties to submit further observations on whether there had been a violation of Article 4 of the Convention. The application was communicated to the Government under Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.
eval_texts: The case was brought by five members of a trade union. They claimed they had been denied the right to claim compensation for overtime work. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights, which ruled in favor of the plaintiffs. The court ruled in favour of the applicants, and the case went to the Supreme Court of Justice, which decided the case was not a violation of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Supreme Court ruled that the case should be dismissed, and ordered the parties to return to the original hearing date of August 9, 2014. The hearing was adjourned until the end of September, when the case could be re-examined by the Court. Workers at the company in question had worked overtime of 139.5 hours in months which had thirty-one calendar days and 135 hours in the remaining months. Their work schedule did not take account of weekends or public holidays as duty‑free shops remained open twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week. They claimed compensation for the overtime hours they had worked beyond the legal working time for the previous five years of their employment. The applicants requested further remuneration for work done on weekends and public holidays and compensation for annual leave that they had not taken. The İzmir Labour Court decided to join each applicant’s proceedings and to seek an expert report. The applicant’s employer had previously been cautioned, on 25 November 1996, by the Ministry of Labour concerning its practices on working hours. The employer did not owe anything to the applicants for weekend and public holiday work as the remuneration for those days had been in accordance with the applicable regulations. The applicants could not claim any compensation for unused annual leave as they were still working at the company and such leave was only payable at the end of a contract. They also submitted that the deduction of three hours of rest per day was not based on fact but was an assumption by the expert. They requested that the court take other evidence into account, including the defendant employer's shift orders which detailed who would work when and for how long. The applicants worked 24 hours in the course of a twenty-four-hour shift. The Court of Cassation quashed the first-instance judgment on 28 October 2008 and remitted the case on the following grounds: ‘It can be seen from the case file that during the summer months [the applicants] worked for 24 hours and subsequently rested for 24. hours; and in the winter months they worked for24 hours and then rested for 48 hours. However, as determined by the well-established case-law of the Grand Chamber of Grand Chamber, the overtime entitlement should be based on the legal working week of forty‑five hours’ The applicants worked continuously for 24 hours. They were awarded almost ninety percent less than the previous expert report had calculated. On 18 March 2010 the Court of Cassation upheld the İzmir Labour Court’s decision without responding to the applicants’ objections. The applicants appealed against the decision and maintained that the fact that they had worked for twenty-four hours had already been confirmed by the legal records of the Ministry of Labour. Although they had proven that fact, the judgment had been based on the presumption that working for more than 14 hours a day was physically impossible. As a result of that interpretation, some of the applicants' claims were dismissed entirely.

name: Nurettin Peker
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42136/06) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been shot in the leg and then beaten up by a number of gendarmes who had been carrying out an operation in the prison where he was being detained. On 11 May 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theapplication at the same time (Article 29 § 1).
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42136/06) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been shot in the leg and then beaten up by a number of gendarmes who had been carrying out an operation in the prison where he was being detained. On 11 May 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applicant's application at the same time. The operation, named “Return to Life’, began at around 4.30 a.m. on 19 December 2000. The applicant was wounded by a bullet and was among those who were taken to the hospital. He was subsequently taken to Gebze State Hospital but was brought back to the prison four days later, before his treatment was complete. The Government's submissions on the facts of the case are published in full at: http://www.goup.org/news/world-joint-prosecution-and-prosecutors-submissions-on-the-facts-of-the case-at-gebze-state-hospitals.html. The applicant and five other inmates who were injured in the operation were also taken to hospital. A doctor examined the applicant at Gebze hospital on 20 December 2000, noted a gunshot wound on his left foot and began treating it. No firearms were found in the prison during the searches carried out in the immediate aftermath of the operation, or during the searched carried out on 12 January, 16 January, 18 January, 19 January, 23 March and 25 May 2001. The applicant and over 200 of his fellow inmates were indicted and accused of obstructing law-enforcement personnel in the execution of their duties and causing criminal damage. The inmate claimed that the gendarmes had opened fire on him. Three pistols were found in the prison. It was possible that the applicant had been shot with one of those pistols. Neither officer S.Y. nor any of the gendarmes under his command had fired shots during the operation. In a statement on 11 June 2002 the applicant repeated his allegations and gave the prosecutor the names of the four friends who had assisted him. The Gebze governor appointed a gendarmerie officer to investigate the allegations. The Regional Administrative Court in Sakarya examined the objection lodged by the applicant against the governor's decision on 10 January 2005, and quashed the decision. It held that a judicial investigation should be carried out. Gebze prison officials refused to take any further action against the two officers. The case was dismissed in 2006. The two men were later released from prison. The incident was never officially investigated by Gebze's police force. The officers were never charged with any crime. They were released from jail in 2004, after the incident was reported to Gebz prison officials, who then decided not to take further action. The men have since been released from the prison, and the case is now closed. The decision was made by the Gebza's police department, not the prison authorities, and is not subject to any further legal action.

name: Dariusz Kwiatek
train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 20204/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 4 May 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant’s pre-trial detention to the Government. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The application was dismissed and the defendant was sentenced to three years in prison.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 20204/02) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 4 May 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant’s pre-trial detention to the Government. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal from May to August 2004. The applicant, Mr Dariusz Kwiatek (“the applicant”), was born in 1970 and lives in Dąbrowa Górnicza. The investigation was terminated on 14 September 2000. On 15 September 2000 the prosecution filed a bill of indictment with the Katowice Regional Court. The applicant was charged with 2 burglaries. The case file comprised at that time some 32 volumes. The prosecution had obtained voluminous evidence, including various expert reports. The first hearing was listed for 22 March 2001 but it was cancelled. On 14 May 2001 the Regional Court ordered that the applicant be held in custody until 15 October 2001, relying on the same grounds as previously. The application was then joined to that of a certain M.K. who had also been charged with burglary. The trial court had not commenced an examination of the merits due to reasons. The applicant and two other co-defendants appealed against that decision. The Court of Appeal upheld the decision. On 22 November 2001 the trial began. However, the Regional Court was only able to hear two defendants. Two subsequent hearings had to be cancelled due to the absence of one of the defence counsel. The applicant was ordered that the applicant be held in custody until 22 February 2002. The Regional Court made an application under Article 263 § 4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to the Katowice Court of Appeals. The application was denied and the applicant was held until 17 January 2002. He is currently serving a three-year sentence. The applicant appealed against the decision of 8 October 2001. On 9 January 2002 the Court of Appeal granted the Regional Court’s application. The applicant was charged with armed robbery, a serious offence for the commission of which an offender was liable to a minimum sentence of 3 years’ imprisonment. However, in reality the charges of armed robbery were brought against other defendants and the applicant had been, and still was, charged with 2 burglaries. The trial court made yet another application for an extension of the applicant's detention until 1 October 2002. The application was granted on 29 May 2002 and the trial court appealed against that decision, but to no avail. The trial court held hearings on the following dates: 31 January, 15 and 21 March, 11 and 25 April, 16 May 2002, 3 and 27 June, 31 July, 29 August and 12 September 2002. Four hearings were cancelled for the following reasons: the absence of some of the co-defendants and defence counsel. On 3 December 2002 the Regional Court closed the trial. On 10 December 2002 it gave judgment. The applicant was convicted of one burglary and sentenced to 2 years’ and 10 months’ imprisonment, which was nearly (less 12 days) the period he had spent in detention on remand. In sentencing the applicant the trial court took into account his two earlier convictions for similar offences.

name: Piotr Rachwalski
train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 47709/99) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged, in particular, that they had been deprived of their liberty during an unlawful search of their apartment. They complained of a breach of Articles 3, 5 and 8 of the Convention. By a decision of 21 October 2008 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Commission and the applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1) The Court ruled in favour of the applicants in October 2008. The case is still pending at the European Court of Human rights in Strasbourg, France.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47709/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged, in particular, that they had been deprived of their liberty during an unlawful search of their apartment and that the police had used excessive and unjustified force towards them. They complained of a breach of Articles 3, 5 and 8 of the Convention. By a decision of 21 October 2008 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The parties do not fully agree about the facts of the case, which may be summarised as follows. As presented by the applicants the case was not decided on the merits. Policemen, armed with truncheons and guarded by police dogs, entered the house, woke up the other occupants and ordered them to stand against the wall. No information was provided about the grounds, purpose or legal basis for the search. During this time the police showered abuse on the students. The applicants requested to be examined by a forensic medicine specialist. It was established that the first applicant had two long bruises on his left arm, and other bruises on the palm of his hand. The second applicant had a blue mark on her bottom (13 by 9 cm) It was stated that these bruises could have been caused by the use of police truncheon. The Wrocław District Prosecutor refused to institute criminal proceedings against the police for abuse of authority. The prosecutor considered that the police action had been justified. The police could have reasonably suspected that the unlocked car had been stolen, even though it had not been reported as such. The further developments had certainly come as a surprise to both the police and other persons involved in the incident. The applicant was most probably hit once. The atmosphere was tense. The owner of the car gave the police the keys and documents to the car. As D. S. was unruly and continued to express objections, the policemen decided to arrest him. While he was being taken into custody by the police, he hit one of them in the face. D. S. had objected in a loud voice to the police intervention. He insisted that the intention of the police was to harass the persons in the house. He had not obeyed the police requests to calm down and the verbal exchange between him and the police officer A. C. had become increasingly heated. The prosecutor considered that this had been justified in the light of D. S’s aggressive behaviour. It was finally noted that the accounts of the facts given by the persons present at the scene, other than the police, were highly divergent, making it impossible to establish the facts of the case. Therefore, the submissions of the other persons could not be considered credible. D. S. argued that he was a law-abiding citizen, a student of two university faculties and a member of the Municipal Council of his town. He had not given any reason to be beaten, verbally insulted and humiliated just at the whim of the police. The Wrocław Regional Prosecutor upheld the contested decision. He considered that the police intervention had been justified in so far as they wanted to verify the identity of the owner of the car. Regardless of whether he had intended to hit A. C. in the face or not, his behaviour could have been perceived as an intentional assault. The identity check of the persons present in the house had been necessary as they had insulted the policemen.

name: Metin Gültekin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 17081/06) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, that their close relative, Toğay Gültekin, had died while doing his compulsory military service owing to the authorities’ failure to ensure prompt access to medical treatment for his serious health problems. On 2 April 2014 the application was communicated to the Government. The application was heard by the Supreme Court of Justice (SCJ) on 11 April 2014. The case was returned to the Court of Appeal for further proceedings.
eval_texts: An application against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that their close relative, Toğay Gültekin, had died while doing his compulsory military service owing to the authorities’ failure to ensure prompt access to medical treatment for his serious health problems. On 2 April 2014 the application was communicated to the Government. The application was lodged by four Turkish nationals. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent. The case is being heard by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) in Strasbourg. Toğay Gültekin died at the GATA Hospital on 27 March 2004. No autopsy was performed. An investigation was carried out at the military unit where he had been doing his military service. The military officers who carried out the investigation concluded that there had been no fault attributable to them in his death. The applicants initiated compensation proceedings against the Ministry of Defence before the Supreme Military Administrative Court (“the Military Administrative court”) They argued, in particular, that Toğay GülTekin had not received prompt or adequate medical care in his regiment. When his condition had deteriorated he was examined by a doctor attached to his regiment but he was not transferred to a hospital specialising in infectious diseases. Toğay Gültekin had been performing his military service and had thus not had the opportunity to leave his military unit and seek medical assistance of his own volition. The authorities had been under an obligation to protect his well-being and to ensure timely medical treatment for him. The applicants argued that it had been these inordinate delays that had caused Toğay Güllekin’s death. The Ministry of Defence maintained that the military authorities had not acted in a negligent fashion when dealing with his medical problems. The court accepted that he had been examined by a doctor at the regiment's infirmary on 20 March 2004 and then sent back to his unit. Military Administrative Court appointed three medical experts to clarify whether the military authorities had acted negligently. Medical experts reached the following conclusion in their report of 20 September 2005: “... An examination of the documents and other information in the file shows that Toğay Gültekin started his military service on 22 August 2003. On 2 January 2004 he was treated for a retractile testicle at Çorlu Military Hospital. He was prescribed medication at the regiment’s infirmary for an upper respiratory tract infection on 5 January 2004. On 17 March 2004 the regimental Infirmary doctor decided to refer him to an infectious diseases clinic, but that was not done. On 20 March 2004 he. was diagnosed with and treated for an infection of the upper respiratory. tract. On 22 March 2004. he was referred to the University Hospital with suspected hepatitis and he was sent there. On 23 March 2004, he was diagnosed. with fulminant hepatitis. He died on 27 March 2004 as a result of fulminants hepatitis.” Toğay Gültekin was contaminated with both hepatitis A and hepatitis B viruses within a short period of time. His liver was infected with both viruses at the same time. This is a condition which worsens the damage to the liver and increases the risk of fulminant hepatitis (fast-deteriorating acute liver failure) A liver transplant is the sole method of ensuring patient survival. The Military Administrative Court dismissed the applicants’ claim. In its decision the court relied on the medical expert report summarised above (see paragraph 18) and concluded that no fault could be attributed to the authorities for Toğay GülTekin’s death. On 28 December 2005 the Military Administrative Court refused to entertain the rectification request lodged by the applicants. in failing to refer Toğay Gültekin to hospital between 17 and 23 March 2004. The court ruled that the military had been derelict in its duty to refer him to hospital and he should have been admitted to hospital. The case was settled out of court in 2005. For more information on the case visit: www.militaryadministrativecourt.gov. The case was heard by the Court's Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The applicant was ordered to indicate the value of her claim on 5 October 1995. The Warsaw Regional Court exempted her partially from the court fees. On 27 February 1996 the Warsaw Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) dismissed her appeal. On 9 October 1996 the defendant co-operative lodged a counter-claim against the applicant. On 17 February 1999 the applicant submitted a request for legal assistance, stating that she had not been able to contact a lawyer chosen by her. At the hearing held on 9 June 1999 the court ordered an expert opinion concerning the construction costs. The applicant's lawyer modified her action and raised additional claims, inter alia, for compensation for the allegedly deceitful taking over of her previous flat. The application was made in 1999. The applicant's house was built on a plot of land in Warsaw. The application was rejected by the Warsaw Regional Court. On 9 December 2002 the Court of Appeal quashed that decision. On 27 January 2003 the Regional Court rejected the applicant's additional claim of 10 April 2002, since she had not paid the due fee. On the same day it ordered an expert opinion. On 10 April 2003 the court granted the applicant partial exemption from court costs. The proceedings are still pending. The court has ruled that the applicant does not need to pay court costs for the claim that she did not pay the court fee for the initial claim.

name: Lynette Copland

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 62617/00) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained of the monitoring of her telephone calls, e-mail correspondence and Internet usage. The Court declared the application partly admissible. The Government stated that the monitoring consisted of analysis of the College telephone bills showing telephone numbers called, the dates and times of the calls, and their length and cost. The case was heard in March 2006 and the applicant filed further observations (Rule 59 § 1 of the Rules of Court). The Government submitted that the monitoring of telephone usage took place for a few months up to about 22 November 1999. The applicant did not comment on the manner in which her Internet usage was monitored but submitted that it took place over a much longer period of time than the Government had admitted. The Government accepted that this monitoring took the form of analysing the websites visited, the times and dates of the visits to the websites and their duration. In November 1999 the applicant became aware that enquiries were being made into her use of e-mail at work when her step-daughter was contacted by the College and asked to supply information about e-mails she had sent to the College. There was no policy in force at the College at the material time regarding the monitoring of telephone, e-mail or Internet usage by employees. The applicant provided the Court with statements from other members of staff alleging inappropriate and intrusive monitoring of their movements. She further believed that the DP became aware of a legally privileged fax that was sent by herself to her solicitors and that her personal movements, both at work and when on annual or sick leave, were the subject of surveillance. The DP has been suspended and the applicant understands that the applicant, who is still employed by the College, understands that  the DP has also been suspended.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 33868/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) Mr Oleg Choumakov (“the applicant’), was arrested on suspicion of having committed a robbery and the murder of a taxi driver. The court found that the grounds previously invoked were still valid and that only the applicant's detention would secure the proper conduct of the investigation. The applicant was born in 1971 and is currently detained in the Gdańsk Detention Centre. The applicant's detention had reached the statutory time-limit of two years. The Regional Court made applications to the Gdańsk Court of Appeal asking for the applicant’s detention to be prolonged beyond that term. On 30 June 2005 the Elbląg Regional Court convicted the applicant and his co‑accused and sentenced them to 25 years’ imprisonment. The applicant lodged an appeal against the judgment. The appeal court quashed the impugned judgment and remitted the case on 21 December 2005. On the same day, the appeal court prolonged the applicants’ detention on remand. On 7 March 2006 his pre-trial detention was further prolonged. The trial court reiterated the grounds given previously: the reasonable suspicion against the applicant. The Elbląg Regional Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to 25 years’ imprisonment. The applicant lodged an appeal. The Gdańsk Court of Appeal allowed the appeal and quashed the impugned judgment. The case was remitted and the applicant remains in detention pending trial. His appeal against that decision was dismissed on 15 January 2008. The court further prolonged the applicant’s detention until 28 June 2008. In addition to the grounds invoked previously, the court found that the applicant and the second co-accused had made an attempt to contact each other illegally and to exchange information about the trial which justified the finding that he might interfere.

The facts of each case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. Mr Hobbs is a United Kingdom national, born in 1921 and living in Southampton. His wife died on 25 February 1998. On 11 October 2000 he contacted the Inland Revenue and applied for widow’s bereavement allowance (“WBA”) for the years 1998/9 and 1999/2000. He was informed that he did not qualify for the tax allowance, since he was a man and the law provided only for payments to widows. Mr Richard was born on 21 May 1957 and lives in Dunfermline. There were two children of the marriage, born on 22 February 1991 and 29 December 1992. Mr Geen, no. 63468/00 lives in Maidenhead. His wife died on 17 October 1995. There were three children of the marriage, born 18 November 1987, 22 August 1989 and 22 April 1992. On 3 July 2000 the applicant applied to the IR for a WBA or equivalent. He was refused by a letter dated 11 July 2000. A paragraph had been added, stating that in or around December 1995 or January 1996 the applicant had made enquiries at his local tax office about entitlement to tax rebates or allowances following bereavement. This information was included in the application form lodged on 29 September 2000. On 26 March 2001 the applicant sent a copy of a letter of refusal from the IR dated 9 July 1996.

The applicants also requested to obtain documentary evidence from the land register. The court fixed a one-month time-limit for the parties to produce the evidence. On 26 March 1998 the court gave judgment. It partly granted the claim of the original plaintiffs’ daughter against the second applicant and dismissed the claims of the first applicant. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1271/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the decision to place her in detention on remand pending her third trial had not been supported by relevant and sufficient reasons. She relied on Article 5 §§ 1 (c) and 3 and Article 8 of the convention. The application was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Government and the applicant each filed written observations (Rule 59 § 1). The applicant was released on bail pending trial to her home where she lived with her three children. The applicant’s second trial began on 17 February 2003. The second trial judge also allowed bail, no objection being made by the prosecution. On 20 March 2003 she was, by a majority verdict of the jury, convicted of murder. The trial judge sentenced her to life imprisonment and committed her to custody. The period of imprisonment that the applicant had to serve before she could have been considered for release was set at fifteen years. The Court of Appeal quashed her conviction and, having heard further submissions, ordered that she be returned upon a fresh indictment for murder before the Crown Court. The applicant applied for bail and the prosecution did not object. In correspondence, she submits that the reasoning of the appeal court was not committed to writing. The Government submitted a copy of the contemporaneous notes of the senior law clerk present at the hearing. The final paragraph of her notes reads as follows: “ CS [Counsel for the prosecution]: no opposition to bail – did attend. LCJ [Lord Chief Justice]: on bail before trial, course of trial, honoured all condits [conditions] prosecution doesn’t oppose. Material difference here – found guilty by jury quashing material irregularity on charge. Doesn't sound directly an issue on bail. Be a prompt retrial. Refused.” The application to the Court of Appeal for leave to appeal against the refusal of bail to the House of Lords was refused on 22 July 2004.

On the basis of further information provided by the prosecution as to who had been watching the trial proceedings in the remote viewing room, the Appeal Court recalled the order of the trial judge and substituted an order for desertion pro loco et tempore, which allowed for the re-indictment of one of the original accused. eval_texts: The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). The Court ruled in favour of the applicant. The decision was made by the Court on 8 July 2003, and the decision is published here in its entirety. The applicant was released from prison in May 1994. He had not paid the money due under the confiscation order, but the order had not been enforced. On 25 June 1996 a warrant was issued for the applicant's arrest to bring him to court for a means inquiry to take place in respect of the sum of GBP 17,670 outstanding on the order. The inquiry took place on 10 July 1996. The proceedings were adjourned at the applicant’s request to allow him to seek legal aid and a Certificate of Inadequacy (which would have meant that he would have to pay back the money). The applicant was found not guilty of any offence. The High Court dismissed the applicant's application for a Certificate of Inadequacy on 18 November 1997. The Magistrates' Court ordered that proceedings to enforce the confiscation order should take place. The proceedings were subsequently adjourned several more times, but the reason for the adjournments is not clear. On 13 May 1998 the case was listed for 3 June 1998, and on the latter date the applicant was committed to prison for 15 months for non-payment of the sum outstanding. The High Court refused his application for judicial review of the magistrates' decision on 7 August 1998. However, as a matter of English law the High Court held the onus was on the applicant to pay, and “any continuing lapse of time is then in the eye of the law a product of the failure to pay"

eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 7 June 1991. It originated in an application (no. 13191/87) against the French Republic lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of that State, Mr Tuan Tran Pham Hoang, on 20 August 1987. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 paras. 1, 2 and 3 (c) (Art 6-1, art. 6-2, 6-3-c). Mr Tuan Tran Pham Hoang, a French national who was born in Saigon in 1963, was unemployed and living at Auln. He sued the French Government for discrimination against him. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 21 April 1992. The Court heard addresses by Mrs Belliard for the Government, Mr Schermers for the Commission and Mr Lestourneaud for the applicant, as well as replies to its question. The hearing was adjourned until 22 April 1992 when Mr Hoang was allowed to apply for a new trial. He was granted bail and returned to France on 21 May 1992. He claimed that he had been denied the right to appeal against the decision of the High Court. On 3 January 1984 he was arrested in Paris with four other people from Hong Kong, Cambodia or Vietnam. They were carrying two bags containing 2,750 grams of heroin base and 85 grams of almost pure heroin, together with a pair of scales, one pan of which bore traces of heroin. Two other people, Mr Jip Quang Duong and Mr Hanh Phuoc, were arrested after weapons and 5kg of caffeine were discovered by police while searching a flat visited by the applicant. The applicant was released under judicial supervision on 6 March 1984. He and the six others mentioned above for trial on the charge that they had “conspired in Paris during 1983-84, in particular up to 3 January, to produce, possess and supply drugs, namely heroin’. The 7 defendants constituted a group of individuals formed with a view to importing heroin base, converting it, possessing it, transporting it and mixing it with caffeine. The heroin subsequently seized was to be transported in Pham’s motor vehicle, and Tran was to drive with it to the home of Jip Quang Duong and Hanh Phuoc, where the 5kg of caffeine were seized. The Director-General's submissions included the following details: “The defendants’ statements and the police surveillance disclosed the following: Cheng Man Ming and Fu Wing Kin left Bangkok together by air on 26 december 1983 with a suitcase with a false bottom containing the heroin.”

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26118/10) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant waved a small placard reading “Casse toi pov’con” (“Get lost, you sad prick”) during a visit to Laval by the President of France. He was prosecuted by the public prosecutor for insulting the President, an offence under section 26 of the Act of 29 July 1881. The court held as follows: “... On the day of the President’s visit ... the defendant ... saw fit to wave asmall placard containing an exact copy, served cold, of a famous retort prompted by a direct affront” The Angers Court of Appeal upheld the lower court’s judgment in its entirety. As to the question of guilt: Actus reus of the offence has been made out. There is no need for lengthy discussion of the fact that describing the President as a ‘sad prick’ [‘pauvre con’] amounts to insulting him. The small placard containing the phrase in question is indisputably a form of publicly conveying a message, which can take place by means of placards or posters on public display. The expression ‘casse toi pov’con’ can be read as ‘you shouldn’t say’. Hervé Eon, a former Socialist elected representative in the département of Mayenne, had recently fought a long-running campaign actively supporting a Turkish family residing unlawfully in national territory. The Court of Appeal further noted that the applicant had declined to apologise, which meant that he could not be given a discharge. It observed that the first-instance court had found that a simple warning was required and had given him a suspended fine of EUR 30 as a matter of principle. It concluded that the penalty imposed was entirely appropriate in view of the nature of the offence and the applicant’s character. The applicant appealed on points of law to the Court of Cassation. The applicant challenged the decision to refuse legal aid in the absence of an arguable ground of appeal. The Government stated that on 15 September 2009 the law firm instructed to represent him had sent the Court of Cassation a letter indicating that it did not intend to file further pleadings in support of the appeal; nor had the applicant filed any pleadings himself. The applicant nevertheless pursued his appeal on points of law to its conclusion. The appeal was declared inadmissible, finding that there were no grounds to warrant its examination. In an order of 15 June 2009 the President of the. Court ofCassation upheld the refusal to grant legal aid.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 68864/01) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Two French nationals, Ms Hermance Merger and Ms Clémentine Cros (‘the applicants’), made the application on 3 November 2000. The first child wanted the money to go to the rest of the family. The court ruled that the money should go to his wife, not to the other children. The applicants appealed to the Court of Cassation. eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 29 May 1995. It originated in an application (no. 22500/93) against the French Republic lodged with the Commission under Article 25. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 8 of the Convention (art. 8). The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings. The President gave the applicants leave, as lawyers, to present their own case. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr L.-E. Pettiti, the elected judge of French nationality. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 April 1996. Mr Gérard Guillot and his wife chose to give their daughter, born on 7 April 1983, the forenames “Fleur de Marie, Armine, Angèle’. The Registrar received the Government's memorial on 27 November 1995. The Court heard addresses by Mr Martínez, Mr Guillat and Mrs Dubrocard. The case was dismissed in a judgment of 7 February 1984 by the Nanterre tribunal de grande instance. The court heard the case again in May 1996. 'Fleur de Marie' is composed of two forenames recognised by French law, which when linked by the preposition 'de' form the name of the heroine of Eugène Sue's Mystères de Paris. A forename may be composed of up to two names already in use, it cannot consist of a combination of two names linked by a preposition since it would cease to be a mere reuse of a traditional boy's or girl's name. The main claim in the application must be dismissed but there is no reason not to grant the claim made in the alternative relating to the forename 'Fleur-Marie', says the Versailles Court of Appeal. The case-law is tending towards a more liberal approach in order to take account of changes in social mores, local customs and family traditions. It is necessary to prevent parents from choosing forenames which are excessively whimsical and so eccentric that the child is likely to be the first victim. This is the case with the forename 'Fleur de Marie', notwithstanding that it was the name of the heroine of a famous literary work. On the other hand, there is no reason not to allow the claim made in the alternative that the fore name should consist of the two forenames ‘Fleur’ and ‘Marie’ juxtaposed.

Kūris, Mr W. Fuhrmann, Mr K. Jungwiert, Mr B. Zupančič, Mrs N. Vajić, Mrs W. Thomassen, Mrs M. Tsatsa-Nikolovska and Mrs S. Botoucharova. In support of their request the applicants referred to Article 4 of the Declaration of Rights of 1974, which guarantees the right to freedom of religion, and Article 9 of the Convention. The traditional wording is still mandatory for other offices, such as that of Captain-Regent or of a member of the government. Law no. 115 of 29 October 1993 introduced a choice for newly elected members of the General Grand Council between the traditional oath and one in which reference to Gospels was replaced by the words ‘on my honour’ The Government raised three preliminary objections and asked the Court to declare the application inadmissible. The full text of the Commission’s opinion is reproduced as an annex to this judgment. in its report of 2 December 1997 (former Article 31 of the Convention), it concluded unanimously that there had been a violation of Article 9. on 7 April 1997. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 72161/01) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant was born in 1941 and lives in Pruszków, Poland. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court decided that there were no grounds for lodging a cassation appeal. The applicant had never had the right to a co-operative apartment which could be assimilated to ownership. She had admitted, both before the first-instance and the appellate court, that at the time of the exchange of apartments she had been aware that her right was only assimilable to the rights arising out of a rental contract. It had been open to her to take steps in order to have her right transformed into an ownership-like right, but she had not done so. In these circumstances, a cassation appeal would not offer any prospects of success. The first instance court was right in finding that the defendant housing co- cooperative was not obliged to pay compensation to the applicant.

In his appeals, he argued that the charges against him were based on unreliable and fabricated evidence. He also relied on his personal circumstances, in particular the need to ensure that his wife, who suffered from psychiatric problems, was cared for. Authorities repeatedly relied on a strong suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences in question, supported by evidence from witnesses and experts. The courts found no special grounds that would justify lifting the applicant's detention and imposing a less severe measure. In one of the decisions dismissing an appeal by the applicant against a decision prolonging his detention, the Court of Appeal noted that “certain witnesses in principle admitted that they had been instructed [about what to say] in their testimony” It did not, however, specify who had exerted pressure on the witnesses or how they had done so. The applicant's pre-trial detention was lifted and he was released on 27 June 2008.

The applicants were represented by Mr C. Şanlı, Mr M. Karabıyık and Mr A. Gündüz, lawyers practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government on 20 December 2005. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention, it decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants argued that the plot of land in question should have been considered as urbanised land (arsa) instead of rural land. Three on-site inspections were conducted and three separate expert reports were received by the court. On 29 December 1997 the First Instance Court awarded the applicants a certain amount of additional compensation. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The application was dismissed on 2 November 2002. The case was decided on 2 December 2005. On 16 June 1998 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment on the ground that the expert reports were not sufficient basis for a judgment. On 9 May 2000 the Gebze Civil Court of First Instance decided that the plot of land was of rural nature. In reaching this decision, the court conducted four more on-site inspections and relied on four additional expert reports. The court awarded the applicants an additional compensation of 22,568,437,760 Turkish liras (TRL) plus interest at the statutory rate, running from 15 October 1996 for Mr Ali Erdem and from 22 October1996 for the other applicants.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no 70516/01) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 12 December 2005 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Agreement, it decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility. The applicants appealed to the Gaziantep. Administrative Court and requested that the decision of 25 March 1997 be annulled. They maintained that they had paid their rent periodically until 1997. They also contended that there was no valid reason to terminate their lease contract. In this connection they maintained that although criminal proceedings had been initiated against them in the eighties for being members of an illegal organisation, namely the PKK, they had all been acquitted of the charges against them. The applicants appealed. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld the judgments of the Gazian Administrative Court on 10 November 2000, 14 September 2000, 26 October 2000, 8 November 2000 and 16 November 2000 respectively.

name: Zdzisław Sikorski
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 46004/99) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the civil proceedings in his case exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 6 of the Convention. By a decision of 24 June 2003 the Court declared the application admissible. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26: the Chamber of the Court. The application was transferred to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5: 2 of Protocol no. 11).
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 46004/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the civil proceedings in his case exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 6 of the Convention. By a decision of 24 June 2003 the Court declared the application admissible. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The court held hearings on 15 May, 28 August and 14 November 1991, 29 January, 22 April, 27 May and 30 September 1992, 23 February and 7 June 1993, 28 March and 25 April 1994. Hearing scheduled for 8 September 1999 was adjourned because of an illness of a court expert. Hearings were held on 14 October and 30 December 1999, 17 January, 29 March, 20 April, 28 April, 18 May, 23 May and 16 June 2000. On 8 November 2000 the Oleśno District Court imposed a fine on an expert for his non-compliance with the time-limit for issuing his opinion. The Supreme Court declined to examine the cassation appeal, considering that it had not been shown that arguable public interest grounds existed which would justify the examination of the appeal. The case continues to this day in the Częstochowa Regional Court.

name: Hüsamettin Keskin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32987/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court declared the case a settled case. The judge elected in respect of Turkey, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28) and was replaced by an ad hoc judge. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32987/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’. consent, the Court ruled that the application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints (applications nos. 26480/95, 28291/95 and 29280/95) The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way). On 30 January 1981 the Erzincan Martial Law Court ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. On 10 May 1982 the Military Public Prosecutor filed a bill of indictment against the applicant and 722 other defendants. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. In a judgment of 24 August 1988 the Martial Law. Court convicted the applicant on account of his involvement in the Dev.Yol. It sentenced the applicant to fifteen years’ imprisonment, permanently debarred. him from employment in the civil service. On 24 June 1997 the Ankara Assize Court decided, under Article 102 of theTurkish Criminal Code, that the criminal proceedings against the. applicant should be discontinued since the prosecution was time‑barred.

name: Ahmet Koç
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32580/96) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the criminal proceedings brought against him had not been concluded within a “reasonable time” He also contended that he had been convicted on the basis of the statements he had made to the police under duress. By a decision of 23 September 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. It retained the applicant's complaints concerning his right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal and declared the remainder of his complaints inadmissible. The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section of the Court.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the criminal proceedings brought against him had not been concluded within a “reasonable time” He further submitted that his right to a fair hearing had been breached because of his conviction by the Ankara Martial Law Court, which lacked independence and impartiality. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 23 September 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. It retained the applicant's complaints concerning his right of fair hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal. The applicant was charged with membership of an illegal armed organisation. The case was referred to the Military Court of Cassation (Askeri Yargıtay) The applicant was sentenced to six years and eight months' imprisonment. He was also permanently debarred from public service. The applicant appealed against the conviction and was dismissed from his post at the Ankara Municipality on account of his conviction. On 11 December 1996 the applicant was permitted to return to his previous post and to work as the head of the research and planning department of the municipality. He is still employed at the municipality as a head of research andplanning.

name: Uğur Çatak
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26718/05) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented by Mr Ç. Bingölbalı, a lawyer practising in İzmir. The Turkish Government (“the Government’s Agent”) were represented by their Agent. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26718/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was expelled from the military academy following a secret security investigation conducted by the Ministry of Defence into him and his family. The Supreme Military Administrative Court refused to annul the expulsion decision. The court acknowledged that the security investigation had revealed that his father had previously been convicted of forgery. It further held that this information justified the applicant's expulsion under the relevant laws and regulations. On 18 January 2005 the applicant requested rectification. The application was granted. The Ministry of Defence filed an action with the İzmir Civil Court against the applicant for the reimbursement of his educational expenses. The applicant was ordered to pay 12,355.61 Turkish liras (TRY) (approximately 6,000 euros (EUR) plus interest running from 7 June 2004 to 14 April 2008. Article 52 of Law no. 1602 on the Supreme Military Administrative Court provides as follows: “The Chambers ... may request the parties or the competent authorities to provide them with all documents and information concerning the cases before them ...” The Prime Minister, the Army Commander-in-Chief or the Competent Minister may refuse to submit the requested documents or information if they concern the security or superior interests of the Republic of Turkey.

name: Elif Karakaya

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5173/05) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Kızılkaya and Mr İ.H.Altan, lawyers practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant was awarded compensation with statutory interest on 27 July 2004. The case was referred to the Court of Jurisdictional Disputes (Uyuşmazlık mahkemesi), which held on 17 November 2003 that the matter fell within the jurisdiction of the military administrative courts. The applicant objected to the amounts stated in the expert report and did not seek rectification. The Supreme Military Administrative Court granted the applicant compensation on 16 June 2004, but did not rectify the amount. The court also awarded the applicant legal aid on 1 June 2000, but this was rejected on 28 June 2000. The Court of Jurisdictional  Disputes found that the case should have been heard by the competent civil administrative court due to its military content and referred the case to the Ankara Administrative Court.

name: Waldemar Flieger
train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 36262/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36262/08) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Mr Waldemar Flieger (‘the applicant’) was indicted before the Świecie District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) on charges of burglaries committed in the period between 9 December 1998 and 17 February 1999. The applicant was born in 1975 and is currently detained at the detention centre in Chełmno. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Bydgoszcz Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) under section 5 of the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. He sought a ruling that the length of the proceedings before the Gliwice District Court had been excessive and an award of just satisfaction in the amount of 15,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) On 20 January 2009 the Świecie District Court sentenced the applicant to one year and three months' imprisonment. It appears that the applicant failed to appeal and the judgment became final in July 2008.

name: Jan Załuska

The case was first heard in May 2006. The applicant filed a complaint under the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. On 27 September 2007 the Warsaw Regional Court awarded the applicant PLN 2,277,838 in compensation for pecuniary damage. Since this judgment was not appealed against, it became final on 19 October 2007. The Warsaw Court of Appeal confirmed that the proceedings in question had indeed been lengthy. The court stated that, although the applicant’s representative had lodged several futile motions which affected the pace of the proceedings, the court took no action to discipline him.

name: Mehmet Reşit Arslan

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 31320/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The application was brought by a Turkish national, Mr Mehmet Reşit Arslan (“the applicant”), on 21 August 2001. He was represented by Ms S. Gürcan, a lawyer practising in Istanbul. The applicant was convicted of membership of an illegal organisation under Article 168 § 1 of the Criminal Code. He maintained that his statements had been taken under torture while in police custody. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of 6 March 2000. The death penalty was commuted to a life sentence. He was sentenced to the death penalty under Article 125 of the criminal code. The applicant appealed the conviction and was convicted on 21 March 2001. He died in prison on 24 July 2007, aged 78. He is survived by his wife, two children and a step-son. The case is described as one of the most notorious torture cases in Turkish history.

name: Marianna Jeruzal

The applicant’s daughter, Mrs Halina Jeruzal‑Kuklińska, informed the Court’S Registry that the applicant had died on 25 November 2002. She stated that she wished to continue the proceedings before the Court in her late mother's stead. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 65888/01) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Marianna Jeruzal (“the applicant”) was born in 1912 and lived in Gdynia in Poland. She died in 2002. The applicant and her husband transferred the ownership of their house and land to their son – Z.J., and kept a lifetime usufruct interest for themselves. Under the terms of the contract Z. J. was supposed to take care of the applicant and. her husband and to provide them with food and medical care. But he had failed to do so. The Gdańsk Regional Court quashed the impugned judgment and remitted the case on 22 December 1995. The defendant lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) On 25 May 1999 the Supreme court gave judgment. On 9 October 2000 the applicant asked to be granted leave to file an appeal out of time and to be assigned a lawyer. The applicant’s legal aid lawyer did not file a cassalation appeal. The case was returned to the Gda’dsk Court of Appeal on 11 May 2000. The application was dismissed on 15 November 2000. Gdańsk Court of Appeal rejected her application. Court considered that in view of the value of the claim, a cassation appeal in the applicant’s case was inadmissible in law. Another legal aid lawyer was involved in the case. In 2000 the court ruled that the appeal was not viable. The case was settled out of court in December 2000. The appeal was dismissed and the application was dismissed. In 2001, the judge dismissed the appeal on the grounds of insufficient evidence. In 2003, the Appeals Court upheld the appeal and ruled in favor of the applicant. In 2012, the Polish government ruled in favour of the appeal.

name: Iordanis Iordanou

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 43685/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the Turkish occupation of the northern part of Cyprus had deprived him of his home and properties. By a decision of 25 June 2002 the Court declared the application admissible. The Court also received comments from the Government of Cyprus, which had exercised its right to intervene (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 1 (b)). The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court then ruled in favour of the applicant. The applicant also owned three plots of land in Karavas, some of which were lemon groves, with olive and carob trees growing on the others. This second house, located at 10, Kanaris Street, consisted of three ground floor rooms, one room upstairs, two wells, one electric water pump and one water storage pump. He claimed that he had been deprived of his property rights, all his property being located in the area which was under the occupation and control of the Turkish military authorities. The latter had prevented him from having access to and from using and possessing his houses and fields. He therefore produced an extract from the registries of the Republic of Cyprus, dated 29 June 1993, and indicating that the property at issue was registered in his name.

name: Maria Kubiszyn
