The Court ruled that the application was not admissible because of the lack of a hearing within areasonable time. The Polish Government was represented by their Agent, Mr Krzysztof Drzewicki.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 37437/97) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Krzysztof Drzewicki, from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that her right to a “hearing within a reasonable time” had not been respected. The court held twelve hearings on the following dates: 26 August, 6 December 1994; 31 January, 21 March, 16 May, 1 September, 28 November 1995; 9 January, 13 February, 19 March, 17 April and 26 April 1996. It heard evidence from at least twelve witnesses. The applicant claimed that her husband had been exclusively responsible for the failure of their marriage and that, therefore, divorce was inadmissible in law. The court further vested custody rights over their minor child with the applicant and obliged her husband to pay maintenance for the child. On 5 January 2001 the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) held a hearing and on the same date it dismissed the applicant's cassation appeal. The case was heard on the following dates: 13 February, 16 March, 24 April 1998. The applicant filed an appeal with the Wrocław Court of Appeal. On 15 May 1998 the Wałbrzych Regional Court pronounced divorce, finding that both spouses had been at fault.

name: Dündar Hasko
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 20578/05) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant alleged, in particular, that the length of the criminal proceedings against him had been incompatible with Article 6 § 1 of the convention and that his right to adversarial proceedings had been breached by the non-communication of the Principal Public Prosecutor’s opinion to him. On 10 February 2010 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the Application at the same time (Article 29 § 1).
eval_texts: The case was brought by a Turkish man claiming that his right to a fair trial had been violated by the Turkish Government. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights. The court ruled that there was insufficient evidence to prove that the claims made by the applicant were false. The judge also ruled that the government had not done enough to ensure the right of the applicant to have his case heard. The decision was appealed to the High Court of Justice, which found in favor of the government. The appeal was dismissed and the case was dismissed again, with the judge concluding that the case should be dismissed on the grounds that the applicant had not shown that he was entitled to a right to be heard. The applicant was found guilty as charged and sentenced to 4 years and 8 months' imprisonment in July 2003. The Istanbul Assize Court re-examined the applicant’s sentence on 13 February 2006 and reduced it to 3 years and 9 months’ imprisonment. The applicant requested the suspension of the execution of his sentence on account of his age and poor state of health. In July 2010, an additional arrest warrant was issued against the applicant. He was sentenced to four years and eight months' prison in July 2009. The judge was convicted of using false powers of attorney knowingly. The verdict was quashed on 8 October 2002 by the Court of Cassation, which upheld the first-instance court's decision.

name: Fatih Taş

eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was the owner and the editor-in-chief of a publishing house, Aram Basım ve Yayıncılık, which published a periodical, Vesta. The applicant and his fellow refugees had informed the Commander of the United Nations (UN) forces in Cyprus of their intentions. They arrived at the check point in the “buffer zone’, on the main road which links Nicosia with Ayios Amvrosios and Kyrenia. There, they asked the UN officer on duty to be allowed to return to their homes, property and villages. They requested the same officer to forward their demand to the Turkish military authorities. The officer replied that the latter had refused their request. The applicant has not been able to go back to his home and property since returning to Cyprus.

It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theApplication at the same time (Article 29 § 3) The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of foreign Affairs. The application was dismissed on 9 July 2004.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 41663/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were born in 1948 and 1955 respectively and live in Glinica. They claimed compensation for the unlawful annulment of a contract by a contract holder. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of foreign Affairs. According to an assessment made by two lawyers, a cassation appeal lacked any prospects of success. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicants sought just satisfaction in the amount of 20,000 Polish zlotys (PLN), that is, PLN 10,000 each. Both parties lodged appeals against the first-instance judgment. It appears that both parties lodged cassation appeals and the case is pending before the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) The court held that the 2004 Act had legal effect as from its entry into force on 17 September 2004. It found that during the relevant part of the proceedings, there had been no inactivity or undue delay on the part of authorities. In that connection, the court. held that there was no breach of the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time in the period after 17 September. 2004.

name: Ramazan Erkenov
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18152/11) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Mr Ramazan Erkenov (‘the applicant’), on 14 January 2011, was detained at the Gaziantep Foreigners’ Removal Centre. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the admissibility and merits of the application. The Russian Government, who were informed of their right to intervene under Article 36 of the. Convention, did not make use of this right. The application was declared inadmissible on 25 September 2014.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18152/11) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Russian Government, who were informed of their right to intervene under Article 36, did not make use of this right. On 25 September 2014 the applicant’s complaints under Article 3, Article 5 and Article 13 were communicated to the Government. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible, pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The application was lodged by a Russian national of Chechen origin, Mr Ramazan Erkenov, on 14 January 2011. The Russian authorities requested the extradition of the applicant. The Gaziantep Assize Court refused that request, holding that the offences in question were of a political nature and that alleged perpetrators of such offences could not be extradited. The applicant met with his lawyer a total of nine times between 3 March 2009 and 27 July 2010 during his detention. On 24 July 2010 the applicant was released on the condition that he leave Turkey within fifteen days. It appears that the applicant left Turkey shortly after his release. The application for asylum was rejected on 26 April 2010. The applications for asylum and a residence permit were also dismissed by the Ministry of the Interior on 10 June 2010.

name: Bayram Güçlü
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 31535/04) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented by Mr H. Dilek and Mr A. Sungurtekin, lawyers practising in Samsun. The Turkish Government (“the Government’s Agent”) were represented by their Agent. On 10 October 2011 the application was communicated to the Government. The case was dismissed on 12 September 2013. It was decided that the applicant was entitled to appeal against the decision of the Court.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1966 and is currently serving a prison sentence in Samsun. On 21 January 2002 the applicant was interrogated by the police at the Narcotics Branch of the Istanbul Security Directorate, in the absence of a lawyer. According to a form explaining arrested persons’ rights, which the applicant signed, he was informed of the charges against him and of his right to remain silent. On 10 October 2011 the application was communicated to the Government of the Republic of Turkey by the applicant's agent. On 22 January 2002 the applicant was taken before the investigating judge at the Istanbul State Security Court, who remanded him in custody. In the absence of a lawyer, the applicant denied the statements he had given to the police and maintained that he had been compelled to sign them without having read them. The court found the applicant guilty of trafficking cocaine and sentenced him to thirty-six years’ imprisonment. In convicting the applicant, it relied on his statements, the statements made by the other members of the criminal organisation, which had been taken during the proceedings against them, and forensics reports on the drugs that had been seized. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court.

name: Henryk Urban
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 23614/08) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that their case had not been heard by an “independent tribunal” The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 30 June 2009 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of theapplication at the same time as its admissibility (former Article 29 § 3 of the convention, now Article 29§ 1)
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that their case had not been heard by an ‘independent tribunal’ The applicants had been granted legal aid and were represented by a lawyer practising in Cracow. The Polish Government (“the Government’s” Agent) was represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility. The first applicant requested that the assessor (asesor sądowy) B. R.-G. withdraw from the case on the ground that she had not accepted a medical certificate excusing his mother from attending a hearing. On 24 September 2007 the Lesko District Court, sitting as a single judge, dismissed the first applicant's request as ill-founded. The applicants appealed. They objected, inter alia, to the fact that their case had been decided by an assessor, alleging that she was not a judge. They referred to the Constitutional Court's judgment of 24 October 2007 and submitted that she could not exercise judicial powers because she did not offer sufficient guarantees of independence.

name: Mustafa Abdi
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 27770/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented by Ms E. Norman of CLC Solicitors, a lawyer practising in London. The United Kingdom Government (the Government) were represented by their Agent, Mr D. Walton of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The application was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The case was decided to be heard by the Court of Appeal. The judge ruled that the applicant should not be expelled to Somalia pending the Court's decision.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 27770/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was convicted of offences of rape and indecency with a child and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. The application was communicated to the Government on 25 May 2009. On 7 December 2010 the Acting President of the Section to which the case was allocated decided to apply Rule 39 of the Rules of Court. The Court decided that it was desirable in the interests of the parties and the proper conduct of the proceedings that the applicant should not be expelled to Somalia pending the Court’s decision. The applicant had claimed to be a member of the Isaaq tribe, which comes from Somaliland, an autonomous region in north-west Somalia. He claimed that his parents were born in Hargeisa, although it was accepted that he was born in Mogadishu. As the applicant did not co-operate with the provision of bio-data, the Government decided that it would be preferable to remove him to Somalia. In November 2004 the applicant refused a formal request to sign such a disclaimer. In July 2006 the Government concluded an agreement with African Express Airlines which made enforced removals to Somalia possible. The first enforced removal to Somalia took place on 30 November 2006. In September 2006 the applicant was granted permission to apply for judicial review. Mr Justice Calvert-Smith ruled that the Secretary of State for the Home Department could only detain a person that he intended to deport for what amounted to a reasonable period. The period of detention from 3 December 2004, which was the date of the applicant’s first review following his refusal to return voluntarily, to 30 June 2006 was found to be unlawful because of its length, the impossibility during that period of achieving removal, and the misleading statements which had misled decision-makers both inside and outside the Home Dept. Both the applicant and the secretary of state were granted leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal. The applicant was issued with removal directions set for 29 November 2006 and sought leave to apply for judicial review of the removal directions. The applicant was granted permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal on 18 December 2009. The applicant remains in immigration detention pending removal. On 6 December 2010 the applicant was issued with removal directions to Somalia. The removal was to take place on 8 December 2010. The Court granted the applicant interim measures under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court to prevent his removal. The current application is only concerned with the first period of detention. 30 June 2006 should have been held to be unlawful. On 13 April 2007 the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal had ordered that he be released from detention on bail. He was released early the following week but was re-detained on 3 April 2008 after breaching his bail conditions. In April 2006 the Home Office introduced a ‘secret’ policy creating a presumption in favour of the detention of Foreign National Prisoners pending their deportation. The policy was not disclosed until mid-2008 and was not formally published until September 2008. The lawfulness of this policy was considered by the Supreme Court in the cases of Walumba Lumba and Kadian Mighty v. Secretary of State for the Home Department [2011] UKSC 12 (see paragraph 37, below) The Supreme Court ruled that the policy constituted a “near blanket ban” on release. The applicant was held from 3 September 2003 to 13 April 2007. During this period there were monthly reviews of the applicant’s detention. The reviews were carried out in November 2003, March 2004, June 2004, September 2004, October 2004 and November 2004.

name: Richard Roy Allan
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained of the use of covert audio and video surveillance within his cell, the prison visiting area and upon a fellow prisoner. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. By a decision of 28 August 2001, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1).
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 48539/99) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained of the use of covert audio and video surveillance within his cell, the prison visiting area and upon a fellow prisoner. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. The applicant and Leroy Grant appeared in custody at the Stockport Magistrates' Court. An anonymous informant told the police that the applicant had been involved in the murder of David Beesley. On 20 February 1995 Detective Chief Inspector Dunn requested permission for the cell and the visiting areas used by the applicant and Grant to be bugged with audio and video technology. The applicant was invited to comment on the recordings made in February and March 1995. He made no comment to any question. According to the applicant, he was interrogated by the police concerning the Kwik-Save robbery. The police told the applicant that he was not obliged to say anything. He availed himself of that right. H. had been fitted with recording devices. H.'s evidence was the assertion that the applicant had admitted his presence at the murder scene. This asserted admission was not part of the recorded interview and was disputed. The thrust of the applicant's case was that he was discussing robberies and did not accede to H.’s efforts to channel their conversation into a discussion of the murder. No evidence, other than the alleged admissions, connected the applicant with the killing of Mr Beesley. The judge concluded that there was evidence on the tapes from which the jury could infer that the. applicant was involved in the events of 3 February 1995, and it was not so unreliable that it could not be left to the jury to assess for themselves. The judge's ruling on the admissibility of the evidence was given on 26 January 1998, after a voir dire (submissions on a point of law in the absence of a jury) The trial judge gave directions on the way in which the jury should assess the reliability of the disputed evidence. He told them that they were to judge whether the police had deliberately wound up the applicant during the interview on 28 June 1995 and how to approach the evidence put forward by H. The prosecution say the contents of the tapes of 28 June can be relied on and are consistent with what H. says [the applicant] had said to him previously. The defence say if you consider the whole picture you simply cannot rely upon H. The applicant was convicted of murder before the Crown Court at Manchester by a majority of ten to two and sentenced to life imprisonment. The applicant lodged a notice of appeal, asserting that the judge ought to have excluded evidence of the audio- and video-recordings of his conversations with Leroy Grant and J.N. and the evidence put forward by H.S. His renewed application was refused by the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) on 18 January 1999, after a hearing at which he was represented by leading counsel. In the court's judgment of that date, Lord Justice Rose found that the trial judge gave a very careful and impeccable ruling as regards the admissibility of the tapes and evidence.

name: Velimir Janosevic
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his rights under Article 6 of the Convention had been violated. The Court heard addresses by Mr Thörnhammar and Ms Kalmerborn. By a decision of 26 September 2000, following the hearing, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The case was then heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 26September 2000. The application was transferred to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol no. 11). The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1).
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 34619/97) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his rights under Article 6 of the Convention had been violated as the Tax Authority's decisions on taxes and tax surcharges had been enforced prior to a court determination of the dispute. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 26 September 2000. Following the hearing, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The Court heard addresses by Mr Thörnhammar and Ms Kalmerborn. Tax Authority increased the applicant's liability to income tax by 286,859 Swedish kronor (SEK) The additional taxes levied on the applicant, including interest and surcharges, totalled SEK 1,020,300, of which SEK 161,261 were surcharges. The amounts relating to value-added tax and employer's contributions were payable on 5 January 1996 and those relating to incomeTax on 10 April 1996. The Tax Authority considers that the prerequisites laid down in section 49, subsection 1(2) or (3), of the Tax Collection Act [Uppbördslagen, 1953:272] for granting a stay of execution have been fulfilled. Tax Authority: "The applicant's ability to pay is open to serious doubt" The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Stockholm, claiming that he should be exempted from the obligation to provide security and granted a stay of execution. The Appeals Court upheld the Tax Authority's decisions of 21 May 1996. The applicant lodged a notice of appeal. On 21 May 1997 the Administrative Court of Appeal in Stockholm refused him leave to appeal against the Court's judgments. The Supreme Administrative Court refused to grant leave to appealed against the Appeals Court's decisions on 3 November 1998. The Appeal Court's decision was upheld on 11 July 1996. The applicant's tax liability as of 22 March 1996 amounted to SEK 653,144, including penalties for late payment (dröjsmålsavgifter) that had accrued since the final date on which payment could have been made. The only property owned by the applicant was some vehicles, but of insufficient value to cover the debt. The applicant appealed to the Svea Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt), claiming, inter alia, that the District Court's decision amounted to a violation of Article 6 of the Convention. Leave to appeal against the appellate court's decision was refused by the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) The whole debt became statute-barred on 31 December 2001, at the end of the fifth year following the day it became due. The applicant was sentenced by the District Court to ten months' imprisonment for tax fraud (skattebedrägeri) and a bookkeeping offence (bokföringsbrott) The judgment was upheld by the Court of Appeal on 16 November 1998. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused on 4 March 1999. Further proceedings concerning the taxes and tax surcharges concerning the applicant were referred to the County Administrative Court for determination in 2000. By a letter of 5 September 2001 the applicant requested an oral hearing at which it was proposed that certain witnesses would give evidence. The County Administrative Court upheld the Tax Authority's decisions of 22 and 27 December 1995. Administrative Court informed the applicant that it did not find a hearing necessary and ordered him to make his final observations in the case in writing. The applicant has appealed to the Administrative Court of Appeal, where the dispute is at present pending. The Court made extensive references to the judgments. of the Supreme Court of 29 November 2000 and the Supreme Administrative Court. of 15 December 2000 (see paragraphs 51-55 below) and concluded that the Swedish provisions on tax surcharges were in conformity with the Convention. It considered that there had been sufficient reasons to impose the surcharges in question and that no legal basis for remitting them had been shown.

name: Joseph Keegan
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 7 April 1993. It originated in an application (no. 16969/90) against Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 1 May 1990. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr B. Walsh, the elected judge of Irish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 7 April 1993. It originated in an application (no. 16969/90) against Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 1 May 1990 by an Irish citizen, Mr Joseph Keegan. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6, 8 and/or 14. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 November 1993. The Registrar consulted the Agent of the Government, the applicant’s lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the procedure (Rules 37 para. 1 and 38). The Court heard addresses by Sir Basil Hall, Ms Browne and Mr Gleeson as well as replies to questions put by several of its members. The proceedings before the Circuit Court were described as follows:. The applicant met his girlfriend Miss V. (‘V’) in May 1986 and they lived together from February 1987 until February 1988. Around Christmas 1987 they decided to have a child. On 22 February 1988 it was confirmed that V. was pregnant. On 29 September 1988 V. gave birth to a daughter S. of whom the applicant was the father. On 17 November 1988 she had the child placed by a registered adoption society with the prospective adopters. The applicant applied to be appointed guardian under section 6A, sub-section 1, of the Guardianship of Infants Act 1964. He also applied for custody of the child. While a married man is a guardian of his children, an unmarried man is not unless so appointed by the court. On 29 May 1989 the Circuit Court appointed the applicant guardian and awarded him custody. The High Court found in July 1989 that the applicant was a fit person to beappointed guardian and that there were no circumstances involving the child which required that the father’s rights be denied. Mr Justice Barron acceded to an application by V. and the prospective adopters to state a case for the opinion of the Supreme Court. Chief Justice Finlay said the High Court had incorrectly construed section 6A of the 1964 Act. He considered that the Act only gave the natural father a right to apply to be guardian. It did not equate his position with that of a married father, he said. The first and paramount consideration in the exercise of the court’s discretion was the welfare of the child, and the blood link between child and father as merely one of the many relevant factors which may be viewed by the court as relevant to that question. He concluded that: “... regard should not be had to the objective of satisfying the wishes and desires of the father to be involved in the guardianship of. High Court resumed its examination of the case in early 1990. It heard evidence of a consultant child psychiatrist who considered that the child would suffer short-term trauma if moved to the applicant’s custody. The matter was then referred back to the High Court for the case to be decided in light of this interpretation. Mr Justice Barron recalled that the applicant wished bona fide to have custody of his daughter and that he felt the existence of an emotional bond. He had also noted that if the child remained with the adopters she would obtain the benefit of a higher standard of living and would be likely to remain at school longer. However, he considered that differences springing solely from socio-economic causes should not be taken into account where one of the claimants is a natural parent. An adoption order was subsequently made in respect of the child. The father's wish and desire to be involved in the guardianship of and to enjoy the society of his child is not a factor which I am to take into account. In these circumstances, the welfare of the infant requires her to remain in her present custody. Accordingly the application for relief must be refused.“The quality of welfare likely to be. achieved with the prospective adopters would not be to an important extent better than that likely to. be achieved by custody with the father. enumerated.” “I cannot hold that the quality of. welfare would be better than the one achieved by the father,” said the judge.

name: Allan Jacobsson
train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr Allan Jacobsson, a Swedish citizen, on 11 January 1984. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 of the Convention and to the declaration whereby Sweden recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Article 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr G. Lagergren, the elected judge of Swedish nationality (Article 43) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the court (Rule 21 para. 3)
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 18 December 1987. It originated in an application (no. 10842/84) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr Allan Jacobsson, a Swedish citizen, on 11 January 1984. The Commission sought a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6, 13, 17 and 18. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr G. Lagergren, the elected judge of Swedish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The Government's memorial and the applicant's memorial were received by the registry on 2 and 9 May 1988, respectively. The President directed on 21 February 1989 that the oral proceedings should commence on 24 May 1989 (Rule 38) The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr Corell for the Government and Mr Gaukur Jörundsson for the Commission and Mr Tullberg, Mr Petrén and Mr Magnusson for the applicant as well as their replies to its questions. The applicant bought a property of 2,644 m², Salem 23:1, in the centre of Rönninge in the municipality of Salem. The first building prohibition under section 35 of the 1947 Act covering the applicant’s property was issued by the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen, ‘the Board’) of the Stockholm County on 21 September 1965. The last decision was taken on 11 July 1985 and was valid until 11 July 1987. On 1 July 1987, with the entry into force of the Plan and Building Act 1987 (Plan - och Bygglagen, “the 1987 Act’), the existing system for prohibitions on construction was abolished and replaced by a new one (see paragraphs 44-45 below). The applicant turned to the Board and requested that the municipality be ordered to adopt a town plan (stadsplan) for the central parts of Rönninge. On 28 June 1979 the Municipal Assembly (kommunfullmäktige) adopted a master plan (generalplan) relating to part of the municipality of Botkyrka. According to the plan, the applicant’s property was supposed to be used for building blocks of flats of more than two storeys. On 15 January 1980 the Building Committee stated, in reply to a request from the applicant, that it was not prepared to grant him an exemption from the building prohibition or a permit to build a one-family house and a garage on the property. The Board rejected the appeal on 25 April 1980. In April 1983 the Board requested the Board to revoke, pursuant to section 168 of the 1947 Act, the right to build according to the subdivision plan. The applicant's property is situated in an area that should be used for the construction of multi-family houses in 1988. The Government rejected the applicant's appeal on 15 December 1983. The applicant appealed to the Board, arguing inter alia that the building prohibition covering his property had ceased to be effective on 6 June 1984. In a decision of 21 August 1984, the Building Committee conceded that a mistake had been made and quashed its decision of 12 June; however, it took a new decision of similar content since a new building prohibition was valid as from 11 July 1984. On 24 April 1986 the Government quashed the Board’s decision, holding that the Committee’'s opinion was not a binding decision and that it could not as such be subject to an appeal. On 10 July 1987 the applicant again filed a request for a preliminary opinion regarding a building permit for his property. The Building Committee decided however, pursuant to the rules laid down in the new 1987 Act, to defer its decision for a period of two years. The validity of the subdivision plan (see paragraph 8 above) remained unaffected. This plan mentioned the possibility of using the area for single or multi-family house development. According to the Government, this is the last step of the preparatory work in the making of a town plan. The building committee decided to defer the decision on the request for two years (see. paragraph 45 below).

name: Steven Phillips
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 41087/98) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, inter alia, that the statutory assumption made against him by the court which issued a confiscation order violated his right to the presumption of innocence. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) It was declared partly admissible on 30 November 2000 [Note by the Registry. The Court’s decision is obtainable from the Registry]. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 8 February 2001.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, inter alia, that the statutory assumption made against him by the court which issued a confiscation order following his conviction for a drug offence violated his right to the presumption of innocence. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 of the Rules of Court) and was declared partly admissible on 30 November 2000. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 8 February 2001. Phillip Phillips was sentenced to nine years' imprisonment in July 1996. He had previously been convicted of a drug-related offence. An inquiry was conducted into the applicant’s means, pursuant to section 2 of the Drug Trafficking Act 1994 (‘the 1994 Act’ – see below) The investigation officer concluded that the applicant had benefited from drug trafficking and that the total benefit was GBP 117,838.27. The applicant was found to have become a director of a newsagents business in July 1992 of which his parents were the sole shareholders. He was the registered owner of five cars, of an estimated total value of approximately GBP 15,000, and spent GBP 2,000 on a BMW 520i in October 1995. The applicant was convicted of car theft and required to pay GBP 25,000 to the insurance company which had indemnified the victims. He claimed that he had sold the house for GBP 50,000 in order to clear this debt and had used the GBP 12,000 residue from the sale to purchase the newsagents premises for his parents because he owed them money too. When he was released from prison in April 1994 he began trading in telephones. This was the source of the GBF 17,000 he had in his building society account. He denied owning any of the cars registered in his name, claiming variously that each had been purchased and sold on behalf of a friend or stolen without insurance. The judge found the prosecution’s allegation that the applicant still owned the house to be correct. The judge held that X's purported purchase payment of GBP 50,000 had in fact been a benefit of drug trafficking. ‘No sensible explanation for the involvement of [X] in that cashing of that cheque was given to me at all, and it is not sensible. Just as the jury did not believe Mr Phillips, neither do I. What has happened here, in my judgment, is a device of just the sort providing a cover to explain the transfer of money which one would expect to find in concealing benefit from drug trafficking,’ the judge said. The judge said he found it. impossible, in his judgment, to see any sensible reason. other than that he did not cash a cheque; that it was a simple payment. The judge also said that he found the purchase of a share of a business for GBP 50,000 entirely without documentation ‘unbelievable’ and a device to conceal the true reason for the payment by [X] to the accused of GBP 28,000. ‘I think family loyalty has overcome his honesty,’ the judge said. “I am satisfied that the GBP 11,400 must be treated as a benefit.” ‘I am satisfied that the GBP 50,000 which he said in evidence was what such a property was worth in 1992, that is to say during the long, flat period’ ‘There is no evidence that it is worth any less now, and I therefore find his realisable share in the equity in that business to be worth GBP50,000.’ In view of the difficulties inherent in realising the applicant’s share of the family business, the judge allowed him three years in which to pay the confiscation order, with a period of two years’ imprisonment to be served in default of payment. ‘I find the amount to be recovered to be that figure’

name: Rolf Gustafson
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 18 December 1995 by the applicant, Mr Rolf Gustafson, a Swedish national. The applicant’s application bringing the case before the Court referred to Article 48 of the Convention (art. 48), as amended by Protocol No. 9 (P9), which has been ratified by Sweden. The object of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mrs E. Palm, the elected judge of Swedish nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 18 December 1995 by the applicant, Mr Rolf Gustafson, a Swedish national. The applicant’s application bringing the case before the Court referred to Article 48 of the Convention (art. 48), as amended by Protocol No. 9 (P9), which has been ratified by Sweden. On 27 April 1996, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members of the Chamber. The applicant claims that on two occasions, in April-June and June‑July 1991, he was the victim of kidnapping and extortion perpetrated by three persons. According to the applicant, one of the alleged perpetrators, a certain Mr L., had wanted to be paid for the part he played with him in the commission of certain economic crimes. The applicant requested the court, pursuant to the provisions of chapter 22 of the Code of Judicial Procedure (Rättegångsbalken: see paragraph 20 below), to order L. to pay him a total of 169,350 Swedish kronor (SEK) in compensation in respect of the following items: (a) material damages to his clothes; (b) SEK 10,000 in non-pecuniary damages. The applicant applied for compensation to the Criminal Damage Compensation Board (Brottsskadenämnden - hereinafter “the Board’) under the Criminal damaged Act 1978. In his application he stated that he had sought compensation for personal injury in the amount of SEK 160,000 in the proceedings against L. The Stockholm District Court convicted L., sentenced him to six years’ imprisonment and ordered him to pay SEK 144,350 in damages to the applicant. The Court of Appeal found that the applicant, in view of his criminal background, could not be deemed a trustworthy person. It followed that the information he had provided on the events which had given rise to his kidnapping and extortion were untrue. On 26 August 1993 the Board rejected the applicant’s compensation claim, stating: “A condition for a grant of compensation is that damage has in fact been caused by crime. The Board ... cannot find it established that [the applicant] has suffered damage as a result of crime. Consequently, compensation for damage caused byCrime cannot be awarded.“ On 11 November 1993 the applicant requested the Board to reconsider its decision. He argued that it was clear from the judgments of the District Court and the Court of Appeal that he had been the victim of a crime and had suffered the damage for which he requested compensation. He did not seek leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) against the decision. Inspector S. had been the principal investigator into the economic offences of which the applicant had previously been convicted. He had interrogated both the applicant and L. on a number of occasions. Inspector S. told the District Court, inter alia: “I was, probably on 4 July 1991, informed [about the alleged kidnapping of the applicant]. A colleague ... telephoned me to say that he had been informed that [the applicant] had been kidnapped ..., that the kidnapping had been staged by [L.] with the help of two ‘gorillas’, ... and that the kidnap had been combined with an extortion threat against [ the applicant] in the amount of SEK 5 million” On 1 June 1994 the Board rejected the applicant’s request, for the following reasons: “The submissions in this case in support of the request for reconsideration are not such as to be a reason for the Board to change its previous decision. Nor is there any other reason for changing the decision.” ‘He had more or less repeated the same evidence he gave to the District Court.’ ‘There was no reason to change the previous decision.' ‘The applicant had not given any further evidence that would support his request for a reconsideration’. ‘. He had given no further evidence than he had given in the previous case.‘.

Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis (No. 2), [1979] 2 All England Law Reports 620; also reported at [ 1979] 2 Weekly Law Reports 700. It emerged that details of a telephone conversation to which Mr. Malone had been a party prior to 22 March 1977 were contained in the note-book of the police officer in charge of the investigations. The evidence against the applicant consisted of detailed oral admissions that he had allegedly made to the police concerning his involvement in the three offences. The jury’s decision was by a majority verdict of ten to two. He received a sentence of ten years for the robbery, and two sentences of eight years each for the burglary offences. All three sentences were to be served concurrently. Leave to appeal against the sentence was granted by a single judge of the Court of Appeal on 5 February 1985. On 21 May 1985 the substantive appeal against sentence was dismissed by the full court. In February 1986, the Director of Public Prosecutions decided that there was insufficient evidence to support criminal charges against three police officers. At the disciplinary hearing, on 13 to 15 June 1988, the tribunal decided there was no case to answer and dismissed the charges. An independent police investigation was ordered in the course of which certain facts came to the attention of the police. The report was requested by the Home Department but its disclosure was refused on the grounds of public interest immunity. The applicant submitted to the Court of Appeal that the verdict should be set aside as unsafe and unsatisfactory because of certain shortcomings in the prosecution case, in particular, that certain information had been withheld by the police. At the trial one of the police witnesses had stated under cross-examination that no fingerprints were found at the scene of the crime. In fact two fingerprints had been found which later turned out to be those of the next door neighbour who was a regular visitor to the house. The applicant had not been informed of this by the prosecution before his trial. A further shortcoming complained of by the applicant related to the fact that the police had shown two volumes of photographs of possible burglars (including a photograph of the applicant) to the elderly victim of the robbery. Court of Appeal examined other impugned shortcomings which it did not consider to cast any doubt on the verdict. Court concluded that there was some slipshod police work in the present case, no doubt because they took the view that here was a man who had admitted these crimes fully, and consequently there was very little need for them to indulge in a further verification of whether what he said was true. Although this is a matter which perhaps casts the police in a somewhat lazy or idle light, we do not think in the circumstances there was anything unsafe or unsatisfactory in the end about these convictions. Consequently, treating this matter as we have to according to section 17 of the Act, we think this appeal fails and must be dismissed.

The case was heard by the Court of Appeal (Högsta domstolen) on 9 November 2010. The Enforcement Authority contacted the applicant in order to plan the sale of the attached sawmill. In his reply a few days later, the applicant stated that he had removed the sawmill from his property and hidden it. The Authority also handed the applicant a summons for questioning on its premises. On 17 May 2010 the Enforcement Authority requested the District Court to detain the applicant because he had refused to cooperate and give the required information. On 27 May 2010, after having held an oral hearing, the Court held a hearing and ordered the applicant to return the saw mill to the Authority. The sawmill was returned to its owner on 28 May 2010. The Court of Appeal found that there were extraordinary reasons to detain the applicant and that detention was proportionate to the aim pursued. The Enforcement Authority appealed to the Court of appeal, maintaining its claims and adding that, according to the preparatory works of the Enforcement Code, it was only necessary that the debtor had received an injunction but refused to comply with it. It further submitted that having regard to the applicant’s stance on the matter, the imposition of a conditional fine would most likely have no effect. Lastly, the Authority stated that it had reported the applicant to the police on the ground that he had committed a breach of an official order when he had removed and hidden the sawmill. The Court of Appeal held an oral hearing on 30 June 2010 and decided to maintain its earlier decision. On 13 July 2010 the District Court reviewed the applicant’s detention and held a new hearing in the case. The Enforcement Authority maintained that the applicant should be kept in detention since he still had not given any information about the location of the sawmill. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal since a new decision had already been taken by the District court at that time. The applicant appealed to the Court of appeal which, on 20 July 2010, rejected the appeal. The appeal was dismissed on 23 July 2010 and the applicant was detained. The District Court found that continued detention of the applicant would be disproportionate to the measures he had taken. The Enforcement Authority appealed to the Court of Appeal which, on 13 August 2010, rejected the appeal. The Supreme Court dismissed the Enforcement Authority’s further appeal and consequently, on 23 September 2010, the District Court struck the case out of its list of cases as the case was closed. On 26 April 2012 the applicant submitted a claim for damages to the Chancellor of Justice (Justitiekanslern), pursuant to the Act on Compensation for Deprivation of Liberty and Other Coercive Measures (Lagen om ersättning vid frihetsberövande och andra tvångsåtgärder, 1998:714), in the amount of SE. The applicant had sought compensation for the suffering he had endured during the 42 days he was deprived of his liberty. He also demanded to be reimbursed SEK 2,940 for costs which had been deducted from his pension during his time in detention. On 15 October 2012 the Chancellor of Justice rejected the claim. The Chancellor noted that the decision to detain the applicant had been taken by a court of law, in accordance with relevant legal provisions. The examination of the case showed no basis for finding that the. decision had been made on erroneous grounds and therefore was incorrect, the Chancellor said. He added that it was incorrect to think the decision was taken on an erroneous basis and therefore the claim was incorrect.
