On 29 May 2001 it was declared admissible by a Chamber of that Section, composed of the following judges: Mr J.-P. Costa, President, Mr W. Fuhrmann, Mr P. Kūris, Mrs F. Tulkens, Mr K. Jungwiert, Sir Nicolas Bratza and Mr. Traja. The applicant was convicted of murder in 1967. He was released on licence in April 1979. His licence required him to cooperate with his probation officer and to remain in the United Kingdom. In September 1980 his licence was revoked and thereafter he was continuously ‘unlawfully at large’ In April 1989 he returned from South Africa in possession of a false passport. He remained in custody, however, due to the revocation of the life licence. In July 1993 he was arrested and remanded in custody on counterfeiting charges. On 19 July 1994 he was convicted on two counts of conspiracy to forge travellers' cheques and passports and sentenced to six years' imprisonment. In 1996 the Parole Board conducted a formal review of the applicant's case and recommended his release on life licence. In 1997 the Secretary of State rejected the Board's recommendation in the following terms. The applicant was granted leave to seek judicial review. On 1 July 1997, but for the revocation of his life licence, the applicant would have been released from prison on the expiry of the sentence for fraud, pursuant to provisions whereby prisoners serving determinate sentences of more than more than 10 years are eligible for release. On 10 June 1997 the applicant was given leave to appeal the decision. The application was successful on the grounds that the conditions of his licence had been breached and he was entitled to a full review. The applicant is now serving the equivalent of a determinate sentence of about five years, albeit in open conditions. This term has not been imposed on him by way of punishment, because he has already served the punitive terms which his previous, very serious, offences have been thought to merit. The term has been imposed because he is thought to present danger to the public, because that is not suggested. It is not submitted that the term imposed bears any relation to the gravity of any future imprisonable offence which the applicant might commit. The imposition of what is in effect a substantial term of imprisonment by the exercise of executive discretion, without trial, lies uneasily with ordinary concepts of the rule of law.” The House of Lords dismissed the applicant's appeal against the Court of Appeal's decision. In his speech, Lord Steyn held that section 35(2) of the 1991 Act conferred a wide administrative discretion on the Secretary of State to decide upon the release on licence of mandatory life prisoners. Lord Buxton, concurring with the latter remarks, added: “The category of imprisonable offence is extremely wide, and can encompass many matters that are wholly unrelated, both in nature and seriousness, to the reasons for the life sentence prisoner being within the power of the State in the first place’” On 16 December 1997 the applicant was moved to open conditions. The applicant was released on licence on 22 December 1998.

name: Joe Anthony Ashendon
train_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the refusal to award them their defence costs, after they had been acquitted in their respective criminal proceedings, was in violation of Article 6 § 2 of the convention. On 23 April 2008 and 2 October 2009 respectively, the Vice-President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to give notice of the applications and to communicate the complaints to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of each application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicants and the Government each filed written observations.
eval_texts: The case originated in two applications (nos. 35730/07 and 4285/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the refusal to award them their defence costs, after they had been acquitted in their respective criminal proceedings, was in violation of Article 6 § 2 of the convention. It was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of each application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The applicants and the Government each filed written observations (Rule 59 § 1). The Court ruled in favour of the first applicant. The first applicant was charged with burglary, rape (by penile penetration), and sexual assault. The prosecution offered no evidence in respect of the burglary charge and a not guilty verdict was recorded. The trial judge’s summing up to the jury contained the following direction: “We all know this is a horrific, a disgusting episode. We all know that, and we all know – there has not been any argument about this, has there? – where moral responsibility lies. ... We are not here to dish out admonitions for immoral conduct, disgusting behaviour. We are here to judge whether a crime has been committed, whether the criminal law of the land has been broken.” The jury acquitted the applicant of the three remaining charges. When the first applicant applied for his costs (which exceeded GBP 100,000 and had been met by his family) his counsel stated: “This is a case in which [the first applicant] was inevitably going to be charged with a criminal offence” In refusing the application, the trial judge said: ‘With regard to a defendant’s costs you [Counsel] are right, the costs should and almost invariably would follow the event. I cannot think of another case in my 35 years’ experience in the criminal courts in which it is more apparent’ The second woman was arrested in 2006 for allegedly conspiring to steal from a company. A tape of a conversation she had with a co-worker was played to the court. The second woman claimed that she did not know what was on the tape or when it was recorded. The case was eventually settled out of court with no admission of wrongdoing on the part of the second woman or her co-defendants. The third woman was acquitted of all charges, but was given a retrial on the same charges, which was dismissed on appeal. The fourth woman was sentenced to four years in prison for her part in the conspiracy. The fifth woman was found not guilty of any of the charges against her. Second applicant was acquitted unanimously of the two counts facing her. Three defendants, including A.R. and C.R., were convicted of the majority of the charges against them. The trial judge refused the application for a defendant’s costs order, pursuant to section 16(2) of the Prosecution of Offences Act 1985 (see relevant domestic law and practice below) He stated: ‘The relevant features, in my judgment, in this case are these: that [the second applicant], acting very much on the advice of her then solicitor [name omitted], exercised her right to silence when answering ‘no comment’ in her police interview’ The trial judge declined to hold an oral hearing on the renewed application and stated that he was unable to make the order for the reasons he had already given. The second applicant renewed her application in writing, relying inter alia on the fact the she had been unable to recall the conversation on the tape recording until the trial had started. In my judgment that is a proper reason for refusing a defendant’s costs order. In no way is that decision meant to indicate that she is in any way guilty of this offence, she is not, she has rightly been acquitted by this jury.” The trial judge concluded by saying that the second applicant's failure to put the phone call into its true context clearly influenced the prosecution decision to bring charges.

name: Carl G. Holm
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 11 December 1992 by the European Commission of Human Rights and on 15 February 1993 by the Government of the Kingdom of Sweden. It originated in an application (no. 14191/88) against Sweden lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Swedish national, Mr Carl G. Holm, on 24 January 1987. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mrs E. Palm, the elected judge of Swedish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 11 December 1992 by the European Commission of Human Rights and on 15 February 1993 by the Government of the Kingdom of Sweden. The object of the request and of the Government’s application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mrs E. Palm, the elected judge of Swedish nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b) The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 June 1993. The Court heard addresses by Mr Ehrenkrona, Mr Gaukur Jörundsson, Mr Malmlöf and the applicant himself. The applicant formed together with others a foundation named Contra. in 1974. According to him its aim was to scrutinise governments of communist regimes in Eastern Europe and the Swedish Social Democratic Workers Party (Sveriges socialdemokratiska arbetareparti - the “SAP’) The author of the book, Mr Sven Ove Hansson, was then employed by the publisher and had previously served as an ideological adviser to the SAP. The applicant brought a private prosecution for aggravated libel (grovt förtal) against Mr Hansson in the District Court (tingsrätten) of Stockholm. In the same proceedings he sued both the author and the publisher for damages, claiming 200,000 Swedish kronor. He contended that the book contained allegations implying that he belonged to certain nazi and fascist groups, calculated to cast doubt on his honour and to expose him to contempt. The impugned passages of the book included allegations which can be summarised as follows: (a) in 1973 the applicant had chaired the youth section of the World Anti-Communist League’s Conference in London, an organisation whose membership was said to consist largely of neo-nazis. A jury was asked to consider whether a criminal offence had been committed. The jury was composed on the basis of a list of two groups of names. The list indicated the jurors’ political affiliations. The first group comprised sixteen persons, seven of whom were members of the SAP, five of the Conservative Party, two of the Liberal Party, and one of the Communist Party. The second group included eight names, of whom four wereMembers of The Social Democratic Party (SAP), two of The Conservative Party and two of The Liberal Party. The applicant, referring to paragraph 9 of Article 13 in Chapter 4 of the Code of Judicial Procedure (rättegångsbalken), filed a complaint with the District Court under Chapter 12, section 8, of the Freedom of the Press Act. The contents of the book were of a political nature and that the case had political undertones. The applicant and the defence each rejected three jurors from the first group and one from the second group. Those eliminated by the applicant were all SAP members and those by the defendants were members of the Conservative Party. The jury had replied in the negative to the questions put to it concerning the alleged unlawfulness of the impugned passages. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 4 December 1986, without stating any reasons. It was not open to the applicant to appeal further against this decision (Chapter 12, section 8, of the Freedom of the Press Act)

name: Tommaso Cuscani
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32771/96) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he did not receive a fair trial on account of the absence of interpretation at his hearing on sentencing. The application was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court, which declared it admissible on 26 June 2001. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The applicant, but not the Government, filed observations on the merit of the case. The case was heard by a Chamber that would consider the case according to Rule 26 of the Rules of Court.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32771/96) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he did not receive a fair trial on account of the absence of interpretation at his hearing on sentencing. The application was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court, which declared it admissible on 26 June 2001. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The case was settled in the High Court of Justice of the Republic of Ireland on 1 August 2012. The case will be heard at a later date. The applicant was granted legal aid on 1 March 1995. The legal aid order covered both the committal hearings and the actual trial. The applicant was represented throughout the proceedings by a Queen's Counsel (“QC”), who was also a Recorder, a very experienced junior counsel and two different firms of solicitors. At the trial on 4 January 1996, the applicant, on the advice of counsel, changed his plea to guilty. The court was informed that the applicant disagreed on the quantum of the sums which formed the basis of the plea. He was also indicted on another count of cheating the public revenue and pleaded guilty to that charge too. The applicant was convicted of fraud and sentenced to four years' imprisonment. He appealed to the Court of Appeal Criminal Division seeking leave to appeal against sentence. The applicant did not maintain in his application that he had been unable to understand the proceedings at the trial or to communicate effectively in court. In his application, the applicant was represented by the same legal team that had defended him at trial. The judge asked whether anyone in court who was fluent in both English and Italian could provide interpretation for the applicant. The court agreed to make use of the applicant's brother, but he was never requested to translate any statement during the course of the hearing. Leave to appeal was refused by the Single Judge on 3 May 1996 and by the full Court of Appeal on 15 July 1996. On 2 September 1996 the applicant sought advice from the President of the Law Society on what action to take against his defence lawyers. He wrote to the Home Secretary, admitting that he had not declared GBP 2,000 per week for staff wages due to the recession, and claiming that the real amount of the fraud was GBP 140,000 and not GBP 800,000. He further complained that his counsel had failed to secure him the services of an interpreter at the trial on 26 January 1996 and that this was of “paramount importance” for the purposes of the plea in mitigation. Commission accepted that the applicant would have been able to understand the generality of the prosecution case, but expressed the view that an interpreter ought to have been present when the case was explained to the applicant by his own representatives. Commission found that too little time had been spent by the applicant's lawyers explaining the case to him. Commission concluded that there were grounds for finding that the plea was uninformed, partly because of his inadequate understanding of the language, and because of the inadequate explanation of the case given to him by his legal representatives. However, the Court of Appeal no longer had the power to allow an appeal against conviction if it did not think the conviction was unsafe.

name: Ingrid Ullrich
train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 66956/01) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Court decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings on 6 May 2003. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The Austrian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Winkler, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Ingrid Ullrich, an Austrian national, filed the application on 12 October 1999.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 66956/01) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the welding work had soiled stored clothes and the salesroom of her boutique and had affected her health. The Austrian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Winkler, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Court decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant applied for damages as regards injuries to her health. She was granted legal aid on 4 March 1999. On 20 April 1999 the court withdrew the legal aid granted to her. On 18 May 1999 the Salzburg Regional Court imposed a fine on the applicant for abuse of process. On 7 March 2000 the Linz Court of Appeal confirmed this decision. On 31 August 2000, upon the parties’ requests, the court appointed two further experts. On 11 December 2000 both of the experts delivered their reports. On 9 February 2001 the court, presided over by another judge, held another hearing and heard and heard the case again. In March 2001 the applicant requested the court to hear another witness. The court adjourned the proceedings sine die in order to obtain an opinion of another expert. During this hearing the applicant’s counsel declared that he would inform the court of the outcome of friendly settlement discussions within four weeks. In the meantime, on 31 August 2001, the defendant's counsel had informed the applicant's counsel that the defendant did not agree with their proposal for a friendly settlement. The applicant's claim had become time-barred as the applicant had not duly continued the proceedings after friendly settlement negotiations had failed in August 2001. On 21 January 2003 and on 25 April 2003 the court held further hearings. On 14 October 2003 the Vienna Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal.

name: Darren Omoregie
train_texts: The case originated in an applications (nos. 265/07) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the decision to expel the first applicant to Nigeria with a prohibition of re-entry into Norway for a period of five years constituted a violation of Article 8. By a decision of 22 November 2007, the Court declared the application admissible.The applicants and the Government each filed further written observations (Rule 59 § 1). The applicants were represented by Mr A. Humlen, a lawyer practising in Oslo. The Government was represented by their Agent, Mrs F. Platou Amble.
eval_texts: The case originated in an applications (nos. 265/07) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the decision to expel the first applicant to Nigeria with a prohibition of re-entry into Norway for a period of five years constituted a violation of Article 8 of the convention. By a decision of 22 November 2007, the Court declared the application admissible. The application was brought by Mr Louis Osaze Darren Omoregie, a Nigerian national; Mrs Elisabeth Skundberg Darren, a Norwegian national; and their daughter Selma. The first applicant applied for a work permit on the ground of family reunification. The Directorate of Immigration rejected the application on 26 April 2003 and ordered him to leave Norway. On 14 May 2003 the first applicant again appealed and requested stay of execution. Local police notified him thereof on 19 October 2003 with an order to leave the country by 30 October 2003. The first and second applicants got married on 2 February 2003. No judicial appeal was lodged against the above decisions, which became final on 30 September 2002. B. Administrative sanction for failure to leave Sweden and ensuing judicial proceedings. C. A. The decision was announced on 30 October 2002 and the application was submitted to the Immigration Appeals Board on 1 October 2002. D. The appeal was dismissed on 7 October 2002, and the applicant was expelled.  Directorate of Immigration warned him that it was contemplating to expel him pursuant to section 29(1)(a) of the Immigration Act. The Directorate considered that he had seriously contravened the provisions of the Act and had evaded implementation of the order to leave the country. The Oslo City Court quashed the Immigration Appeals Board's decision of 21 July 2004 as being invalid. It found that the applicant's alleged ignorance of the unlawfulness of his gainful occupation was no excuse. It decided to prohibit the first applicant from re-entry into Norway for five years, with a possibility of re- entry on application - normally only after two years. It also dismissed his appeal against the Directorate's rejection of his application for a work permit. The High Court found it established that the applicant had stayed lawfully in Norway from 25 August 2001 to 30 September 2002. It was undisputed that his stay was unlawful from 30 September or 1 October 2002 until 14 February 2003 when he applied for family reunification. The first applicant disputed that he had evaded a decision to leave the country and had only omitted to voluntarily comply with the decision. However, the High Court considered that also such an omission constituted evasion for the purposes of the act, although it was less serious than going under ground. Even if the first applicant could apply for re-entry after two years, he would most probably only be granted permission to come for shorter visits. The High Court observed that the central issue was the one of proportionality. It noted that the first applicant's links to Norway were very limited. At the time of the impugned decision he had lived there for less than three years, parts of the time unlawfully. Already after less than two years he had been warned of expulsion. His stay in Norway had been very short and could not have given him any legitimate expectation of being able to live there. This was not significantly altered by his marriage to the second applicant, which had been entered into shortly before the disputed decision. It was not uncommon for a person whose expulsion had been decided to marry a Norwegian citizen and use this as an argument to have the expulsion order invalidated. The High Court considered that the balance of interest was not in his favour. The High Court, taking into account the Strasbourg Court's case law, did not find that the disputed decision would be incompatible with Article 8 of the Convention. The applicants complained that the first applicant's expulsion would entail a splitting of the family in breach of Article 8. The couple had a child, Selma, who is the third applicant. The Appeals Leave Committee of the Supreme Court refused the applicant leave to appeal, finding it obvious that the appeal had no prospects of success. The Board found that quashing the refusal of re-entry was not required in the interest of the third. applicant. The Immigration Appeals Board dismissed an appeal by the first applicant against a rejection by the Directorate of Immigration of 30 October 2006. The request had been made on the basis of a provision in the Immigration Regulation which was applicable to cases of unmarried parents and therefore did not cover the applicants' case. On 7 March 2007 the Implementation Group of the Oslo Police District expelled the first applicants back to Nigeria. The application was decided not to apply Rule 39 of the Rules of Court because the circumstances underlying the application were not of the kind to which, in the Court's practice, Rule 39 was applied. The applicants' lawyer informed the Court that they wished to maintain their application notwithstanding the refusal to apply Rules 39.

name: Kamal Bader
train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 13284/04) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Four Syrian nationals alleged that, if deported from Sweden to Syria, the first applicant would face a real risk of being arrested and executed contrary to Articles 2 and 3. The applicants, who had been granted legal aid, were represented by Mr K. Larsson, a lawyer practising in Karlskrona. The Swedish Government (“the Government’s Agent”) was represented by their Agent, Ms E. Jagander, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 13284/04) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that, if deported from Sweden to Syria, the first applicant would face a real risk of being arrested and executed contrary to Articles 2 and 3. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Government filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court declared the application admissible on 26 October 2004. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) and the case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. The applicants claimed that they had left Syria legally, flying from Damascus to Turkey and then on to Stockholm. They had travelled using their own passports but had destroyed them upon their arrival in Sweden. The Migration Board rejected the family's application for asylum and their request for residence permits and ordered their deportation to Syria. The applicants appealed to the Aliens Appeals Board (Utlänningsnämnden), relying on the same grounds as they had before the Migration Board and adding that Kurds were being persecuted and discriminated against in Syria. On 16 September 2003 the Aliens appeals Board dismissed the appeal on theSame grounds as the Migration board, stating that the new reasons advanced by the applicants did not alter the position. The first applicant had been convicted of threatening behaviour against his four-year-old daughter and a brother-in-law. He appealed to the Court of Appeal (hovrätten) of Skåne and Blekinge, which on 24 February 2004 upheld the conviction and the suspended sentence. In January 2004 the family lodged a new application for asylum to the Aliens Appeals Board and requested a stay of execution of the deportation order. They referred to a judgment that had been delivered on 17 November 2003 by the Regional Court in Aleppo which stated that the first applicant was convicted, in absentia, of complicity in a murder. They were also ordered to pay 1,000,000 Syrian pounds to the victim's family. The Aliens Appeals Board requested the Swedish embassy in Syria to verify whether the judgment was authentic. They further enquired if a reprieve was possible and whether death sentences were normally carried out in Syria. A local lawyer (förtroendeadvokat) they had engaged had confirmed that the judgement was authentic and had carried out research into the Syrian criminal law on sentences for murder and manslaughter. The embassy said that the lawyer had also stated that it was not unusual for the Syrian courts to impose the maximum sentence possible when an accused failed to appear for trial after being summoned to do so. It added that, according to their sources, it appeared that the accused had to be present in person in order to obtain a retrial. The court rejected the application for asylum on the basis that it was unlikely that it would be granted. The court also ruled that the first applicant would not be granted asylum if he returned to Syria. The case was settled on the grounds that the man had been married to another person. The first applicant was sentenced to death by lethal injection, but it was overturned on appeal. The appeal was dismissed on the ground that the sentence was not justified. The judge said that the case was the result of a miscarriage of justice, and that the death penalty was not available to the man. The trial was thrown out on appeal, but the judge said it was likely the case would be re-filed. The stay of execution of the deportation order until further notice is still in force. The dissenting member of the Aliens Appeals Board considered that, having regard to all the facts of the case, the applicants did have a well-founded fear that the first applicant would be executed if returned to Syria. The family should therefore be granted residence permits in Sweden. On 19 April 2004, following the Court's indication under Rule 39, the Migration Board granted a stay of Execution of the Deportation Order until further Notice. The stay is currently in force and remains in place until the family can apply for a permanent residence permit to stay in Sweden again.

name: Jürgen Schneider

In respect of the first two offences the Administrative Court remitted the case. regards speeding but quashed the sentence relating to this offence; (b) quashes the conviction and sentence as to the unjustified use of broad-beam lamps; and (c) refused to deal with the complaint relating to the conviction for breaching the requirement to drive in the right-hand lane. The applicant did not lodge a complaint. with the Administrative court or the Constitutional Court. The hearing was held in the absence of the defence.

name: Vereinigung Bildender Künstler
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 68354/01) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant association alleged that the Austrian courts' decisions forbidding it to continue exhibiting a painting by Otto Mühl had violated its right to freedom of expression under Article 10. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Court declared the application admissible by a decision of 30 June 2005. But neither the applicant association nor the Government filed further written observations (Rule 59 § 1).
eval_texts: The application was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant association alleged that the Austrian courts' decisions forbidding it to continue exhibiting a painting by Otto Mühl had violated its right to freedom of expression. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26: 1. By a decision of 30 June 2005 the Court declared the application admissible. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal on 17 November 2005. The decision was delivered by the President of the Supreme Court of Germany, Hans-Joachim Kohl. The painting was damaged by a visitor, who covered with red paint the part which showed, among others, Mr Meischberger. He claimed the painting debased him and his political activities and made statements as to his allegedly loose sexual life. On 6 August 1999 the Vienna Commercial Court (Handelsgericht) dismissed Mr Meischerberger's action. It noted that it had initially been intended to show. Mr Jörg Haider, in sexual positions with two other FPÖ politicians. He was shown gripping the. ejaculating penis of Mr Haider while at the same time being touched by two otherFPÖ. politicians and ejaculating on Mother Teresa. The right of the applicant association to freedom of artistic expression outweighed Mr Meischberger's personal interests. The court also noted that the painting showed numerous other persons, among them friends and benefactors of the painter, and also representatives of the FPÖ party. The limits of artistic freedom were exceeded when the image of a person was substantially deformed by wholly imaginary elements without it being evident, the court said. The painting in question could therefore be seen as a kind of counter-attack (Gegenschlag). The court further added that there appeared to be no danger of recurrence (Wiederholungsgefahr) as the painting had been partly covered by red paint. The painting in the present case was not intended to be a parable or even an exaggerated criticism conveying a basic message. It therefore did not fall within the scope of Article 10 of the Convention, but in fact constituted a debasement of Mr Meischberger's public standing (Entwürdigung öffentlichen Ansehens) The applicant association could not justify the exhibition of the painting under the artistic freedom protected by Article 17a of the Basic Law (Staatsgrundsgesetz) The Supreme Court rejected an appeal by the applicant association as it did not concern a legal question of considerable interest.

name: Armand Atlan
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36533/97) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that they had been denied a fair trial in breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 10 October 2000 the Chamber declared the application admissible and decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The applicants were represented before the Court by Mr H. Brown, a lawyer practising in Ruislip, Middlesex. A man named Willi Smolny flew from Brazil to London via Copenhagen. He had with him a black suitcase containing 18 kilograms of cocaine. Thierry and Mr Terrasson were arrested by customs officers at Heathrow. The two men were carrying two similar-looking suitcases, which customs officers found to contain cocaine. Both men were charged with possession with intent to sell or smuggle the drug. They were released on bail, but a third man, Armand, who had not travelled with them, was arrested at the airport in Los Angeles. The case is described as 'one of the worst drug busts in the history of Britain' Armand Terrasson, who was on his way to Antwerp, was arrested at Heathrow. He claimed to have taken his own, not Mr Smolny’s, black suitcase from the carousel. He said that he had travelled alone to Copenhagen, taking with him a black suitcase, to meet a married woman friend. He was unable to meet her because her husband was home, so he returned immediately to London. The prosecution case was that Armand had organised the importation, using MrSmolny as the courier from Brazil to Copenhagen and London. He had instructed Mr Terrass on, with Thierry as ‘minder’, to collect Mr Smalny's suitcase as if in mistake for his own. All four defendants pleaded not guilty and gave evidence. The applicants maintained that Armand worked principally as a jewel trader, but that he did not keep written records because he systematically avoided paying taxes and duties in Brazil. The illegality of his jewel trading had motivated their lies during their initial interviews with customs officers. The defence centred around a dispute between Armand and a rival jewel trader based in Brazil called Rudi Steiner. They claimed that, in order to avoid repaying his debt, he had arranged falsely to implicate them in the importation of cocaine. But they had no evidence to connect Mr Steiner to Mr Molny’s suitcase full of drugs or to substantiate the suggestion he was a Customs and Excise informer. Brazilian businessman Steiner sent a representative across the world to deliver diamonds worth thousands of dollars in exchange for a sample of the diamonds. Steiner's representative was caught with 18 kilos of cocaine in a suitcase that was identical to the one used in the arrest of Morgan. He believed the diamonds were antiques and works of art, but the drugs were actually cocaine. The diamonds were intended to be sold in a London jewellery store, but they were used to pay for Smolny's flight and hotel stay in Denmark and the return journey to London. The cocaine was intended for the British Customs Service, but Steiner set them up in order to get them to believe they were carrying antiques, he says. The jury convicted the applicants and Mr Terrasson of importing the cocaine. Mr Smolny was acquitted. In spring 1994 the applicants learned from the French press that a Swiss undercover police officer, Commissioner Cattaneo, had written a report. In early 1995 the applicants’ solicitor obtained a copy of the report. It mentioned Rudi Steiner, describing him as one of three regular informers of the Brazilian, Danish and French police. He was said to have an interest in stolen jewels and a long-term involvement in the traffic from Brazil to Europe of large quantities of cocaine, which he was able freely to obtain from the Brazilian police. The applicants added a further ground of appeal coupled with an application for leave to call fresh evidence. They maintained that the Mato Grosso Report substantiated their suggestion at trial that Mr Steiner had access both to stolen jewels and cocaine. In their submission, the fact that the jury had not had before it evidence relating to these matters, and the judge, ignorant of the true facts, rendered their convictions unsafe. The applicants objected to the holding of an ex parte hearing, in writing on 27 November 1995 and orally before the Court of Appeal on 7 December 1995, submitting inter alia that the court was a tribunal of both fact and law and could be adversely influenced by material which was wrong. The applicants' solicitor was able to obtain a number of documents relating to the Italian proceedings. These included transcripts of interviews with Mr Steiner, arrest warrants and a list of his previous convictions. He also obtained a statement from Commissioner Cattaneo, the Swiss police officer who had prepared the Mato Grosso Report. In his statement the Commissioner confirmed the authenticity of the report. He stated that he had been introduced to Mr. Steiner by a Danish police officer and had become Mr Steiners’ “handler”, passing information to the British authorities. According to the Commissioner’s statement, his British “contact” had been a customs officer named Martin Crago, whom he had contacted at the British Embassy in Brasilia. Court of Appeal ruled that justice did not require disclosure by the Crown of the public interest immunity evidence. Court of Appeal dismissed the application for leave to appeal on 20 February 1997. 'Little, if any, of the material [put before the applicants’ counsel] would have been admissible at the trial,' the court said. 'Much of it is wholly irrelevant to the central issue in this case, namely whether British Customs and Excise officers conspired with Steiner to ‘frame’ the Atlans' 'Steiner. denied that he had been Commissioner Cattaneo’s contact and declined to answer any question about Mr Steiner. Prosecuting counsel suggested that the only way Steiner could have been sure of achieving such an end would have been to persuade the officers to ‘plant’ the drug on, or falsely attribute it to, Thierry or Terrasson. There are also a number of other questions indicating the impossibility of the Atlans’ defence. Why, if they thought they were to collect diamonds from Steiner, not drugs, did they check their luggage onto the return flight without apparently enquiring by telephone why he had not turned up or whether he had been delayed? Why did Smolny make indirect telephone contact with someone on Armand’s telephone number in Brazil on the day of the importation? Prosecuting counsel's submission provides a logical and complete answer to the complaint based on Steiner’s alleged role as an informer and drug smuggler. His only possible line of defence, though, for the reasons we have given, is a wholly unrealistic one. The evidence against them, which had been thoroughly and robustly tested at the trial, was overwhelming. Their involvement in the high value and high risk activity of drug smuggling, not some black market dealing in gems under Brazilian law, was clear. Whatever Steiner's possible role, the Atlans’ guilty participation in cocaine smuggling is clear. ...”

name: Wolfgang Ohneberg
train_texts: The case originated in an application under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Neither the Appeals Commission nor the Constitutional Court had held an oral hearing. It was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29) The case was decided by the Supreme Court of Austria on November 14, 2009. The decision was the first in a long line of cases to be heard in the High Court of Justice of the United States of America. The case will be heard on November 24, 2010. The hearing will be the first of its kind in the U.S. and will be followed by a series of hearings.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 of the convention because neither the Appeals Commission nor the Constitutional Court had held an oral hearing. The applicant worked for the Bregenz Tax Authority (Finanzamt) as a civil servant. He was the head of a tax assessment division (Leiter der Veranlagungsabteilung) The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicant was transferred to the post of specialist without any team-leading responsibilities. The job profile did not state that any employees or civil servants were to be under his direct supervision. The applicant appealed against the decision to the Appeals Commission on 18 May 2006. He argued, inter alia, that his actual work had not changed sufficiently to justify the lower grade. The Appeals Commission replied on 30 October 2006 and stated, referring to the Constitutional Court’s case-law, that the rights and obligations. arising from employment in public service did not amount to civil rights and. obligations. The appeals Commission dismissed the applicant's appeal on 21 July 2006. In June 2007 the Constitutional Court ruled that the complaint was not in violation of Article 6 of the Constitution. The Constitutional Court found that there was no legal basis for the complaint to be brought. The decision was overturned on 21 August 2007. The case was decided by a 2-1 vote with the majority of members of the Court in favour of the complaint. The majority of the court found that the claim had been made on the basis of the law of the land. The court ruled that no action should be taken against the owner of the right to appeal against the decision. The appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal and the case was dismissed.

name: Vincent Kelly
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30054/96) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants, next-of-kin of nine men killed during a security force operation at Loughgall on 8 May 1987, alleged that their relatives had been kill unjustifiably. They invoked Articles 2, 6, 14 and 13 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol no. 11). The case was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30054/96) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants, next-of-kin of nine men killed during a security force operation at Loughgall on 8 May 1987, alleged that their relatives had been kill unjustifiably. They invoked Articles 2, 6, 14 and 13 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The proceedings in the present case should be conducted simultaneously with those in the cases of Jordan v. the United UK ( no. 24746/94) and McKerr v the United. Kingdom (No. 28883/95) The application was made to the Human Rights Commission on 23 March 2000. A hearing took place in public on 4 April 2000. The applicants accepted that the summaries below are an accurate reflection of the written statements made by the official personnel involved, without making any admission as to the credibility, consistency and veracity of these statements. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court heard addresses by Mr Weatherup and Mr Korff. The application was declared admissible by a decision of 4 April2000. The court ruled that the application was admissible and dismissed the Government's objections. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights. The RUC station, which operated on a part-time basis only, was opened as normal at 9 a.m. on 8 May 1987. Soldiers O, P, Q and R were instructed to position themselves in a wooded area to the south of the Loughgall Road, near what is known as Ballygasey Cottage. Soldiers S, T and U were positioned to the rear of St Luke’s Church. Three armed men who said they were from the IRA entered the house of the Mackle family in Aghinlig Upper, Dungannon. At about 6.30 p.m., a vehicle pulled up outside and a fourth man arrived. It appears that a bomb containing 300 to 400 pounds of explosives was prepared in the yard of the house. A blue Hiace van came from the Loughgall direction and parked outside the station. A man, dressed in blue overalls and wearing a balaclava, emerged from the rear of the van. He raised his rifle and began to shoot at the RUC station. Soldiers A to E, who had positioned themselves at windows on the first floor of the station began to return fire without warning. Soldier B received a facial injury from flying glass after a window by which he was standing was broken by gunfire. One of the IRA men drove the digger through the front gate and Soldier B, having spotted this, fired a short burst at the driver. The digger stopped and shortly afterwards there was an explosion. Soldiers A, B, D and E moved towards the front of the RUC station and continued to fire at the men near the van. Constables B and C were led outside by Constable A and Soldier C, who administered first aid to them. Soldier F also left the station by the rear and did not take any part in the shooting. Some of the soldiers stated that they came under fire. Shortly after the bomb exploded, Soldiers K and R observed what they thought was a gunman lying in the grass behind the police station. He failed to stand up when challenged to do so, and both soldiers fired several rounds at what turned out to be a large lump of wood. The bodies were wearing blue boiler suits except where specified otherwise. The first body (Patrick Kelly) was found lying on his back still moving. There were two significantly bullet damaged vehicles, a blue Toyota Hiace van (with approximately 125 bullet holes in the bodywork) and a white Citroen car. In the vicinity of the junction of Clovenden Road/Ballygasey Road there were bullet damaged Vauxhall Cavalier and Ford estate cars. Other vehicles near the scene of the attack included a red Sierra 15 metres from position 6, occupied by a woman and her daughter. A blue Escort about 70 metres from the scene which was empty. Post mortem examination revealed at least a dozen wounds to the torso and head. Pathologist observed at least twenty separate missile wounds (i.e. bullet and fragment) and found that discharge abrasion on an entry wound on the front of the neck indicated that when the gun was discharged the muzzle was within several feet of the body. There were four loaded rifles and one shotgun found in the van. Three of the stocks were folded. The sixth body (Eugene Kelly), which had massive head damage and multiple injuries elsewhere, was seated in the driver seat. There was a revolver lying between the driver’s seat and his door. The seventh body (Declan Arthurs) was lying in a lane-way opposite the premises of the Loughgall Football Club. The police took possession of the firearms used by Soldiers A to X. In total, 678 spent cartridge cases were recovered, 78 of which were from IRA weapons. Two forensic doctors carried out post mortem examinations of the bodies. The RUC forwarded a report to the Director of Public Prosecutions for Northern Ireland (the DPP) on the outcome of their RUC investigation. On 22 September 1988, he concluded that the evidence did not warrant the prosecution of any person involved in the shootings. Judgments were given by the Court of Appeal on 6 December 1990 and by the House of Lords on 22 September 1990. The inquest was adjourned on 24 September 1990, pending the determination of the Devine case, which concerned the powers of Coroners and the procedure at inquests. The inquest into the deaths of the three men was held on 30 May 1995 in public before a Coroner and a jury of 10 members. The RUC and Ministry of Defence were represented. The Coroner made available the maps and photographs but did not permit counsel (other than those instructed on the Coroner’s behalf) to see witness statements until the witness was giving evidence. On the same day of the inquest, counsel for the six families asked for the proceedings to be adjourned to allow them to seek judicial review of the decision to refuse access to the witness statements. This step was taken on 31 May 1995 following consultation with the families. The family of Declan Arthurs sought judicial review of the Coroner’s decisions not to allow the legal representatives to see witness statements before they gave evidence. The judge placed considerable emphasis on the character of an inquest as a fact finding exercise and not a method of apportioning guilt. It was concluded on 2 June 1995 that all nine men had died from serious and multiple gun shot wounds. In his judgment of 24 May 1996, Mr Justice McCollum in the High Court refused to quash the coroner's decisions or the jury verdict. The families of Antony Hughes, Kevin Antony McKearney, Michael Gormley, Seamus Donnelly, Gerard O’Callaghan and Eugene Kelly filed civil proceedings against the Ministry of Defence.

name: Johann Achleitner
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 53911/00) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Winkler, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The First Section declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 53911/00) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants run a fishing farm in Schalchen, Austria. They claim that the regulation works on a small river in the vicinity of the applicants' estate without permission under the Water Act (Wasserrechtsgesetz 1959) constituted an interference with their water-rights. On 20 June 2002 the First Section declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicants' predecessors filed a request for transfer of jurisdiction (Devolutionsantrag) as the District Authority failed to decide within the statutory six months time-limit. The Federal Minister for Agriculture and Forestry (Bundesminister für Land- und Forstwirtschaft) allowed the appeal as a consequence of which the Regional Governor had to take a decision on the merits. The Administrative Court, upon a complaint lodged by the applicants, quashed this decision and found that the administrative authorities had not properly decided on the appeal. The case was appealed to the German Supreme Court, which ruled in favour of the applicants in 1979. The applicants appealed against the decision to grant ex post permission for the regulation works. The applicants lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court as well as with the Administrative Court. Several technical experts were appointed in order to establish whether the regulation Works had damaged the well. The Federal Minister had to take a decision on the merits. whether the applicants' water rights had been prejudiced by the regulationWorks. The Minister found that the Regulation works had not damaged the applicants's well and dismissed the request for compensation. The applicant challenged the experts appointed by the Federal Minister for bias (Ablehnungsantrag) on 27 April 2000. The appeal was dismissed on 14 October 1996, after having held hearings on 1 and 2 July 1996. The proceedings are still pending. the applicants agreed with the Federal Minister on the further conduct of the proceedings. The Federal Minister would furnish a questionnaire to the expert in order that he supplemented his report. Thereafter the applicants would be given the opportunity to comment on the revised report and another hearing would be held. The applicants agreed that the hearing should be adjourned until a later date to allow the expert to make his report available to the applicants. The hearing was to be held at the end of February. The proceedings are currently pending and the applicants are waiting to hear from the expert on how to proceed with the case. The hearings are expected to last for up to two weeks.

name: Torsten Leander
train_texts: The present case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 11 July 1985. The case originated in an application (no. 9248/81) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission on 2 November 1980 under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Swedish citizen. The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed violations by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8, 10 and 13 of the Convention. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. G. Lagergren, the elected judge of Swedish nationality.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 9248/81) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission on 2 November 1980 under Article 25. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby Sweden recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Art. 46) The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed violations by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8, 10 and 13. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. G. Lagergren, the elected judge of Swedish nationality, and Mr. R. Ryssdal. President of the Chamber ascertained, through the Registrar, the views of the Agent of the Swedish Government (“the Government’), the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for the applicant regarding the need for a written procedure. On 12 December 1985, he directed that the lawyer and, should he so decide, the Agent should each have until 4 February 1986 to file a memorial. The applicant’s memorial was received at the registry on 3 February. By letter the same day, the agent of the Government stated that the Government did not intend to file any memorial. On 21 March, the Secretary to the Commission informed the Registrar that the De delegate would present his observations at the hearing. On 28 April, the Commission communicated to the Registrar a number of documents whose production he had requested on the instructions of the President. The hearing was held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg on the appointed day. Torsten Leander was employed as a temporary technician at the Naval Museum at Karlskrona in the south of Sweden. He alleged that on 3 September he was told to leave his work pending the outcome of a personnel control. The Government contended that in employing Mr. Leander the Director had committed two mistakes. It was not in accordance with the procedure prescribed in the Ordinance and the relevant regulations issued thereunder to employ a person before the personnel control had been undertaken. The Museum possesses several storage rooms and historical objects within the area for the security of which the Chief of the Naval Base (örlogsbaschefen) is responsible. According to the information received by the Commander-in-Chief of the Navy, the person holding the post in question must have freedom to circulate within areas subject to special restrictions. The applicant complained to the Government and asked that the assessment of the Commander-in-Chief of the Navy be cancelled. The Government requested the opinion of the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces (överbefälhavaren), who in turn consulted the commander of the navy. “The decision whether or not to employ you is taken in a procedure distinct from the present one,” the Commander in Chief said.“However, according to his information, the Director of the Museum required the person employed in the post in question to have free access to, and freedom to circulate in, the Naval Base and that accordingly, on 21 September 1979, he had taken the decision not to accept the applicant” The employment of Mr. Leander during this time, 15 August - 1 September 1979, did not involve any access to the Naval Base. The Commander-in-Chief of the Navy has said that he does not oppose such employment. The Director of the Naval Museum has, however, affirmed the requirement that Mr Leander should have access to. the Naval base. In view of the above and the fact that, if Mr.  Leander was given access toThe Naval Base, he would have access. to secret installations and information, the Commander-In-Chief decided not to accept the applicant. The opinion of the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces was accompanied by a secret annex, containing the information on Mr. leander released by the National Police Board (rikspolisstyrelsen). This annex was never communicated to the applicant and has not been included in the material submitted to the Court. The National Police Board did not see any cause to apply this provision in the case of the applicant as no special reasons were found. The Government do not examine Leander’s request for a revised assessment of his person and take no measure in regard to any other part of his petition. Leander has lodged no appeal with the Government in respect of appointment. His request that the Government should declare him acceptable for the provisional employment concerned cannot therefore be examined. At the relevant time, he had not belonged to any political party since 1976. Earlier he had been a member of the Swedish Communist Party. He had also been a. member of an association publishing a radical. During his military service, in 1971-72, he had been active in the soldiers’ union. According to him, the union conference in 1972 had been infiltrated by the security police. His only criminal conviction stems from his time in military service and consisted of a fine of 10 Swedish Crowns for having been late for a military parade. The applicant asserted however that, according to unanimous statements by responsible officials, none of the above-mentioned circumstances should have been the cause for the unfavourable outcome of the personnel control. He had also beenActive in the Swedish Building Workers’ Association and he had travelled a couple of times in Eastern Europe.

name: Michael Thaler
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 58141/00) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the Regional Appeals Commission which decided on his claims for doctor’s fees lacked independence and impartiality. By a decision of 15 September 2003 the Court declared the application admissible. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed First Section (Rule 52 § 1) The case was heard by the Court of Appeal from 1 January to 3 February 2004.
eval_texts: An Austrian national, Mr Michael Thaler (‘the applicant’), filed an application under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the Regional Appeals Commission which decided on his claims for doctor’s fees lacked independence and impartiality. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26§ 1. By a decision of 15 September 2003 the Court declared the application admissible. In November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25§ 1) This case was assigned to the newly composed First Section (Rule52 § 1). The applicant lodged proceedings against the Tyrol Regional Health Insurance Board. He claimed that it had to pay some ATS 18 million (about 1,3 million euros) as the doctor’s fees provided for in the general agreement were far too low. The Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint on 17 December 1999. It did not accept that the Regional Appeals Commission's decision had violated the applicant's constitutional rights. The second set of proceedings was heard by the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) in 2000. The ECHR found that the ECH may be considered as an independent and impartial tribunal because of the composition of the Regional Appeals Commission. The Constitutional Court found no indication that the members of the Regional Appeals Commission lacked independence or impartiality. ‘A violation of the required impartiality could, thus, ... be due to specific circumstances in the individual case resulting, for example from an official or organisational dependence of the appointed member,’ the court said. The Court said it could only exist if the appointed assessors had been involved in the preparation of the general agreement or if there were other specific reasons raising legitimate doubts about their independence and impartiality in determining certain legal matters. The court ruled that members were not bound by any instructions and that there was no evidence that the Commission was not impartial.

name: Eliza Söderman
train_texts: The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Swedish national, Ms Eliza Söderman (‘the applicant’), on 21 January 2008. The applicant alleged that the Swedish State had failed to comply with its obligation under Article 8 of the convention to provide her with remedies against her stepfather’s violation of her personal integrity when he had attempted secretly to film her naked in their bathroom when she was 14 years old. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. On 21 June 2012 a Chamber composed of Dean Spielmann, President, Elisabet Fura, Karel Jungwiert, Mark Villiger and Ann Power-Forde delivered its judgment.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5786/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the Swedish State had failed to comply with its obligation under Article 8. The case was referred to the Grand Chamber in accordance with Article 43. The Grand Chamber unanimously declared it admissible, holding, by four votes to three, that there had been no violation of that provision. The joint dissenting opinion of Judges Spielmann, Villiger and Power-Forde was annexed to the judgment. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Its President acceded to the applicant’s request not to have her name disclosed. The application was brought by a woman who was sexually molested by her stepfather when she was 14-years-old. The Government and the Human Rights Centre of Ghent were granted leave by the President of the Grand Chamber to intervene in the written procedure. The Court heard addresses by Mr Crafoord, Mr Lewis, Mr Södergren and Mr Rönquist, as well as their replies to questions put by Judges Ziemele, Sicilianos, Pinto de Albuquerque and Zupančič. The case was heard in public in the human rights building, Strasbourg, on 3 April 2013 (Rule 59 § 3). The applicant, her stepfather, her mother and her cousin gave evidence before the District Court of Falun (Falu Tingsrätt) in 2006. The applicant, represented by counsel, submitted a claim for damages of 25,000 Swedish kronor (SEK): SEK 15,000 in compensation for violation of her personal integrity and SEK 10,000 for pain and suffering, to be joined to the criminal proceedings. She based her private claim on “the criminal act for which her stepDad was being prosecuted”, without invoking any specific sections of the Tort Liability Act. She had not reported the incident to the police until 2004, when she heard that the applicant’s cousin had also experienced incidents with the accused. The applicant’s stepfather was given a suspended sentence combined with seventy-five hours’ compulsory community service. He was ordered to pay the applicant damages in the amount of SEK 20,000. The Court of Appeal acquitted him on the counts of sexual molestation allegedly committed against the applicant. The court found it established that he had had a sexual intention in hiding the camera in the laundry basket and directing it at the part of the bathroom where it was usual to undress. The buzzing sound from the camera heard by the applicant strongly suggested that the camera was switched on and was actually recording. Whether a recording had actually been made, however, was unclear. A man filmed his sleeping girlfriend while he masturbated. The man was acquitted of sexual molestation because he had not intended his girlfriend to find out about the filming. The isolated act of filming was not a crime in itself, as in Swedish law there was no general prohibition against filming an individual without his or her consent. The Court of Appeal went on to point out that the act might, at least theoretically, have constituted the crime of attempted child pornography (försök till barnpornografibrott) considering the applicant’s age. In conclusion, despite finding his behaviour extremely reprehensible, he was acquitted and the applicant's claim for damages dismissed.

name: Gösta Håkansson
train_texts: The case was brought before the Court on 14 December 1988 by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and on 27 January 1989 by the Government of the Kingdom of Sweden. The case originated in an application (no. 11855/85) against Sweden lodged with the Commission in 1984 by Mr Gösta Håkansson and Mr Sune Sturesson. The purpose of the request and of the Government’s application was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6, 13 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (P1-1).
eval_texts: The case was brought before the Court on 14 December 1988 by the European Commission of Human Rights. The Government of the Kingdom of Sweden brought the case on 27 January 1989. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them. The case originated in an application (no. 11855/85) against Sweden lodged with the Commission in 1984 by Mr Gösta Håkansson and Mr Sune Sturesson, both Swedish citizens. The purpose of the request and of the Government’s application was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6, 13 and 14. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr Corell for the Government, by Mr Rozakis for the Commission and by Mr Ravnsborg for the applicants. The applicants’ replies were received at the registry on 20 October 1989 and the Government’s comments thereon on 20 November 1989. On 4 December 1989 the President rejected an application from the Government to file additional evidence and on 23 January 1990 the Chamber rejected a similar application. The application was returned to the Court on 20 December 1989. The hearing was adjourned until 30 January 1990. The property had been seized in July 1979 in order to secure the payment of the previous owners’ debts to three banks. According to a valuation made public before the auction, the market value (saluvärde) of the property was estimated at 140,000 SEK. The applicants submitted three affidavits, each of which was signed in 1989 by a person who had been present either at the auction or at the public viewing. On the same day the applicants submitted a request to the County Agricultural Board for a permit to retain the estate Risböke 1:3. The application was denied. The property was sold at an auction in 1980 for 240,000 Swedish crowns (SEK) On 15 February 1980 the County Agricultural Board rejected the applicants’ request on the ground that the estate was a “rationalisation unit’ (rationaliseringsfastighet) which ought to be used for the purpose of consolidating other properties in the area. The applicants appealed to the National Board of Agriculture (lantbruksstyrelsen), which rejected the appeal on 5 September 1980. A new request, dated 4 January 1982, for a permit to retain Risböke 1:3 was rejected by the County agricultural board on 25 January 1982. The Board concluded that the real estate at issue lacks the prerequisites for remaining as a separate cultivation unit. The applicants brought proceedings before the Real Estate Court (fastighetsdomstolen) of Växjö requesting that the State redeem the Risböke 1:3 in accordance with section 14 of the 1979 Act. In a judgment of 11 December 1981 the court rejected the claim, stating that in view of the clear wording of section 14 this provision could not be applied by analogy to the applicants’ situation. In April 1984 the Senior Land Surveyor (överlantmätaren) of the County of Kronoberg made a new valuation of the property, resulting in an estimated market value of 125,000 SEK. On 10 November 1983 the County Administrative Board ordered the compulsory resale by auction. The application to buy Risböke 1:3 was made in April 1984. The Enforcement Office determined that the estate had a value of 125,000 SEK. The applicants challenged this before the Göta Court of Appeal but the court dismissed the action on 4 June 1984. On 26 June 1984, at the applicants’ request, the County Administrative Board appointed two special valuers (see paragraph 37 below) In their report of October 1984, the valuers concluded that the property had an estimated market value of 172,000SEK. After the costs of the valuation and the auction had been deducted the applicants received 155,486.50 SEK (“the 1985 auction’) The Court of Appeal refused to grant the application for the right to hold a hearing. The application had been made under the terms of the Land Ordinance. The Court's decision to refuse to grant it was upheld by the Court of Appeals. The case was appealed to the Supreme Court of Sweden. The appeal was denied and the case was returned to the Court. The decision was not made public until after the appeal had been dismissed. The result is that the case is no longer before the Court, and the appeal is not a legal challenge to the decision to hand over the case to the court, but rather a matter of public record.

The legal framework covering applications for bail, including appeals, did in Mr Justice Gibbs view enable her to take proceedings whereby the lawfulness of her detention could be decided speedily by a court. There was, in his judgment, nothing even arguably to be found in the wording of Article 5§ 4 which entitled an applicant to be present at such proceedings in all instances. Where prosecution appeals against refusal of bail were concerned, Rule 19.17 (4) provided a Convention compatible procedure to ensure that no injustice was caused to an applicant in cases in which he or she was not permitted to bePresent.

name: Einar Strömblad

The application was assigned to the newly composed Fifth Section of the Court on 1 February 2011. The proceedings relating to custody and rights of contact relate to the case of Mr Einar Strömblad and his daughter, N., who was born in Sweden in 2003. The Court of Appeal of Skåne and Blekinge upheld the lower court’s decision in full. It found that no circumstances had been presented which indicated the decision was not in the best interests of the child. N. should live with her mother, he wanted contact rights to be exercised on a regular basis according to a specific schedule. The parties were left to agree on where it would be best for N. and the applicant to meet. In this respect, the court emphasised that L. had a great responsibility to ensure that N. would be able to see the applicant. This decision was final on 13 December 2005. The applicant requested the District Court to change its interim decision, inter alia, in respect of N’s place of residence and the contact rights. He claimed that the interim decision in force had made it impossible for him to create meaningful contact with N., since it was too expensive to travel to Prague every other weekend. The Court of Appeal rejected the appeal, noting that it was not legally possible for it to decide where a child should live; it could only decide with whom. In 2006 the Social Council made an investigation concerning the custody of N. and contact to her, but the Court did not find the results satisfactory. In July 2007, the Court mandated a company, Access Borders SE, to investigate N.'s living conditions in the Czech Republic. L. took a number of procedural decisions, inter alia, rejecting L.’s request to have all documents in the case-file translated into Czech. The court decided that L. should have the sole custody of N. and granted the applicant a right of contact with N. four days in a row on a monthly basis, which should gradually be increased. The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Court of Appeal, which refused leave to appeal on 29 September 2010. On 8 December 2010 the Supreme Court refused leave for the applicant to appeal against the decision of the District Court. The District Court held that both the applicant and L. were suitable parents. It concluded that the fact that N. had not seen her father for the last five years was to a large extent caused by L.'s behaviour. In June 2006 L. sent a notification of change of address to the Swedish Tax Authority (Skatteverket) on N.’s behalf. Since parents who have joint custody of a child need to agree on a change of. address for the child, L. agreed to move N. to Prague. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal, claiming that the District Court should have focused on the actual removal of N. from Sweden by L. and not on the retention. In his view, the removal had been unlawful and the Hague Convention was therefore applicable. On 1 February 2007 the Supreme Court rejected the application. The applicant opposed the change of N’s place of residence in the Swedish population register (folkbokföringen) since he considered the removal of N. to be unlawful and the custody proceedings were still ongoing. The applicant appealed against the decision to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Skåne. The Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal. The case is still pending in the High Court of Justice of the Swedish Court of Appeal in Gothenburg, which could not hear the appeal due to the lack of a joint appeal by the applicant and L. The application has been adjourned pending further proceedings.

The applicant appealed against an order allowing him to be exempted from military service under section 24(3) of the Military Service Act. He argued that he performed a function within the Jehovah’s Witnesses which was equivalent to that of members of a recognised religious society. To restrict such a privilege to members of recognised religious societies was not objectively justified and was therefore in breach of the Federal Constitution. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court against the order. He submitted in particular that by virtue of the 1998 Act, the Jehovah's Witnesses had been granted the status of a “registered religious community’. The ten-year period for a successful application for recognition under the Recognition Act (Anerkennungsgesetz) lacked objective justification, he claimed. The Constitutional Court refused to deal with the complaint for lack of prospects of success. He then filed a request for recognition as a conscientious objector (Zivildiensterklärung), which was granted.
