name: C. Langum Becker
train_texts: The applicant alleged that she had been compelled to give evidence that would have enabled one or more journalistic sources to be identified. The case originated in an application (no. 21272/12) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 13 March 2012. The Norwegian Government were represented by Mr C. Reusch of the Attorney General’s Office (Civil Matters) as their Agent. The applicant was born in 1980 and lives in Oslo and is represented before the Court by Mr V. Strømme, a lawyer practising in Oslo.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that she had been compelled to give evidence that would have enabled one or more journalistic sources to be identified, in violation of her right under Article 10 to receive and impart information. The Norwegian Government were represented by Mr C. Reusch of the Attorney General’s Office (Civil Matters) as their Agent. The case was heard by the Norwegian Supreme Court on 29 October 2013 and the judgment was handed down on 6 November 2013. The decision was delivered by the Chief Justice, who said that the application had been a ‘misrepresentation of facts’. The Oslo stock exchange suspected market manipulation. Mr X confirmed that he had initiated the letter and been the source of the article in DN.no. The applicant refused to answer questions about possible contacts between her and Mr X and other sources, if any, related to the publication by DN. no on 25 August 2007. She argued that she was under no obligation to give evidence on those points. The prosecutor requested that the court impose on the applicant to testify against Mr X. A. an order to testify. B. Mr X’s conviction at first instance. C. The application of Mr X to the High Court. A. The appeal against the order would not be forwarded to the. High Court until after the City Court's judgment in. the case against Mr X had been delivered. D. Mr X was sentenced to one year and six months’ imprisonment, of which nine months were suspended for a probationary period of two years. Mr X appealed to the Borgarting High Court (lagmannsrett) against the City Court’s assessment of the evidence and application of the law in relation to the issue of guilt, its procedure and the sentence (see paragraphs 34-36 below) An appeal by the applicant to the Supreme Court was rejected by three votes to two on 30 September 2011 (Norsk Retstidende – Rt. 2011 page 1266). The appeal had been directed at the High Court's assessment of evidence as well as its application of law. An obligation on the press to give evidence in such cases was not thought likely to weaken the public’s general trust that the press would protect its sources. The situation under review did not concern the disclosure of sources but rather whether the person’S role had become known by other means. Once an informant had confirmed that he was the source, this fact would become known. Should the recipient of the information then refuse to giving evidence, this would normally appear futile. In such a situation, an exemption from the obligation to given evidence would in reality not constitute a protection against having to disclose the source but rather a right to avoid contributing. The majority held that this provision did not apply when the source had come forward and had confirmed his or her role. If the state of the evidence was such that confirmation by the journalist of the identity of the source could not be said to assist in identifying the source, it seemed unquestionable to maintain the obligation to testify. The principal justification for source protection, as elaborated by the Court in its case-law, was based on the consequences that the disclosure of a source’s identity might have for the free flow of information. The majority further noted that there was no decision where the Court had examined the situation where the source hadn't come forward. The legal question at hand was whether a journalist might rely on source protection if the source, without the journalist having revealed it, could be identified with more or less certainty by other evidence. The wording of Article 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was absolute and granted members of the press, broadcasting and other media the right to “refuse to answer questions concerning who is ... the source”. The protection of sources by journalists was, according to the European Court’s case-law, “one of the basic conditions for press freedom” (Goodwin, cited above, § 39). If journalists were allowed to protect their sources, they would obtain information enabling them to uncover matters in society that were worthy of criticism more easily. Mr X had stated that he was the source. A situation where someone claimed to be the source ought to be considered in the same way as where the source consented to disclosure of his or her identity. Mr X’s appeal against the City Court's judgment of 3 March 2011 (see paragraph 17 above) was examined by the High Court, which summoned and heard the applicant as a witness on 13 January. The judge ruled that freedom of speech did not protect only information and views that were positively received, but also those which offended, shocked or disturbed the State or parts of the population. Therefore, the fundamental right of journalists to protect their sources could not be dependent on the sources’ motives. The High Court, by a decision of 25 January 2012, ordered the applicant to pay a fine of 30,000 Norwegian kroner (NOK), approximately 3,700 euro (EUR) for an offence against the good order of court proceedings. The applicant did not appeal against that decision. By a judgment of the same date, the High Court convicted Mr X on the charges and sentenced him to one year and six months’ imprisonment. When important social and economic events happen in Norway, the courts are more likely to take a more active role in ensuring that justice is done. The Court of Appeal ruled that the applicant should not have been allowed to refuse to answer questions about her contacts with Mr X. In 2011 the UN Human Rights Committee adopted General Comment no. 34 concerning Article 19 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (CCPR/C/GC/34), which reads, inter alia, “States parties should recognize and respect that element of the right of freedom of expression that embraces the limited journalistic privilege not to disclose information sources” The provisions of this section apply correspondingly to any director or employee of any broadcasting agency. The Supreme Court interprets the provision in the light of Article 10 of the Convention. Some authorities refer to a journalistic ‘privilege’ not to disclosed a source’s identity, but both reporter and source enjoy rights that may be limited. National laws should ensure that protections apply strictly, with extremely limited exceptions. Restrictions must be genuinely exceptional and subject to the highest standards, implemented by judicial authorities only. Such situations should be limited to investigations of the most serious crimes or the protection of the life of other individuals. Revealing or coercing the revelation of the identity of a source creates disincentives for disclosure, dries up further sources to report a story accurately and damages an important tool of accountability. Under Belgian law, journalists and editorial staff may be compelled by a judge to disclose information sources only if they are of a nature to prevent crimes that pose a serious threat to the physical integrity of one or more persons. A. The disclosure of information identifying a source should not be deemed necessary unless it can be convincingly established that: i. reasonable alternative measures to the disclosure do not exist or have been exhausted by the persons or public authorities that seek the disclosure, and ii. the legitimate interest in the disclosure clearly outweighs the public interest. b. The above requirements should be applied at all stages of any proceedings where the right of non-disclosure might be invoked. c. In order to protect the identity of a source adequately, it is necessary to protect all kinds of information which are likely to lead to the identification of a. source.

name: Martin John Edwards
train_texts: The case originated in two applications against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that they had been denied fair trials, contrary to Article 6 of the Convention, as a result of the incitement of offences by agents provocateurs. The applications were transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 10 September 2002, following a hearing on admissibility and the merits, the Court declared the applications admissible. On 1 July 2003 the Court decided to join the two applications (Rule 43 § 1).
eval_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that they had been denied fair trials, contrary to Article 6 of the Convention. The applications were transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 10 September 2002, following a hearing on admissibility and the merits, the Court declared the applications admissible. On 1 July 2003 the Court decided to join the two applications (Rule 43 § 1) The application was brought by two United Kingdom nationals, Mr Martin John Edwards (“the first applicant”) and Mr Michael Lewis (‘the second applicant’) The applicants were represented by Mr P. Maynard, a lawyer practising in Tonbridge. The first applicant's defence was that at the time of his arrest he believed he was taking part in a transaction to sell stolen jewellery. He alleged that his participation had been organised by a man named Geoffrey Lerway. On 7 April 1995 the applicant was convicted in Snaresbrook Crown Court of possessing a Class A drug with intent to supply and was sentenced to nine years' imprisonment. The first applicant agreed to accompany Lerway to a public house where, at approximately 12.45 p.m., a red Jaguar car and a white van drew up. In the van was a briefcase containing 4.83 kilograms of 50% pure heroin. Of all the participants in the above transaction, only the applicant was arrested and charged. The applicant suspects that the other participants were undercover police officers or informers acting on police instructions, but their identities and status have never been revealed to him. At the time of the alleged dealings, Lerway was on bail to the Middlesex Crown Court in respect of a large scale conspiracy to supply cannabis. It was known to the applicant that Lerway had acted as a participating police informer in that case and it was further known that the police officers involved in the applicant's case had also investigated the conspiracy. The Government revealed for the first time that the material placed before the trial judge included information indicating that the applicant had been involved with heroin before the start of the undercover operation. The applicant denies any prior involvement in drug dealing. the public interest immunity evidence was not disclosed to the applicant during the domestic proceedings, either at first instance or on appeal. The defence made an application to the trial judge to exclude the evidence of Graham, on the basis that the applicant had been entrapped into committing the offence. The judge held that in the course of the ex parte application he had heard nothing and seen no material which would have assisted the defence in their argument that evidence should be excluded under section 78 on grounds of entrapment. Following his conviction the applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal on the ground, inter alia, that the judge had been wrong to refuse to order disclosure. The applicant was charged with possession of forged currency. He claimed he had been entrapped by undercover police officers. The judge refused to grant a stay or to order further disclosure of information. He also ruled that most of the information sought was subject to public interest immunity. The case against the applicant is expected to be heard at a later date. A second submission was then made on the applicant's behalf to exclude the evidence of undercover police officers under section 78 of PACE. It became apparent that most of the areas of cross examination necessary to develop the submission were not to be allowed. Accordingly, the submission was withdrawn and the applicant entered guilty pleas to the indictment on 12 November 1996. On 20 November 1996 he was sentenced to a total of four and a half years' imprisonment. In those circumstances, I advise that there are no grounds of appeal against conviction. The applicant had no prospects of success in appealing against conviction, since he would have to demonstrate that the convictions were unsafe before an appeal could succeed.

name: Mary Theresa Shanaghan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 37715/97) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that her son Patrick Shanaghan was killed by an unknown gunman in circumstances disclosing collusion by members of the security forces. She invoked Articles 2, 13 and 14 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The proceedings in the present case should be conducted simultaneously with those in the cases of Hugh Jordan v the United. Kingdom, no. 24746/94, McKerr v the. United Kingdom,. no. 28883/95 and Kelly and Others v. the United UK, no, 30054/96 (see judgments of the same date)
eval_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that her son Patrick Shanaghan was killed by an unknown gunman in circumstances disclosing collusion by members of the security forces. She invoked Articles 2, 13 and 14 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The proceedings in the present case should be conducted simultaneously with those in the cases of Hugh Jordan v. the United Kingdom, no. 24746/94, McKerr v the United UK,No. 28883/95 and Kelly and Others v the U.K. No. 30054/96. Patrick Shanaghan was a thirty-year-old Catholic and active member of Sinn Fein when he was killed. Between 15 April 1985 and 19 May 1991 he was arrested and detained pursuant to investigations into acts of terrorism in Northern Ireland. Six of the ten arrests resulted in detention for four or more days. He was never charged with any crime. Patrick Shanaghan gave several written statements to his solicitors alleging physical assaults by RUC officers while in custody, including being punched in the back, punched under the chin with a clenched fist, stabbed in the throat with extended fingers, slapped in the face, and being hit and kicked in the testicles. Patrick Shanaghan instituted proceedings against the Chief Constable of the RUC for alleged assault, battery, trespass to the person, unlawful arrest and unlawful imprisonment in respect of his detention from 9 to 15 April 1986. The applicant also claimed that there was an attempt on Patrick Shanaghan's life, on 17 February 1989, but that he managed to escape. The RUC were called but no charges were brought against a suspect for the murder attempt. On 10 December 1990, a RUC detective informed him that security force documentation containing information about him, including a photographic montage, had accidentally fallen out of the back of an army vehicle. He was advised to take measures for his personal safety as there was a risk that the material had come into the hands of loyalist paramilitaries. Patrick Shanaghan was stopped and questioned by RUC and UDR officers on a daily basis. The Shanaghan family home, which the applicant shared with her son, was searched sixteen times between 1985 and 1991. According to the applicant, sometimes the RUC would not even enter certain rooms indicating that the search was not a concerted effort to locate and seize illegal material but was carried out solely to harass the family. The applicant alleged that the behaviour of the police at the scene was not consonant with any concern for her son's life or proper police procedures. She claimed that no ambulance was called to the scene and that the police prevented a priest approaching to give the last rites. Patrick Shanaghan died from a bullet wound to the chest. RUC discovered a car which they believed had been used by the people involved in the shooting. However, a forensic and fingerprint examination disclosed no evidence to connect it with any person suspected of the murder. Enquiries showed that the car had been recently bought for cash by unknown persons from a private vendor. Several suspects had been arrested and interviewed but no evidence of admission had been obtained from them. The inquest was heard over six days, between 26 March and 20 June 1996. It was presided over by the Coroner, who said the cause of death was not known. The High Court quashed the Coroner's decision to admit evidence from a forensic science consultant who criticised the RUC for not taking a plaster-cast of car tyre impressions found at the scene of the crime. The Coroner accepted that the evidence should be admitted. The RUC Chief Constable applied for judicial review of those decisions. The High Court ruled that it was not germane to the question of how Patrick Shanaghan met his death. It said the evidence was relevant to the possible criticism of the standard of the police investigation and that that goes well beyond the scope of the inquiry of the coroner. The case was decided by a jury and a lawyer, with the R UC represented by counsel and a solicitor. Patrick Shanaghan died on 12 August 1991 from a bullet wound to the chest. The Coroner refused to admit in evidence statements made by Patrick Shanaghan to his solicitors. The applicant made a complaint about the conduct of the RUC at the scene of the shooting in denying Dr Stewart access to the body. This complaint was investigated by an assistant chief constable, under the supervision of the Independent Commission for Police Complaints (the ICPC) As a result, the Inspector concerned was given advice which was recorded in the Divisional Discipline Book. The RUC conducted further enquiries and reported to the Director of Public Prosecutions (the DPP) Inquiry into circumstances surrounding the murder was organised by family and friends after the conclusion of the inquest. The inquiry was conducted by the Castlederg-Aghyaran Justice Group and chaired by a retired United States Judge, Andrew Somers. The witnesses included family, local residents and friends of the deceased. Evidence was given alleging that police officers had frequently stopped Patrick Shanaghan in the street and issued threats. The judge concluded that the applicant had been murdered by the British Government and, more specifically, with the collusion of the RUC. The applicant claimed damages for loss and damage sustained by her and the estate of her son by reason, inter alia, of negligence.

name: Liban Mohamud Ahmed
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 59727/13) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented by Mr Z. Yazdani of Deighton Pierce Glynn Solicitors, Mr R. Husain QC of Matrix Chambers, and Ms L. Dubinsky of Doughty Street Chambers. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms A. McLeod. The application was communicated to the Government on 15 October 2014. The case was heard by Mr Justice O’Brien, who concluded that the Government’s actions were unlawful.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 59727/13) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) by a Somali national Mr Liban Mohamud Ahmed. The applicant provided the immigration authorities with a false name and a false immigration history in order to avoid being sent back to the Netherlands. On 15 October 2014 the application was communicated to the Government. The application was dismissed on 30 June 2008 and his appeal rights were exhausted on 8 July 2008. The case was decided in favour of the applicant and he was granted exceptional leave to remain in the United Kingdom. Deportation order signed on 29 October 2008 and he was thereafter detained under paragraph 2(2) of Schedule 3 to the Immigration Act 1971 pending his removal from the United Kingdom. On 2 June 2009 removal directions were set for 17 June 2009. They were cancelled on 16 June 2009 when the applicant made an application to this Court (application no. 26023/09), which granted an interim measure under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court. The form from July 2009 includes the following statement in reference to the Rule 39 measure: “Whilst this means that enforced removal is not possible, [the applicant] could reduce the length of time he spends in detention by withdrawing voluntarily” A similar point features in some, if not all, of the later forms. The applicant filed a claim for judicial review, contending that his ongoing detention was unlawful. Pursuant to the principles set down by the High Court in R. v. Durham Prison Governor ex parte Hardial Singh [1984] 1 WLR 704 (see section on domestic law below), the Secretary of State cannot lawfully detain a person pending removal for longer than a reasonable period. In a judgment dated 14 November 2011 the Administrative Court dismissed the claim. It noted that in deciding whether or not there was a realistic prospect that deportation would take place within a reasonable time, the risk of absconding or re-offending were ‘of paramount importance’ The Administrative Court noted that the interim measure under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, was awaiting a lead judgment on returns to Mogadishu. The court also considered whether alternatives to detention could be used such as electronic tagging, monitoring by telephone and regular reporting. However, given the applicant’s history of absconding, it concluded that the alternatives would not have been sufficient and there was an absence of adequate assurances from the applicant. The applicant was granted permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal. On appeal, he restated his arguments concerning the Hardial Singh principles which had been advanced in the court below. He also submitted that the detention was vitiated by two public law errors that bore directly on the decision to detain him. The Court of Appeal conducted an extensive review of the circumstances of the case. It took into consideration the fact that the Rule 39 measure applied in the applicant’s case did not involve any specific assessment of risk towards him by this Court. Lord Justice Elias dissented on one point only: acknowledging that “there is no one right answer to the question what is a reasonable period”, he believed that the period of two weeks which elapsed following the judgment in Sufi and Elmi was a ‘reasonable period’ for the applicant to be held in detention. It accepted that although it was not possible to say when the proceedings before the Court would be concluded, there was nonetheless a reasonable prospect of removal being effected within a reasonable time. Court accepted that if the applicant were able to show that the decisions to maintain his detention were vitiated by public law he would succeed in establishing that the detention was unlawful and would have a claim of false imprisonment. Court of Appeal found that although some of the passages in the review forms were not very happily expressed, they did not involve any legal error. Court found that Article 5 § 1(f) of the Convention added nothing of substance in the present case. Supreme Court refused the applicant leave to appeal on 26 March 2013. Court rejected the applicant’s assertion that Mikolenko v. Estonia, no. 10664/05, 8 October 2009 was authority for the proposition that the lack of a realistic prospect of deportation within a defined period rendered detention unlawful.

name: Fazia Ali
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40378/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1980 and lives in Birmingham. She is represented before the Court by Mr M. McIlvaney of the Community Law Partnership. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms R. Tomlinson of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The application was communicated to the Government on 7 November 2012 and the case was heard on 13 December 2012. The case was adjourned until 15 January 2013.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40378/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, a parent of two young children, is a homeless person in priority need of accommodation within the meaning of Part VII of the Housing Act 1996 (“the 1996 Act’). Birmingham City Council determined that the applicant was homeless, eligible for assistance and not intentionally homeless. The authority therefore accepted that it owed the applicant the “main housing duty” to provide accommodation to her and her family. On 7 November 2012 the application was communicated to the Government. The applicant viewed the property on 19 March 2007 but declined the offer as she was not happy with the condition of the communal area. By letter dated 21 March 2007 the Council notified the applicant that, by reason of her rejection of its offer, pursuant to section 193 of the Housing Act its duty to her under Part VII of the 1996 Act had been discharged. While the applicant’s case was pending before the review panel, a further offer of accommodation was made to her pursuant to a different scheme, namely the scheme for the provision of housing accommodation. She did not accept this offer. The applicant appealed to Birmingham County Court. The jurisdiction exercised by the County Court under section 204 was that of judicial review. In her grounds of appeal the applicant claimed that the Council had discharged its main housing duty. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal and then to the Supreme Court. At each level, the grounds of appeal were that the decision taken by the Council’s Homelessness Review Officer had constituted a determination of the applicant's civil rights. In Runa Begum the House of Lords found that judicial review provided ‘sufficiency of review’ for the purposes of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The judge noted that the only ground of appeal argued before him was that the letter of offer had failed to arrive. Although it was not specifically stated in the correspondence between the Council and the applicant, the judge appeared to consider whether or not the Council had discharged its duty under section 193(7) The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal. The applicant submitted that the present case could be distinguished from that of Runa Begum because it concerned the simple question of a finding of primary fact rather than an evaluative judgment. The House of Lords stressed that although the Officer had been called upon to resolve some disputed factual issues, these findings of fact were “only staging posts on the way to the much broader judgments” concerning local conditions and the availability of alternative accommodation. Thomas LJ stated that: “It is far from easy to draw the distinction advanced in practice. A finding of suitability is itself a finding based on conclusions ofPrimary fact’ Thomas LJ held that the decision of the House of Lords in Runa Begum applied to all County Court appeals under section 204 of the 1996 Act, no matter whether the decision turned on a simple issue of primary fact or not. He said the decision in Tsfayo, which concerned the housing benefit scheme, did not affect appeals brought in homelessness cases. LJ said the present scope of the appeal provides a real measure of protection for homeless appellants. He concluded that the Strasbourg Court relied on the decision. in reaching its conclusion and said nothing that cast doubt on the correctness of the. decision. The decision was unanimous. The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal, finding that the determination by the Council, that its duty to secure accommodation for the applicant had ceased, was not a determination of her civil rights within the meaning of Article 6.1. Lord Hope of Craighead stated that: “... I would be prepared now to hold that cases where the award of services or benefits in kind is not an individual right of which the applicant can consider himself the holder, do not engage article 6(1)” The HBRB was not independent of the parties. Finally when the housing benefits scheme was looked upon as a whole, it was readily apparent that a conclusion could be reached, in contradistinction to the scheme under Part VII of the Housing Act, that the particular scheme was not compliant with Article 6 (1) Lord Hope said separating simple, formal questions of ‘gateway’ facts from expert assessment of suitability would needlessly complicate a scheme designed to be simple to administer. The court went on to observe that the fact that a County Court did not have a full fact-finding jurisdiction when hearing an appeal under section 204 of the 1996 Act did not mean that the applicant was deprived of what was required to satisfy the guarantees of Article 6 of the Convention.Unlike the County Court, the Supreme Court appeared to consider whether or not the Council had discharged its duty to the applicant under section 193(5); however, it appeared to accept that a formal letter of offer was required by that subsection.

name: Ulrich Sommer
train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 73607/13) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the public prosecution office had collected and stored information about his professional bank account in a manner which was disproportionate. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr H.-J. Behrens and Mrs K. Behr, of the Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection. The application was communicated to the Government on 3 February 2016. The decision was handed down on 7 March 2016.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the public prosecution office had collected and stored information about his professional bank account in a manner which was disproportionate. The application was communicated to the Government on 3 February 2016. The German Federal Bar Association (Bundesrechtsanwaltskammer) had been granted leave by the Vice‑President to intervene as third party (Article 36 § 2 of. the Convention and Rule 44 of the Rules of Court) The case was settled on 8 February 2016 at the Court of Appeal in Dusseldorf. The public prosecutor asked for a list of all transactions concerning the applicant’s bank account from 1 January 2009 until that day. He based his request for information on Articles 161a, 51 and 70 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (hereinafter ‘the CCP’) The public prosecutor did not order the bank to submit the information, but pointed to the obligations of witnesses set out in the CCP and the possible consequences of non‑compliance. The bank complied with both requests for information and submitted the information to the public prosecution office. The information received was analysed by the police and the public prosecutor. A list of fifty-three transactions deemed to be relevant was included in the investigation file as evidence. The applicant, as the lawyer of the accused, was granted access to the investigation file. From the case file he learned, for the first time, of the investigative measures concerning his own bank account. He asked the Chief Public Prosecutor to hand over to him all data received from the bank and destroy all related data at the public prosecution office. The applicant appealed against the decision. The court found that the investigation was lawful, that the bank had provided the information voluntarily, and that the documents could therefore only be returned to the bank. The Regional Court also decided to separate the documents in question from the general court file and only grant access to them if reasons proving sufficient interest were provided. The Hamm Court of Appeal confirmed the decision of the Regional Court. It found that the decision was proportionate and that the safeguards were not applicable. The Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant’s constitutional complaint, without providing reasons (case no. 2 BvR 2268/12) The court ruled that the bank could not be considered a person assisting the applicant or a person involved in the professional activities of the applicant under Article 53a of the CCP (see paragraph 27 below). The judge concluded that the application was not valid as the bank had acted voluntarily and there had been sufficient suspicion for such an extensive analysis of his banking transactions.

name: Michael Stechauner
train_texts: The case was brought to the Court of Appeal under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). The case was dismissed on the grounds that the application had not been heard properly. The case is now being appealed to the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, France. The application was dismissed by the Court on July 4, 2008. The decision was overturned on July 5, 2008, on a technicality. It was decided that the case could not be heard again until after the appeal had been heard by the ECHR. The hearing was heard on July 7, 2008 and the case was settled on July 8, 2008 with the decision to dismiss the case. The appeal was dismissed again on July 13, 2009.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 20087/06) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the proceedings concerning his doctor’s fees had not been dealt with within a reasonable time and that the Regional Appeals Commission which dealt with his case was not impartial or independent. The Lower Austrian Health Insurance Board refused to reimburse echocardiologic and sonographic examinations as the applicant was not a specialist doctor but a general practitioner. On 2 May 2008 the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. The application was examined at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The applicant had claimed payment for echocardiologic and sonographic services amounting to EUR 1,169.75 for the second quarter of 1998. On 25 November 1998 the Regional Appeals Commission refused to grant the applicant’s claims concerning the third and fourth quarters of 1997 and the first quarter of1998. The applicant complained to the Constitutional Court that there had not been a public hearing. The Constitutional Court set aside the contested decision for the third quarter of 1997 on 27 November 2000. On 19 September 2001 the newly composed Regional AppealsCommission rejected the applicant's claims for the first and second quarters of 1998, owing to a tie in the Joint Arbitration Committee. The Constitutional Court found no violation of the right to a fair hearing and upheld the contested decision. It held that the assessors of the Regional Appeals Commission were independent in exercising their duties and that no circumstances giving rise to doubts about their impartiality or independence had arisen in the present case. The mere fact that assessors were members of Regional Medical Associations or Regional Health Insurance Boards which had provisions of the same content in their general agreements was not sufficient to cast doubt on their impartialities. This decision was served on counsel on 29 November 2005 and was served to the applicant’s counsel on 27 September 2005. The applicant complained to the Constitutional Court, alleging a breach of the principle of equal treatment and lack of independence.

name: Max Myer Kingsley
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35605/97) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the proceedings before the Gaming Board Panel were in violation of Article 6 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. The Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of 14 September 1999, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. The case was dismissed by the Court of Justice on 14 December 1999. It was decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35605/97) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the proceedings before the Gaming Board Panel were in violation of Article 6 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 14 September 1999, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The Chamber having decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine), the parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. London Clubs Ltd. lodged objections with the clerk to the Licensing Magistrates, with regard to LCL’s annual application for renewal of the licences it held. The Gaming Board also made cancellation applications in respect of the existing licences held by LCL. A meeting was held between the Gaming Board and the non-executive directors of LCL and their legal advisors on 26 March 1992. As a result of this meeting, the applicant and the other executive directors (with the exception of the finance director) resigned with effect from 30 April 1992, on the understanding that such resignation was involuntary and constituted dismissal by London Clubs. Subsequently an agreement was reached. whereby LCL would apply for new licences for the casinos, via re-constituted operating companies, to which application the Gaming. Board would not object. If the applications were successful and new licences were granted by the. Licensing magistrates, LCLwould undertake to surrender its existing licences, thereby avoiding the necessity for the applications for cancellation or renewal to be heard.  Lady Littler's speech referred to London Clubs and commented that the practices we and the Police had regarded as unacceptable had ceased. The Gaming Board alleged that the “persons’ referred to were minority shareholders and no reference to the applicant was intended. The applicant did not accept this explanation, however defamation proceedings were not commenced. By a letter dated 23 April 1993, the Gaming Board informed the applicant formally that it was “minded to revoke’ the applicant’s Section 19 certificates and that the applicant would be given the opportunity to state his case against revocation either in writing or orally. The hearing had, in fact, never taken place. The Gaming Board had already publicly expressed the view (at the hearing before the Licensing Magistrates) that the applicant was not a fit and proper person to remain as an executive director of London Clubs. The Gaming Board rejected the request for an independent tribunal and a Section 19 hearing commenced on 11 April 1994 before a panel of three, all members of the Gaming Board (“the Panel”). The hearing was conducted in private and lasted for seven and a half days. The effect of the revocation of the Section 19 certificates was that the. applicant was unable to obtain employment in any sector of the gaming industry in the United. Kingdom or in any jurisdiction which had a. relationship with the United Kingdom gaming authorities. Mr Justice Jowitt delivered three separate judgments in respect of the applicant’s appeal. The first judgment dealt with the scope of the phrase ‘a fit and proper person’ in Schedule 5 of the Gaming Act 1968. The second judgment considered the applicant's claim that he had a ‘legitimate expectation’ that the Gaming Board would be precluded from taking account of any breaches of its guidelines unless the breaches were unlawful. The third judgment which dealt with “Wednesbury challenges and allegations of bias runs to 165 pages.57 pages of the third judgment were devoted to the issue of bias. The application for judicial review was dismissed on 11 January 1996. Jowitt J. described the test of bias under English law in the following terms. It is a two stage test. The applicant has first to show from the evidence that there is an appearance of bias. Having done so, he has to go on to show that on a proper examination by the court of the evidence before it there is demonstrated a real danger of injustice having occurred. Injustice will have occurred as a result of bias if ‘the decision-maker unfairly regarded with disfavour the case of a party to the issue under consideration by him’. R. v. Inner West London Coroner Ex parte Dallaglio [1994] 4 All ER 139. Jowitt J. concluded that there was no unconscious bias on the part of any of the Panel members. He said: “When a body is charged by statute with the power or duty to make a decision in circumstances in which a question of bias arises, the decision will not be liable to be impugned on account of bias”. Jowitt said that if, contrary to his finding, there was unconscious bias, the “doctrine of necessity” fell to be considered. He concluded that, on the evidence before him, he could not say that the applicant had established that there is a real danger of injustice having occurred as a result of bias. Jowitt J. rejected the application for leave to appeal on the grounds that no useful reference could have been made to an independent tribunal which did not involve an impermissible delegation. The Court of Appeal refused an application to appeal from JowittJ.'s decision. Morritt L.J. (with whom Hobhouse L. J. agreed) held, on the “doctrine of necessity,” as follows: “I am prepared to assume in favour of [the applicant] that he would have an arguable case sufficient to justify leave to Appeal”. The applicant failed to establish that the Panel’s decision was irrational or unreasonable or to make out any sufficient ground for judicial review. ‘The question of bias, therefore, depends on the very limited point on whether it is arguable that Jowitt J was wrong in that respect. I am bound to say that, on that limited point, I think he was manifestly right.’ ‘The decision for the Board was, at the end of the day, whether or not Mr Kingsley was a fit and proper person. That could not be delegated to an independent panel and if they were actuated by bias, apparent or real, then the decision would still have to be made by them' ‘There is no arguable point, susceptible on this part of the case, which would justify giving leave to appeal’

name: John Edward Seton
train_texts: The applicant was born in 1983 and is currently detained at HMP Whitemoor. He is represented before the Court by Mr G. Bloxsome, a lawyer practising in Croydon with Blackfords LLP. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Grainger of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The case originated in an application (no. 55287/10) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) on 13 September 2010.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 55287/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr John Edward Seton (“the applicant’s case was that he had been involved in a drug deal with Mr Pearman and Mr Bartlett. The applicant was convicted for the murder of a Mr Jon Bartlett and a co-defendant, Mr Lee Osborne, was tried and acquitted of assisting an offender. Mr Seton is currently detained at HMP Whitemoor and is represented before the Court by a lawyer practising in Croydon with Blackfords LLP. The applicant’s trial for the murder of Mr Bartlett started on 11 August 2008. At the trial it was accepted by the applicant that the real issue for the jury was whether he or Mr Pearman was the murderer. The defence objected to their admission in evidence but the judge ruled that they should be admitted. The judge stated that he was satisfied the evidence had extremely strong probative value as Mr PearMan ‘appeared to be expressing genuine outrage’ at being implicated in a murder in which he was in no way involved’. The admission of the phone calls was made pursuant to section 114(1)(d) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003. The judge indicated that Mr Pearman could not be called because he refused to give evidence. He noted that all the enquiries carried out by the police to date had confirmed his lack of involvement in the killing. The judge said that he did not consider that there would be any real prejudice to the applicant from the tapes being played. At trial, in addition to playing the tapes, the prosecution led evidence that the applicant and victim were known to each other and were both involved in drug dealing on a substantial scale. Items connected to drug dealing were recovered from Mr Bartlett’s home, one of which was a list of debts. The applicant appeared on this list and he was shown as owing the victim GBP 24,000. Witnesses also saw a white van in the vicinity of the shooting at the relevant time. The van had orange writing on the side, and was similar, if not identical, to the van that had been hired from AVA on the same date. Cell site evidence also demonstrated that the applicant and his co-accused were in the. vicinity of a road where the Vectra was found between 8.01 p.m. and 8.17 p.M. Phone evidence was led by the prosecution with the intention of showing that the. applicant’s mobile telephone was in the nearby area at the time of the murder. CCTV footage showed the applicant arriving in the white AVA van, wearing a baseball cap and making telephone calls to an associate at 1.47 a.m. The number dialled by the applicant was in the vicinity of the cell site covering the road where the Vectra was found. The prosecution’s case was that Mr Pearman, a man in his fifties, did not match the description of the gunman given by the eye-witnesses. The trial judge directed the jury as follows: “It is for you to decide what weight, if any, you attach to this evidence” Jury asked and were allowed to hear the tapes of Mr Pearman’s telephone calls again. On 26 August 2008, by a majority, the jury convicted the applicant of murder. He was sentenced to life imprisonment with a minimum term of thirty years. He appealed against conviction to the Court of Appeal. The appeal was initially considered and rejected by a single judge in February 2009. The application was renewed before the full court on 14 November 2009 and leave to appeal was granted. In doing so, the court found it to be arguable that the trial judge did not make sufficient investigations with regard to the production of Pearman. Full court heard the case and dismissed the appeal, reserving its judgment. The judgment was delivered on 12 March 2010. In relation to the tapes of Mr Pearman’s telephone calls, the court observed: “It is contended on behalf of the Appellant [the present applicant] that the tapes should not have been admitted without calling, or trying to call, Pearman to give evidence. ... The difficulty with this submission is the judge's finding of fact that Pearman would not give evidence” The judge considered this evidence to be important and to have strong probative value. We do not know whether the jury shared this view. The defence were able to say, as they did, that the statements were self-serving, made by a serious criminal. The Court of Appeal said that because of the lateness of the allegation, the telephone records for telephones used in the murder only went back to 23 April 2006. The judge’s decision was not marred by legal error; he took all relevant matters into account; and the decision to admit the recordings in evidence was not one that no judge could sensibly have made. For these reasons, we reject this ground of appeal. The safety of the conviction was also upheld. The evidence against the Appellant may have been circumstantial, but it was overwhelming. The police uncovered no evidence of any link between Pearman and either the Appeller or Bartlett, despite exhaustive enquiries. Evidence of Rita Willott was not challenged and was read at the trial. The weight of the evidence points clearly to a young man such as the Appellant rather than Pearman. The evidence relating to the purchase of the Vectra and the hire of the AVA van on the day of the murder supports the prosecution case. The cell phone evidence showed Seton to be in the vicinity of the. murder when it was committed. Thus, quite apart from the evidence of Pearman’s telephone. calls, we had no doubt as to the safety of the conviction of the Appnellant.‘On 6 March 2010 the applicant was informed that the Court of Appeal had refused to certify questions of general public importance for the consideration of the Supreme Court’

name: Ivar Ringvold
train_texts: The case was lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’s”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) on 5 December 1996. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 2 of the. Convention on account of the national court's decision, despite. his acquittal on criminal charges, to order him to pay compensation to the victim. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 17 September 2002.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 34964/97) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 2 of the Convention on account of the national court’s decision, despite his acquittal on criminal charges, to order him to pay compensation to the victim. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 17 September 2002 (Rule 59 § 2). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr H. Harborg, Attorney-General's Office (Civil Matters), Agent, Mr F. Elgesem, Advokat, Counsel/Adviser, and (b) Mr S. Næss. Criminal proceedings were instituted before the Eidsivating High Court (lagmannsrett) which heard the case between 16 and 18 February 1994. The High Court, noting that the jury had answered the questions concerning criminal guilt in the negative, acquitted the applicant of the charges. It also rejected G.’s compensation claim of (up to) 110,000 Norwegian kroner (NOK) for non-pecuniary damage. G. subsequently appealed to the Supreme Court (Høyesterett) under the rules of the 1915 Code of Civil Procedure (tvistemålsloven) against the refusal to award compensation. In the appeal proceedings before the Supreme Court, G.’s lawyer requested that documents produced in the context of the criminal case be submitted as evidence. The Supreme Court then ordered the taking of oral evidence by the Oslo City Court (byrett) Evidence was taken between 26 and 30 June 1995, 18 and 20 October 1995, 20 November 1995 and 3 January 1996, during which time more than twenty witnesses were heard. The ruling cannot be perceived as a general procedural bar against the production of the case documents from criminal proceedings in a later case. In my view, the request for submission of thecriminal-case documents in question must therefore be granted. The first voting judge, Mrs Justice Gjølstad, stated on behalf of a unanimous court, inter alia: “In so far as the appeal concerns the merits, two general questions arise, namely the relationship to the acquittal in the criminal case (see Article 6 § 2 of the Convention) and the requirement of proof in such cases.” This arrangement is intended to make it easier for the injured party to have a civil compensation claim examined, but it does not preclude the possibility of making such a claim in separate civil proceedings instead. Contrary to what followed from the old Code of Criminal Procedure, it is not a condition for the examination of civil compensation claims that the accused person should have been convicted in respect of the charge. Justice Gjølstad: I cannot see that the arrangement under Norwegian criminal procedural law, whereby it is possible to have civil compensation claims determined after an acquittal, gives rise to any particular problems. The Supreme Court had regard to the video recording of the judicial examination of the alleged victim in the criminal proceedings before the High Court. It found that the evidence satisfied the standard of proof, establishing that sexual abuse had occurred and that, on the balance of probabilities, it was clear that the applicant was the abuser. Accordingly, there was a basis for awarding the victim compensation under section 3-5(1)(b) of the Damage Compensation Act. G. found that several infringements had occurred and that, even though their extent was not possible to ascertain with precision, there had been serious violations involving a certain use of force or threats. as a result of which G. had sustained damage. G. also found that there were serious violations that were not controllable with precision and that they had been committed by various members of the public at a number of locations around the world. The court said that the extent of the violations was not able to be determined with precision but that they were serious and that G had been involved in a series of incidents. It also said that G. was involved in at least one instance in which the use of a weapon or force was excessive and that this had had a negative effect on the relationship between the two.

name: Maria Buckland
train_texts: The case was brought against the Government of the United Kingdom. The case was made on 12 August 2008. The Court of Appeal ruled in favor of the Government on 3 May 2011. The decision has been appealed and will be heard again in April 2013. This is the latest in a long line of legal challenges to the Court's decision to rule in favour of the government in this case. The original appeal was brought by the Government in 2008, and was dismissed on May 3, 2011. This time, the case has been brought again, and the decision will be decided again on May 14, 2013. The court will hear the case again on June 6, 2013, and decide whether or not to order the Government to reconsider.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40060/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the Court of Appeal’s decision to dismiss her appeal and uphold the judgment making a possession order constituted an unjustified breach of her right to respect for her home and her family life and discriminated against her. The application was communicated to the Government on 3 May 2011. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicant was born in 1959 and lives in Cardiff. The Gypsy Council issued a notice of termination of licence to the applicant which expired on 6 February 2005. The Gypsy Council issued a claim for possession against the applicant and five members of her extended family, including her parents, in Neath Port Talbot County Court. In a witness statement lodged prior to the hearing, the applicant indicated that she intended to leave the site when her parents left. Judge Bidder QC gave a judgment on the preliminary issue of whether the applicant could challenge the making of a possession order in her case. He considered himself bound by the decision of the House of Lords in Kay and Price (see paragraph 42 below), which had examined the effect of this Court’s judgment in Connors v. the United Kingdom, no. 66746/01. The judge asked the parties to consider the date of 4th November 2006 being the date on which the [applicant’s] parents are required to leave. He was, however, satisfied that her son, who resided part of the time with her, had been involved in an incident on site in which he threatened someone with a gun, although it was not clear whether the gun had been real or merely an imitation. He made an order for possession against the applicant and suspended enforcement of the possession order against her until the same time and date. However, he was clear that the behaviour of [her son] on this site and his attitude towards the Farrows is such that I have to impose conditions on her continued possession. In November 2007 a bill which would amend the Mobile Homes Act 1983 (“the 1983 Act’) was introduced to Parliament. The effect of the proposed amendment was to allow a defendant in possession proceedings such as the applicant to challenge before the County Court the reasonableness of making a possession order. Lord Justice Dyson noted: “42. The significance of the amendment is that a claimant’s decision to seek possession does not involve summary eviction without judicial scrutiny of the justification of the claim to possession” On 12 December 2007 the applicant's appeal was dismissed. The real difference between the present case and Connors is not that the appellant had been in occupation for a shorter period than was the family in Connors ... On any view, the site was her home and had been for a substantial period of time. Dyson LJ concluded that since the amendment to the 1968 Act, it was difficult to conceive of a case in which a public law defence would succeed. He accepted that the vulnerable position of gypsies as a minority meant that “some special consideration should be given to their needs and different lifestyle” (citing Connors, § 83). He found that the main reason for the narrowing of the margin of appreciation in Connors was that the complete absence of any procedural safeguards was a serious interference with the applicant’s Article 8 rights. However, the precise scope of these safeguards was in his view, a matter for the national authorities to determine. He considered that provided that a reasonable degree of protection was afforded by the domestic law, the Strasbourg Court would not interfere. The court had no jurisdiction to take the reasons into account in deciding whether to order the occupant’s eviction. Absent a public law challenge, the occupant had no opportunity to challenge the reasons given by the local authority for seeking possession. The court has a wide discretion under subsection (2) to impose conditions when making an order for suspension. More generous safeguards could have been introduced (and they will be when the 1983 Act is amended) But the amendment goes far enough to meet the real thrust of the criticisms made in Connors. Dyson LJ found that the decision to provide the procedural safeguards introduced by the amendment of section 4 of the 1968 Act was within the margin of appreciation available to the United Kingdom. Dyson LJ considered that by addressing the lack of procedural safeguards for gypsies of local authority sites, the amendment had also gone a long way to meeting the discrimination point. While discrimination would not be cured completely until the 1983 Act was amended, it had been much mitigated. Thus to the extent that the discrimination persisted, the decision not to eliminate it altogether fell within the margin of appreciation accorded to the contracting States. The House of Lords refused the applicant’s request for permission to appeal. The applicant left Cae Garw caravan site for alternative accommodation on land owned by her brother. She claims that her departure was the result of the refusal of leave to appeal and in the face of further threats of eviction.

name: Dennis Sibson
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 21 February 1992. It originated in an application (no. 14327/88) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr Dennis Sibson, a British citizen, on 17 October 1988. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 11 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent him.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 21 February 1992. It originated in an application (no. 14327/88) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 17 October 1988. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 11 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 26 October 1992. The Court heard addresses by Mr Eadie for the Government, Mr Marxer for the Commission and Mr Bowers for the applicant. Both the Government and the applicant filed a written reply to a question put by the Court. Mr Sibson, who was born in 1929, was employed by Courtaulds Northern Spinning Ltd (“CNS“) from November 1973 as a textile worker. The hearing was adjourned until after 20 January 1993, when the applicant’s comments on those observations were heard. Until the events giving rise to the present case, the applicant was a member of the Transport and General Workers Union. He was based at its depot at Greengate, Lancashire, together with between forty and fifty other drivers. In March 1985 a fellow driver, Mr D., allegedly accused Mr Sibson of having “milked the funds’ of the union whilst he was branch secretary. The applicant lodged with the local TGWU branch a complaint to the effect that Mr D. had “disseminated false statements tending to depreciate“ him as one of its officers, but it was dismissed by the branch adjudication panel on 20 July 1985. The applicant was offered a transfer to Chadderton, where his earnings would be similar to those at Greengate. He refused to accept the offer and suggested that the management should dismiss him. Mr Dear refused to do that, and added that if the applicant reported to Greengate for work, he would be sent home without pay. Mr Sibson, citing his solicitor’s advice that that would constitute constructive dismissal, then said that he would resign with immediate effect, which he did by letter of the same date. He then lodged with the Industrial Tribunal a complaint of unfair dismissal against CNS and TGWU. His representative in these proceedings was not legally qualified, legal aid not being available for this purpose. Industrial Tribunal unanimously accepted the complaint of unfair dismissal. Mr Sibson was entitled to refuse to rejoin TGWU because there was no closed shop agreement in force. Court of Appeal concluded that CNS had acted within its contractual rights in requiring the applicant to transfer to a nearby depot. CNS could not be regarded as having been constructively dismissed. For confidential support call the Samaritans in the UK on 08457 90 90 90, visit a local Samaritans branch or see www.samaritans.org for details. In the U.S. call the National Suicide Prevention Line on 1-800-273-8255 or visit www.suicidepreventionlifeline.org. On 15 April 1988 Mr Sibson applied for legal aid to appeal to the House of Lords. On 30 June legal aid was granted for the purpose of obtaining counsel’s opinion on the merits of an appeal. On 8 August counsel advised that there were no reasonable prospects of success and that leave to appeal would not be given. Further legal aid is refused on 19 August. No question of unfair dismissal therefore arose. . No questions of unfair termination or unfair dismissal arose. No dispute over the outcome of the appeal was ever brought to a court of law. The case was dismissed on 9 September 1988. The appeal was rejected on 11 September 1989.

name: Gisela Kirsten
train_texts: The case was brought to the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights. The case was heard on May 30, 2005. The decision was made to rule on the merits of the case and not on the constitutionality of the application. The Court ruled in favour of the government's application on May 31, 2005, and the case was dismissed on June 2, 2005 at 3:00pm. The ruling was made on the basis that the application was not consistent with the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) Article 34 provides for the protection of human rights. The application was made under Article 29 of the ECHR, which states that the right to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness is a fundamental right.
eval_texts: The case was brought by a woman who had worked as a dancer in the German Democratic Republic. She applied for an old-age allowance from the German government. The case was decided in favor of the woman by the German Court of Appeal. The court ruled that the former dancer should receive the allowance. The judge extended the deadline to 1 June 2007 and ordered that the prosecution serve any further response within four weeks. A procedural hearing was agreed for 6 July 2007. On 1 November 2007 the parties appeared before the judge. The matter was further adjourned at hearings that took place in November 2007 and December 2007. The substantive hearing was listed for 20 July 2008, with a time estimate of two weeks, but in fact lasted four days from 22 to 24 July 2008. The judge delivered his ruling on the confiscation on 19 December 2008. He identified the total amount of the applicant’s benefit from criminal conduct as GBP 1,840,563. He found the principal realisable asset to be a farm, which was valued at GBP 690,000. The Court of Appeal granted leave to appeal but dismissed the appeal itself. The court upheld the confiscation order and found no violation of Article 6 § 1. It is. now for the applicant to seek other remedies.C. The judge erred in including the current value of the farm within the benefit figure of the proceeds of drug trafficking. The delay in the disposal of the. confiscation proceedings had breached his right to a fair trial and to a trial. within a reasonable time under Article 6.§ 1 of the Convention. C. The period from the applicant’s arrest in January 1999 to the. conclusion of his first trial on 31 August 2000 was wholly unexceptional and reasonable. Court of Appeal considered that there would have been a hearing of the confiscation question in about the spring or early summer of 2002. Court of Appeal noted that the various grounds advanced by the applicant fell away one by one over that period, but one of them remained and was not finally laid to rest until November 2006. Court concluded that the appeal on this ground, as on the others, had always been without any proper basis or merit. It is this additional period to which we referred prospectively earlier on as an example of the defendant taking the course that he is quite entitled to do – leaving no legal stone unturned – but adding to the passage of time as a result. name: Prem Singh

On 19 December 1991 the Board decided against recommending Mr Singh’s immediate release. Mr Singh received a more detailed explanation of his recall in a letter from the chief probation officer. The reason given for his recall was not the alleged offences (which were a matter for the court), but rather his failure to provide accurate information about his circumstances to his supervising probation officers. Mr Singh asked for his case to be reconsidered in the light of this development, and the Secretary of State referred it back to the Parole Board. On 30 July 1992 the Board again declined to recommend Mr Singh’s release. He was not told the reasons for this decision. The applicant sought judicial review (see paragraph 47 below) of the two decisions. On 20 April 1993 the Divisional Court quashed the decision of 19 December 1991 on the ground that there had been a breach of natural justice because of the Board's failure to disclose to Mr Singh all the reports before it. Prem Singh was released from prison in 1994. He was not permitted to be present at the review. The Secretary of State did not agree to his release. Mr Singh applied for a judicial review of this decision, but he withdrew his application because he had been offered an early review of his case by the Parole Board. In June 1994 the Par parole board reconsidered Mr Singh’s case in accordance with section 35 (2) of the Criminal Justice Act 1991 (see paragraph 35 below). Mr Singh entered detailed representations and the file before the Board was disclosed to him; it contained recent reports from probation officers, from a psychologist working with Mr Singh and from the Local Review Committee. All the reports which made a specific recommendation were in favour of the applicant's release as soon as possible. Prem Singh was recalled to prison in 1990 'following serious breaches of the trust placed in [him] as a life licensee' The Secretary of State was unable to assess accurately whether he was still a threat to the public because he had spent the three and a quarter years since his recall in a closed prison. name: Terence Perkins

The appeal on grounds (b) and (g) also fail. The decision turns on the following main issues. Whether, if the development is inappropriate to the green belt, there are any special circumstances to justify the granting of planning permission. Whether the appeal buildings enhance or preserve the character or appearance of the conservation area. I shall also consider the effect of the development on the countryside surrounding the village. The Court of Appeal rules that the buildings should not be granted planning permission to be built on the site in Higher Whitley, Vale Royal Borough, Vale of Wight, Hertfordshire. The appeal was dismissed by the High Court on 8 March 1991, the judge, Mr Lionel Read, QC, finding inter alia as follows: “A principal argument on behalf of the applicant at the inquiry under [ground] (b) was that the erection of the two buildings was permitted development under the General Development Order’. The applicant does not challenge the inspector’s decision under ground (b). Nevertheless paragraphs 14 and 15 of the decision letter, where he is still dealing with that ground, are relevant to the court's consideration of his decision on grounds (a) and (g) ... ... In my judgment ... it cannot be said that the inspector failed to take into account the fact that the applicant might, within his General. Development Order rights, erect buildings of a broadly similar nature. He addressed that very consideration in terms at paragraph 15. Inspector extended the applicant’s time for complying with the enforcement notice under ground (h) The question whether the alterations proposed to a building were, as he evidently thought, a ‘matter of cosmetics’ and would not meet the main objections was entirely a matter of planning judgment for him. It is to be remembered that, in order to stay within his General Development Order rights, the applicant must erect replacement buildings which, by their appearance and layout, could be considered as designed for the purposes of agriculture. If they are, their effect on the green belt, the countryside and the conservation area is irrelevant to the exercise of that right. I find no error of law and I dismiss the application.

name: Mary Kehoe
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 2010/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that there had been unreasonable delay in enforcing the financial obligations of her ex-partner in respect of child support. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 2010/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that there had been unreasonable delay in enforcing the financial obligations of her ex-partner in respect of child support. The Court declared the application partly admissible as regarded the applicant’s complaint of lack of access to court, and inadmissible as. regarded her children. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The case was settled out of court. An interim maintenance assessment (IMA) was issued with effect from 5 October 1995. Mr K’s liability changed many times after that date, inter alia as his employment changed and it proved difficult to obtain information. By March 1996 arrears of GBP 4,244 had accumulated. The CSA negotiated an agreement with Mr K that he would pay under the IMA, GBP 124.33 per week plus GBP 25.67 towardsArrears. The order was discontinued when regular payments were resumed. The judge ruled that the CSA had made a series of errors in its handling of the case. The case was closed on 13 January 2003 with effect from 30 September 2002. Mr K admitted owing GBP 6,329.24 for the period 25 May 1995 to 11 September 2000. He agreed to pay the former sum by 8 July 2003 and the latter sum at GBP 500 per month from November 2002. A payment of GBP 1,500 was made on 30 December 2002. The applicant brought proceedings under the Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA), seeking a declaration that the provisions of the Child Support Act 1991 were incompatible with Article 6 § 1 of the Convention as they denied a parent with care of children access to court in connection with disputes. The Court of Appeal upheld the Secretary of State's appeal and dismissed the applicant's cross-appeal. The House of Lords, by a majority of four to one, rejected the applicant’s appeal in 2005. The applicant had no legal right in domestic law to a child maintenance payment of any particular amount or at all. She was unable to assert that she had an arguable civil right under Article 6 which entitled her to a determination by a court. The judge had erred in finding she had a right to damages to supplement her limited right of judicial review. The damages could only be awarded where the Act was incompatible with Article 6, and the Act did not become incompatible because of a lack of entitlement to damages. The state has an interest, most directly in cases where public funds are disbursed, but also more generally that children should be adequately supported. The 1991 Act cannot in my opinion be interpreted as conferring any right on a parent in the position of Mrs [K]. She is of course the person to whom child maintenance will be paid, directly or indirectly and subject to any deduction of benefit. But the right which she had enjoyed under the former legislation was removed, and the right to recover the maintenance has been vested in the CSA.“Baroness Hale of Richmond, dissenting, found that prior to the 1991 Act a father had, at common law, a duty to maintain his legitimate minor children. Baroness Hale noted that there was undoubtedly a legitimate aim. The non-enforceability by the custodial parent in non-benefit cases was not a necessary feature of comparable child support schemes elsewhere in the common law world. She concluded that this was just the sort of policy choice in a socio-economic field which the courts were usually prepared to leave to the judgment of Parliament. She would therefore have allowed the appeal and restored Mr Justice Wall’s order. Meanwhile, all money owed to the applicant was paid by 27 April 2005 and her case was closed. The case was eventually settled out of court in a settlement worth more than £1million.

name: Erich Kiefer
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by an Austrian national, Erich Kiefer (“the applicant”) on 30 December 1998.
