The case concerns the duration of the proceedings instituted by the proponent and whether they were terminated within a ‘reasonable time’
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by an Austrian national, Erich Kiefer (“the applicant”) on 30 December 1998. It originated in an application (no. 27353/95) against Switzerland lodged by the applicant with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant is represented by Mr B. Gachnang, a lawyer practising in Lucerne in Switzerland. The Swiss Government are represented by their Agent, Mr Ph. Boillat. The case concerns the duration of the proceedings instituted by the. applicant and whether they were terminated within a ‘reasonable time’ as required by Article 6. In 1983 the applicant suffered an injury and became partly disabled. On 7 November 1985 he requested pension benefits from the Swiss Invalidity Insurance. The Compensation Office dismissed the applicant's request on 23 December 1987, as he was only partly hindered in exercising his profession as a lorry driver. In 1989, various reports were filed by Austrian experts. The applicant requested the Austrian authorities to undertake a most thorough examination of his case by means of a further medical expert. In 1990 the Austrian orthopaedist Dr. L.-K. submitted a report on 7 February 1990. The case was referred back to the Swiss Compensation Office for renewed examination. The Invalidity Insurance Commission considered in its proposal of 19 July 1990 that the applicant had not sufficiently demonstrated his invalidity. The applicant was granted a time-limit of 30 days to reply. On 7 April 1993 the Compensation Office dismissed the applicant's request for pension benefits as he had not been insured at the time concerned. On 10 May 1993 he filed an appeal against this decision which was dismissed by the Federal Appeals Commission for Old Age, Survivors and Invalidity Health Insurance on 21 February 1993. In October 1992 the applicant was issued a preliminary decision (Vorbescheid) according to which he was not insured when the injury had occurred for which reason a formal condition for granting an invalidity pension had not be met. The applicant filed an administrative law appeal on 5 April 1994. The appeal was dismissed on 18 November 1994 by the Federal Insurance Court. The applicant applied to the Commission on 13 April 1995, complaining under Article 6 § 1 about the length of social security proceedings. The Commission declared the application admissible on 16 April 1998. In its report of 21 October 1998 (former Article 31), it expressed the unanimous opinion that there had been a violation of Article 6§ 1. The decision of 23 December 1987 refused to grant a pension on the grounds that there was no invalidity, without even dealing with the allegedly missing insurance quality. The conduct of the authorities, and in particular the result of this conduct, breaches good faith and must be described as arbitrary.

name: Nadine Mladoschovitz

eval_texts: The applicants alleged a violation of Article 6 of the Convention in proceedings concerning the enforcement of their claims for maintenance against their father. Apparently the debtor fell into arrears with maintenance payments (Unterhaltsrückstand) amounting to the sum of EUR 3,006. The applicants were represented by Mr R. Gabl, a lawyer practising in Linz. name: Juri Maslov
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1638/03) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1638/03) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the residence prohibition against him violated his right to respect for his private and family life. The Court ruled that the application was not admissible because the Bulgarian Government did not make use of their right to intervene. The decision was upheld by the Court. The case was heard by the German Court of Appeal. The verdict was upheld on the basis that the Austrian Government had not made use of its right to intervention. The applicant was convicted of 18 counts of partially completed and partially attempted aggravated burglary and sentenced to 15 months’ imprisonment. The Vienna Juvenile Court noted the applicant’s confession as a mitigating circumstance, the number of offences committed as well as the rapid relapse into crime after the last conviction as aggravating circumstances. The applicant served his prison term until 24 May 2002. He did not benefit from early release. On 3 January 2001 the Vienna Federal Police Authority (Bundespolizeidirektion) imposed a ten years’ residence prohibition on the applicant. He appealed. He submitted that the residence prohibition violated his rights under Article 8 of the Convention as he had come to Austria at the age of six. The applicant came to Austria at the age of six, had attended school in Austria and was not able to speak Bulgarian. The Administrative Court dismissed the complaint and found that the residence prohibition was justified under Article 8 of the Convention. The Constitutional Court declined to deal with the complaint for lack of prospects of success. On 22 December 2003 the applicant was deported to Sofia. He was arrested on 27 November 2003 and deported on December 22, 2003. His case was heard by the Court of Appeal of the Federal Court of Justice of the Republic of Austria, which was the last court to hear the case before it was referred to the Supreme Court.

name: Jaroslaw Niedzwiecki

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 58453/00) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. In 1997 the applicant obtained an unlimited residence permit (Aufenthaltsberechtigung) The applicant lodged an action with the Würzburg Social Court (Sozialgericht), claiming that he had been residing in Germany since 1987 and that he should, therefore, have the right to child benefits. The Social Court confirmed that only aliens with an unlimited. residence permit or with a provisional residence permit were entitled to the payment of child benefits under. Section 1 of the Child Benefits Act, as in force until 31 December 1995. The court further pointed out that this distinction did not violate the German Basic Law. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint combined with a request for an interim measure. He claimed that the relevant provision of the Federal Child Benefits Act was discriminatory and racist. He alleged that the refusal of his request for child benefits infringed the principle of social justice (Sozialstaatsprinzip) The proceedings before the Tax Court are still pending. The proceedings concerning claims after 1 January 1996 have been transferred to the Nuremberg Tax Court (Finanzgericht) The application was dismissed on points of law on 18 March 1999. The case was appealed to the Federal Social Court on 3 July 2001. It was decided that it was not competent to deal with the applicant’s claims regarding child benefits for the period after January 1996.

name: Johann Ferihumer

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30547/03) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he had been violated in his right to freedom of expression under Article 10. The Court declared the application admissible in February 2006. The application was brought by Johann Ferihumer, the father of a pupil of a secondary school in Grieskirchen. The School Committee (Schulgemeinschaftsausschuss) of the school decided not to send pupils on a one week trip to Tuscany or Prague. Teachers brought proceedings against the applicant for insult and damage to their reputation before the Peuersbach District Court. The court noted that it was true that, in the course of time, the atmosphere between the pupils and teachers at the Grieskirchen secondary school had been strained. The spokesperson of the pupils had complained that the teachers did not take her seriously and avoided any discussion about the boycott measures with her. 'Not only this: the teachers apply pressure on pupils and parents to an intolerable extent. This amounts in fact to an abuse of their authority. Who is surprised that the school speaker was at the end of her tether?' The Wels Regional Court dismissed the appeal. It noted that the statement at issue constituted a statement of fact susceptible of proof. The injunction at issue did, therefore, not violate the applicant's right to freedom of expression. The court further ordered the applicant to pay the costs of the proceedings. This decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 13 March 2003. The judge said that the teachers had themselves attracted the attention of the public by their boycott measures which had provoked criticism and resistance. It was, on the contrary, because of the teachers' unbending attitude concerning the boycott measures that pupils and parents had finally resigned and agreed to the compromise.

name: Farida Kathoon Khan

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38030/12) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. In November 2009 the applicant was granted privileges in the hospital, for example she was granted days of leave, which had not led to any complaints. She also started working full‑time in the laundry department of the clinic. This was possible due to her improved mental health. But she had to stay away from her family for the duration of her treatment. Her condition has since improved but she still has problems with her eyesight and her speech. The judge ruled that she must stay in contact with her relatives and take her medication as soon as she can. So far, no date for the applicant’s removal to Pakistan has been set. 19 September 2013 that a petition to the parliament of the Land of Hesse in this matter had not been successful. No date has yet been set for his removal from Hesse to Pakistan. name: Nigel Eastaway

eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that there had been a violation of his right to a hearing within a reasonable time. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. By a decision of 18 November 2003, the Court declared the application admissible. The Chamber having decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine), the parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. The parties replied to the parties’ observations in writing. The Secretary of State’s evidence was completed and served on the applicant on 14 December 1992. On 13 May 1993 the applicant applied to strike out the proceedings. The applicant and one other defendant were acquitted, and two defendants were convicted. On appeal, the two convictions were quashed in February 1995. In November 1995 Mr Davies was granted leave to appeal out of time to the Court of Appeal. His substantive appeal was dismissed by that court on 24 May 1996. The appeal to the High Court brought by the first defendant to the disqualification proceeding, Mr Davies, against the Registrar's decision of 27 January 1994, was dismissed on 2 May 1995. The defendants were ordered to serve their evidence by January 1997. The case was adjourned until February 1998. The court ruled that it was in the public interest for the case to continue. The defendants were allowed to give further evidence until July 1998. At this point the case was closed and the defendants were cleared of all charges. The judge ruled that the case should be dismissed. The trial has now been adjourned again until April 1998. the case is expected to be settled in May or June 1998, if not earlier. The jury was set to hear evidence from both sides at a later date. The verdicts are expected on April 25. The applicant attempted to negotiate a ‘Carecraft’ settlement with the Secretary of State. The secretary of state refused to discontinue the proceedings on the grounds that they had already exceeded the ‘reasonable time’ provision in Article 6 of the Convention. The matter was set down for trial on 4 October 1999. The applicant applied for judicial review of the legality of the decision of 30 June 1999. It was refused by the Court of Appeal on 15 March 2000. Lord Justice Buxton described the application as ‘misconceived’, because the arguments on delay could, and should, have been made in the course of the disqualification proceedings and not in separate proceedings. The application was heard by the Vice-Chancellor on 7 February 2001, and judgment was delivered dismissing it on 15 February 2001. Mr Eastaway had applied in the Companies Court to strike out or dismiss the disqualification proceedings on the ground of violation of the reasonable time provision in Article 6 § 1. The applicant appealed to the House of Lords, which granted leave on 11 July 2000. The House heard the applicant’s appeal on 18 October 2000, and on 2 November 2000 delivered judgment dismissing it. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the House had no jurisdiction to hear an appeal from the Court of Appeal refusing leave to apply for judicial review (R v. Secretary of State for Trade and Industry, ex parte Eastaway [2000] 1 WLR 2222). The application was brought by Eastaway against the Secretary of State for the Privy Council. He was convicted of breaching his Convention rights under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Mr Eastaway claimed he was not entitled to a fair trial and that the delay was not due to his actions but to avoid a fair and public hearing. The application was dismissed by the Vice-Chancellor and appealed to the Court of Appeal. The appeal was dismissed and the proceedings against the applicant were terminated on 4 June 2001. The applicant signed an undertaking giving him a period of disqualification of four and a half years. The undertaking was accepted and the case was terminated on 25 June 2001, with the disqualification period commencing in May 2001.

name: Samuel Betteridge
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1497/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he did not have a speedy review of the lawfulness of his detention. The application was communicated to the Government on 14 December 2010. It was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Chivers Solicitors, a firm of lawyers based in Bingley. The United Kingdom Government were represented by their Agent, Ms A. Sornarajah, of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1497/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he did not have a speedy review of the lawfulness of his detention. He was originally sentenced to life imprisonment with a tariff (i.e. minimum term to be served before eligibility for release arose) of five years. Upon appeal, this was reduced to a sentence of imprisonment for public protection (“IPP” – see paragraphs 22-23 below) The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Chivers Solicitors, a firm of lawyers based in Bingley. The applicant’s tariff expired on 18 December 2008, by which time no Parole Board review had taken place. The applicant challenged, by way of judicial review proceedings, the delay in fixing a Parole board hearing. The hearing was eventually rescheduled for September 2009. The panel was not satisfied that sufficient evidence exists that your risk of sexual and/or violent offending has yet reduced to a level such that that risk can be safely managed out of closed conditions. They feared that there had been an underestimate of risk and insufficient attention to the sadistic elements of the offences in other assessments. They would therefore counsel against the formulaic approach in this case. The High Court handed down its judgment in the judicial review proceedings on 23 June 2009. The judge outlined the background to the applicant’s claim, as follows: “4. a breach, having regard in particular to the fact that the pre-tariff advisory opinion of the Parole Board had effectively made it clear there was no chance of release upon expiry of the tariff (see paragraph 7 above)” The judge considered that it followed “inevitably” from it that the panel, if asked, would not conceivably have directed the applicant's release. In fact it is common ground that Article 5(4) of the European Convention on Human Rights requires there to be a speedy hearing an independent judicial body. ‘Speedy’ does not indicate a particular period, and I accept entirely that it is fact sensitive. What may be required in a particular case may not be needed in another, depending upon the circumstances. In this case the cause has been the lack of man power in the Parole Board which has meant that it has been unable to provide the necessary panel. That is hardly surprising having regard to the importance of ensuring not only that those who should be released are released, but that those which should not be are not released.’ ‘It will take time for the position to be improved: that is inevitable. ... It may well be that it could be said that steps ought perhaps to have been taken at an earlier stage ... Nevertheless, that is historical, and as I say there is now a recognition’ The applicant had originally sought a mandatory order requiring that his case be heard in September. The judge agreed with the decision not to pursue the claim for such an order, observing that it would be inappropriate for an individual, seeking judicial review, to “jump the queue” at the expense of those who did not seek judicial review. The applicant’s legal representative accepted that it was “not of the greatest importance” whether a declaration was granted or not, because the terms of the judgment could show what the situation was. He decided: “In all the circumstances I do not think that it is necessary for me to make any formal declaration in the circumstances of this case” Judge says measures put in place to alleviate the problem will not have immediate effect. He says it is not now appropriate for any prisoner to take proceedings against the Parole Board alleging breaches of Article 5(4) Unless there are very special circumstances, something has gone badly wrong despite the new arrangements in that prisoner’s particular case. It will not be helpful, either to the prisoner or to the court, if claims are brought which in reality, because of the existing situation, are not likely to achieve any sensible redress and merely add to costs. The court cannot do the impossible. We cannot make orders which are only going to create difficulties for others and are not in any way desirable. The applicant was advised by his counsel that no appeal would be successful as the Court of Appeal would be bound to conclude that it could not prioritise any individual case. The Parole Board recommended that the applicant be moved to open conditions. The Secretary of State accepted the recommendation. The applicant was released in September 2009. He was released on bail in January 2010. He has been remanded in custody until the end of August 2014. He is currently serving a two-and-a-half-year suspended sentence for a drugs offence. The judge said that under. special circumstances, claims of this nature should now be discouraged. The court welcomes the steps that are clearly being taken now to. ensure that that situation does not continue.

name: Eie Enhorn

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56529/00) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of his liberty in breach of Article 5. The application was initially allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26:. The Government, but not the applicant, filed observations on the merits (Rule 59): the Court changed the composition of its Sections on 1 November 2004. The applicant kept three appointments with the county medical officer in September 1994 and one in November 1994. He failed to appear as summoned five times during October and November 1994 and was ordered to be kept in compulsory isolation in a hospital for up to three months. The applicant is prohibited from giving blood and donating organs or sperm. The court's record of the applicant's statement reads, inter alia, as follows: “After learning about his HIV infection he had hardly had any sexual relationships. Henceforward he would only have sexual relations with other HIV infected persons.” It appears to be in dispute whether the instructions were included in the applicant’s medical record as prescribed by section 16 of the 1988 Act. The County Administrative Court ordered that the applicant should be kept in compulsory isolation for up to three months pursuant to section 38 of the 1988 Act. The order took effect immediately, but the applicant failed to report to the hospital. The applicant absconded from the hospital several times, first on 25 April 1995. On 27 September 1995 he ran away again and was at large until the police found him on 28 May 1996. He ran away for a fourth time on 26 February 1997 and was not returned until 26 February 1999. During the period from 26 February until 2 March 1999 the applicant was detained in his room. According to the record of a hearing held in camera on 20 April 1999, the applicant explained that before 1994 he had had ten to twelve sexual relations per year. The owner of the farm hostel gave evidence on the applicant's behalf. The applicant had drunk approximately six strong beers a week and never got drunk. He dreamt of living on his own in a flat, supporting himself on sickness benefit. He had lost all sexual desire and would in future have to decline all sexual relations. If he were to be exempted from compulsory isolation he would follow the instructions issued by the county medical officer. The most recent laboratory test, carried out on 18 March 1999, indicated that the applicant had a healthy liver. It was noted that subsequent to his return the applicant’s liver had improved.” A statement was submitted to the court by a consulting psychiatric chief physician, P.N., connected to the special care facility at the hospital to which the applicant had been admitted. After the applicant's involuntary return, he had attempted to establish contact with him three times, but in vain. On the latest occasion, in March 1999, he claimed that the applicant made a lunge at him. The chances of eliminating or limiting the continuous risk of the infection being spread by means of a prolonged placement in isolation in accordance with the Act are deemed – all facts considered – to have not yet completely vanished. During the last two years when he was on the run, [the applicant] sought medical treatment twice and it has been established that both times he said that he had the HIV virus. The County Administrative Court delivered its judgment, finding against the applicant for the following reasons: “[The applicant] is HIV-positive and thus carries the HIV infection. He has been subjected to compulsory isolation since February 1995 and has during this period absconded from the hospital on several occasions – on the latest occasion for more than two years. During these two years he has used a false name and has been living a very secluded life, obviously owing to the risk of being discovered. A life at liberty makes great demands upon the person carrying the infection.” As regards the laboratory tests concerning the applicant's liver, the county medical officer found these to be of doubtful value, since they had been performed in connection with the compulsory isolation of the applicant. The Court finds that there is good reason to suppose that, if he remains free, [the applicant] will not comply with the practical instructions issued and that this entails a risk of the infection spreading. The Court has not been convinced that [ the applicant] is not misusing alcohol. The applicant again absconded, leaving his whereabouts unknown. In the meantime, he had appealed against the above judgment to the Administrative Court of Appeal, before which he relied on an opinion of 14 May 1999 by the aforementioned chief physician and specialist in psychiatry, C.G., which stated, inter alia, the following: “The opinions [by other psychiatrists and one psychologist] resulting from previous examinations were fairly unanimous in their conclusion that [The applicant] was a man with a paranoid personality disorder, who misused alcohol” The applicant had been celibate since 1996 and had no longer any particular sexual desires or fantasies. He preferred sexual contact with boys around the age of 17. His attitude towards medication against the HIV infection was negative. The Administrative Court of Appeal found against the applicant in 1999. Leave to appeal against the judgment was refused by the Supreme Administrative Court (Reger) In conclusion, C.G. found that the applicant fulfilled the criteria for a paranoid personality disorder, and that, judging from previous information, the applicant suffered from misuse of alcohol but not from alcohol dependency. The applicant could be described in everyday terms as an odd person, but not as mentally ill. Several applications for an extension of the applicant's compulsory isolation were submitted by the county medical officer after June 1999. On 12 December 2001 an application was turned down by the County Administrative Court. The application referred to the fact that the applicant’s whereabouts were unknown and that therefore no information was available regarding his behaviour, state of health and so on. It appears that since 2002 the. applicant's whereabouts have been known, but that the competent county medical. officer has made the assessment that there are no grounds for the applicant.'s further involuntary placement in isolation. ingsrätten) on 5 October 1999. It is now known that the man's location is unknown.

name: Helmut Entleitner
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29544/95) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained that, in proceedings concerning a share of an agricultural association, the agricultural authorities lacked independence and impartiality. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 12 October 1999 the Chamber declared the application admissible. The case was decided on 31 October 1999 by the Court of Justice of the European Union. The decision was in accordance with Article 27 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29544/95) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained that, in proceedings concerning a share of an agricultural association, the agricultural authorities lacked independence and impartiality. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 12 October 1999 the Chamber declared the application admissible. The case was heard by the Third Section of the Court. The judge ruled that the application was admissible and the case was dismissed. The matter has been referred to the International Court of Justice. The share passed with a transfer of the land to a third party in 1949 (as rectified in 1952) The question of the grazing rights had to be determined by reference to the ownership of theLand on 29 April 1868, as that was the last time they were officially mentioned. On 14 March 1995 the Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint rejecting at the same time, in accordance with section 39(2) no. 6 of the Administrative court Act (Verwaltungsgerichtshofgesetz) The judgment was served on the applicant's representative on 31 March 1995. The applicant did not own the land - that is, the applicant didn't own grazing rights.

name: Sahro Osman
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38058/09) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Danish authorities’ refusal to reinstate her residence permit in Denmark was in breach of Articles 3 and 8. The Danish Government (the Government) were represented by their Agent, Mr Thomas Winkler, from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and their Co-Agent, Mrs Nina Holst-Christensen. On 1 February 2011 the Court changed the composition of its Sections and the above application was assigned to the newly composed First Section.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38058/09) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Danish authorities’ refusal to reinstate her residence permit in Denmark was in breach of Articles 3 and 8 of the convention. The Danish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Thomas Winkler, from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and their Co-Agent, Mrs Nina Holst-Christensen, from Ministry of Justice. The application was assigned to the newly composed First Section of the Court. Immigration Service found that the applicant’s residence permit had lapsed pursuant to section 17 of the Aliens Act because she had been absent from Denmark for more than twelve consecutive months. They also considered that she was not entitled to a new residence permit under section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Alien Act, in force at the relevant time, since the applicant was 17 years old. Finally, it found that no special circumstances existed to grant her a residence permitUnder section 9 c, section 9(2) of theAlien Act, under which she was applying for family reunification, she had not contacted the Immigration Service until August 2005. The applicant appealed against the decision by the Migration Service of 21 December 2006. The Immigration Service received a questionnaire from the applicant dated 12 July 2007 used for requests for exemption from the authorities revoking a residence permit. It stated, inter alia, that it had been the applicant’s parents’ decision that she should leave Denmark at the relevant time; that the applicant spoke Danish, but could not read or write the language; that she was very afraid and could not reside in her country of origin as there was unrest. The applicant did not specify that she had actually returned to Denmark, but her signature was dated as set out above in Esbjerg, Denmark. Immigration Service brought case before Copenhagen City Court before which the case was decided on the documents submitted. On 25 April 2008 it found against the applicant. Decision was appealed against to the High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret), henceforth the applicant remained in Kenya. It added that section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Aliens Act had been amended, limiting the right to family re-unification to children under 15 years instead of under 18 years. It found that such decision did not contravene Article 8 of the Convention as invoked by the applicant, and that the case would not have a different outcome. The applicant's parents sent her voluntarily to Kenya to live with family for an indefinite period. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) was refused on 19 January 2008. The applicant was advised to leave Denmark pursuant to section 30 of the Alien’s Act and the possibility of submitting an application for asylum under section 7 of the Aliens Act. The application should be submitted in person to the Immigration Service or the police. So far the applicant has not applied for asylum. The High Court upheld the City Court's decision in October 2008, but said it could not review a final administrative decision of refusal of a residence permit under section 9c, subsection 1.

name: Adele Ursula Price
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that her committal to prison and her treatment in detention violated Article 3 of the convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 12 September 2000 the Chamber declared the application admissible. The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine), and the parties replied to the other in writing. The Court's decision is obtainable from the Registry.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that her committal to prison and her treatment in detention violated Article 3 of the convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. In 2000 the Chamber declared the application admissible. No hearing on the merits was required. The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The Court's decision is obtainable from the Registry [Note by the Registry]. The applicant is four-limb deficient as a result of phocomelia due to thalidomide. The applicant alleges that she was forced to sleep in her wheelchair since the bed was hard and would have caused pain in her hips. She also alleges she was unable to use the toilet since it was higher than her wheelchair and therefore inaccessible. She was offered a hot drink and a meal but refused both. The doctor's note of his examination of the applicant at 12.35 a.m. states: “Patient complained of feeling cold, headache and queasy (no food since admission – offered but refused). Talking quite sensibly, not obviously hypothermia, seated in wheelchair. Tells me unable to lie flat and sleeps on sofa, sitting up, at home’ The applicant was not placed in a normal cell in New Hall, Wakefield, but was instead detained in the prison's health care centre. Her cell had a wider door for wheelchair access, handles for the disabled in the toilet recess and a hydraulic hospital bed. The applicant slept until 7 a.m., when she was moved to another cell and offered food and drink, which she refused. She was taken to New Hall Women's Prison and detained until the afternoon of 23 January 1995. On arrival at the prison the applicant completed a medical questionnaire. She stated that she had health worries but that they were ‘under control – takes it as it comes’ A 'continuous medical record' on the applicant was kept during her detention. The first entry, dated 21 January 1995, stated: ‘I asked duty Governor, Mr Ellis, to give permission for a battery charger for Adele's wheelchair to be brought in if we could arrange it’ The applicant alleged that on the evening of 21 January1995 she was lifted onto the toilet by a female prison officer, but was then left sitting on the toilet for over three hours until she agreed to allow a male nursing officer to clean her and help her off the toilet. The Government submitted that there was no medical condition to admit her to hospital with. Adele claimed she was exposed to two male prison nursing officers. The Government denied that these incidents occurred. The applicant was allowed to serve half her sentence under the Criminal Justice Act 1991. She needed catheterising due to urine retention before her release. Her medical record states that she was due for release this afternoon as soon as transport arrangements can be made. The remission provisions in sections 45 and 33 of the criminal justice Act 1991 meant that the applicant had only to serve three and a half days of her sentence. She was released on January 23, 1995, after serving half of the sentence imposed by the Supreme Court. She is currently serving a sentence of six months in prison. The applicant claimed to have suffered health problems for ten weeks as a result of her treatment in detention. She has not provided direct medical evidence in support of this claim. She was granted legal aid, limited to obtaining evidence and seeking counsel's opinion as to merits and quantum. Her counsel referred to the difficulties which the applicant was likely to face in proving that she had suffered the ill-treatment which she alleged, and that, even if successful, damages were not likely to exceed 3,000 pounds sterling. In the light of this advice, the applicant's legal aid certificate was discharged on 13 May 1996. She had some complaints about her sleeping arrangements. Said that Gv Ellis had said that she could sleep on a chair and have her cell door open all night.

name: Johannes Werner
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 28 October 1996 and by the Government of the Republic of Austria on 25 November 1996. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 31 of Rules of Court B). The lawyer was given leave by the President to use the German language. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 28 October 1996 and by the Government of the Republic of Austria on 25 November 1996. It originated in an application (no. 21835/93) against Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by an Austrian national, Mr Johannes Werner, on 16 March 1993. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 31 of Rules of Court B). The lawyer was given leave by the President to use the German language (Rule 28 § 3). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The hearing in this case and in the Szücs case took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 June 1997. The Court heard addresses by Mr Weitzel, Mr Bürstmayr, Mr Schreiner, Mr Cede and Mrs Gartner. Commission had produced various documents relating to the proceedings before it, as requested by the Registrar on the President’s instructions. A graphologist found that it was unlikely that the signatures on the payment slips for the purchases made with the stolen credit card were in Mr Werner's hand and that witnesses called by the public prosecutor did not have sufficiently clear memories. The applicant and Mr and Mrs Hauser sought compensation from the State for the pecuniary damage sustained on account of their detention. A Vienna Regional Court refused their compensation claims on the ground that, contrary to the requirements of section 2 (1) (b) of the 1969 Act, the suspicion concerning them had not been dispelled. The pair appealed against that decision to the Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) The appeal was dismissed on 29 October 1992. It ruled that suspicion must be dispelled sufficiently to establish that the detained person is not punishable, and cannot be prosecuted, in respect of the conduct in which he was detained. There is no justification for giving the appellants, as they demanded, the opportunity to prove their innocence by taking further evidence. The evidence they propose to adduce cannot be considered likely to lead to such a result. The witnesses it was proposed to call have already been interviewed by the police. The conditions which must be met under section 2 (1) (b) of the Compensation (Criminal Proceedings) Act in order to be able to claim compensation have accordingly not been satisfied. The appellants’ claims must therefore fail.” No representative of the principal public prosecutor’s office attended the deliberations. The main reason why the prosecution was abandoned was that with the passing of time those witnesses’ memories had begun to falter.

name: Maria Gollner
train_texts: The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that civil proceedings concerning her lasted unreasonably long. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided for in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of 21 November 2000, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Court ruled in favour of the applicant and the Austrian Government, and ruled that the application was admissible and that the case should be heard.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49455/99) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that civil proceedings concerning her lasted unreasonably long. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 21 November 2000 the Court declared the application partly admissible. As of 1 November 2001 the application was allocation to the First Section. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided for in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. The case was first heard on 28 April 1995. On 8 August 1995 a further hearing was held. On 7 September 1995 the court requested the expert to supplement his opinion which he did on 23 October 1995. Following two requests by the applicant for extensions of the time-limit, she submitted her comments on the supplemented expert opinion on 10 January 1996. On 14 August 1996 the District Court gave judgment, partly dismissing the applicant’s claim. Following her appeal, the St. Pölten Regional Court quashed the decision for procedural errors on 13 December 1996 and referred the case back. The applicant appealed against this decision and filed a motion challenging the judge for bias. On 24 March 1998 the appeal was dismissed by the Vienna Court of Appeal. On 29 October 1998 the motions for provisional maintenance were partly dismissed by the District Court. On 23 November 1998 the applicant appealed against this decision. On 3 March 1999 the St. Pölten Regional Court quashed the Court’s judgment of 24 September 1998 for procedural errors and referred the case back. On 15 April 1999 the applicant lodged a further appeal and requested that it be given suspensive effect to preserve the status quo before the Regional Court's decision. A further hearing scheduled for 1 December 1999 was cancelled due to the judge's illness. Further hearings were held on 3 May 2000 and 15 June 2000. The judgment was served on 13 February 2001.

name: Josef Prinz
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 2 November 1998. It originated in an application (23867/94) against Austria lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 by Mr Josef Prinz, an Austrian national. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c) On 14 January 1999 the Panel of the Grand Chamber decided that the application would be examined by one of the Sections. After consulting the Agent of the Government and the applicant, the Chamber decided not to hold a hearing in the case.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 2 November 1998. It originated in an application (23867/94) against Austria lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 by Mr Josef Prinz, an Austrian national, on 28 March 1994. The applicant and the Government of Austria are represented by their Agent, Mr F. Cede, Ambassador, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c) The Regional Court found that the applicant had intimidated numerous persons by threats of murder, but that he could not be held responsible because he was suffering from a mental illness. The applicant had, in several letters addressed to judicial authorities and lawyers, respectively, stated his intention to murder particular judges and lawyers. He had a system of fixed ideas and a missionary devotion to the implementation of his plans. His mental disturbances, combined with the further symptoms of aggressiveness, his cruelty and recklessness, entailed a high risk for third persons. The Regional Court considered that it had not been required to hear the judges and other victims concerned, as requested by the applicant. The Supreme Court found that the rejection by the trial court of the applicant's requests for the taking of evidence did not impair the rights of the defence. The question of whether the victims had in fact been intimidated had been irrelevant. The Supreme Court also confirmed the legal qualification of the offences committed by the applicant. The Regional Court had found that his threats of murder were of such a nature as to intimidate third persons in general. Considering his mental illness, there was also a risk of further offences of the same kind. The written judgment was served upon the applicant’s official defence counsel on 29 October 1993. The applicant's defence counsel did not request that the applicant be permitted to attend the Supreme Court hearing. The decision was received at the registry of the Krems District and Regional Court on 17 March 1994. In this respect, the Supreme Court considered that the prognosis was reliably founded on the expert psychiatric opinions and was confirmed by the general impression conveyed by the applicant's criminal acts. the future, which he had submitted in his plea of nullity. The decision was made after a hearing held at the Registry on March 17, 1994, with the verdict read out on March 18, 1994. The judge ruled that the applicant did not have a psychiatric condition and therefore could not have committed the crimes he was charged with. The case was settled out of court on March 25, 1994 and the sentence was commuted to a fine.

name: James Dowsett
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 39482/98) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of a fair trial by virtue of the prosecution’s failure to disclose all material evidence in their possession. By a decision of 14 May 2002, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The Court ruled that the application was admissible, and that the applicant had been entitled to a trial by jury.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 39482/98) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of a fair trial by virtue of the prosecution’s failure to disclose all material evidence in their possession. On 22 March 1989 at Norwich Crown Court the applicant was convicted of the murder of Christopher Nugent and sentenced to life imprisonment. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section on 1 November 2001. The Court declared the application admissible on 14 May 2002. Nugent and Gray were convicted of conspiracy to commit murder. The pair were accused of paying for the murder of another man in exchange for money. The two men claimed that they were not involved in the murder but were forced to pay for the damage done to the victim's body. The case was settled out of court and the men were released from prison in 1998. The trial heard that some of the evidence was false, and the jury was unable to reach a verdict on the rest of the case because of the lack of evidence. They were convicted by a jury of three men and sentenced to 10 years in prison. They are still serving their sentence, which includes three years in jail. The Government submitted that the evidence which was not disclosed at first instance, but was disclosed prior to the applicant’s appeal, fell into two categories. The first type of evidence derived from the Holmes computer system used by the police officers conducting the murder inquiry to store and cross-reference all the information obtained in the course of the inquiry. The second category of evidence related to the parallel investigation into mortgage fraud by a number of people, including the applicant and Nugent. In respect of some of the items in this article, the Government has chosen not to publish the names of any of the people named in the Government's submission. Document no. 580 subsequently came into the applicant’s possession. It is a letter, dated 12 April 1988, from a firm of solicitors acting for Gray addressed to Detective Chief Inspector Baldry of the Suffolk Constabulary. No reason was given to explain the decision to include the document in the list of withheld evidence. Non-disclosure of evidence at trial, particularly evidence discovered in the parallel mortgage fraud investigation, was one of the applicant's grounds of appeal to the Court of Appeal. The applicant also relied on the fact that the trial judge had omitted to direct the jury that a person may lie for reasons unconnected with his guilt in relation to the offence. Court of Appeal dismissed appeal on 29 March 1994. No miscarriage of justice had occurred. Nugent’s dishonesty was made perfectly plain to the jury. The applicant believed that an inducement was promised to Gray by the prosecuting authorities in exchange for his testifying against him. The Court of Appeal concluded: “There was overwhelming evidence that the appellant initiated a plot against the victim Nugent. There was likewise strong evidence that he had indicated what he wanted was to get rid of Nugent...’” The alleged significance of document no. 580 was never determined. The application was dismissed on 28 March 1994, and Gray was sentenced to life in prison with a minimum of 25 years. Stephen Gray was jailed for 11 years for the murder of John Nugent. He was released in 1999. Stephen Runham, who provided the murder weapon and drove the get-away car, received a tariff of 16 years. The Government denied that any inducement was offered to Gray. Under cover of a letter dated 27 June 2001, they sent to the Court undated statements from three senior officers in the Suffolk Constabulary who had been involved in the murder investigation. The Court heard that all one hundred and one pages of the document were written with Mr Gray’s consent and without any form of inducement. The court heard that Gray hoped that his honesty at the trial would one day assist him to make a successful application for parole. Detective Chief Inspector Abrahams, also now retired, said in his statement: “I did not personally offer Gray any inducement or arrangement relating to his sentence’ ‘I do remember that Gray at one time was on hunger strike in prison and that we helped his wife to visit him in prison. How this help was given I do not remember - it may have been in the role of carrying messages to and from” ‘Gray was a very dangerous murderer who I considered enjoyed carrying out his ‘murder’ contract with Mr Dowsett. This matter was so grave that no such undertaking could honestly have been given.’ Gary Runham did the groundwork in planning Nugent’s murder and propositioned Gray at a later stage to do the actual killing. The jury unanimously found Dowsett guilty of murder and he was sentenced to life imprisonment. Gray appeared as a prosecution witness but Runham didn’t. The matter was investigated by an outside Police Force and was found by the DPP [Director of Public Prosecutions] and the PCA to be totally unsubstantiated. The above is to the best of my recollection. I do not know what tariffs were set by the Judge in his sentencing of all three defendants but I assume credit was given for Gray and Runham's guilty pleas.

name: Franz Bachmayer
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36650/05) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were represented by Mr E. Proksch, a lawyer practising in Wien. The Austrian Government (the Government’s Agent) was represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Tichy, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs. On 28 August 2008 the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 1).
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36650/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants have an inalienable and indefinite right to the use of wood (Einforstungsrecht) from certain plots of land now owned by the Republic of Austria and managed by the Austrian Federal Forestry Administration. In 1870 and 1876 the applicant's predecessors were granted the right to exchange their right to use the wood for ownership of the land. The Austrian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Tichy, Head of the International Law Department. The first applicant and Jakob Bachmayer concluded a contract on the transfer of the rights of the latter to the second applicant on 16 January 1991. Subsequently, on 30 April 1986, they filed a request for transfer of jurisdiction (Devolutionsantrag) The Supreme Land Reform Board (Oberster Agrarsenat – Supreme Board) dismissed the request on 2 July 1986, because the questions at issue were of a high complexity and several expert opinions were required. They filed a complaint against this decision with the Administrative Court, which was dismissed on 8 October 1991. On 15 April 1992, after having held oral hearings in 1991 and 1992, the Regional Board dismissed the appeal against the Office of the Regional Governor of 27 June 1985 as regards “count 2” of the decision. The Austrian Federal Forestry Administration lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court on 31 January 2003. The case is still pending before that court. The applicants filed a complaint against the Supreme Land Reform Board's decision to quash the Office of the Regional Governor's decision of 27 June 1985. On 6 June 2006 the Constitutional court declined to deal with the applicants' complaint for lack of prospects of success and, upon their request, transferred the case to the Administrative Court. The application was dismissed and the case was returned back to the Regional Govt. decision. The decision was quashed on 7 November 2005 and remitted the case back to that authority. The court held that the legal provision under review was not in accordance with the Federal Constitution and quashed the decision of the impugned authority of 4 December 2002.

name: Franz Steininger
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 21539/07) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that no tribunal had decided on the imposition of surcharges for unpaid contributions to the Austrian Agricultural Marketing Association. On 23 October 2008 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The case was decided to be heard by the Court of Appeal on 8 October 2013. The verdict was published on 8 November 2013.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that no tribunal had decided on the imposition of surcharges for unpaid contributions to the Austrian Agricultural Marketing Association. The Austrian Government is represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Tichy, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for European and International Affairs. The application was communicated to the Government on 23 October 2008. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The case was dismissed on 17 July 2006 without holding a hearing. The Federal Minister found that after the decision of the European Commission of 30 June 2004 (C(2004)2037), the applicant company was in a position to know precisely which charges it had to pay. The Federal Minister referred further to the Administrative Court’s decision of 20 March 2006, no. 2005/17/230, according to which also the levying of AMA contributions was in accordance with the relevant provisions of EU law. On 25 July 2006 AMA dismissed the request for suspension of the enforcement. The applicant company complained, inter alia, that the surcharge imposed violated its constitutional right to property. It complained further that no public hearing had been held. On 25 September 2006 the Constitutional Court declined to deal with the applicant company’s complaint under Article 144 of the Federal Constitution for lack of prospect of success. As the authorities imposing the surcharges had failed to hold an oral hearing, the applicant. company asked the Administrative Court for a public hearing. The Administrative Court dismissed the. applicant company's complaint on 30 January 2007 and held. as follows: “The present case does not differ in the questions of relevance to the decision. from the one decided by the. Administrative Court on 20 March 2006, no. 2005/17/230. Pursuant to Section 43(2) of the Administrative. Court Act reference is made to it. For the reasons set out in that decision the breach of law. complained of by the applicantCompany also does not exist in view of the present complaint, for which reason. it can be dismissed without further proceedings in camera.”

name: Herbert Tuma
train_texts: The case was made against Austria under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The application was made on 22 May 2007. It was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The decision was made to uphold the application. The case was heard by the European Court of Justice on 26 March 2009. The court ruled on 27 March 2009 that the application was not in breach of Article 34. eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. name: Kristina Sheffield

Ryssdal, decided that a single Chamber should be constituted to consider both cases simultaneously. The first applicant, Miss Kristina Sheffield, is a British citizen born in 1946 and currently resident in London. At birth the applicant was registered as being of the male sex. Prior to her gender reassignment treatment (see paragraph 13 below) she was married. She has one daughter from that marriage, which is now dissolved. The applicant’s former spouse applied to the court to have her contact with her daughter terminated. She states that the judge granted the application on the basis that contact with a transsexual would not be beneficial. The Grand Chamber decided on 25 April 1998 that it was not necessary to hold a further hearing following the relinquishment of jurisdiction by the original Chamber. Her new name has been entered on her passport and driving licence, her birth certificate and various records including social- security and police records continue to record her original name and gender. She has not seen her daughter since then, a period of some twelve years. She was dismissed by her employers in 1986 as a direct consequence of her gender reassignment and has found it impossible to obtain employment in the respondent State. She also notes that she is obliged under the Perjury Act 1911 to disclose her former sexual identity in certain contexts under pain of criminal sanction. The applicant sought to discover whether these personal details were held on police computer files. She did not pursue the enquiry. The second applicant, Miss Rachel Horsham, is a British citizen born in 1946. She has been living in the Netherlands since 1974 and acquired Netherlands citizenship by naturalisation in September 1993. The second applicant was registered at birth as being of the male sex. She left the United Kingdom in 1971 as she was concerned about the consequences of being identified as a transsexual. Thereafter she led her life abroad as a female. From 1990 she received psychotherapy and hormonal treatment and finally underwent gender reassignment surgery on 21 May 1992 at the Free University Hospital, Amsterdam. The British consulate issued a new passport to the applicant recording her new name and her sex as female. She states that she is forced to live in exile because of the legal situation in the UK. Under English law, a person is entitled to adopt such first names or surname as he or she wishes. Under section 11(b) of the Matrimonial Causes Act 1973 any marriage where the parties are not respectively male and female is void. The criteria for determining the sex of a child at birth are not defined in the Act. The practice of the Registrar is to use exclusively the biological criteria (chromosomal, gonadal and genital) as laid down by Mr Justice Ormrod in the above-mentioned case of Corbett v. Corbett. The sex of the child must be entered on the birth certificate. A birth certificate accordingly constitutes a document revealing not current identity but historical facts. The 1953 Act provides for the correction by the Registrar of clerical errors or factual errors. The official position is that an amendment may only be made if the error occurred when the birth was registered. The fact that it may become evident later in a person’s life that his or her “psychological” sex is in conflict with the biological criteria is not considered to imply that the initial entry at birth was a factual error. No error is accepted to exist in the birth entry of a person who undergoes medical and surgical treatment to enable that person to assume the role of the opposite sex. A transsexual continues to be recorded for social security, national insurance and employment purposes as being of the sex recorded at birth. The ECJ ruled that there had been a violation of Article 8 of the Convention. The majority of member States now make provision for such recognition. Only four (including the United Kingdom) do not permit a change to be made to a person’s birth certificate to reflect the re-assigned sex of that person. The ruling of the ECJ was applied by the Employment Appeal Tribunal in a decision handed down on 27 June 1997 (Chessington World of Adventures Ltd v. Reed [1997] 1 Industrial Law Reports) ( paragraphs 21–22) (Liberty's observations on the legal recognition of transsexuals in comparative law) In her application to the Commission lodged on 4 August 1993, Miss Horsham alleged that the refusal of the respondent State to give legal recognition to her status as a woman following gender reassignment surgery gave rise to violations of Articles 3, 8, 12, 13 and 14 of the Convention. The full text of the Commission’s opinions in the two cases and of the dissenting opinions contained in the reports is reproduced as an annex to this judgment. name: Sarah Boyle

This Unit had been set up on an experimental basis to treat selected long-term prisoners and prisoners with violent propensities (see paragraph 32 below) The Unit had a maximum of eight prisoners and was characterised by a more liberal regime. In particular, he discovered that he had special abilities in working with people and in sculpture, writing and other areas of artistic activity. Mr. Boyle was transferred to a Training for Freedom Hostel within the prison in November 1981. He was released on 1 November 1982. As from October 1980 until his release, he was in the lowest security category (Category D) A full vegetarian diet was available at Saughton Prison and no complaint was made by Mr. Boyle to the Governor or to the Secretary of State for Scotland as to its adequacy. The applicants also asserted before the Commission that on occasions the prison censorship officer read out aloud in front of other inmates letters from Mrs Boyle, laughing or making comments about her. Boyle did not make any complaint to the Governor of the Prison or the Secretary of State regarding the manner in which his mail was read. His petition was rejected on the basis that there was a general prohibition of the passing on by a prisoner of material intended for publication or for use on wireless or television. The Government have subsequently acknowledged that in fact this rule was applied in error, since the letter in question was addressed to a person connected with the public media. name: Graham Gaskin

The City Council then refused to disclose the documents, saying they were ‘unprofessional’ and ‘in the public interest’ ‘I regret I do not feel able to help you further. last analysis, for the provider of information, retrospectively collected, to release or refuse to release, in their absolute discretion, the information supplied from the ‘confidential’ embargo originally accorded to it. The reasons for releasing or not releasing are irrelevant whether they are good, bad or indifferent.’ ‘The Government, the effect of Regulation 9 (3) is that, in future, case records will be compiled on the basis that the information contained therein is liable to be disclosed, except in so far as disclosure would be likely to reveal the identity of the informant or another third party' ‘By virtue of section 2 (4) of the Access to Personal Files Act 1987, the 1989 Regulations apply only to information recorded after 1 April 1989. name: Gerard Patrick O’Hara

The applicant was released without charge on 3 January 1986 at 9 p.m., after six days and 13 hours in custody. He was interviewed on thirty-four occasions. The applicant instituted a civil action for damages before the High Court in Northern Ireland in respect of, inter alia, assault, seizure of documents, false imprisonment and unlawful arrest. It was common ground that the murder was a terrorist offence. The superior officer was not called as a witness in the proceedings. He had been told by his superior officer, Inspector B., that the applicant was involved in the murder and stated that these were the reasonable grounds for suspecting the applicant. He did not state that Inspector B. had told him the grounds for his own suspicion. Judge McCollum found that there had been an unlawful taking of the applicant’s notes by a police officer and awarded Mr O’Hara GBP 100 in damages. He rejected the applicant's claims of assault and ill-treatment, finding that he had not satisfied him on the balance of probabilities that his version of events was right and that of the police officers wrong. The judge found on the evidence that the detective constable had a suspicion that the [applicant] was involved in the murder of Kurt Konig and that this suspicion was reasonably based on information given to him by a superior officers at the briefing that morning. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the decision of the High Court that reasonable suspicion could be derived from information provided by a superior officer. “Notwithstanding his concern that more detail of the briefing had not been given, the learned trial judge was able to conclude: ‘(1) that the arresting officer ... did have a suspicion that the [applicant] was involved in a terrorist murder and it was implicit that that suspicion was genuinely held by him.’ These were factual findings and clearly contained all the essential proofs that the respondent was required to adduce to constitute lawful arrest under section 12(1)(b) of the Act” An appeal to the House of Lords against the decision of the Court of Appeal was dismissed on 12 December 1996. In his judgment, Lord Hope of Craighead held that it was not necessary for an arresting officer to possess all the information which had led to the decision to arrest. Lord Steyn stated, inter alia, concerning the general principles: “Certain general propositions about the powers of constables under a section such as section 12(1) can now be summarised. (1) In order to have a reasonable suspicion the constable need not have evidence amounting to a prima facie case. (2) Hearsay information may therefore afford a constable reasonable grounds to arrest, and such information may come from other officers. (3) The information which causes the. constable to be suspicious of the individual must be in existence to the knowledge of the police officer at. the time he makes the arrest. (4) The executive ‘discretion’ to arrest or not ... vests in the constables, who is engaged on the decision. to arrest and not in his superior officers. "How can the badge of superior officers and the fact that he gave an order make a difference? ... In practice it follows that a constable must be given some basis for a request to arrest someone under a provision such as section 12(1), e.g. a report from an informer’s report," he said. The judge added: “It is accepted, and rightly accepted, that a mere request to arrests without any further information by an equal ranking officer, or a junior officer, is incapable of amounting to reasonable grounds for the necessary suspicion.” The judge said the decision was “a matter of principle” and not a matter of law.

name: Hroar Anton Hansen

On 28 June 2007 the applicant instituted civil proceedings before the City Court against Ekheim Invest claiming that he had title to 50% of the Ekheim estate. The applicant referred to legal doctrine, according to which a judgment as a main rule only had legal force in the relationship between the parties to the proceedings. In the period since 2001 the estate had increased so greatly in value that. the Court now had to assess the ownership issue independently of the conclusion reached in. the 2001 judgment. At that time the mortgages on the property had clearly exceeded its value and it had therefore been unproblematic to hold. that, in light of an on-going bankruptcy at the time, the applicant would not have been in a better position in the time of the bankruptcy. The applicant appealed against the City Court’s judgment of 21 January 2008 to the Borgarting High Court (lagmannsrett) The High Court concluded that it refused to admit the appeal (“Anken nektes fremmet”), giving the following reasons: “The High Court finds it clear that the appeal will not succeed, and that its admission should therefore be refused pursuant to Article 29-13(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure.” The applicant appealed the decision to the Supreme Court, but it was not heard until 11 June 2008. The applicant was successful in his appeal against the decision of the High Court. The 2005 Code of Civil Procedure (Tvisteloven) entered into force on 1 January 2008. The conditions for the High Court granting leave to appeal and for refusing the admission of an appeal (“Krav til samtykke. Nektelse”) were set out in Article 29-13. The Supreme Court found it clear that the appeal would not succeed and therefore rejected the appeal under Article 30-9 (2) The Appeals Leave Committee of the Supreme Court (Høyesteretts ankeutvalg) argued notably that the refusal of admission of the appeal lacked reasons. The Ministry of Justice observed that, whilst the right to appellate review of a decision on the merits was an important safeguard, an unlimited and extensive right in this respect could be counterproductive to the rule of law. The committee submitting draft statutory provisions recognised that there was a need to stop clearly unmeritorious appeals to the High Court in order to avoid additional considerable costs being incurred by the parties and by the judiciary. The aim of introducing a merits filtering mechanism before the High. Court, in addition to the already existing leave to appeal requirements, was to promote the interests of procedural economy. The High Court's role in appeal proceedings in a civil case was not to examine the case afresh but to review the first-instance court's decision. It was not a condition for refusing admission of the appeal that the High Court agreed with the City Court’s reasoning or was of the view that its reasoning would stand after the review of the case. The United Nations Human Rights Committee communicated its “Views” on a communication (no. 1542/2007) lodged by Mr Abdel Kereem Hassan Aboushanif under the Protocol to the 1966 International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights concerning the lack of reasoning in a decision by a Norwegian High Court. The Norwegian Supreme Court ruled that every High Court decision refusing admission of an appeal under the Code of Criminal Procedure ought to be reasoned. Omitting to provide reasons “impair[ed] the effective exercise of the right to have one’s conviction reviewed”. The requirement of reasons was a necessary safeguard for ensuring a substantial review. Ensuing developments in the Supreme Court's case-law as well as legislative change are likely to lead to a change in the Norwegian Human Rights Act. The Human Rights Committee considers that, in the circumstances of the case, the lack of a duly reasoned judgment, even if in brief form, provides a justification for the court's decision that the appeal would be unsuccessful. The Supreme Court quashed a High Court decision refusing admission of an appeal on the basis of Article 29-13 (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. A majority of seven members considered the subject matter in relation to Article 88 of the Constitution, according to which the Supreme Court was to adjudicate in final instance. The majority observed that this provision left the legislator great latitude in organising the national system of judicial remedies as it deemed appropriate. The extent of the reasoning required would vary considerably, depending on the nature of the particular case, ranging from a couple of sentences to more extensive reasoning of a legal or factual character. There were also other mechanisms that could ensure the. Supreme Court the necessary control. Supreme Court’s competence to review the High Court procedure encompassed questions of whether a breach had occurred of expressly stated rules of procedure. The Supreme Court was empowered to fully examine the application of the law and the assessment of the evidence. This also covered whether in the light of the points of law raised in the case was justifiable for the high court to refuse admission of the appeal. No constitutional obligation to give reasons for a High Court refusal to admit an appeal could be justified by the interests of the Supreme Court procedure, says the majority of the court. The majority relied on systemic considerations and what they considered as clear presumptions on the part of the legislator. The Norwegian Supreme Court ruled that the obligation to state reasons for a refusal of admission of an appeal under Article 29-13 (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure also extended to civil cases. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 8400/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Crown case was that D.G. had been summoned to the scene by the applicant and another co-accused, M.H., using a mobile telephone belonging to D.M. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the Crown's evidence regarding the alleged phone calls came from a number of sources. Crown case involved video recordings from closed circuit television (CCTV) cameras near the scene. From a combination of video recordings and mobile telephone records for M.H.'s telephone, the Crown contended that the applicant could be seen making certain calls. There was also eye witness evidence of him making at least one of the critical calls. The applicant's case at trial was that he had made no calls on M. H.'s mobile telephone. However, he said that he was a drug dealer using his own telephone and that the calls were made for his own criminal purposes and were nothing to do with the summoning of D.G. The jury asked to be shown the video evidence again on the second day of their deliberations. The judge agreed that the recordings could be taken into the jury room and played there by the jury if required. The prosecution argued that the jury should be able to watch the video on their own. The jury retired and the case was adjourned until the next day. The case was decided in favour of the applicant by a majority verdict of not guilty. The verdict was quashed on appeal by the Court of Appeal in March 2013. The trial continued until the end of the trial in April 2013.
