Judge instructed the jury to return and directed them as follows: “Ladies and gentlemen, we are going to leave [Officer M] in this court with you, and he will play any part of the video that you have seen. He will play it as you think fit. Remember that there is more than one camera that operates – that sometimes you are viewing camera no. 1, and I think at other times camera No. 2.” “There is to be no other communication with him – or any communication from him – than simply asking him to play you what you want to see,” the judge added. Jury left alone in the court room with Officer M at 2.05 p.m. to begin reviewing the video evidence. Jury spent almost two hours viewing the video recordings in the presence of Officer M. When the court reconvened, leading counsel for the applicant directed the judge's attention to various authorities, including Archbold's Criminal Pleading, Evidence and Practice. Judge: 'The unusual circumstance is this ...: we cannot put the equipment in the jury room' The judge agreed to reconvene at 4 p. m. as he did not wish to interrupt the jury's viewing of the video Evidence. The jury were allowed to watch the video footage for the remainder of the trial. Counsel for the applicant suggested that the police officer could continue to operate the equipment but that the presence of a jury bailiff in the jury room would ensure that there was no communication between the parties. Judge: 'I am merely looking at the peculiar situation that arises here, and the simple fact of the matter, if we boil it down to first principles, is quite simply this: throughout this afternoon, there has, in fact, been an outsider in the Jury retiring room' Judge: ‘And that is the first problem ... The second problem is that the jury could not work the equipment.' Prosecutor: 'And the problem is this: that those who sit behind the dock are essentially put on trust in relation to the police Officer's lack of communication' Judge observed that there was a need to protect the privacy of the jury while preserving the integrity of the situation. He pointed out that “the die had been cast” and that: “... either the procedure in the circumstances of this particular case is acceptable, or it is not.” It was then suggested that either the jury themselves be instructed how to use the equipment or that the video be played in open court in the presence of the judge. The following morning, a solution was agreed which would allow the jury to operate the equipment themselves, with information provided to assist them in locating the part of the recordings that they wished to view. The jury subsequently viewed the video recordings alone for about an hour. They continued their deliberations for the rest of the day and into the following morning. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal on 20 June 2006. The jury found the applicant guilty of attempted murder and making threats to kill. He was sentenced to 25 years in prison for attempted murder. His co-accused, M.H., was found not guilty. The applicant appealed, arguing that the approach taken to the viewing of the video recording amounted to a fundamental infringement of the integrity of the jury's deliberations. The court noted that the officer in question was a serving police officer. He had not been called as a witness. Court of Appeal refused to receive witness statement from Officer M which had not been seen by the applicant or his lawyers. The court examined the trial transcript and said it had absolutely no doubt that assent to the presence of Officer M while the jury viewed the CCTV footage was given by all counsel concerned. The Court observed that this was not a case where any bias, or apparent bias, was in question. The question was whether the conviction was safe, and in particular whether the unusual course taken meant that there was an unacceptable risk that the jury may have come under improper extraneous influence after the close of evidence in the case. A fair trial required that a jury should not be improperly influenced. Jurors should not be able to influence the outcome of a case, says the Court of Appeal. The court noted that the approach adopted in the present case occurred with the authority of the judge and with the consent of all parties. The safeguard of the integrity of the jury system lies in the respect that jurors have for the serious oath that they have taken, rather than in requiring formal rules attempting to insulate them from contact with the outside world, the court said. “No question arose as to the applicant's right to a fair trial being waived. Such a right could only be waived after a full investigation of the facts, in particular as to whether the applicant was fully apprised of the options available,” said the court. The court noted that the jury had been in any way inhibited by the presence of the police officer: they spent considerable time viewing the recordings. The jury continued to view the recordings alone the following morning and clearly gave further consideration to them. The significance was that: “... the jury arrived, after prolonged deliberation, at discriminating verdicts” The court concluded that on the facts of this case, whether or not what occurred should have happened – and we will come to that in a moment – the hypothetical informed and fair minded observer would be aware of all the factors to which we have called attention and he would, we are satisfied, not believe that there was a real danger. Jurors commonly ask questions on all manner of topics. Some of them call for the jury to be reminded of a particular area of evidence. They must, we are quite satisfied, as jurors be entitled to review precisely the same material as has been put in evidence in court. If the necessary equipment can be provided in any particular court by agreement as to compatibility of machinery between parties and the court, then so much the better. If in the last resort it really is the case that the recorded material simply is incapable of being played on any machinery which the jury can take into the retiring room, then we think that the normal course should be followed. eval_texts: The case originated in two applications (nos. 41516/10 and 75702/13) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) Two British nationals, Mr Charles Bernard O’Neill and Mr William Hugh Lauchlan (‘the applicants’), on 15 July 2010 and 28 November 2013 respectively. The first applicant was born in 1962 and is currently detained in HMP Glenochil in Scotland. The second applicant wasborn in 1976 and is now detained in. HMP Edinburgh. The United Kingdom Government were represented by their Agent, Mr P. McKell of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The applicants' complaints concerning the length of their criminal proceedings were communicated to the Government on 13 November 2012. The applicants were detained by the police under section 14 of the Criminal Procedure (Scotland) Act 1995 on 17 September 1998. They were interviewed separately by police officers for over five hours. During these interviews they were directly accused of the murder of A.M. Both applicants asked police officers if they were going to be charged with the murder, but received indications to the contrary. Following the interviews, neither applicant was arrested or charged with any offence owing to insufficient evidence. In April 2004 the applicants were arrested in Spain in connection with the apparent abduction of a fourteen year old boy. In November 2004 both applicants appeared on indictment in respect of offences contrary to the Sex Offenders Act 1997. They pled guilty and on 4 April 2005 they were sentenced to a further three years’ imprisonment. The applicants were charged with the murder of A.M. and with concealing and disposing of her body in an attempt to pervert the course of justice. They appeared on petition at Kilmarnock Sheriff Court were they were committed for further examination and remanded in custody. A Proof of Life report was produced on 18 November 2005 (supplemented on 5 January 2006), which concluded that A. M. had been dead since approximately June 1997. The twelve-month period for bringing proceedings expired on 4 April 2006 and the Lord Advocate did not seek an extension of time. By November 2006 both applicants had served the custodial element of their earlier criminal sentences and were released from prison. C.M. disappeared in Spain in November 2007 and returned to the UK in November 2008. The police continued to conduct periodic reviews of the decision to take ‘no proceedings meantime’ in respect of the 2005 petition. Central Scotland Police formed ‘Operation Aspen’, the objective of which was to look for evidence of further sexual offending by the applicants. New evidence came to light concerning the circumstances of A.M’s disappearance and the applicants’ sexual offending. Crown Counsel concluded that there had been a material change in the prospects of securing a conviction against both applicants on the murder charges contained in the earlier 2005 petition on 9 September 2008. On 10 September 2008 the applicants were served with an indictment. Both applicants were convicted of. sexual offences charges and sentenced to periods of. imprisonment ranging from eight to ten years to run concurrently. Both appealed against conviction and sentence. The applicants’ trials took place between 19 April 2010 and 13 May 2010. They were sentenced to life imprisonment for murder, with a tariff of thirty years for the first applicant and twenty-six years for. the second applicant. The first applicant also argued that the murder charge against him should be dismissed for reason of delay. However, the court refused to dismiss the charge, finding, inter alia, that proceedings had begun on 5 April 2005; that the “reasonable time” permitted by Article 6 had not been exceeded. The first applicant lodged a Note of Appeal on 2 September 2010, containing numerous grounds and sub-grounds on a wide range of issues regarding all the charges. The sifting judges granted him leave to appeal against his sentence for murder, but not against his conviction. The applicants subsequently applied under section 107(8) of the Criminal Procedure (Scotland) Act 1995 (“the 1995 Act’) for leave to reinstate grounds which the judges had found to be unarguable, including those relating to the length of proceedings. The main issue before the Supreme Court was whether the applicants could be said to have been “charged” on 17 September 1998 or whether the appropriate “starting point” for the purposes of Article 6 § 1 was 5 April 2005. Supreme Court observed that as the “fair trial” guarantee under Article 6 was distinct from the ‘reasonable-time’ guarantee it had to be approached separately. The court concluded that the correct “starting point” in the applicants’ proceedings was 5 April 2005 and the case was remitted to the Appeal Court. The Appeal Court dismissed the first applicant’s appeal against conviction and sentence on 27 March 2014, and the second applicant‘s appeal on 19 June 2014. name: Günther Paul Litwin
train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 29090/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a stateless person, Mr Günther Paul Litwin. The applicant alleged that he had been denied access to the appeal courts, contrary to Article 6 of the convention. The case was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) on 29 March 2010. The application was decided on the merits and admissible by the Court on 30 June 2010.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29090/06) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been denied access to the appeal courts. The court, following a proposal made by the applicant’s counsel, promised a maximum penalty of nine‑and‑a‑half years’ imprisonment in exchange for his right to appeal. The Government did not take part in the agreement reached, and the public prosecutor did not attend the hearing. The content of the agreement is in dispute between the parties. The applicant was convicted of aggravated extortion, aggravated robbery and attempted aggravated robbery (two counts of each offence) and dangerous bodily injury (one count) and sentenced to nine-and-a-half years' imprisonment. The court considered the fact that the applicant had eventually waived his right to the confiscated assets and had thus delivered a major proportion of his criminal profits as a mitigating factor. The applicant subsequently appointed new counsel. On 12 April 2001 the applicant’s new counsel applied for restitution of the status quo ante and lodged an appeal on points of law, arguing that the waiver of the right to appeal had been invalid because it had not complied with the requirements of the Federal Court of Justice's case-law. The applicant claimed that the waiver of the right to appeal had been declared before delivery of the judgment and had been invalid for this reason. The Court of Justice did not find it necessary to establish whether the waiver had been part of a negotiated agreement, as this fact did not call into question the validity of the waiver as such. The only decisive factor was whether the accused had been unduly influenced when waiving his right to appeals. In the present case, there was no indication that there had been such undue influence. The applicant could not be granted restitution of the status quo ante. The decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 5 July 2001. A German man claims he was unduly influenced when waiving his right to appeal in exchange for a maximum penalty of nine-and-a-half years' imprisonment. The Federal Constitutional Court (file no. 2 BvR 1339/01) refused to admit the constitutional complaint for examination without giving further reasons. This decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 4 December 2003. The court ruled that the process had been arbitrary, not been in accordance with the statutory provisions governing the confiscation of assets in criminal proceedings and had also constituted a violation of the right to an effective remedy. On 20 November 2003 the Federal Constitutional. Court ( file no.2 Bvr 1339 /01), relying on the relevant provisions of its rules of procedure, refused to admitted the constitutional. complaint.

name: Bengt Hellborg
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) and this case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. The Court declared the application partly admissible.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his right to the peaceful enjoyment of his possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 had been violated as he was not permitted to build a second house on his property. He complained about the length of the related proceedings before the administrative authorities and courts and also about the refusal of the Supreme Administrative Court to hold an oral hearing. By a decision of 30 November 2004, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required. The applicant’s late father had applied on 13 June 1989 to the Building Committee (byggnadsnämnden) of Lund for tentative approval (förhandsbesked) of a plan to divide Humanisten 1 and build a new one-family house. The purpose of such an approval, issued under Chapter 8, section 34 of the 1987 Act, was to give a property owner who was planning a building project the possibility to obtain an advance assessment of whether the planned measures may be permitted at all. In assessing an application for a building permit made within two years after the grant of tentative approval, the Building committee was bound by the determinations made in that approval. On 15 April 1992 the Building Committee granted the applicant a tentative approval of a plan to divide the plot – Humanisten 1 – and to build a new one-family house. Several of the applicant’s neighbours opposed the measure with reference to the special character of the neighbourhood. The Land Survey recommended that the property plan be repealed in order to facilitate a division of the property enabling the applicant to construct a new house on the resulting new plot. A new property plan would not be required; repeal of the existing plan would be sufficient and the division would be consistent with the detailed development plan and be suitable for its purpose. It appears that those proceedings were at a standstill until January 1997 (see section 4 below) The Government quashed the Board’s decision to repeal the property plan. for Humanisten 1. The Government observe that the entire block has long been occupied by buildings in accordance with the city plan and plot divisions. .... The Government find that the suitability of the intended change of the property and the development conditions within the block ought to be examined through a new detailed development plan for the area in which the size and situation of the buildings can also be regulated to a sufficient extent. In view of this and everything else which has emerged in the case, the Government find. that the decision to repealed the propertyPlan should be quashed. Supreme Administrative Court ruled that the Government’s decision was not unlawful and confirmed it. Court held that the decision to quash the lower instances’ decisions regarding the property plan does not conflict with any legal rule in the manner claimed by the applicant. The application for re-opening of the case was refused by the Supreme Administrative Court on 10 April 2002. The adoption of a new detailed development plan and related proceedings was also ruled not unlawful. The Court found that the adoption of the plan was within the scope of jurisdiction of the authorities in planning matters. It should therefore be upheld. The case was dismissed on the grounds that the case could be examined and decided without holding an oral hearing. The applicant appealed against the decision to the Board, which on 18 January 1999 upheld the Council’s decision. The applicant made a further appeal to the Government, which was rejected on 23 June 2004. The Board found that the public interest in protecting the cultural heritage of the neighbourhood outweighed the applicant's private interest. It quashed the Building Committee's 15 April 1992 decision on the grounds that the tentative approval was contrary to the existing property plan and detailed development plan. The neighbours claimed that, although they were affected by the decision, the Committee had failed to hear them in the case or inform them about the decision. In a decision of 31 March 2000, the Board first found. that the neighbours were entitled to appeal against the tentative approving and was satisfied that they had done so within the required time-limit. 10 February 1999 to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Skåne. In September he asked the court to give priority to the case. In November 2000 the applicant appealed against both judgments to the Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten), in Gothenburg. On 15 September 2004 the Supreme Administrative Court refused the applicant leave to appeal in both cases. In separate proceedings in 1997, 1997, the applicant sought a declaratory judgment establishing liability in relation to the building permit. The applicant was awarded a settlement of £2.2 million in 1998. He was also awarded a further £1.5 million in 1999. The applicant requested the District Court (tingsrätten) of Lund to declare that the Municipality of Lund was liable to pay him compensation for both actual and potential damage caused. The District Court found that the Building Committee had disregarded a clear and unambiguous provision in the 1987 Act. Since the applicable plans did not allow the grant of a building permit and since an amendment to the plan could not be a condition attached to a tentative approval, such approval should not have been granted. The Municipality appealed to the Court of Appeal (hovrätten) of Skåne and Blekinge. By judgment of 13 October 1998 the Court declared that the municipality was liable for the applicant's damages. In 2001 the applicant instituted civil proceedings against the Municipality requesting compensation in an amount of SEK 3,000,000 for the damage he had suffered due to the refusal to grant him the building permit. The Municipality contested the request. The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Court of Appeal, which on 23 May 2005 refused the applicant leave to appeal. The Supreme Court of Sweden dismissed the applicant's appeal against the decision in May 2005. The case is still pending in the District Court of Lund and the applicant is seeking compensation for the damages he claims he has suffered as a result of the refusal of a building permit to build a new house.

name: Franz Osinger

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 54645/00) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that there was no public hearing in the succession proceedings. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 26 June 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine) and that the parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section, the Chamber that would consider the case. The farm was found to be a hereditary one (Erbhof) within the meaning of the Agricultural Succession Act 1958 (Anerbengesetz) The applicant filed an application to be appointed as its principal heir. An expert concluded that the farm should not be considered hereditary. The other heirs appealed. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals and upheld the Regional Court's finding. The parties of the hereditary proceedings did not reach an agreement, an estate curator (Verlassenschaftskur) was appointed to look after the farm. The farm was sold in 1993 and is now owned by a private company. The estate curator is still at the farm today. The applicant already owned part of another hereditary farm. The District Court dismissed the applicant's request to be appointed as principal heir. The applicant appealed and submitted a new private expert opinion. An estate curator was appointed and the succession proceedings were suspended. On 10 June 1999 the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant's appeal on points of law. This decision was served on the applicant's lawyer on 14 July 1999. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the applicant did not meet the requirements to be a principal heir because he already owned a part of a hereditary farm, and that he did not have sufficient evidence to be considered as such.

name: Duncan Lustig-Prean
train_texts: The case originated in two applications against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Both applicants complained that the investigations into their homosexuality and their discharge from the Royal Navy constituted violations of Article 8 of the Covention. The applications were joined to two similar applications (nos. 33985/96 and 33986/96, Smith v. the United UK and Grady v the United States) The Commission granted Mr Beckett on 23 January 1998 the right to appeal to the European Court of Justice (“ECJ”) on the question of the applicability of the Council Directive on the Implementation of the Principle of Equal Treatment for Men and Women.
eval_texts: The case originated in two applications against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Both applicants complained that the investigations into their homosexuality and their discharge from the Royal Navy on the sole ground that they are homosexual constituted violations of Article 8 of the Covention taken alone and in conjunction with Article 14. The Government, represented by Mr M. Eaton and, subsequently, by Mr C. Whomersley, both Agents, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, submitted their observations on 17 October 1997. The Commission decided to adjourn the applications pending the outcome of a reference to the European Court of Justice (“ECJ”) pursuant to Article 177 of the Treaty of Rome. The High Court delivered its judgment withdrawing its reference in the case of R. v. Secretary of State for Defence, ex parte Perkins (13 July 1998) The applications fall to be examined by the Court in accordance with the provisions of Article 5 of the Protocol No. 11. On 4 May 1999 the President of the Chamber decided to grant Mr Lustig-Prean legal aid. The hearing in this case took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 18 May 1999. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr C. Whomersley, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr J. Eadie, Counsel, Ms J. Betteley, Ms. Pfieffer, Advisers. The first applicant joined the Royal Navy Reserve as a radio operator in 1982. He became a midshipman in the executive branch of the navy in 1983. In 1994 the applicant attained the rank of lieutenant-commander. The applicant was interviewed on 13 June 1994 by personnel from the service police about his sexual orientation for approximately 20 minutes. He was asked, inter alia, whether he had had homosexual contact with service personnel (at least four questions on this subject) and whether his parents knew of his homosexuality. He then confirmed that he was homosexual, acknowledging that he had been a practising homosexual since his teenage years. The application was denied. The second applicant joined the Royal Navy in 1989. In 1991 he became a substantive weapons engineering mechanic. On 16 December 1994 the Admiralty Board informed the applicant that it had decided to terminate his commission and to discharge him, administratively, from the navy with effect from 17 January 1995. The ground for his discharge was his sexual orientation. The applicant’s commission was removed and most of the bonus which he had received with that promotion was recouped by the naval authorities (£4,875 out of £6,000). His term of service would otherwise have terminated in 2009, with the possibility of renewal. He left the ship ‘with a well-deserved reputation for outstanding professional ability and admirable personal qualities’ The applicant’s report dated 27 November 1992 noted that he displayed potential in a number of areas essential to good leadership. In May 1993 the applicant had been refused time off to deal with a personal matter (he wished to collect his Aids test results) and consequently he spoke with the chaplain, to whom he admitted his sexual orientation. He was then called for interview by the service police. The applicant immediately confirmed his homosexuality, later clarifying that he first had “niggling doubts” about hissexual orientation approximately two and a half years previously. The interview was suspended pending the search. During the search, slides (of himself, his partner and some of his service friends) and personal postcards were seized. The service police report completed after the applicant’s interview included several internal documents where it was noted that the applicant, in openly declaring his homosexuality and his relationship with a civilian, had effectively disposed “of any immediate potential security concern” For that reason, it was considered in the report that “no cause was identified for conducting a security interview with Beckett” That report also accepted that a case for fraudulent entry into the armed forces would be inappropriate given the date when the applicant had discovered his homosexuality. The applicants’ judicial review proceedings (R.C. v. Ministry of Defence, ex parte Smith and Others 2 Weeky Law Reports 305) The High Court dismissed the application for judicial review. Lord Justice Simon Brown gave the main judgment of the court. He noted that the cases illustrated the hardships resulting from the absolute policy against homosexuals in the armed forces. All four of the applicants had exemplary service records, some with reports written in glowing terms. In his view, the tide of history was against the Ministry of Defence. He further observed that it was improbable, whatever the High Court would say, that the policy could survive for much longer and added, “I doubt whether most of those present in court throughout the proceedings now believe otherwise.” The case was heard at the Royal Courts of Justice in London. For confidential support call the Samaritans in the UK on 08457 90 90 90, visit a local Samaritans branch or click here for details. Simon Brown LJ also found that the Equal Treatment Directive was not applicable to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. He also observed that the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, Israel, Germany, France, Norway, Sweden, Austria and the Netherlands permitted homosexuals into the armed forces. A brief analysis of the Convention’s case-law led the judge to comment that he strongly suspected that, as far as the United Kingdom's obligations were concerned, the days of the policy were numbered. It followed that the applications had to be rejected “ albeit with hesitation and regret”. In exercising merely a secondary judgment, this Court is bound to act with some reticence. Our approach must reflect, not overlook, where responsibility ultimately lies for the defence of the realm. In August 1995 a consultation paper was circulated by the Ministry of Defence to ‘management’ levels in the armed forces relating to the policy against homosexuals in those forces. It was indicated that the case was likely to progress to the European courts and that the applicants in the judicial review proceedings had argued that the Ministry’s position was “bereft of factual evidence’ On 3 November 1995 the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal. The Master of the Rolls, Sir Thomas Bingham, delivered the main judgment (with which the two other judges of the Court. of Appeal agreed) He considered that the court may not interfere with the exercise of an administrative discretion on substantive grounds save where the court is satisfied that the decision is unreasonable in the sense that it is beyond the range of responses open to a reasonable decision- maker. Master of the Rolls: Court must not shrink from its fundamental duty to ‘do right to all manner of people’ He noted that the case concerned innate qualities of a very personal kind, that the decisions of which the applicants complained had had a profound effect on their careers and prospects and that the applicants’ rights as human beings were very much in issue. However, he concluded that the policy could not be considered “irrational” at the time the applicants were discharged from the armed forces, finding that the threshold of irrationality was “a high one” and that it had not been crossed in this case. “It is, inevitably, common ground that the United Kingdom’s obligation, binding in international law, to respect and ensure compliance with [Article 8 of the Convention] is not”. Henry LJ of the Court of Appeal agreed with the judgment of the Master of the Rolls and, in particular, with the latter’s approach to the irrationality test and with his view on the inability of the court to resolve Convention issues. He questioned the utility of a debate as to the likely fate of the ‘longstanding’ policy of the Ministry of Defence before the European Court of Human Rights with which the primary adjudicating role on the Convention lay. Thorpe LJ agreed with both preceding judgments and with the views expressed on the rationality test to be applied and on its application in the particular case. He also found that the Equal Treatment Directive did not apply to complaints in relation to sexual orientation. In December 1995 Mr Lustig-Prean issued proceedings in the Industrial Tribunal claiming unfair dismissal and sexual discrimination contrary to the Sexual Discrimination Act 1975. Those proceedings were adjourned pending the above-described application for leave to appeal to the House of Lords. In December 1997 Mr Beckett also issued proceedings claiming sexual discrimination. In the light of subsequent decisions of the ECJ and of the domestic courts, the second applicant subsequently requested the withdrawal of those proceedings which were, on 27 August 1998, dismissed by the Industrial tribunal. The applicants’ Industrial Tribunal proceedings were dismissed on 25 April 1996. The appeals committee of the Appeals Committee of the House. of Lords refused leave to Appeal to the Lords on 19 March 1996.

name: Douglas Gary Vinter

eval_texts: The case originated in three applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the whole life orders which had been imposed on them violated Articles 3, 5, 6 and 7 of the convention. The Court decided to give notice of the applications to the Government and rule on the admissibility and merits of the cases at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The applications were filed by Douglas Gary Vinter, Jeremy Neville Bamber and Peter Howard Moore. The Government was represented by their Agent, Ms L. Dauban of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The power to release a prisoner is provided for in section 30(1) of the Crime (Sentences) Act 1997. The Secretary of State will only exercise his discretion on compassionate grounds when the prisoner is terminally ill or seriously incapacitated. All three applicants maintain that these whole life orders, as they apply to their cases, are incompatible inter alia with Articles 3 and 5 § 4 of the Convention. The High Court may set a minimum term of imprisonment or make a whole life order. The applicants are currently serving mandatory sentences of life imprisonment for murder. The first applicant was sentenced to life imprisonment on 20 May 1996, the first applicant’s case this order was made by the trial judge under the current practice. First applicant was sentenced to life in prison for the murder of a work colleague. Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 25 June 2009. First applicant pleaded guilty to murder and instructed his counsel not to make any submissions in mitigation lest it add to the grief of the victim’s family. He was given the mandatory life sentence and made a whole life order. The court considered the general principles for determining the minimum term of a mandatory life term (as set out in schedule 21 to the 2003 Act: see relevant domestic law and practice below). It found that, given the circumstances of the offence, there was no reason whatever to depart from the normal principle enshrined in thenormal principle. The second applicant's parents, his adoptive sister and her two young children were shot and killed in 1985. The second applicant was subsequently charged and, on 28 October 1986, convicted of the murders. In 1988, the Secretary of State imposed a whole life tariff. In 2008, following the entry into force of section 276 and schedule 22 to the 2003 Act, the second applicant applied to the High Court for review of the whole life order. The High Court found that there was no reason to depart from the views of the Lord Chief Justice and the secretary of State. It therefore imposed a name order and sentence of life in prison. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 14 May 2009. The Court of Appeal found that the whole life order imposed by the High Court was not only correct but, for the purposes of punishment and retribution, fully justified. The review procedure created by the 2003 Act was compatible with Article 7 of the Convention as, properly construed, the relevant statutory provisions meant a prisoner could not be disadvantaged by the outcome of the review. The applicant, himself a homosexual, was alleged to have committed the murders for his own sexual gratification. Each victim was stabbed many times with a large combat knife which the third applicant had bought for that purpose. He made extensive admissions about all four murders to the police. The police had been recommending that the second applicant should never be released. The Secretary of State had been entitled to choose between those recommendations or to adopt neither of them. The applicant’s defence was that the murders had been committed by someone else, though he admitted to having been present at all the murders save for that of the second victim. The High Court found that, since the case involved the murder of two or more persons, sexual or sadistic conduct and a substantial degree of premeditation, under schedule 21 the starting point was a whole life order. There were no mitigating features and even the Lord Chief Justice, in recommending a minimum term of thirty years, had shared the trial judge's view that it might never be safe to release the third applicant. The court added that no issue of arbitrariness arose and whether such a sentence was disproportionate depended on the facts of each case. Third applicant applied to the Court of Appeal to certify that its judgment concerned a point of law of general public importance which ought to be considered by the House of Lords. On 14 August 2009, he was informed that, because the Court. of Appeal had refused his application for permission to appeal against sentence, an application to certify a point. of law for the House. of Lords could not be made. The trial judge said: “A man in a police cell is entitled to privacy just as much as a man sitting at his fireside in his own home” There is no statute which provides for lawful bugging of police cells nor to prohibit such an action, he said. The weight of his loss of privacy is another matter which I may take into account, the judge added. The judge rejected five safeguards that should have been afforded to the accused if the bugging was to be lawful. He said that if they were to be required in each case, no covert listening would ever be realistic or possible. The trial judge added: ‘Such evidence can in serious cases such as this be very very serious’ The applicant together with three others was convicted on 20 July 2000 of various robbery and firearms offences. The appeal was dismissed on 13 February 2002, dismissing the appeal. The trial court considered the evidence of a Chief Superintendent who testified that he believed that, on 10 October 2002, the applicant was a member of the IRA. The applicant made an application for an inquiry into PK’s sources arguing that his trial would be unfair if he did not know these sources and the evidence against him (Rowe and Davis v. the United Kingdom [GC], no. 28901/95, ECHR 2000-II). The prosecution, which had no access to the confidential source material, opposed the applicant's request on the basis of the principle of informer privilege. The SCC found that, while it was unthinkable that information that would threaten lives or State security would be disclosed, the admission of PK's evidence without any inquiry into its basis would unfairly balance the trial in favour of the prosecution. Chief Superintendent PK had 25 years' service as a police officer most of which was devoted to combating subversion. It was difficult to imagine anyone better informed on the subject in the country. The SCC was persuaded beyond any doubt by the belief evidence of PK that the accused were members of the IRA as charged. The trial court held that the demands of justice required that it should not convict solely on the basis of PK’s evidence so the SCC went on to examine whether there was evidence which supported and corroborated the belief of PK. It found that there was nothing in the files that would assist the defence in proving the innocence of their clients. Packaging from a Rayovac torch and a receipt dated 10 October 2002 were later found in the Nissan Micra when it was searched. The SCC considered that the above evidence showed that both accused were aware of, or acquiesced in, unlawful activities in Corke Abbey. However, it was of the view that those activities could equally be ascribed to persons engaged in organised crime as opposed to those engaged in subversive crime. The court accepted a piece of paper containing the drawing of a key and a telephone number which the court accepted was that of MB, the owner of the Nissan Almera with the false number plates. It was also satisfied, having heard abundant evidence which included sightings of the applicant and his co-accused together in the middle of the night, that they were ‘well known’ to each other. The court was satisfied that not only were the relevant statutory provisions invoked and adequately explained to each accused but each was given an opportunity to protest in the event that he had not understood that explanation, an opportunity which was ignored. It was clear to the court that each was deliberately and offensively ignoring all that was being asked of them. The video-recordings of the interviews were shown to the trial court. It noted that, not only did each remain totally silent during the course of interview, but each appeared to take no ostensible interest whatsoever in what was going on. They sat bolt upright showing remarkable self-control throughout, in that their only movement was an occasional blink of the eyes but they made no effort to engage with the interviewers. The trial court had no doubt as to the materiality of a vast number of the questions put to each accused and it was clear that each had made no effort whatsoever to answer them. For example, each accused was asked to affirm or deny that he was a member of the IRA. Each was asked whether he knew the men arrested at Corke Abbey on the night of 10 October 2002. The court was satisfied that their silence amounted to corroboration of the belief evidence given by Chief Superintendent PK. It was persuaded beyond all reasonable doubt that each of the accused was guilty of charged. The trial court added that it was not convinced that, standing alone, either the activities at Corce Abbey or the documentation found upon a search of their homes necessarily indicated activities or membership of an unlawful organisation.  applicant was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment. Appeal to the Court of Criminal Appeal (‘CCA’) was refused. Court found no evidence that would have assisted the accused and the material examined constituted a good basis for the belief of the Chief Superintendent. CCA rejected the submission that the SCC, which decided on guilt or innocence, should not have carried out this review having regard to this Court’s case-law. It was not at all satisfied that a restriction on the ability to cross-examine the Chief. Superintendent, arising from his claim of privilege in respect of the underlying sources of information. upon which his belief was based because of a threat to life or to the. on-going security of the State, did not ipso facto constitute a breach of Article 38. The CCA held that there was no reason to conclude that anything found in the material examined by the trial court was influential on that court in making its judgment, let alone inspiring anything determinative of the guilt of either accused. A statement to the contrary was explicitly made by the. trial court and was to be found in. the judgment itself. The facts upon which the trial. court relied were all proven beyond reasonable doubt and, indeed, there had. been no serious challenge to the prosecution evidence of the facts, connections and. associations so found. The court was fully entitled to have found that the applicant was associated with the events at Corke Abbey and its conclusion, in the circumstances, was a safe and valid one. The trial court was entitled to look at the established facts, when taken in conjunction with the inferences which it had properly drawn to see whether these supported or corroborated the belief evidence. On 26 October 2007 the CCA delivered its (second) decision and refused the application for a section 29 certificate. It summarised this Court’s findings in the above-cited case in which it found a violation of Article 6 to the effect that. the entitlement to disclosure is not an absolute right and that, in any criminal proceedings, there may be competing interests, such as national security, which must be weighed against the rights of the witnesses. The CCA concluded that the approach taken by the trial court in the applicant’s case was clearly within the ambit of the case-law of the Strasbourg Court which required that the withholding of any such documentation had to remain at all times in the supervisory control of judges themselves. The CCA rejected the submission that the trial judges had had no regard at all to the documentary source material. There was no requirement to disclose documents which did not damage the prosecution or assist the defence. The applicant had not sought to have the appeal court examine or consider the Chief Superintendent's documentation in order to ascertain whether the trial Judges had misdirected themselves in respect of the documents or the documents. name: Colin Laskey
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 11 December 1995. It originated in three applications (nos. 21627/93, 21826/93 and 21974/93) lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 14 December 1992 by three British nationals. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 8 of the Convention. The late Mr Laskey’s father and the two other applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent them (Rule 30).
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 11 December 1995. It originated in three applications (nos. 21627/93, 21826/93 and 21974/93) lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 14 December 1992 by three British nationals. The late Mr Laskey’s father and the two other applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent them. On 8 February 1996, in the presence of the Registrar, the President of the Court, Mr R. Ryssdal, drew by lot the names of the other seven members of the Chamber. Rights International, a New York-based non-governmental human rights organisation, submitted written comments on specified aspects of the case. The comments were received on 16 August 1996. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 21 October 1996. Mr Laskey, Mr Jaggard and Mr Brown, all British citizens, were born in 1943, 1947 and 1935 respectively. They were charged with a series of offences, including assault and wounding, relating to sado-masochistic activities that had taken place over a ten-year period. One of the charges involved a defendant who was not yet 21 years old - the age of consent to male homosexual practices at the time. The activities were consensual and were conducted in private for no apparent purpose other than the achievement of sexual gratification. There were instances of branding and infliction of injuries which resulted in the flow of blood and which left scarring. Video cameras were used to record events and the tapes copied and distributed amongst members of the group. The prosecution was largely based on the contents of those videotapes. The applicants pleaded guilty to the assault charges after the trial judge ruled that they could not rely on the consent of the “victims’ as an answer to the prosecution case. On 19 December 1990, the defendants were convicted and sentenced to terms of imprisonment. The applicants appealed against conviction and sentence. On 11 March 1993, the appeal, known as the case of R. v. Brown ([1993] 2 All England Law Reports 75), was dismissed by a majority of the House of Lords. Lord Templeman, in the majority, held after reviewing the case-law that: “... the authorities dealing with the intentional infliction of bodily harm do not establish that consent is a defence to a charge under the Act of 1861’” The Court of Appeal, Criminal Division, dismissed the appeals against conviction on 19 February 1992. Since, however, the court found that the applicants did not appreciate that their actions in inflicting injuries were criminal, reduced sentences were imposed. It is an offence for a person to abuse his own body and mind by taking drugs. The violence of sado-masochistic encounters involves the indulgence of cruelty by sadists and the degradation of victims. Such violence is injurious to the participants and unpredictably dangerous. Society is entitled and bound to protect itself against a cult of violence. Pleasure derived from the infliction of pain is an evil thing. Cruelty is uncivilised.“Lord Jauncey of Tullichettle found that the line falls properly to be drawn between assault at common law and the offence of assault occasioning actual bodily harm created by section 47 of the 1861 Act. It would appear to be good luck rather than good judgment which has prevented serious injury from occurring. Wounds can easily become septic if not properly treated, the free flow of blood from a person who is HIV-positive or who has AIDS can infect another. An inflicter who is carried away by sexual excitement or by drink or drugs could very easily inflict pain and injury beyond the level to which the receiver had consented. The possibility of proselytisation and corruption of young men is a real danger even in the case of these appellants. The taking of video recordings of such activities suggests that secrecy may not be as strict as the appellants claimed to your Lordships. Lord Slynn of Hadley found adults were able to consent to acts done in private which did not result in serious bodily harm. He agreed that it was in the end a matter of policy in an area where social and moral factors were extremely important and where attitudes could change. It was however for the legislature to decide whether such conduct should be brought within the criminal law and not for the courts in the interests of “paternalism’. All the applicants lost their jobs and Mr Jaggard required extensive psychiatric treatment. The proceedings were given widespread press coverage and were given extensive coverage by the BBC and the Daily Mail.

name: Andreas Jäggi

The case was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The decision was made to uphold the ruling. In 1976, shortly after his death, a blood-type analysis did not rule out his being the latter’s father. In 1997 the applicant contacted the Geneva University Institute of Forensic Medicine to have a private paternity test carried out, but his request was refused. In 1999 the applicant applied to the Canton of Geneva Court of First Instance for revision of the judgment of 30 January 1948. In the course of the proceedings he also requested a DNA test on the mortal remains of A.H. The Federal Court adopted a judgment, served on 22 December 1999, in which the applicant was found not to be the biological father. The applicant, who is 60 years old, has been able to develop his personality and pursue a large portion of his existence without suffering any medically attested damage to his physical or mental health. The Court of Justice was therefore entitled to restrict the applicant’s personal freedom by taking into consideration that of the respondents, in view of the lack of public interest in having this parental tie established. The Federal Court observed that there were no consequences of a civil-law nature that could justify implementing the measure sought. “The right to know one's parentage cannot be absolute in scope but must be weighed against the interests relating to protection of the personal freedom of others,” the court said.

name: Juri Maslov
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1638/03) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the imposition of an exclusion order on him and his expulsion to Bulgaria violated his right to respect for private and family life. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) on 2 June 2005. On 22 March 2007 a Chamber of that Section, composed of Christos Rozakis, Loukis Loucaides, Nina Vajić, Elisabeth Steiner, Khanlar Hajiyev, Dean Spielmann, Sverre Erik Jebens, judges, and of Søren Nielsen, Section Registrar, delivered a judgment in which it held, by four votes to three, that there had been a violation.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the imposition of an exclusion order on him and his expulsion to Bulgaria violated his right to respect for private and family life. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. On 22 March 2007 a Chamber of that Section delivered a judgment in which it held, by four votes to three, that there had been a violation of Article 8 of the convention. The respondent Government should pay the applicant 5,759.96 euros in respect of costs and expenses. The applicant was born in 1984 and currently lives in Bulgaria. He was convicted on 22 counts of aggravated gang burglary in 1999. The sentence was accompanied by an order to undergo drug therapy. The applicant was sentenced to eighteen months’ imprisonment, 13 of which were suspended on probation. The Court heard addresses by Mr Deuretsbacher and Mr Trauttmansdorff, as well as their answers to questions put by a number of judges. András Sajó, substitute judge, replaced Riza Türmen, who was unable to take part in the further consideration of the case (Rule 24. § 3). The applicant was convicted on 18 counts of aggravated burglary and attempted aggravated burglary. The Vienna Juvenile Court remanded him in custody. On 3 January 2001 the Vienna Federal Police Authority (Bundespolizeidirektion) imposed a ten-year exclusion order on the applicant. On 17 August 2001 the applicant lodged complaints with the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) and the Constitutional Court. The appeal was dismissed by the Vienna Public Security Authority (Sicherheitsdirektions) on 19 July 2001. The applicant was sentenced to 15 months in prison and served his prison term. The applicant came to Austria only at the age of six, had attended school in Austria and could not speak Bulgarian. He had no relatives or other social contacts in Bulgaria and stressed the fact that he was still a minor. The Administrative Court dismissed the complaint and found that the exclusion order was justified under Article 8 § 2 of the Convention. The Constitutional Court declined to deal with the applicant’s complaint for lack of prospects of success. On 22 December 2003 the applicant was deported to Sofia. According to information given by counsel at the hearing, the applicant did not commit any further offences in Bulgaria. The Government informed the Court that the inclusion order will expire on 3 January 2011, that is ten years after its issue.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35115/97) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that in criminal proceedings against him, relating to charges of threatening behaviour, he did not have a public hearing. By a decision of 15 June 2000 the Chamber declared the application partly admissible [Note by the Registry. The Court's decision is obtainable from the Registry]. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court heard addresses by Mr Blum, Mr Okresek and Mrs Schindler.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35115/97) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that in criminal proceedings against him, relating to charges of threatening behaviour, he did not have a public hearing as the trial was held in the prison where he was detained. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 15 June 2000 the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 29 August 2000. The Court heard addresses by Mr Blum, Mr Okresek and Mrs Schindler. On 8 May 1995, when prison personnel at Garsten carried out the necessary reception formalities, the applicant refused to cooperate and demanded to be returned to Stein Prison. On account of these incidents, criminal proceedings on charges of threatening behaviour (gefährliche Drohung) were instituted against the applicant. The Steyr Regional Court (Landesgericht) decided to hold the hearing in Garsten Prison, which is situated about 5 km from Steyr. It set down 29 January 1996 as the date for the trial. The summons indicating the date and place of the hearing was served on the applicant and his official defence counsel a month before the hearing. The applicant, assisted by counsel, pleaded not guilty. The court heard the four prison officers to whom the applicant had allegedly addressed threats as witnesses. Neither the applicant nor his counsel complained about a lack of publicity at that time. Following the hearing, the Regional Court convicted the applicant of threatening behaviour, finding that he had on three occasions threatened prison personnel with arson or assault. The applicant filed an appeal on points of law and fact, as well as against sentence (Berufung wegen Nichtigkeit, Schuld und Strafe). He complained, in particular, as a ground of nullity, that the hearing on 29 January 1996 had not been public since it took place in the closed area of Garsten Prison. The Court of Appeal found the applicant had committed the offence of threatening behaviour. The sentence was commensurate with the applicant's guilt, the court said. The applicant was found guilty of threatening prison personnel with arson or assault. He was sentenced to 10 years in prison, plus two years' probation. The application was heard in a closed area of the prison, but the trial was open to the public. The judge had not been informed of any potential spectators at the start of the hearing. The appeal was denied on appeal on points of fact, according to the court of appeal. The trial was adjourned until September 19th, when it will resume.

The Commission produced various documents as requested by the Registrar. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 February 1994. Mr Karlheinz Schmidt, a German national who was born in 1939, lives at Tettnang, in the Land of Baden-Württemberg. On 30 April 1982 the relevant municipal authorities required him to pay a fire service levy of 75 German marks (DM) for 1982. This decision was based on section 43 of the Land Fire Brigades Act, as amended on 27 November 1978 (Feuerwehrgesetz) The decision to impose a levy on women was in breach of the Constitution. The Administrative Appeals Court dismissed the appeal on points of law. The Constitutional Court was not able to refer the case back to the Administrative Court again. The case was settled in the Supreme Court of Germany in 1986. The court ruled that a tax on women is not contrary to the Constitution, but that it must be paid by men, and not women. The Supreme Court's decision was appealed to the Constitutional Court, which upheld the decision. The appeal was dismissed and the case was lost. The decision was made to impose the levy on men instead of women. It was upheld by the Court of Appeal. Mr Schmidt applied finally to the Federal Constitutional Court, which on 31 January 1987, sitting as a panel of three members, declined to accept the appeal for adjudication. It noted, inter alia: “... The Federal Constitutional court has already held, in its judgment of 17 October 1961 ..., concerning the provision which corresponds to the present section 43 para. 2, first sentence, of the Baden-Württemberg Fire Brigades Act, that there had been no violation of the principle of equal treatment.” The fact that the obligation to serve in the fire brigade was limited to the male residents of a municipality still continued to be objectively justified on account of the risks inherent in service.

name: Sladjan Nacic
train_texts: The application was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) on 18 March 2010. eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained that deportation of the first, second and fourth applicants to Kosovo or Serbia would be in violation of Articles 3 and 8 of the convention. They are of Roma descent and lived in the village of Kosovo Polje. Following the outbreak of war in 1999, the first applicant refused to participate in the fighting and hid from the armed forces. The other applicants were subjected to threats and beatings by Serbian military. Finally, they were driven out of their home by Albanian militia and fled by train to Suvi Do, another village in Kosovo. The applicants had felt harassed in Kosovo because of their being Roma, but they had not been subjected to any persecution, allegedly due to their isolation. They applied for asylum and permanent residence permits on arrival in Sweden. The Board found that neither the general situation in Kosovo nor that in Serbia was such that it in itself constituted grounds for granting asylum. The applicants were not to be considered as refugees or as in need of any other specific protection, according to the Migration Board (Migrationsverket) The Board noted that the first applicant’s mother was Serb, that none of the family members spoke Romani or had any contact with other Roma, and that they had only socialised with Serbs in Kosovo.  applications were made on behalf of three young people from Kosovo and Serbia. The applicants submitted several medical certificates regarding the first, second and third applicants. According to the certificates, there was a risk that they might commit suicide if they were to be expelled from Sweden. The Migration Court rejected the appeal, upholding the Board’s reasoning and conclusion, adding the following. The third applicant would soon be 18 years old. He was depressed and could hardly interact with other persons. He isolated himself at home and became apathetic. In June 2008, he attempted suicide by overdose of anti-depressants. There would be a serious risk of another suicide attempt. The applicants had been subjected to persecution in Kosovo due to their ethnicity and that this had caused their health problems. Their possibilities to receive proper care if sent back were limited, especially regarding the third applicant. Their health had deteriorated, as allegedly shown by several medical certificates submitted. On 23 November 2009 the Migration Court of Appeal delivered its judgment. It found that the medical certificates showed that he suffered from severe mental illness, that he was unlikely to get better in the foreseeable future and that the necessary treatment presupposed he was in a safe, secure and stable environment. The court quashed the lower court’s judgment and granted him a permanent residence permit. The applicants submitted new medical certificates concerning the first, the second and the third applicants. The documents available also showed that the condition for the third applicant’s well-being was a safe, secure and stable environment. The Migration Board rejected the request as it found that the applicants had invoked no new circumstances of importance and that there were no impediments to the enforcement of the first,. second and fourth applicants’ deportation order. The applicants requested the Court to indicate to the Swedish Government under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court a suspension of the applicants' deportation to Kosovo or Serbia. The court ruled that all applicants should be granted permanent residence permits. On 16 June 2011, the applicants submitted new medical certificates issued by Ann-Marie Nyberg and dated June 2011. According to these, the first applicant had been feeling slightly better since the family had moved from the children’s home to an apartment in Trollhättan in December 2010. However, he still suffered from feelings of futility and despair. He was diagnosed with grave depression, depressive devitalisation and complex PTSD. The second applicant had recently been feeling worse again due to her fear of a possible deportation. The third applicant had gradually been feeling better since he had been granted a residence permit. His positive development had been halted by the threat of disruption of the family and he showed clear signs of falling into depression again.

eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 12 March 1999. It originated in an application (27052/95) lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 of the Convention by Mr Eric Jasper, a British national. The applicant is represented by Ms Mary Cunneen of Liberty. The Government of the United Kingdom are represented by their Agent, Mr Martin Eaton, Deputy Legal Adviser at the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. On 1 April 1999 Mr L. Wildhaber, the President of the Court, acting under Rule 24 §§ 3-5 determined the composition of the Grand Chamber to include, ex officio, himself, and Mrs E. Palm, the Vice-President. The applicant was serving a prison sentence at the time of the application. Three tonnes of cannabis resin was imported into the United Kingdom concealed in a consignment of frozen meat on a lorry travelling from Zeebrugge to Dover. The meat was delivered to West Kent Cold Storage at Dunton Green, near Sevenoaks in Kent. On 1 July 1993 Customs and Excise officers were keeping the applicant under observation. At approximately 6 a.m. he was followed from his home in Walthamstow, East London, to a. lorry park at Beckton, where he collected an articulated lorry and. refrigerated trailor which he had bought the previous month. The Court heard addresses by Mr Cranston and Mr Emmerson and also replies to questions put by several of its members. The applicant made two brief visits to the garage during the morning, and then returned at approximately 1 p.m. Four of the pallets, containing a large quantity of cannabis resin, had been opened and left to defrost in the unrefrigerated garage. Six of the ten pallets of meat were still on the lorry in a frozen state, although the refrigerator motor was not operative. The applicant told Customs officers that he worked as a haulage contractor and had not known that the meat contained cannabis. The prosecution made an ex parte application to the trial judge to withhold material in its possession on the grounds of public interest immunity. The trial judge examined the material in question and ruled that it should not be disclosed. Prosecution counsel provided answer to questions 9(iii) and (vi), informing the defence that there had been no such observations and no “information received” from an informant. Defence applied to the trial judge for an order that the prosecution should provide the information requested. Prosecution counsel: “I contend that I am not required to reveal to any person whether there has been any interception of communications under the [Interception of Communications] Act [see paragraphs 31-34 below]” That position was upheld by the trialJudge who, in his ruling of 24 January 1994, said: ‘I am confident I have done what is required of me in respect of it’ The applicant did not give evidence at his trial. The defence case was that he had no knowledge of the cannabis hidden in the consignment and was acting as an innocent haulier of the goods. On 31 January 1994 the applicant was convicted of the offence charged and on 21 March 1994 he was sentenced to ten years' imprisonment. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal, on the following grounds: “It was clear that not all unused material had been disclosed. ... In open court it was stated on behalf of the defendant that the unused material was of potential importance to his defence’. The Crown had declined to answer the question whether any potentially relevant material, apart from the subject-matter of the ex parte application, had not been disclosed, on grounds that to do so would reveal whether or not there had been a telephone intercept. The Court of Appeal declined to order the disclosure of the transcript of the ex parte hearing of 14 January 1994 to the defence. The application was made on the ground that the matters which emerged during the ex-parte hearing are relevant, or likely to have been relevant, to the defense of Mr Jasper. The court said that the judge knew precisely the scope of the application and listened with the greatest possible care to the matters. He tested those matters, and he came to the conclusion that the ruling which he made was appropriate in all the circumstances. It is abundantly clear from the transcript that he throughout was very careful to ensure and to explore whether the material was relevant. In these circumstances, it is impossible to say whether or not the material is relevant.” On 28 March 1995 the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal. The first ground of appeal, namely the non-disclosure of relevant evidence, was rejected. The court continued: “This was a case of enormous strength so far as the prosecution were concerned. The appellant had been caught red handed with a huge amount of cannabis resin. He was exercising a proprietorial form of control over the packages’ contents. By opening them he was allowing what were ostensibly their sole contents to defreeze, with a risk (to put it no higher) of their becoming valueless. ... It is difficult, if not impossible, to see what other inference than that he was indeed guilty of the offence charged any reasonable jury could have reached. We dismiss this appeal”

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 76900/01) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The parties did not submit further observations on the merits. The Salzburg Federal Police Authority prohibited the meeting on the ground that it would endanger public order and security. Like a number of other organisations, Comradeship IV traditionally held a commemoration ceremony at the city's municipal cemetery on All Saints' Day. The disruption of this and other commemoration ceremonies was likely to offend the religious feelings of members of the public visiting the cemetery, the authority noted. The association's members were mainly former SS soldiers killed in the Second World War and they had commemorated them for more than forty years by laying a wreath in front of the war memorial at the cemetery. In the past few years, organisations had organised protest campaigns with the aim of disrupting the ceremony. The Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) dismissed a complaint by the applicant alleging violations of his rights to freedom of assembly, freedom of expression and freedom of religion. It went on to say that the prohibition of the proposed meeting would not be justified if its sole purpose were to protect the Comradeship IV commemoration ceremony. The authorities had also had regard to the fact that the gathering had in previous years been the target of activities aimed at disrupting it which had caused considerable nuisance to other visitors of the cemetery and had each time required police intervention. The decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 5 February 2001.

eval_texts: Cases originated in two application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. First applicant alleged that his trial for indecent assault had been unfair because one of the two women who made complaints against him died before the trial and her statement to the police was read to the jury. Second applicant claimed that his. trial for wounding with intent to do grievous bodily harm had been. unfair because the statement of one witness who feared attending trial was. read to a jury. A hearing in both cases took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 8 January 2008. Dr Al-Khawaja was charged on two counts of indecent assault on two female patients while they were allegedly under hypnosis. One of the complainants, S.T., committed suicide (taken to be unrelated to the assault) before the trial but, several months after the alleged assault, had made a statement to the police. The judge stated that the contents of the statement were crucial to the prosecution on count one as there was no other direct evidence of what took place. The jury heard evidence from a number of different witnesses and the defence were given the opportunity to cross-examine other witnesses who had produced similar fact evidence. The applicant was convicted by a unanimous verdict on both counts of indecent assault. The Court of Appeal concluded on 3 November 2005 that the applicant's right to a fair trial had not been infringed. The appeal centred on the pre-trial ruling to admit S.T.'s statement as evidence. It was also submitted that, in his summing up, the trial judge did not give adequate directions to the jury as to the consequential disadvantage of this evidence to the applicant. On 6 September 2005 the appeal was dismissed. The court held that admissibility of evidence is primarily a matter of domestic law. This was not a case where the witness had absented himself, whether through fear or otherwise, or had required anonymity. The reason was death, which has a finality which brings in considerations of its own. The Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords but certified that a point of law of general public importance was involved in the decision. The applicant was charged with wounding with intent and also with attempting to pervert the course of justice. The court also considered that the applicant had been able to attack the accuracy of the deceased complainant's statement by exploring the inconsistencies between it and the evidence given by witnesses and experts. On 7 February 2005, the Court of Lords refused the applicant's petition to appeal the decision to the Supreme Court of England and Wales. Mr Tahery B. was born in 1975. On 19 May 2004 he was. involved in a fight with S. during which it is alleged that the. applicant stabbed S. three times in the back. When witnesses were questioned at the scene, no-one claimed to have seen the applicant stab S. T. was too fearful to attend trial before the jury and that he should qualify for special measures. The trial judge heard evidence from a police officer conducting the case who testified that the Iranian community was close-knit and that T.'s fear was genuine. T. himself gave evidence to the judge from behind a screen. In ruling that leave should be given for the statement to be read to the jury, the trial judge stated: “I am satisfied in those circumstances upon the criminal standard of proof that this witness is genuinely in fear’. Challenge of a statement can be caused by evidence given in rebuttal; by either the defendant, if he chooses to do so, or by any other bystander – and we know that there were some – who were on the street at that time. T.'s witness statement was read to the jury in his absence. The applicant also gave evidence. On 29 April 2005, the applicant was convicted by a majority verdict, principally of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm. He was later sentenced to nine years' imprisonment to be served concurrently with a term of fifteen months' imprisonment for doing an act intended to pervert the course of justice. The appeal judges were satisfied that if they were to refuse leave, under the CJA 2003, to have T.'s statement read at trial there would be unfairness to the prosecution. The court upheld the reasoning at the full Court of Appeal.  leave to appeal on conviction was refused on 24 January 2006. The Court of Appeal held that the jury was informed of all matters necessary to its decision-making process. The applicant's sentence was reduced to seven years' imprisonment. The court ruled that the trial judge had explicitly warned the jury in detail as to how they should treat this evidence and properly directed them as to what they should consider in reaching their verdict. It was also stated that there was available not only cross-examination of other prosecution witnesses but also evidence from the applicant himself and the potential for evidence from other bystanders in order to prevent unfairness. The judge ruled that even a proper direction by the judge could not cure the unfairness, but that a jury was told all the information necessary to reach a verdict.
