It was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 of the Rules of Court) A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building on 4 April 2000. The Government was represented by their Agent, Mr C. Whomersley of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The Northern Ireland Human Rights Commission was given leave by the President to intervene. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court heard addresses by Mr Weatherup and Mr Treacy. The applicant’s son, Pearse Jordan, aged 22, was shot and killed in Belfast by an officer of the Royal Ulster Constabulary (the RUC), later identified as Sergeant A. Jordan. The facts of the case, in particular concerning what happened when Peare Jordan was shot on 25 November 1992, are in dispute between the parties. The Court ruled the application admissible on 4 April 2000, and the case was dismissed by the Court of Appeal on 12 December 2000. Four civilians stopped as they heard a crash behind them. Pearse Jordan emerged from the immobilised car, and appeared shaken. He staggered across the road towards the four men followed by four police officers. An officer about 12 feet away fired a number of shots at him. The civilians heard no warning shout or challenge given by any of the officers. The police carried out a search of the car. The four witnesses followed the ambulance which took Pearse. Jordan to hospital where they stated that they were subjected to hostile and threatening remarks by. members of the security forces. An official RUC statement stated that a deputy superintendent of the RUC from outside Belfast would investigate the shooting. Sergeant A was in charge of teams on the ground which were going to intervene if possible to intercept the munitions. He was carrying a Smith and Wesson 59 pistol and a MP5 Heckler and Koch. The car possibly reached the speed of 60, maybe 70 miles per hour at the fastest. They were in a built up area, in traffic so it was difficult to judge. The Orion slowed falling behind and then shot past on the passenger side, accelerating down the Falls Road in the direction of the city. Sergeant A told his driver to pursue him and force him off the road. They switched on their police klaxon but had no blue flashing light on the car and none of them were wearing their police caps. Sergeant A said that he called out “Police. Halt.” or “Halt. Police” The driver of the Orion turned around towards him. He could not see the man’s hands which were below his waist. He feared the man was armed as he had spun round so quickly. He fired a short burst from his MP5 at the trunk of the man. The driver fell flat, toppling over. It was realised at that stage that he was seriously injured. Sergeant A quickly searched the car, while other security force personnel administered first aid to the driver. The military took over the first aid. Sergeant A had a clear view of the deceased from the waist up. When the deceased turned to face him, he did not make any movements towards him. His arms were down and his hands out of sight. In that short space of time, he formed the opinion that the deceased was a threat to his life. He was certain that there were no viable alternatives to discharging his own weapon.Forensic examinations of the cars involved in the incident were carried out. Interviews were conducted with the other police officers and army personnel involved. Only officer D heard shouting coming from the call sign 8 direction before the shooting. Inspector M gave a statement of 6 December 1992. The RUC concluded its inquiry into Pearse Jordan's death in May 1993. Its report on the investigation was submitted to the Director of Public Prosecutions (the DPP) The DPP’s department issued to the Chief Constable of the RUC a direction of ‘no prosecution’ in respect of the fatal shooting. Following that decision, the Coroner decided to hold an inquest. The inquest began on 4 January 1995 and was adjourned until May 1995. The applicant and his family were not provided with any indication as to the nature of the. RUC’S findings. The Coroner ruled that the evidence was insufficient to warrant the preferment of disciplinary charges against the police officers concerned. Defence issued a certificate in which he identified information whose disclosure at the inquest he believed would be contrary to the public interest on grounds of national security. Defence made an application that the identities of certain military witnesses be withheld and that they should give their evidence from behind a screen. On 4 January 1995, the Coroner’s inquest commenced. The Coroner sat for three and a half days, hearing evidence from 19 witnesses, including the applicant, 8 civilians, Soldiers V, W and X, 7 police officers and a pathologist. The applicant and his family were represented by a solicitor and counsel. The RUC were represented. The applicant’s legal representatives made an application for the Coroner to discharge himself from the Inquest on the grounds that he was not conducting the inquest fairly. The Coroner refused the application. The applicant sought orders of certiorari to quash inter alia. the refusal to give the next of kin access to the statements of the witnesses. before they gave evidence at the inquest. The application was heard on 9 and 10 November 1995, and Lord Justice Carswell refused the applicant's claims. In doing so he had regard to the inquisitorial nature of inquest proceedings. He referred to the remarks of Griffiths J in Ex parte Peach: “A coroner's inquest is an inquest with a very limited objective indeed.” The applicant appealed against the decision of Lord Justice Carswell. The appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland on 28 June 1996. The applicant’s application for leave to appeal to the House of Lords was refused on 4 October 1996. Final judgment was given in the case of Sharon Lavery v. the Secretary of State and the Legal Aid Department, in which a challenge concerning the unavailability of legal aid for inquests was dismissed. The inquest was due to recommence on 1 December 1997. It was adjourned on 19 November 1997 by the Coroner, after consultation with the parties, pending the outcome of a judicial review application in the High Court. The applicant was granted legal aid to pursue a civil action for compensation in the High Court. On 5 October 1995, the applicant served a statement of claim in the civil proceedings. The applicant did not reply to this request until a date unspecified subsequent to 27 August 1998. On 8 October 1999, the Crown Solicitor wrote to the applicant seeking consent to a remittal of the civil action to trial. The case is currently at the discovery stage but that this cannot be concluded until the inquest is terminated. In addition to the witnesses who gave evidence in January 1995, 12 police officers and Soldier Y involved in the anti-terrorist operation in which Pearse Jordan died, forensic experts and three police officers involved in RUC investigation into the shooting.

During preliminary investigations, which concerned a network of more than 300 firms, about 1,800 bank accounts were examined and about 8,000 volumes of documents were seized and studied. A special computer programme was designed in order to cope with the large volume of data. Most of the time was consumed by the preparation of an expert opinion, whereby the team of accounting experts first had to clear the balance sheets of the companies. name: Anthony M. Tyrer

The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Sir Gerald Fitzmaurice, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the conventions) and Mr. G. Balladore Pallieri, the President of the Court.
eval_texts: The Tyrer case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights. The case originated in an application against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission on 21 September 1972. The purpose of the Commission’s request is to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether or not the facts of the case disclose a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 3 (art. 3) of the Convention. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Sir Gerald Fitzmaurice, the elected judge of British nationality and Mr. G. Balladore Pallieri, the President of the Court. The Government of the Isle of Man requested that the Chamber should carry out an investigation on the spot in the Island pursuant to Rule 38 para. 2 of the Rules of Court. At a meeting held in private in Strasbourg on 13 December 1977, the Chamber resolved to defer its decision on this request until after the oral hearings. The oral hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 17 January 1978. There appeared before the Court: Mr. D.H. ANDERSON, Legal Counsellor, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr. L.J. BLOM-COOPER, Q.C., Mr. J.W. Corrin, Attorney-General. Anthony Tyrer pleaded guilty to unlawful assault on a senior pupil. He was sentenced to three strokes of the birch. His father lost his self-control and went for one of the policemen and had to be restrained. The applicant’s skin was sore for about a week and a half afterwards. His appeal was dismissed on the afternoon of 28 April 1972. The court considered that an unprovoked assault occasioning actual bodily harm was always very serious and that there were no reasons for interfering with the sentence. The Court decided that the very fully information which had been supplied to the Court concerning this case rendered it unnecessary to carry out the investigation requested. The applicant was sentenced pursuant to section 56 (1) of the Petty Sessions and Summary Jurisdiction Act 1927. The sentence was governed by the following provisions: “(a) the instrument used shall, in the case of a child, be a cane, and in any other case shall be a birch rod.“ The expressions “child“ and “young person“ mean, respectively, an individual of or over the age of 10 and under 14 and an individuals of or under 14. The court in its sentence shall specify the number of strokes to be inflicted, being not more than six strokes. The whipping shall be inflicted privately as soon as practicable after sentence. A medical practitioner shall be present during a birching and may at his discretion order the stopping of the punishment at any time. A report of the facts shall be forwarded immediately to His Excellency. The Isle of Man is not a part of the United Kingdom but a dependency of the Crown with its own government, legislature and courts. The Island’s parliament, the Court of Tynwald, is one of the oldest in Europe. It consists of a Lieutenant-Governor appointed by and representing the Crown, an Upper House (the Legislative Council) and a Lower House ( the Lower House) The punishment is to be inflicted over ordinary cloth trousers in all cases irrespective of the offender's age. Judicial corporal punishment of adults and juveniles was abolished in England, Wales and Scotland in 1948. The punishment remained in existence in the Isle of Man. In May 1977, by thirty-one votes for and only one against, Tynwald passed a resolution. A privately organised petition in favour of the retention of judicial corporal. punishment had obtained 31,000 signatures from amongst the approximate total of 45,000. persons entitled to vote on the Island. Since 1969, since 1969 its application has apparently been restricted in practice to offences of violence. It was considered a deterrent to hooligans visiting the Island as tourists and, more generally, a means of preserving law and order. The name and address of a juvenile sentenced in the Isle of Man, whether to corporal punishment or otherwise, are not published. The average number of crimes of violence to the person per annum was: between 1966 and 1968 - 35; between 1969 and 1971 - 52; between 1972 and 1974 - 59; and between 1975 and 1977 - 56. At the 1976 census, the Island’s population stood at 60,496. In the three years 1975 to 1977, only one young male was convicted of a crime of violence. The applicant also claimed damages as well as repeal of the legislation concerned. The Commission, having considered ex officio that the facts of the case raised issues of discrimination on grounds of sex and gender, ruled in favour of the applicant. The Commission declared the judicial corporal punishment inflicted on the applicant was degrading and was in breach of Article 3 (art. 3) of the Convention. The Commission declared inadmissible the remainder of the application. The applicant took no further part in the proceedings. The case raised questions of a general character affecting the observance of the. Convention which necessitated a further examination of the issues involved’. The report contains one separate opinion which expresses the opinion that there were not any significant social or cultural differences between the Isle of Man and the United Kingdom which could be relevant to the application of Article. 3 (Art. 63-3) in this case.

name: David Adetoro
train_texts: The case was brought by a U.S. citizen against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The court ruled that the applicant was not entitled to a hearing. The application was made on October 30, 2006, and the hearing was held on October 31, 2008. The case was settled on October 24, 2008, with the decision of the Court of Appeal being quashed. The judge said that the application was not in the public interest and that it should not have been heard. The appeal was dismissed and the case was dismissed on October 26, 2009, and a new hearing was set up.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he did not have a fair trial as a result of the trial judge's misdirection to the jury on the drawing of adverse inferences as regards his refusal to answer questions during police interviews. The evidence against the applicant was almost entirely circumstantial and the case relied heavily on evidence from a police surveillance exercise carried out over a period of about one year. The Government were represented by their Agent, Ms J. Gladstone, of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The case was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to rob and other offences arising out of the conspiracy. During the interviews, he was asked to give an explanation for his movements as recorded by the police in their surveillance exercise, his association with a variety of individuals and his whereabouts at the time of the robberies. On each occasion, he replied “no comment”. The judge directed the jury as to the burden of proof and the standard of proof in the case: “...The burden [of proof] lies upon the prosecution throughout the case, to prove their case against the defendant. The defendant does not have to prove anything at all, there is no burden upon him to proveanything” The judge went on to deal with the questioning of the applicant by the police. He noted that the applicant had not answered questions put to him during the police interviews, replying ‘no comment’ to each of the questions posed. The judge concluded with the following direction: “I have to tell you as a matter of law, that the fact that a defendant tells a lie, is not of itself, evidence of guilt.” There were six hours – if I've added it up correctly – of interviews between the police and the defendant, from the day of his arrest in March through to June of last year and at each of those various interviews, he was cautioned. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal arguing that the summing up contained a Lucas direction (a direction to the jury in relation to lies – see paragraph 33) The judge noted that he was satisfied that Mr Adetoro was involved in the sixth robbery. He was a 'rather clever and determined liar' and his alibi 'fell apart' The judge was not prepared to place reliance on anything he said and made no finding in respect of Mr Shearer and Mr Stephenson's presence or absence in the circumstances of the fifth robbery. The judge concluded that the applicant was guilty of the offences charged and sentenced him to 26 years' imprisonment. The applicant's appeal against conviction was dismissed. However, his sentence was reduced to 22 years' imprisonment. The Court of Appeal disagreed and found that, despite the misdirection by the trial judge, the conviction was safe. It distinguished between cases where an accused exercised his right to silence pursuant to legal advice or because he was tired or ill and those where, as in the present case, the reason for not answering questions was linked to the applicant's silence at the police interviews. The main ground of appeal was that the direction on adverse inferences was defective in that the jury were not directed that an adverse inference could only be drawn where it was satisfied that the real reason for the applicants silence was that he had no answer to the questions asked. The court also noted that the judge had given the jury an unnecessary Lucas direction. The jury were told that if they thought there was an innocent explanation for any such lie told by the appellant they should not hold it against him. So, as the jury must have concluded that the appellant's explanation for his silence ('I wanted to protect others') was a lie, following the judge's direction they would have had to consider whether there was a innocent explanation before they could have used it as supportive of the Crown's case. If they did draw adverse inferences against the appellant following the directions which they were given, they could only have done so if they considered that he had no or no sustainable answer to the questions he was asked. The applicant's appeal against conviction was dismissed on 7 June 2006. The Court of Appeal found the evidence against the applicant to be overwhelming. The appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court of England and Wales. The Appeal Court held that the evidence was overwhelming and that the correct direction would have tipped the balance in favour of the applicant. The application was dismissed and the case was dismissed from the court of appeal on June 7, 2006, and the appeal was settled out of court in August 2006. It was the first case of its kind to be heard in the High Court. The case was decided by the Appeal Court, which agreed with the earlier judgment of the Court of appeal.

London Clubs would apply for new licences for the casinos via reconstituted operating companies. If the applications were successful and new licences were granted, LCL would undertake to surrender its existing licences, thereby avoiding the necessity for the applications for cancellation or renewal to be heard. The Gaming Board issued LCL with certificates of consent, which LCL was statutorily obliged to obtain from the Gaming Board as a prerequisite to making an application to the Licensing Magistrates. Objections were made by a rival casino owner. However, these objections were rejected and new licence were granted in October 1992, after a three-day hearing. Lady Littler, Chairman of theGaming Board, addressed the British Casino Association at its annual luncheon. Her speech referred to London Clubs and commented: “We [the Gaming Board] satisfied ourselves that the practices we and the Police had regarded as unacceptable had ceased” The Gaming Board was considering whether the applicant was a fit and proper person to hold the Board's certificate of approval. By a letter dated 23 April 1993, the Gaming Board informed the applicant formally that it was “minded to revoke” the applicant's section 19 certificates. The applicant did not accept this explanation, but did not institute defamation proceedings. to were minority shareholders and no reference to the applicantwas intended. The Gaming Board had already publicly expressed the view (at the hearing before the Licensing Magistrates) that the applicant wasn't fit to remain an executive director of London Clubs. As such, the applicant contended, the gaming Board could not be the judge of a section 19 hearing. The Gaming Board rejected the request for an independent tribunal. The application for judicial review was dismissed on 11 January 1996 by Mr Justice Jowitt after a hearing lasting over sixteen days. The effect of the revocation of the section 19 certificates was that the applicant was unable to obtain employment in any sector of the gaming industry in the United Kingdom or in any jurisdiction which had a relationship with the UK gaming authorities. The first judgment dealt with the applicant's appeal. The decision was challenged on the grounds that the Panel was biased, or had the appearance of bias, and that its findings were vitiated by errors of law and were irrational. Mr Justice Jowitt dealt with the applicant's “Wednesbury’ challenges to the findings in respect of the various complaints made of him. The judge found that the Board's conclusion – that what took place amounted to an agreement between Mr S. and LCL, such that section 16 was breached – was a conclusion it was entitled to reach. Fifty-seven pages of the third judgment were devoted to the issue of bias. The grounds on which leave to move for judicial review were granted asserted firstly that. the Board could not and did not approach its decision with objectivity and impartiality. Secondly, it was asserted that whether or not there was actual bias the applicant reasonably believed there was and that the. Board should have had regard to the appearance of bias which had been created. There was a disagreement between the parties as to the approach the court should adopt when bias is alleged. It is a two-stage test. The applicant has first to show from the evidence that there is an appearance of bias (R. v. Inner West London Coroner, ex parte Dallaglio [1994] 4 All England Law Reports 139) The question on which the court must reach its own factual conclusion is this: is there a real danger of injustice having occurred as a result of bias? By “real” is meant not without substance. A real danger clearly involves more than a minimal risk, less than a probability. One could, I think, as well speak of a real risk or a real possibility. Mr Justice Jowitt found that there was no unconscious bias on the part of any of the Panel members. He indicated that if, contrary to his finding, there was unconscious bias, the doctrine of necessity would apply, and the decision would stand. The decision will not be liable to be impugned on account of bias provided that: (i) if only some of those charged with the power or duty to decide are potentially affected by bias such of them as can lawfully withdraw do so, and (ii) those of the decision-makers who are potentiallyaffected by bias use their best endeavours to avoid the effect of bias. Mr Justice Jowitt rejected the submission, on the grounds that no useful reference could have been made to an independent tribunal which did not involve an impermissible delegation. Lord Justice Morritt (with whom Lord Justice Hobhouse agreed) held that there was a real risk that the decision of the tribunal had been actuated by bias. The decision for the Board was, at the end of the day, whether or not Mr Kingsley was a fit and proper person. That could not be delegated to anIndependent panel and if they were actuated. by bias, apparent or real, then the decision would still have to be made by them. "There is no arguable point, susceptible on this part of the case, which would justify giving leave to appeal," says the judge. The decision has to be made by the Board and could not be delegated to an independent tribunal. There has been no meaningful independent panel and the decision would stand, the judge says. "It seems to me that there is noarguable point," he adds, "which would justifyGiving leave to appealed.” The hearing will take place at a later date and the case is expected to be heard later this year. The final decision will be made on whether to appeal the decision to the European Court of Justice.

name: Arnold Fragner

The applicant alleged that the proceedings concerning his doctor's fees had not been dealt with within a reasonable time and that the Regional Appeals Commission which dealt with his case was not impartial or independent. The case began with an application for the transfer of jurisdiction (Devolutionsantrag) to the Regional Appeals Commission (Landesberufungskommission) before the Joint Arbitration Committee (Paritätische Schiedskommissions) on 4 September 1996. The Appeals Commission dismissed the applicant's claim as it found that the applicant had failed to obtain the necessary visa from a chief physician. The applicant then filed a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) and on 13 October 1999 that court quashed the Appeals Commission's decision. On 3 May 2000 the applicant filed a request for proceedings to be resumed and, on 8 November 2000, the appeals commission held an oral hearing in which it decided to appoint an expert for examining the question of urgency of the chirurgical interventions forming the basis of the dispute. The applicant complained to the Constitutional Court, alleging a breach of the principle of equal treatment. The Constitutional Court found no violation of the right to a fair trial and upheld the contested decision. It held that the assessors of the Regional Appeals Commission were independent in exercising their function and no circumstances giving rise to doubts about their impartiality and independence had arisen in the present case. This decision was served on counsel on 29 November 2005. The decision was made on 27 September 2005, and the appeal was heard on 11 November 2005, with the verdict served on 9 December 2005, the day before the appeal hearing was due to begin. name: Sandro Nerva

The application was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court, which declared it admissible on 11 September 2001. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine).
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42295/98) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged, in particular, that their rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and under Article 14 of the Convention had been breached given that the domestic courts of the respondent State had ruled that money which was left to them as tips by customers passed to their employer to be used as it wished. The application was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court, which declared it admissible on 11 September 2001. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The applicants were employed as waiters at the time. When the applicants received a tip in cash directly from a customer, the money was placed in a box called a ‘tronc’ and distributed proportionately among the waiters. In 1979, following an inspection from the tax authorities, the applicants’ employer was required to treat tips left by cheque or credit card within the ‘Pay-As-You-Earn’ (“PAYE’) system. The applicants submitted that the staff agreement to the new system was not intended to alter the fact that the gratuities were to be paid in full to employees. At the relevant time there was a legal requirement that various categories of workers, including waiting staff like the applicants, be paid a minimum sum as remuneration. The applicants sued their employer for breach of contract and challenged the employer’s right to count the tips included in cheque or credit card payments. In his judgment, the employer obtained the legal title to a tip paid by credit card or cheque, with the result that it became the employer's property. If the applicants’ claim was upheld, the consequence would have been that their employer had been paying them less that the statutory minimum over a period of years. Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal. Lord Justice Staughton observed that the relevant legislation embodied the rule that what was paid by the employer and not by any other person counted as remuneration. He considered that the same reasoning could not apply to tips built into payments made by cheque or credit card to their employer since the amounts became the latter’s property. In his view, tips paid in this manner should count against the minimum remunerative requirement.Lord Justice Aldous dissented. He accepted that the amount was paid to the employer. However, in his opinion the intention of the customer was the same. Lord Justice Aldous stated that there was no difference in principle between tips paid in cash and tips paid by cheque or credit card. In his opinion, the only difference was that in the latter cases the employer acted as agent for the customer and, when doing so, had to carry out its duties under the relevant tax legislation. However, the fact that tax on cheque and credit card tips was deducted under the PAYE system, instead of being paid by the waiters, did not affect the relationship between customer and employee. The applicants’ counsel was given the opportunity to speak to the petition for leave and to address the employer’s written objections.

eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court in accordance with the provisions applicable prior to the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that planning and enforcement measures taken against them in respect of their occupation of their land in their caravans violated their right to respect for home, family life and private life. They also complained that they were subject to discrimination as gypsies. The panel of the Grand Chamber determined that the case should be decided by the Grand chamber. The applicants and the Government each filed a memorial. Third-party comments were also received from the European Roma Rights Centre. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 May 2000. The Court heard addresses by Mr Drabble and Mr Pannick. The applicants wished for their children to be brought up in a stable environment which would facilitate the continuity of their education. They now have four children, Jody born in 1983, and a son and daughter born in 1998. The case was heard in the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg on 29 November 2000 (Rule 59 § 2). The applicants are gypsies by birth. The applicants were refused a place on any local authorised site. They camped outside one official site for 5-6 weeks hoping to be offered a plot. No place was offered and court proceedings were brought against them by the Borough to secure their eviction from the land. The Government stated that the Borough has no knowledge or record of any request by the applicants for a pitch in 1982. They moved into the caravan occupied by the first applicant’s mother on a permitted gypsy site and sold their own caravan. The caravan was however small and conditions became intolerable. Having nowhere else to go, the applicants in or about 1983 reluctantly applied for permanent accommodation and accepted the offer of a council flat. The applicants made a further application for planning permission which was refused on 11 December 1989. A public enquiry was held before a Planning Inspector on 26 March 1991. The Inspector refused their appeal on 24 April 1991 and the applicants were penalised in costs on the basis that it was identical to the previous application. The applicants conceded that the only action taken since the 1989 decision by or on behalf of the family to find another site or accommodation, was a telephone call … to the [Borough] Counsel for the borough assured the inquiry that the [applicants’] family would be offered short-term housing. This is the position the family have faced for a long time. The mobile home would remain intrusively visible from Lenham Road and Baker lane. There is nowhere within the site at which a mobile home could be positioned without causing equally serious harm. No new gypsy sites have been opened in Maidstone since 1967. There are still gypsy families parked on unauthorised sites in the Maidstone area. The provision of private sites should be encouraged. Kent County Council support the provision ofprivate sites. So does Government policy. There should be a flexible attitude to such planning applications. As was said in a Parliamentary answer in 1987, well-run gypsy. sites, once established, seldom give cause for serious complaints. ‘Designated’ authorities like Maidstone may still need to make extra provision in their area. The applicants terminated their council tenancy to move onto land not permitted for residential use contrary to the advice of the Housing and Planning Departments. They were told that there was a waiting list for places on official sites but that since they were intentionally homeless they could not put their names on it for 2 years. The applicants left their land and travelled to Whitstable, Kent close to where some of the second applicant’s family had stationed their caravans. On the site there was no sanitation or electricity and there was an infestation of rats. The Borough took the decision to seek an injunction in the High Court restraining the applicants from stationing their caravan on their land. On 24 July 1992, a fine of GBP 350 was imposed on each applicant. The applicants' names were placed on the waiting list at the end of 1992 but they removed their names from that list in January 1993. On 17 December 1992, the applicants returned to their land, where the children could resume their education at their previous school. The applicants applied for judicial review to quash the injunction proceedings on the basis that the decision to pursue the injunction against them was unreasonable. On 6 May 1994, the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal. On or about 30 October 1996 the applicants withdrew their application. In February 1997, the applicant sold their land. They also sold their caravan at a substantial undervalue. They went to live temporarily in the caravan occupied by the second applicant’s brother. The applicants suffered headaches, anxiety, claustrophobia and depression requiring them to seek medical treatment. They were both prescribed medication which did not however resolve their physical sense of confinement. The applicants bought a touring caravan, which they stationed on the land of the second applicant’s brother. They took every opportunity they could to travel in the traditional style during school holidays, attending traditional gypsy fairs to continue horse trading activities. They have bought another plot of land in Yalding, Kent, with the intention of resuming their traditional life and intend to apply for planning permission for a new caravan park. The application for permission to build a caravan park for the applicants is still pending.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) by an Irish citizen, Mr William Condron, and a British citizen, Mrs Karen Condron. The applicants alleged that they were denied a fair hearing on account of the fact that the trial judge left the jury with the option of drawing an adverse inference from their silence during police interview. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) by a decision of 7 September 1999. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 January 2000 (Rule 59 § 2). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr C. Whomersley, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr D. Pannick QC, Mr M. Shaw, Counsel, Ms S. Chakrabati, Counsel and Mr I. Chisholm. The applicants were arrested at 12.45 p.m. on 28 April 1995. In the flat were found sixteen wraps of heroin weighing between 0.07 and 0.09 g. A further quantity of heroin was found weighing 1.19 g in the flat. The applicants' solicitor, Mr Delbourgo, noted that the first applicant, who seemed to be in the early stages of withdrawal, was unfit to be interviewed. However, after a 10- to 15-minute examination, the Force Medical Examiner, Dr Youlten, stated that the applicant was fit for interview. The second applicant was also seen to have withdrawal symptoms but again was stated by the Force medical Examiner to be thinking clearly and able to answer questions. The applicants were asked to explain their actions in apparently passing to, and being passed items from, flat 50. Both simply responded to these questions with the words ‘no comment’ Both applicants gave evidence at the trial and said that the heroin found in the flat had been for their own personal use and had been purchased in bulk by the first applicant the evening before their arrest. The defence case for the applicants was that they were not fit to be interviewed because they were suffering from drug withdrawal symptoms. The judge considered that Mr Delbourgo had been wrong in his analysis that the applicants had been unfit to be questioned and allowed their interviews to stand as evidence. When asked about the incident recorded on 26 April 1995 in which the second applicant was seen receiving and then returning a packet to the occupant of flat 50, the applicants gave explanations which they had not mentioned to the police in their interviews. The first applicant stated that no drugs had ever passed between the flats and that the packet contained either cigarettes or money. The second applicant said that it was simply an exchange of a packet of cigarettes. Other items had been passed this way since it was easier than having to go along the walkway of the front of each flat. When asked why they had made no comment to police questions during interview, both applicants stated that their solicitor's advice that they were not in a condition to do so, given their withdrawal from heroin. The applicants were each convicted by a majority of nine to one of being concerned in supplying heroin and possessing heroin with intent to supply. The first applicant was sentenced to a total of four years. The applicants' conviction and appeal were upheld by the Court of Appeal. The prosecution case was that in the circumstances when each of these defendants were questioned on these topics, he or she could reasonably be expected to have mentioned what they said in court. The defendants explained that their 'no comment' answers, speaking generally because of course they put it in more detail, the [applicants] said they were suffering from withdrawal symptoms and relied on Mr Delbourgo, their solicitor's advice. The applicants appealed to the Court of Appeal on two primary grounds: the inclusion of the police interviews and the contents of the judge's direction. The applicants' counsel contended that the trial judge should have excluded the “no comment” interviews as they were a direct result of following their solicitor's honest advice. James Curtis, the co-accused, was acquitted on both charges. The second applicant was sentenced to a total of three years' imprisonment. The trial judge allowed the jury to draw adverse inferences from the applicants' failure to answer questions at the interview. The judge, as the fact-finding tribunal in the voir dire (submissions on a point of law in the absence of the jury), had been correct in his decision to include the notes of interviews in evidence. The Court of Appeal did not find that this lacuna in the summing-up meant that the convictions were unsafe, having regard to the weight of the other evidence. Lord Justice Stuart-Smith explained in this connection: “We have already referred to the substantial, almost overwhelming evidence of drug supply from what was found in the [applicants'] house.” The acquittal of Curtis shows that the jury regarded the evidence of the interviews as insignificant. Curtis also failed to answer questions in interview. The applicants' appeal in its judgment delivered on 17 October 1996 was dismissed by the Court of appeals. The appeal was dismissed on 16 October 1996.

During the battle of Mount Tumbledown he witnessed the death and mutilation of several of his friends and was himself injured in the wrist by a mortar-shell blast. As a result of these experiences he suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder (“PTSD”) which manifested itself by flashbacks, nightmares, feelings of anxiety, insomnia and outbursts of anger. This disorder was not diagnosed until after the events of 29 July 1990 (see paragraph 10 below) The Court heard addresses by Mr Bratza, Mr Mackenzie and Mr Havers. Lance-sergeant, who had become a lance-Sergeant, was sent with his regiment to Northern Ireland. On 29 July 1990, after a heavy drinking session, he held members of his own unit at pistol point and threatened to kill himself and some of his colleagues. He fired two shots, which were not aimed at anyone and hit a television set, and subsequently surrendered the pistol. He was then arrested. On 31 July 1990 an ex-naval psychiatrist, Dr McKinnon, examined Mr Findlay and found that he was responsible for his actions at the time of the incident. However, a combination of stresses (including his back injury and posting to. Northern Ireland) together with his heavy drinking on the day, had led to an “almost inevitable’ event. Mr Findlay was remanded for trial on eight charges arising out of the incident of 29 July 1990 and decided that he should be tried by general court martial. He was acquitted of all charges against him by the jury on 22 July 1991. Mr Findlay appeared before the general court martial, at Regent’s Park Barracks in London, on 11 November 1991. He pleaded guilty to three charges of common assault (a civilian offence), two charges of conduct to the prejudice of good order and military discipline (a military offence) He was sentenced to two years’ imprisonment, reduction from the original sentence of two years. General Court Martial (Regent’s Park Barracks), ex parte Alexander Findlay, CO/1092/12/2/2). The judge advocate was hostile to Mr Findlay on two occasions during the hearing. The magazine appealed to the Supreme Court (Høyesterett), which by judgment of 2 September 2008 found against the applicants, by three votes to two. Mr Justice U.S. gave the following reasons, which in the main were endorsed by the two other members of the majority: “I have concluded that the appeal should be allowed.’’ “The provision in section 3-6 refers, at any rate primarily, to violation of section 390. In my view, there is no need to consider whether, as contended by [the applicants], there is a need to redress for violation of privacy.” The couple had not been informed beforehand that there were plans to publicise the wedding, nor were they asked for their consent. The article as a whole contains information about the couple and their child. The relationships between the family and their friends are clearly of a personal nature. There would have been no question of violation of privacy if consent to publication had been obtained. The next question is whether the article was unlawful. This question must be decided on the basis of an overall evaluation of the article, cf. paragraph 64 of the Big Brother judgment with further references.. In my assessment of legality I also refer, as was done in the Plata judgment, paragraphs 57 and 58: ‘... When the penal provision applies to violation of Privacy, this necessarily implies that the issue that arises is that of legality’ The European Convention on Human Rights is incorporated into internal Norwegian law in the Human Rights Act. Both Article 8 relating to respect for private and family life and Article 10 relating to the right to freedom of expression are central to the present case. The article in question clearly has a purely entertainment value. In the assessment of legality, protection under Article 8 is the most relevant principle to be weighed. (40) I will now examine the circumstances in the present Case in relation to the issue of legality. The issue is whether in spite of this there are grounds for saying there is no right to publication of details of the subjects’ private life. A wedding is a public affirmation that two persons intend to live together and has legal consequences in many different sectors of society. Information about a wedding does not in itself involve a violation of privacy if it is given in a neutral form and based on a reliable source. The Court reiterates the fundamental importance of protecting private life from the point of view of the development of every human being’s personality. That protection extends beyond the private family circle and also includes a social dimension. It considers that anyone, even if they are known to the general public, must be able to enjoy a ‘legitimate expectation’ of protection of and respect for their private life. Se og Hør ran several articles featuring photos taken from different sources together with speculation and gossip. The magazine also described the relationship between the parties during their life together, which was an invasion of their private life as a couple. A wedding is a very significant personal experience for the bridal couple, an experience that includes their families, friends and other persons close to them. The wedding ceremony and celebrations are therefore clearly part of private and family life and thus in principle should be protected. But in my opinion this consideration is only one aspect of the case. I shall now examine more closely the way the wedding was conducted. The bride arrived at the islet in a rowing boat, with six bridesmaids on board. There she was greeted by her future husband and by a men. The wedding was organised in a very unusual way and took place in an area accessible to the public under the Outdoor Recreation Act. After the ceremony the bride and groom had to step from rock to rock in order to reach the shore, which the bride accomplished in bare feet. The situation would not have been any better if the photography had taken place somewhere closer, or from a place where the photographer and journalist could have been seen by the wedding party. This could have disturbed the whole wedding. Nor was the photographing in the nature of a breach of confidence, as it would have been if for example any of the participants had published personal photos taken during or in connection with the wedding. Mr Justice T. gave the following reasons which in the main were endorsed by the other member of the minority: “(58) I am substantially in agreement with the first-voting judge’s general interpretation of section 3-6 of the Damages Act and section 390 of the Penal Code. (59) I will first examine whether the subject of the article in Se og Hør can be considered to be ‘a personal matter’ in the meaning of section 390. (60) The case raises difficult and uncertain legal questions, clarification of which is in the public interest, cf. section 20-2, third paragraph, a, of the Code of Civil Procedure. Weddings have always been a subject of general interest. It is not unusual for the couple to wish to share their wedding and its arrangements only with those closest to them. In my view the desire to hold a private wedding should be respected in the sense that the wedding ceremony should be regarded as a personal matter within the meaning of section 390. The wedding party was held at a hotel on Tjøme, which in this context is clearly a private area. The islet where the events reported by Se og Hør, and the marriage itself, took place is a relatively short walk away and directly linked with the hotel’s property. The article included a description of the guests and the couple’s families, together with the names of well-known figures. The names of guests with children were also given, and pictures were shown. I regard these as the personal touch that the bridal couple had wished to give their wedding. I agree with the first-voting judge that the publication of personal matters is justified in cases where it does not contribute to public debate. However, when matters of a personal nature such as those in question here are published, they must have at least a minimum of public interest if the invasion of privacy is to be considered legitimate. Although the desire to entertain is in itself legitimate, its nature does not justify overriding the affected parties’ desire to protect their privacy. The opposite parties have demanded that the amount decided by the Court of Appeal should be maintained. I am of the opinion that the article in Se og Hør cannot be justified on the basis of an assessment of legality. Since I know that I am in the minority, I will not formulate a final conclusion. I have no objections to the amounts decided on. (70) For these reasons, the opposite parties are entitled to redress for pain and suffering from the appellants.” The amount decided on by the court of appeal is to be maintained at the same level as the original amount. The amount to be paid to the opposite party has not yet been decided.

name: James Valentin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26461/06) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the bankruptcy proceedings against him were not terminated within a reasonable time. By a decision of 22 January 2008, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Danish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs Nina Holst-Christensen. The Court ruled that the application was not admissible, but the applicant and the Government each filed further written observations (Rule 59 § 1).
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26461/06) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the bankruptcy proceedings against him were not terminated within a reasonable time. The Court declared the application partly admissible in January 2008. The application was made by a Danish national, Mr James Valentin (“the applicant”), on 15 June 2006. The Government was represented by their Agent, Mrs Nina Holst-Christensen (”the Government’s Agent”). The Partnership’s assets, including the individual partners’ assets, were estimated at about 8 million Danish kroner (DKK) The Partnership estate was closed on 5 December 1995 with distribution of dividends. Court sessions were held on 6 November, 6 and 21 December 1995, 14 February and 17 April 1996. The Bankruptcy Court adjourned the proceedings pending the preparation of accounts. The accounts were being prepared, but could not be completed until, inter alia, the outcome of proceedings initiated by the Ministry of Taxation against Hugo Petersen’S Børsmæglerselskab A/S. The latter proceedings were finalised in 1999. The bankruptcy proceedings against the other partners of the Partnership were terminated in 1997. The Bankruptcy Court decided to postpone the approval of the accounts. An amount of approximately DKK 5.4 million remained for distribution to so-called section 98 claims. The applicant’s dispute with the tax authorities did not affect the assets available for distribution. The accounts were approved in May 1998 and the estate was closed in March 1998. During the period between November 1998 and October 1999 an amount of DKK 750,000 was made available to the applicant. Before the final deadline for notifying claims in the estate, which the applicant missed, a distribution on account was made in respect of the ordinary claims. Thirty-two Partnership creditors lodged claims for interest in the estate. Eight creditors then issued a writ against the bankruptcy estate, and the applicant intervened as a third party. On 2 May 2001, the Bankruptcy Court passed judgment in the eight lead cases, and at a meeting of creditors on 22 May 2001 the creditors declared that they did not wish to appeal against the judgments unless the applicant did so. The applicant subsequently appealed against the judgment to the High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret), hereafter the High court. The High Court ruled in favour of the applicant and the creditors on 21 May 2001. The application was dismissed on 8 November 2001. The applicant objected to the Bankruptcy Court closing the estate. He appealed against the finalisation of the estate in accordance with section 149 to the High Court, which found against him on 22 March 2002. It appears that the applicant failed to request leave to appeal against this decision to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) The Ministry of Justice (Justits Justice) disputed the Government's account of the case. The case was settled in December 2005, and the applicant was awarded DKK 100,000. The application was dismissed in April 2006, with the applicant awarded the remaining assets of his estate and the costs of administration. The appeal proceedings against the applicant were dismissed in September 2005. The application was made by a former employee of the company. The company had filed for bankruptcy in 2011. The case is still pending in the bankruptcy court. The judge invited the applicant to raise his complaints about the length of the bankruptcy proceedings before the court, where the case was pending. The applicant complained about the duration of the proceedings, the judge said. The application was eventually dismissed on June 25, 2012. The court is still awaiting a decision on whether to allow the company to file for bankruptcy. The hearing is expected to be held again on July 4, 2012, according to the court's website. It is not known when the case will be heard again.

name: Ronald Grant Jones
train_texts: The case originated in two applications (nos. 34356/06 and 40528/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, that the grant of immunity in civil proceedings to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in the case of Mr Jones and to the individual defendants in both cases amounted to a disproportionate interference with their right of access to a court. The Redress Trust (REDRESS), Amnesty International, the International Centre for the Legal Protection of human Rights (Interights) and JUSTICE (“the third-party interveners”) were given leave by the President of the Chamber to intervene in the written procedure.
eval_texts: The case originated in two applications (nos. 34356/06 and 40528/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, that the grant of immunity in civil proceedings to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in the case of Mr Jones and to the individual defendants in both cases amounted to a disproportionate interference with their right of access to a court. The Redress Trust (REDRESS), Amnesty International, the International Centre for the Legal Protection of human Rights (Interights) and JUSTICE were given leave by the President of the Chamber to intervene in the written procedure. Two men claim they were tortured in Saudi Arabia. They say they were beaten with a cane and given mind-altering drugs. They were taken to Saudi Arabia for treatment. Two of the men are still in the custody of the Saudi government. The third man has been released on bail. He is now seeking compensation for his injuries. The case has been referred to the International Court of Justice, which will decide if the case should be heard in the UK or the US. The judge will decide whether or not to hear the case, and the date of the hearing will be set at a later date. The court will also decide whether the case will be heard by the British or Saudi courts, or the American courts. The two cases were joined and on 28 October 2004 the Court of Appeal published its judgment. It unanimously dismissed Mr Jones’s appeal from the decision of the Master to refuse permission to serve Saudi Arabia outside the jurisdiction. But it allowed the appeals in respect of the refusal of permission in each case to serve the individual defendants. The applicants appealed to the Court. of Appeal with the leave of theMaster. Lord Justice Mance, with whom Lord Phillips and Lord Justice Neuberger agreed, refused to depart from this Court’S ruling in Al‑Adsani v. the United Kingdom [GC], no. 35763/97, ECHR 2001‑XI. Torture was to be regarded as outside the scope of any proper exercise of sovereign authority or with international crime, let alone with systematic torture. He did not accept that the definition of torture in Article 1 of the Convention against Torture was fatal to the applicants’ claims. He noted that the House of Lords in Pinochet (No. 3) had considered that there would be no immunity from criminal prosecution in respect of an individual officer who had committed torture abroad in an official context. Mance LJ did not consider it significant that Lieutenant Colonel Abdul Aziz had been described in Mr Jones’s claim as the “servant or agent” of Saudi Arabia. Mance LJ considered that whether any claim in the English courts against individuals could proceed was better determined not by reference to immunity. He was of the view that the legislation and case-law of the United States of America militated strongly against any such settled principle. He considered the dicta in the separate opinion of Judges Higgins, Kooijmans and Buergenthal to the judgment of the International Court of Justice in the ‘Arrest Warrant’ case to provide further confirmation that there was no settled international practice in this area. He acknowledged that the courts of one State were not expected to. pursue any civil claim. But he concluded that it might be disproportionate to maintain a blanket refusal of recourse to the civil courts of another jurisdiction. Mance LJ concluded that giving blanket effect to a foreign State’s claim to State immunity ratione materiae in respect of a State official alleged to have committed acts of systematic torture could deprive the right of access to a court under Article 6 of real meaning. He considered that the judgment in Pinochet (No. 3) (see paragraphs 44-56 below) had shown that torture could no longer fall within the scope of the official duties. Lord Phillips agreed with the conclusions of Mance L J as regards both the claim against Saudi Arabia and the claims against the individual officials. He therefore allowed the applicants’ appeals inrespect of the individual defendants and remitted them for further argument, concluding: “96. ...” Saudi Arabia appealed to the House of Lords against the decision of the Court of Appeal in respect of the individual defendants. Mr Jones appealed against the. decision in respect to his claim against Saudi Arabia itself. On 14 June 2006, the House. of Lords unanimously allowed Saudi Arabia’s appeal and dismissed. the appeal by Mr Jones. Lord Bingham considered that there was a “wealth of authority” in the United Kingdom and elsewhere to show that a State was entitled to claim immunity for its servants or agents. The fact that conduct was unlawful or objectionable was not, of itself, a ground for refusing immunity. In some borderline cases there could be doubt whether the. conduct of an individual, although a servant or agent, had a sufficient connection with a State to entitle it to claim. immunity for his conduct. Lord Bingham disagreed with the applicants’ submission that torture could not be a governmental or official act since, under Article 1 of the Convention against Torture, torture had to be inflicted by or with the connivance of a public official or other person acting in an official capacity. The applicants referred to a substantial body of authority showing that the courts of the United States would not recognise acts performed by individual officials as being carried out for the purposes of immunity. Lord Bingham considered the first to be of slight legal authority, the second to be an obiter dictum and the third not to be accurate statement of international law. Lord Bingham found that the prohibition of torture did not override all other rules of international law. Article 14 of the Convention against Torture did not provide for universal civil jurisdiction. There was no evidence that States had recognised or given effect to any international-law obligation to exercise universal jurisdiction over claims arising from alleged breaches of peremptory norms of law. For these reasons, Lord Bingham agreed with the Court of Appeal that the claim brought by Mr Jones against Saudi Arabia was to be dismissed. In respect of the individual defendants, he found the conclusion of the Appeal on the torture claims could not be sustained. He considered that the court had incorrectly departed from the position in its previous ruling in Propend that the acts of State officials were to be considered the act of the State itself. In Lord Bingham’s view both errors resulted from a misreading of Pinochet (No. 3) (see paragraph 44-56 below) Lord Hoffmann, concurring in the judgment, considered that there was no automatic conflict between the jus cogens prohibition on torture and the law of State immunity. Saudi Arabia, in claiming immunity, was not justifying torture but merely objecting to the jurisdiction of the English courts in deciding whether it had used torture or not. The distinction between criminal proceedings (which were the subject of universal jurisdiction) and civil proceedings ( which were not) was “fundamental” and one that could not be “wished away”. Lord Hoffmann found Lord Justice Mance’s conclusion that the Convention against Torture did not lend acts of torture any official character to be unsatisfactory. He also considered inappropriate the Court of Appeal's proposed approach to the exercise of jurisdiction. He concluded that it would be “invidious in the extreme for the judicial branch of government to decide that it will allow the investigation of allegations of torture against the officials of one foreign state but not against those of another” He considered that it was necessary to show that international law did not require immunity against civil suit to be accorded to officials who were alleged to have committed torture.

name: Folke Schmidt
train_texts: The Schmidt and Dahlström case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (hereinafter referred to as ‘the Commission’). The case originated in an application against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission by two Swedish subjects, Mr. Folke Schmidt and Mr. Hans Dahlstrøm, on 9 June 1972. The Court deemed it conducive to the proper administration of justice to constitute a single Chamber to consider both the present case and that of the Swedish Engine Drivers’ Union (Rule 21 para. 6). On 15 October 1974, the President of the Court drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of five of the seven judges required to sit as members of the Chamber.
eval_texts: The Schmidt and Dahlström case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (hereinafter referred to as ‘the Commission’). The case originated in an application against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission by two Swedish subjects on 9 June 1972. The President of the Court deemed it conducive to the proper administration of justice to constitute a single Chamber to consider both the present case and that of the Swedish Engine Drivers’ Union. The five judges so selected were Mr H. Mosler, Mr E. Rodenbourg, Mr. A. Favre, Mr G. Wiarda and Mr. P. O’Donoghue. The oral hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building in Strasbourg on 25 September 1975. There appeared before the Court: Mr. H. DANELIUS, Head of the Legal Department at the Ministry for Foreign Affairs, Agent; Mr. B. HÅRDEFELT, Chief Legal Adviser at the. Ministry of Finance. The Commission produced the document recently called for by the Court. The Court heard the addresses of Mr. Fawcett, Mr. Schmidt for the Commission and Mr. Danelius for the Government, as well as their replies to questions put by the. Court and several judges. Swedish workers and employers in the private sector have traditionally enjoyed the right to form and join trade unions and associations. In 1971, after expiry of one collective agreement and during negotiations for a new agreement, the applicants’ unions called selective strikes not affecting the sectors in which worked the applicants, who thus did not come out on strike. Mr. Schmidt and Mr. Dahlström complain that they, as members of the “belligerent“ unions, were denied certain retroactive benefits paid to members of other trade union and to non-union employees who had not participated in the strikes. The case will be heard by the Labour Court. The Act of 1936 guarantees two distinct rights to the parties on the labour market. The right to organise is defined in Section 3 of the Act as being the right of employers and employees to belong to an employers’ organisation or a trade union. It imposes on the other party an obligation to enter into negotiations, to attend meetings for negotiations and, where necessary, to make proposals for the settlement of the issues involved. This provision is applicable to all trade unions. As from 1 January 1966, the 1965 State Officials Act (statstjänstemannalag) has virtually assimilated State employees to employees in the private sector. The Act made the 1928 Collective Agreement Act, the 1928 Labour Court Act and the 1936 Act on the Right to Organise and Negotiate applicable in the public sector. The Act provided for collective agreements to be concluded, subject to certain exceptions, between the National Collective Bargaining Office (Statens Avtalsverk) and the organisations of State employees. The Ministry of Finance has a nominee on the governing board of the Office. The few independent trade unions represent only about 2,000 State employees in all. Insofar as they are union members at all, university teachers and army officers generally belong to SACO and SR respectively. Negotiations in the public sector of the labour market are centralised in that they are conducted by the federations on behalf of their member unions. Collective agreements in Sweden are normally concluded for a period of two or three years. For various reasons, however, the new collective agreement is often concluded some time after the previous agreement has expired. The new agreement has often specifically provided that its terms shall apply retroactively as from the date of expiry of previous agreement. In the case of a strike during the bargaining period, employers have customarily refused to grant retroactive benefits in order to deter unions from taking industrial action in the future.  collective action may not be taken by the different trade unions independently but rather on the basis of a decision by, or after receiving the approval of, the federation concerned. The question whether an individual employee has any means of challenging his union’s decision to go on strike is a matter exclusively governed by the internal rules of the union concerned. These may provide for a right to ask for a secret ballot or for other rights to object to the union's decisions to take industrial action. The law described above at paragraphs 10 to 17 has in recent years undergone various changes which, being subsequent to the facts at issue, are not relevant for the present case. Previous collective agreement was reinstated on 13 March 1971 for a period of six weeks. All strikes and lock-outs terminated forthwith. In June 1971 in a new global agreement for the years 1971 to 1973. According to this agreement, certain posts were upgraded and the salary scales were generally increased retroactively as from 1 January 1971. Clause 18, however, provided for an exception in this respect: “Officials who were members between 1 January and 12 March 1971 (or any part of this period) of organisations that organised industrial action... shall not be entitled to the increased wage benefits applicable under the agreement, unless the Collective Bargaining Office decides otherwise” SACO and SR brought an action against the State under the 1936 Act on the Right to Organise and Negotiate. Mr. Dahlström, who was upgraded under the new agreement, was affected for the whole period up to 12 March 1971. During these periods the applicants performed work for a lower salary than that paid to other employees who were in the same salary brackets but not members of SACO or SR. Their financial losses amounted to Kr. 300 and Kr. 1,000 respectively. In its judgment of 22 December 1971, the Labour Court unanimously rejected the claim of the applicants’ unions. The Court first confirmed the parties’ common view that the right to organise did not exclude the possibility for strikes. The Court found that no such purpose on the part of the State could be established. No support had appeared for the idea that the State intended to induce members of SACO and SR to switch over to TCO-S and SF. The Court assumed that the latter organisations would also have been refused retroactivity if they had organised industrial action during the process of negotiations. Any procedure designed to refuse the benefit of retroactivity generally to non-union employees in sectors where SACo and SR were dominant or representative could have become very complicated and time-consuming. The State would be barred from upholding the principle that a strike destroys retroactivity in any other way than by refusing retroactive validity for agreements with respect to all employee organisations. The applicants complained that in the particular circumstances the Government’s policy regarding payment of retroactive benefits had amounted to preferential treatment. The Commission declared the application admissible by a decision of 18 October 1972. In its report of 17 July 1974, the Commission: (i) confirmed its opinion, previously expressed in the report in the Swedish Engine Drivers’ Union case, that Article 11 para. 1 (art. 11-1) may legitimately extend to cover State responsibility in the field of labour-management relations and thus to provide some protection for unions against interference by employers. (ii) expressed the opinion: ‘In view of the preceding finding, the. Commission was not called upon to examine whether the action complained of was justified under Article 11. para. 2.’ The report found that the differential treatment complained of was in the circumstances justified as an industrial relations policy. The report contains a separate concurring opinion. It found that there had been no violation of Article 14 read in conjunction with Article 11 para. 1 (art. 14+11-1). The report also found that it had been justified as a matter of industrial relations. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) for further action. The ECHR ruled that the case should be referred back to the ECH for further proceedings. The decision was upheld and the case was adjourned until January 24, 2015.

name: Richard John Powell
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 16 March 1989. It originated in an application (no. 9310/81) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. The object of the request was to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 13 (art. 13) of the Convention. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and sought leave, which was granted by the President of the Court, to be represented by a university law lecturer from the UK.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 16 March 1989. It originated in an application (no. 9310/81) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. The object of the request was to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 13 (art. 13) of the Convention. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and sought leave, which was granted by the President of the Court, to be represented by a university law lecturer from the UK. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir Vincent Evans, the elected judge of British nationality. Hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr Bratza for the Government, by Mr Busuttil for the Commission and by Ms Hampson for the applicants, as well as their replies to its questions. Various documents were lodged at the registry by the Government and the applicants on the day of the hearing and on different dates between 10 October 1989 and 4 January 1990. The first applicant, Richard John Powell, is a director of a mining concern and lives with his family at Esher, Surrey, in a house which he bought in 1957. Since 1972 it has lain under a flight departure route from Heathrow in operation for about one third of the year. Since 1984 the house has been within a lower NNI contour. About 6,500 people around Heathrow Airport experience a noise exposure equal to or greater than that suffered by Mr Rayner and his family. The NNI is a long-term average measure of noise exposure which is used in the United Kingdom to assess the disturbance from aircraft noise to communities near airports. It takes account of two features of the noise, namely the average noisiness and the number of aircraft heard during an average summer day. The flights which determine the NNI at any point on the ground are those which take place between 06.00 and 18.00 hours Greenwich Mean Time during the three busy summer months. No development whatsoever is permitted within the 60 NNI and over contours (high noise-annoyance zone) It is to be noted that the NNI calculation reflects a logarithmic element in the PNdB scale, which has the result that every increase of 10 in that scale represents approximately a doubling of the loudness. The Government’s policy, as stated in the 1985 “Airports Policy“ White Paper, is that they are “not prepared to make any commitments at this stage on the question of a fifth terminal at Heathrow but will keep the matter under review“ (Command Paper, Cmnd 9542, paragraph 5.19). The British Airports Authority, being a public statutory body, did not have power to acquire property near an airport. The Noise Abatement Act 1960 specifically exempts aircraft noise from its protection. An action will lie at common law for nuisance in respect of an activity which unreasonably interferes with the use and enjoyment of land, for example an activity causing annoyance through noise. If liability is established, damages may be awarded or, in certain circumstances, an injunction granted. There being no relevant new or altered development in the case of Heathrow Airport there was no need for such a scheme to be introduced in the first place. The liability of aircraft operators is further limited by the Civil Aviation Act 1982. The 1982 Act does not exclude all liability on the part of aircraft operators for trespass and nuisance caused by aircraft in flight. The exemption applies only in respect of aircraft flying at a reasonable height above the ground. The main forum for international co-operation seeking to make aircraft quieter is the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) The broad thrust of ICAO’s work has been towards the development of a series of standards, leading to the phasing out of aircraft unable to meet them. These standards are not operative within the I CAO member States unless and until they are given effect in national legislation. In the United Kingdom effect is given to them by means of an Air Navigation (Noise Certification) Order. A 1984 Order gave effect to new ICAO standards and to regulations based upon recommendations of the European Civil Aviation Conference. In the event of an infringement of the noise limit, the Airport informs the airline by letter and sends a copy to the Department of Transport.
