The present reality is that I cannot foresee any circumstance in which the undisclosed material, that is the material undisclosed to the trial judge, would be of assistance to the defence. But it may be that the defence may advance a proposition or raise an issue that might by remote possibility make that so, and I think if the Crown concedes that that's the position then the Crown should make the matter known. The trial judge rejected both applications. the defence of entrapment, further disclosure was required. The trial judge found that taking the circumstantial evidence and the inferences to be drawn from it, he was satisfied of the applicant's guilt of the two offences beyond reasonable doubt. On 12 November 2002 the applicant was convicted by the trial judge, without a jury, of two offences: possession of firearms and ammunition with intent, contrary to Article 17 of the Firearms (NI) Order 1981; and possession of articles for a purpose connected with terrorism. The applicant was sentenced to concurrent terms of imprisonment of twelve years and two years respectively. The applicant appealed against his conviction on both charges. On 28 October 2004, the Court of Appeal in Northern Ireland unanimously dismissed the appeal. The non-disclosed material was not considered by the Court before it gave judgment. Instead, it considered the House of Lords ruling in R. v. H and C [2004] A.C. 134 (see paragraph 32 below) and reviewed this Court's judgments in Rowe and Davis and Jasper, both cited above; Fitt v the United Kingdom [GC], no. 29777/96, ECHR 2000‑II; Edwards and Lewis v the UK, no. 39647/98 and 40461/98, 22 July 2003. The Court of Appeal found that the applicant's defence of entrapment was well known to the trial judge, the prosecution, and the disclosure judge and no other issue had been identified that might sound on the question of disclosure. The disclosure judge had been unable to envisage any circumstances in which the non-disclosed material could assist the defence either by enhancing the case that was being made for the applicant or by undermining or weakening the prosecution case. It agreed with the disclosureJudge that there had been no need for special counsel to be appointed and there was nothing to indicate that the material characterised as wholly irrelevant to the applicant’s defence might have suddenly become relevant. It rejected the. applicant's contention that the. disclosure judge should have obtained a daily transcript of the trial and examined it for any sign of material that might have assisted the applicant. Court of Appeal refused to certify a point of law of general importance or grant leave to appeal to the House of Lords. Court of Appeal dismissed appeal on 19 November 2004. Court had the opportunity to assess matters and give their explanations as to the circumstances in which they came to be involved with the applicant. Court also had the chance to assess and rule on the appeal's merits. court of appeal dismissed appeal and ruled in favour of the applicant in 2004. court also refused to certified a point  of law on general importance. court ruled in favor of the claimant and ruled that the case should go to the Supreme Court of Justice rather than the Court of appeal.

name: Jane Smith
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court, in accordance with the provisions applicable prior to the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case originated in an application (no. 25154/94) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 of the Convention by a British citizen, Mrs Jane Smith (“the applicant”), on 4 May 1994. The applicant alleged that planning and enforcement measures taken against her in respect of her occupation of her land in her caravans violated her right to respect for home, her family and private life.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court, in accordance with the provisions applicable prior to the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case originated in an application (no. 25154/94) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 of the Convention by a British citizen, Mrs Jane Smith (“the applicant”), on 4 May 1994. The applicant alleged that planning and enforcement measures taken against her in respect of her occupation of her land in her caravans violated her right to respect for home, her family and private life. The applicant and the Government each filed a memorial. Third-party comments were also received from European Roma Rights Centre. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 May 2000. The applicant is a gypsy by birth. Since her birth she has travelled constantly, mainly in the Surrey area, with her family in search of work. They regard travelling as detrimental to both the health of their family and to the education of their children. They have five children, born in 1975, 1977, 1982, 1989 and 1994. The Court heard addresses by Mr Drabble and Mr Pannick. In 1988, the High Court had granted a declaration that Surrey County Council was in breach of its duty under section 6 of the Caravan Sites Act 1968 to provide provision for gypsies. In March 1993, the applicant bought land known as 111A Almners Road, Runnymede. It was a portion of a garden in a Green Belt area where there was already some residential development. The applicant moved a mobile home onto the land and took up residence with her family. In 1996 the applicant’s uncle, Jasper Smith, a member of the Gypsy Council, stated that he had attempted on numerous occasions prior to 1993 to obtain a site on an official site on behalf of the applicant without success. The previous owner of 111A Almners Road, also a gypsy, had been refused planning permission in January 1993 to live on the land in a caravan. The Council considered that the stationing of a caravan would be detrimental to the character of the Green Belt. The applicant was aware of this situation and the fact that the previous owner had appealed to the Secretary of State for the Environment against the refusal of planning permission and the enforcement order. An Inspector appointed by the Department of Environment heard evidence and representations from the applicant and the Council. By a letter dated 3 June 1993, the Inspector dismissed the appeal. “10. The mobile home is situated on an enclosed plot of land fronting Almners road, adjacent to No. 111. This land is separated from the adjacent house by a screen fence, which continues along the rear boundary of the appeal site’ The appeals site lies within the south west sector of the Metropolitan Green Belt. Structure Plan 1989 and policy PE2 of the Replacement Structure Plan 1992 provide that gypsy caravan sites may be appropriate and necessary in the green belt, but they will not be considered acceptable as of right. Despite the support of some nearby residents, I consider that the discernible presence of the unauthorised development on the appeals site is harmful to the appearance of this mainly rural location. … In light of this and its particular impact on the aims of green belt policy, I conclude … that the use of the land for a residential caravan site for a mobile home and associated operational development is not appropriate to this part of the Met. There are no plans to change the status of the green belt. There is no need to change it because it is already there. There are plans to make it more accessible to people who need it. The green belt is a place to live, not a place for people to live. It is an important place to work and to raise a family. It has been around for a long time, and it is good to see it being used again and again. It's a good place to raise children, but it is not a great place for a family to live and work. It would be a shame to see people suffer because they can't get to their family’s home. The applicant applied to the Council for planning permission to build a bungalow. The Council refused planning permission. The applicant remained on her land in the caravan as the family had not been offered a place on an official campsite and thus had no alternative legal site to place their caravan. Injunction proceedings were instituted against the applicant and her family by the Council. On 5 September 1994, the Council obtained an injunction in the High Court requiring the family to move off their land immediately. In light of the new Criminal Justice and Public Order Act, the applicant, in fear of being on the roadside, applied to be placed on the local authority homeless list on 4 August 1994. The applicant has applied for accommodation in a more natural environment but no offer has yet been made. The Council had previously offered three alternative pieces of land which were subsequently withdrawn due to a methane gas leak, boggy ground and vicinity to a rubbish dump. The local authority has stated that, in the event that the applicant is forced to leave the site, the authority will provide temporary accommodation for her until permanent accommodation becomes available. However, in view of the restrictions on development within the Green Belt, all accommodation offered will be in urban areas. The statistics for 1994 showed that the official sites in the area catered for 44 caravans while there were another 26Caravans on unauthorised sites. 70% of the County was Green Belt, 20% urban and 10% countryside beyond the Green Belt. Areas of outstanding natural beauty (AONB) or designated landscape value (ADLV) account for 40% of County. According to the diagram, the Runnymede area consists entirely of Green Belt and urban centres. The applicant submitted that all the area of the Council was in the Metropolitan Green Belt area. The Government stated that only a large part of it was. The diagram and materials submitted from the Surrey Structure Plan 1994 indicates that 70% of. the County was Green Belt,. 20%Urban and 10%.

name: Ulf Arne Hammern
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30287/96) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 2 of the Convention on account of the reasoning relied on by the Norwegian courts in refusing his compensation claim. The Norwegian Government were represented by Mr F. Elgesem, who acted as Agent until he left the Attorney-General's Office (Civil Matters) in June 2002. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 17 September 2002 (Rule 59 § 2). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr H. Harborg, Attorney- General's Office, (Civil matters) Agent, and (b) Mr K. Kallerud, Counsel/Adviser.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 2 of the. Convention on account of the reasoning relied on by the Norwegian courts in refusing his. compensation claim with respect to damage sustained in criminal. proceedings in which he had been acquitted. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 17 September 2002. The Court heard addresses by Mr Krokeide (counsel for Mr O, who pleaded the common issues relevant to both his case and that of Mr Hammern), Mr Wiig and Mr Elgesem. The applicant spent three periods in pre-trial detention – respectively 7, 7 and 32 days – a total of 46 days. He denied the accusations and was suspended from his post at Botngård kindergarten in Bjugn. The court found him guilty of sexual abuse, but not guilty of any other charges. The case was heard in the Court of Appeal in Copenhagen. The Court of Appeals is the highest court in Denmark. The jury was made up of the Attorney-General's Office (Civil matters) and the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutors. The applicant's trial took place before the Frostating High Court (lagmannsrett), sitting with three judges and a jury, over a period of 43 days, between 15 November 1993 and 31 January 1994. After the jury had answered all of the 25 questions relating to the indictment in the negative, the applicant was acquitted. The applicant subsequently filed a petition with the High Court, claiming compensation under Articles 444 to 446 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court ordered the State to award him the entirety of his claim of NOK 45,000 in compensation for pecuniary damage under Article 445. However, on the basis of an assessment, the relevant parts of which are quoted in the Supreme Court's (Høyesterett) decision cited below (paragraph 23) the applicant appealed against this decision. The Appeals Selection Committee, considering that the applicant's appeal concerned the High Court's application of Article 444 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, rejected the appeal. The Appeals Selection. Committee 's decision contained assumptions of criminal liability and that, consequently, it violated Article 6. § 2 of the Convention. The compensation case must be determined on an independent basis and the rules on evidence applying in such compensation cases do not differ from those which apply to ordinary compensation claims. The Supreme Court concluded that the rules in Article 444 were not, as such, contrary to Article 6 ° 2 of the Convention. He requested the Supreme Court to quash the High. Court's decision. The Appeals Selection Committee said the High Court had to justify why it had rejected the compensation claim. The Committee said that the reasoning must be formulated in the light of the conditions for compensation as mentioned above. The High Court was aware of the rules in Article 6 § 2 of the Convention, the European Court's Sekanina judgment and the 1994 decision of the Supreme Court, the Committee said. The committee said it would base itself on this view in its assessment of the present case. The case is a compensation claim brought by Mr Hammern. The question is whether he is able to show that he did not carry out the acts which were referred to in the indictment. Mr Hammern was charged with sexual abuse of 10 children. The children themselves gave statements to their parents, during the judicial examinations and to a psychologist, about abuse by Mr Hammern. Children markedly changed their behaviour, inter alia, in the form of bedwetting, refusing or expressing fear about going to the kindergarten. Several children had a sore crotch, sore abdomen and, on one or several occasions, blood on their underwear. The High Court does not find any reason to go further into the discussion about the possibility of paedophilia. It is not only the so-called real paedophiles who commit abuse against children. The Appeals Selection Committee finds that the High Court' s reasoning does not go further than is necessary to carry out a careful examination of the compensation claim. The Committee once more emphasises that a refusal to award compensation under Article 444 does not imply that the previous acquittal is being undermined.” In the light of the foregoing, the appeal must be rejected,” the committee concluded. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, France, on September 13, 2013. The court ruled in favour of the accused, and the case was adjourned until October 15, 2013, to allow the case to be heard by a full court.

name: Raphael Rowe
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 12 March 1999. It originated in an application (no. 28901/95) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 by two British nationals. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 of the Convention. A panel of the Grand Chamber decided on 31 March 1999 that the case would be examined by the Grand chamber of the Court. The Grand Chamber included ex officio Sir Nicolas Bratza, the judge elected in respect of the UK.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 12 March 1999. It originated in an application (no. 28901/95) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 by two British nationals. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 of the Convention. The Grand Chamber included ex officio Sir Nicolas Bratza, the President of the Court, Mrs E. Palm and Mr J.‑P. Costa. Hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 October 1999. The Court heard addresses by Mr Emmerson and Mr Cranston and also their replies to questions put by several of its members. The offences occurred during the night of 15 to 16 December 1988, a series of offences occurred in Surrey, England. The first, which may have occurred sometime after 1.30 a.m., involved an attack on two men in a parked car in a field near a public house in Fickleshall. Just after the conclusion of sexual activities between the two men (Mr Ely and Mr Hurburgh), two masked men appeared. Three masked robbers arrived at the Napier household in Oxted. Two of them went into Timothy Napier's room; one had a knife, the other a gun. Richard Napier was forced back upstairs to the bedroom where his wife was waiting. A knife was pointed at her and she was told to remove her rings and jewellery or her fingers would be cut off. The other two robbers ransacked the room before all three fled taking Timothy's Toyota car. Hurburgh's car was found abandoned nearby. Police received information that the persons responsible for the murder and other offences were living at 25 Lawrie Park Road, Sydenham. Raphael Rowe, Michael Davis and Randolph Johnson lived at No. 25. Mark Jobbins, Norman Duncan and Shane Griffin also lived at the address. Duncan and Griffin sniffed glue on a regular basis. All three had criminal records. Rowe, Davis and Johnson were black. Jobbinson and Duncan were white. Johnson was white. Rowe and Davis were both black. Johnson is white. They were all black. The three men were arrested on suspicion of aggravated burglary. A number of items from the Spicer/Almond robbery, including two eternity rings, a yellow metal watch strap and a lady's watch, were found in Rowe's wastepaper basket. Rowe's girlfriend, 16-year-old school student and girlfriend of Rowe, produced to the police a number ofthings from the robbery. The trial of the two applicants and Johnson took place at the Central Criminal Court in February 1990. The prosecution relied substantially upon the evidence of the Jobbins Group. The latter admitted having jointly stolen the Spitfire which had been found abandoned near the scene of the first robbery and murder. They also admitted driving the Renault and Cavalier stolen at the last robbery to a field in Sidcup where they had set fire to them. The trial concluded with the acquittal of Johnson and the conviction of the other two applicants. The case was heard in front of a jury of 11 men and six women. The jury returned a verdict of not guilty, and the sentence was quashed. All three of the accused denied any involvement in the offences. Defence argued that many of the witnesses for the prosecution were unreliable. It was argued that if anyone from No. 25 had been responsible for the crimes, it was the Jobbins Group, and they had given a deliberately false account to the police in order to implicate the accused and thus exonerate themselves. The defence referred to the substantial reward which had been offered as a factor which may have motivated prosecution witnesses to give evidence. The jury returned a verdict of not guilty and sentenced the three men to life in prison with a minimum term of 20 years. The sentence was suspended for 25 years. The applicants and Johnson appealed on the grounds that their convictions were unsafe and unsatisfactory because of weaknesses and inconsistencies in the evidence against them. The disclosure procedure to be followed when the prosecution was in possession of material which it believed should not be disclosed to the defence had been changed by the judgment in R.V., R and R. V. The case was re-canvassed before a differently constituted Court of Appeal on 14 and 15 January 1993. The Lord Chief Justice, Lord Taylor, participated in both hearings. The appeal was heard ex parte and the application was rejected. The applicants were convicted of murder, assault occasioning grievous bodily harm, and robbery. The applicants applied to the Court of Appeal for leave to appeal to the House of Lords, but this application was refused on 30 September 1993. In 1994 the applicants applied for a review of the safety of their convictions. In April 1997 the Criminal Cases Review was carried out. This resulted in an ex parte application which was heard in camera. This application was upheld and referred to by Watkins LJ in his final judgment in these terms: 'We upheld the claim and refused to order disclosure of any kind for reasons we gave on 22nd June and which are recorded' The application was dismissed and the applicants were not allowed to appeal. The Criminal Appeal Commission (“the CCRC”) was set up under the Criminal Appeal Act 1995. In August 1997 the CCRC appointed an officer from Greater Manchester Police to investigate the events surrounding the prosecution of the applicants and Johnson. The investigating officer's report was submitted in January 1999. The CCRC found, inter alia, that Duncan was a long-standing police informant, who, on 18 December 1988 had approached a Sussex police officer and told him that the applicants were responsible for the crimes of 15 to 16 December 1988. Duncan had received a reward of GBP 10,300, in addition to police protection between 18 and 22 December 1988 and immunity from prosecution in relation to his admitted participation as an accessory to the offences.

name: David Frederick Bullen
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 3383/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were charged with involvement in a money laundering scheme together with a third co-accused. The application was lodged on 19 January 2006 by two British nationals, Mr David Frederick Bullen and Mr Kamlesh Kumar Soneji. On 14 June 2007 the Acting President of the Chamber of the Fourth Section to which the case had been allocated decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the case at the same time. The case was listed for the confiscation hearing with a time-estimate of five working days. Adjournment pending R. v. Steele and Shevki. until after passing sentence was fixed for 30 October 2000, outside the six-month period required under section 72A of the CJA 1988. The applicants objected that the court lacked jurisdiction to hear the. proceedings on the grounds that more than six months had elapsed since their convictions. and that the judge had not considered whether there were ‘exceptional circumstances’ warranting the imposition of the. confiscation orders outside the statutory time-limit. The confiscation proceedings were adjourned until 5 February 2001. The Court of Appeal heard and dismissed Mr E’s appeal against conviction. Mr E. was seeking leave to appeal to the House of Lords. The substantive hearing of the confiscation hearing was again adjourned. The Crown Court imposed a confiscation order on the second applicant in the amount of GBP 75,350. The first applicant lodged an application for appeal on the same grounds as the second. The proceedings were adjourned to 28 January 2002 with a time estimate of three weeks. The confiscation proceedings were again listed for mention before the trial judge on 30 March 2001. The hearing was fixed to begin on 15 October 2001. On 7 February 2002 the first applicant was ordered to pay GBP 375,000. The Court of Appeal allowed the applicants’ appeals and quashed the confiscation orders and default sentences of imprisonment. They noted that on 29 June 2000, defence counsel for the second applicant and the co-accused Mr. E. had requested an early hearing at the Crown Court. However, the earliest date that the trial judge would be available was the week beginning 30 October 2000. There was no evidence of any enquiry from 24 March 2000 onwards into whether a space could be found for the confiscated hearing during the six-month period. Neither had there been any analysis of any factors which might amount to exceptional circumstances. The trial judge had also “candidly acknowledged more than once” that there were no exceptional circumstances to justify the imposition of a confiscation order. The Court of Appeal certified that a point of law of general public importance was involved in the decisions. The House of Lords observed that the core problem before it was whether, as a matter of statutory construction, failure to comply with a statutory time-limit would have the effect of invalidating an act. In London and Clydeside Estates Ltd v. Aberdeen District Council [1980] 1 WLR 182, 189E-190C, Lord Hailsham had emphasised that it was within the courts’ inherently discretionary jurisdiction to determine the nature of a particular statutory requirement. The prime purpose behind the statutory provision for confiscation orders was to recover any financial benefit that an offender might have obtained from his criminal conduct. In October 2005 the Court of Appeal re-imposed the confiscation orders and sentences of imprisonment in default on the applicants. The prejudice to the applicants was not significant and was outweighed by the countervailing public interest in not allowing convicted offenders to escape confiscation for what were no more than bona fide errors in the judicial process. In any event, there would always be the safeguard of judicial review should there be an apparent abuse of process. The Crown Court had postponed its final decision on confiscation Orders in good faith. In the present case, the Crown court had postponed the final decision in goodfaith. The public interest was outweighing the prejudice to applicants and they were not prejudiced by the prejudice. The court could not have intended to disable a court from making a confiscation order after sentence.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28135/95) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, inter alia, that he was ill-treated while in detention. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The case was decided by the Court of Appeal. The applicant was interviewed five times by two teams of two detectives. The doctor gave the applicant two tablets (a mild analgesic) and prescribed four such tablets a day if required. During the sixth interview the applicant broke his silence and gave detailed answers to a number of questions admitting to his involvement in the assembly and planting of the bomb. The applicant was medically examined that evening at 8.20 p.m. during the seventh interview. He signed a lengthy statement which. described in considerable detail his part in the conspiracy to plant and detonate the. bomb. His solicitor made notes on the applicant's allegations of ill-treatment. The solicitor chose not to pass these complaints on to the police. The applicant, along with others, was charged at Belfast Magistrates' Court with conspiracy to cause explosions, possession of explosives with intent, conspiracy to murder and membership of the Irish Republican Army. The trial of the applicant and his co-accused began at Belfast Crown Court before a single judge sitting without a jury. The prosecution case was based on the admissions made by the applicant in interview and, in particular, the written statements signed by him. The applicant applied under section 8 of the Northern Ireland (Emergency Provisions) Act 1978 (as amended) to have the admissions and statement made during questioning excluded on the basis of his alleged ill-treatment. The voir dire ended on 23 October 1990 when the trial judge rejected the application. On 21 December 1990 the trial judge gave judgment. He noted that the only evidence against the applicant was the admissions and statement made while in custody at Castlereagh police station. The trial judge summarised the applicant's evidence of ill-treatment and this summary was later accepted on appeal by the applicant as constituting an accurate account of his evidence in this respect. On the question of general credibility the judge found that the applicant had repeatedly lied to the court, whereas the detectives involved were not at all shaken by a rigorous cross-examination in their firm denials. As to the ESDA evidence, he found it impossible to accept that ill- treatment of the nature alleged by the. applicant could have gone on without it being picked up by the cameras in the room where the applicant. was questioned. The trial judge rejected the applicant's allegations of ill-treatment. On 11 January 1991 the applicant was sentenced to twenty years' imprisonment. The applicant's appeal against conviction was heard by the Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland on 16 June 1993. The court concluded that it was satisfied that the applicant had not been ill-treated and that his conviction was neither unsafe nor unsatisfactory. On 17 December 1993 the applicant’s appeal against his sentence was rejected. The findings in the medical report drawn up at the hospital on 8 May 2006 were consistent with the previous report and indicated that the injuries inflicted on the applicant had not caused him any permanent physical damage. The report stated in particular that a woman who resembled the female applicant had quarrelled with and pushed a police officer during the incidents. There was no indication of an assault against the applicants against the police officers. The Izmir public prosecutor decided not to prosecute the police officers involved in the incidents. The public prosecutor held that the injuries mentioned in the applicants’ medical reports were not life-threatening and only required simple medical treatment. The second applicant had applied to the Izmir Branch of the Human Rights Foundation of Turkey (İnsan Hakları Vakfı) on 3 May 2006 for further medical examinations. On the same day the applicant gave his statements before the Public Prosecutor at the Istanbul State Security Court. He reiterated his account of the events, but denied certain parts of his police statements, whereby he had admitted to being a member of a criminal organisation. He did not indicate anything with regard to his alleged ill‑treatment. The Public Prosecutor filed an indictment against the applicant on 21 June 2001, accusing him of armed robbery, membership of ariminal organisation and illegally carrying weapons. In 2001, the applicant claimed the indictment had not been served on him and that he had not fully understood the charges against him. He further retracted the previous statements he had made before the police and the Public Prosecutor. The Public Prosecutor submitted his written opinion to the Istanbul State Security Court. He stated that the telephones of two of the accused had been intercepted and that the conversations between them and with the applicant had revealed that the latter had threatened them. Finally, relying on the telephone recordings and the statements of the other accused, the Public prosecutor proposed that the applicant should be found guilty as charged. The applicant requested the examination of two witnesses, A.V.O. and a certain İ.D.Y. The Court of Cassation found the applicant guilty as charged and sentenced him to twenty years and ten months' imprisonment and a judicial fine. The applicant appealed against the judgment, arguing that the court had failed to hear any witnesses on his behalf and that it had restricted his right to defend himself during the course of the proceedings. On 12 April 2004 the Court of. Cassation upheld the judgment after holding a hearing, during which the applicant was. not present. the outcome of the court proceedings. The judge ruled that the applicant’s guilt had been established on the basis of an overall assessment of the evidence at its disposal, without specifying which particular evidence it relied on.

He was stripped naked, immersed in cold water and beaten with a truncheon on various parts of his body, including the soles of his feet. His hands were tied with a blanket and he was strung up by his arms and subjected to a form of torture known as “Palestinian hanging” The applicant was examined by a medical expert who observed two ecchymosises of 2-3 cm on both sides of the applicant's hips and an allergic dermatitis on his right hand. The applicant filed further petitions alleging that he had been subjected to ill‑treatment while in police custody. The Istanbul public prosecutor initiated an investigation into the applicant's allegations of ill-treatment. The applicant surrendered a 7.65 mm calibre pistol and seven bullets to the police officers. Several weapons and organisational documents were found and seized in the course of the police operation. On 26 November 1996 the Istanbul State Security Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to twelve years and six months' imprisonment. The judge noted that the applicant had maintained during the hearings that he supported the ideology of the PKK and believed that the PKK was the legitimate representative of Kurdistan. The judgment of the first-instance court became final in respect of the applicant since he did not appeal against it.

The Court considers it useful to outline the circumstances under which the parliamentary elections of 22 July 2007 took place. In early May 2007 the Turkish Parliament decided to hold early parliamentary elections. This followed a political crisis resulting from Parliament’s inability to elect a new President of the Republic. In the elections the AKP, the CHP and the MHP managed to get over the 10% threshold. More than sixty independent candidates stood for election in about forty provincial constituencies. The strong showing by independent candidates was one of the main features of the elections of 22 July 2007. There were none in the National Assembly in 1980 but 1999 saw them return, when there were three. In 2002 nine independent MPs were elected from a national total of 260 independent candidates. In the elections in July 2007, twenty-seven independent MP were elected, and more than twenty ‘thousand hopes’ candidates were elected after obtaining approximately 2.23% of the votes cast. The applicant lodged with the Higher Electoral Council a request for the annulment of the Decree du 27 May 2007. Election broadcasts were authorised from 15 to 21 July 2007, that is to say during the week before the elections. The applicant stressed that one peculiarity of the 22 July 2007 elections had been the large number of independent candidates standing. He considered that this unprecedented phenomenon had stemmed, firstly, from the 10% electoral threshold imposed during the parliamentary elections, and secondly, from dissatisfaction felt by most people at the material time with the performance of the political parties, whether in power or in opposition. The application was dismissed on the basis of Article 94 II a) of Law no. 298.

He suggested that the high-ranking officers in question should set up a political party on retirement and present their political projects to the people. The applicant submitted an objection as to the jurisdiction of the Military Court to try him, on the grounds of his civilian status and relying on the Convention and his right to freedom of expression. The Military Court declined jurisdiction in favour of the Bakırköy Assize Court. The commanding officer of the Third Army Corps lodged an appeal on points of law against the decision to decline jurisdiction. The Court of Cassation quashed the decision declining jurisdiction and referred the case back to the military court. The applicant was not apprised of the appeals by the commanding officer and the Military Prosecutor, both of which were added to the case file. The case was referred to the Military Court of First Instance, which declined jurisdiction. The commanding officer of the Third Army Corps lodged a fresh appeal on points of law against the decision declining jurisdiction. By a judgment of 11 March 2008, the latter court declined jurisdiction and referred the case to the Bakırköy 2nd Criminal Court, which held jurisdiction for offences committed via the press. The application was dismissed and the case was returned to the Prosecutor's Office. The case was then referred again to the Second Criminal Court by the Court of Appeal, which refused to hear the case. The applicant was sentenced to five years in prison. Bakırköy 2nd Criminal Court referred the case to the BakırKöy 16th Criminal Court on the grounds that that court was the former Bağcılar 2nd criminal Court. By a judgment of 12 March 2009 the Bak Turkish 16th criminal Court referred a jurisdictional dispute to the Bak Turkish Assize Court. The Bak Turkish Assizes Court decided in favour of the Bak Turkish Criminal Court. The case was then referred back to the 2nd criminal court, which declared the proceedings statute-barred under Article 95 § 4 of the Military Criminal Code.

Mr Faruk Kalaç, a Turkish citizen born in 1939, pursued a career as judge advocate in the air force. In 1990 he was serving, with the rank of group captain, as the high command’s director of legal affairs. The Supreme Military Council (Yüksek Askeri Sûrasi), composed of the Prime Minister, the Minister of Defence, the Chief of Staff and the eleven highest-ranking generals in the armed forces, ordered the compulsory retirement of three officers and twenty-eight non-commissioned officers for breaches of discipline and scandalous conduct. The decision, which was based on section 50 (c) of the Military Personnel Act, was made on 1 August 1990. The decision was made by the Supreme Court of the Republic of Colombia on 30 May 1991. The decision was based on the principle that members of the armed forces should be subject to the same rules as the rest of the population. The court ruled that the decision was not in breach of the Constitution, as it did not constitute a violation of the right to freedom of speech and the right of the family to bear arms. The case was appealed by the Ministry of Defence, and the case was dismissed on 9 January 1992. It was the first time a case of this kind had been heard in the court of cassation, which is a process of appeals against decisions made by a court.

Under Article 314 §§ 2 and 3 of the Civil Code “Gözüm” was registered as the surname of E. The Civil Code intended to treat the legal relationship between the adoptive parents and the adopted child as ‘a biological relationship’ This was not possible in the case of single-parent adoptions, where either a mother or a father was absent. The Court of Cassation upheld the decision of the court below in a judgment which made no mention of the legislative change. The applicant applied to the registry office for the registration of her forename as that of the mother of E., relying on Article 20 § 4 of the new Regulation. She told the police officers that when her husband had failed to come home the previous evening she had telephoned the local prosecutor and asked him whether herhusband had been arrested. Unbeknown to her, some half an hour later her husband's body had been found by soldiers in a ditch in the vicinity of the nearby town of Güroymak. He was blindfolded and there was a gunshot wound on his face. Doctors established the cause of death as cerebrovascular haemorrhagic shock caused by the gunshot wound. and the body which, according to the doctors, had been caused by physical trauma. The applicants sent letters to the offices of the Van and Tatvan prosecutors and asked to be provided with information regarding the steps taken in the investigation over the course of the previous ten years. The Van prosecutor’s office decided that it had no jurisdiction ratione loci to investigate the incident and forwarded the applicants’ letter (mentioned in the preceding paragraph) to the office of the prosecutor in Tatvan. On 24 July 2003 the Güroymak prosecutor took a decision of non-jurisdiction ratione materiae. The application was brought against the Ministry of the Interior. The applicants argued that the perpetrators of the killing had not been found, despite the fact that more than one year had elapsed since the incident. The Van Administrative Court decided to award compensation to the applicants, in accordance with Article 125 of the Constitution (see paragraphs 32-34 below). It held that when carrying out their duties the public authorities had an obligation to take the necessary measures to prevent the death of the applicant’s relative. The compensation proceedings were settled in December 1997. The application was dismissed by the Security Court in July 2003. The case was reopened in April 2009 and the applicants are still seeking compensation. The Ministry of the Interior appealed, arguing that it had not failed in that obligation because the reason for the killing and the identity of its perpetrators had not yet been established. For the public authorities to be said to have failed in their obligation, it was necessary to establish that they had either not performed their duties at all, or failed to perform them in a timely manner, or had performed them in an unsatisfactory fashion. The applicants lodged an appeal with the Supreme Administrative Court against the decision and argued that a citizen need not officially seek protection from the authorities in order to trigger the State's obligation to protect such a citizen’s life. The Ministry was therefore responsible for the pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage arising from the failures on its part. The final decision was served on the applicants on 3 January 2006. The fact that some eight years after the killing the perpetrators had still not been identified was an indication that the public Authorities had failed in their duties. The appeal was rejected and the case was returned to the Appeals Court.

The Court further emphasised that it was not bound by the classification made by the administration and that it made its own assessment as to whether the confidentiality was justified in each case. The Kayseri Civil Court ordered the applicant to pay the Ministry of Defence 5,050,500,000 Turkish liras (TRL) (approximately 3,000 euros (EUR)), plus interest running from 8 April 2003. A description of the relevant domestic law can be found in the decision of Karayiğit v. Turkey ((dec.), no. 45874/05, 23 September 2008). The court ruled that the applicant had paid the Defence Ministry for the reimbursement of his educational expenses. The court also ruled that there was a right to compensation for the loss of the applicant's education, as well as interest.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1448/04) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants maintained that the manner in which the compulsory lessons in religious culture and ethics were taught infringed their rights. In a decision of 6 June 2006, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 3 October 2006 (Rule 59 § 3 of the Rules of Court). The Court heard addresses by Mr Genç and Mr Özmen. The court ruled in favor of the applicants. Alevism is a belief or philosophy influenced by other cultures, religions and philosophies. It represents one of the most widespread faiths in Turkey after the Hanafite branch of Islam. It advocates close contact with nature, tolerance, modesty and love for one's neighbour, within the Islamic faith. Alevis reject the sharia (code of laws in orthodox Islam) and the sunna (forms of behaviour and formal rules of orthodox Islam), and do not consider the pilgrimage to Mecca as a religious obligation. According to Alevism, Allah created Adam in his image and all his manifestations in this world are in human form. Allah is neither in the sky nor in paradise, but in the centre of the human heart. The Turkish government made religious education a compulsory subject in primary and upper secondary schools. The Supreme Court of Turkey ruled that this was against the law. The court also ruled that the teaching of religious education was not a violation of the Turkish constitution. The ruling was upheld by the High Court of Justice of Turkey. The decision was made based on a legal interpretation of the law, not the law as a whole. The Court's decision was appealed, but the appeal was rejected by the Supreme Court. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights, which ruled in favor of the school's right to teach religious education as a compulsory part of the education.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 25801/94) against Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged principally that her home and property had been destroyed during an operation by gendarmes carried out in her village in south-east Turkey. The application was declared admissible by the Commission on 23 May 1996. In its report of 6 September 1999, the Commission expressed the opinion that there had been a violation of Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. The case was referred to the Court on 23 October 1999. Mr Türmen, the judge elected in respect of Turkey, withdrew from sitting in the case. The Government accordingly appointed Mr F. Gölcüklü to sit as an ad hoc judge. The facts of the case, particularly concerning events on or about 8 November 1993 when the gendarmes carried out an operation at Çitlibahçe, were disputed by the parties. The Commission, pursuant to former Article 28 § 1 (a) of the Convention, conducted an investigation with the assistance of the parties and heard witnesses in Ankara on 7 February 1997. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The Commission’s findings of fact are set out in its report of 6 September 1999 and summarised below (Section A). The applicant accepts the Commission's findings of Fact (Section B) PKK terrorists went to the village of Dadaş in the Hazro district and took away five teachers. All, save one of the teachers, were shot. The imam’s brother, though wounded, survived. The gendarme commander who gave evidence before the Delegates denied that this occurred but recalled that he had destroyed hemp crops. The Commission did not make any finding in regard to this aspect as it was not the subject-matter of any specific complaint. The Delegates found the applicant to be a convincing witness, an elderly, simple and unsophisticated lady who was on the whole credible. Her oral testimony was largely consistent with the statement given by her to the Human Rights Association shortly after the incident. The Commission found in conclusion that the applicant’s property, furniture and possessions were deliberately burnt and destroyed during an operation by security forces in the village of Çitlibahçe on 8 November 1993. The Commission did not find the matters referred to by the Government as being indicative of bad faith or as materially undermining the credibility and reliability of the applicant and her witnesses. The possessions burned included a fridge, television, kitchen utensils, household goods, and produce (including tobacco, wheat, barley, lentils, and winter provisions). The applicant and other villagers went to Diy. The commission accepted the evidence of the applicants as regards its principal elements. The Government emphasised the terrorism which was prevalent in this region from the early 1990’s and created a public danger threatening the life of the nation. The applicant had made no complaint to the public prosecutor about the alleged burning of her house and property by the gendarmes during the operation on 8 February 1993. The Government submitted a copy of the statement taken by the Diyarbakır public prosecutor from the applicant via an interpreter on 10 October 1995. This had not been provided to the Commission. The Hazro Administrative Council began an investigation and found that her claims were unsubstantiated. She acknowledged that the thumbprint on the document was hers and that she did not remember who took the statement. As regarded the events, she could not remember the exact date but about two years before 20 or more army vehicles had been seen. After the village burned down, she went to Diyarbakır. She said that she thought her application was going to Ankara to claim her rights. She was illiterate and ignorant and did not know anything about European human rights. When she made a statement to the HRA, there had been a lot of people with her and they described the events also. The application which had been read out was accurate though and she had no complaints to make about the person who wrote it down. She did not want to start a case in Europe in the way that he [the public prosecutor] had explained. It was for the State to look after her rights, she said.

The Istanbul Regional Administrative Court set aside the District Governor’s decision of non-authorisation on the ground that the investigation into the applicants’ allegations was inadequate. On 15 July 2002 the Bahçelievler District Governor refused authorisation for the prosecution of the accused police officers. The applicants appealed against this decision. On 17 December 2002 the Eyüp Assize Court dismissed the applicants’ appeal. This decision was notified to the applicants on 26 February 2003. The application was dismissed on 17 December 2003. For more details on this case, please visit: http://www.cnn.com/2013/10/24/world/features/europe/stories/stories-top-stories/story-of-the-police-trial-and-sustained-decision-to-not-prosecute-two-officers.html#storylink=c.

name: Derya Gazioğlu

eval_texts: Four Turkish nationals took part in an anti-war demonstration in Istanbul in October 2003. They were arrested and taken into police custody where they remained until their release the following day. The applicants allege that they were subjected to ill-treatment during their arrest and their detention in custody. They claim that the intervention of a number of police officers and the force used by those police officers against them in a demonstration in which they were taking part had been in violation of their rights under Articles 3 and 11 of the Convention. The application was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the. Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) The applicants were brought before the Bakırköy prosecutor. With the exception of the third applicant, the applicants complained of ill-treatment. The applicants told the prosecutor that by attending the demonstration they had been exercising their democratic rights. They also alleged that the police had arrested them without any previous warnings. The fourth applicant complained that he had been beaten up by the police officers. Ten police officers denied having been at the demonstration or having seen any of the demonstrators. The remaining officer, police chief M.T., said he had not taken part in the dispersal of the demonstration but had questioned the applicants in a police station. On 14 April 2004 the Bakırköy prosecutor decided to close the investigation into the applicants’ allegations of ill-treatment. He denied having ill-treated any of the arrestees or having sworn at them. The applicants' objection against the prosecutor’s decision was rejected by the Eyüp Assize Court on 8 December 2004. On 28 January 2008 the BakTurkish Criminal Court of First Instance acquitted the applicants, holding that they had exercised their democratic rights and not committed any offences. This decision stated that it was to be served on the applicants. According to a hand-written note on this decision, it was communicated to the applicants on 9 February 2005.

name: Leyla Şahin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 44774/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 2 July 2002 the Chamber declared the application admissible. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 19 November 2002. The Court heard addresses by Mr Grosz, Mr Alpaslan and Mr Güran. Both the applicant and the Government each filed written observations on the merits.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that a ban on wearing the Islamic headscarf in higher-education institutions violated her rights and freedoms. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court. The Government and the applicant each filed written observations on the merits. The Court heard addresses by Mr Grosz, Mr Alpaslan, Mr Yildiz and Mr Güran. The application was declared admissible by a decision of 2 July 2002. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 19 November 2002 (Rule 59 § 3). The case was brought by a woman who says she was forced to wear the headscarf because she was a Muslim. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights. The court ruled that the woman was entitled to wear a head scarf as long as it did not interfere with her constitutional rights. The woman was able to continue wearing the head scarf for a further four years. She was allowed to wear it for another four years, but was not allowed to leave the university campus unless she showed up for a lecture. In the end, the court found her not guilty of any crime and allowed her to continue to wear her head scarf. The judge ruled that she was not entitled to be a member of the university. The applicant was refused admission to a neurology lecture and on 10 June 1998 to a written examination on public health, again for the same reason. She lodged an application for an order setting aside the circular of 23 February 1998. The Istanbul Administrative Court dismissed the application, holding that by virtue of section 13(b) of the Higher-Education Act (Law no. 2547 – see paragraph 50 below) a university vice chancellor, as the executive organ of the university, had power to regulate students’ dress in order to maintain order. The Administrative Court held that neither the regulation in issue, nor the individual measures, could be considered illegal. On 19 April 2001 the Supreme Administrative court dismissed an appeal by the applicant on points of law. The applicant was suspended from Vienna University for a semester for taking part in an unauthorised assembly. Istanbul University argued that the disciplinary penalty was lawful as the reason for the applicant’s one-semester suspension. The Istanbul Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's application to have the penalty quashed. The applicant was granted an amnesty releasing her from all the disciplinary penalties and their effects. On 28 September 2000 the Supreme Administrative Court held that the aforementioned legislation made it unnecessary to examine the merits of the appeal on points of law against the judgment of 30 November 1999. The application was dismissed on the grounds that there was no case on the merits.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was being searched for on suspicion of membership of an armed illegal organisation, namely the Hizbullah. According to the applicant, during his detention in police custody he was allegedly stripped naked and his testicles were squeezed. He was also hosed with water, beaten with the butt of a gun, subjected to electric shocks and hung by his arms. On 7 September 2010 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theApplication at the same time. The applicant was accused of membership of an armed illegal organisation. He was also accused of involvement in activities which undermined the constitutional order of the State. On 28 February 2008 the Diyarbakır Assize Court pronounced its judgment. It convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The applicant appealed. On 27 May 2010 the Court of Cassation upheld the first-instance court’s judgment. The case was heard in front of a panel of judges from the Diyarbakir State Security Court. The hearing was adjourned until 2 October 2011. The judges noted in the minutes that the applicant had five purple bruises on his right hand. The court further stated that if the applicant's lawyer wished to lodge a separate complaint with the public prosecutor, a certified copy of the minutes should be annexed. The applicant claimed that he had been hosed with pressurised water, hung by his arms and subjected to electric shocks. He also maintained that his testicles had been squeezed and cigarettes had been extinguished on his hand. The Forensic Medicine Institute reported that the injuries on the applicant’s body, as indicated in the three medical reports, could have been sustained as a result of a fall, in the course of resisting the officers during his arrest, or resulted from a blow with a blunt object. In April 2009 the Diyarbakır Public Prosecutor, finding the applicant's allegations unsubstantiated, issued a decision not to prosecute. The case was. dismissed by the Siverek Assize Court. The case was adjourned until November 14, 2014. The trial was held at the Siverek Court of Appeal, in the town of Siverek. It was the first trial of its kind in the area. The jury returned a verdict of not guilty by reason of misadventure. The appeal was dismissed on November 13, 2013. The conviction was overturned on appeal on November 15, 2013, on appeal. The verdict was returned on November 16, 2013 on appeal, and the appeal was thrown out on November 17, 2013 by the court of appeal.

On 23 June 2003 the applicant was brought before the Nusaybin Public Prosecutor, where he reiterated the statement he had made to the police. On 7 July 2003 the Public Prosecutor at the Diyarbakır State Security Court filed an indictment with that court accusing the applicant of aiding and abetting the PKK/KADEK, and F.A. of membership of that organisation. At the sixth hearing, held on 1 April 2004, the applicant’s lawyer requested his release, claiming that the only piece of evidence found against him was F.S.’S statements made during the preliminary investigation stage. The case against the applicant was transferred to the Diyarbakır Assize Court. The applicant appealed the conviction of aiding and abetting the PKK/KADEK. In December 2008 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court and sentenced him to four years and six months’ imprisonment. The new Criminal Code entered into force on 1 June 2005 (Law no. 5237) The assize court held that under the new criminal code the act of aiding or abetting an illegal organisation constituted the offence of membership of anillegal organisation and thus carried a higher sentence. It stated that the applicant. was therefore being convicted under Article 169 of the former Criminal Code, which was more favourable to him than the corresponding provisions of the new. Criminal Code.

name: Elena Riera Blume
train_texts: Seven Spanish nationals, Ms Elena Riera Blume, Ms Concepción Riera, Ms María Luz Casado Perez, Ms Daría Amelía Casado. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 37680/97) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The application concerned the detention of the applicants, who are presumed members of a “sect” for nearly ten days following a preliminary investigation directed by Barcelona investigating judge no. 6. The applicants relied on Articles 3, 5, 8 and 9 of the Convention. On 9 March 1999 the Chamber declared admissible the complaints of six of the applicant’s, namely Ms Elena Riera Blume, Ms Concepción. Blume and Ms Daría Amelía Casado Perez, and Ms María Teresa Sales Aige. Riera Blume and Others v. Spain (dec.), no. 37680/97, ECHR 1999-II. The applicants, Ms Elena Riera. Blume, Ms Concepción Riera Blumes, Ms María Luz. Casado Perez, Ms Daría Amelía Casado. Perez,Ms María Teresa Sales Aige and Mr. Javier Bruna Reverter, were accused of deprivation of liberty and interference with their right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion. The Court found that there was no basis on which such a settlement could be reached. It declared the remainder of their application inadmissible. It decided that if there was not a friendly settlement, a public hearing would be held. Sales Aige, Javier Bruna Reverter, were arrested in 1984 for being members of a religious sect. The applicants, born in Valencia in the 1950s and 1960s, are now in their 60s and 70s. They were arrested after a public safety department infiltrated the sect, the CEIS. The group had allegedly brought about a change of personality in their followers. It was alleged that they had been inciting them to prostitution and other activities designed to obtain money for the organisation. The applications were released and all those detained during the searches were questioned by police before they were released to their families. In some cases the applicants were also interned in a psychiatric centre. The applicants were allegedly subjected to a process of ‘deprogramming’ by a psychologist and a psychiatrist at the request of Pro Juventud. They were taken to individual rooms under the supervision of persons recruited for the purpose, one of whom remained permanently in each room. On 30 June 1984 the applicants left the hotel. The applicants lodged a criminal complaint alleging false imprisonment, offences against the exercise of personal rights, falsification of documents, usurpation of functions and misappropriation of goods. The Barcelona Audiencia Provincial acquitted the accused, holding that the acts complained of had been prompted by a philanthropic, legitimate and well-intentioned motive and that there had been no intention of depriving them of their liberty. The applicants lodged an appeal (recurso de amparo) with the Constitutional Court. In their appeal they alleged violations of the right to religious freedom (Article 16 of the Constitution) and the rights of the defence during their detention. They asked the court to quash the judgments of the Audiencia Provincial and the Supreme Court, to order the officials complained of to pay five million pesetas as compensation for the damage sustained and to make a declaration to the effect that the Generalitat of Catalonia was liable in default.“The offence of false imprisonment cannot be said to have been committed since, firstly, there was no intention on the part of the defendants to deprive anybody of his or her liberty.” Mr José Victor Riera Blume was held to have withdrawn on account of failure, through his own fault, to comply with a formal requirement. The court added that the decisions being challenged had not infringed any of the rights relied on by the five remaining appellants, seeing that they were limited to declaring that the acts with which the defendants were charged did not amount to the offences for which they were being prosecuted. The Constitutional Court pointed out, firstly, that there was no fundamental right to have a person convicted and, secondly, that it could not protect fundamental rights by quashing final substantive judgments whereby defendants had been acquitted. It also pointed out that, according to its case-law, the Constitution did not confer a right to secure criminal convictions of third parties.
