In a judgment of 30 June 2005, the court dismissed that objection, considering that the civil action continued when the offender’s death occurred after a decision on the criminal prosecution had been given. The Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation quashed and annulled the judgment in October 2003. The profit had been 94,100,000 French francs (FRF), or 14,345,452.52 euros (EUR), without any real added value for the injured companies. The applicant, E.P.L., Lambda and the Principal Public Prosecutor at the Court of Appeal appealed on points of law. In support of his appeal the applicant argued that there had been a violation of Article 6 of the Convention because the criminal court had no authority to judge the matter after his father’s death. The advocate-general at the. Court of Cassation concluded that the Versailles Court of appeal had no. authority toJudge the civil action after J.-L. Lagardère's death. In a judgment of 25 October 2006 the Court of Cassation declared the Principal Public Prosecutor’s appeal inadmissible and rejected those lodged by the applicant and E.P.L. The Court of Appeal had “found Jean‑Luc Lagardère guilty’. In other words, in order for the criminal court to be able to rule, in both the criminal and the civil proceedings, there is a condition: the effective participation of the accused in his trial. This meant that the accused had to have had an effective opportunity to submit his arguments in full concerning the presence and the solidity of all the constituent elements of the offence.

name: Ruvhten Sijte
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 39013/04) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, that they had not had effective access to court and that the length of the national proceedings had been unreasonable. By a decision of 17 February 2009, the Court declared the application partly admissible and the applicants and the Government each filed further written observations (Rule 59 § 1). The applicants were represented by Mr J. Södergren and Mr C. Crafoord, lawyers practising in Stockholm. The Swedish Government was represented by their Agent, Mr C.-H. Ehrenkrona, of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, that they had not had effective access to court and that the length of the national proceedings had been unreasonable. By a decision of 17 February 2009, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The application was filed by four Swedish Sami villages (samebyar): Handölsdalen,. Mittådalen, Tåssåsen and Ruvhten Sijte (formerly Tännäs) (“the applicants”) Swedish Sami villages have been fighting for years for the right to winter grazing on their land. The issue of winter grazing has been a controversial one in Sweden. The borders of the herding area are controversial and have not been statutorily defined, especially as concerns the winter grazing land. One-third of the surface of Sweden is divided into all-year land and winter grazingLandowners sought a declaratory judgment that the villages had no right to reindeer grazing without a valid contract concluded between the landowner and the village. The villages claimed that they had a right toWinter grazing based on prescription from time immemorial and international law. The parties exchanged views on questions of evidence and submitted specifications of supplementary evidence. The main hearing started on 18 September and ended on 25 October 1995. The District Court issued a 192-page judgment on 21 February 1996. It found that, from the 16th to the late 19th century, there had not been any winter grazing which had established a right for the Sami to such grazing on the relevant properties. The court found that a right to real property could not legally be established through “custom” and that aright to winter grazing on properties in the area was not legally established. During the hearing, as well as on seven previous occasions, the court struck out the case in regard to some of the landowners following withdrawal of the action. The Sami villages appealed to the Court of Appeal (hovrätten) of Nedre Norrland. They demanded that the District Court's judgment be quashed and that the decision on litigation costs not be enforced. The landowners responded and requested that the villages not be allowed to invoke circumstances in their defence that had not been presented to the court. The court concluded that there was no right of the Sami. villages to reindeer grazing on the plaintiffs' land without a valid contract and accordingly gave. judgment in favour of the landowners. The villages were ordered to pay approximately 4,000,000 Swedish kronor (SEK; about 400,000 euros (EUR) The Sami villages claimed that there was a procedural hindrance (rättegångshinder) as they lacked the capacity to act as parties in relation to the issue concerned by the proceedings in question. By a decision of 4 November 1997, the Court of Appeal rejected this claim. On 1 December 1997 the villages appealed against that decision to the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) The Supreme Court refused the villages leave to appeal on 18 February 1999. In February 2000 the villages reiterated their demand that the District Court's judgment be quashed and the case remitted. In January 2001 the court ordered the parties to make submissions on the question of which landowners were to be considered opposite parties in the appellate proceedings. The main hearing in the Court of Appeal was held between 1 and 31 October 2001 and lasted 16 days. On 18 June 2001 the villages adduced some written evidence not previously presented. The landowners objected to that evidence but, by a decision of 5 September 2001, the court allowed the villages to present it. Following some landowners' withdrawal of. their action and the Idre Nya Sami village's withdrawal of its appeal, the Court. of Appeal struck out the case and set aside the District Court's judgment. In February 2002 the court ordered the applicants to pay the plaintiffs' legal costs in the appellate proceedings, amounting to approximately SEK 2,900,000 (about EUR 290,000) Sami villages claim that a right to winter grazing based on prescription from time immemorial has come into being as Sami have been in Härjedalen since prehistoric times. Reindeer management took on a completely nomadic form in the late sixteenth century or, at all events, during the seventeenth century, and it can be assumed that even then, in the winter, depending on the weather conditions and access to food, the reindeer wandered in search of food. The Court of Appeal examined extensive evidence dating back several hundred years and drew the following conclusions. The right toWinter Grazing could not require that reindeers grazed in a particular area every winter. A basic condition for that right was that the area had been used in such a way that every instance of grazing could be seen as part of a recurring pattern. The Sami Fund (Samefonden) has granted the applicants a loan of SEK 14,700,000 (approximately EUR 1,470,000) to pay the litigation costs incurred in the domestic proceedings. The loan, which is free of interest, is due on 30 November 2010. The appeal was completed on 22 May 2002. On 29 April 2004 the Supreme Court refused the applicants leave to appeal. The application for a right to use the relevant properties on the basis of prescription from time immemorial was rejected. The applicants appealed to the. Supreme Court on 19 March 2002. Their appeal was concluded on 22May 2002. In the following months, they submitted documents as to the question of who was to represent them before the Supreme. Court.

name: Carola van Kück
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35968/97) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that German court decisions refusing her claims for reimbursement of gender reassignment measures were in breach of her right to a fair trial. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 18 October 2001 the Chamber declared the application admissible. This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35968/97) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that German court decisions refusing her claims for reimbursement of gender reassignment measures and also the related proceedings were in breach of her right to a fair trial. She relied on Articles 6 § 1, 8, 13 and 14 of the Convention. The case was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case. By a decision of 18 October 2001, the Chamber declared the application admissible. This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section. In 1992 the applicant, represented by counsel, brought an action with the Berlin Regional Court against a German health insurance company. She claimed reimbursement of pharmaceutical expenses for hormone treatment. As an employee of the Berlin Land, she was entitled to allowances covering half of her medical expenses; the private health insurance was to cover the other half. She requested a declaratory judgment to the effect that the defendant company was liable to reimburse 50% of the expenses for gender reassignment operations. In his conclusions, Dr H. confirmed that the applicant was a male-to-female transsexual and that her transsexuality had to be regarded as a disease. He further indicated that gender. reassignment surgery was not the only possible medical treatment in cases of transsexuality. The applicant was a male-to-female transsexual and that her condition had to be regarded as a disease. Expert concluded that the gender reassignment operation formed part of the curative treatment of a mental disease. The court was not convinced that, on account of the applicant’s resistance to therapy, the intended operation was the only possible treatment. On 11 October 1993 the applicant lodged an appeal with the Berlin Court of Appeal. In its reasoning, the court found that the applicant ought first to have had recourse to an extensive course of 50 to 100 psychotherapy sessions, as proposed by the psychiatric expert Prof. D. The applicant is now living as a woman. In November 1994 the applicant underwent gender reassignment surgery. The Court of Appeal valued the claims at stake at 28,455.92 German marks. According to the opinion of the expert Dr H., her transsexuality constituted a disease, a matter not in dispute between the parties to the proceedings. The applicant had therefore failed to prove that the conditions for reimbursement of medical treatment were met in her case. The case was dismissed following an oral hearing, on 27 January 1995. The appeal was dismissed after the applicant’s appeal was rejected on the grounds that the expert had not confirmed the necessity of gender reassignment measures. The claimant had unsuccessfully attended between twenty-four and thirty-five psychotherapy sessions. Court of Appeal concluded that the applicant had failed to prove the necessity of her treatment. Court of Appeal further considered that, in any event, the applicant was not entitled to reimbursement under clause 5.1(b) of the General Insurance Conditions on the ground that she had herself deliberately caused the disease, as argued by the defendant in earlier submissions. The applicant was born as a male child and did not claim that she was a female on account of chromosomal factors. On account of her male orientation, she had been able to resist feelings that she would have preferred to be a girl and that this would have been more appropriate, and had controlled her emotional life at an early stage. The German Transsexuals Act (Gesetz über die Änderung der Vornamen und die Feststellung der Geschlechtszugehörigkeit in besonderen Fällen) of 10 September 1980 (Federal Gazette I, p. 1654) was adopted following the decision of 11 October 1978 of the Federal Constitutional Court. The applicant was born a man but realised he was infertile and wanted to be a woman. She took female hormones without medical advice, assistance or instruction. In 1996 the Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant’s constitutional complaint. The German health insurance system has been governed by the Social Security Act, Book V, Health Insurance (Sozialgesetzbuch, Fünftes Buch, Gesetzliche Kranken-versicherung) since 1989. Under the relevant provisions, persons insured under the health system are entitled to medical treatment which is necessary in order to diagnose or to cure a disease. The basic rules for private health insurance, as for any other private insurance, are laid down in the Insurance Contract Act (Gesetz über den Versicheringerungsvertnung) (B. v. 7). Private health insurance covers expenses for curative treatment which is medically necessary on account of a disease or injuries suffered as a result of an accident. The insurer is exempted from liability if the insured person has deliberately caused his or her own disease or accident (section 178.l). The contractual relations are standardised in general insurance conditions. The European Court of Justice (ECJ) found that discrimination arising from gender reassignment constituted discrimination on grounds of sex and, accordingly, Article 5 § 1 of Council Directive 76/207/EEC of 9 February 1976, precluded dismissal of a transsexual for a reason related to a gender reassignment. ECJ: Community law as it stands at present does not cover discrimination based on sexual orientation. “Discrimination based on the fact that a person belongs to a particular sex, is limited to the case of a worker’s gender reassignment and does not therefore apply to differences of treatment based on a person's sexual orientation,” it says. ‘The refusal by an employer to allow travel concessions to the person of the same sex with whom a worker has a stable relationship ... does not constitute discrimination prohibited by Article 119 of the Treaty or Directive 75/117,’ it adds. The ECJ concludes that such discrimination is to be prohibited.

Franz Weber, a Swiss journalist, lives at Clarens, in the Canton of Vaud. The applicant and one of the associations he runs, Helvetia Nostra, lodged a complaint alleging defamation against R.M., who had written a letter published in the letters column of the. newspaper L’Est vaudois under the headline ‘Franz. Weber is fooling you’. The Court heard addresses by Mr Boillat and Mr Vautier for the Government, by Mr Trechsel for the Commission and by Mr Schaller for the applicant, as well as their replies to its questions. R.M. was charged with defamation and committed for trial in 1982, but the case was dismissed. R.M.'s behaviour borders on the 'criminal', says the former head of Helvetia Nostra. He says the list of municipal taxpayers is not published and it is easy to hide behind that sort of censorship and live by devious means. ‘We have had enough of playing into the hands of people who sponge off us,’ he writes. “You would be amazed at the distrust of the whole country’s democratically - and how democratically! - elected authorities,” he adds. On 3 March 1982 the daily newspapers Gazette de Lausanne, 24 heures and Tribune/Le Matin reported what the applicant had said. Mr Weber had already divulged the first three items of information at a press conference in Berne on 11 May 1981, during which he denounced “the plot hatched against him by the Vaud authorities in order to intimidate him’ The President of the Cassation Division imposed a fine of 300 Swiss francs on him, together with a probationary period of a year for the purposes of deletion of the fine from the cantonal register. He also stated that he had lodged a challenge and a complaint against the investigating judge. The court in Vaud ruled that Mr Weber's disclosure of criminal complaints had been lodged was not information about an investigation. The court said that disclosure of a criminal complaint is not caught by Article 185 CC, more particularly where it has been decided to take no action on the complaint. Mr Weber himself admits that the breach of the confidentiality of the investigation was intentional. The proceedings in the Criminal Cassation Division of the Vaud Cantonal Court were dismissed on 15 October 1982. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that there was no need to deal with it in the present proceedings as criminal proceedings will shortly be time-barred. The matter which was to be kept confidential was known to a limited or indefinite number of people because confidentiality had already been breached. Mr Weber lodged a public-law appeal with the Federal Court. He relied on Articles 10 and 6 (art. 10, art. 6) of the Convention. In his view, Article 6 applied because of the criminal nature of the fine. On this point cantonal law differed from federal law. The appellant was therefore rightly convicted. ...“ Finally, the Criminal Cassation Division set aside of its own motion the entry of thefine in the cantonal register.’’. The proceedings in the Federal. Court were held at the Court of Appeal in Lausanne, Switzerland. The hearing was held at the Court of cassation, which is located at the Prosecutor’s Office. The applicant maintained that Article 185 of the Vaud Code of Criminal Procedure (Vaud CCP) violates freedom of expression. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal on 16 November 1983. It noted in particular that such restrictions are "permissible where they are necessary in a democratic society" The rule enacted in Article 185 Vaud CCP clearly conforms to these principles. A weighing of the competing interests at stake leads to the same conclusions. The prohibition against communicating information about an investigation until its completion and the penalties attaching to the offence are undoubtedly consistent with the proportionality principle. The applicant had grounds for rebelling against the sometimes unorthodox course taken by the proceedings against him. He successfully availed himself of the usual remedies. The fine was convertible into ten days’ imprisonment under Article 12 of the Vaud Order on the recovery of fines and their conversion into imprisonment. The possibility of conversion into a custodial sentence makes no difference, since conversion is possible only in the event of the appellant’s refusing to pay the fine out of sheer unwillingness. The safeguards provided for in Article 6 § 1 (art. 6-1) ECHR were therefore not applicable in the instant case. The fine imposed was not a negligible one, but it nonetheless came into the category of penalties which by their nature, duration or manner of execution are deemed not to be appreciably detrimental.

The Cologne Court of Appeal reversed the Regional Court's judgment and ordered the agency to accede to the applicant's request, which it did a month later. The applicant answered in detail the replies to the press release and the agency's press release in detail. In both cases, the courts refused to accept for adjudication his applications on the ground that they had no prospects of success. In October 1989, the Cologne court of Appeal ruled in favour of the applicant, and his application was dismissed. Jacubowski sent thirteen articles from newspapers with large circulations to forty newspaper publishers and newspaper, radio and television journalists. The articles gave critical accounts of his dismissal, the circumstances surrounding it and the ddp’s activities in general. They reported in particular that the dDP's financial position had worsened again since the bankruptcy in April 1983. Some of its clients were preparing to dispense with its services, mainly because of their poor standard and the lack of certain technical facilities. The pending court proceedings will ensure that all the details finally become clear. I should be glad to be able to meet you in person before too long, in order to discuss not only the past but also future developments in the German 'news market' The court held that in his circular the respondent had repeated in his own name the allegations made in the attached articles. The judgment was based on section 1 of the 1909 Act, which provides: “Any person who, in the course of business commits, for purposes of competition, acts contrary to accepted moral standards may be enjoined from further engaging in those acts and held liable for damages’’ The court said, inter alia: � “... the respondent sent his circular of 25 September 1984 for purposes. of competition in thecourse of business’. It went on to hold that he would have to “compensate the [E. company] for all the damage that the acts [in question] ha[d] caused and [would] cause the [ddp]’ The respondent had already been planning for a long time to set up his own agency. The circular and newspaper cuttings were sent out about a month later to selected addressees. A few months later the respondent’s new agency was set up. The last paragraph of the circular likewise makes the competitive intention clear. It shows that the respondent intended to provoke discussion not only with a view to correcting assertions concerning himself that were possibly false, but also to promote his future activities as a competitor of the [ddp]. It is not apparent what else the respondent could have meant when he wrote that he wished to discuss ‘not only the past but also future developments in the German “news market”’ Mr Jacubowski had needlessly handicapped (behinderte unnötig) a competitor and accordingly infringed section 1 of the 1909 Act. It does not appear that there was any such reason to disparage the [ddp] by taking up the unfavourable comments on its activities in the Horizont article. The information was, moreover, of a business nature, but this did not mean that it ceased to be an opinion whose expression was protected by Article 5 para. 1, first sentence, of the Basic Law. This provision therefore had to be weighed against section 1, on which the prohibition had been founded. The distribution of the applicant’s circular can hardly be regarded as an attempt to influence public opinion. Rather it was designed almost exclusively to promote his private business interests and to secure or improve his competitive position in the news market. In principle, freedom of expression takes precedence over rights protected by ordinary laws in so far as the statement is part of the ongoing discussion of questions of public importance. The fact that an interest is made to prevail by means which are in principle protected under Article 5 para. 1 of the Basic Law cannot justify subordinating to it the other interest, which is entitled to the protection of an ordinary law. The person concerned thus has no right to have doubtful issues in the case clarified, writes the judge. The court would have been preferable had the Innsbruck District Court stated this explicitly and without ambiguity, he adds. The judgment was reproduced in an Austrian legal journal but the applicant's identity was not revealed. An order issued by the competent civil court took the case-file into consideration. The costs of the procedure, and notably the costs of a medical opinion, were borne by the State. The applicant himself had to pay his lawyer's fees and his own expenses. The public prosecutor is required by law to inquire into the correctness of any report (Anzeige) of an offence. In district court proceedings there is no formal process of investigation and no special procedure of accusation. All that is required is a written or oral application from the district prosecutor seeking the imposition of a penalty. The decision terminating proceedings is governed by section 451 par. 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which provides: ‘If the court is satisfied that the conditions laid down in section 42 are met, it shall terminate the proceedings by a decision. The public prosecutor may lodge an appeal against any such decision ...’ In cases before a district court, the decision whether or not the conditions of paragraph (1) hereof are met shall be taken by the court; where the court decides in the affirmative it shall bring the proceedings to a close. Section 42 was introduced into the new Austrian Penal Code which entered into force on 1 January 1975. The Supreme Court and the great majority of legal commentators regard it as a clause which is not concerned with mere procedure but which provides a substantive ground for exonerating the accused. A decision taken by a court in pursuance of section 42 to terminate proceedings is not entered in the criminal record of the person concerned. The file relating to a case closed in this manner may be used in other legal (and disciplinary) proceedings, as may, in principle, the case-file in any legal action whatever its outcome. The Government contested these assertions, save apparently as regards the possibility of having access to the register of names. The Commission accepted the application on 6 July 1979. name: Manuel Tejedor García
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 28 October 1996. The applicant designated the lawyers who would represent him (Rule 30). The lawyers were given leave by the President to use the Spanish language in the written procedure.

In a decision (auto) of 4 December 1990 the investigating judge rejected MrGallego’s observations and held that the application had been made in time. The judge said it would be better to test the evidence at an adversarial. hearing. The application had to be deemed to have been made within the statutory three-day time-limit (see paragraph 16 below) On 12 February 1991 the investigating judge made a final discontinuance order (Articles 637 no. 2 and 790 no. 6 of the CCP) in respect of the two guardia civil officers accused by the ANPU. In the applicant’s case, he ordered an oral hearing and committed the applicant for trial in the Audiencia Provincial. On 12 November 1991 Mr Tejedor García appealed on points of law on the ground, inter alia, that the public prosecutor's application against the decision of 10 September 1990 had been made out of time. On 28 May 1993 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal. In its view, no violation of Article 24 § 1 of the Spanish Constitution existed in this case. The Constitutional Court ruled that the application was not in breach of the law. The court said the application had been made on the basis of a broad interpretation of the constitution. It found that the interpretation was consistent with the law and not an issue of constitutionality. The decision was made after an appeal was made to the High Court. The High Court said that the case should not have been allowed to be heard without an appeal. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that it was not based on the law as it stood. name: Juan Manuel Palomo Sánchez
train_texts: The case originated in six applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained that they had been dismissed by way of reprisal for belonging to a trade union and on account of its demands. They relied on Articles 10 and 11 of the convention. The applications were allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). On 11 December 2008 the President of the Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. On 17 November 2009 the Chamber decided, under Rule 42 § 1, to join the proceedings in the applications.
eval_texts: The case originated in six applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were represented before the Court by Mr L. García Quinteiro, a lawyer practising in Barcelona. The Spanish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr F. Irurzun Montoro, State Counsel. The applications were allocated to the Third Section of the Court. On 17 November 2009 the Chamber, composed of Josep Casadevall, Elisabet Fura, Corneliu Bîrsan, Alvina Gyulumyan, Egbert Myjer, Luis López Guerra and Ann Power, judges, and Santiago Quesada, Section Registrar, decided to join the proceedings in the applications. The applicants and the Government filed memorials before the Grand Chamber. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 8 December 2010 (Rule 59 § 3). The Court heard addresses by them. The applicants sought to secure recognition by the employer of their special “salaried worker” status, as confirmed by judgments of 2 May and 30 December 1995 of the High Court of Justice of Catalonia, in order to be covered by the corresponding social-security regime. They were employed as delivery men by the company P., against which they brought several sets of proceedings in employment tribunals. Representatives of a committee of non- salaried delivery staff in the company had testified against them in those proceedings. The applicants joined the union’s executive committee. The union published a monthly newsletter. On the cover of the newsletter, a cartoon with speech bubbles showed a caricature of the human resources manager, G., sitting behind a desk under which a person on all fours could be seen from behind. The applicants challenged that decision before Barcelona Employment Tribunal no. 17, which, in a judgment of 8 November 2002, dismissed their claims and found that the dismissals were justified. No changes concerning the appointment of the union members or their duties have taken place since the union was formed in August 2001. The trade union NAA is now based in Barcelona. The tribunal noted that the text was a response to what had happened during proceedings brought by the applicants before Barcelona Employment Tribunal no. 13, in which A. and B. had appeared as witnesses against the applicants’ interests and in favour of their employer. The article entitled “When you’ve rented out your arse you can’t shit when you please” read as follows: “If you belong to a works council and you have to sign agreements with your employers that will never be honoured, just to keep you quiet, and agree to changes that only benefit their cronies, and to pay cuts and other sell-outs” You can see the injustices meted out on your colleagues, the totally irrational way of dealing with their problems and the constant persecution to which they are subjected. But you say nothing, for fear of drawing attention to yourself. Your lips are sealed just like your anal sphincter, because you’ve rented out your arse and you can’t shit when you please. You could break everything up, tear it to pieces, crush and demolish it all ... but your hands are tied by credits, IOUs and debts. You are crushed by your new SUV, your children’s after-school activities, and the twenty-five year mortgage on your semi-detached house. And you let yourself be humiliated, you swallow your pride, you shut up and you accept. The High Court of Justice of Catalonia upheld the judgment under appeal in so far as it concerned the applicants. The court referred, among other things, to the limits imposed by the principle of good faith between parties to a contract of employment. In a decision of 11 March 2004, the Supreme Court of Spain rejected the applicants’ appeal. The applicants lodged an appeal on points of law, seeking harmonisation of the relevant case-law. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that the dismissal was based on serious misconduct as provided for by law and that the applicants' fundamental rights had not been breached. The Supreme Court ruled that the appeal was not successful. Relying on Article 24 (right to a fair hearing) of the Spanish Constitution, the applicants lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court. The Constitutional Court found the appeal inadmissible for lack of constitutional content. The court dismissed their appeal on the ground that the decision produced for purposes of comparison, namely a judgment of the High Court of Justice of Madrid of 31 July 1992, was not pertinent. The decision reads as follows: “... there is not enough evidence to show that the [appellants’] dismissal was an act of reprisal on the part of the respondent company’s ...”  constitutional protection afforded by Article 20 § 1 (a) of the Constitution does not, however, extend to absolutely vexatious expressions. The Court to the conclusion that the appellants’ right to freedom of expression has not been infringed. “They used that right in an excessive manner by means of value judgments expressed through cartoons and comments that were offensive and humiliating for the persons concerned and impugned their honour and reputation,” the court said. The court concluded that the cartoons were not necessary for others to form an opinion about the facts of which the appellant wished to complain, and were therefore gratuitous.

name: Swiadi Schatschaschwili
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 9154/10) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Georgian national, Mr Swiadi Schatschaschwili. The applicant alleged, in particular, that neither he nor counsel had been granted an opportunity at any stage of the criminal proceedings instituted against him to examine the only direct witnesses and victims of the crime allegedly committed by him in Göttingen in February 2007. The Court advised the parties on 14 January 2014 that it would continue processing the application.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 9154/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr H. Meyer-Mews, a lawyer practising in Bremen. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs K. Behr, Regierungsdirektorin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The Court advised the parties on 14 January 2014 that it would continue processing the application under the name Schatschaschwili v. Germany. The crimes were committed in Kassel on 14 October 2006 and in Göttingen on 3 February 2007 respectively. The Regional Court found it established that the applicant, acting jointly with an unidentified accomplice and according to a previously agreed plan, entered by force into an apartment. The men were aware that the apartment was used for prostitution and expected its two female occupants to keep valuables and cash in there. The applicant then threatened to shoot the women should they not disclose where they were keeping any additional money. The court imposed an accumulated prison sentence (Gesamtfreiheitsstrafe) of nine years and six months. The applicant and his accomplice gained access to O. and P.’s apartment pretending to be potential clients. Once inside the apartment B. produced a knife that he had carried along in his jacket. Fearing for her life O. opened the safe from which B. removed EUR 300 and also handed over the contents of her wallet in the amount of EUR 250. B. then left the apartment at around 8.30 p.m. taking the money. P. tried to escape from the perpetrators but jumped from the balcony located approximately two meters off the ground and ran away. The applicant jumped after her but abandoned the chase after some minutes when passers-by appeared nearby on the street. The Regional Court based its finding of facts regarding the first crime committed in Kassel on the statements made by the victims L. and I. on the occasion of their police interrogations as well as in the course of the subsequent trial. Both witnesses had identified the applicant without any hesitation as the perpetrator who had carried the gun when presented with his photo. The Regional Court found L and I’s testimonies to be consistent and credible and noted that they were supported by the statements of the police officers who had attended the crime scene and had interviewed the victims. The said article provides for such possibility in the event insurmountable. of the German Code of Criminal Procedure (see Relevant domestic law below) Witnesses O. and P. had been summoned to appear before the Regional Court on 24 August 2007, the third day of the trial. They both had refused to attend the hearing relying on medical certificates dated 9 August 2007 that indicated their unstable post‑traumatic emotional and psychological condition. The Regional Court asked for the witnesses to be heard by a court in Latvia and the hearing to be transmitted by voice and image. However, a witness hearing scheduled by the competent Latvian court for 13 February 2008 was cancelled shortly before on the ground that the witnesses had demonstrated that they were still suffering from post-traumatic disorders. The witnesses had further claimed that following threats by the accused they feared possible acts of revenge. The Regional Court concluded that it was impossible to have the witnesses examined in the foreseeable future. A further objection against the introduction of the witnesses’ pre-trial statements by counsel of one of the co-accused was rejected by the Regional Court. The trial as a whole had been fair and had complied with the requirements of Article 6 § 3 (d) of the Convention. The court was thus not prevented from admitting O. and P.’s pre- trial statements as evidence in the proceedings. It also held that notwithstanding the resulting restrictions for the defence, the trial had beenFair and complied with Article 6§ 3. Regional Court: O. and P. had given detailed and coherent descriptions of the circumstances of the crime. Minor contradictions in their statements could be explained by their concern not to disclose their illegal residence status and activities to the authorities. The court observed that the witnesses’ attention during the incident had been focussed on the further perpetrator carrying the knife and that the applicant himself had only stayed a short period of time in the apartment. Their inability to identify the applicant also showed that the Witnesses, as opposed to the defence’s allegations, had not testified with a view to incriminating him. O. had not answered the door when the neighbours were ringing the bell. Another neighbour, an elderly woman, had called on her and asked her to accompany her to their flat to investigate what had happened. The Regional Court noted that neither the defence nor the court itself had had an opportunity to observe the main witnesses’ demeanour at trial or by means of an audio-visual examination. The court further emphasised that when taking into account the testimonies. given by the witnesses' neighbour E. and their friend L. it had paid special attention to the fact that their statements constituted hearsay evidence and had to be assessed particularly carefully. The link between the evidence obtained in the course of such separate investigations and the crime at issue could only be made after O. and P. had reported the incident of 3 February 2007 to the police. The applicant and the co-accused had denied any participation in the robbery as such or any premeditated criminal activity in this respect. The applicant had testified that he and B. had come to the apartment with a view to making use of the women’s services as prostitutes. He further had conceded that he had followed P. when she escaped over the balcony in order to prevent her from calling the neighbours or the police since he had been afraid of getting problems in view of his criminal record and the problems he had previously had with prostitutes. The Federal Public Prosecutor General (Generalbundesanwalt) moved that the applicant's appeal on points of law be dismissed by the Federal Court of Justice. The applicant was convicted of murder in Germany in 2007. He appealed the conviction. The Federal Court of Justice dismissed the appeal on points of law as manifestly ill-founded. In October 2009 the Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant’s constitutional complaint against the decisions of the Federal Court. The applicant has since left prison and returned to his life in prison. The case is still pending in the Supreme Court of Germany. The verdict is expected to be delivered later this year or early in the new year. name: María Dolores Ruiz-Mateos
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court first by the Government of the Kingdom of Spain and then by the European Commission of Human Rights on 20 and 21 February 1992. It originated in an application (no. 12952/87) against Spain lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by six Spanish nationals on 5 May 1987. The object of the application and the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 (Art. 6-1). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr J. M. Morenilla, the elected judge of Spanish nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court first by the Government of the Kingdom of Spain and then by the European Commission of Human Rights on 20 and 21 February 1992. It originated in an application (no. 12952/87) against Spain lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by six Spanish nationals on 5 May 1987. The object of the application and the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent them (Rule 30). The President of the Court gave the lawyers leave to use the Spanish language. Mr Rafael de Mendizábal Allende, judge at the Supreme Court, was appointed as ad hoc judge. Mr Morenilla stated that he wished to withdraw pursuant to Rule 24 para. 2, because he had represented the Government before the Commission as Agent. The Chamber decided under Rule 51 to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The case was brought by five brothers and a sister, who held 100% of the shares in RUMASA S.A. The Government ordered the expropriation in the public interest of all the shares. The case gave rise to an appeal to the Constitutional Court (recurso de inconstit) The Court heard addresses by the Government, by Mr Pellonpää for the Commission and by Mr García Montes, Mr Sánchez Pardo and Mr Ruhlmann for the applicants, as well as their replies to its questions. The lawyers for the applicant and the Government’s representatives produced various documents. The Court ruled in favour of the applicants. Law no. 7/1983 of 29 June 1983, published a day later in the Official State Gazette (Boletín Oficial del Estado), had replaced the legislative decree. Articles 1 and 2 thereof ordered the immediate expropriation and transfer of possession of the companies concerned. The aim of these measures was to protect the public interest because, in order to finance the group’s companies, its banks had taken risks considered to be disproportionate in relation to their solvency. A group of deputies contested its constitutional validity. The Constitutional Court dismissed the deputies’ appeal by a judgment of 2 December 1983, adopted with the President's casting vote. In a dissenting opinion, six members of the court expressed the view that the expropriated procedure followed was contrary to the Constitution. On 21 March 1984 the first applicant had requested Court no. 18 to refer to the Constitutional Court a question on the conformity of Articles 1 and 2 of Law no. 7/1983 with Articles 14, 24 and 33 of the Constitution. The court held hearings on 18 June and 17 September 1984. In the opinion of the first-instance court, the decision on the merits of the dispute depended on the validity of the provisions in issue. The Constitutional Court found the question admissible on 17 October 1984; it then gave notice of the question to the Chamber of Deputies, the Senate, the Government and the Attorney General. The applicants submitted two memorials, respectively eighty-five and thirty-seven pages long. José María Ruiz-Mateos challenged two judges for lack of impartiality. The Constitutional Court dismissed the challenge on the ground that the judges lacked locus standi. By a judgment of 19 December 1986, it held that Articles 1 and 2 of Law no. 7/1983 were compatible with Article 24 of the Constitution. Although this admittedly meant that the persons concerned suffered restrictions on the judicial protection of their rights, it was always open to them to contest the measure in the administrative courts and to ask those courts to refer a question to the Constitutional Court on the constitutional conformity of such action. In addition an appeal (amparo), was also made to the Supreme Court of Justice. The appeal proceedings began on 26 June 1988. The hearing was initially set down for 21 October, but was adjourned at the request of the applicants’ lawyer, who was unable to attend. The applicants sought a stay of the proceedings until the European Commission and Court of Human Rights had had an opportunity to rule on their application to Strasbourg. The Audiencia provincial referred the question to the Constitutional Court on 9 July 1989. The latter court declared it admissible on 31 October 1989, then communicated it to the institutions. On 7 July 1989 it overruled the applicant’s objection to this decision. The application was dismissed on 22 December 1986. The following day that court dismissed the action for restitution. Constitutional Court found contested articles of Law no. 7/1983 to be compatible with Articles 14 and 33 para. 3 of the Constitution. Two judges expressed a dissenting opinion. Constitutional Court has jurisdiction over the whole of Spanish territory and is competent to hear appeals against alleged unconstitutionality of laws and regulations having the force of law. The Audiencia provincial was notified of this on 25 January 1991 and set down a hearing for 22 February. The court dismissed their appeal by a judgment of 25 February. On 6 March the applicants lodged an application for the interpretation of that judgment. Their application was dismissed on 11 March 1991. The relevant Articles of the 1978 Constitution are worded as follows. Only the rights guaranteed under Articles 14 to 29 of the Constitution may be the subject of an amparo appeal. The judgments of the Constitutional Court shall be published in the Official State Gazette, together with any dissenting opinions. They have the force of res judicata with effect from the day following their publication, and no appeal may be brought against them. Those which declare the unconstitutionality of a law or of a rule with force of law, and all those which do not merely recognise an individual right, shall be fully binding on all persons. Unless the judgment rules otherwise, that part of the law not affected by unconst Constitutionality shall remain in force. ‘A question as to constitutionality referred to the Constitutional Court by a judge or court must be accompanied by a certified copy of the main file and, in so far as there are any, the observations provided for in the preceding article’ ‘No appeal shall lie against this decision. The Court may declare the question inadmissible, in a decision stating its reasons, after hearing only the Attorney General, when the procedural requirements are not satisfied or when the question is manifestly ill-founded’. ‘The court shall give judgment within 15 days, except when it considers a longer period, which may not exceed thirty days, to be necessary, in which case it must state the reasons for its decision. The Commission declared the first complaint admissible and the remainder of the application (no. 12952/87) inadmissible. The Commission expressed the opinion that there had been a violation of Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) inasmuch as the applicants had not been given a fair hearing.
