name: Johann Aigner
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the criminal proceedings against him had been unfair because the Austrian courts refused to grant his request for the further hearing of witnesses. By a decision of 15 February 2007 the Court declared the application admissible.Neither the applicant nor the Government filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The application was rejected by the Court on 14 February 2007. The case was dismissed on 14 April 2007. It was decided that the application was not admissible and the case was thrown out of court.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28328/03) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the criminal proceedings against him had been unfair because the Austrian courts refused to grant his request for the further hearing of witnesses. By a decision of 15 February 2007 the Court declared the application admissible. The application was filed by an Austrian national, Mr Johann Aigner (“the applicant”), on 16 August 2003. The Austrian Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Tichy. In 2001 the Graz Regional Court convicted the applicant of attempted rape with violence. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof), which upheld his plea of nullity and quashed the conviction. It found that the proceedings before the Regional Court were defective under Article 258 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Strafprozeßrechtsordnung) The Regional Court then resumed the proceedings in a new composition. At hearings on 1 July, 26 August, 15 October and 19 November 2002, it heard evidence from the applicant and further witnesses. These witnesses included Mr S, a waiter working in one of the pubs which the applicant had visited with Mrs K, and Mrs P, the innkeeper of another pub. Mrs K refused to give evidence and requested that the statements she had made to the police and the investigating judge be read out instead. The Court also granted the applicant’s request for the video recording of her deposition before the investigatingJudge to be shown. However, when played, the video Recording turned out to be a blank tape. The court dismissed the applicant's requests for the further taking of evidence. It did not consider it useful to visit the scene as the room in question was no longer in the state it had been in at the material time. Lastly, it dismissed the request for Mrs K to be called again to give further evidence as she had refused to giving evidence at the trial and there was no indication she would change her mind. The Regional Court, sitting in a formation of two professional judges and two lay judges, convicted the applicant of attempted rape with violence. It noted that Mrs K had been under the influence of alcohol to a considerable degree at the time of the events. The court did not believe the applicant’s account that he had invited Mrs K for drinks all afternoon and then to his room out of sympathy for her. The judge sentenced the applicant to three years’ imprisonment. Referring to a psychiatric expert opinion, it further ordered that he be detained in an institution for mentally ill offenders. The applicant filed a plea of nullity with the Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) in which he complained about the dismissal of his requests for further evidence. On 20 February 2003 the Supreme Court rejected the applicant’s plea of nullity. The Graz Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) dismissed the applicant's appeal, but granted the Public Prosecutor's cross-appeal and increased the sentence to four years’ imprisonment. The applicant had not submitted any reasons why Mrs K would be prepared to give evidence after refusing to do so at the trial on 1 July 2002. Article 258 of the 1975 Code of Criminal Procedure (Strafprozessordnung) provides that all evidence must in principle be taken at the Trial. In particular, witnesses and experts must make their statements orally before the court. Documents may only be used as evidence if they have been read out in court. Victims of sexual offences by the accused are exempted from giving evidence at the trial if there has been an adversarial hearing of the victim in the preliminary proceedings. This provision was introduced as part of the 1998 reform of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Prior to this reform, only minors aged under 14 at the time of an alleged sexual offence were exempted from Giving evidence at trial. The argument in favour of increasing procedural safeguards for the alleged victims of sexual offence is the danger of the court proceedings causing damage and traumatisation to the victim. However, it would also appear to be in the interest of victims aged over 14 for them to be questioned only once, as making a statement places a heavy mental burden on them. The European Court of Justice has ruled that particularly vulnerable victims receive ‘specific treatment best suited to their circumstances’ The aim is to ensure that victims are questioned “only insofar as necessary for the purpose of criminal proceedings’ ‘Victims may be entitled to testify in a manner enabling that objective to be achieved, by any appropriate means compatible with its basic legal principles,’ the court ruled. ‘A court should be able, in respect ofparticularly vulnerable victims, to use a special procedure if it best corresponds to the situation of the victims’‘ ‘The hearing arrangements must be capable of guaranteeing to all victims treatment which pays due respect to their individual dignity and gives them the opportunity to be heard and to supply evidence’

name: Martin Brunnthaler
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged in particular that the proceedings relating to his request for an industrial licence for chimney sweeping lasted unreasonably long. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 16 June 2005, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Court then ruled that the application was not admissible, and the case was returned to the Government. The case was heard by the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the. Convention) The Chamber was constituted as provided in Rule 26 of the Rules of Court.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 45289/99) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged in particular that the proceedings relating to his request for an industrial licence for chimney sweeping lasted unreasonably long. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Court declared the application partly admissible in a decision of 16 June 2005. The case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section on 1 November 2004. The Court ruled that the application was not admissible. On 3 June 1993 the Federal Minister allowed his request for transfer but dismissed his application for the industrial licence under the Trade Act (Gewerbeordnung). Referring to the submissions of the competent municipalities, he noted that there was no need for further chimney sweepers in the concerned area. On 20 July 1993 the applicant filed a complaint with the Administrative Court. He complained in particular that the. Federal Minister had not made sufficient investigations for his findings. The applicant filed against this decision with the Constitutional Court. On 1 July 1998 the Regional Governor allowed the reinstitution into proceedings. The Federal Minister for Economic Affairs dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 3 September 1999. The Linz Municipal Office, on 23 January 1997, again dismissed the applicant’s request for an industrial licence. The Regional Governor confirmed this decision on 21 July 1997. On 30 September 1997 the Constitutional Court declined to deal with the applicant's complaint. The case was transferred to the Administrative Court. On 9 September 1998 the Administrative court dismissed the complaint as being unfounded. This decision was served on the applicant and his counsel on 21 September 1998. The applicant has appealed the decision. The application has been adjourned until October 28, 2009. The appeal was dismissed on October 18, 2009, and the application was dropped. The decision was made after the applicant filed further submissions.

name: Mateo Cruz Gorraiz Lizarraga
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 62543/00) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained that they had not had a fair hearing in the judicial proceedings brought by them to halt construction of the Itoiz dam. They also complained that the Autonomous Community law in question had been enacted with a view to preventing execution of a Supreme Court judgment which had become final. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 62543/00) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Five Spanish nationals, Mr Mateo Cruz Gorraiz Lizarraga, Mrs Catalina Echamendi Erro, Mr Francisco Javier Gorraz Echamendis, and Mr Fermín Luis Gorra Zegarra, applied to the Court on 12 September 2000. The applicants were represented by Mr M.J. Baumont Aristu and Mr J.L.Beaumont Aristou, lawyers practising in Pamplona and Madrid. The case originated in an engineering project of February 1989 for the construction of a dam in Itoiz (Navarre province) which would result in the flooding of three nature reserves and a number of small villages. According to the Government, the total number of landowners affected by the dam's construction is 159. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The application was declared admissible and reserved its position on the Government's preliminary questions as to whether the first five applicants lacked ‘victim’ status and had failed to exhaust domestic remedies. In April 2003 the Chamber decided, having regard to the circumstances of the case, to dismiss a Rule 39 request submitted by the applicants. The Audiencia Nacional partly upheld the appeal in a judgment of 29 September 1995. The court also accepted the request for precise designation of the protection zones around the nature reserves affected by the dam. In a decision of 6 March 1996, the court prohibited the filling of the reservoir and displacement of the population concerned. In June 1996 the parliament of the Autonomous Community of Navarre (parlamento foral de Navarra) passed Autonomous community law (foral) no. 9/1996 on natural sites in Navarre. This law amended Aut autonomous Community Law no. 6/1987 of 10 April 1987. The Supreme Court definitively cancelled the dam project in so far as it concerned the 500-metre protection zones around nature reserves RN 9, 10 and 11. As a result of the judgment, the size of the planned dam, and thus of the area to be flooded, was reduced. The village of Itoiz, where the applicants' immovable property was located, was saved from flooding. In application of the Supreme Court's judgment, by a decision of 4 September 1997, the Audiencia Nacional declared final the interim enforcement measures ordered on 6 March 1996 concerning the prohibition on filling the reservoir and other related work. The applicant association contested the authorities' argument, claiming that the Autonomous Community law of 1996 was inapplicable in the instant case. By a decision of 21 May 1998, the Constitutional Court declared the application inadmissible on account of certain errors in its presentation which could nonetheless be corrected. The Audiencia Nacional summoned the parties on 28 May 1998 so that it could hear their submissions on certain aspects of the Aut autonomous Community law whose constitutionality had been challenged. The constitutional court declared the issues raised in the preliminary question admissible on 21 July 1998. Under section 37(2) of the Judicature Act, it gave notice of the questions to the Chamber of Deputies, the Senate and the government and parliament of Navarre. The Constitutional Court held that the impugned provisions of the Autonomous Community law of 1996 were compatible with the Constitution. The Speaker of the Senate asked that the Senate be considered a party to the proceedings and offered its assistance. The Audiencia Nacional forwarded to the Constitutional Court the written pleadings submitted by the applicant association during the proceedings before it. The Constitutional Court's judgment of 14 March 2000 was published on 13 April 2000. It was based on a judgment of the Supreme Court of Navarre delivered in accordance with Navarre Aut autonomous Community Law no. 6/1987. It observed at the outset that enforcement of that judgment had become impossible since the entry into force of the law.  Constitutional Court considered that in the meantime a new law had been passed amending the legal system applicable to the peripheral protection zones. It found that both the Supreme Court's judgment of 14 July 1997 and the new Autonomous Community law of 1996 were intended to guarantee the existence of a peripheral protection zone around the three nature reserves affected by the dam's construction. Accordingly, it held that the balance of general interests had been respected and that there was no clear lack of proportion between the conflicting interests. Consequently, the impugned provisions could not be held to be contrary to Article 24 § 1 of the Constitution. It added that the new law did not amount to ad causam legislation, being general in form and in substance. The Constitutional Court dismissed the application for a preliminary ruling. The judgment was published in the Official Gazette on 14 April 2000. out that laws could be challenged before the Constitutional Court through the remedy provided for in Article 163 of the Constitution. The application was dismissed after it was found to be not in the public interest. The case was heard by a panel of three judges, who found in favor of the applicant. The appeal was dismissed and the judgment was made public in April 2000, after it had been heard by the panel for more than a week. The judge made the decision to dismiss the application, and the decision was made for the case to go to the court of appeal.

name: Louise O’Keeffe
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35810/09) against Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Ms Louise O’Keeffe (‘the applicant’), on 16 June 2009. The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court. Ann Power-Forde, the judge elected in respect of Ireland, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). On 13 June 2012 the President of the Chamber decided to appoint Mr Justice Charleton to sit as an ad hoc judge. On 20 September 2012 that Chamber (Angelika Nußberger, substitute judge, replaced Ganna Yudkivska who was unable to take part in the further consideration of the case) relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35810/09) against Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant mainly complained under Article 3 that the system of primary education had failed to protect her from sexual abuse by a teacher in 1973. She also relied on Article 8 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1, both alone and in conjunction with Article 14. The Chamber, unanimously, struck out the complaints regarding the length of the domestic proceedings and the lack of an effective domestic remedy in that regard, given the friendly settlement reached between the parties on those issues. It also declared admissible the remaining complaints. The applicant attended Dunderrow National School from 1968. The school was owned, through trustees, by the Catholic Bishop of the Diocese of Cork and Ross. The manager (S.), acting on behalf of the bishop, was the local parish priest. The applicant and the Government each filed further observations on the merits. The Irish Human Rights Commission and the European Centre for Law and Justice had been given leave by the President of the Chamber to intervene in the written procedure and their submissions to the Chamber were admitted to the Grand Chamber file. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 6 March 2013 (Rule 59 § 3). In 1971 a parent of a child complained to the manager that L.H. had sexually abused her child. That complaint was not reported to the police, to the Department or to any other State authority and was not acted upon by the manager. In September 1973 other parents brought to the applicant’s parents’ attention similar allegations. Those allegations were not reported at that time. The applicant suppressed the sexual abuse. While she had significant psychological difficulties, she did not associate those with the abuse. In 1996 she was contacted by the police who were investigating a complaint made in 1995 by a former pupil of Dunderrow National School. In 1998 he pleaded guilty to twenty-one sample charges and was sentenced to imprisonment. His licence to teach was withdrawn by the Minister for Education (‘the Minister’) under Rule 108 of the National School Rules 1965. An initial award (44,814.14 euros (EUR) was made by a single judge. The applicant appealed to a CICT panel. She claimed that the CICT gave her the option of continuing her appeal (at the risk of finding that her CICT application would be rejected as out of time) or of accepting the initial offer. The award was made on an ex gratia basis. Since the State is never a party to CICT proceedings, it became aware of this award later. The High Court awarded the applicant damages in the sum of EUR 305,104. The first payment was received in November 2007 so that she has been paid in the region of EUR 31,000 to date. She registered a judgment mortgage against that part of the family home owned by L.H. The State Defendants applied for a direction to strike out the case. The High Court judge, in response to the applicant’s complaint regarding the absence of a State system for adverting to and addressing sexual abuse in national schools, asked Counsel for the applicant as follows: “What evidence do I have, or what should I have deduce[d] from the evidence that has been given?” The High Court accepted the State Defendants’ application in March 2004. On 20 January 2006 the High Court delivered judgment. It found that the action was not statute barred. It also concluded that the State was not vicariously liable for the sexual assaults perpetrated by L.H. given the relationship between the State and the denominational management of national schools. In May 2006 the applicant appealed to the Supreme Court. Her Notice of Appeal challenged the finding on vicarious liability. By a majority judgment of 19 December 2008 (Hardiman J and Fennelly J, with whom Chief Justice Murray and Mr Justice. Mr Justice Fennley J agreed), the appeal was dismissed. The costs of the proceedings were awarded against the applicant. Dissenting churches and the Catholic Church wished to ensure that children of their denominations be educated in schools controlled by the denomination and not by the State. Those churches were “remarkably successful” in achieving this aim. State funding was accorded on a proportionate basis to all denominational schools, the population was at the time overwhelmingly Catholic so that the majority of national schools had Catholic patrons and managers. The Catholic Church had responded that there could be no interference whatever with the “inherited tradition of managerial rights of schooling”. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and the case is now mooted for a new generation. Hardiman J referred to the ‘urgent desire’ of the denominations to maintain their role in primary education. As a result there were approximately 3,000 national schools in Ireland. Most were under the control of Catholic patrons and managers, a few were underThe control of other denominations and even fewer were controlled by non-denominational groups. Hardiman J noted that, in recent times and after more than a century and a half, the provision of education was belatedly placed on a statutory basis by the Education Act 1998. Prior to that Act the system had been administered by the 1965 Rules as well as by other ministerial letters, circulars and notes. Hardiman J concluded that, having regard to the relevant test for vicarious liability and to the above-described arrangements for the control and management of national schools, the State Defendants were not liable to the applicant for the wrongs committed against her. The relationship of L.H. and the State – a “triangular one with the Church’ – was entirely sui generis and a product of Ireland’s unique historical experience. The manager was “the nominee of the patron, that is of a power other than the Minister and he did not inform the Minister of any difficulties with, or complaints about, [L.H.]” Hardiman J: The Minister can hardly be responsible for a failure to ‘cease’ a course of action of whose existence he was quite unaware. Kenny J: In my view the Constitution specifically envisages, not indeed a delegation but a ceding of the actual running of schools to the interests represented by the patron and the manager. Fennelly J: Cases of sexual abuse had preoccupied the criminal courts and the Supreme Court for many years and it was surprising that that court was confronted for the first time with questions relating to the liability of institutions including the State for sexual abuse of schoolchildren in a national school by a teacher. Fennelly J said the system was not a State system but rather a “State-supported system’ He noted the clear division of power between the State (funding and fixing the curriculum) and the manager (day-to-day running of the school including hiring and firing teachers) He concluded that the State was not vicariously liable for the acts of L.H. or for the failure of the manager to report the 1971 complaint to the State.Geoghegan J dissented. He accepted that neither the Department nor its inspectors had any knowledge of the assaults. He considered that, for all practical purposes, most primary education in Ireland took the form of a joint enterprise between Church and State. Geoghegan J relied, notably, on the role of school inspectors. If an allegation of sexual assault by a teacher on a national-school pupil was considered well-founded by an inquiry set up by the Department, it could lead to the withdrawal of recognition or to a police investigation. The Supreme Court vacated the High Court order for costs against the applicant since it was not disputed that hers was an important and complex test case. It determined that each party had to bear its own costs related to the action against the State Defendants. The applicant was legally represented throughout the civil proceedings, although she did not have legal aid. She was awarded damages of more than £30,000.

name: Stuart Gray
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49278/09) against the United Kingdom and the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) Two British nationals, Mr Stuart Gray and Mr Rory Gray, on 10 September 2009, complained that shortcomings in the British health system in connection with the recruitment of locum doctors had led to their father’s death as a consequence of medical malpractice by German locum doctor U. U. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the admissibility and merits of the application. The application was declared partly inadmissible on 18 December 2012.
eval_texts: Two British nationals, Mr Stuart Gray and Mr Rory Gray, lodged an application with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. They complained that shortcomings in the British health system in connection with the recruitment of locum doctors had led to their father’s death. The application was declared partly inadmissible on 18 December 2012 as being manifestly ill-founded. The applicants and the German Government each filed observations on the admissibility and merits of the application. The case was heard by the Supreme Court of the European Court of Justice, which concluded that the application was not admissible. The applicants are the sons of the late David Gray (hereinafter referred to as “Mr Gray” or “the deceased”) who died in the evening of 16 February 2008 at the age of 71 at his home in Cambridgeshire, United Kingdom. Mr Gray suffered from kidney stones and from 2004 on he had regularly been attended at home by his doctor, a General Practitioner. The GP had routinely administered injections of opiates, in particular pethidine at a dosage of 100mg, for pain relief. On several occasions between 2006 and 2008 Mr Gray had recourse to out-of-hours medical services by “Take Care Now’ (“TCN”), a private agency that recruits locum doctors within the United Kingdom or from abroad. Dr U., a German national, had recently been recruited by TCN through an agency on a self-employed basis to provide out-of-hours care. U., at the time aged 65, had qualified as a doctor in Germany in 1972 where he was practising as an aesthetic surgeon. For the purpose of working as a locum doctor in the United Kingdom he had obtained registration with the British General Medical Council (GMC) in 2006. U. administered 100mg of diamorphine from the respective ampoule included in the palliative care box by intra‑muscular injection. Two hours after U. had left, Mr Gray’s partner realised that he was no longer breathing and called an ambulance. The attending emergency services confirmed that Mr Gray had died. U. was suspended from the British medical register on an interim basis. He explained that when treating the deceased he had committed a grave mistake with fatal outcome that had resulted from the confusion between the drugs pethidine and diamorphine. A post mortem report issued on 25 June 2008 by a forensic pathologist in the United Kingdom. established as the cause of Mr Gray’s death diamorphin poisoning in association with alcohol intoxication as well as hypertensive heart disease and myocardial fibrosis. The criminal proceedings were instituted against U. in the U.K. and Germany. U. apologised for the medical malpractice in connection with the deceased's treatment. Cambridgeshire Constabulary made an application for assistance to the German Federal Office of Criminal Investigation (Bundeskriminalamt) on 5 March 2008. The CPS asked the German authorities to carry out the respective investigations. Bochum Chief Public Prosecutor ex officio initiated preliminary criminal proceedings (Ermittlungsverfahren) against U. in Germany under file no. 49 Js 174/08 on suspicion of having negligently caused the death of Mr Gray. U. is charged with manslaughter, i.e. the unlawful killing of a human being, an offence contrary to Common Law and punishable on conviction by a term of life imprisonment. In July 2008 German and British police officers visited U. at his surgery in Witten, Germany, and informed him that criminal investigations were pending against him in Germany and the United Kingdom. The originals of the protocols of the witness hearings conducted as well as the material obtained in the course of the investigations were handed over to Cambridgeshire police. A forensic expert opinion was obtained from a professor of Essen university hospital on the question whether the treatment of the deceased by U. had complied with medical standards. In his final report issued on 18 September 2008 the expert confirmed that the cause of Mr Gray’s death had been an overdose of diamorphine. U. not sufficiently investigated the cause of Mr Gray’s acute pain and had not verified whether the medication administered and its dosage had been an appropriate therapy under the circumstances. The expert concluded that U.’S treatment of the deceased had thus been inadequate and had violated basic principles of medical care. Cambridgeshire Constabulary requested the German public prosecution authorities to assure that no criminal proceedings would be instituted against U. in Germany prior to finalisation of the investigations in the United Kingdom. German prosecution authorities informed Cambridgedgeshire police that they had been obliged by operation of law to institute preliminary criminal proceedings against U in Germany. The second applicant and the first applicant filed a complaint in November 2008 against U. acting as joint plaintiffs to the prosecution (Nebenkläger) The complaint was made under file no. 49 Js 174/08 against U., with the latter’s apology letter of 10 July 2008 sent to the Bochum prosecution authorities. On 27 February 2009 an arrest warrant was issued against U by the Huntingdon Magistrates’ Court, Cambridgeshire. On 12 March 2009 the Colchester Magistrates' Court issued a European Arrest Warrant (”EAW’) against U for allegedly having caused the death of Mr Gray with an overdose of morphine. U. had nevertheless committed a grave error in the deceased’s treatment and had thus violated basic principles of the medical profession. The EAW was forwarded by the British authorities to the German Federal Office of Criminal Investigation on 13 March 2009. On 20 March 2009 the Witten District Court issued the penal order (file no. 49 Js 174/08) against U. as applied for by the prosecution authorities. By a decision of the same day, the District Court determined that the probation period for U. was two years starting from the date the penal Order became final. The CPS asked the Ministry of Justice of the Land of North Rhine-Westphalia for information why the EAW had not yet been executed and for clarification whether any criminal or other proceedings were conducted, pending or envisaged. U. had been convicted by final decision of a German court for the offence underlying the extradition request and the sentence imposed upon him was currently in the process of being executed. His extradition would therefore be contrary to the ban on double jeopardy as reflected in section 9 (1) no. 1 of the Act on Cooperation in Criminal Matters. The Hamm Higher Regional Court, endorsing the reasoning of the Hamm General Prosecution Authorities, declared U.’s extradition inadmissible on 14 May 2009. No appeal having been lodged by U., the penal order of 20 March 2009 became final in accordance with Article 410 of the German Code of Criminal Procedure (see Relevant domestic and international law and practice below). Criminal investigations in the United Kingdom were discontinued. The Westphalia-Lippe Medical Association applied for the opening of disciplinary proceedings against U. for breach of his professional duties in connection with the incidents on 16 February 2008. The proceedings regarding U.’s fitness to practice medicine before the Arnsberg District Government were discontinued at the end of 2010. A decision dated 27 April 2011 of the competent Münster Administrative Court sitting in a special formation as disciplinary jurisdiction for the healthcare professions reprimanded U. under file no. 49 Js 174/08. U. committed himself to refrain from practising medicine abroad in the future. An Inquest into the circumstances of the incident was held by the Cambridgeshire Coroner from 14 January to 4 February 2010. U. in particular for having committed a grave error in the treatment of Mr Gray, and fined him 7,000 EUR. The GMC Fitness to Practice Panel considered that U. had breached several of the basic principles of good medical practice and decided to formally strike U.’s name from the medical register in the United Kingdom. The applicants’ compensation claims were settled with respect to all three defendants by consent orders of December 2009, January and August 2010. The decision became final on 4 June 2011.

name: Hans Dichand
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29271/95) against the Republic of Austria lodged on 28 September 1995 with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that an injunction prohibiting them from repeating certain statements they had published in a periodical violated their right to freedom of expression. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 9 January 2001 the Chamber declared the application admissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court effected a change in the composition of its Sections, but the present case remained with the former Chamber of Section III.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29271/95) against the Republic of Austria lodged on 28 September 1995 with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that an injunction prohibiting them from repeating certain statements they had published in a periodical violated their right to freedom of expression. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The applicant, but not the Government, submitted additional observations on the merits. The Court decided that no hearing was required. The case remained with the former Chamber of Section III, which had declared the application admissible. The applicants belong to a large media group which at the relevant time was in strong competition with another media group represented by Mr Michael Graff, a lawyer practising in Vienna. Mr Graff was from 1982 to 1987 secretary general of the Austrian People’s Party (Österreichische Volkspartei) and, from 1983 to 1995, a Member of Parliament for that party. In 1989 several Austrian laws were amended by the Extended Pecuniary Limits Amendment Act (Erweiterte Wertgrenzen-Novelle). The Government Bill (Regierungsvorlage) provided for an amendment to Section 359 § 1 of the Enforcement Act (Exekutionsordnung) Dumas took it for granted that he had to give up his law firm when he became a member of the government. Only Mr Graff, who is obviously thick-skinned, does not intend to comply with these moral concepts. The People’s Party does not have to fear the ‘Krone’ but its voters, who will continue turning away from it if the party shows itself incapable of establishing order within its own ranks. Cato.” [German] “Moral 93 Roland Dumas war, bevor er Frankreichs Außenminister wurde, einer der bekanntesten und er erheblich. und erheblicher. Dr. Graff verwaltete zum Beispiel das gigantische Erbe Picassos, vertrat Kreisky and einen österreichischen Außenminister. Für Dumas war es ganz selbstverständlich, daß er sein Rechtsanwaltsbüro aufgeben mußte, als er in die Regierung eintrat. Ein Anwalt darf nicht an der Entstehung von Gesetzen beteiligt sein, die seinen Mandanten Vorteile bringen. Damit in solchen Fällen nicht ein bestimmter Verdacht entstehen kann, der keineswegs begründet sein muß. M.G. Graff brought injunction proceedings under Section 1330 of the Austrian Civil Code (Allgemeines Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch) against the three applicants. He requested that the applicants be prohibited from stating or repeating that he “does not intend to comply with moral concepts existing in democracies all over the world” The applicants’ appeal against this decision was to no avail. In September 1994 the Vienna Commercial Court granted a permanent injunction. It ordered the applicants not to repeat the impugned statements and to retract the statements in one edition of the “Neue Kronen‑Zeitung” The court found that the statement contained in the first paragraph of the newspaper article was an insult. The court concluded that the applicants could not successfully rely on Article 10 of the Convention. The interference with the applicants’ rights under this provision was justified in order to protect Mr Graff’s good reputation, which could be prejudiced by such untruthful statements. The applicants were the owners of several monthly magazines. Unlike daily newspapers, these magazines were usually on the market longer. If one of the applicants. magazines, for instance, had violated the Unfair Competition Act (Bundesgesetz gegen den unl), the court said. Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) dismissed the applicants’ appeal in 1994. It found that the Commercial Court had correctly taken the necessary evidence and assessed the relevant facts. The applicants also submitted that the impugned article constituted a criticism of Mr Graff’s behaviour as a politician and was therefore protected by the freedom of expression guaranteed by Article 10 of the Convention. But the contested statements were not value judgments, but (political) criticism based on alleged facts. Such criticism was only acceptable if the underlying facts were true. Since the applicants had failed to prove the truth of these facts, they could not rely on these facts. Supreme Court rejected as inadmissible the applicants’ extraordinary appeal on points of law (außerordentliche Revision) The court pointed out that disparagement by means of untrue statements, even if made in the course of political debate, went beyond acceptable (political) criticism and could not be justified by a weighing of interests or by invoking the right to freedom of expression. This decision was served on the applicants on 10 April 1995. Article 10 of the Convention was upheld by the Supreme Court on 9 March 1995. The decision was made by the Court of Appeal on 13 March 1995, and the application was dismissed.

name: Bernd Karl Baumann
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 33592/96) against France lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights on 21 July 1995. The applicant complained that he had been denied access to a tribunal, within the meaning of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, or an effective remedy. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The case was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52:1 of the Rules of Court). On 14 March 2000 the Chamber declared the application admissible. The Court has ruled in favour of the applicant.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 33592/96) against France lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained that he had been denied access to a tribunal, within the meaning of Article 6 of the Convention. He also alleged a breach of his right to freedom of movement as a result of the seizure and subsequent confiscation of his passport. On 14 March 2000 the Chamber declared the application admissible. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. It turned out that on 27 November 1993 Strasbourg police officers spotted an occupied vehicle parked in a car park. The case was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. On-the-spot investigation established that other transactions had taken place and that the two arrested men used to meet in a hotel in Brumath (Bas-Rhin) The investigators seized a German passport in the applicant's name, 7,700 German marks (DEM) and 2,150 French francs (FRF) found in Miss C.E.'s handbag. O.H. and S.B. were committed for trial at the Strasbourg Criminal Court where they were tried and convicted on 13 June 1994. The applicant could not therefore lodge an application for the return of his possessions with the criminal court trying the case. C.E. requested the public prosecutor to return the seized DEM 7,700 and FRF 2,150 on the ground that the money belonged to her and that she was not in any way involved in the criminal proceedings. The public prosecutor refused her request on the grounds that the items had been confiscated by order of the Criminal Court in its judgment of 13 June 1994 in the proceedings against O.H. and S.B. received no reply. In a letter of 29 April 1996 she renewed her request, stating among other things: “my ex-boyfriend has put me in a difficult position which has seriously changed my life ... I have incurred debts because of him ... it is very important for me to recover my money...”

name: Gabriel Magee
train_texts: The case originated in three applications (nos. 26289/12, 29062/12 and 29891/12) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The first and second applicants were represented by KRW Law-LLP, a firm of solicitors based in Belfast. The third applicant was represented by Mr P. Moriarty of O’Connor and Moriarty Solicitors. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government’s Agent”) were represented in the case by their Agent, Ms M. Addis of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office.
eval_texts: The case originated in three applications (nos. 26289/12, 29062/12 and 29891/12) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The first and third applicants were arrested under section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000 (“the 2000 Act”) on suspicion of involvement in the murder of a police officer on 9 March 2009. They were detained at Antrim police station on the same day. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the admissibility and merits of the cases (Rule 59 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Court Judge granted warrants authorising a five-day extension of detention. Each of the applicants was interviewed on twelve occasions in the following five days. In her reasoning, Judge Philpott noted that the relevant forensic evidence was central to the investigation and that the investigation was being carried out diligently and expeditiously. The second applicant was arrested under section 41 of the 2000 Act on suspicion of involvement in the murder of two soldiers at Masserene Barracks, Antrim, on 7 March 2009. He was detained at Antrim Police Station on the same day. On 15 March 2009 the DPP made an application to the County Court for a warrant extending the second applicant’s detention as the results of a number of forensic tests were pending. The applicants sought permission to apply for judicial review of Judge Philpott’s decisions of 21 and 22 March 2009 granting further extensions to the warrants authorising their detention. The High Court of Northern Ireland heard the applications on 25 March 2009. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the judge had failed to address the question of whether the detention of the applicants was required while the results of the forensic examinations were expected. The applicants also claimed that Schedule 8 of the 2000 Act was incompatible with Article 5 of the Convention. The review of the lawfulness of the detention had to embrace an examination of the basis of the arrest, otherwise a person could be detained for up to twenty-eight days without there having been any judicial review. The High Court of Northern Ireland found no basis for the submission that Schedule 8 was incompatible with Article 5 of the Convention. The court accepted, however, that a review of the lawfulness of the arrest need not involve a detailed analysis of the decision to arrest. The Court held that, although there was no doubt that the “competent legal authority” referred to in Article 5 § 1 (c) was the magistrate in the United Kingdom, it did not necessarily have to be a person with power to conduct the trial of any eventual criminal charge. The judges also found that, as paragraph 32 of the 2000 Act provided that there must be reasonable grounds for believing that the further detention of a person was necessary, it therefore contained a requirement of proportionality. High Court of Northern Ireland ruled on 24 February 2011. Case involved whether detention for more than four days was compatible with rights under the European Convention on Human Rights. High Court also ruled that there was no authority which supported the applicants’ contention that Article 5 required that a detained person be charged well before the expiry of the twenty‑eight day period contemplated in the 2000 Act. The High Court ruled that the ‘judge or other officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power’ within the meaning of Article 5(3) of the Convention was not ‘the competent legal authority’ referred to in the case. The applicants were released without charge on 25 March 2009. The first and third applicants were not subsequently charged with any offence related to the murder of the police officer. The second applicant was immediately rearrested and interviewed over the following two days. On 7 November 2011 the second applicant stood trial before a judge sitting without a jury. On 20 January 2012 he was acquitted on all counts of the indictment. The applicants’ release from detention was upheld by the Court of Appeal. However, the High Court refused leave to appeal to the Supreme Court. The applications did not raise an arguable point of law of general public importance. The application for bail was refused.

name: Christof Stollenwerk
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 8844/12) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) on 9 February 2012. The applicant alleged that the principle of equality of arms had been violated because the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal had taken decisions on 3 and 25 February 2011 relating to the continuation of his detention. The German Government were represented by one of their Agents, Mr H.-J. Behrens, Ministerialrat, of the Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection. On 16 March 2016 the complaint concerning Article 5 § 4 of the convention was communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the principle of equality of arms had been violated because the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal had taken decisions on 3 and 25 February 2011 relating to the continuation of his detention. The German Government were represented by one of their Agents, Mr H.-J. Behrens, Ministerialrat of the Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection. On 16 March 2016 the complaint concerning Article 5 § 4 of the convention was communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The applicant was convicted of smuggling drugs into Germany and trafficking (dealt with as a single offence instead of two separate offences) and sentenced to two years and six months’ imprisonment. On 13 December 2010 he lodged an appeal against the judgment. On 28 January 2011 the Düsseldorf Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office (Generalstaatsanwaltschaft – “the prosecution authorities”) submitted written observations to the Court of Appeal, requesting the dismissal of the appeal of 5 January 2011. On 25 February 2011 the Court. of Appeal dismissed the request for a subsequent hearing as inadmissible. The decision of the Court of Appeal was based on the fact that there had been no opportunity to respond to the request for an inquiry. The decision was not based on facts, but on the lack of opportunity to comment on the request. The court's decision was made on the basis that the request had been made without sufficient information. The Court's decision is therefore the result of a legal challenge to the decision made by the court, which was upheld by the Supreme Court. The case was settled in the High Court of Justice on July 31, 2011. The appeal was upheld on August 6, 2011, and the decision is now on its way to the European Court of Appeals.

name: Alfred Worm
