The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 31).
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 4 July 1996 and by the Government of the Republic of Austria (‘the Government’) on 11 September 1996. It originated in an application (no. 22714/93) against Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by an Austrian national, Mr Alfred Worm, on 28 July 1993. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him. Hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 April 1997. The Court heard addresses by Mr Geus, Mr Masser and Mr Cede and also replies to its questions. The applicant was working for Profil, an Austrian periodical dealing mostly with politics. For several years he investigated and reported on the case of Mr Hannes Androsch, a former Vice-Chancellor and Minister of Finance. He was found guilty of making false statements as a witness on two occasions. The court found that he wrongly stated that certain amounts of money had been put at his disposal by a Mr S., whereas in fact they had been transferred from anonymous bank accounts operated by his wife and himself. Hannes Androsch was convicted of having evaded taxes between 1973 and 1981. He was sentenced to a fine of 1.8 million Austrian schillings (ATS). The atmosphere during the trial was glacial. ‘Above all, there were to be no mistakes during the proceedings. The case was to be handled with common prudence, properly and to the best of our knowledge and belief – but not with kid gloves!’ (Mr Heinz Tschernutter, tax investigator and witness, when asked what principles had governed the hearing of the Androsh case.) On the day before the trial [the Austrian newspaper] Die Presse dropped the bombshell that was meant to shake all Austria. Lawyer Herbert Schachter was quoted as saying: ‘I’m sure that Dr Andosch will present his case in an impressive manner’ Judge Zeilinger knows the file inside out, as was clear from each of his questions. The public prosecutor, Matousek, is able to find his way around in the dark generated by the ‘international legal adviser's’ murky financial deals. Anyone venturing into the maze of Androsch's accounts containing undeclared money is amazed by the structure's simplicity. It is not only wholly lacking in sophistication but is almost astoundingly crude. The alleged tax evasion was perhaps ‘long-term’ but by no means ‘ingenious and sophisticated’. While Androsh was Finance Minister, until January 1981, he could rely on the zealous but unlawful obedience of a number of powerful officials. It has been known since 1980 that Androsch evaded taxes. The tax officials Walter Handerek, Heinz Tschernutter and Gerhard Berner, who reopened the file between 1985 and 1988, were treated by defending counsel Herbert Schachter as though they were the accused. It is both symptomatic and revealing that Andosch told the trial court again and again that ‘seven inspections’ had been carried out and on each occasion had found in his favour. The legal proceedings which were adjourned on Friday furnished further proof that for years the accused escaped prosecution thanks to the zealous obedience of officials. Everyone except him is to blame for this. Androsh has become so completely immersed in the role of the innocent victim that he cannot subjectively conceive of ever having been the guilty party. Androsch's defence in court was disgraceful. After so many years one would at least have expected properly constructed arguments. Each time Judge Zeilinger asked him a specific question he either took refuge in lapses of memory or blamed his ‘adoptive father’ He even trotted out the late Sir Arthur Stein, the explorer of the Silk Road, from whom he claims to have received a legacy. He paid less and less attention to the judge's questions and treated the public prosecutor with increasingly provocative contempt. He turned to look more and more often at the public in the gallery, seeking approval, and his gestures increasingly reminded one of the self-satisfied, powerful Vice-Chancellor and Finance Minister. Judge Zeilinger had prepared for this trial keenly and diligently. By citing facts he kept forcing Androsch into corners from which he could only escape by taking refuge in memory lapses. There comes, however, a point in every trial after which the court expects some sign of understanding. It hopes for a trace of humility that may be appraised as a mitigating circumstance. The defendant has shown no humility to date, not even for a second. But he now has a few weeks to consider whether it is consonant with the principles of a State based on the rule of law for a Finance Minister and his family to have at their disposal accounts containing millions in undeclared funds. The Vienna Regional Criminal Court acquitted the applicant. The article analysed the conduct of the presiding judge, the public prosecutor, defence counsel and in particular the accused, Mr Androsch, almost as a psychologist would have done. It appeared from the article that the applicant assumed that the investigations carried out by the tax authorities were correct. He subjected the statements made by the accused at the trial to a critical psychological analysis. However, his way of writing and the wording used were not capable of influencing these proceedings. The court found that it was clear for every reader, who was vaguely familiar with the issue, that. the applicant, who had been working for Profil for many years, had intensively dealt with the so-called “Causa Androsh” and frequently reported on it. The court convicted the applicant of having exercised prohibited influence on criminal proceedings and imposed on him forty day-fines of ATS 1,200 each, that is ATS 48,000, or twenty days' imprisonment in default of payment. The publishing firm was made jointly and severally liable for payment of the fine. The Court of Appeal also contested the Regional Court's assumption that everybody, including the lay judges, knew the applicant's long-standing commitment in the Androsch case and would therefore not be influenced by his article. It observed that “the objective element of the offence defined in section 23 of the Media Act is constituted not only by unfavourable comment on evidence but also by favourable comment” The court found that the applicant's expertise and involvement in the subject matter rather reinforced the impression that he had written the article with the intention of influencing the outcome of the proceedings. He had researched into the case since 1978 and had written more than a hundred articles about it. From the beginning he had been convinced that Mr Androsch had committed tax evasion. It was in no way certain that the lay judges regularly read Profil. On the contrary, in spectacular proceedings like the ones in issue, it happened frequently that lay judges would follow the reports in papers they did not usually read. The objective element of the offence defined in section 23 of the Media Act is accordingly made out. As regards the subjective element, it should be. observed that it is hard to understand why the court below should have concluded that there was no intention to influence the outcome. of the trial.

name: Aysel Aydin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 16637/07) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that her criminal conviction violated her right to freedom of expression. The President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the case at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The Turkish Government did not express any wish to intervene under Article 36 § 1 of the convention. The German Government were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel of the Federal Ministry of Justice.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that her criminal conviction violated her right to freedom of expression. The Turkish Government did not express any wish to intervene under Article 36 § 1 of the convention. The case was decided on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29): The application was upheld by the Court on 16 April 2007. The ruling was made by the President of the Fifth Section, who was also decided to rule on the merits and admissibilities of the case. The decision was published on 26 March 1994. The PKK's executives changed their strategy and declared an end to the armed battle against Turkish army entities. For two years the PKK has been using exclusively political means to fight for a peaceful and democratic solution to the Kurdish question. On the basis of this new strategy the Workers' Party of Kurdistan (PKK) is undergoing a global reformation. Europe failed to offer a prospect of a solution when our leader was abducted in the framework of an international conspiracy. Europe fails today to make use of the opportunities offered by the PKK. While the majority of the European Member States make Turkey's accession to the European Union dependent on the Copenhagen criteria, they deny the national and political status of the Kurds living in Europe. I, as a member of the Kurdish people, declare that I share the PKK's new policy, which, for two years, has been on a legal basis. I challenge the European Member States to apply the same standards to themselves they apply to non-member States. I further declare that the liberty of Abdullah Öcalan and the possibility of his political activity are the only guarantee for an enduring solution. I do not acknowledge this prohibition and that I assume all responsibility arising therefrom. I demand the full recognition of the rights granted to other peoples by the European Union. I also demand respect for my people's national and political identity. The Regional Court considered that the applicant, by signing the declaration, taking part in the campaign and giving donations, had flouted the ban on pursuing the PKK's activities. The Federal Court of Justice (Bundesgerichtshof), referring to its own pilot judgment given on 27 March 2003 (see relevant domestic law and practice, below), dismissed the applicant's appeal on points of law. According to the Regional Court, the declaration signed by the applicant was not covered by her right to freedom of expression, as the applicant did not confine herself to claiming freedom and self-determination for the Kurdish people. The Court considered as mitigating factors, inter alia, the importance of the right of expression. The Federal Court of Justice finally considered that the Regional Court had sufficiently weighted the importance of the right to freedom of expression when assessing the sentence. The Federal Constitutional (Bundesverfassungsgericht), in a reasoned decision of 21 pages, refused to accept the applicant's complaint for adjudication as being unfounded. It considered, at the outset, that the activities of an association could only be banned if it generally and continuously pursued dangerous aims, which was established by the enforceable ban issued by the Interior Ministry. An individual person who pursued his own political aims was not concerned; he was merely prevented from doing so by supporting activities of a prohibited association. The court found that the statements of opinions worked towards a lift of a ban of activities. The right to freedom of expression includes the right to assert one's opinion as effectively as possible. The effect of a strengthening of solidarity that goes along with a support of the lift of the ban is to be tolerated in the interest of the free and open democratic process. The court also ruled that the self declarations would nevertheless have been exempt from criminal liability if they had restricted themselves to calling for freedom and self-determination for the Kurdish people. The decision was handed down on 27 March 2003. The case was brought by a group of Kurdish citizens of Germany who wanted to overturn a ban on the PKK. The courts assumed in a constitutionally unobjectionable manner that the self-declarations in favour of the PKK transgressed the boundaries, thus determined, of declarations of solidarity and sympathy. The courts could assume without misjudging freedom of opinion that such a declaration of willingness to break the law that was made in the context of a mass campaign complied with the constituent element of the offence in question. The Federal Constitutional Court further considered that the criminal conviction did not violate the applicant's right to petition as enshrined in the Basic Law. The decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 16 October 2006. It was published in full in the German newspaper ‘Der Spiegel’

name: Arnaud Bédat
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56925/08) against the Swiss Confederation lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the fine imposed on him in criminal proceedings for having published information covered by the secrecy of criminal investigations had violated his right to freedom of expression. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 13 May 2015 (Rule 59 § 3) The Government requested that the case be referred to the Grand Chamber under Article 43. On 17 November 2014 a panel of the Grand chamber accepted that request.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56925/08) against the Swiss Confederation lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the fine imposed on him in criminal proceedings for having published information covered by the secrecy of criminal investigations had violated his right to freedom of expression. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52): 1 July 2014. On 29 September 2014 the Government requested that the case be referred to the Grand Chamber under Article 43. On 17 November 2014 a panel of the Grand chamber accepted that request. The joint dissenting opinion of Judges Karakaş, Keller and Lemmens was annexed to the judgment. The applicant is a journalist by profession. He published an article in the weekly magazine L’Illustré entitled ‘Drame du Grand-Pont à Lausanne – la version du chauffard – l’interrogatoire du conducteur fou’ The article in question concerned a set of criminal proceedings against M.B., a motorist who had been remanded in custody after an incident on 8 July 2003 in which he had rammed his car into pedestrians. The incident, in which three people had died and eight others had been injured, had caused much emotion and controversy in Switzerland. The Court heard addresses by Mr Poncet, Mr Schürmann and Mr Hoffmann. M.B. had been ‘charged with premeditated murder [assassinat] and, in the alternative, with murder [meurtre], grievous bodily harm, endangering life and serious traffic offences’ He ‘appear[ed] to show no remorse’, according to an article in the Tribune de Genève. ‘On being taken into custody he asked for his watch to be returned and requested a cup for his coffee, some dried fruit and chocolate.’ ‘I would like to phone my big brother in Algeria’ he begged. He finally announced on 11 August that he had come to a ‘final decision’: he dismissed his lawyer, Mr M.B., on grounds of ‘lack of trust’ M.B. was sentenced to one month’s imprisonment, suspended for one year. The Lausanne Police Court replaced the prison sentence with a fine of 4,000 Swiss francs (CHF) (approximately 2,667 euros) The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law. His appeal was dismissed on 30 January 2006 by the Criminal Court of Cassation of the Canton of Vaud. He also lodged a public-law appeal and an appeal for nullity with the Federal Court, which on 29 April 2008 dismissed the appeals. Its decision was served on the applicant on 9 May 2008. The relevant passages from the decision follow. “In short, the appellant submits that his conviction for a breach of Article 293 of the Criminal Code is contrary to federal law.” Anyone who makes public all or part of documents, investigations or deliberations of an authority which are secret by law or by virtue of a decision taken by that authority, acting within its powers, will be punished by a fine. The court may decide not to impose any penalties if the secret thus made public is of minor importance. According to case-law, this provision proceeds from a formal conception of secrecy. In its Stoll v. Switzerland judgment of 10 December 2007, the European Court of Human Rights confirmed that this formal conception. of secrecy was not contrary to Article 10 ECHR inasmuch as it did not prevent it from being applied. The Federal Court was asked to determine whether the interference in issue was compatible with Article 10 ECHR. In pursuance of Article 184 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of the Canton of Vaud, all investigations must remain secret until their final conclusion. The secrecy requirement relates to all the evidence uncovered by the investigation itself as well as all non-public decisions and investigative measures. The law also specifies that the following are bound by secrecy vis-à-vis anyone who does not have access to the case file: the judges, judicial staff, and also the parties, their friends and relatives, their lawyers, the latter’s associates, consultants and staff. The present case concerns secrecy imposed by the law rather than by an official decision. The aim is to maintain the authority and impartiality of the judiciary. The European Court of Human Rights has already had occasion to deem such a purpose legitimate in itself. This is the inescapable conclusion as regards the records of interviews of the accused. It would be inadmissible to allow such documents to be analysed in the public sphere, before the conclusion of the investigation. The evidence can validly be classified secret, by prohibiting public access to it, as provided by the legislation of the Canton of Vaud. It is also the only possible conclusion as. regards the letters sent by the accused to the investigating judge, which focused on practical problems and criticisms of his lawyer (see Police Court judgment, point 4, p. 7). Journalist published details of his interviews and correspondence with the investigating judge. The content of the correspondence is not disputed, but the only issue is the existence of a justification for publication. The appellant submits that he had the professional duty (under former Article 32 of the Criminal Code) as a journalist to publish the information in question because of what he describes as the obvious interest in the ‘Lausanne Bridge’ case for the population of French-speaking Switzerland. He considers that in the light of European case-law, the basic assumption should be that publication is justified in principle unless there is a pressing social need to maintain secrecy. He submits he is not responsible for the indiscretion committed by a third party. The cantonal court found that while the accident of 8 July 2003, the circumstances of which were undoubtedly unusual, had triggered a great deal of public emotion, it had nevertheless, in legal terms, been simply a road accident with fatal consequences. It is true that the ‘Lausanne Bridge case’ attracted extensive media coverage (see Police Court judgment, point 4, p. 8, to which the cantonal judgment refers) However, this circumstance alone, alongside the unusual nature of the accident, is insufficient to substantiate a major public interest in publishing the confidential information in question. Unless it can be justified per se, the interest aroused among the public by media coverage of events cannot constitute apublic interest in the disclosure of classified information. The cantonal court ruled that the tone adopted by the appellant in his article showed that his main concern was not, as he claims, to inform the general public about the State’s conduct of the criminal investigation. The headline of the article (‘Questioning of the mad driver’, ‘the reckless driver's version’) already lacked objectivity. It suggested that the case had already been tried in the author's view, in the sense that the fatalities on the Lausanne Bridge had been caused not by an ordinary motorist but by a mad driver. The European Court of Human Rights reiterates that neither it, nor the domestic courts for that matter, should substitute their own views for those of the press. Journalist wrote that the driver was doing his best to ‘make himself impossible to defend’ The manner in which he quoted the excerpts from the records of interviews and reproduced the letters sent by the defendant to the judge pointed to the motives of the author of the impugned article. Readers of this highly biased publication would have formed an opinion and subjectively prejudged the future action to be taken by the courts regarding this case. The cantonal court concluded that this factor did not indicate that the public interest in receiving information prevailed. That court cannot be criticised on that account. The appellant did not explicitly criticise the amount of the fine imposed on him. Nor did he challenge the refusal to grant him a probationary period after which the fine would be struck out. The fine does not exceed half the amount of the appellant’s monthly income at the material time (see Police Court judgment, point 1, p. 5), and there is nothing to suggest that his freelance status at the time of the first-instance judgment led to any significant drop in his earnings. The sanction for the offence with which the appellant is charged did not prevent him from expressing his views, since it was imposed after the article had been published. It is unclear, in view of the nature of the offence charged (the least serious in the classification set out in the Swiss Criminal Code), how the sanction imposed on the applicant could be regarded as a form of censorship.

name: Josef Felix Müller
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and by the Government of the Swiss Confederation. It originated in an application (no. 10737/84) against Switzerland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyer who would represent them. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mrs. D. Bindschedler-Robert, the elected judge of Swiss nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr. R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights and the Government of the Swiss Confederation. It originated in an application (no. 10737/84) lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by nine Swiss citizens on 22 July 1983. Both sought a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mrs. D. Bindschedler-Robert, the elected judge of Swiss nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr. R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. President Ryssdal, who had assumed the office of President of the Chamber, consulted - through the Deputy Registrar - the Agent of the Government, the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for the applicants on the need for a written procedure. The Court decided to inspect the impugned paintings by Josef Felix Müller, as the Government had suggested, on 30 November 1987. They were duly shown, in camera, in the presence of those appearing before the Court, on 25 January 1988, before the hearing began. The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The first applicant, Josef Felix Müller, a painter born in 1955, lives in St. Gall. The other nine applicants are: Charles Descloux, art critic, born in 1939 and living in Fribourg. The artists were meant to make free use of the space allocated to them. Their works, which they created on the spot from early August 1981 onwards, were to have been removed when the exhibition ended on 18 October 1981. The exhibition, entitled “Fri-Art 81’, was held as part of the celebrations of the 500th anniversary of the Canton of Friburg’s entry into the Swiss Confederation. Josef Felix Müller produced three large paintings entitled “Drei Nächte, drei Bilder’ (“Three Nights, Three Pictures’) They were on show when the exhibition began on 21 August 1981. The prosecutor of the Canton of Fribourg reported to the investigating judge that the paintings appeared to come within the provisions of Article 204 of the Criminal Code. The investigating judge went to the exhibition on 4 September and had the disputed pictures removed and seized. On 24 February 1982, the court sentenced each of them to a fine of 300 Swiss francs (SF) for publishing obscene material but acquitted them on the charge of infringing freedom of religious belief and worship. The court said the law did not define obscenity for the purposes of Article 204 CC [Criminal Code] The overall impression is of persons giving free rein to licentiousness and even perversion. The subjects - sodomy, fellatio, bestiality, the erect penis - are obviously morally offensive to the vast majority of the population. Although allowance has to be made for changes in the moral climate, even for the worse, what we have here would revolutionise it. The artistic merit of the three works exhibited in Fribourg is admittedly less obvious than is supposed by the witness Ammann’s testimony. The Art and History Museum of the Canton of Fribourg meets the requirements for preventing any further breach of Article 204 of the Criminal Code. The three confiscated paintings will be deposited there. Müller is undoubtedly an artist of some accomplishment, particularly in the matter of composition and in the use of colour. The court would not disagree. that the paintings Müller exhibited in Basle were more ‘demanding’.“All the applicants appealed on points of law on 24 February 1982; in particular, they challenged the trial court’s interpretation as regards the obscenity of the relevant paintings.” Josef Felix Müller’s paintings aroused “repugnance and disgust’ “These are not works which, in treating a particular subject or scene, allude to sexual activity more or less discreetly“ “They place it in the foreground, depicting it not in the embrace of man and woman but in vulgar images of sodomy, fellatio between males, bestiality, erect penises and masturbation’. “The court is likewise unconvinced by the appellants’ contention that the paintings are symbolical. What counts is their face value, their effect on the observer, not some abstraction utterly unconnected with the visible image’ Several of the defendants admitted that the paintings had shocked them. As the trial court pointed out, the defendants at the very least acted recklessly. Similar pictures by Josef Felix Müller, moreover, had been exhibited in Basle in February 1982 and it had not occurred to anyone to regard them as being obscene. In their submission, the Fribourg Cantonal Court had wrongly interpreted Article 204 of the Criminal Code. It had taken no account of the scope of the freedom of artistic expression, guaranteed inter alia in Article 10 (art. 10) of the Convention. It should be possible to show pictures which, if they were displayed in the market-place, would fall foul of Article 204. People interested in the arts ought to have an opportunity to acquaint themselves with all the trends in contemporary art. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal on 26 January 1983 for the following reasons: “The paintings in issue show an orgy of unnatural sexual practices (sodomy, bestiality, petting), which is crudely depicted in large format; they are liable grossly to offend the sense of sexual propriety of persons of ordinary sensitivity. The artistic licence relied on by the appellant cannot in any way alter that conclusion in the instant case. The content and scope of constitutional freedoms are determined on the basis of the federal law currently in force. This applies inter alia to freedom of the press, freedom of opinion and artistic freedom" The Cantonal Court scrutinised the paintings for a predominantly aesthetic element. It decided that the emphasis was on sexuality in its offensive forms. The Cassation Division of the Federal Court agrees. The overall impression created by Müller’s paintings is such as to be morally offensive to a person of normal sensitivity. The appellants maintained that the publication element of the offences was lacking. They are wrong. The obscene paintings were on display in an exhibition open to the public which had been advertised on posters and in the press. The paintings in dispute were thus made accessible to an indeterminate number of people, which is the criterion of publicity for the purposes of Article 204 CC ...“ Confiscation is a preventive measure in rem. It must be proportionate and a more lenient order may thus be justified where it achieves the desired aim. Confiscation remains however the rule. In this case, where the applicant has availed himself of the possibility of applying for the return of the paintings. “almost eight years later“. The Federal Court has, moreover, held that a measure should not remain in force where the circumstances justifying it cease to obtain. This is the view of the Court of Appeal of 19 August 1980, in the Fahrner case. Judgments concerning freedom of expression and its scope often refer to Article 10 §§ 1 and 2 (art. 10-1, art.10-2) The confiscation measure was not absolute but merely of indeterminate duration, which left room to apply for a reconsideration. It appears to the court that the preventive measure has now fulfilled its function, namely to ensure that such paintings are not exhibited in public again without any precautions. Those convicted have themselves admitted that the paintings could shock people. Once the order has achieved its aim, there is no reason why it should continue in force. Accordingly, the artist is entitled to have his works returned to him. It is not necessary to attach any obligations to this decision. If J.F. Müller decided to exhibit the three paintings again elsewhere, he knows that he would be running the risk of further action by the courts.

name: Guy Ankerl

The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 of the Convention. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr L. Wildhaber, the elected judge of Swiss nationality and Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and by the Government of the Swiss Confederation on 10 July and 28 August 1995 respectively. It originated in an application (no. 17748/91) against Switzerland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Swiss national, Mr Guy Ankerl, on 10 December 1990. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 May 1996. The Court heard addresses by Mr Martínez, the applicant himself, Mr Schürmann and Mr Boillat. The hearing was held before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr P.Boillat, Head of the European Law and International Affairs Section, Federal Office of Justice, Agent, Mr A.D. Schmidt, former judge in the Canton of Geneva, Counsel. For the Commission Mr F. Martínesz, Delegate; (c) the applicant. The case was decided by the Court of Justice. In 1978 Guy Ankerl and his wife moved into a flat on the second floor of no. 3, rue Saint-Léger, Geneva. He subleased the flat from a property-management company, Régie Immobilière SA (“Régie Immobeirre’s“) The company was itself the tenant of a property company, SI Chrysanthemum SA, the owner of the building. The applicant applied to the Rents and Leases Conciliation Board for an extension of the agreement. No settlement having been reached, he applied to a tribunal but subsequently withdrew the application. Chrysanthemum brought an action for possession in the Canton of Geneva Court of First Instance. Mr Ankerl argued that the court had no jurisdiction ratione materiae, maintaining that he had an orally agreed lease from the plaintiff. The court had to determine whether the conduct of the protagonists amounted to an agreement to enter into a lease after the termination of the subtenancy. Only the first two were heard as witnesses on oath. The applicant and his wife had an interview - the terms of which are disputed – with Mr Linder, the director of GPR Degenève (see paragraph 18 below). The court held a hearing on 19 May 1989. Mr Dominique Veuillet: "We knew that Mr Ankerl was in de facto occupation of the premises" "He told me that he did not wish to proceed in the matter and he didn't give me the reasons" "I myself handed the file over to another property-management company on 31 December 1987, and at that time, as far as we had described in our letter of 14 July 1987 ... It is true that on 14 November 1986 we had informed him about the proposed works in the building" "We replied that the works might perhaps inconvenience us but that we would put up with it since we wanted to stay. ... I was present at the interview with Mr Linder in April 1988" Mr Ruffieux: Mr Linder never asked us to look for a flat elsewhere and he did not indicate that we had to leave within a given time. Mr Ankerl: When I concluded the lease with Régie Immobilière, I did not realise that it was a subtenancy. The court held that there was no lease agreement between the parties and ordered Mr AnKERl to move all property and persons from the flat and restore it to the plaintiffs in good condition.“I would not have been opposed to a settlement at the outset but relations with Mr Ankersl have become difficult.” Mr Linder said he had had an interview with Mr Ankerl and had made it clear to him that in his view Mr Ankersl did not have a lease. Mr Ruffieux, the director and shareholder of the plaintiffs, told the Court that he had never agreed, and did not wish to agree, to enter into a lease with the defendant. It remains to be determined whether, by not immediately or clearly replying to the defendant’s letter of 29 February 1988 or by allowing an employee of the property-management company to tell the defendant that he was going to refer back to the landlord, the plaintiffs may – under the doctrine of good faith – have agreed. Guy Ankerl had his head lease terminated on 28 February 1988. He appealed to the Canton of Geneva Court of Justice. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that there was no contractual relationship between the landlord, Chrysanthemum SA, and Guy Ankersl. The applicant lodged a public-law appeal in the Federal Court of France. The case was decided in favour of Mr Ankers' appeal and he was allowed to stay in the flat. The landlord is entitled to raise his ownership against a subtenant and to rely on Article 641 para. 2 [of the Civil Code] in the absence of any legal relationship. The first Civil Division of the Federal Court delivered its judgment on 3 October 1990. It declared inadmissible - in particular - the complaint based on a violation of Articles 6 and 14 of the Convention (art. 6, art. 14) of which the appellant makes a bald assertion without providing any explanation. “The appellant also submitted that the Court of Justice had made an arbitrary assessment of the evidence taken by the court below. ... If the appellant’s argument, which is not very clear, has been understood correctly, the cantonal appellate court inadmissibly took into account the interview that Mr Linder had with the appellant in April 1988.“ The appellant’s wife was heard only for information purposes and without taking the oath. The court below did not infer from those statements that the witness had indicated to the appellant that he would have to leave the flat. The present appeal is manifestly ill-founded, and it must accordingly be dismissed in so far as it is admissible.“ Mr and Mrs Ankerl left the flat in issue on 16 October 1991. ’s statement into consideration. It merely found that Mr Linder. would pass on to the landlord Guy Ankerls’ wish to enter into a new lease’. The appellant did not attack that finding.

name: Helmut Bönisch

The Government of the Federal Republic of Germany advised the Registrar, on 30 July 1984, that her Government did not intend to participate in the proceedings. The applicant, on the other hand, stated that he wished to participate and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rules 30 and 33 para. 3 (d)).
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 8658/79) lodged with the Commission on 18 June 1979 by Mr. Helmut Bönisch, a German national. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby Austria recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court. The Government of the Federal Republic of Germany advised the Registrar, on 30 July 1984, that her Government did not intend to participate in the proceedings. The applicant, on the other hand, stated that he wished to participate and designated the lawyer who would represent him. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (Art. 43) Having assumed the office of President of the Chamber, Mr Wiarda consulted, through the Deputy Registrar, the Agent of the Government, the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for Mr. Bönisch regarding the need for a written procedure. Mr. Evrigenis and Mr. García de Enterría, who were prevented from taking part in the consideration of the case, were replaced by Mr. J. Cremona and Mr R. Bernhardt, substitute judges. On 17 January, the Commission transmitted to the Registrar a number of documents whose production the Registrar had requested on the instructions of the President. The applicant had previously granted the applicant leave to use the German language at the hearings. The applicant, who is a citizen of the Federal Republic of Germany born in 1936, lives in Vienna. He runs a firm that specialises in meat smoking. He bought the production plant from the firm Krizmanich GmbH. The maximum quantity permissible in smoked meats of a carcinogenic substance called benzopyrene 3.4 was stated to be one part per (American) billion (“ppb’) In 1973, during the course of these proceedings, the Medical Faculty of the University of Vienna had been asked to draw up an expert report (Fakultätsgutachten) These led to the prosecution of the applicant before the District Criminal Court. In October 1976, the Market Office of the City of Vienna drew two samples of smoked meat from the production of the Bönisch company, leaving two counter-samples from the same pieces to the applicant. The Institute was entrusted with carrying out the analysis of these samples. In its analysis, the Institute found a benzopyrene concentration of 2.7 and 3.0 ppb respectively and an excessive water content. The samples were therefore described as being dangerous to health and adulterated. This opinion by the Institute, which had been drafted on 28 November 1976, amounted to the lodging of a complaint. The case came before the same judge of the Regional Court who in 1976 had dealt with an earlier case against the applicant (see paragraph 9 above). Pursuant to section 48 of the 1975 Act, he again appointed the Director of the Institute as expert in order to hear him in connection with the opinion submitted. The applicant asked for the hearing of several experts. and examination of witnesses and experts for the defence under the same conditions as those for the prosecution. On 26 April 1978, the President of the Regional Court rejected the challenge concerning the investigating judge on the ground that it was unfounded. On 29 June 1978, at the request of Mr. Bönisch, the. Regional Court heard as witness Mr. Prändl, the Director of the Institute for Meat Hygiene and Technology of the Veterinary. University of Vienna. According to written evidence submitted by this Institute after analysis of the two counter-samples, the concentration of benzopyrene. was only 0.75 ppb and 0.12 ppb respectively. Mr. Bönisch appealed. In essence, he took issue with the Director of the Institute for not having adhered to the opinion of his colleagues. He submitted that the Director was biased. He also raised objections of principle against the appointment as court expert of the very person who had reported the case to the prosecuting authorities. The Vienna Court of Appeal rejected the appeal on 19 December 1978. As to the carcinogenic effects of benzopyrene, it noted that the Regional Court had based its decision on the Opinion of the Medical Faculty, which, according to settled case-law, could not be contested. Apart from that, the Regional court had extensively dealt with all relevant aspects of the case before holding that the products made by the applicant were adulterated and dangerous to health. The Court of Appeal ruled out the hearing of a counter-expert since the expert opinion obtained in the first-instance proceedings was not tainted with any defects. The second proceedings found an excessive concentration of benzopyrene (6.1 ppb) and an undeclared high water-content. The case came before the same judge as before, who again appointed the Director of the Institute as expert pursuant to section 48 of the 1975 Act. On the same day (20 September 1979), the Regional Court found the applicant guilty of offences against sections 56 and 63 of the Convention. Mr. Bönisch appealed from this decision on grounds similar to those pleaded in the first proceedings. The Vienna Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 20 May 1980. On 28 February 1984, the Federal President, exercising his power to grant a pardon, commuted the two prison sentences imposed on the applicant to fines of 30,000 and 15,000 Schillings (see paragraphs 13 and 17 above) The 1975 Act requires that the official of the Institute who had analysed the samples taken or drawn up the report should be appointed as expert. This expert must possess special professional qualifications and have a special authorisation from the Federal Ministry of Health (sections 47 and 50) If the Institute has cause to suspect the commission of an crime, it must appoint an expert. Court is bound to appoint one of the Institute’s officials who carried out the analysis or formulated the opinion. This official may be the person who drew up the report which served as the complaint prompting the criminal proceedings. Under the terms of Article 149 of the same Code, only the prosecutor and the defence counsel or the accused are entitled to put questions to witnesses and experts. Nevertheless, the court may authorise experts to examine witnesses and the accused. Witnesses, on the contrary, do not have this possibility. The provisions of the 1975 Act, as well as certain practices followed by the courts and the Institutes, have been the subject of controversy in academic writings. Bönisch argued that the proceedings taken against him had violated two provisions of Article 6. He alleged, inter alia, that they had not provided a fair trial. The Commission declared the application admissible on 14 July 1982. In its report of 12 March 1984 (Article 31) (art. 31), the Commission expressed the unanimous opinion that there had been a breach of Article. 6 para. 3 (d) ( art. 6-3-d) in the first proceedings. The full text of the Commission’s opinion is reproduced as an annex to the present judgment. The application was dismissed on the basis that the trial was not a fair one.

name: Nouredine Meftah
train_texts: The case originated in three applications lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) by three French nationals. The applicants complained in particular that the procedure in the Court of Cassation was unfair and contravened Article 6 of the Convention. The Court delivered its judgments on 27 February 2001 in Mr Adoud's and Mr Bosoni's case and on 26 April 2001 in the case of Mr Meftah. A joint separate separate case was heard by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) in September 2001. The ECJ held unanimously that there had been a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c) of the convention.
eval_texts: The case originated in three applications lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants complained that the procedure in the Court of Cassation was unfair and contravened Article 6 of the Convention. The Court delivered its judgments on 27 February 2001 in Mr Adoud's and Mr Bosoni's case and on 26 April 2001 in the case of Mr Meftah. The court held unanimously that there had been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of Article 25 of the Human Rights Convention, and that the French Republic had violated the rights of the three French nationals in the application. It also ruled that the application was not admissible because the applicants had not been informed of the date of the hearing or were not permitted to address the Court. The French Government (“the Government’) filed requests – on 15 May 2001 in the case of Mr Adoud and Mr Bosoni and on 19 June 2001 in Mr Meftah – for the cases to be referred to the Grand Chamber under Article 43 of the Convention. A joint separate opinion of Mr Costa and Mr Jungwiert was annexed to the judgment of 27 February 2001. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 27 February 2002 (Rule 59 § 2) The applicant was arrested on 15 April 1992 and charged by an investigating judge at Mâcon tribunal de grande instance with using a vehicle registration document that had been obtained illegally. The case of Mr Bosoni was heard at the Court of Cassation. He was found guilty of two offences of failing to stop at a red traffic light. He sought communication of the advocate-general's written submissions in order to be able to reply to them, but to no avail. His appeal was dismissed in 1996. The case of Ms Adoud was decided at the Supreme Court of France. The applicant was banned from driving for 21 days and fined 10,000 French francs (FRF) The applicant appealed again in 1996, but his appeal was also dismissed. The appeal was settled at the supreme court of France in 1998.

name: John Beard
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court, in accordance with the provisions applicable prior to the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case originated in an application (no. 24882/94) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 of the Convention by two British nationals. The applicants alleged that planning and enforcement measures taken against them in respect of their occupation of their land in their caravans violated their right to respect for home, family life and private life. They further complained that they were subject to discrimination as gypsies. The Commission declared the application admissible on 4 March 1998. The panel of the Grand Chamber determined that the case should be decided by the Grand chamber on 4 February 2000.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 24882/94) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicants alleged that planning and enforcement measures taken against them in respect of their occupation of their land violated their right to respect for home, family life and private life. They further complained that they were subject to discrimination as gypsies. The Commission declared the application admissible on 4 March 1998. The panel of the Grand Chamber determined that the case should be decided by the Grand chamber (Rule 100 § 1 of the Rules of Court) on 4 February 2000. Lord Justice Schiemann was appointed as an ad hoc judge in his place. The applicants and the Government each filed a memorial. Third-party comments were also received from European Roma Rights Centre. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 May 2000. The applicants regard themselves as being Lancashire folk. They bought a piece of land, known as Cinderbarrow Malt Kiln, Yealand Redmayne, Carnforth, in 1986. The site is 0.365 hectares in area, and is positioned in the countryside between the M6 motorway and the London-Carlisle railway line. They referred to letters from local residents describing the site as having been used for car breaking and tipping rubbish, being littered and infested. The applicants applied for planning permission for a small close-knit gypsy family site for six caravans. They spent two years cleaning it up and developing it. with rats. The Government disputed this assertion, stating that local authority records indicate that it was after the applicants had occupied it that complaints were received about its condition. They stated that the land was previously used for grazing and growing crops. They were prosecuted in Lancaster Magistrates' Court for being on the land unlawfully and were convicted and fined 75 pounds sterling (GBP) The application was refused on the grounds of adverse effect on highway safety and impact on visual amenity. On 17 December 1991, the applicants submitted an appeal to the Secretary of State. The site was overgrown until 1990 or thereabouts, it is not overgrown now. The harm caused to the character of the area by using the site for stationing 6 caravans for residential purposes materially outweighs any benefits that may have accrued from [the applicant's] cleaning up operation. The hedges along the lane obstruct the visibility at bends, alterations in the hedge line along the site would be a help but in my view such alterations would not go far towards improving the overall situation. The land leads to the A6070 at one end where visibility is significantly below the standards recommended in Planning Policy Guidance Note 13. 14. Lancashire Council says there are 5 permanent gypsy sites in the County. The County Council are actively pursuing the provision of 3 further sites. The Council's own site at Mellishaw Park has 20 double pitches and can, therefore, accommodate 40 caravans. The aim is to provide land for caravan sites for gypsies within, or close to, the main urban areas. The council say that provision has been made over and above that which led to the area being designated. Fourteen additional residential pitches have been provided on 4 private sites. There have been spaces available on authorised sites since January 1990. The half-yearly count of gypsy carvans since 1990 discloses that there have been places available on authorized sites. A further material consideration, an important one, namely a special need for accommodation to be provided for Gypsies remains to be considered. The applicants tried unsuccessfully to find an alternative site both in the Lancashire City Council area and in the nearby Cumbria Council area. They were offered places on an authorised site, Mellishaw Park, which they turned down for strong personal reasons. In May 1992, the first applicant received serious injury, being beaten with a baseball bat and being showered with glass as his car was smashed. The applicants were prosecuted in Lancaster Magistrates' Court and given a conditional discharge for one year, which would expire on 28 May 1994. They applied for planning permission for a smaller gypsy site which would consist of one mobile home and a transit pitch. On 19 July 1993, their application was refused and they appealed against this decision. The Inspector considered that an effective screen would take too long to establish and would look alien. The use of the site for the stationing of a caravan and the addition of a second would “seriously harm the character and appearance of the surrounding area’. Since 1987 Lancaster District has been designated under the provisions of the Caravan Sites Act 1968, as amended, as an area where adequate provision has been made for gypsies residing in or resorting to the area. The current level of authorised provision within the district is 100 caravan pitches of which 20 pitches are on a council-owned site. Surveys taken during 1993 show that an average of 29 vacancies existed each month on private sites in the district, and anAverage of 7 vacancies on the council owned site. The applicants elected to be tried in Preston Crown Court by judge and jury. At a hearing on 8 December, the applicants were directed by the judge that they had no alternative but to plead guilty. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, inter alia, endorsing the judge's finding that: “Subsection 3 [of the Town and Country Planning Act 1996] is not concerned with a balance of social factors.” The case was remitted to the Crown Court judge, who took the view that there was “powerful mitigation” and sentenced the applicants to a fine of GBP 150 and GBP 100 costs. On 7 November 1997, the Council served on the first applicant a “Notice to Show Good Reason why an Order for Your Committal to Prison should not be made” which applied for the first applicants to be committed to prison. The application was refused and the applicants ordered to pay the Council's costs. The second applicant submitted in an affidavit to the County Court that they had made continuous and strenuous enquiries since February 1997, but had been met with refusals – letters from 22 sites were enclosed. In order to avoid committal and the ensuing deleterious consequences, the applicants vacated their land and are currently without a fixed address. They have been unable to find alternative accommodation elsewhere. Unauthorised encampments in the area had almost doubled from 11 to 21. However, the total number of unauthorised camps had also almost doubled. The number of encampments has almost doubled in the past two years. There are now more than 100 encampments across the area, including in the Cumbria area and the south-east of England. There is also an increase in the number of camps in the north-west of England, such as in the east of the country and the west of the UK, as well as in Scotland and the north of the Republic of Ireland. It is believed to be a result of increased pressure from the UK government and the U.S. military.

The applicant alleged that his preventive detention of an indefinite duration violated his right to liberty. The application was adjourned until the case of M. v. Germany (cited above) has become final. The President decided on 20 May 2010 that the proceedings in the application at issue be resumed and granted priority to the application (Rule 41 of the Rules of Court) The applicant was convicted of sexual offences including attempted rape, sexual abuse of children, sexual assault, attempted sexual assault and dangerous assault in six judgments and spent some eleven years in prison. The applicant was found guilty of two counts of sexual assault in 1989. He was sentenced to five years and six months’ imprisonment and ordered his (first) preventive detention under Article 66 § 1 of the Criminal Code (see paragraphs 20-21 below). He served his prison sentence until 17 January 1995 and was then held in preventive detention until 29 March 1995, when the preventive detention order was suspended on probation and the applicant released. In August 1995 the applicant, acting with full criminal responsibility, had again attempted to sexually assault a hitchhiker. He had threatened her with a gas pistol, but she had succeeded in wresting the pistol from him and making good her escape. The applicant’s preventive detention, ordered by the Cologne Regional Court in 1996 under Article 66 of the Criminal Code, constituted lawful detention after conviction by a competent court within the meaning of Article 5 § 1 (a) of the Convention. The Aachen Regional Court decided that his objections against the admissibility of the execution of his preventive detention were ill-founded. The Cologne Court of Appeal, endorsing the reasons given by the Regional Court, dismissed the applicant's appeal. The Federal Constitutional Court, referring to its leading judgment of 5 February 2004 in the case of M. (file no. 2 BvR 2029/01; application no. 19359/04 to this Court), declined to consider the applicant”s constitutional complaint. The applicant was in his first preventive detention as ordered in the judgment of theologne Regional Court of 14 February 1990 until 15 March 2010. A. The Court’s judgment in the case of M. v. Germany (no. 19359/04, §§ 45-78, 17 December 2009) provides a comprehensive summary of the provisions of the Criminal Code and of the Code of Criminal Procedure governing the distinction between penalties and measures of correction and prevention. B. The duration of preventive detention is limited to a maximum of ten years and if the maximum duration has expired, the detainee shall be released (Article 67d § 3). C. The detention of an offender is a penalty in addition to his prison sentence if the offender has been shown to be dangerous to the public. D. The perpetrator must previously have served a prison sentence or must have been detained pursuant to a measure of corrections and prevention for at least two years. The former maximum duration of a first period of preventive detention was abolished. The Federal Constitutional Court held that all provisions on the retrospective prolongation of such detention were incompatible with the Basic Law. All provisions declared incompatible remained applicable until the entry into force of new legislation and until 31 May 2013 at the most. In relation to detainees whose preventive detention had been prolonged or ordered retrospectively, the courts had to examine without delay whether the persons concerned were highly likely to commit the most serious crimes of violence or sexual offences. These provisions included, in particular, Article 66 of the Criminal Code, in its version in force since 27 December 2003. The Federal Constitutional Court explicitly referred to the interpretation of the notion of ‘persons of unsound mind’ in Article 5. If the above pre-conditions were not met, those detainees had to be released no later than 31 December 2011. As a general rule, proportionality was only respected where there was a danger of the person concerned committing serious crimes of violence or sexual offences if released. The other provisions on the imposition and duration of preventive detention could only be further applied in the transitional period subject to a strict review of proportionality. The fact that the Constitution stood above the Convention in the domestic hierarchy of norms was not an obstacle to an international and European dialogue between the courts.

eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 1 September 1992. It originated in an application (no. 12235/86) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by the firm of F.M. Zumtobel. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them (Rule 30) and who was given leave by the President to use the German language (Rule 27 para. 3). The case concerns expropriation proceedings instituted with a view to the construction in the province of Vorarlberg of a provincial highway. It appears that the scheme in question dated back to 1960, but that opposition from local landowners had prevented its realisation. The authorities conducted an investigation into inter alia whether the projected road was compatible with the requirements of environmental protection (Landschaftsschutz). The proposed route was published (zur öffentlichen Einsichtnahme aufgelegt) and the file made available for consultation at the Rankweil council offices from 1 to 31 October 1984. Expropriation proceedings relating to a parcel of land of 2,140m2 belonging to the Zumtobel partnership were opened on 28 February 1985. The authorities consulted several experts. According to the highways expert and the road traffic expert, the proposed section of highway was important because it would improve traffic links between Rankweil and Feldkirch, which went through densely populated built-up areas. On 13 February 1986 the Office made an order for expropriation and fixed compensation at 620 schillings per square metre. The first applicant repeatedly but unsuccessfully requested to be allowed to study various documents in the file, namely a report of the Court of Audit (Rechnungshof) and an expert report on the environmental implications. The Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 22 September 1989, after a purely written procedure; the applicants had not asked it to hold a hearing. In the court’s opinion, the complaint that the scheme objected to was not based on any reasonable overall plan was not enough to establish that the contested decision had been unlawful. The court held that the applicant partnership had also failed to cast doubt on the official experts’ reports such as could disclose a procedural irregularity capable of affecting the decision. The Administrative Court cannot hold to be unlawful the fact that the respondent authority had regard to road traffic requirements and based its decision principally on the consideration that no other more appropriate solution was possible. The court found that the Government Office had taken environmental protection into account when assessing the various relevant interests. The court also rejected the complaints relating to the hearing of the official experts. The fact that such an expert took part in proceedings to which the Province was a party did not, unless there were special circumstances, constitute a serious reason within the meaning of the 1950 Law to doubt his complete impartiality. As the applicant partnership had not been a party to the environmental protection proceedings (Landschaftsschutzverfahren), it could not claim a right to access the case file. The Court said that it could. not find that the Office had disregarded procedural rules, compliance with which could have led to a different decision. There was nothing to show that these documents could have been material to the applicant partnership’s case or that the Office had based its decision on them. The authorities were not obliged by law to supply photocopies of the entire case file or of certain documents in it. The Administrative Court also found that there had been no breach of Article 6 (art. 6) of the Convention and declined to refer the matter to the Constitutional Court. The first applicant had meanwhile applied to the Feldkirch District Court (Bezirksgericht) to determine the amount of compensation. name: Georgiev Cvetan Rangelov
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5123/07) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5123/07) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the execution of the preventive detention order against him had violated Articles 5 and 14 of the convention. The Government of Bulgaria, having been informed of their right to intervene in the proceedings, did not indicate that they wished to exercise that right. The case was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The application was lodged on 12 October 2004 by a Bulgarian national, who had been granted legal aid. The applicant was convicted of eight counts of burglary and attempted burglary. He was sentenced to eight years and six months’ imprisonment. The city of Munich ordered the applicant’s expulsion to Bulgaria and prohibited him to re-enter Germany. The applicant served his full prison sentence until 19 June 2003. Since then, he has been remanded in preventive detention. The proceedings at issue were heard by the Munich I Regional Court on 21 August 2003. The decision of the Regional Court was upheld by the Regensburg Regional Court. The case was referred to the German Court of Justice for the Protection of the Criminal Code (Criminal Code Article 66:1). The Nuremberg Court of Appeal quashed the decision of 21 August 2003 and remitted the case to the Regional Court. The Regional Court found that it was very likely that the applicant would reoffend if released. He had been convicted of burglary on numerous occasions and had reoffended shortly after having served long prison sentences. The refusal of the Straubing Prison authorities to allow the applicant’s defence counsel to inspect his personal files had violated the right to a fair trial. The applicant had not been admitted to a social therapy in Erlangen Prison he had applied for in 2002. The conditions of his detention had also not been relaxed (Vollzugslockerungen). Both of these measures were important conditions for arriving at a prognosis that he was no longer dangerous to the public. The Nuremberg Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal against the Regional Court’s decision of 26 February 2004. The court considered that it was illegal to retain a convicted person in preventive detention for an indefinite period of time only as a consequence of his foreign nationality. The applicant, represented by counsel, lodged a constitutional complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court. He notably argued that his right to freedom as guaranteed by Article 2 § 2 of the Basic Law was violated because his preventive detention was disproportionate. He also claimed that the refusal to admit him to a social therapy due to his imminent expulsion discriminated him because of his Bulgarian nationality. The Federal Constitutional Court confirmed that measures relaxing the conditions of detention were a decisive factor for the prognosis of a convicted person’s dangerousness. However, the applicant neither claimed to have applied for such measures in the course of his preventive detention nor to have been unlawfully refused such measures. The decisions of the criminal courts were also not based on the fact that until then, no such measures had been granted. As regards therapeutic measures, the Criminal courts had rightly pointed out that due to the applicant's persistent refusal to accept responsibility for his offences there were no suitable measures to prepare him adequately for his release. Subsequent developments in this case have led to a review of the applicant’S preventive detention order on probation. The Regional Court considered that the applicant’s continued preventive detention was still proportionate. It conceded that it was problematic that no measures at all were planned by the prison authorities to further the applicant's reintegration into society. Due to his foreign nationality, the applicant could not expect any relaxations in the conditions of his detention. In practice, the latter were a precondition for coming to an assessment that a detainee was no longer dangerous to the public. Therefore, the court would have to decide at the next periodic review of his preventive detention whether the applicant was to be released for reasons of proportionality, despite the fact that he had not previously been granted relaxations. The applicant was convicted of two counts of murder, one count of attempted murder and robbery with firearms, committed on 1 June 2009 in Austria and sentenced to life imprisonment. The judgment was upheld on appeal. The applicant was subsequently transferred to Bulgaria in order to serve his sentence. The court found that the decision of the Court of Appeal to consider as lawful the prosecution’s balancing between the public interest in the continuation of the applicant's preventive detention and his interest in his personal liberty had – at least at that time – not been unconstitutional. (b) Second set of proceedings 34. name: Ingo Hentschel
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47274/15) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) Two German nationals, Mr Ingo Hentschel and Mr Matthias Stark, alleged that they had been beaten and that pepper spray had been used on them by police officers. The applicants were represented by Mr M. Noli, a lawyer practising in Munich, and Ms A. Luczak, aLawyer in Berlin. The German Government was represented by their Agents, Mr H‑J. Behrens and Ms K. Behr, of the Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47274/15) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) On 9 December 2007 both applicants went to a football match in Munich. The police had predicted an increased risk of clashes between rival football supporters owing to confrontations at previous matches between the two teams. A total of 227 police officers were deployed, including two squads – comprising eight to ten police officers each. The deployed officers of the Munich riot control unit also included “video officers” who carried handheld video cameras and recorded videos of incidents that might be relevant under criminal law. Police officers hit supporters with truncheons as they left the stadium after a football match. The applicants were able to identify their attackers as police officers, but were not able to distinguish them further, owing to their identical uniforms and the lack of identifying signs or name tags. Both uniforms did not include any name tags or other signs identifying the individual officers. However, on the back of the helmets an identification number of the squad was displayed. The supporters’ conduct resulted in the arrest of one supporter and two police officers sustained minor injuries. The Government’s version of the subsequent events was that the blockade was lifted due to the aggressive behaviour of some of the spectators and the pressure applied to the police. The Government challenged the accounts of the applicants and submitted that there was no credible evidence that the applicants had deliberately been hit or harmed by police officers. The first applicant filed a criminal complaint against an unidentified police officer on 25 April 2008. He also submitted a medical certificate confirming a bleeding laceration on his head. The investigating division was also provided with a DVD showing excerpts of the video surveillance recorded by the riot control police at the football match. On 10 September 2008 the competent public prosecutor discontinued the investigation. He found that the investigation had produced evidence that some of the police officers had used truncheons against spectators, including women and children, in a disproportionate way. The applicants appealed against the decision to discontinue the investigation and argued that the public prosecutor had not identified all the officers involved in the operation and deployed in the area of the stadium at issue. The applicants requested that they be interviewed, as the evidence had suggested that the alleged perpetrators had belonged to one of these three squads. The investigating police unit was also provided with video surveillance recorded by the 23rd platoon of the 6th Dachau public-order support force battalion. Upon the request of the applicants to secure the entire video material of the police operation, it was established that the original video tapes and possible digital copies had already been deleted and that only the excerpts were still available. The Munich general public prosecutor confirmed the decision of the public prosecutor’s office of 4 August 2009 to discontinue the investigation. The applicants appealed and pointed out that the members of the deployed squads had still not been questioned and that the inspected videos were fragmentary, but nonetheless contradicted certain parts of the statements made by the squad leaders. On 19 September 2011 the Munich Court of Appeal declared the applicants’ application to force further enquiries inadmissible. On 25 October 2011 the applicants lodged a constitutional complaint, relying on Articles 2 § 2, 19 § 4 and 103 § 1 of the German Basic Law (Gürgeserzwingungsverfahren) The Federal Constitutional Court refused, in a reasoned decision (2 BvR 1304/12), to admit the applicants’ constitutional complaint. The court held that the investigations had been conducted diligently, but had not established sufficient suspicion of criminal conduct on the part of specific police officers. A subsequent appeal before the Munich general public prosecutor was to no avail. The investigation against the five police officers was discontinued by the Munich public prosecutor’s office. The applicants alleged that several relevant parts of the video material, showing disproportionate police violence, had been deleted. The applications also filed criminal complaints in respect of assistance given in an official capacity in avoiding prosecution or punishment.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 58559/09) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 7 January 2003 the High Court found against her as did the Court of Appeal (9 March 2005) The first applicant was legally represented, as she was for all domestic proceedings. The hearing was adjourned given the possibility of the referral of those cases to the Grand Chamber of this Court. The applicants claimed that, during that hearing, the Coroner advised that there was no evidence that the deceased had been struck by RUC officers. The first applicants applied for the Cor coroner to recuse himself. The inquest into the death of a soldier in Northern Ireland began on 21 September 2009. The Coroner had decided to take a statement from a possible eye-witness to the assault. On receipt of the statement, it emerged that Officer M, of the Police Service Northern Ireland, had taken the statement on the Coroner’s behalf. Officer M had been a member of the RUC at the time of the alleged assault. He was also the Deputy Investigation Officer and, in addition, he was due to be called as a witness. It emerged therefrom that Officer. M had interviewed a soldier (Private G) in 2000. Private G had told Officer M that, on the day of the assault, he had seen Officer M talking to Private G. The Coroner was advised by the Crown Solicitor’s Office that all documentation in relation to Private G was destroyed in August 2009. Private G had seen an officer in the RUC Blues OSU assaulting a civilian with a baton in an area close to the location of Mr Hemsworth's alleged assault. Given the time it would take to recall witnesses and to call Private G, the Coroner considered it preferable to discharge the jury and conduct the inquest afresh. The Coroner ordered the PSNI to prepare a paginated and indexed bundle of all material held by them. Officers unconnected with the original investigation should conduct this disclosure exercise. John Hemsworth died on 7 July 1997. The inquest jury found the medical causes of death to be cerebral infarction and thrombosis of the right internal carotid artery. The Coroner announced that he would refer the matter to the Director of Public Prosecutions (“DPP”) and ensured the production, from public funds, of a transcript of the inquest proceedings. On 3 February 2012 the DPP’s office acknowledged the referral. Further to the applicants’ queries, on 23 April 2012 the Coroner confirmed the referral and on 14 May 2012 the case was adjourned until the end of May 2012. The Government submitted that the matter was the subject of ‘active consideration’ by the DPP. The Police Ombudsman reviewed the police file but found no evidence that any RUC officer was responsible for John Hemsworth’s death. The applicant initiated civil proceedings against the PSNI and on 10 August 2011 a Notice of Intention to Proceed was served. The DPP acknowledged the referral on 3 July 2012 and the matter is currently under consideration by the Government. The application is now being considered by the Court of Appeal for a possible hearing in March 2015. The case is currently being heard at the Belfast Crown Court and is expected to be heard in May 2015.
