eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 28 January 1986. It originated in an application (no. 9912/82) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of that State, Mr. Uli Lutz, on 14 June 1982. The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 2 (Art. 6-2) The President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the Englert and Nölkenbockhoff cases should be considered by the same Chamber. The Court held a preparatory meeting immediately beforehand. The Government’s memorial was lodged with the registry on 13 November 1986. The applicant informed the Registrar on the same day that he would not be filing a memorial. On 29 November, the Chamber decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. The Court heard addresses by Mrs. Maier for the Government, by Mr. Weitzel for the Commission and by. Mr. Wingerter and Mr. Hohbach for the applicant, as well as their replies to its questions. The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. On 15 December, the Secretary to the Commission told the Registrar that the Delegate would submit his observations at the hearing. Uli Lutz, a German national born in 1959, lives in Heilbronn-Horkheim. On 10 October 1980, he was riding a motor cycle and was involved in a road accident. According to the police report (Verkehrs-Ordnungswidrigkeiten-Anzeige), he had attempted to overtake a car, although the traffic situation was unclear. The result had been a collision which caused damage to both vehicles. On 9 December 1980, on the basis of thePolice report, the HeilBronn Police Authority imposed on Mr. Lutz a fine (Geldbusse) of DM 125, to which were added costs of DM 14. The decision was based on section 24 of the Road Traffic Act (Strassenverkehrsgesetz - see paragraph 38 below) The driver of the car was likewise fined for a “regulatory offence’ (Ordnungswidrigkeit) on 9 December 1980. Two days later, Mr. Lutz, who was represented by Mr. Wingerter, lodged an objection (Einspruch) against the decision. The appropriate authority in Heilbronn forwarded the objection to the public prosecutor’s office on 23 January 1981. On 24 July 1981, the court informed the applicant that it intended to discontinue the proceedings as they were time-barred. The costs of the proceedings shall be borne by the Treasury. The defendant shall bear his own necessary costs and expenses. The decision on costs is based on Article 467 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, taken together with section 46 of the Act on ‘regulatory offences’. As the file stands, the defendant would most probably have been convicted of an offence against the Road Traffic Regulations (Nach Lage der Akten wäre der Betroffene mit hoher Wahrscheinlichkeit wegen eines Verstosses gegen die StVO verurteilt worden). That being so, it would be unjust (unbillig) to award his necessary costs. Mr. Lutz had himself admitted to the police that he was not expecting the car which was moving out to the left onto the road in front of him to make a U-turn. The court held that in such circumstances it would have been unjust to award the defendant’s necessary costs and expenses against the Treasury. Mr Lutz then applied to the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) but on 2 February 1982 a bench of three judges refused to entertain the application, holding that it had insufficient prospects of success. In the Constitutional Court’S view, the decisions of the District Court and the Regional Court did not offend the presumption of innocence. The presumption of innocence precluded taking measures against a defendant (Beschuldigter) that amounted in effect to a penalty (Strafe) This rule was not infringed where the necessary costs and expenses of a party who had been proceeded against in respect of a ‘regulatory offence’ were not awarded against the Treasury in the event of the proceedings being discontinued. “The decision not to order the Treasury to pay the costs and. expenses of the party concerned obviously cannot be regarded as a punishment (Bestrafung) or even be equated with. such,” said the court in a judgment.
