eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4619/12) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that the ban on wearing in public places clothing designed to conceal the face deprived her of the possibility of wearing the full-face veil. The Government were given notice of the above-mentioned complaints and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal on 9 July 2015, and the verdict was delivered on 9 August 2015. The judge ruled in favour of the applicant. Wearing a mask is forbidden at all times, at any public meeting and in all public places and in public thoroughfares. A helmet, balaclava or other headgear may be worn where authorised by the legislation on the safety of workers or other legislation. The three municipalities submitted that the impugned provision sought to guarantee public safety and not to regulate or restrict the exercise of any form of worship. The Conseil d’État, refusing to follow the judgment no. 213.849 of 15 June 2011, refused to follow this decision. The ban was upheld by the Court of Appeal. The judgment was served on the applicant on 23 June 2011. the opinion of the auditeur, dismissed the application for annulment of the provision. The applicant appealed against the judgment. He was denied appeal. The appeal was dismissed. The judge said that the judgment was correct and that the application had been dismissed. He added that the judge was also of the opinion that the ruling was not in breach of the law. The judgement was set aside on 22 June 2011 and the appeal was rejected on 24 June 2011, and the case was dismissed on 1 July 2011. The case was settled in the Supreme Court of Ireland on 15 July 2011, with the judgment delivered by the judge on 22 August 2011. It was the first time that the case had been heard by the High Court.

name: Herbert Wille
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court, as established under former Article 19 of the Convention, by the European Commission of Human Rights and by the Liechtenstein Government. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 10 and 13. The applicant designated the lawyers who would represent him (Rule 36). The lawyers were given leave by the President of the Grand Chamber, Mrs Palm, to use the German language (Rule 34):. The Grand Chamber included ex officio Mr L. Ferrari Bravo, Mr I. Cabral Barreto, Mr W. Fuhrmann, Mrs N. Vajic, Mr J. Hedigan, Mrs W. Thomassen, Mrs M. Tsatsa-Nikolovska, Mr T. Pantîru, Mr E. Levits and Mr K. Traja.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court, as established under former Article 19 of the Convention, by the European Commission of Human Rights and by the Liechtenstein Government. It originated in an application (no. 28396/95) against the Principality of Liech Tenstein lodged with the Commission. The Grand Chamber included ex officio the judge elected in respect of Lie Chtenstein and the Vice-Presidents of the Court. The applicant designated the lawyers who would represent him (Rule 36). The lawyers were given leave by the President of the Grand Chamber, Mrs Palm, to use the German language (Rule 34 § 34). In 1992 a controversy arose between His Serene Highness Prince Hans-Adam II of Liechtenstein (“the Prince’s”) and the government on political competences. The matter was settled on the basis of a common declaration by the Prince, the Diet (Landtag) and government. The applicant had not stood for re-election in May 1993, and he was appointed President of the Liech tenstein Administrative Court (Verwaltungsbeschwerdeinstanz) in December 1993 for a fixed term of office (see paragraph 26 below) In February 1995, in the context of a series of lectures on questions of constitutional jurisdiction and fundamental rights, the applicant gave a public lecture. On 27 February 1995 the Prince addressed a letter to the applicant concerning the above lecture, as summarised in the article published in the Liechtensteiner Volksblatt. The applicant expressed the view that the Constitutional Court was competent to decide on the “interpretation of the Constitution in case of disagreement between the Prince (government) and the Diet”. The letter, written on heraldic letter paper, read as follows: “Vaduz, I was astonished to read the report in the 17 February issue of the. ‘Nature and Functions of the Lie chtenstein Constitutional Court’. I assume that the statements you made on the Court's areas of responsibility have been correctly reproduced in this report’ Prince Hans-Adam II of Liechtenstein wrote to Herbert Wille saying he had lost his confidence in the government. Wille was appointed President of the Administrative Court on the Diet’s recommendation. He said the court has no competence to decide as a court of interpretation in the event of a disagreement between the Prince and the people (the Diet) In my eyes your attitude, Dr Wille, makes you unsuitable for public office. I do not intend to get involved in a long public or private debate with you, but I should like to inform you in good time that I shall not appoint you again to a public office should you be proposed by the Diet or any other body. Ihre Aussagen über die Zuständigkeitsbereiche des Staatsgerichtshofes in diesem Bericht korrekt wiedergegeben wurden. Sie werden sich bestimmt noch an die Auseinandersetzung zwischen der Regierung and mir vor dem 28. Oktober 1992 erinnern. Sie haben dazumal sinngemäss geantwortet, dass Sie mit diesen Teilen der Verfassung sowieso nicht einverstanden seien. "Ich habe diese unentschuldbare Haltung gegenüber unserer Verfassung eingesehen", sagt Dr. Wille. "Ich hoffe, dass sie mein Vertrauen verloren hat. Ich habe nicht die Absicht, mich mit Ihnen öffentlich üffentliches Amt. Leider muss ich aufgrund des Berichtes im Liechtensteiner Volksblatt nun feststellen, das Sie sich nach wie vor nicht an die Verfasung gebunden fühlen" "Ihre Auffassungen vertreten, die eindeutig geggen Sinn und Wortlaut der VerfAssung verstossen,    erzielt wurde", says Dr.Wille. Hans-Adam II. Fürst von Liechtenstein’s office as President of the Administrative Court was called into question. The applicant concluded that the declaration made by the Prince that he did not intend to appoint the applicant to a public office, amounted to an interference with his rights to freedom of opinion and to thought. He denied having ever made a statement to the effect that he. did not consider himself bound by the Constitution or parts thereof. He further explained his research on the competences of the Constitutional Court in constitutional matters. According to him, the expression of an opinion not shared by the. Prince could not be regarded as a failure to comply with the Constitution. The Prince had known Mr Wille for many years and considered it appropriate to state the reasons for his decision regarding him. The decision no longer to appoint him to the office of President of one of the highest courts, on account of his attitude in the past as well as the opinions expressed by him, did not amount to an interference with his rights to freedom of expression and to thought. All citizens were free to propose and to plead for amendments to constitutional or other legal provisions. However, MrWille, during his term of office as a member of the government and in his lecture, had not availed himself of such constitutional and democratic means, but had simply ignored those parts of the Constitution with which he disagreed. Confusing the terms “Government” and “Diet” with “Prince” or “people” would undermine the rule of law. In a democratic State based on the rule of law, a distinction had to be drawn between freedom of expression and the means used by an individual for imposing his views in such a society. The Prince considered that Mr Wille, having regard to his education and professional experience, knew that the terms ‘people’ (“Volk”), “Diet” (‘Landtag’) and “Prince” were clearly defined in the Constitution. The applicant’s contention that these terms were interchangeable would jeopardise the Constitution and the constitutional State as a whole, the Prince said. The applicant is currently employed as a researcher by the Liechtenstein-Institut. The Prince refused to accept the proposed appointment of Mr Wille as President of the Administrative Court. The applicant is now an associate judge of the Court. He is still employed by the Institute. The application was rejected by the Diet on 14 April 1997. It was proposed that the applicant be appointed again as President, but the Prince rejected the proposal. The appointment was rejected again on 19 April 1997, and the application was not accepted again. The position of President of Administrative Court is currently vacant. The current position is that of associate judge at the Court of Appeal.

name: Muñoz Díaz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49151/07) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mrs María Luisa Muñoz Díaz complained about a refusal to grant her a survivor’s pension, following the death of M.D., also a Rom of Spanish nationality, on the sole ground that they were not a married couple under Spanish law. The Court heard addresses by Mr Blasco Lozano, Ms Queipo de Llano López‑Cózar and Mr S. Sánchez Lorente.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, a Rom of Spanish nationality, complained about a refusal to grant her a survivor’s pension, following the death of her husband. She alleged that there had been a violation of Article 14 of the. Convention taken in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 12 of. the Convention. The Court heard addresses by Mr Blasco Lozano, Ms Queipo de Llano López-Cózar and Mr S. Sánchez Lorente. The couple were married according to their community’s own rites. The marriage was solemnised in accordance with Roma customs and cultural traditions. On 14 October 1986 the applicant and her family were granted first-category large-family status. The couple had six children, who were registered in the family record book issued to the couple by the Spanish civil registration authorities (Registro civil) on 11 August 1983. On 24 December 2000 the applicant's husband died. He was a builder and at the time of his death had been working and paying social security contributions for nineteen years, three months and eight days, supporting his wife (registered as such) and his six children as his dependants. He had been issued with a social security benefit card, stamped by Agency no. 7 of Madrid.  applicant filed a claim with the Labour Court. In a judgment dated 30 May 2002 of Labour Court no. 12 of Madrid, she was granted an entitlement to receive a survivor’s pension with a base rate of 903.29 euros per month, her Roma marriage thus being recognised as having civil effects. Roma marriages are not registered in the Civil Register because they have not been regarded by the State as a feature of the ethnic culture which has existed in our country for centuries. ... Directive 2000/43/EC implementing the principle of equal treatment between persons irrespective of racial or ethnic origin is applicable to the present case, where the denied benefit derives from the employment relationship of the insured person who died from natural causes while he was still working. The INSS appealed. In a judgment of 7 November 2002, the Madrid Higher Court of Justice quashed the impugned judgment. “... A distinction must be made between the legislation that is in force and is applicable at all times and what may be considered desirable by a given sector of society. ... A marriage solemnised solely and exclusively according to Roma rites is not covered by any of the above-mentioned cases, as even though an ethnic group is concerned, the norms or formalities of that group do not produce any legal effect outside its own environment and are not enshrined in the law’s law.” Roma marriage does not correspond, in the current framework of our law, to the nature of the marriages referred to above. Section 174 of the LGSS requires that a person be the spouse of the deceased in order to benefit from the survivor’s pension, and the notion of spouse has been interpreted strictly according to an established constitutional and ordinary case-law. A couple living together de facto as husband and wife and many others who, in reality, are not married under the applicable law, are excluded from the benefit of that pension. ... A marriage can only be one that is solemnised civilly or religiously according to the terms set out above. ... The morality of the rite or its conformity with public order are not called into question. The court ruled that 'discrimination by absence of differentiation' did not arise from Article 14 of the Spanish Constitution. The court also rejected the idea that the recognition of the civil effects of a marital relationship created by certain specific religious rites, but not one that has been solemnised according to Roma rites and customs, may entail directly or indirectly, the alleged ethnic discrimination. The law establishes a general possibility – neutral from a racial and ethnic point of view – of marrying in the civil form, and that the legislature, the court said. in the case of the surviving spouse, did not prohibit such an extension of the survivor’s pension to other forms of partnership. Dissenting opinion appended to judgment no. 199/2004 found a violation of the right to equality. It referred to a case concerning the widower of a civil servant. The parties had expressly refused such registration of their marital relationship which had been solemnised in a religious form. The case-law of the Constitutional Court did not take into account the rites, practices or customs of a specific ethnic group, the dissenting judge said. The guarantee of equality required measures of positive discrimination in favour of the underprivileged minority, he added. The dissenting judge concluded as follows: “It is disproportionate for the Spanish State, which took into consideration the applicant and her Roma family by issuing them with a family record book, granting them large-family status, affording health-care assistance to her and her six children and collecting the corresponding contributions from her Roma husband for nineteen years, three months and eight days, now to refuse to recognise them’ On 3 December 2008, under the third amendment of Law no. 40/2007 of 4 December 2007 pertaining to certain social security measures, the applicant was granted a survivor’s pension with effect from 1 January 2007, as the partner of M.D. the Roma marriage. The relevant provisions of the Spanish Constitution are as follows: Article 14 “Spaniards shall be equal before the law; they may not be discriminated against in any way on account of birth, race, sex, religion, opinion or any other condition or personal or social circumstance” Article 16 “1. Freedom of ideas, religion and worship shall be guaranteed to individuals and communities without any restrictions on its expression.” The Spanish Civil Code provides for the right to marry in Spain and abroad. A surviving spouse is entitled to a survivor’s pension in the event of nullity of a marriage. This entitlement is in proportion to the period of his or her cohabitation with the insured person, provided he or she has not acted in bad faith and has not remarried. The law also allows the head of the household, his spouse and four or more children to be classified as a large family. For more information on the law, go to: www.cnn.com/2013/07/26/politics/spanish-marriage-law/index.html. Law no. 40/2007 of 4 December 2007 on social security measures, amending the LGSS, reads as follows: Third transitional amendment “Exceptionally, a survivor’s pension shall be granted where the death of the insured person occurred before the entry into force of the present Act’’ The recognition of the pension entitlement will take effect from 1 January 2007, subject to the fulfilment of all the conditions provided for in the present provision. Marriages solemnised according to the rites of those religious denominations are therefore recognised by the Government. Married couples can claim a survivor's pension if they live together as unmarried partners for at least six years prior to the death. The Council of Europe’s Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities, opened for signature on 1 February 1995, contains the following provisions in particular. Article 1 “The protection of national minorities and of the rights and freedoms of persons belonging to those minorities forms an integral part of the international protection of human rights, and as such falls within the scope of international cooperation” Article 5 “1. The Parties undertake to promote the conditions necessary to maintain and develop their culture, and to preserve the essential elements of their identity, namely their religion, language, traditions and cultural heritage.” The measures adopted in accordance with paragraph 2 shall not be considered to be an act of discrimination. Spain signed the Convention on the day that it was opened for signature and ratified it on 1 September 1995. It came into force in respect of Spain on 1 February 1998. The Convention states that the Spanish government shall refrain from policies or practices aimed at assimilation of persons belonging to national minorities against their will and shall protect these persons from any action aimed at such assimilation. It also says that it will protect the rights of Spanish citizens who are not citizens of the Spanish Republic but of a different nation. Spain is one of seven countries to sign and ratify the Convention. The other seven are: Australia, Britain, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Norway and Portugal.

name: Paule Perez
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47287/99) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that at the end of the investigation during which she was joined as a civil party, the procedure before the Court of Cassation had not been fair. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. On 5 June 2003 a Chamber of that Section, composed of the following judges, relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber. The Grand Chamber decided that there was no need to hold the case. The case was declared admissible on 30 January 2003.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47287/99) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged, in particular, that at the end of the investigation during which she was joined as a civil party, the procedure before the Court of Cassation had not been fair. On 5 June 2003 a Chamber of that Section, composed of the following judges, relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber, neither of the parties having objected to relinquishment (Article 30) The Grand Chamber decided that the application was admissible. An investigation was begun on the grounds of assault with an offensive weapon resulting in total unfitness for work for more than eight days (reduced to less than that during the investigation). The applicant joined the proceedings as a civil party. On 14 March 1997 the Saint-Pierre investigating judge ruled that there was no case to answer. He found that the applicant's son, “who had allegedly given her the injection, had left the département to return to his dental practice abroad, in Gabon”, that “he had given his mother an injection of a substance which was medically harmless at that dosage...”. The decision was apparently served on the applicant on the same day by registered post. On 7 April 1997 the applicant went to the investigating judge's registry and, claiming that she had not received a copy of the decision, refused to sign the notice of appeal drafted by the registrar. The Indictment Division of the Court of Appeal of Saint-Denis-de-la-Réunion found that the applicant had appealed “by letter addressed to and received by the investigatingJudge's registry”, and she had gone to the registry on the same day and refused tosign the notice. She alleged that there had been a breach of Articles 592, 575-6, 593 and 646 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In a judgment of 21 April 1998, the Criminal Division ofthe Court of Cassation dismissed her appeal. The case was dismissed on the grounds that it was served out of time. The Court of Appeal ruled that the appeal of 7 April 1997 against the decision that there was no case to answer served on 14 March 1997 was ‘out of time in accordance with the conditions laid down in Article 183 of the Code of Criminal Procedure; ...’ The case was heard in the High Court in London. The verdict was returned on 8 April 1997. The case is still pending appeal in the Supreme Court of England and Wales. It was dismissed by the Appeal Court on 6 April 1998. The Appeal Court ruled on 7 April 1999 that the case had not been served in the time required by Article 183.

name: Eliane van Glabeke
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38287/02) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented by Afcap (French association against psychiatric abuse) The French Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs E. Belliard, Director of Legal Affairs at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 4 January 2005 the Second Section decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Government submitted that the applicant had been ‘picked up’ on the public highway by a police officer who had asked for her to be admitted to hospital. The applicant disputed that account and stated that she had been arrested while cycling to the shops and taken to the police station. She submitted that after her admission at the hospital she had immediately been undressed and made to lie down with all four limbs attached to the bedposts in a seclusion cell. She had not undergone a medical examination on arrival but had been injected with unknown substances. The Second Section decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The parties have been unable to establish the date on which the letter was received. Lille State Counsel's Office decided to take no further action on that application as it was devoid of purpose. On 28 March 2002 Afcap in turn applied to the President of the Lille Court of Appeal for the immediate discharge of her daughter. The decision was made not to take further action and she was released to return to her family. The case was heard before the High Court of Justice on 2 April 2002. The judge ruled that the case should be referred to the court of Appeal as a matter of law and not to the Government of South Africa for further action. The court of appeal was ordered to make a decision on the application.

name: Burghard Theodor Mooren
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 11364/03) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Burghard Theodor Mooren (“the applicant”), on 26 March 2003, complained that, in the proceedings for review of his pre-trial detention, the Court of Appeal had unlawfully deprived him of his liberty. He claimed that his defence counsel had been refused access to the investigation files. The Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention, it decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant had been granted legal aid and was represented by Mr D. Hagmann, a lawyer practising in Mönchengladbach. The German Government were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The application was rejected on the grounds that it did not meet the requirements of Article 34. The District Court noted that the applicant, who had availed himself of the right to remain silent, was strongly suspected of tax evasion. He had to be placed in pre-trial detention because of a danger of collusion (Verdunkelungsgefahr) (see section 112 § 2 no. 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure – paragraph 41 below) The documents seized were incomplete. The applicant argued that there was no risk of collusion or of his absconding. Should the court nevertheless consider that he might abscond if released he was ready to comply with any conditions imposed by the court, such as handing over his identity papers. Mönchengladbach District Court upheld the arrest warrant. It found that there was still a risk that, if released, the applicant would tamper with factual evidence or interfere with witnesses. The Regional Court found that it was impossible to assess whether the information given in this manner would be sufficient. On 16 September 2002 the applicant, represented by counsel, lodged a further appeal against the detention order. The Court of Appeal's decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 16 September. The applicant was sentenced to three years in prison and a fine of £250,000. He is currently awaiting sentencing and his trial is expected to begin in January 2015. The Düsseldorf Court of Appeal quashed the detention order issued by the District Court on 25 July 2002. Pursuant to section 114 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the facts leading to a strong suspicion that the accused had committed a particular offence had to be given to the applicant. The applicant claimed that he had a constitutional right to be. given access to the facts and evidence on which the detention. order was based. The case has been remitted back to the Mönchengladbach District Court for further proceedings. The application was dismissed on appeal in July 2002 and the applicant was detained again on 9 September 2002. The decision was upheld by the Regional Court on 17 September 2002 but the applicant appealed. In order to comply with the constitutional rights to be heard and to a fair trial, the facts and evidence on which the suspicion and the reasons for the defendant’s detention on remand were based had to be described in sufficient detail to enable the accused to comment on them and defend himself effectively. The Court of Appeal noted that, in its decisions on the applicant's detention, the District Court had, however, merely stated that the applicant was strongly suspected of tax evasion “on the basis of the business records seized when his home was searched”. It should, at minimum, have summarised the results of the evaluation of those records. be set out in the detention order. The applicant’s counsel complained that he had not been granted access to the case files before the hearing. The Mönchengladbach District Court then issued a fresh detention order against the applicant. It stated that there was a strong suspicion that the applicant had evaded taxes on some twenty occasions between 1991 and June 2002. He faced a lengthy prison sentence which could no longer be suspended on probation, had not notified the authorities of his place of residence for several years and had claimed that he was living in the Netherlands. The District Court suspended the execution of the order to release the applicant at the request of the Public Prosecutor's Office, which had immediately lodged an appeal. The Mönchengladbach Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal against the detention order on 7 November 2002. The applicant lodged a further appeal on 8 November 2002 complaining that his counsel had still not been granted access to the case files. On 18 November 2002 the Public Prosecutor's Office granted the applicant's counsel access to his case files for inspection. On 10 December 2002 the applicant withdrew his further appeal. He argued in particular that his right to liberty, the deprivation of which was only constitutional if it was in accordance with the law, had been breached by his illegal detention. The impugned decisions disregarded both the case-law of the Federal Constitutional Court and the Basic Law. The Court of Appeal’s refusal to quash the detention order and to take a decision itself had also breached his right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time. On 9 March 2005 the Mönchengladbach District Court convicted the applicant on eight counts of tax evasion and sentenced him to a total of one year and eight months’ imprisonment suspended on probation. The court found that the applicant, who had confessed to the offences, had evaded turnover taxes of DEM 129,795, income Taxes of DEM 344,802 and trade taxes of Dem 55,165. The Federal Constitutional Court, without giving further reasons, declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint against the detention orders.

name: María Gloria Pérez de Rada Cavanilles
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 15 December 1997. It originated in an application (no. 28090/95) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by a Spanish national. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr J.M. Morenilla, the elected judge of Spanish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention), and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 15 December 1997. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1. The applicant was designated before the Commission by the initials M.P., the applicant subsequently agreed to the disclosure of her identity. On 26 January 1998 the Agent of the Spanish Government (‘the Government’) was given leave by the President to use the Spanish language at the hearing. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr J.M. Morenilla, the elected judge of Spanish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention), and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The applicant had been in dispute with a neighbour concerning a view over her property at Lumbier in the province of Navarre. In the agreement the neighbour, who had only a life interest in the building he occupied, undertook to block the view from his patio over the applicant’s property within six months. When that period expired without the neighbour having carried out his undertaking, the applicant applied to the Aoiz Court of First Instance for enforcement of the agreement. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 June 1998. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr J. Borrego BorreGO, Head of the Legal Service for the European Commission and Court of Human Rights, Ministry of Justice, Agent; (b), for the Commission M. F. Martínez, Delegate. The agreement was defective because one of the parties had no capacity to conclude such an agreement. The judge added that there was nothing to prevent an agreement being concluded with the person who had the necessary capacity. The decision was at last served on the applicant in the person of her domestic help, since she herself was out at the time. The application against the decision of 7 September 1993 at Lumbier was dismissed on the ground that the neighbour, who was merely a life tenant, could not carry out the works needed to block the view without the consent of the reversioner. The applicant appealed the decision, saying that the defendant had not brought any action to have the agreement set aside. On 30 November 1993 the applicant lodged a reposición application and, in the alternative, an ordinary appeal against the decision of 7 September 1993 with the registry of the duty court in Madrid. Noticing, however, that the application should have been lodged at the Aoiz Court of First Instance, the head of the registry crossed out the stamp, thereby invalidating it. On the same day, the applicant sent, by registered letter with advice of delivery, the same repos clawón application to the court. The court dismissed the application and upheld the impugned decision, on the ground that it had not been lodged within the prescribed period of three days. The applicant filed an appeal with the Navarre Audiencia Provincial, which dismissed it in a decision of 23 December 1994. On 20 January 1995 the applicant lodged an amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court, relying on the right to protection by the courts. The application was declared inadmissible on the following grounds:. the reposición application had been determined and not at the same time as that application, and. that it was accordingly pointless to consider whether it had been lodged timeously;. the applicant was not represented by a lawyer; and. the application was filed at a post office rather than the registry of the court or with the duty judge. An action to have the terms of a settlement agreement declared void may be brought on the same grounds as one for annulling contracts. Such an action must be brought in the appropriate court within fifteen days of the conclusion of the agreement, using the procedure corresponding to the amount in dispute. The relevant provisions of the Judicature Act are the following: Section 11 “1. The rules of good faith must be complied with in all proceedings.” Section 270 “Procedural documents, decisions and judgments shall be served on all the parties to a case’s parties’ names and on any persons referred to in them or who may be prejudiced thereby” The law on administrative matters states that applications, pleadings and communications sent by members of the public to public administrative bodies may be filed at post offices. The rules on the postal service, as enacted in Decree no. 1653/1964 of 14 May 1964, provide: Article 205 “Acceptance of applications and documents sent to administrative institutions …” The documents and applications in question shall be submitted in an open envelope. The official who accepts the item for despatch shall stamp it with the date in the upper left-hand corner of the main document, so that the name of the post office and the date of submission are clearly visible. Mrs Pérez de Rada Cavanilles applied to the Commission on 20 June 1995. She alleged that the Spanish courts’ strict application of the rules of procedure had prevented her from availing herself of the existing remedies. The Commission declared the application (no. 28090/95) admissible on 25 November 1996. In its report of 21 October 1997 (Article 31), it expressed the unanimous opinion that there had been a violation of Article 6 § 1. The full text of the Commission’s opinion is reproduced as an annex to this judgment. The Government asked the Court to hold that the dismissal of the application against the judgment of 7 September 1993 had not violated the rights guaranteed in Article 6§ 1 of the Convention.

name: María Iglesias Gil
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56673/00) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were represented before the Court by Mr J. Thomas Mulet, of the Palma de Mallorca Bar. The Spanish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. J. Borrego Borregone, Head of the Legal Department for Human Rights at the Ministry of Justice. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 10 December 2002 (Rule 59 § 3)
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56673/00) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mrs María Iglesias Gil and A.U.I. were represented before the Court by Mr J. Thomas Mulet, of the Palma de Mallorca Bar. The Spanish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. J. Borrego BorreGO. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits. María Iglesias Gil is the mother of A.U.I., who was born in 1995. A.A. abducted his son during an access visit and left Spain with him. After passing through France and Belgium, he travelled with the child by air to the United States. The first applicant lodged a criminal complaint with Vigo investigating judge no. 5 alleging child abduction and applied to be joined to the proceedings as a civil party. The investigating judge made orders for a nationwide search to be made for the child and for its immediate return to its mother. The Vigo Family Court awarded the first applicant custody and the father access to the child. The family court refused to issue an international search and arrest warrant for criminal contempt. The judge said that it was not clear whether there had been an offence of criminal contempt, as the alleged offences of coercion and extortion had not been made out. He also said that an international arrest warrant was not justified as the conduct complained of appeared to come within Article 622 of the Criminal Code, which characterises it as a minor offence. The investigating judge also examined whether a person could be prosecuted for the abduction of a minor for whom he had joint parental responsibility. He found that this was not possible under the case-law as the only offences that could be committed in such circumstances were criminal contempt and extortion. No new facts have emerged since then that would justify reclassifying the offence. No international search and arrest warrant can be issued as it is not an offence that comes within the extradition treaties. An appeal by the first applicant was dismissed by the Pontevedra Audiencia Provincial on 9 November 1998. In a decision of 2 June 1999, the Constitutional Court dismissed her appeal as manifestly ill-founded, holding that she had not stated why she disagreed with the reasoned decisions of the lower courts. The first applicant sought amparo relief under Articles 24 (right to a fair hearing), 15 and 17 of the Constitution, and the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child of 1989. An application for an order requiring investigating judge no. 5 to stand down was dismissed in a decision of 20 November 1997. A.U.A. did not return his son A.I. to his mother at the end of the period he was allowed by the family court. In her submission, the investigating judge had directly infringed both her and her son’s right to private and family life, and her right to judicial protection. The first applicant had confined herself to contesting the decisions of the criminal courts which, in reasoned and well-founded decisions, had decided to make a provisional discharge order in respect of her criminal complaint of child abduction, while renewing certain preventive measures. The Vigo Family Court withdrew parental responsibility from A.U.A. and awarded the first applicant full parental responsibility. Since 1 February 1997, the whereabouts of both father and child have been unknown, which means that the child has been removed from the applicant’s custody in breach of a court order. The first applicant saw her son for the first time since his abduction in February 1997. On 30 September 2000 Vigo investigating judge no. 6 made a provisional discharge order. On an appeal by the first applicants, that order was quashed by the Pontevedra Audiencia Provincial in a decision of 15 May 2001.Renewal of contact between first applicant and her son, the return of the child and further criminal complaints have all been unsuccessful. The first applicant was able to recover her child with police assistance on A.U.A.’s return to Vigo with the child. She said that for a time she was forced to go into hiding with her son in a shelter for women. The first applicant lodged a criminal complaint with the Vigo investigating judge against the first applicant and her parents alleging aggravated contempt. On 14 July 2000 the Family Court granted A.u.a. detention pending trial. The case has been referred to the High Court of Spain for further proceedings. The application is expected to be heard by the Spanish Court of Appeal in September 2014. Article 1: "Contracting States shall take all appropriate measures to secure within their territories the implementation of the objects of the Convention" Article 2: "For this purpose they shall use the most expeditious procedures available" Article 3: "The removal or the retention of a child is to be considered wrongful where: (a) it is in breach of rights of custody attributed to a person, an institution or any other body, either jointly or alone, under the law of the State in which the child was habitually resident immediately before the removal or retention" Article 4: "A Contracting State shall designate a Central Authority to discharge the duties which are imposed by the Convention upon such authorities’” Article 8: “Any person, institution or other body claiming that a child has been removed or retained in breach of custody rights may apply.” Article 11: ‘The judicial or administrative authorities of Contracting States shall act expeditiously in proceedings for the return of children.’ Article 13: � “Notwithstanding the provisions of the preceding Article, the judicial or. administrative authority of the requested State is not bound to order the return. of the child’s” The U.N. Convention on the Return of Children came into force in 1997. It provides for a process for a child to be returned to a parent or guardian if they have been wrongfully removed, retained or removed. Law no. 1/1996 of 15 January 1996 on the legal protection of minors, amending the Civil Code and Code of Civil Procedure (published in the Official Gazette of 17 January 1996) The relevant provisions of this Law provide: Section 3 “Minors shall enjoy the rights afforded them by the Constitution and international treaties ratified by Spain.” Article 158 “The court shall, on its own initiative, or on an application by the child, a parent or the public prosecutor, order the following measures: ... (2) appropriate action on a transfer of custody to avoid the unsettling the child in a way that is harmful” Spanish courts have refused to characterise a failure by a person with parental responsibility for a minor to return the child as false imprisonment or kidnapping. Under the case-law, a person guilty of such conduct may only be prosecuted for criminal contempt or extortion under Article 556 of the Criminal Code, for which the punishment is six months’ to one year’s imprisonment. The Law inserted a new Article 225 bis in the Criminal code, worded as follows: “1. A parent who, without any justification, abducts his or her minor child shall be liable on conviction to between two and four years’ imprisonment” The penalties stated in this Article shall also apply to any person from whom the minor is descended or any relative of the parent by blood or marriage up to the second degree who has committed the aforementioned acts. The sentence is expected to be in the upper half of the range set out in paragraph 1. (ii) failing to return a minor in material breach of an obligation arising under a judicial or administrative decision. The penalty is likely to be higher than the sentence given in the first paragraph of this Article. The penalties also apply. to any. person from which the minor. is descended. or any relatives of the minor by blood and marriage. up to a second degree.

name: Leci Gani
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 61800/08) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that he had not been given a proper and adequate opportunity, during either the investigative stage or the hearing, to challenge and question the victim, the sole witness against him in relation to all the crimes for which he had been convicted, with the exception of the forgery of official documents. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The Court informed the Albanian Government of their right under Article 36 § 1 of the convention to intervene in the proceedings.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 61800/08) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant, Mr Leci Gani, was born in 1975 and is currently serving a term of imprisonment in the Spanish prison of Quatre Camins in La Roca del Vallès (Barcelona) The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The Albanian Government did not inform the Court of their wish to intervene. The hearing before the Barcelona Audiencia Provincial took place on 19 April 2006. N. attended the hearing after undergoing a psychological diagnosis which established her suitability to testify in court. She had started to answer the questions posed by the public prosecutor when her statement had to be interrupted. She was said to be suffering from post‑traumatic stress symptoms that were hindering her from testifying. Those symptoms were medically confirmed after the hearing. The court had already adjourned the hearing once before, following a similar reaction on the part of N. As a consequence, it had provided her with psychological assistance before and during the hearing to allow for her full examination, but to no avail. The court had previously attempted – perhaps to the point of excess – to exhaust all remedies to obtain her statement. It had made use of all the psychological support that the presence of officials from the victims’ service could provide. The efforts were fruitless, however, and the witness’s resolved will to collaborate was prevented by one of the most horrific cases of psychological annihilation of a victim that this court has ever witnessed in its long professional experience. Only continuous breaks and recesses and an excessive effort on her part enabled her to make, in more that an hour, some progress in her statement, which came to a dramatic end as she was telling the court about the episode of a cold-water bath with which she had been tortured. Barcelona Audiencia Provincial ordered that the statements which had been taken from her during the investigation stage of the proceedings be read out. The applicant gave his alternative account of the facts. The court found that on 4 April 2004 the applicant had gone to N.’s apartment and had made death threats when she had not let him in to see their son. Upon leaving the apartment, he had twice knocked a car belonging to J., a close male friend of N., causing damage to the vehicle. On 6 April 2004 at around 1 a.m., the. applicant had broken in through a window. He had punched J., who had been there with N., and then hit N. repeatedly. N. had been tied, immersed in icy water, thrown on a bed and raped vaginally and anally. The applicant was sentenced as the principal offender for: (i) making very serious threats to N., to fifteen months’ imprisonment; (ii) breaking and entering into N’s home using violence and coercion, to two and a half years’ prison. He was also fined EUR 30,525 for damages. The court found that, when the applicant had been arrested at Prat de Llobregat Airport (Barcelona), he had been carrying false identification documents. The credibility of her testimony was enhanced by the weakness of the applicant's statement. The trial court also relied on other evidence, such as the contradictions of a hearsay witness for the defence. The Supreme Court quashed the Audiencia Provincial’s judgment. The court considered that the use as evidence of the victim's pre-trial statements had not infringed the applicant's right to defend himself. The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court reduced the penalty imposed on the applicant in respect of kidnapping. It also lessened the classification of the offence of making threats and reduced the sentence. The trial court had first tried to resolve the problem by staying the hearing and ordering a medical examination of the witness with a view to excluding any possibility of feigning on her part. When the same difficulties had recurred at the final hearing, the appeal was lodged. Supreme Court: Trial courts should take special care in assessing victims’ statements. In a decision served on 3 July 2008, the appeal was declared inadmissible for being devoid of any constitutional content. The Supreme Court added that the delay with which N. had reported the facts to the police could be explained by her fear and by the fact that she had had a child with the applicant. It also contended that it did not find in N.’s statement any alteration or substantial change which could be deemed as rendering it inconsistent and thus weakening its validity. In the light of those considerations, the Supreme Court was satisfied that the Audiencia Provincial had acted cautiously enough when assessing N’'s statement.

name: Siegmund Karner
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40016/98) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the Supreme Court's decision not to recognise his right to succeed to a tenancy after the death of his companion amounted to discrimination on the ground of his sexual orientation. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). By a decision of 11 September 2001 the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. On 7 December 2001 the President of the Chamber granted ILGA-Europe (The European Region of the International Lesbian and Gay Association), Liberty and Stonewall leave to intervene as third parties.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the Supreme Court's decision not to recognise his right to succeed to a tenancy after the death of his companion amounted to discrimination on the ground of his sexual orientation. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). By a decision of 11 September 2001 the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. On 7 December 2001 the President of the Chamber granted ILGA-Europe (The European Region of the International Lesbian and Gay Association), Liberty and Stonewall leave to intervene as third parties. In 1994 Mr W. died after designating the applicant as his heir. In 1995 the landlord of the flat brought proceedings against the applicant for termination of the tenancy. On 6 January 1996 the Favoriten District Court dismissed the action. It considered that section 14(3) of the Rent Act (Mietrechtsgesetz) was also applicable to a homosexual relationship. On 5 December 1996 the Supreme Court granted the landlord's appeal, quashed the lower court's decision and terminated the lease. In 2000 the applicant died and his mother waived her right to succeed to the estate. He asked the Court not to strike the application out of its list before the public notary handling the applicant's estate had traced other heirs.

name: Arnaldo Otegi Mondragon
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 2034/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the decision of the Supreme Court finding him guilty of serious insult against the King of Spain amounted to an unjustified infringement of his right to freedom of expression. The Court examined the information available to it, it decided that no hearing was necessary. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1 of the convention). On 7 June 2009 the applicant requested the Court to hold a public hearing.
eval_texts: The applicant alleged that the decision of the Supreme Court finding him guilty of serious insult against the King of Spain amounted to an unjustified infringement of his right to freedom of expression. The Court examined the information available to it, and decided that no hearing was necessary. The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) The applicant was represented by Mr D. Rouget and Ms J. Goirizelaia Ordorika, lawyers practising in Saint-Jean-de-Luz and Bilbao respectively. The Spanish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr I. Blasco. The Basque Country High Court of Justice has decided to try the applicant. The prosecutor lodged a criminal complaint against the applicant for “serious insult against the King’. The applicant argued that his remarks had constituted political criticism directed against the Head of the government of the Basques Country. He said that to say that the King of Spain was the Supreme Head. of the Civil Guard did not imply any intention to undermine dignity or honour; it was merely. merely a matter of opinion. The criminal proceedings in the Basque. Country High court of Justice began on 6 April 2003. The trial is expected to last a few weeks. The judge will decide whether or not the applicant should be tried. The High Court of Justice found the applicant not guilty of the charges against him. The court found that his remarks had been ‘clearly offensive, improper, unjust, ignominious and divorced from reality’ The application had sought to express political criticism in the context of freedom of expression, one of the foundations of the rule of law and democracy. This is not an issue concerning the private life of the Head of State but one of rejection of the ties of political power deriving from the hereditary nature of the institution which he personally symbolises. The Constitution does not guarantee the right of expression solely in relation to certain points of view that are considered correct. Public prosecutor lodged an appeal on points of law to the Supreme Court. He argued that the law protected the honour of the King as a specific individual possessed of personal dignity. In the view of the public prosecutor, it was clear that the King had been performing official duties. That did not deprive him of the right to respect for his honour, he said. The Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the lower court, making several references to the Court's case-law. It sentenced the applicant to one year’s imprisonment, suspended his right to stand for election for the duration of the sentence and ordered him to pay a fine. The judge agreed with the Basque Country High Court of Justice that the remarks had not targeted the King’s private life or his personal honour. The judge pointed out that the limits of freedom of expression were wider with regard to institutions since the latter did not possess honour. In view of the seriousness of the insulting comments and the fact that the applicant had deliberately expressed them in public, the Supreme Court sentenced him to one year's imprisonment. The amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court was dismissed. The applicant lodged an appeal alleging, inter alia, a breach of his right of expression (Article 20 § 1 (a) The Supreme Court’s judgment had incorrectly weighed the competing interests at stake. The statements in question had not been disproportionate in the context in which they had been uttered. The Constitutional Court noted at the outset that the right to freedom of expression did not encompass a right to proffer insults. It pointed out in that connection that the Constitution did not prohibit the use of hurtful expressions in all circumstances. However, freedom ofexpression did not protect vexatious expressions which, regardless of their veracity, were offensive and ignominious and were not pertinent for the purpose of conveying the opinions or information in question. The Supreme Court considered that the weighing of the competing rights at stake had been carried out in an appropriate manner by the Supreme Court. The King occupied a neutral position in political debate. This implied that he was owed institutional respect of a kind that was ‘substantively’ different from that due to other State institutions. The Constitutional Court held that the applicant’s remarks, on account of their obviously derogatory nature, had clearly gone beyond what could be considered legitimate. The applicant was imprisoned on 8 June 2007 after the Supreme Court upheld a judgment of the Audiencia Nacional of 27 April 2006 sentencing him to fifteen months’ imprisonment. According to the Government, his sentence was remitted on 16 July 2009. He is currently in pre-trial detention in connection with other criminal proceedings.

name: Lütfü Pakelli
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 8398/78) against that State lodged with the Commission on 5 October 1978 under Article 25 (art. 25) of the Convention by a Turkish national. The application invited the Court to hold that there had been no such breach. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. R. Bernhardt, the elected judge of German nationality (Article 43) and Mr. G. Wiarda, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b) ofThe Rules of Court). On 28 May 1982 the President drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of the five other members.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 8398/78) against that State lodged with the Commission on 5 October 1978 under Article 25 (art. 25) of the Convention. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. R. Bernhardt, the elected judge of German nationality, and Mr. G. Wiarda, the President of the Court. The application invited the Court to hold that there had been no such breach of Article 6 para. 3 (c) (Art. 6-3-c) The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and the Government of the Federal Republic of Germany. The hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 November. Immediately before they opened, the Chamber had held a preparatory meeting. The Court heard addresses by Mrs. Maier and Mr. Riess for the Government and by Mr. Frowein and Mr Wingerter for the Commission, as well as their replies to its questions. On 20 December, the Commission transmitted to the Court the applicant’s claims under Article 50 (art. 50) of the Convention. On 26 November, in response to a request which he had made on the instructions of the President, the Registrar received certain documents from the Commission. On 9 June 1982, having particular regard to their concurring statements, he concluded that there was no need for memorials to be filed. The applicant, a Turkish national born in 1937, is currently living in Turkey. He was resident in the Federal Republic of Germany from 1964 to 1976. On 3O April, the court sentenced Mr. Pakelli to two years’ and three months’ imprisonment for an offence against the Narcotics Act and for tax evasion. It was found to be proved that in the spring of 1972 the accused had illegally imported into Germany sixteen kilograms of cannabis resin of Turkish origin, hidden in his car. The trial opened before the Heilbronn Regional Court on 7 April 1976. The applicant was defended by Mr. Wingerter and, at certain moments, by Mr Rauschenbusch, a member of the same firm. Mr. Rauschenbusch was found guilty of murdering a Turkish man in 1974. He appealed the conviction on grounds that he was wrongly convicted. His defence counsel was Mr. Wingerter, who had previously defended another man convicted of being Mr. Pakelli's accomplice. In a letter to the Federal Court, Mr Rauschensbusch complained solely of procedural errors. He listed nineteen, most of which concerned decisions of the Heilbronn Regional Court refusing to appoint an expert or to summon, question or have questions put to witnesses. The last of the alleged errors related to Article 146 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It considered that Article 146 prevented Mr.RauschenBusch, just as it did Mr Wingerters, from acting in the case as officially defence counsel. On application by the Federal public prosecutor’s office, the Federal Court decided on 13 October 1977 to hold a hearing (Hauptverhandlung) on 29 November. Mr. Rauschenbusch and his client, who had returned to Turkey, were notified of this on 17 October. In his view, an accused (Angeklagter) who was at liberty was not entitled to such an appointment for hearings in an appeal on a point of law. There was no legal requirement at that stage for him either to appear in person or to be represented by a lawyer (Article 350 paras. 2 and 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure). Mr. Rauschenbusch said Mr. Pakelli was obviously (offensichtlich) not in a position to pay a lawyer. He had come to the Federal Republic as a migrant worker and had returned to Turkey after spending a long (laengeren) period in Heilbronn prison. It was evident that he had no savings. According to the minutes, the Federal Court heard the judge acting as rapporteur and then the submissions (Ausfuhrungen) of an official of the Federal public prosecutor’s office (Bundesanwaltschaft) in favour of rejecting the appeal. The Federal Court, referring to a judgment of its 3rd Criminal Chamber, added that an appeal on a point of law based on that Article could succeed only if the representation of several accused by one and the same lawyer proved to be really incompatible, in the circumstances of the case, with the duties of the defence. And on this occasion it had not been established that there was any conflict of interests. The Federal Court then rejected the remainder of the complaints: some were examined in detail and held to be without foundation and the others were considered more briefly. The judgment, which was ten pages in length, was served on Mr. Rauschenbusch on 21 December 1977. The Constitutional Court found nothing arbitrary in the decision of the President of the 1st Criminal Chamber of the Federal Court. The case was not “serious’, within the meaning of the above-mentioned judgment of 19 October 1977. Mr. Pakelli could have remained in the Federal Republic of Germany and attended the hearing, if need be with the assistance of an interpreter. The official appointment of a lawyer by the trial court covers not only the proceedings before that court but also the written stage of any appeal on a point of law. The trial court will also make a special appointment for the latter stage, if necessary. An appointment will also be made in other cases, either by the court of its own motion or at the accused’s request. An accused who is at liberty may appear in person or be represented by a lawyer at the appeal hearing (Article 350 para. 2). According to the case-law of the Federal Court, defence counsel can be assigned to him only under Article 140 para.2. The Federal Constitutional Court has held that defence counsel is to be appointed by the court of its own motion and at the expense of the State in serious cases. The court concerned may dispose of an appeal on a point of law without hearings in the following cases only: Where it finds the appeal inadmissible (Article 349 para. 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure);. Where, on a reasoned application by the public prosecutor’s office, the court considers unanimously that the appeal is manifestly ill-founded;. and. Where the court finds unanimously that an appeal filed in the interests of the accused is well-founded. Appeal hearings open with the rapporteur’s address. The appellant is heard first and the last address to the court is always made by the accused. Article 350 para. 1 requires that the accused and his lawyer be informed of the date and place of the hearing. “Common defence counsel’ (gemeinschaftliche Verteidigung) does not allow several accused to be defended by a common defence counsel. The 1st Criminal Chamber followed these precedents in its judgment of 29 November 1977 in the present case (see paragraph 17 above). The Government stated that this interpretation has since been accepted by all the Criminal Chambers of the Federal Court. On 16 May 1980, the Commission granted Mr. Pakelli free legal aid on the basis of a declaration of means dated 9 September 1979 and confirmed by certificates from the competent authorities. The Commission declared the application admissible in so far as it related to the rejection of the applicant’s request that a lawyer be officially appointed for the hearing before the Federal Court. In its report of 12 December 1981 (Article 31), the Commission expressed the unanimous opinion that the applicant had been the victim of a violation of Article 6 para. 3 (c) (art. 6-3-c) and, by eleven votes to one, that it was not required to determine whether there had also been breach of the right to a fair trial.

name: Thérèse Berger
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 48221/99) against the French Republic lodged with the European Court of Human Rights. The applicant complained, in particular, of the unfairness of criminal proceedings before the Court of Cassation in which she had been a civil party seeking damages. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 10 July 2001, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections. This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. Both the applicant and the Government filed written observations on the merits of the case.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 48221/99) lodged with the European Court of Human Rights under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant complained of the unfairness of criminal proceedings before the Court of Cassation in which she had been a civil party seeking damages. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Both the applicant and the Government filed written observations on the merits of the case (Rule 59 § 1) The Court declared the application partly admissible on 10 July 2001. The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 50 § 1). On 7 May 1997 the applicant appealed against that order. She was represented by counsel. Both parts of the reporting judge's report had been sent to the advocate-general prior to the hearing. The Court of Cassation declared the appeal inadmissible on the following grounds. It found that there was insufficient evidence that anyone had committed the alleged offences of fraudulent breach of trust and fraud or any other offence. None of the grounds of appeal, which amount to contesting the validity of the judges' findings of fact and of law, corresponds to any of the situations in which a civil party may appeal against a judgment of an indictment division in the absence of an appeal by the prosecution.

name: Alois Hauser-Sporn
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court decided to communicate the complaints concerning the length of the proceedings and the lack of remedies in that respect to the Government. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. In this respect, the Court opted to reject the Government's request to discontinue the application of Article 29 § 3 of the Court's Convention. The case was decided by the Court on 19 September 2005. The decision was made on the application's merits, and the application was dismissed.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court decided to communicate the complaints concerning the length of the proceedings and the lack of remedies in that respect to the Government. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. In this respect, it decided to reject the Government's request to discontinue the application of Article 29 § 3 of the convention. The applicant was found guilty under Article 88 of the Criminal Code of having negligently caused bodily harm and of having abandoned the victim. He was sentenced to a fine of ATS 3,200 (approximately EUR 230), suspended on probation. The incident took place in 1995. The police chief was fined for failing to report the incident. The case was settled in court in 1997 and the fine was reduced to $2,000. The judge ruled that the offence was not in breach of Article 4 of the Road Traffic Act. The court also found that the police officer did not have to report it to the police. The decision was upheld by the Court of Appeal in 2000. The original case was decided by a majority vote, with the judge agreeing to reduce the fine from $3,500 to $1,500. The appeal was dismissed on 7 September 1998. The Supreme Court ruled against the appeal on 6 October 1998. The case was heard in the Administrative Court of Germany. The fine did not exceed EUR 726 and no important legal question was at stake. The IAP submitted its observations in reply on 9 April 2001. The Administrative Court refused, under section 33(a) of the. Administrative Court Act, to deal with the applicant's complaint. This decision was served on the. applicant's counsel on 6 November 2003. The complaint was settled out of court in a settlement of more than EUR 1,000,000. The case was decided out of courtroom by a single judge. The applicant was allowed to appeal to the Supreme Court of the Federal Court of Justice.

name: Wim Capeau
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42914/98) against the Kingdom of Belgium lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights on 29 May 1998. The applicant complained of a violation of Articles 5 § 1 (c), 6 § 2 and 14 of the Convention, contending that the statutory requirement to establish his innocence by adducing factual evidence or submitting legal argument to that effect was incompatible with the presumption of innocence. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The Chamber declared the application partly admissible.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42914/98) against the Kingdom of Belgium lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The Belgian national, Mr Wim Capeau (“the applicant”), on 29 May 1998, complained of a violation of Articles 5, 6 and 14 of the Convention. The applicant claimed that the statutory requirement to establish his innocence by adducing factual evidence or submitting legal argument to that effect was incompatible with the presumption of innocence. By a decision of 6 April 2004, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Government filed observations on the merits of the case (Rule 59 § 1). The applicant did not submit any observations within the time allowed. On 25 October 1996 the applicant claimed compensation for unwarranted pre-trial detention, relying on the Law of 13 March 1973. On 12 May 1997 the Minister of Justice refused the applicant's claim on the ground that he had not “established his innocence by adducing factual evidence or submitting legal argument to that effect’. On 4 July 1997 the applicant contested the Minister's decision by means of an application to the Unwarranted Pre-trial Detention Appeals Board. The Appeals Board upheld the refusal of his claim by a decision taken on the same day and served on the applicant on 29 March 1998. It noted that the grounds for presuming the guilt of the applicant, who had always denied committing the offence he stood accused of, had been held to be insufficient to justify committing him for trial.

name: Jean-Claude Gacon
train_texts: The case was brought against the Government of France under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The case was heard in the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, France. The French government argued that the application was a breach of Article 34. The Court agreed that it was a violation of the right to appeal to the Supreme Court. The application was rejected and the case was referred back to the French Government for further action. The appeal was later dismissed. The decision was made to appeal the decision to the Court of Justice of France, not to the court of public opinion. The Supreme Court of France made the decision on the basis that the decision was based on the merits of the case, and not on a technicality.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1092/04) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the additional time granted to the Principal Public Prosecutor for appealing against a judgment of the Criminal Court amounted to a breach of the principle of equality of arms. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the convention) The case was heard by the Court of Cassation Bar on 16 October 2006. The decision was made to allow the application to be heard. The applicant and his brother were committed to stand trial in the Lyons Criminal Court. They were charged with having deceived the social security scheme and the relevant health insurance offices through fraudulent practices. The Lyon Criminal Court held that the prosecution had lapsed as the offence of professional collusion was covered by an automatic amnesty, and that it lacked jurisdiction to examine the claims of the civil parties. The applicant was accordingly acquitted. The Principal Public Prosecutor lodged an appeal against the judgment on 20 April 2001, availing himself of the two-month time-limit granted to him for that purpose by Article 505 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Court of Appeal ruled that the appeal was inadmissible on the grounds that it was incompatible with the guarantees of Article 6 of the Convention. The applicant was sentenced to a suspended term of two years’ imprisonment. He was also ordered to pay a fine of 120,000 euros (EUR) and stripped of his civic, civil and family rights for five years. The applicant appealed on points of law, arguing that the time available to the Principal Public Prosecutor for lodging an appeal under Article 505 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was incompatible with Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. In a judgment of 25 June 2003 the Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant's appeal, holding that the two-month time-limit for an appeal was not in breach of Article 6.

The report contained the names of people implicated in drug trafficking in Morocco. It related how, over a period of ten years, there had been a tenfold increase in the area of land that had historically been used for cannabis production in the region of Er Rif. The report contained twelve chapters with the following titles: “Cannabis in Morocco – the historical background”, “The characteristics of cannabis growing” and ‘The ‘war on drugs’ ’. The book was referred to in the newspaper Le Monde on 25 May 1994. The article was relatively short (it ran to some thirty or so lines in two columns), but gave details of the report. Le Monde published an article about a report commissioned by the European Union. The report said that Morocco was the world’s leading exporter of cannabis. The King of Morocco asked for criminal proceedings to be instituted against Le Monde. Both the editor-in-chief and the author of the article were acquitted of insulting a foreign head of State by the Paris Criminal Court in 1996. The court found that the journalist had merely quoted extracts from what was undisputedly a reliable report, without distorting or misinterpreting it or making groundless attacks. In a judgment of 6 March 1997, the Paris Court of Appeal, while recognising that ‘in just a few years Morocco has become the world's leading cannabis exporter’, accepted that he had acted in good faith. Le Monde found guilty of insulting a foreign head of State and sentenced to fines of 5,000 French francs (FRF) each. They were ordered to pay King Hassan II, who had successfully applied to be joined as a civil party to the proceedings, FRF 1 in damages and FRF 10,000 pursuant to Article 475-1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Court of Appeal also ordered Le Monde to make additional reparation in the form of a report publishing details of the convictions. The applicants appealed on points of law against that judgment. In a judgment of 20 October 1998, the Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation dismissed their appeal. The Court of Appeal found that the charge of duplicity had been repeated twice. The article portrayed Morocco as the world’s leading hashish exporter and alleged direct responsibility on the part of the Moroccan government and members of the royal family, was tainted with malicious intent, the court said. The court said the article had been made ‘to dramatic effect solely in order to preserve the country’'s image’ and ‘the insistence on drawing the reader’’ to the King in person was ‘malicious intent’. ‘Pernicious statements had been. made to dramatise. his country [was] viewed, and the charge that pernicious. statements were made to dramatic effect was made to preserve. the country's image,’ the court added.
