The case was brought by Mr Karl Obermeier, who resides at Linz, who was formerly employed by a private insurance company (‘the company’) In 1974 a dispute arose between the applicant and the company concerning various paid activities which it proposed to withdraw from him. Mr Obermeier instituted proceedings in the Vienna Labour Court (Arbeitsgericht). On 10 March 1978, the day following the first hearing, he was suspended from his duties by his employer. The company considered that it was entitled to take such a decision at any time without giving reasons. The first round of the proceedings concerning the applicant’s suspension was heard at the Linz Labour Court on 9 March 1981. The court dismissed the remainder of the appeal, finding that, under Article 228 of the Code of Civil Procedure (Zivilprozessordnung), a declaratory judgment may bear only on the existence of a legal relationship. On 21 May 1980 Mr Obermeier had been declared disabled for the purposes of that Act. On 8 May 1981, the company had sought the authorisation of the Disabled Persons Board for the applicant’s dismissal. Following a hearing, the Board gave its consent to the dismissal on 8 July 1981, finding that the relationship of trust between the parties had been irremediably undermined. The Provincial Governor (Landeshauptmann) for Upper Austria confirmed the Board's decision on 16 October 1981. The applicant then appealed to the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) which dismissed his appeal on 9 March 1983. The European Commission of Human Rights declared the application inadmissible on 12 March 1986. The company pleaded Mr Obermeier’s lack of a legal interest (Rechtsschutzbedürfnis) in the revocation of his suspension, since in the meantime he had been dismissed. The applicant, for his part, challenged the lawfulness of his dismissal. He stressed in particular that it had been pronounced before the authorisation from the Disabled Persons Board had become final, as the case was still pending before the Administrative Court. The company sent to the applicant, on 21 December 1984, a further notification of dismissal, which was to take effect on 30 June 1985. On appeal by the applicant appealed on points of law to the Supreme Court which, on 23 October 1984, quashed the decisions of the labour courts. The applicant appealed on points of law to the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) which, on 25 November 1985, referred the case to the Administrative Court. The latter court allowed the appeal on 21 May 1986, finding that the company had committed an error of law by dismissing Mr Obermeier before the authorisation had become final. On 1 June 1986, the Provincial Governor confirmed the Board’s decision of 14 March 1985. The applicant then asked the Board to declare, pursuant to sections 8 to 12 of the Disabled Persons (Employment) Act, that his employment contract subsisted. The Board and Provincial Governor found, on 10 February 1986 and 12 January 1987 respectively, that they lacked jurisdiction. The Supreme Court did not take into account the applicant’s appeal to the Constitutional Court and the Administrative Court. The parties did not appeal from this decision. The Labour Court found that Mr Obermeier had never been validly dismissed. It took the view that the effects of the prior authorisation given by the Board were not permanent and that such authorisation could provide the legal basis only for a dismissal which was closely linked to it. The Supreme Court stated that it was not for the civil courts to review the decisions of the administrative authorities. On the contrary, they were required to base their own judgments on such decisions, without any further examination. The applicant claimed that he had cited at the hearing, as an additional ground for the invalidity of his dismissal, disregard of clause 33 § 9 of the collective agreement. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 29 June, holding that section 105 of the Industrial Relations Act did not apply to a disabled person. The applicant then instituted new proceedings in the Linz Regional Court, sitting as a social and labour court. The court dismissed the action on 23 September 1988, finding that the agreement given by the works council in 1981 was also valid in relation to the 1984 dismissal. The Court of Appeal, and subsequently the Supreme Court, dismissed Mr Obermeier. Mr Obermeier's application was dismissed by the Administrative Court on 21 May 1986. He then applied to the labour courts for the reopening of the proceedings concerning his suspension, proceedings which had been terminated by the Supreme Court on 15 July 1986. The Supreme Court quashed these two decisions but dismissed his application on 14 March 1990, on the ground that the judicial decisions which had closed the proceedings in which the applicant had already contested the validity of his dismissal were final. name: Herwig C. Emmer-Reissig

The case was heard in the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten) on 29 June 1989. The court ruled that the case was not an administrative matter involving the exercise of public power. As a result, the Swedish Touring Club was no longer mentioned in the Act. name: Dorothea Vogt
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 11 March 1994 and by the German Government on 29 March 1994. It originated in an application (no. 17851/91) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a German national, Mrs Dorothea Vogt, on 13 February 1991. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention and also, in the case of the Commission's request, of Article 14.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 11 March 1994 and by the German Government on 29 March 1994. It originated in an application (no. 17851/91) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a German national, Mrs Dorothea Vogt, on 13 February 1991. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention and also, in the case of the Commission's request, of Article 14. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 February 1995. The Grand Chamber comprised as ex officio members the President and the Vice-President, Mr Bernhardt, who in this case was already sitting as national judge. The names of the remaining ten judges were drawn by lot by the President in the presence of the Registrar on 27 January 1995, namely Mr F. Gölcüklü, Mr R. Macdonald, Mr A. Spielmann, Mr J. De Meyer, Mr I. Foighel, Mr M.A. Lopes Rocha, Mr D. Gotchev and Mr P. Kuris. Mrs Dorothea Vogt was a German national born in 1949. She was a member of the German Communist Party (Deutsche Kommunistische Partei - “DKP’) She taught German and French in a State secondary school in Jever, Lower Saxony. In an assessment report drawn up in March 1981 her capabilities and work were described as entirely satisfactory. The Court heard addresses by Mr Trechsel, Mr Becker, Mr Jäckel, Mr Damman and Mr Meyer-Ladewig, and replies to a question put by it. Disciplinary proceedings against Mrs Vogt will be heard at a later date. The applicant had been a member of the Bremen/North Lower Saxony regional branch (Bezirksorganisation) of the DKP since the end of 1983. She had stood in the 1982 elections to the Landtag of the Land of LowerSaxony as a DKP candidate. Mrs Vogt was accused of also failing to comply with her duties as a civil servant in that she had taken part in and addressed the 7th party congress in Nuremberg in January 1984. The proceedings were stayed on 15 July 1985 in order to widen the investigations to include further instances of the applicant's political activity that had come to light in the meantime. From October 1986 Mrs Vogt was paid only 60 per cent of her salary. The applicant argued that her conduct could not amount to a failure to fulfil her duties as a civil servant. By being a member of the party and carrying out activities on its behalf she had availed herself of the right of all citizens to engage in political activity. She had always carried out such activity within the law and within the limits laid down in the Constitution. Her action to promote peace within the Federal Republic of Germany and in its external relations and her combat against neo-fascism were in no way indicative of an anti-constitutional stance. The DKP, whose aims had always been wrongly alleged (but never proven) to be anti- constitutional, was found guilty of a breach of duty. Disciplinary proceedings against Mrs Vogt breached International Labour Organisation (ILO) Convention No. 111 concerning discrimination in respect of employment and occupation. It also violated Article 10 (art. 10) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Disciplinary Division found that the applicant had failed to comply with her duty of political loyalty and ordered her dismissal as a disciplinary measure. It granted her a sum equivalent to 75 per cent of her pension entitlement at that date, to be paid for a six-month period. A party could be held to be anti-constitutional even if it had not been banned by the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) under Article 21 para. 2 of the Basic Law (Grundgesetz) Duty of political loyalty, which admittedly restricted civil servants' fundamental rights, was one of the traditional principles of the civil service and had constitutional status by virtue of Article 33 para. 5 of the Basic Law. The rule did not apply to measures, such as disciplinary proceedings, which initially had a different purpose and restricted the freedom to stand for election to, and to sit as a member of, parliament only as an indirect and unavoidable consequence of their implementation. The Disciplinary Division finally ordered that Mrs Vogt should be paid 75 per cent of her pension allowance for a period of six months. It did so in recognition of the fact that apart from her breach of the duty of loyalty Mrs Vog t had always performed her duties unexceptionably and enthusiastically and needed some income. The court held that the applicant's reference to Article 5 para. 1 of the Basic Law, which secured the right to freedom of expression, was not relevant. Mrs Vogt's conduct had been unlawful. By holding such a senior political post within the DKP, she necessarily espoused anti-constitutional aims and had therefore to be considered to be opposed to the Constitution herself. The same approach applied in cases where a person had already been appointed to a permanent civil service post. It was not possible to support both systems at the same time. Even though Mrs Vogts sought above all to support the constitutional system, she was not allowed to do so. The DKP's aims were admittedly not all anti-constitutional; some of them were compatible with the Basic Law. However, civil servants could not, as a means of furthering their own political objectives, make use of a party with anti- constitutional aims and help it to come to power. It appears doubtful whether the view of the Constitution espoused by the official and described above reflects accurately the principles enshrined in the Basic law. It is not necessary to resolve that question here. In its judgment banning the former Communist Party (KPD) (BVerfGE 5, p. 85), the Federal Constitutional Court held that the 'tactics of conflict' employed by the former KPD were incompatible with the free democratic constitutional system. The court also considered that the applicant's commitment to changing the DKP's policies could not exculpate her. The political loyalty owed by civil servants entailed a duty for them to dissociate themselves from groups which criticised or cast aspersions on the State and the existing constitutional system. The attitude of civil servants who, even if they campaigned within DKP for the renunciation of aims that were contrary to the Constitution, showed outside the party, through the political offices they held, that they unreservedly supported its programme and policy, was incompatible with such a duty. Mrs Vogt had knowingly breached her professional obligations, the Disciplinary Court found. Her dismissal had therefore been justified. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint (Verfassungsbeschwerde) with the Federal Constitutional Court. The court decided on 7 August 1990 not to entertain the constitutional complaint, on the ground that it had insufficient prospects of success. The disciplinary tribunals had been entitled to find that the DKP's aims were anti-constitutional, notwithstanding the provisions of Article 21 para. 2 of the Basic Law. The basis of trust necessary for Mrs Vogt to continue to work as a civil servant was lacking, despite the fact that she had declared herself to be in favour of a change in the party's policy. The applicant's dismissal had not amounted to a breach of the principle of proportionality as regards her constitutional rights. From 1987 to 1991 the applicant worked as a playwright and drama teacher at the North Lower Saxony regional theatre (Landesbühne) in Wilhelmshaven. From 1 February 1991 she was reinstated in her post as a teacher for the LowerSaxony education authority. The Land government had beforehand repealed the decree on the employment of extremists in the Lower Saxonic civil service (Ministerpräsidentenbeschluß - also known as the Radikalenerlaß - see paragraph 32 below) and had published regulations for dealing with “earlier cases“ (see paragraph 33 below)

It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The application was dismissed on 16 September 2008 and the Government was ordered to pay compensation to the applicants.

name: Theodor Klasen
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant died on 21 April 2005. On 11 May 2005 his lawyer informed the Registrar that his wife from a second marriage, Mrs Pauline Klasen, wished to continue with the case. By letter of 12 July 2005, the Government objected to her being allowed to do so. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fifth Section (Rule 25 § 1 and Rule 52 § 1) on 1 April 2006. On 27 October 2004 the Court decided to communicate the application. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 75204/01) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Mr Theodor Klasen, was born in 1933 and lived in Mülheim. He worked between 1964 and the beginning of 1974 with asbestos insulators for the T Company. During this period, the workers of this company who were exposed to asbestos dust while working had to clean their clothes themselves. This was done by the applicant's first wife Mrs Gisela Klasan. On 6 March 1991 she applied to the Düsseldorf Health Insurance Association for compensation payments, claiming that her illness was the consequence of her husband's work clothes. Mrs Gisela Klasen filed an objection against this decision which was rejected on 13 December 1991 by the Appeals Board of the Health Insurance Association. The court found that she had not been an employee herself, nor had she acted like an employee. She had cleaned her husband's clothes on ground of their living together, but not with a view to acting for her husband’s employer. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint alleging that the social courts' interpretation of Section 539 of the Social Security Act was discriminatory. The Federal Constitutional Court invited the Federal Parliament, the Federal Council (Bundesrat) and the Federal Government to submit their written observations on the constitutional complaint. Court refused to admit the complaint because it lacked reasonable prospects of success. The court held that the contested interpretation of Section 539 of the Social Security Act did not violate the applicant's constitutional rights. It also argued that it was incumbent on the legislator to determine to which extent the industrial health insurance should cover third persons. It further pointed out that a constitutional complaint could not be based on an alleged violation of the European Convention on Human Rights. This decision was notified to the applicant’s lawyer on 28 March 2001. It was announced to the public on 6 April 2001 and made public on 8 April 2001. The case was heard at the High Court in Wellington, New Zealand.

name: Emrah Emre
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5056/10) against the Swiss Confederation lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he was the victim of a violation of his right to respect for private and family life. The Turkish Government did not avail themselves of their right to intervene in the proceedings. The application was assigned to the second Section of the Court. It was decided, under Article 29 § 1, that the Chamber would rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The decision was announced on 1 February 2011.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 5056/10) against the Swiss Confederation lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he was the victim of a violation of his right to respect for private and family life. The Turkish Government did not avail themselves of their right to intervene in the proceedings. The application was assigned to the second Section of the Court. The case was decided on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time by the President of the First Section on 22 April 2010. The Court’s Sections were reorganised on 1 February 2011. In a decision of 2 June 2003 the Aliens Department for the Canton of Neuchâtel ordered the applicant’s administrative removal for an indefinite duration. On 20 October 2004 the applicant was deported to Turkey. After returning to Switzerland illegally in May or June 2005, he was arrested and taken into custody on 1 July 2005 pursuant to arrest warrants issued on the basis of his criminal convictions. In a judgment of 22 May 2008, which became final on 22 August, the First Section of the Court unanimously declared admissible the complaint under Article 8 and found that there had been a violation of that provision. On that basis, it held that Switzerland had to pay the applicant the sums of 3,000 euros (EUR) for non-pecuniary damage and EUR 4,650 for the costs and expenses he had incurred ‘in the domestic proceedings and before the Court’ The Court notes that the criminal activities in question were spread over a wide period (from 1994 to 2004) and that the two suspended sentences of 12 November 1997 and 10 November 1999 were activated in view of the further offences committed by the applicant. The Court observes that some of the conduct attributed to the applicant dated back to his adolescence and some to a relatively young age. It is undeniable that the convictions for wounding weigh heavily against him. Concerning the weapons offence, however, it appears to have been constituted merely by the possession of a tear-gas canister. As to the road traffic offences, whilst they may well constitute a potential danger they should nevertheless be taken seriously. It has not been established that it was the applicant who stabbed a security guard with a knife during the attack on the discotheque in 2000. The applicant arrived in Switzerland on 21 September 1986, before the age of six. At the time of the Federal Court’s judgment of 3 May 2004 he was twenty-three and a half. His criminal activities were spread over a considerable period. The domestic courts noted that he had not shown any awareness of his criminal activities. He had refused to follow his psychotherapy. His parents and brothers, one of whom had Swiss nationality, lived in the country. There is some debate between parties as to his professional integration in Switzerland. The applicant had spent most of his life in Switzerland, including all his school years, and that his parents andBrothers had Swiss citizenship. The Court notes that the applicant showed signs of ‘an emotionally labile personality disorder, with impulsive and borderline elements, together with a phobic anxiety disorder’ vis-à-vis the prospect of his deportation. The applicant argued that his illness, having involved suicide attempts, could not be adequately treated in Turkey. The Government, for their part, claimed the contrary, considering that his family would still be able to support him financially from Switzerland. The Court does not feel obliged to settle this question. The views of the parties to the proceedings differ on this point. The arguments of the applicant and of the Government differ on the matter, and the Court is not convinced that his brief stay in Turkey after his first removal may be taken into consideration. The Court does not rule out the possibility that the applicant’s health problems could be treated adequately in Turkey. It finds that the respondent State cannot be regarded as having struck a fair balance between the interests of the applicant and his family. As to the possibility for the applicant to request that the exclusion order be suspended temporarily or permanently rescinded, the Court finds that this possibility remains purely speculative at present. The permanent nature of the expulsion measure was considered by the Court in concluding that the measure had been disproportionate. The Court observes that the application is directed against his administrative removal, the duration of which it finds particularly harsh. It notes that in the present case the Police Court and the Criminal Court of Cassation of the Canton of Neuchâtel ordered the applicant's deportation for a period of seven years (see paragraph 11 above). The court also quashed the 12 December 2003 judgment of the Administrative Court of the Canton of Neuchâtel. The European Court of Human Rights awarded Emre the compensation by way of just satisfaction. The payment of such compensation does not, however, necessarily release the State concerned from its obligation under Article 46 ECHR to comply with the judgments of the European Court. In the present case, the Federal Court upholds a request for revision, it gives two separate decisions in succession, even though it generally does so in a single judgment. In the first, referred to as the rescindant, it annuls the judgment of which revision is sought; in the second, known as the rescisoire, it rules afresh on the application previously referred to it. The annulment decision puts an end to the revision procedure as such and leads to the re-opening of the previous proceedings. This is the principle of restitutio in integrum, which has the practical effect of limiting the freedom of States in the choice of means by which to remedy a violation of the Convention. The applicant's links with Turkey were at that time weaker than those he enjoyed with Switzerland. The applicant’s presence in Switzerland represented a particularly serious danger for public order and security. The only appropriate solution in order to alleviate the effects of the impugned measure against the deportee would consist in limiting the duration of the exclusion. 4.3 Consequently, it is justified to limit the removal measure ordered against the applicant to a period of ten years with effect from the removal decision of 2 June 2003. After such time he will be able to lodge an application for leave to remain, which will be examined by the European Court of Human Rights. On 11 September 2009 the applicant married a German national. As a result of that marriage he has obtained a German residence permit. name: Alan Martin
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Articles 3 and 6 of the Convention about his trial by court-martial. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. The case was adjourned pending the judgment of the Grand Chamber in Grieves v. the United Kingdom [GC], no. 57067/00, ECHR 2003‑XII. The parties each filed observations on the admissibility and the merits of the complaints. The applications were heard by a Chamber that would consider the case in light of the judgment in Morris v the United UK, no. 38784/97, E CHR 2002‑I.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40426/98) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Articles 3 and 6 of the Convention about his trial by court-martial. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. The parties each filed observations on the admissibility and the merits of the complaints. The case was adjourned pending the judgment of the Grand Chamber in Grieves v. the United Kingdom [GC], no. 57067/00, ECHR 2003‑XII. The Court ruled in favour of the applicant in the case against the UK Government. The applicant was living with his family in Germany, where his father was an Army Corporal serving in the Support Unit of the Rhine Garrison. On 8 February 1994 the applicant was charged with the murder of a young civilian woman. The German authorities waived jurisdiction pursuant to the NATO Status of Forces Agreement 1951. The applicant was returned to Germany in time for his court-martial which commenced on 21 April 1995. Despite his father’s return, the applicant remained subject to military law as the proceedings had already commenced (see paragraph 26 below). The applicant returned to England in April 1994 where he was detained. His father was discharged from the army in November 1994. The trial ended with the applicant’s conviction on 3 May 1995. In accordance with the provisions of the Army Act 1995, the verdict of the court-martial was confirmed by a Confirming Officer (see paragraph 28 below) The applicant appealed to the Courts-Martial Appeal Court, which had the power to quash the conviction if it considered it unsafe. The Lord Chief Justice, Lord Bingham of Cornhill, giving judgment on 30 July 1996, held, dismissing the appeal: “... We have some considerable sympathy with the appellant's complaint.” The appeal court certified a question of law for law. The House of Lords granted leave to appeal. Lords Slynn of Hadley and Hope of Craighead expressed the view that at first sight the decision to prosecute the applicant—a civilian aged only 17 at the time of the murder—by court-martial had been inappropriate. Lord Hope explained the utility of the 1955 Act in view of the greatly increased opportunities which were by then available for families and other civilian personnel to accompany the forces when serving overseas. On 16 December 1997 the Lords unanimously dismissed the appeal. The application was dismissed by the Court of Appeal on 16 December 1998. The appeal was dismissed on 19 December 1998 by the Supreme Court of Justice. Many of the witnesses were German and that they could not be forced to attend a trial in England. The defence had not yet indicated what evidence would be agreed. It cannot be assumed that the Director would have been willing to take proceedings in England without knowing more about the factors which he would have wished to take into account. He added that one of the forensic scientists who was responsible for examining secretions and bloodstains was being difficult to deal with and would only attend meetings if they were arranged through the German public prosecutor in the nearest large town. ... I have not forgotten that Lord Bingham of Cornhill CJ [see paragraph 18 above] said in his judgment that it was clear, with the benefit of hindsight, that the trial could have been conducted in Englandwithout due difficulty. There is no sound basis for thinking that, at the time when a decision about this would have had to have been taken, a prosecution in the English courts within a reasonable time would have been seen to be practicable. The alternatives lay between taking proceedings by way of court-martial in Germany, leaving the matter in the hands of the German public prosecutor or taking no proceedings at all. ... Conclusion ... The proceedings were conducted within the rules laid down by Parliament. ...” — The NATO Status of Forces Agreement 1951. — The Army Act 1955. — “(1) Any person subject to military law who commits a civil offence, whether in the United Kingdom or elsewhere, shall be guilty of an offence against this section”. Trial of those who have ceased to be subject to military law is expressly provided for by section 131 of the Act. Since the Armed Forces Act 1976, where a civilian defendant is to be tried, civilian Crown servants can be detailed as members of the court-martial. Most criminal offences allegedly committed by a civilian dependent would be tried by a Standing Civilian Court (similar to a Magistrates’ Court), with trial by court-Martial reserved for the most serious offences. The law and procedures which applied generally to the applicant’s court- Martial were contained in the Army Act 1955, the Rules of Procedure (Army) 1972 and the Queen's Regulations 1975. The basic rule of the common law is that the jurisdiction of the criminal courts in the United Kingdom is confined to crimes committed within the territory of each court. An exception is provided by section 9 of the 1861 Act, which gives jurisdiction to British courts in respect of alleged murders and manslaughters committed by British citizens anywhere in the world. The Offences against the Person Act 1861 is cited as a reason for the ban on the use of capital punishment in the UK. For more information on the ban, visit www.justices.org.uk or go to the website of the European Court of Human Rights (ECH) for more information.

eval_texts: The case was brought by a mother of a young girl who was banned from wearing a headscarf to school. The mother claimed that the ban breached her right to freedom of movement. The family appealed the decision, but it was upheld by the Court of Appeal. The judge said the girl's right to wear a head scarf was not infringed by the ban. The applicant's parents appealed against the Director of Education's decision to expel her. The Nantes Administrative Court of Appeal dismissed their appeal, on the same grounds as the lower court, finding that the applicant, by behaving as she had done, had overstepped the limits of the right to express and manifest her religious beliefs on the school premises. The applicant indicated that she subsequently took correspondence courses in order to continue her school studies. Her parents lodged an appeal on points of law with the Conseil d'Etat, relying, inter alia, on their daughter's right to freedom of conscience and expression and expression of her religion. name: Wolfgang Adam Wenner
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 62303/13) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the refusal to grant him drug substitution treatment during his imprisonment, including a refusal to have such treatment examined by an external medical expert, had breached Article 3 of the convention. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by one of their Agents, Mr H.‑J. Behrens, of the Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection. The application was communicated to the Government on 17 June 2014. The Court of Appeal ruled in favour of the applicant.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the refusal to grant him drug substitution treatment during his imprisonment had breached Article 3 of the convention. He has been continuously addicted to heroin since 1973, when he was aged 17. On 3 June 2009 the Augsburg Regional Court convicted the applicant of drug trafficking, sentenced him to three years and six months’ imprisonment and, having regard to a previous conviction, to another two years and 6 months‘ imprisonment. It further ordered the applicant’s placement in a drug detoxification facility, to be executed. The applicant was transferred back to Kaisheim Prison on 30 April 2010. The prison doctors gave him various painkillers for chronic pain resulting from his polyneuropathy, on a daily basis. During his detention, the pain in his feet, neck and spine became such that, at least during certain periods, he spent most of his time in bed. An external doctor for internal medicine, H., on the prison authorities’ request in October 2010. did not consider any changes in the treatment of the applicant’s HIV and hepatitis C infections necessary. He suggested that the prison medical service reconsider the possibility of drug substitution treatment. The applicant was examined by a doctor specialised in drug addiction therapy to that end. The applicant claimed that drug substitution treatment was the only adequate treatment for his medical condition. Substitution also helped to protect other prisoners from infection when using the same needles as he did for the consumption of drugs. Detoxification caused the person concerned serious physical strain and extreme mental stress and should only be attempted in cases of a very short opioid dependence. It had to be clarified whether, in the applicant’s case, further treatment for the hepatitis C from which he suffered was necessary. The decision of the prison authorities to refuse the applicant drug substitution therapy was a miscarriage of justice. It should not have been allowed to take place in the first place. The applicant was severely addicted to drugs. He was placed in a drug rehabilitation centre for five months before his transfer to Kaisheim Prison. He had been treated by medical experts with considerable knowledge of drug addiction treatment. The prison authorities argued that substitution treatment was neither necessary from a medical point of view nor a suitable measure for the applicant’s rehabilitation. After three years in detention, he no longer suffered from physical withdrawal symptoms. His condition with regard to his HIV and hepatitis C infections was stable and did not require any therapy. As suggested by the prison doctor, the applicant should use the opportunity to wean himself off opioids, such as heroin and its substitutes. The applicant appealed against the decision of the prison authorities to the Augsburg Regional Court. He argued that the authorities of Kaisheim Prison, where no substitution treatment had ever been provided, had omitted to examine the medical necessity of drug substitution therapy. He also argued that under the applicable administrative rules for substitution treatment in prison in the Land of Baden-Württemberg, he would be provided with drug substitution treatment. The Munich Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal as ill‑founded. On 10 September 2012 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court. The applicant’s objection against the Court of appeal‘s decision was rejected. The applicant complained that his right to respect for his physical integrity under the Basic Law had been breached. He complained that he was denied drug substitution therapy, the only suitable therapy to treat his chronic pain. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant’s constitutional complaint without giving reasons (file no. 2 BvR 2263/12) On 3 December 2014 the applicant was released. When examined by a doctor on 5 December 2014 he tested positive for methadone and cocaine. The doctor confirmed that the applicant would receive drug substitution treatment from 8 December 2014 onwards. The applicant was advised to be taken to a drug rehabilitation clinic immediately on his release in order to prevent him from taking an overdose of heroine.

name: Claude Mazurek
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 34406/97) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. On 4 May 1999 the Chamber declared the application admissible and decided to invite the parties to submit their observations on the merits at a hearing. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 12 October 1999. The applicant, Mr Claude Mazurek (“the applicant”), appeared before the Court. The application was dismissed by the Court on 8 November 1998. The case was dismissed again on 9 November 1998, after an extension of the time allowed, and the applicant replied on 22 April 1998. After the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention on 1 November 1998 the case was again dismissed.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 34406/97) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The application was examined by the Court following the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention on 1 November 1998. On 4 May 1999 the Chamber declared the application admissible and decided to invite the parties to submit their observations on the merits at a hearing. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mrs M. Dubrocard, Deputy Director, Human Rights Division, Legal Affairs Department, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Agent, and for the applicant Mr A. Ottan, of the Montpellier Bar, Counsel. Claude Mazurek was born in 1942 and lives at La Grande-Motte. His mother died on 1 August 1990 of HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) encephalopathy. She left two children: a son, Alain, born out of wedlock in 1936 and legitimised by his mother’s marriage in 1937. Alain brought an action against the applicant in the Nîmes tribunal de grande instance seeking an order that his mother's estate be divided by a notary. In a judgment of 21 January 1993 the court ordered the estate to be divided. With regard to the applicant's rights, it referred to Article 760 of the Civil Code. The court ruled that Article 760 did not discriminate against children born into a marriage. It said that the money had been intended to be given to the child's mother. But the court said the money should be returned to the mother, as it was part of the child’s inheritance. The court said that it was not intended to discriminate against the child, but to protect the interests of his parents. The decision was made in line with Article 8 and Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), which protects the rights of children born to unmarried mothers and fathers. The ruling was upheld by the European Court of Human Rights. The applicant appealed on points of law to the Court of Cassation, which delivered its judgment on 25 June 1996. The court was properly entitled to hold that it was not the intention of the legislature to discriminate between children on the grounds of their birth, but to ensure minimum compliance with the marital obligations of a married parent with regard to his or her legitimate children. The applicant’s complaint of unjustified discrimination on grounds of birth between children born in wedlock and children born out of wedlock, contrary to Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention, was dismissed. In respect of the complaint that the. Court of Appeal had ordered the sum transferred to the applicant‘s account to be returned to the estate to be divided, the Court. of. Cassation held that in deciding that the facts of the case had not shown any intention on the part of the deceased to bestow a gift on her son in. advance of the division of her estate, the court had determined an issue which it alone had jurisdiction to determine.

name: Roger Ekeberg
train_texts: The case originated in five applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained that they did not have a fair and impartial hearing before the Borgarting High Court. The Chamber decided to join the proceedings in the applications. By a decision of 11 July 2006, the Court declared the applications admissible. The Government, but not the applicants, filed further written observations (Rule 59 § 1). The Court ruled that the applications were admissible and dismissed the Government's written observations. The decision was upheld by the Supreme Court on 25 September 2003. The case was decided in favour of the applicants and against the Norwegian Government.
eval_texts: The case originated in five applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained that they did not have a fair and impartial hearing before the Borgarting High Court. The Chamber decided to join the proceedings in the applications (Rule 42 § 1) By a decision of 11 July 2006, the Court declared the applications admissible. All the applicants, but the fifth, were members of a motor cycle club named “Screwdrivers”, which was based in Hamar and was, at the time of the events giving rise to the proceedings described below, the “Hang-Around Club” of the Hells Angels. A Volkswagen Transporter was loaded with explosives that were detonated. The force of the explosion had been such that metal and rubber parts of the vehicle had hit and killed the driver of a passing car. The building had burned down to the ground and a neighbouring property had been severely damaged, several vehicles had been totally or largely destroyed. The total damage had amounted to at least NOK 2,000,000. The applicants were indicted (count II) under Article 161(1) and (2) for the acquisition, confection or storage of explosives, or for aiding or abetting thereto, with the knowledge that the explosives had been intended to be used for the commission of the offence. The High Court found it correct to assess whether there were grounds for imprisonment on the basis of law enforcement considerations pursuant to Article 172. The decision included the following reasons: “The City Court has ordered detention of [the fourth applicant] on the ground of danger of evasion, see Article 171 (1) no. 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and the defence counsel's first supporting letter concerned imprisonment on this ground.” The defence counsel has alleged that the conviction is based on a statement of a co-defendant which is contradicted by other statements and evidence. The basic condition stated in Article 172 is regarded as having been met. The High Court bases its judgment, as in the Borgarting High Court's ruling of 28 June 2001 in the Orderud case (appeal case 01-02109) The High Court has found that the law enforcement considerations which form the basis of Article 172 are so prominent here that the accused should remain in prison also after judgment. The accused's personal and family circumstances pointed out by the defence counsel cannot be given sufficient weight in the opposite direction, and continued imprisonment cannot be said to be a disproportionate measure under Article 170A. Unless it is of importance for the decision regarding whether or not the accused is to be released, especially in relation to the consideration of proportionality, the regime he is now subject to is found to be of no importance to the High Court's assessment.” The High Court also considered decisions included in Rt 2000, page 371, page 1664 and page 1905. The prosecution appealed against the acquittals of the first, second and third applicants on count II. The High Court was sitting with a jury of 11 members (reduced to 10 on the fifth day as one of the jury members was disqualified, see below) and with 3 professional judges, one of whom was Judge G. The jury answered all the questions in the affirmative, except for one regarding count II with respect to the fourth applicant. The professional judges decided to pass judgment and convicted all five applicants on counts I and III. For each applicant, the number of days spent in provisional detention was to be deducted from the sentence. Finally, the three professional judges awarded NOK 120,000 in compensation for non-pecuniary damage to the husband of the woman killed by the explosion. The Supreme Court unanimously rejected both appeal grounds, on procedure and sentencing, on 25 September 2003. The first voting judge, Mr Justice Støle, gave inter alia the following reasons: “(13) I will first deal with the allegation that High Court judge, Judge G., was disqualified. ... (14) From the outset, I find reason to point out that our rules of procedure for criminal cases in a High Court that sits with a jury are based on a distribution of functions. (15) Following the landmark judgment by the European Court of Human Rights on 24 May 1989 in the case Hauschildt v Denmark (application no. 10486/83), there is extensive Supreme Court case law on this.” The question of imprisonment was decided during the investigation and without a conviction by any court. same applies to the presiding judge in a High Court case involving a jury. In Rt-1996-925, the. presiding judge of the High Court was, with dissenting votes, also regarded as being disqualified in a. situation where the order to remand the accused in custody had been made after there was a. conviction by a first instance court. But here the objection on the grounds of disqualification is not aimed at the presiding. judge, but at one of the other two professional judges who took part. The question now is whether the other professional judges in a high Court that is convened with a jury are to be regarded as disqualified under section 108 of the Administration of Courts Act due to the fact that they have previously been involved in applying Article 172 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Judge G. of the High Court was not disqualified. It is true that all the professional judges take part in the assessment of whether the jury's decision is to form the basis of the judgment. However, such a setting aside of decisions does not determine the question of guilt and is also so exceptional that, in my opinion, it cannot be given any significance worth mentioning in this context. The jury was constituted with 11 members, according to Article 355 (2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. juror W. contacted a policeman she knew and asked if she could sit on the jury even though she had been questioned by the police on one occasion. Jury member W. reported to the police as a witness and told the police about her observations in close connection to the day of the explosion. Her observations are of such a nature that it can be questioned whether she is impartial in this case. After this, W. withdrew from the jury and the hearing continued with the remaining 10 jury members. The question here is whether W.'s presence as a member of the jury during the first four days of the hearing may have influenced the jury's verdict. I agree with the High Court that W. was prejudiced, but the question is then whether the other 10 members of the Jury became prejudiced as a result of W. serving on the jury. The jury members will regularly be told by the presiding judge that, when deciding on the question of guilt, they must only place emphasis on what is stated as evidence in court. There is no corresponding barrier to the jury members discussing the case among themselves – even continuously during the court hearing. I refer to the fact that W. was at no time called as a witness in the case, by either the prosecuting authority or the defendants. The prosecutor has stated to the Supreme Court that the observations she had told to the police on 10 July 1997 – including about parts of the vehicle in question's licence number – were clarified early on as being of no importance to the further investigation.

name: Edmund Schönenberger

eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights and by the Government of the Swiss Confederation. It originated in an application (no. 11368/85) against Switzerland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Swiss national and a Turkish national. Both sought a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 8. The Commission also sought a Decision under Article 10. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mrs. D. Bindschedler-Robert, the elected judge of Swiss nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr. Jacot-Guillarmod and Mr. Levi for the Government, Mr. Trechsel for the Commission and Mr Schönenberger, Ms. Hug and Mr Garbade for the applicants. At the hearing, the Commission, the Government and the applicants lodged with the registry various documents, either at the President’s request or on their own initiative. The first applicant, Edmund Schönnberger, who is a Swiss citizen born in 1942, practises as a Rechtsanwalt. Mehmet Durmaz, who is a Turkish national born in 1950, lives at Onex, in Switzerland. He is a taxi-driver. in Zürich. On 16 February 1984, acting on a statement by one O, the district prosecutor (Bezirksanwalt) for Pfäffikon issued a warrant for his arrest. The applicant was arrested on the same day by the Geneva police. He was questioned and also confronted with other suspects on 23 and 24 February. On each occasion he cooperated by answering all the questions put to him. On 24 February, she asked Mr. Schönenberger to take charge of Mr. Durmazer’s defence. On 28 February she expressed the hope that the “lawyer’ - whose name she did not mention - “would look after [him]’ The district prosecutor probably received the letter and enclosure for Mr. Durmaz on Monday 27 February, but kept them from him without telling him that he had received them. Anything you say may be used in evidence against you. If you choose to remain silent, the district prosecutor will have to prove your guilt by other means (witnesses, etc.) He will usually then try to influence you by arguing that in that case you will remain in custody on remand until such time as he has questioned witnesses, other suspects, etc. If this does not worry you, it will be to your advantage to exercise your right not to make any statement. At all events, be patient: you will have-have to be released at some stage! Yours faithfully ...“ Mr. Durmaz was freed on 23 March 1984. On 29 May 1985 the Zürich district prosecutor ordered that he had no case to answer as it could not be excluded beyond all possible doubt that someone else had been mistaken for him. In respect of his detention on remand, the prosecutor awarded him 3,000 Swiss francs (CHF) which was increased to 3,565 CHF on 30 October 1985. The appeals against the Pfäffikon district prosecutor’s order of 1 March 1984 were dismissed by the presiding judge. The applicants lodged a public-law appeal with the Federal Court against the decision of the Department of Justice. In the Canton of Zürich, the monitoring of correspondence with persons in custody is governed by section 53 of the District Prisons Ordinance of 19 April 1972. Section 53(3) reads as follows (translation from German): “No correspondence with co-prisoners and former co- Prisoners (except for close relatives) shall be allowed. Letters jeopardising the purpose of detention or prison security shall not be forwarded.’ The Federal Court held that the disputed measure was a disproportionate restriction on freedom of correspondence and on the rights of the defence. It consequently set aside the Department of Justice’s decision and awarded the applicants costs of 500 CHF. The applicants applied to the Commission on 10 January 1985 (application no. 11368/85). They claimed that the Pfäffikon district prosecutor’s stopping of the letter from Mr. Schönenberger to Mr. Durmaz had violated their right to respect for their correspondence (Article 8 of the Convention) (art. 8) and their freedom of expression (Article 10) The general principle laid down in the disputed ordinance cannot be criticised as being unconstitutional, at least not if regard is had to the fact that correspondence with the supervising authorities and defence lawyers is not subject to any marked degree of control. Commission declared the application admissible on 4 March 1986. In its report of 12 December 1986, the Commission expressed the unanimous opinion that there had been a breach of Article 8 (art. 8) and that no separate issue arose under Article 10. The full text of the Commission’s opinion is reproduced as an annex to this judgment. At the hearing, the Government confirmed the submissions contained in their written pleadings. In them they invited the Court ‘to conclude that in the present case the non-forwarding of the letter in issue addressed by the first applicant to the second applicant, who was detained on remand and did not know the sender’

name: Qadam Shah Mohammadi
train_texts: The application was brought by an Afghan national. He claimed that he was being forced to return to Hungary. The case was heard by the Court of Arbitration for Human Rights. The judge ruled that the application should be dismissed until further notice. He also requested that the Hungarian Government provide information on the status of the applicant’s case. This information was provided by the Hungarian government. The application was denied by the judge and the case was returned to the Austrian Government for further proceedings. The decision was made under Rule 41 of the Rules of Court. The Hungarian Government was requested to provide information about the asylum proceedings against the applicant. The request was denied.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 71932/12) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his forced transfer to Hungary under the Dublin II Regulation would subject him to inhuman and degrading treatment. The Court decided to apply Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, indicating to the Government that it was desirable in the interests of the parties and the proper conduct of the proceedings not to expel the applicant to Hungary until further notice. The application was decided to communicate the application to the Austrian Government and to grant priority to the application. The applicant left Afghanistan for Austria in October 2011. He claims he was forced to lodge an asylum request and placed in an open camp. On 15 December 2011 the Traiskirchen Federal Asylum Office (Bundes­asylamt) rejected the applicant’s asylum request. On 11 January 2012 the Asylum Court (Asylgerichtshof) quashed that decision. It stated that the Asylum Office had failed to update its country information regarding the risk of refoulement of asylum‑seekers from Hungary to Serbia. Furthermore, the decision had not established the legal framework under which the asylum application was to be made. Hungary expelled asylum-seekers to Serbia, if their first asylum proceedings were terminated and there was no obstacle under the non-refoulement rule. A person lodging a subsequent asylum request was not allowed to remain in Hungary. The Hungarian authorities stated that they did not have a list of safe third countries and evaluated each case individually. In most cases Serbia was considered to be a safe third country. The Asylum Office concluded that it hence did not consider itself legally obliged to make use of the sovereignty clause and rejected the asylum request. The applicant’s appeal against that decision, but on 24 September 2012 the Asylum Court awarded suspensive effect to that decision. Hungary had discontinued his proceedings on 24 October 2011. The asylum court assumed that because of Hungary’s acceptance of jurisdiction the applicant would have access to asylum proceedings on the merits in Hungary. It pointed out that the Hungarian authorities had informed the Asylum Office that they had planned an age assessment, but could not carry it out because the applicant had left the country. On 20 November 2012 the Court applied an interim measure under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court and requested the Austrian Government to stay the applicant's transfer to Hungary until further notice. The Austrian Government complied with this request. The Court noted a lack of sources in the UNHCR's letter and referred to the recently updated country information. The Court notes that on 1 January 2014 Regulation (EU) No 604/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council (“the Dublin III Regulation’) entered into force. At the time of the decision by the Austrian authorities to expel the applicant to Hungary, the Dublin II Regulation was the applicable legal basis. Unaccompanied minors were placed in a children’s home in Fót, where care and education were provided to them according to their age. Having regard to the fact that the applicant would turn 18, it was very unlikely that a guardian would be appointed for him upon his return. The aim is to avoid multiple applications and to guarantee that each asylum-seeker's case is dealt with by a single member State. Under the Dublin II Regulation, the member State responsible for examining an asylum application of an unaccompanied minor shall be that where a member of his or her family is legally present. In the absence of a family member, theMember State responsible. for examining the application is that where the minor has lodged his. or her application for asylum. International documents describing the. conditions of detention and reception of asylum-seekers in Hungary are extensively summarised. in the judgment in Mohammed v. Austria (no. 2283/12, §§ 32-50, 6 June 2013). In the paragraphs that follow, the most relevant information will be reiterated, and new developments after the adoption of that judgment will be taken into account. Hungary ’s continuing policy and practice of considering Serbia as a safe third country and returning asylum-seekers to that country without conducting an examination of the merits of their claims. The UNHCR noted that the number of asylum‑seekers detained had significantly declined in 2012. Asylum-seekers who applied for asylum immediately upon their arrival, or at the latest during their first interview with the immigration police, were no longer detained. People who failed to apply immediately, or who otherwise failed to communicate such an intention, continued to be subject to detention for the duration of the entire asylum proceedings. The Hungarian Helsinki Committee commented on legislative changes in Hungary which entered into force on 1 July 2013. It raised concerns that there might be a threat that asylum- seekers were placed in alien policing detention upon return to Hungary. Hungary's Asylum Act provides for a newly created detention regime called “asylum detention’ The proposed detention regime for asylum‑seekers would also foresee the detention of first-time asylum-seekers as well as those whose cases had started even before the adoption of the proposed regulations. Detention was up to the discretion of the Office of Immigration and Nationality. In this note, the Hungarian Helsinki Committee concluded that the amendments introducing a separate detention regime had seriously weakened the judicial review of immigration and asylum detention and the right to appeal in asylum proceedings. The amendments also failed to ensure adequate reception conditions, the committee said. The committee's report was published on the Asylum Information Database (AIDA) on 30 April 2014. Between July and December 2013, 1762 asylum-seekers were detained under the asylum detention regime. The maximum period of asylum detention is six months. Vulnerable people were not excluded from detention, with the exception of unaccompanied children. Alternatives to detention were available in the form of bail, a designated place to stay, and periodic reporting obligations. But the Hungarian Helsinki Committee criticised that the scope of application of bail as alternative to asylum detention was not defined clearly enough, which it feared could result in the non-application of this measure in practice. After the introduction of that regime, asylum detention facilities were usually at full capacity. It calculated that on average, approximately 26% of all asylum-seeking were in asylum detention, while the number of male asylum- Seekers increased to around 42%. Detainees complained about inadequate housing conditions, lack of equipment and cleaning materials, inadequate water quality, and difficulties in practising their religion. The majority of the social workers hardly spoke any foreign languages and were mainly performing administrative tasks rather than engaging with the detainees. The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention expressed its concern that there had been a significant focus on detaining asylum-seekers in Hungary. It highlighted the pressure and challenges faced by Hungary as a transit country, having seen a radical increase in the numbers of asylum- seekers in 2013 alone. The legislative changes to the Asylum Act that had come into effect in July 2013 had led to some positive changes, such as asylum detention being based on individual assessment. The Working Group called to the Hungarian Government’s attention the fact that the situation of asylum-seekers and migrants in irregular situations needed robust improvements. It recommended that the measures introduced by the recent law, which were considered to be positive, should be implemented in a clear and defined manner. Detention should not be the common and first resort and should be for the shortest possible duration, especially when genuine Asylum-seekers may be overlooked or detained unnecessarily without proper justification, the Working Group said in a letter to the government. ‑seekers. The issue of prolonging the detention of an asylum-seeker and the lack of proper judicial review were consistently raised during interviews it conducted.

eval_texts: The case originated in two applications (nos. 36812/97 and 40104/98) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that the non-enforcement of the final return order under the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction had violated their rights under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention. The applications were transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The applicant and the Government each filed written observations on the admissibility and merits. The Court decided to join the applications and to communicate them to the respondent Government. The court found that the first applicant's wife had wrongfully removed the child within the meaning of Article 3 of the Hague Convention. The court dismissed the mother's claim that the child's return would entail a grave risk of physical or psychological harm. It considered that the second applicant's return could not be hindered by the fact that the mother was her main person of reference and that returning could cause a massive trauma affecting her development. 26 September 2002 the Court declared the applications admissible. The case was heard in the Graz District Civil Court (Bezirksgericht für Zivilrechtssachen) and the decision was made on 20 December 1995. First applicant filed an application for enforcement of the return order of 20 December 1995. First applicant started divorce proceedings before the Oakland Circuit Court (Michigan) By a decision of 16 April 1996, the court pronounced a default judgment of divorce. Further, it awarded the first applicant sole custody of the second applicant. Second applicant should reside with first applicant in the event of her return. The fact that the publication involved only a reprint of the criminal information did not exculpate the applicant. It went far beyond the mere reporting of a criminal suspicion to publish the text of the information in a periodical and thus to make it accessible to the general public. There was no justification for doing so. The applicant could not invoke a legal duty under Article 114 of the Criminal Code, namely to draw the public’s attention to the (allegedly) Nazi mentality of a high-ranking official of a governing party. That allegation came under the general rule that a person who made an attack of this kind through the media had to prove that it was true. Vienna Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal (Berufung) The case did not concern the (possibly incorrect) legal qualification of his statements, but allegations putting a stain on his character which objectively could not be inferred from those statements. The publication in the form of a criminal information was intended to ensure that the accusation as to his character made therein would have a particularly telling effect on the average reader. The fact that a short report on the criminal information against this politician would not have been punishable did not justify the conclusion that a full reprint of it was not punishable either. Neither the right to report a criminal suspicion (Article 86 para. 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure - see paragraph 27) nor the right of journalists to publish a criminal report were to be infringed. The written text of the judgment was served upon the applicant on 7 January 1985. Mr Grabher-Meyer requested the Attorney-General (Generalprokurator) to file a plea of nullity for the preservation of the law (Nichtigkeitsbeschwerde zur Wahrung des Gesetzes) but he was informed on 9 January 1986 that the Attorney General did not intend to take any action. Neither the exception provided for in Article 114 para. 2 of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 25 below) justified the publication because it was not appropriate (mangels Anlassadäquanz): it had been insinuated, without a sufficient basis in the facts, that Mr Graber Meyer held National Socialist attitudes.

name: Brigitte Heinisch

The parties each filed observations on the admissibility and merits of the application. The President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the subject at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The parties replied to those third-party submissions.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28274/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that her dismissal without notice from her employment as a geriatric nurse infringed her right to freedom of expression. She had brought a criminal complaint against her employer alleging deficiencies in the institutional care provided. The application was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The applicant and the Government each filed observations on theAdmissibility of the Application. The parties replied to those third-party submissions (Rule 44 § 6) The applicant had been working in a geriatric nursing home operated by Vivantes. In 2002 the Medical Review Board of the Health Insurance Fund (Medizinischer Dienst der Krankenkassen, hereinafter referred to as ‘MDK’) established serious shortcomings in the daily care provided there. The MDK threatened to terminate the service agreement with the applicant’s employer. Subsequently, restructuring took place and the applicant was dismissed. The case is currently before the European Court of Justice (ECJ) and is expected to be settled by the end of the year. Vivantes GmbH has deceived family members, because the care provided does not in any way correspond to or justify the fees paid. Vivantes has systematically tried to cover up the existing problems and urged staff to falsify records of services rendered. The applicant’s complaint referred to the report produced by the MDK following their visit in 2003, and stated that she would be willing to attest to the bad conditions at the nursing home. It further included statements by the applicant concerning overworking and referred to minutes of a team meeting advising staff, in order to avoid disciplinary consequences, not to disclose staff shortages and time pressures to patients and their relatives. Brigitte was dismissed from her job at Vivantes Forum for Senior Citizens on account of her repeated illness, with effect from 31 March 2005. The applicant challenged the dismissal before the Berlin Labour Court (file No. 35 Ca 3077/05) The applicant contacted friends and also her trade union, Vereinte Dienstleistungsgewerkschaft (ver.di). On 27 January 2005 they issued a leaflet headed as follows: “Vivantes wants to intimidate colleagues!! Not with us! Immediate revocation of the dismissal of our colleague Brigitte who used to work for Vivantes” The applicant was heard as a witness by the public prosecution in preliminary investigation proceedings against Vivantes. The preliminary proceedings were again discontinued on 26 May 2005 pursuant to Article 170 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The applicant’s claim of 25 February 2005 was then extended accordingly. The Berlin Labour Court (Arbeitsgericht) established that the employment contract had not been terminated by the dismissal of 9 February 2005 since this could not be justified under Article 626 of the German Civil Code (Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch) and section 1(1) of the Unfair Dismissal Act (Kündigungsschutzgesetz - see “Relevant domestic law and practice” below) German law does not contain general provisions governing the disclosure of deficiencies in enterprises or institutions. An extraordinary dismissal of an employee for having lodged a criminal complaint against his or her employer may be based on Article 626 of the German Civil Code. An employment relationship may be terminated by either party to the contract without complying with a notice period for a “compelling reason” (wichtiger Grund). Facts must be present on the basis of which the party giving notice cannot reasonably be expected to continue the employment until the end of the notice period or to the agreed end of that relationship. The Federal Constitutional Court refused, without stating further reasons, to accept her constitutional complaint for adjudication. Employment termination is unlawful if it is socially unjustified. Case-law of the Federal Constitutional Court and Federal Labour Court was cited in the decision. The court held that, in accordance with the rule of law, the discharge of a citizen’s duty to give evidence in criminal investigations could not in itself entail disadvantages under civil law. The employee's motives for lodging the complaint were of particular significance. A complaint lodged by an employee must not constitute a disproportionate reaction in response to the employer's conduct. Indications of a disproportionate Reaction by the complainant employee could be the justification of the complaint. The motivation of the person lodging the. complaint or the failure to have previously drawn attention to the impugned deficiencies internally. within the enterprise. The court ruled that a complaint lodged solely to cause damage to the employer or to ‘wear him or her down’ could constitute a disproportionate reaction depending on the charges underlying the complaint. The Council of Europe stressed the importance of ‘whistle-blowing’ as an opportunity to strengthen accountability, and bolster the fight against corruption and mismanagement, both in the public and private sectors. Article 170 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides for the following outcomes of investigation proceedings: “(1) If the investigations offer sufficient reason for bringing public charges, the public prosecution office shall submit a bill of indictment to the competent court.” 6.1.3. It should codify relevant issues in the following areas of law:. employment law – in particular protection against unfair dismissals and other forms of employment-related retaliation;. both public and private sector whistle-blowers ..., and the media. 6.2.4. This legislation should protect anyone who, in good faith, makes use of existing internal whistle-Blowing channels from any form of retaliation (unfair dismissal, harassment or any other punitive or discriminatory treatment) The above guidelines were also referred to in the Parliamentary Assembly’s related Recommendation 1916 (2010) 38. Article 24 of the Revised European Social Charter has been ratified by twenty-four of the Council of Europe's member States. Germany has not ratified ILO Convention No. 158. 40. These include the Council of Europe’s Criminal Law Convention on Corruption and Civil Law Convention On Corruption or the United Nations Convention against Corruption. Germany has not yet ratified the Convention. or regulations or recourse to competent administrative authorities; ...”.
