name: Sylviane Stefanelli
train_texts: The case was brought against the Republic of San Marino under Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Government of the Republic complained that there had been no public hearing at first instance or on appeal. The application was declared admissible and inadmissible on 1 June 1999. The case was heard by the European Commission of Human rights, which ruled in favour of the Government on 12 February 1999. It was the first case of its kind to be heard in the European Human Rights Court of Appeal. The decision was appealed by the Government and the case was decided by the Court of Appeals on 14 March 2000. The judge ruled that the Government's case was admissible.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35396/97) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention of the unfairness of criminal proceedings that had been brought against her. The Court declared the application admissible as regards the lack of a public hearing at first instance and on appeal and inadmissible as to the remainder. The application was examined by the Court after the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention on 1 November 1998. The Government submitted their observations on 12 February 1999 and the applicant replied on 15 March 1999. The case was decided on 1 June 1999. The applicant is a San Marinese national. She was suspected of offences connected with the illegal sale of milk for zootechnical use. The applicant appealed and lodged her grounds of appeal on 12 August 1996. The first-instance judge delivered his verdict without holding a public hearing and in the accused’s absence. He sentenced her to four years and six months’ imprisonment. He also ruled that she was dangerous and imposed a court supervision order as a security measure. In his decision, he rejected the allegation of a violation of fundamental principles on the ground that the legislation in issue had been amended in November 1992. The decision was made public on 18 November 1996. The judge upheld the conviction on the merits but reduced the sentence to three years’ imprisonment. He also quashed the declaration that the applicant was dangerous and the security measure. and it was for the legislature to decide whether or not the reform applied to pending proceedings or, as it in fact decided, only to new proceedings. The judge also upheld the charge of possession of an instrument of crime with intent to offend. and the conviction was quashed on the grounds that the charge was a ‘political act’ and was ‘substantive’. and ‘unlawful.’ The judge said the sentence of three years was “an appropriate sentence”.

name: Iradj Kuhlen-Rafsandjani
train_texts: The case originated in three applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the length of two sets of proceedings concerning custody of his children had been excessive. On 9 December 2009 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applied at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The German Government were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, Federal Ministry of Justice.
eval_texts: The case originated in three applications (nos. 21980/06, 26944/07 and 36948/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Iradj Kuhlen-Rafsandjani alleged that the length of two sets of proceedings concerning custody of his children had been excessive. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Ms C. Krüger-Rauch, a lawyer practising in Schifferstadt. The German Government were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, Federal Ministry of Justice. The proceedings concerning custody of the children and the applicant's contact rights began in 1998. The parties agreed to the commissioning of an expert opinion on a possible regulation of custody and contact rights. They further agreed that until the completion of the expert opinion the contact of the applicant with his children should be provisionally regulated by the acting judge in cooperation with the Kleve child protection agency (Kinderschutzbund). On 28 April 1999 the parties agreed that the contact between the applicant and his children would be temporarily restricted until the expert opinions were completed. The proceedings were to a large extent conducted jointly until the. applicant's former wife's petition for divorce was granted by a judgment dated 29 November 2001. The mother requested sole custody of the children for the duration of the separation of the spouses. Court ordered an expert opinion on the question of what attribution of custody rights and – should sole custody be awarded to the mother – what contact with their father would be in the children's best interest. The mother had previously cancelled appointments for appraisals in connection with the drawing up of the expert opinion, thereby delaying its completion. In view of the repeated disputes between the parents and the fact that the children had been living with the mother for a considerable time and were settled, the expert recommended that sole custody was transferred to her. Nevertheless, it appears that regular contact between the father and the children ceased temporarily during the year 2000 (Aufenthaltsbestimmungsrecht) In November 2000, in the separate custody proceedings, the District Court decided to provisionally grant sole custody of the children to the mother. The applicant asked to be granted contact rights in accordance with his request as reformulated on 18 October 2000. In addition to regular contact at the weekends, the applicant asked for the right to spend the second Christmas holiday and half of each of the summer, autumn and Easter holidays with his children. The Düsseldorf Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's request for legal aid in the appellate proceedings on the ground that his claim was devoid of any prospect of success. In view of the tensions and lack of cooperation between the parents, the transfer of sole custody was in the children's best interest. The application was brought by the wife of the father of the children. She had filed for divorce from her husband, and the children had been left in the care of their mother. The court awarded the mother sole custody and the right to determine the children's place of residence to a guardian. The children attended the hearing but were not heard by the Court of Appeal. The case was heard in Düsseldorf in May and June 2002. The application was dismissed in August 2001. In March 2002 the applicant appealed against the decision to leave sole custody to the mother and to give the children to the District Youth Welfare Office. The appeal was dismissed on 26 June 2002, but the appeal was heard again in May 2002. The proceedings regarding the applicant's contact rights following the divorce took place in Düsseldorf. The applicant, represented by his counsel, and his former wife entered into a court settlement (Prozessvergleich) stipulating that the applicant should have contact with the children every fortnight on Saturdays or Sundays from 2 p.m. in the mother's presence. The parties further agreed that with effect from 2003 they would plan at least one holiday per year with theChildren at approximately the same place and time, so as to enable the applicant to meet the children regularly for a period of several days during the holidays. Appeal dismissed and settlement confirmed that the settlement was neither invalid nor void. For the period until finalisation of the expert opinion the applicant was granted unaccompanied contact with the children every fortnight on Saturdays or Sundays from 10.00 a.m to 6 p.m. The court refrained from regulating the applicant's contact rights for the holidays since at the hearing of 11 March 2005 the children had objected to spending holidays alone with their father. It specified that in reaching its conclusion it could not rely on an expert opinion because the father had refused to be examined by the appointed expert. The applicant objected to the new expert on the ground that she did not have the necessary professional qualifications. The applicant filed a request to spend summer holidays with his children at his home in Heidelberg from 23 July to 3 August 2008. By a decision of 6 June 2008 the District Court rejected the request since the children had objected to spending the holidays with him. On 19 August 2008 the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal dismissed an appeal against that decision, since because of the passage of time a decision in the matter was no longer required. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the constitutional complaint (file no. 1 BvR 1716/01) concerning the separate custody proceedings (5 F 283/98) in which the applicant challenged the provisional attribution of sole custody. The Federal Constitutional Court held that the applicant's parental rights as guaranteed by the Basic Law included an obligation for the courts to conduct custody proceedings in such a way as to obtain a reliable basis for a decision founded on the child's wellbeing. The court pointed out that it was questionable in the case at hand whether the proceedings had satisfied these requirements since the lower courts had not given any convincing reasons why the children had not been heard. However, there was no need to take a decision in this respect because in any event the applicant could not claim to have suffered a particularly serious disadvantage since his complaint did not have any prospect of success even if remitted to lower courts. The applicant made an application on behalf of and in the name of his children for the regulation of the children's contact rights with respect to their father. The application was dismissed as inadmissible on the ground that the determination of contact arrangements between the father and the children was already the subject of proceedings under file no. 5 F 272/98. The applicant argued that the grandparents were setting the children against him and obstructing the exercise of his contact rights. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint (File no. 1 BvR 2127/01) by a decision of 7 December 2005, served on the applicant in December 2005. The application was rejected by the District Court on 22 March 2001. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint that his parental rights had been violated by the decisions of the lower courts. It held that the right to determine the contact of the children with third persons was part of the right of custody which had been awarded solely to the mother. In view of the close relationship between the mother, children and the grandparents and the fact that the grandparents assumed a considerable part of child care, a prohibition of contact with the children was neither practicable nor in the children's best interest. The Court held that preventing contact between the children and their grandparents could in no way help to ensure regular contact between. the applicant and his children but would to the contrary further obstruct such an aim.

name: Apostolos Ioannis Mangouras
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the sum set for bail in his case had been excessive and had been fixed without his personal circumstances being taken into consideration. The Greek Government, who had been invited to submit written observations on the case, did not express any wish to exercise that right. Alejandro Saiz Arnaiz, ad hoc judge, delivered a judgment in which it held unanimously that the case was not admissibility and merits of the case were not considered. The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court.
eval_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the sum set for bail in his case had been excessive and had been fixed without his personal circumstances being taken into consideration. The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court. The case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section. On 8 January 2009 the Chamber, composed of Josep Casadevall, Elisabet Fura, Corneliu Bîrsan, Boštjan M. Zupančič, Egbert Myjer, Ineta Ziemele, judges, and Alejandro Saiz Arnaiz, ad hoc judge, delivered a judgment. The case was referred to the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights. The Grand Chamber ruled unanimously that there had been no violation of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 September 2009. The applicant was born in 1935 and lives in Greece. On 13 November 2002 the ship Prestige, flying the flag of the Bahamas, was sailing in the Spanish exclusive economic zone off the coast of Galicia, carrying 70,000 tonnes of fuel oil. At a distance of 28 miles from the applicant, the ship was found to have breached Article 5 of the convention. The oil spill blackened beaches and cliffs, destroyed marine life, adversely affected water quality and had an immediate environmental impact on numerous animal species. The spillage of the ship’s cargo caused an ecological disaster whose effects on marine flora and fauna lasted for several months. The shores of the Atlantic coast of Cantabria and Galicia were severely polluted by the numerous waves of oil which were washed up. The applicant's conduct could constitute an offence of causing damage to natural resources and the environment and one of failing to comply with the instructions of the administrative authorities. A judge remanded the applicant in custody and set bail at 3,000,000 euros (EUR), after finding that the facts of the case disclosed sufficient indicative evidence. Investigation has produced sufficient indicative evidence to suggest that Mr Apostolos Mangouras could be criminally responsible for the offences in question. All the evidence indicates that the severe damage to the Prestige was caused by the unforeseeable phenomenon of a storm surge. It is also clear that the ship’s Master, by repeatedly ignoring the instructions of the port authorities, hampered meaningful joint efforts to lessen the extremely serious risks. It should be stressed that the steps taken hitherto and the conclusions to be drawn for the purposes of this decision are of a wholly provisional nature and that many further steps and much more expert evidence will be needed in order to fully elucidate the facts. Bail is necessary and unavoidable, in the present circumstances, to fix bail. Bail cannot, for the time being at least, be replaced by a less restrictive measure. An appeal by the applicant was dismissed on 3 January 2003 by the Corunna Audiencia Provincial on the ground that there was sufficient evidence to charge the applicant with serious offences and that the amount of bail was justified by the unusual circumstances of the case. The court pointed out that the applicant had been remanded in custody on account of his “alleged involvement in his ‘allegedly involvement in the leak in the vessel’” The Audiencia Provincial dismissed the ground of appeal based on the applicability of Article 230 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea of 10 December 1982. The judge ordered the applicant’s provisional release after eighty-three days in detention, subject to the following conditions: “(a) that the applicant be granted bail in the amount of EUR 3,000,000” The judge recorded the lodging of a bank guarantee in an amount corresponding to the sum set for bail, which was provided as a one-off, spontaneous humanitarian gesture by the London Steamship Owners’ Mutual Insurance Association Limited (“the London P and I Club”) London P and I Club and ship’s owner paid out EUR 22,777,986 in compensation for the damage for which they were civilly liable. The applicant complained of the amount set for bail, arguing that it had been excessive and disproportionate in view of his financial circumstances. He alleged that the amount had been fixed without account being taken of his personal circumstances, in disregard of the requirements of the court's case-law. By a reasoned decision (auto) of 29 September 2003, the Constitutional Court declared the appeal inadmissible. For confidential support call the Samaritans on 08457 90 90 90, visit a local Samaritans branch or see www.samaritans.org for details. The court took into consideration the national and international disaster caused by the oil spill, the fact that the accused is a non‑national and that he has no ties in Spain. It follows that bail was fixed on the basis of criteria of proportionality ... The exceptional amount reflects the exceptional nature of the situation.” Subsequently, in March 2005, the Spanish authorities authorised the applicant’s return to his country of origin, where he is now living, on condition that the Greek authorities ensured his compliance with the periodic supervision to which he had been subject. The applicant is therefore required to report every two weeks to a police station on the island of Icaria.

name: Karl-Heinz Bergmann
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the retrospective prolongation of his preventive detention, beyond the former statutory ten-year maximum duration, breached his right to liberty. The Government of Germany was represented by two of its Agents. The case was heard by the European Court of Human rights (ECHR) on 17 June 2014. The decision was returned to the ECHR and the case was dismissed on 17 July 2014. eval_texts: A German national was detained under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. He alleged that the retrospective prolongation of his preventive detention breached his right to liberty. The case originated in an application (no. 23279/14) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court on 18 March 2014. The application was communicated to the Government on 17 June 2014. Here we look at the circumstances surrounding the case. The applicant was born in 1943 and is currently detained in the centre for persons in preventive detention on the premises of Rosdorf Prison (hereinafter the ‘Rosdorf preventive detention centre’). He was convicted by the criminal courts five times. The applicant stabbed a female cyclist in the back in a life-threatening manner for sexual gratification. Still drunk, he had then broken into a house, strangulated a four-year-old girl and had injured her with a knife below the waist. The Regional Court found that at the time of committing the offences, the applicant had been in a state of diminished criminal responsibility. The court endorsed the experts’ finding that the applicant’s personality disorder could no longer be treated because his sexually deviant aggressive behaviour had lasted for decades. He therefore presented a danger to the general public. Public security could therefore be better safeguarded by placing him in preventive detention. The Lüneburg Regional Court ordered the continuation of the applicant’s preventive detention at regular intervals. By 11 June 2011 he had served ten years in preventive detention. The Regional Court further ordered the Rosdorf Prison authorities to offer the applicant, within three months of the date on which its decision became final, a specific anti-hormonal therapy with medication aimed at reducing his sadistic fantasies and his libido, and thus his dangerousness. It noted that at the time of his last offence on 3 October 1985, his first placement in preventive Detention could not exceed ten years. It was only following the entry into force of the Combating of Sexual Offences and Other Dangerous Offences Act on 31 January 1998 (see paragraph 51 below) that the courts responsible for the execution of sentences could prolong preventive detention without any maximum duration. The Regional Court considered that the prolongation of the preventive detention of the applicant, who had been detained for almost thirty years, was still proportionate in view of the considerable threat he posed to the public. It noted that the applicant’s detention in a supervised residence, which it had suggested in its previous decision, was not possible in practice. The Regional Court found that, as required by section 316f(2), second sentence, of the Introductory Act to the Criminal Code, there was still a very high risk that, owing to specific circumstances relating to his personality and his conduct, the applicant would if released commit the most serious sexually motivated violent offences. The Celle Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal. It confirmed that the requirements laid down in section 316f(2), second sentence, of the Introductory Act to the Criminal Code for ordering the continuation of the applicant's preventive detention had been met. The court held that the applicant was suffering from a mental disorder as defined in section 1(1) of the Therapy Detention Act. Specific disorders affecting a person's personality, conduct, sexual preference and control of impulses were covered by the notion of ‘mental disorder’ in the Act. The decision was made on 2 September 2013, and the appeal was dismissed on 3 September 2013. The applicant argued that under the European Court of Human Rights’ well-established case-law the retrospective prolongation of a person’s preventive detention – a penalty – beyond the former ten-year time-limit breached the prohibition on retrospective punishment under Article 7 of the Convention. He claimed that the order for the continuation of his preventive detention violated his constitutional right to liberty. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint without giving reasons (file no. 2 BvR 2182/13). The decision was served on the applicant’S counsel on 7 November 2013. The decision of the Federal constitutional Court is published here. The applicant was detained under the Therapy Detention Act. He had repeatedly refused treatment with medication to diminish his libido. The applicant had participated in group therapy sessions run by a doctor and in a social skills training course. He stopped attending the group for addicts and refused to take medication for fear of side effects. Since 2 June 2013 the applicant has been detained in the new Rosdorf centre for the mentally ill. He is currently being held under Article 67d § 3 of the Criminal Code, read in conjunction with section 316f(2), second sentence, of the Introductory Act to the Criminal code. The conditions of the applicant’s preventive detention at issue are described below. The conception of preventive detention in the centre was developed in order to comply with the constitutional requirement to differentiate between preventive detention and imprisonment. Detainees are placed in apartment units measuring some 23 square metres containing two furnished rooms and a bathroom. The rooms are equipped with a controlled access to the internet including e-mail, telephone, television, CD and DVD player and radio. There are common rooms for residential groups consisting of some seven detainees, which include a kitchen, a dining room, a television room and rooms for games, handicraft work and exercise. The outdoor premises, measuring some 1,600 square metres, can be used for sports, recreation or gardening. Persons in preventive detention may work, but are not obliged to do so. The applicant has refused regular and repeated offers to start a treatment with medication to reduce his libido, which had been recommended by expert W. in 2013, for fear of side effects. In December 2014 he showed willing for the first time to take up such treatment. He proved reliable during leave from the detention centre under escort on a number of occasions under escort. He did not take part in any structured leisure activities and spent most of his day alone watching television. He declined repeated invitations to take part In group sessions of the treatment programme for offenders. The applicant no longer participated in any therapy measures from August 2014. He is being held at the Rosdorf detention centre.

name: Falter Zeitschriften GmbH

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 3084/07) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant company alleged that a court judgment under the Media Act ordering it to pay damages had infringed its right to freedom of expression under Article 10. The Austrian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Tichy, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for European and International Affairs. The application was communicated to the Government on 29 January 2009. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). Elaine B. (name changed, ed.) had been ill-treated by police officers in Cameroon, kicked by them in the abdomen and placed with 18 other women in ‘stinking, damp cells’ She had survived her escape on a container ship, during which she ‘nearly went mad’ The case takes on a political dimension because it exposes conditions in the Traiskirchen centre. One year later only the victim is still before the courts. The chronicling of a judicial scandal. A few fellow Cameroonians, as well as the campaigning lawyer W.R. and his colleague R.H., are continuing to stand by her. ‘Otherwise I would have killed myself’, says Elaine. The Traiskirchen centre in Germany is home to 1,000 asylum seekers. Security officers at the centre later state in court that female asylum seekers could be paid for quick sex. They also tell of pimps rolling up to the centre in their cars. The sexual exploitation seems to have been unbearable. ‘Please help us!’ pleaded the women. The Interior Ministry stated at the time that the police were confronted with a ‘wall of silence’. The woman who claimed that she had been raped by a security officer was dismissed for sexual assault. The centre director F.S. later commented on the attacks in the washrooms of the women’s quarters by telling the court: ‘According to our information such incidents are very common’ Elaine B. describes with precision how the man locked the door and removed the key. She tells of the pains in her lower abdomen afterwards and how she washed herself with warm water for weeks. She immediately identifies the security officer in a photo. For the first interview in the interview room no trained interpreter can be found. In their minutes the police officers at times refer to Elaine B. not by her name but as ‘the nigger woman’ She is repeatedly linked to prostitution. The court heard that the woman was intimidated and seemed very anxious’, recalls District Inspector W.S., who investigated the case, a year later in court. Elaine B. denies this version of events. She says that she had other things on her mind at the time. She felt repelled by this fat man with a moustache who smelled of alcohol, she was afraid of him. If she had really been hoping to be granted asylum, why would she then have defamed the security officer? Next to take the witness stand are the employees of the bakery. name: Sait Berisha

The Vice-President of the Second Section, to which the case was allocated, decided to grant priority to the application under Rule 41.

They established that the applicants had not conducted themselves correctly with regard to the application, and accordingly they were no longer entitled to family reunification. The first applicant informed the Migration Office that R. and L. had been living in Switzerland illegally since 15 August 2009 and that it had been urgent to bring them to the respondent State because L.’s chances of recovery were better in Switzerland. The applicants had brought the children to Switzerland illegally despite the negative decision of the Migration Office of 28 April 2009. The Migration Office also reiterated that the children’s existence had previously been concealed from the Swiss authorities, and that the paternity of the first applicant had not been established. In addition, the legal requirements for family reunification had not be met. The children had lived their entire lives in their home country of Kosovo, where they had attended school. The applicants had waited quite a while before applying for a residence permit, and they had not cited any other important family reasons for seeking reunification. It remained doubtful whether it had always been the applicants’ true intention to construct family life in Switzerland. The children were to be returned to their home country of Kosovo. The U.S. government says that the children are not entitled to stay. They claim they are being forced to leave the country. The case is still pending. Cantonal Court asked the Swiss embassy in Pristina to send it a copy of the visa application the second applicant had made on 13 March 2007, in which she had allegedly mentioned the existence of her three children. In its answer the embassy informed the Cantonal Court that it could not provide a copy because in accordance with internal instructions it had been destroyed after two years. The domestic law indicated that the request for residence permits on the ground of family reunification for R. and L. had been submitted late. Residence permits could therefore only be issued to them if there were important family reasons as set out in Article 47 (4) of the Foreign Nationals Act. R. was allowed entry into high school (le lycée) the following school year. B. was also allowed entry to high school the following year. L. was granted a permanent residency permit on 16 July 2012. The choice-of-law rule, in so far as it refers to the personal law, is not discriminatory and is compliant with Articles 8 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights and with international law. The Cologne Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal against the Regional Court’s decision of 14 June 2007. The court referred to a report dated 21 February 2006 by a medical expert, Sch., whom it had previously consulted. The latter had found that the applicant suffered from a personality disorder. This finding, which was still valid, was at the root of his previous offences and was the reason why he risked committing further offences if released. As he had no family or friends outside prison, he could, if anything, be placed in a supervised residence (betreute Wohneinrichtung), but it could not be ascertained whether he was sufficiently ready to cooperate. The Court of Appeal noted that the negative prognosis as to the applicant’s future conduct could partly have been caused by misconduct on the part of the Aachen Prison management. The public interest in the detention of the applicant, who still risked committing serious property offences, continued to prevail over his own interest in personal liberty. The applicant's age and his state of health did not call into question his continued dangerousness. There was still a risk of his committing serious acts of fraud, an offence which he was able to commit despite his illnesses. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint (file no. 2 BvR 2124/07) The Hamm Court of Appeal upheld a decision of the Aachen Regional Court dated 25 March 2008 in which the latter had found that the prison authorities’ refusal to grant the applicant’s request for leave under escort was unlawful. The applicant was released, on 8 January 2010, by which date he would have spent ten years in that form of detention (Article 67d § 3 of the Criminal Code – see paragraph 51 below) It found that there was no risk that the applicant would commit serious offences resulting in considerable psychological or physical harm to the victims if released. The courts had repeatedly considered that he might commit only non-violent property offences if release. He died on 25 January 2010 and has been living in a residential care home in Erkelenz since then. accordingly, on 25 January 2010. He died on January 25, 2010, at the age of 77, after a long battle with cancer. He now lives in a care home with his wife and two children in an elderly care home. name: Michael Becker
train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained, in particular, that in the proceedings for the withdrawing of his driving licence he did not have a hearing before the Administrative Court. The Government were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Tichy, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Europe, Integration and Foreign Affairs. The application was communicated to the Government on 28 September 2009. The case was decided on 8 April 2012 by the Court of Appeal, with the majority of the decision in favour of the Austrian Government.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained, in particular, that in the proceedings for the withdrawing of his driving licence he did not have a hearing before the Administrative Court. The Austrian Government were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Tichy, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Europe, Integration and Foreign Affairs. The case was settled in favour of the applicant on a majority of the grounds raised by the Court of Appeal and the Government on a minority of the basis of the principle of freedom of expression. The applicant argued that the DAA should have obtained the report of a technical expert on the functioning of the breathlyser. The Lower Austria Regional Governor (Landeshauptmann) dismissed the applicant’s appeal. The applicant was ordered to follow driver improvement training before his driving licence would be returned. The Regional Governor concluded that refusing to undergo a breathalyser test was as serious as driving under the influence of alcohol because it prevented the authorities from verifying whether a person was actually drunk. The appeal had no suspensive effect because it was necessary to avoid the risk that a person lacking trustworthiness for road traffic might drive. The DAA issued a penal order (Straferkenntnis) and imposed a fine for refusal to take the breathalyser test. On 30 April 2001 the applicant appealed. On 27 September 2007 the Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint. Since no decision had been taken within the prescribed time limit of 15 months after the lodging of the appeal, the fine imposed by the DAA had expired ipso iure. The Administrative Court found that an oral hearing was not likely to contribute to the clarification of the case. The applicant had failed to raise any substantial arguments against these findings and had not shown that the assessment of the evidence carried out by the authorities was contradictory or implausible.

name: Albert Hénaf
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 65436/01) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 13 November 2000. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 24 January 2002 the Chamber declared the application admissible, while noting that the objections raised by the Government were inseparable from the examination of the merits.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant alleged that he had been subjected to treatment contrary to Article 3 of the convention. He was due for release from September 2001 onwards according to him, and from 17 February 2002 according to the Government. By a decision of 24 January 2002 the Chamber declared the application admissible, while noting that the objections raised by the Government were inseparable from the examination of the merits. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr R. Abraham, Director of Legal Affairs at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. In November 2000 the prisoner was taken to hospital with swollen glands in his throat. Two police officers were waiting for him at the hospital in order to supervise and guard him. For the rest of the day the prisoner remained handcuffed but not shackled. He filed a complaint against the police officers who had guarded him while he was in hospital. He alleged a violation of Article 803 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and of Article 3 of the Convention. The complaint also alleged ‘serious ill-treatment’, ‘assault’ and ‘torture’. The case is still being heard by the European Court of Human Rights. The application for legal aid was registered on 8 December and refused on 15 December 2000. On 11 April 2001 the applicant appealed on points of law against that judgment. The proceedings are currently pending before the Court of Cassation. Having been released on 1 October 2001 after completing his sentence, the applicant has subsequently been imprisoned in the context of separate proceedings. The applicant has since been released from prison. He is currently serving a three-year prison sentence. He has appealed against the order for payment of a security inadmissible for failure to comply with Article 503 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, by which an appeal by a prisoner must be lodged through the prison governor.

name: Christina Riepl
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 37040/02) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Winkler, Head of the International Law Departement at the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs. On 12 November 2003 the Court decided to communicate the application. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 37040/02) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) by two Austrian nationals, Franz and Christina Riepl. The applicants were born in 1935 and 1939 respectively and live in Freistadt. They applied for a building permit for an adjoining building with a garage on their property in April 1994. The Municipal Council granted the appeal and refused the building permit. The Regional Government dismissed the applicants’ appeal and remitted the case back to the Municipal Council. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicants reached an agreement with the Municipal Council to pay the fees incurred by the applicants’ representation in the proceedings so far. The applicants amended their request for a building permit in accordance with the newly established building scheme (Bebauungsplan) The Municipal Council quashed the building permit of 16 August 1994 and remitted the case back to the Mayor of Freistadt on 28 May 2001. On 15 January 2002 the applicants submitted the corrected plans for a double garage with a parking area. This decision was served upon the applicants' counsel on 4 April 2002. The application was rejected by the Regional Government on 8 October 2001.

name: Del Sol
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 46800/99) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the refusal of her application for legal aid to appeal to the Court of Cassation had infringed her right of access to a court. By a decision of 3 April 2001, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The case remained with the Chamber constituted within the former Third Section.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) The applicant alleged that the refusal of her application for legal aid to appeal to the Court of Cassation had infringed her right of access to a court. Paris Court of Appeal upheld all the provisions of the impugned judgment, with the exception of the decision relating to maintenance, which was reduced to FRF 1,000 monthly. The applicant's husband satisfied all the conditions on which the admissibility of the divorce petition depended, as he had offered to assign to the applicant his rights in property which the couple jointly owned in Italy. It further held that the applicant had failed to show that the divorce would cause her exceptional hardship, either psychologically or materially. The President of the Court of Cassation upheld the decision, holding that the Legal Aid Office had “found no arguable ground of appeal after assessing the facts of the case’.

name: Walter Buchholz

Balladore Pallieri, the President of the Court.

The case originated in an application against that State lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights in 1976. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. H. Mosler, the elected judge of German nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43) and Mr. G. Balladore Pallieri, the President of the Court (Rule 21 par. 3) (b) of the Rules of Court. On 4 October, the. President drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of the five other members, namely Mr. Thór Vilhjálmsson. and Mrs. Bindschedler-Robert. The Government’s memorial was received at the registry on 5 December. On 15 December, the Secretary to the Commission advised the Registrar that the Delegate would present his observations at the hearings. The oral hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 27 January. The Court heard addresses by Mrs. Maier for the Government and by Mr. Gaukur Jörundsson and Mr. Sojka for the Commission, as well as their replies to questions put by the Court. On 6 February, the Agent of the Government. and the applicant’S lawyer supplemented in writing their answers to certain questions put to them at the. hearings. Mr. Buchholz was born in 1918 and lives in Hamburg. He was mainly employed as a driver until the end of 1963 and thereafter as, in particular, controller of branch establishments. On 28 June 1974, he was given notice that he was dismissed with effect from 31 December of the same year as a result of rationalisation measures. On 10 July 1974, the applicant commenced an action before the Hamburg Labour Court claiming that his dismissal was “socially unjustified“ (“sozial ungerechtfertigt“) within the meaning of section 1 of the Unfair Dismissal Act (Kündigungsschutzgesetz) The Hamburg Labour Court delivered judgment on 8 January 1975 immediately after hearing the final submissions of the parties. It held that neither the notice of 28 June 1974 nor the extraordinary notice of 30 September 1974 had terminated the applicant’s contract. The Court also rejected an alternative request by the defendants for discharge (Auflösungsantrag) of the contract of employment in pursuance of section 7 of the Unfair Dismissal Act. It ordered the defendants to pay Mr. Buchholz DM 5,700 arrears of wages but dismissed the claim for future salary. The judgment was notified in writing to the parties on 25 February 1975. Court of Appeal on 13 March 1975. Court also raised the possibility of employing Mr. Buchholz in some other capacity. Court directed the defendants to submit within one month a chart setting out the firm’s commercial staff structure, indicating for each post whether it was suitable for the applicant and, if not, the reason why. The applicant was given one month to reply. The defendants filed the chart, with accompanying explanations, on 31 July; then, on 6 August, they replied to a written pleading from Mr. Buchanan. On 20 August 1975, the Court of Appeal ruled in favor of the defendants. Court of appeal on 16 May 1975 set the case down for hearing. The Court of Appeal decided to hold a hearing on 19 March 1976. It proposed a settlement whereby the contract of employment would be considered as having terminated on 31 December 1974 and the defendants would pay the applicant a lump sum of DM 34,200. The Court called on the parties to state their views by 30 April. By memorandum of 7 April, the defendants refused the settlement proposal; they referred to the “undisputed’ fact that the two notices of 30 September 1974 had been served on the applicant on the same day. On 12 November 1975, the applicant’s lawyer addressed to the Parliament (Bürgerschaft) of the Free and Hanseatic City of Hamburg a petition seeking measures to expedite proceedings before the labour courts. Mr. Buchholz denied that he had actually received the two notices of 30 September on that day. He asked the Court to question on his wife on this point, which was material for the purposes of Article 626 of the Civil Code (see paragraph 15 above). The Court acceded to this request. On 29 September the Court granted free legal aid for the applicant’s defence against the main appeal; it reserved its decision as regards his cross-appeal (see paragraphs 31 and 32 below) The applicant had sought from the Constitutional Court an order requiring the Court of Appeal to bring its consideration of the matter. The Court nevertheless decided that Mr. Buch holz, as well as the chief executive of the Dependorf firm and the four witnesses nominated by the defendants, should be heard on 11 January 1977. The case-file was sent to the Federal Constitutional Court. The presiding judge of the Third Chamber of the Labour Court of Appeal, which was dealing with the applicant’s case, retired on 19 November. The Court refused leave for the constitutional application to proceed: even supposing the application to be admissible, it did not offer sufficient prospects of success. The applicant wrote on 5 February to the Secretary to the. Commission - his petition to the Commission having been lodged on 18 December 1976 - to complain. of this decision, but according to the Government there is no trace in the record of the case. of his having entered any such objection before the Court of. Appeal. The Labour Court of Appeal delivered its judgment. It allowed the defendants’ appeal and dismissed the applicant’s cross-appeal, awarding the costs of the proceedings against him. On 26 April 1979, the Federal Court, after hearing the parties, proposed a settlement whereby the contract of employment would be considered as having terminated on 31 December 1974. The proposal was rejected by the defendants. On 10 May 1979, Mr. Buchholz challenged the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) The Federal Court dismissed the petition for review as unfounded. On 12 September, the applicant applied for free legal aid; his application was granted on 12 September. On 20 September, he asked for leave to petition notwithstanding expiry of the legal time-limit. The applicant complained of the length of the proceedings before the various labour courts, citing this factor as the cause of the contested decision. this decision before the Federal Constitutional Court alleging violation of several basic rights. The applicant claimed that the judgment being challenged was unsustainable as far as its reasoning was concerned (sachlich unhaltbar) and constituted an unacceptable domestic sanction intended to punish him for having taken his case to the Commission. On 19 July, the Constitutional Court refused leave for the constitutional application to proceed on the ground that it was inadmissible. As in 1976 (see paragraph 28 above), the Court had sat in judgment as a panel of three judges. The labour courts of appeal experienced a significant increase in their workload between 1974 and 1976. The incidence of appeals from labour court judgments rose, as compared with the previous year, by 23.1 per cent in 1974. The average length of proceedings progressed from 2.88 months in 1974 to 3.20 months in 1975, but then fell to 2.98 months in 1976, 2.79 months in 1977 and 2.53 months in 1978. The Government tabled in the legislative assemblies in 1978 a Bill designed, amongst other things, to expedite proceedings before the labour courts. The resultant Act entered into force on 1 July 1979. On 7 December 1977, the Commission declared the application admissible. The Commission expressed the opinion that the requirements of Article 6 par. 1 (art. 6-1) had not been observed. No issue arose under Articles 3, 8, or 12. The Government made the following final submission at the hearings on 27 January 1981: “[We] request a finding that the Convention has not been violated in the instant case.’” “The Government. requests a finding. that the convention has not be violated. in this instant case’. “ ‘We. request aFinding that the. Convention hasnot been violated’,’ said the Government. ‘‘[We]. request a. finding that [the] Convention hasNot been violated.

name: Ingrid Hoffmann
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 13 April 1992. It originated in an application (no. 12875/87) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by an Austrian, Mrs Ingrid Hoffmann, on 20 February 1987. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8, 9 and 14 of the Convention. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality, and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 13 April 1992. It originated in an application (no. 12875/87) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by an Austrian, Mrs Ingrid Hoffmann, on 20 February 1987. The applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent her (Rule 30). The President gave him leave to use the German language during the proceedings (Rule 27 para. 3). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality, and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 January 1993. Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court, replaced Mr Ryssdal, who was unable to attend. There appeared before the Court: for the Government Mr W. Okresek, Federal Chancellery, Agent, Mr F. Haug, Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs, Adviser; for the Commission Mrs J. Liddy, Delegate; and for the applicant Mrs Ingrid Hoffmann. The Court heard their addresses as well as replies to the questions of some of its members. The hearing was the first of its kind in the European Court of Human Rights. The applicant claimed that she was better placed to take care of the children, being in a position to devote herself to them completely. She alleged that Mr S. did not even provide for their maintenance, as he was both legally and morally bound to do. She acknowledged, however, that she intended to bring the children up in her own faith. The children had stronger emotional ties with the applicant, having lived with her for a year and a half already, and separating them from her might cause them psychological harm. It followed that it was preferable to leave the children with the mother. By decision of 8 January 1986, the District Court granted parental rights to the applicant. In no case are parents’ religious convictions as such a relevant criterion in deciding on parental rights and duties pursuant to Article 177 para. 2 of the Civil Code. These rights cannot be refused to a parent or withheld from him for the sole reason that he or she belongs to a religious minority. In the concrete case it needs to be examined whether the mother’s religious convictions have a negative influence on her upbringing of the children which should be taken into account. It appears in particular that Ingrid S. would not allow blood transfusions to be given to her children; that for herself she rejects communal celebration of such customary holidays as Christmas or Easter. The Regional Court rejected the appeal by decision of 14 March 1986. The mother’s religious convictions do not deprive Martin and Sandra of the possibility of celebrating these holidays in the usual way, so that no detriment to the children can be found in this regard either. Careful consideration must lead to the conclusion that in spite of more difficult social integration, as discussed above, it appears to be more in the interest of the children's welfare to grant parental rights to the mother than to transfer them to the father. The Jehovah's Witnesses, formerly known as Serious Bible Students, are not outlawed in Austria; it may therefore be assumed that their objectives neither infringe the law nor offend morality. Father's objections against assigning parental rights and duties to the mother cannot in the final instance be decisive. New points raised on appeal cannot cast doubt on the first-instance decision as regards the children’s welfare. The appellant overlooks the fact that, in view of the paramount importance of the children's welfare, the way in which they reached the place where they are currently being taken care of is not necessarily decisive. Even illegal conduct would be of relevance only to the extent that it might, in an individual case, be possible to infer therefrom a lack of suitability for care or upbringing. No expert medical opinion was sought regarding the question, which was raised anew on appeal, of blood transfusions. Mr S. lodged an appeal on points of law (außerordentlicher Revisionsrekurs) with the Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) The Supreme Court overturned the judgment of the Innsbruck Regional Court, granting parental rights to Mr S. instead of the applicant. It gave the following reasons: “The appellant has not hitherto claimed that the children belonged to the Roman Catholic faith; however, he has stated, and it has in fact been established, that the mother is bringing them up according to the principles of the Jehovah’s Witnesses’ teaching”. The children do not belong to the faith of the Jehovah’s Witnesses, their education according to the principles of this sect contravenes Article 2, paragraph 2, of the 1921 Act. The lower courts also failed in their decisions to give due consideration to the children's welfare. The stress caused by being transferred to the care of the other parent, which in any case is usually transitory, has to be accepted in their own best interests. The file contains no documentary basis for the assumption that a change to another carer ‘would with a high degree of probability cause the children serious psychological harm’ ... . Even though it is preferable for young children to be taken care of by their mother, this applies only provided that all other things are equal. The Jehovah’s Witnesses form a particular religious movement. It originated in America in the 1870s. A central feature of doctrine is the belief that the Holy Scriptures in the original Hebrew and Greek are the revealed word of Jehovah God and must be taken as literal truth. The refusal to accept blood transfusions is based on several scriptural references, most notably Acts 15: 28-29, which reads: “For we ourselves have favored adding no further burden to you, except these necessary things, to keep abstaining from things sacrificed to idols and from blood and from things strangled and from fornication. If you carefully keep yourselves from these things ...“

name: Franz Xaver Kronfeldner
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 21906/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the retrospective extension of his preventive detention from a period of ten years, which had been the maximum for such detention under the legal provisions applicable at the time of his offence, violated Article 5. The President decided on 20 May 2010 that the proceedings in the application at issue be resumed and granted priority to the application (Rule 41 of the Rules of Court). In view of the fact that the judgment of 17 December 2009 in the case of M. v. Germany became final on 10 May 2010, the Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Franz Xaver Kronfeldner alleged, in particular, that the retrospective extension of his preventive detention from a period of ten years, which had been the maximum for such detention under the legal provisions applicable at the time of his offence, violated Article 5. The applicant was born in 1958 and was in Straubing Prison until his preventive. detention was declared terminated and his provisional detention in a suitable institution under. the Therapy Detention Act was ordered on 28 November 2011. He is currently detained in StraUBing Psychiatric Hospital. Regensburg Regional Court convicted the applicant of rape. It sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment and ordered his placement in preventive detention pursuant to Article 66 § 1 of the Criminal Code. The court found that in July 1989, some four months after his release from prison, the applicant had raped a woman whom he had come across in Regensburg at night. The applicant was accordingly transferred to Straubing Psychiatric Hospital on 15 December 2005. On 25 October 2007 the Regensberg Regional Court prolonged the execution of the applicant’s preventive detention in a psychiatric hospital. The execution of his preventive detention was interrupted in order to execute the case. Regensburg Regional Court considered that it was very likely that the applicant, if released, would commit further serious offences resulting in considerable physical or psychological harm to the victims. The court quashed its decision of 26 October 2005 to execute the applicant’s preventive detention in a psychiatric hospital and decided to retransfer the applicant to prison in accordance with Article 67a § 3 of the Criminal Code. The applicant was accordingly transferred from Straubing Psychiatric Hospital to Straubed Prison on 19 June 2008. The decision of the Nuremberg Court of Appeal was made on 22 July 2008 and the applicant was sentenced to another sentence of imprisonment. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal as ill‑founded. The reasons why the applicant's therapy in Straubing Psychiatric Hospital had not been successful were irrelevant for the question whether there was still a risk that the applicant, if released, might commit further sexual offences. The psychiatric expert report drawn up by expert K. was clear and conclusive and complied with the minimum standards required for such reports. The court further referred to the leading judgment dated 5 February 2004 of the Federal Constitutional Court, in which the latter had considered the retroactive extension of a convicted person's preventive detention beyond a period of ten years to be constitutional. The applicant was considered by the Straubing Prison authorities to be a self-confident, demanding and mistrustful person. Since July 2009 he has been working in the prison’s furniture factory. From 2002 to 2004 he participated in a discussion group in prison. The applicant did not make any of the therapies available – notably a group or possibly individual social therapy for sexual offenders – for lack of motivation. He consistently refused the treatment offered, questioning the therapists’ expertise. He was not granted any relaxations in the execution of the preventive detention order against him for fear of abuse. The Federal Court of Justice decided to adjourn the case pending a decision of its grand senate on the legal question at issue. The Nuremberg Court of Appeal quashed the decision of the Regensburg Regional Court of 26 July 2010. It found that, having regard to the criteria set up by the Federal Constitutional Court in its judgment dated 4 May 2011, the applicant’s preventive detention was disproportionate. It had not been shown that the applicant, owing to specific circumstances, was highly likely to commit the most serious crimes of violence or sexual offences if released. The applicant had not previously been placed in a psychiatric hospital under section 1 of the Bavarian (Mentally Ill Persons’) Placement Act (see paragraph 39 below). The applicant was transferred to Straubing Psychiatric Hospital thereupon. The court in the case of M. v. Germany (no. 19359/04, §§ 45-78, 17 December 2009) orders preventive detention in addition to a prison sentence. The perpetrator must have been sentenced twice already, to at least one year’s imprisonment in each case, for intentional offences committed prior to the new offence. A comprehensive assessment of the perpetrator and his acts must reveal that, owing to his propensity to commit serious offences, the perpetrator presents a danger to the general public. The court can review at any time whether the further execution of the preventive detention order should be suspended and a measure of probation applied. If the maximum duration has expired, the detainee shall be released. The detention of mentally ill persons is provided for, first of all, in the Criminal Code as a measure of correction and prevention if the detention is ordered in relation to an unlawful act committed by the person concerned. The former maximum duration of a first period of preventive detention was abolished. Transfer for enforcement of a different measure of corrections and prevention than the measure ordered in the judgment against the person is permitted. The court may quash that decision if it later emerges that no success can be achieved by placing the person in a psychiatric hospital or a detoxification facility (Article 67a § 3). The duration of the placement is determined by the provisions which apply to the measure. A court may order a person’s placement in a psychiatric hospital at the request of the authorities of a town or county if the person concerned is mentally ill and thereby poses a severe threat to public security and order. Such an order may only be executed as long as no measure under Article 63 of the Criminal Code has been taken (section 1 § 2 of the said Act) The Federal Constitutional Court held that all provisions on the retrospective prolongation of the complainants’ preventive detention beyond the former ten-year maximum period were constitutional. The Act on Therapy and Detention of Mentally Disturbed Violent Offenders (Therapy Detention Act – Gesetz zur Therapierung und Unterbringung psychisch gestörter Gewalttäter) entered into force. The Federal Constitutional Court held that all provisions of the Criminal Code on the imposition and duration of preventive detention at issue were incompatible with the fundamental right to liberty. It found that those provisions did not satisfy the constitutional requirement of establishing a difference between preventive detention and detention for serving a term of imprisonment (Abstandsgebot) These provisions included, in particular, Article 66 of the criminal Code in its version in force since 27 December 2003. The court ruled that the provisions declared incompatible with Basic Law remained applicable until the entry into force of new legislation and until 31 May 2013 at the most. In relation to detainees whose preventive detention had been prolonged or ordered retrospectively, the courts had to examine without delay whether the persons concerned were highly likely to commit the most serious crimes of violence or sexual offences. The Federal Constitutional Court relied on the interpretation of Article 5 and Article 7 of the Convention. It stressed, in particular, that the constitutional requirement of establishing a difference between preventive detention and detention for serving a term of imprisonment required an individualised and intensified offer of therapy and care to the persons concerned. In line with the Court’s findings in the case of M. v. Germany, it was necessary to provide a high level of care by a team of multi-disciplinary staff and to offer the detainees an Individualised therapy if the standard therapies available in the institution did not have prospects of success. The Court attempted to avoid breaches of the convention in its interpretation of the Constitution.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 9120/80) against the Republic of Austria, lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 1 September 1980. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr. G. Wiarda, the President of the Court (Rule 21 § 3 (b)). On 27 March 1985, the. President drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of the five other members, namely. Mrs. D. Bindschedler-Robert, J. Pinheiro Farinha, Mr E. García de Enterría, and Mrs. J. pinheiro. President Wiarda asked the Government, the Delegate of the Commission and Mr. Unterpertinger’s representative for their views on the need for a written procedure. The Government and the applicant produced documents at the hearings. The hearings were held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard their addresses as well as their replies to its questions. The applicant, an Austrian national born in 1938, lives in Wörgl. He complains of criminal proceedings brought against him. The hearing was held in Strasbourg on 3 February 1986. It was adjourned until 5 March 1986. The applicant claims his wife and step-daughter attacked him with a paper-knife and gashed his forehead close to his eyebrow. He admitted that he had pushed his wife at the time and had tried unsuccessfully to slap his step- daughter in the face. The two women had fought back, and she had pulled her step-father’s hair but had not hit him; she had not seen her mother strike him with the paper- knife. Miss Tappeiner admitted having called her father a ‘convict’ that morning, and said he had responded by slapping her in the. face, but without injuring her. She added that a doctor had issued a certificate in respect of her own injury. Alois Unterpertinger was suspected of causing actual bodily harm (Körperverletzung) in 1979. His wife and step-daughter were accused of attacking him with a paper-knife during a quarrel. He himself had allegedly hit his step- daughter in the face and scratched her slightly just below the right eye. The incident was reported to the Wörgl police on 14 September 1979. The applicant’s injuries had been described as “slight’ by the doctor, according to the police report. He had appeared in person at the police station ten minutes later holding a paper knife. The report was accompanied by several documents. Alois Unterpertinger accused of kicking his wife in the arm. His wife claimed he had broken her thumb in a fight on 9 September. The court acquitted her on 28 January 1980 after hearing evidence from her and her husband. Innsbruck Public Prosecutor’s Department decided on 9 November 1979 to open an investigation against the applicant in respect of the two incidents. The investigation (Vorerhebungen) began on 10 November 1979. On 3 December 1979, Mrs. Unter pertinger appeared before a judge at Kufstein, who told her that, as the wife of the accused (Beschuldigter), she was entitled to refuse to give evidence. The case was heard on 10 March 1980 by a judge of the Innsbruck Regional Court (Landesgericht), sitting alone. The applicant pleaded not guilty. He admitted that he had hit his step-daughter on the head, but not that she had injured her. He added that he was not sufficiently agile to have been able to kick her thumb. The Regional Court then called Mrs. Unterpertinger and Miss Tappeiner. On being told by the court of their right to refuse to give evidence (see paragraph 16 above), they replied that they wished to avail themselves of that right. At the request of the Public Prosecutor’s Department, the documents it had mentioned in its application for leave to prosecute (Strafantrag) were read out. Mr. Unterpertinger was found guilty of causing actual bodily harm and causing grievous bodily harm to his wife. He was sentenced to six months’ imprisonment. He appealed on 9 April 1980. The court found no mitigating circumstances; on the contrary, it saw the applicant’s criminal record as an aggravating circumstance. The appeal proceedings were held at Kufstein, in Berlin, Germany, on 10 March 1980. Mr UnterPertinger claimed that the judgment of 10 March was null and void. In spite of Article 152 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, his former wife and step-daughter, whose statements to the police had formed the sole basis of his conviction, had not been informed at the time of the conviction. The Court of Appeal sat on 4 June 1980. The applicant requested that evidence should be taken from several witnesses, including two doctors, a police officer, a neighbour and his own mother, step-daughter and former wife. The court decided to re-examine the evidence submitted to the court of first instance and to supplement it (Wiederholung und Ergänzung) by having the file on the divorce proceedings read out and hearing testimony from the wife of Mr. Unterpertinger’s brother. She was unable to say whether the applicant’'s former wife had had a bandage on her. Court refused to admit the remaining evidence proffered, as to part, on the ground that the circumstances to which it related were of no importance. Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal immediately after the hearing on 4 June 1980. The victims’ statements to the police were plausible and credible; their account of the incident was logically coherent. The sentence imposed was consistent with the degree of his guilt (schuld) Mr. Unterpertinger was convicted on the two counts against him and sentenced to two years in prison. He served his sentence in prison in 1983 and was released on licence in 1988. He is still serving his prison sentence. The applicant served his sentence from 22 September 1980 to 22 March 1981. The Commission declared the application admissible on 8 July 1983. In its report of 11 October 1984, the Commission expressed the opinion that there had been no breach of paragraph 3 (d) of Article 6 (art. 6-3-d) The full text of the Commission’s opinion and of the separate opinions contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to the present judgment. At the hearing on 17 February 1986, the Court was requested by the Government, “to hold that in the present case the provisions of the European Convention on Human Rights have not been violated“

name: Stavroula Boca
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the civil proceedings to which she had been a party had been excessively long. The Court declared the application admissible and invited the parties to submit additional observations on one question (Rule 59 § 1). The Government filed their written observations within the time allowed, but the applicant did not. The case was assigned to the newly composed First Section of the Court on 1 November 2001. It was decided in favour of the applicant by a majority of three to one, with the Government dissenting.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the civil proceedings to which she had been a party had been excessively long. The application relates to two sets of proceedings. The first concerns the divorce proceedings proper before the court of first instance. The second concerns the interim measures in respect of which Article 1280 of the Judicial Code gives the summary applications court special power and jurisdiction to hear applications for interim measures. The case was decided in favour of the applicant on 12 June 2001. The Belgian Government did not file their written observations within the time allowed, but the applicant did. The case was heard by the Brussels Court of First Instance on 17 March 1998. The parties filed their main pleadings before the hearing of 17 June 1998. At the hearing the applicant's husband stated that he was withdrawing his appeal. On 16 May 2000 the parties filed joint pleadings with the registry of the Court of Appeal stating that they intended to withdraw from the proceedings. The divorce decree was registered on 24 October 2000. The court gave judgment on 16 March 2000 acknowledging that the appeal had been withdrawn. The case was settled by the High Court of Justice on 19 April 2003. The judge ruled that the father of the couple's two children had had custody of the children since the couple had separated in 1995. The mother had been granted renewed contact with the children. The parties have agreed to continue to comply with the interim measures set out in the order of 26 June 1998. that counsel for the parties had stated at the hearing that the parties would continue to Compliance with interim measures. The parties are expected to meet the terms of the order by the end of the year. The case has been adjourned until September 6, 2013. The hearing was due to take place at the High Court in London, England, and is expected to last for around two weeks. It is hoped that the case will be settled within the next few weeks. name: Viera Sramek
train_texts: The present case was referred to the Court, within the period of three months laid down by Articles 32 para. 1 and 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The purpose of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1.
