eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 8790/79) against Austria lodged with the Commission on 19 September 1979 under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mrs. Viera Sramek, a United States citizen. The purpose of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1. In response to the inquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyer who would represent her (Rule 30). The Court heard addresses by Mr. Türk, Legal Adviser in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Agent, Mr. M. Matzka, Federal Chancellery, and Mr. G. Liebl, Office of the Government of the Tyrol. During the course of the hearings, the Government filed a document. The Court decided on 27 March that the proceedings should continue without resumption of hearings (Rule 26). The Chamber decided under Rule 50 of the Rules of Court to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. The Government also replied to two supplementary questions which the Registrar had addressed to them on the instructions of the President. The applicant, who is a United States citizen, lives in Munich in the Federal Republic of Germany. Wishing to build a holiday residence in Hopfgarten, a village in the Austrian Tyrol, she approached, with the assistance of municipal officials, the owners of a plot of land which had until then been used for agricultural purposes. Sale negotiations began in 1971 and apparently led, in 1973, to an initial contract. One year later, Mrs. Sramek paid to the vendors the greater part of the agreed price. However, the definitive contract was not drawn up until 13 January 1977. The contract could not take effect unless it were approved by the local Real Property Transactions Authority (Grundverkehrsbehörde) There were, in fact, already 110 foreign landowners in Hopfgarten and it could be seen from a series of decisions of the Regional Authority that this municipality was one of those where the danger of foreign domination was imminent. The contract in question was therefore contrary to social and economic interests within the meaning of the above-mentioned Act. The applicant received a copy of the appeal but did not file any observations in reply. According to the minutes of the hearing, the rapporteur presented the facts and read out the expert opinions and observations received during the course of the investigation; the latter concerned, inter alia, the percentage of the parcels of land in HopFGarten which was in foreign hands. The applicant stated that she had signed the initial contract (Erstvertrag), which could not then be found, on 13 March 1973. The Transactions Officer then requested the Authority to uphold his appeal on the ground that as there was already a risk of foreign domination in Hopfgarten, the acquisition of the land in question would be contrary to social and political interests. The Regional Authority upheld the appeal: referring to the above-mentioned section 4(2)(a) of the 1970/1973 Act, it refused to approve the transfer of title. Its decision (Bescheid) was dated 16 June. The Authority noted firstly that according to a statement from the municipality of HopFGarten, which had not been challenged at the hearing, there were 110 foreign landowners. There were 4,800 inhabitants and 1,100 families in the locality. Mrs. Sramek was intending to use the land in question for the construction of a holiday residence. The acquisition contemplated was therefore prejudicial to economic and social interests and thus fell foul of, in particular, section 4(2)(a) of the 1970/1973 Act. The Regional Authority rejected the applicant’s argument that she had already concluded a contract in 1973, that is at a time when American citizens were treated on an equal footing with Austrians by virtue of a bilateral treaty dating from 1928. In its view, the 1928 treaty had not established any equality between citizens of the two States in the area concerned. Mrs. Sramek alleged that the Regional Authority had applied section 4(2)(a) of the 1970/1973 Act in a misconceived (denkunmöglich) manner by adopting an illogical approach. The Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal on 3 March 1979 (Erkenntnisse und Beschlüsse des Verfassungsgerichtshofes, 1979, vol. 44, no. 8501). It took the view that the Authority was indeed a “tribunal“ within the meaning of Article 6 (art. 6) ofThe Convention. It gave decisions which the executive could neither annul nor vary. The Constitutional Court gave judgment without holding a hearing. The Government stated that during the last ten years or so the Regional Authority had not approved any acquisition of real property in Hopfgarten by a foreigner. They supplied a list of thirteen refusals in the period between July 1973 and February 1983. According to the applicant, the list was insufficiently detailed to be conclusive. In the Tyrol (see paragraph 9 above), section 15(1) of the 1970/1973 Act obliges the purchaser to seek such approval within two months of the conclusion of the contract. No entry can be made in the land register until the transaction has been approved by the competent authority. The decisions of the Farm Commission are taken by majority vote (section 13(2) of the 1970/1973 Act); they are subject to appeal to the Regional Authority. If the case is referred to it, the Regional Real Property Transactions Authority established at the Office of the Land Government takes a decision as the second and final instance. Its membership varies according to the subject-matter of the contract to be examined. In the case of agricultural or forestry land - whether the buyer be Austrian or foreign - its voting members are: “(a) a person experienced in real property transaction matters, who shall act as chairman; (b) a member of the judiciary (Richterstand)” constitutional court held that the Act did not fix the duration of the members’ term of office, conferred on the said Government the power of appointing the members. The Tyrolean legislature amended, by the same Act of 28 November 1973, the provisions in section 13 concerning, inter alia, exercise of the office of member of the Regional Authority. Only Austrian citizens who have reached the age of 25 years and are in full possession of their legal rights shall be eligible for appointment as members or substitute members. Persons who by reason of a criminal conviction are disqualified from jury service or from acting as lay assessors shall be ineligible. Re-appointment is possible. Members and substitute members shall hold office for three years. Procedure before the Real Property Transactions Authorities is governed by the General Administrative Procedure Act 1950 (Allgemeines Verwaltungsverfahrensgesetz) The parties are entitled to consult the case-file and must be given an opportunity of presenting their arguments. The parties have the right to be heard (rechtliches Gehör) and, inter alia, to adduce their arguments and evidence and comment on facts presented and submissions made by other persons appearing, witnesses or experts. In certain circumstances which may give reason to doubt his impartiality, the civil servant concerned must arrange to be replaced (section 7). Under Article 3 para. 1, the Authorities shall deliberate and vote in the absence of the parties, if appropriate after oral hearings. The right to consult the case-file (Akteneinsicht), guaranteed by Article 17 of the General Administrative Procedure Act, does not extend. The authorities’ resolutions (Beschlüsse) must be recorded, but may be altered as long as they remain unpublished. Decisions of a Regional Authority may be challenged before the Constitutional Court but not before the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) The full text of the Commission’s opinion and of the separate opinion contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to the present judgment. The Republic of Austria requested the Court “to hold that in the present case the provisions of paragraph 1 of Article 6 (art. 6-1) of the Convention ... were not violated”. “As a consequence, as a consequence the facts underlying the dispute do not indicate any breach by the Republic ofAustria of its obligations under the Convention’, the Government said. The Court agreed to hear the case and ruled in favour of Austria in January 1984. The case was settled in March 1984, with the Austrian government calling for the case to be re-opened. The U.S. government appealed the decision to the European Court of Human Rights.

Fifoot, Legal Counsellor, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Barrister-at-Law, Agent and Counsel, Sir Francis Vallat, K.C.M.G., Q.C., Professor of International Law, King's College, London. Sidney Elmer Golder was convicted in 1965 of robbery with violence and was sentenced to 15 years' imprisonment. In 1969 he was serving his sentence in Parkhurst Prison on the Isle of Wight. On the evening of 24 October 1969 a serious disturbance occurred in a recreation area of the prison where Golder happened to be. On 26 October Golder, together with other prisoners suspected of having participated in the disturbance, was segregated from the main body of prisoners. On 28 and 30 October, Golder. was interviewed by police officers. At the second of these interviews he was. informed that it had been alleged that he had assaulted a prison officer; he. was warned that “the facts would be reported in order that consideration could be given’. The facts of the case may be summarised as follows. Golder wrote to a Chief Constable on 4 November 1969 about the disturbance of 24 October and the ensuing hardships it had entailed for him. But the prison governor stopped these letters since Golder had failed to raise the subject-matter thereof through the authorised channels beforehand. On 7 November, another prison officer reported that: “... during the riot of that night I spent the majority of the time in the T.V. room with the prisoners who were not participating in the disturbance. Golder was in this room with me and to the best of my knowledge took no part in the riot. His presence with me can be borne out by officer ... who observed us both from the outside.“ In England the matter of contacts of convicted prisoners with persons outside their place of detention is governed by the Prison Act 1952. The rules made by the Home Secretary in the exercise of this power are the Prison Rules 1964, which were laid before Parliament and have the status of a Statutory Instrument. The relevant provisions concerning communications between prisoners and persons outside prison are contained in Rules 33, 34 and 37 as follows: “Letters and visits generally Rule 33 (1) The Secretary of State may, with a view to securing discipline and good order or the prevention of crime in the interests of any persons, impose restrictions, either generally or in a particular case, upon the communications to be permitted. Golder was released from prison on parole on 12 July 1972. The case was brought before the European Court of Human Rights. Golder was sentenced to 20 years in prison for fraud. He was also sentenced to 10 years for perverting the course of justice. The Court ruled that Golder had a right to access to a lawyer and that the restrictions imposed by the UK authorities were inconsistent with Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) The Government made objection to this opinion of the Commission but stated in their memorial that they no longer wished to argue the issue. The final submissions were made to the Court at the oral hearing on 12 October 1974. The right of access to the courts is not unlimited in the case of persons under detention. The Government submit that in consequence the refusal of the United Kingdom Government to allow the applicant in this case to consult a lawyer was not a violation of Article 6 (art. 6) The Government further submit that control over the applicant’s correspondence while he was in prison was a necessary consequence of the deprivation of his liberty. The Court is requested to reply to the questions: (1) Does Article 6 para. 6-1 of the European Convention on Human Rights secure to persons desiring to institute civil proceedings a right to access the courts? (2) If Article. 6 is found to confer a right, does the Court hold that the restriction imposed was within the degree of restraint permitted by law? Convicted prisoner who wishes to write to his lawyer in order to institute civil proceedings rely on the protection given in Article 8 (art. 8) of the Convention to respect for correspondence. Does the facts of the present case disclose the existence of a violation of Article 6 and of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights?“Do the answers given to the foregoing questions, according to the Facts of the Present Case, disclose theexistence of a violated right of access to a lawyer?” asks the European Court of Human Rights in a ruling on the case. The question is answered at the end of the article.

name: Antonius Adrianus van der Tang
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 18 July 1994 by the Government of the Kingdom of Spain. eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 18 July 1994 by the Government of the Kingdom of Spain. It originated in an application (no. 19382/92) lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Netherlands national, Mr Antonius Adrianus van der Tang, on 2 December 1991. The applicant had complained of the unreasonable length of pre-trial detention but who had absconded and evaded trial after being released on bail. The Commission's request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (Art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby Spain recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court. Antonius Adrianus van der Tang was found driving a lorry which contained 1,300 kg of hashish. He was also found in possession of a pistol with its serial number chiselled off and of a radio pre-tuned to a station which coincided with that of another set found. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg on 20 February 1995. The Court heard addresses by the Government, the applicant's lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission as well as replies to its questions. The hearing was the first to be held in the European Court of Human Rights since it was established. Mr van der Tang was arrested on 25 May 1989 in Bayona, Vigo. He had only been driving for about ten minutes when he was arrested. The drugs were in the possession of Luciano Núñez, who was also arrested (see paragraph 32 below) At least eight more people were subsequently detained for allegedly being involved in a three-stage operation to deliver about 7,000 kg of hashish. An appeal by the applicant against this order appears to have been dismissed on 25 September 1989. The applicant's detention was confirmed on 18 November 1989 (auto de procesamiento) A judge decided that the available evidence was sufficient to charge the applicant with an offence against public health and unlawful possession of a firearm. Mr van der Tang lodged with investigating judge no. 1 his first applications for provisional release. Arguing that he had throughout been unaware of the real nature of the consignment. He insisted that he was not involved with any drug-trafficking organisation. He further complained that during his four-month detention he had only been questioned twice by the judge - in May and June 1989. The ground for the decision was the seriousness of the offences - illegal possession of a firearm and drug trafficking in large quantities. The second offence in itself attracting a prison sentence of “prisión menor en su grado medio’ (that is, from two years, four months and one day to four years and two months) Authorities had launched a nationwide operation (Operación Nécora) to combat a large-scale drug-trafficking organisation. Central investigating judge no. 5 in the Audiencia Nacional, Madrid, was put in charge of the overall investigation. The applicant's case was considered to be closely linked with other files relating to NéCora and was therefore transferred to Madrid on 29 October 1990. He was now charged not only with an offence against public health and unlawful possession of a firearm of foreign origin (see paragraph 10 above) but also with smuggling and criminal association (sections 173 and 174 of the Criminal Code) An appeal by the applicant against these orders which included a request for release was eventually rejected on 8 July 1991. Van der Tang was detained in January 1991. In March 1991 he applied for his detention to be extended to four years. The application was dismissed by the Constitutional Court in September 1991. Mr van der Tang filed a new application for release on bail in April 1992. The case was sent to the Third Criminal Division of the Audiencia Nacional for trial. Van der Tang has been in detention for over three years. He was released on bail on 11 June 1992 subject to the following conditions: (a) the applicant was to pay in cash a security of 8 million pesetas; (b) he was to give an address and inform the court of any subsequent change; and (c) he wasn't to leave Spanish territory. He could have been tried in Galicia several months ago, when the Pontevedra public prosecutor did not oppose his provisional release. It is possible to rule out his being able to conceal or suppress evidence. The court simply took the view that it was just another factor which, combined with the accused's lack of close ties with Spain, could lend support to the idea that he might be likely to seek to evade trial. This type of fear, which is always relative, cannot in such circumstances have the effect of inexorably making the accused serve in advance the sentence which may be imposed on him. This is particularly so as the accused has shown, at least to some extent, that he is able to remain on Spanish territory. On 23 December 1992 the applicant. travelled by car from Spain to the Netherlands. to spend Christmas with his family. This request was refused by the Audiencia Nacional on 24 November 1992 in view of the obvious risk of absconding. On 9 July 1993 the police informed the court that the applicant's whereabouts were unknown. The court ordered the applicant and his surety - his wife - to appear before it on 23 July 1993 at a hearing concerning the forfeiture of the bail. However, the summons could not be served on him, as he no longer lived at the address he had originally given the Spanish authorities. By that time the case file ran to more than 22,000 pages. In respect of the applicant, the public prosecutor demanded a total prison sentence of fourteen years and a fine of 60 million pesetas. On 31 July 1993 the Audiencia Nacional, noting that the applicant had failed to comply with the conditions attached to his release, dismissed the objection and ordered his arrest. The trial took place in Madrid from 20 September 1993 to 24 May 1994. Mr van der Tang did not attend it and could therefore not be tried pursuant to section 841 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Luciano Núñez (see paragraph 8 above) was held to have played a leading role in importing very large quantities of hashish. He was accordingly sentenced to a total of thirteen years' imprisonment and a fine of 100 million pesetas.

name: Asim Sahin

On 11 October 2001 the Chamber delivered its judgment in which it held, by five votes to two, that there had been a violation of Article 8 of the Convention. He relied on Articles 8 and 14 of the convention.

The Turkish Government, who had been informed of their right to intervene under Article 36, did not make use of this right. The application was communicated to the Government on 18 October 2012 and the Government made its observations on the admissibility and merits of the application. In 1999 a similar association was founded in Germany under the name of Deniz Feneri Dernegi e.V. (hereinafter ‘Deniz Fengi’) by G., one of the other shareholders and managing directors of Euro 7 Fernseh- und Marketing GmbH. During that programme, broadcast in Turkey and in Germany, the association reported on charitable aid projects being run by it and appealed for monetary donations. In 2006 the Frankfurt am Main prosecution authorities (Staatsanwaltschaft) launched investigations against the applicant and several co-suspects, including G., on suspicion of fraudulently using the majority of funds donated to the associations. The court’s findings were primarily based on confessions made by T., E. and G. following a plea bargain reached between the court, the prosecution authorities and the defence. The court was therefore satisifed that G. had not been at the top of the criminal organisation‘s hierarchy but had received orders from its leaders residing in Turkey. The judgment refers on several occasions to the role that the heads of the. criminal organisation in Turkey played in connection with the use of donated funds for non-charitable. purposes. In that context the applicant is given the full first and last name of the accused. Part VI stipulates that the accused are to bear the costs of the proceedings. Parts IV and V contain the legal assessment of the offences committed by the accused and the determination of their relative guilt. The most relevant passages of the judgment in parts II to V of its reasoning read as follows: “The accused G. and the persons in charge of Kanal 7 in Turkey were ... aware that donations collected in the German association’s [Deniz Feneri] name would only partly be used for charitable purposes or social projects.” The accused T. was not aware of the exact amount of donated funds that had been used for non-charitable purposes. However he endorsed appeals for further donations while knowing that they were to a large extent going to beused for unauthorised purposes. The separately prosecuted Zekeriya Karaman was accorded a pre-eminent role in this respect. The circumstances of the case (Sachverhalt) have been established (steht fest) on the basis of the confessions made by the accused and further evidence obtained in the course of the trial as set out in the record of the hearing. The Chamber did not follow G.’s submissions that he alone had decided on the unauthorised use of donated funds without consulting the persons behind the scenes in Turkey. The accused T. is guilty of fraud committed in his capacity as successive joint offender (in sukzessiver Mittäterschaft) pursuant to Articles 263 and 25 § 2 of the German Criminal Code. T. was an executing organ rather than a decision maker (mehr ausführendes als bestimmendes Organ) in the fraud. He could not decide alone on the unauthorised use of the donated funds but only develop ideas that ultimately had to be approved by the persons behind the scenes in Turkey. [T.’s] confession was not limited to his own participation in the commission of the offence. He also revealed his knowledge regarding the background and in particular concerning the personsbehind the scenes. By keeping unofficial accounts [E.] made a significant contribution to the functioning of the overall system. (p. 30) The Federal Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s constitutional complaint as inadmissible (file no. 2 BvR 2540/08). The Constitutional Court reiterated its established case-law according to which, by virtue of the constitutionally guaranteed principle of the presumption of innocence, no measures effectively amounting to a penalty could be taken against an accused without his guilt having been established beforehand in the course of a fair trial. However, in the context of criminal proceedings the presumption. of innocence did not prevent the law-enforcement authorities from making an assessment. as to whether and to what degree a person could be suspected of. having committed a criminal offence. Claim was brought against the applicant by Turkish authorities in 2009. A request for legal assistance was sent to the Turkish authorities on 20 January 2009 with a view to obtaining the applicant’s examination in Turkey. No information was submitted to the Court as regards compliance with that request. The applicant could not be regarded as guilty on the basis of that judgment and was still protected by the principle of the presumption of innocence. The fact that the establishment of the facts by the Regional Court not only concerned the accused, who were convicted at the end of the proceedings, but also the applicant was an inevitable consequence of the fact that in complex criminal proceedings it was hardly ever possible to conduct and terminate proceedings against all the accused simultaneously.

The Convention on the Extradition of Criminals between Switzerland and the Republic of Argentina, signed on 21 November 1906, has been binding on both countries since 1912. It lays down the formal and substantive conditions applying to extradition between the two countries. It does not, either expressly or tacitly, deal with the methods to be used by the courts for supervising detention with a view to extradition. It is therefore Swiss law which applies on this point. At the time of the facts in question and until 31 December 1982, the instrument applicable was an Act of 1892. The Federal Court was involved in extradition proceedings in two sets of circumstances. If the arrested person protested against the extradition itself by raising an objection based on the Act, a treaty or a declaration of reciprocity, the court was competent to rule on the merits of the extradition. It was also responsible for ruling on any request for provisional release lodged by the person who was detained with a view to extradition. The Office could grant release if this appeared to be required by the circumstances (section 25, first paragraph) If the Court refused to authorise extradition, the Office was bound by that decision. On the other hand, for important reasons of political expediency, the Court could still refuse to extradite the person concerned. In 1968 the Swiss Government drew attention to a number of shortcomings in the 1892 Act from the point of view of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Federal Court agreed to interpret sections 22 to 25 of the Act in such a way as to establish the general and exclusive jurisdiction of the Federal Court. The transitional arrangements introduced as a result of the exchange of letters were enshrined in the Federal Act of 20 March 1981 on International Mutual Assistance in Criminal Matters. The Indictments Chamber of the Federal Court rules not only on appeals against warrants for arrest with a view to extradition. The Office is now competent to rule at first instance (section 55, first paragraph) If, however, the person concerned claims that he “is being proceeded against because of a political offence’, the decision rests with the Federal court. The Commission declared the application admissible on 18 November 1983. In its report adopted on 13 December 1984, the Commission expressed the unanimous opinion that there had been a breach of Article 5 para. 4 (art. 5-4), since the requirements of procedure and speed had not been complied with in the proceedings in question. “. , either as concerns the procedure applied or as. concerns the requirement of ‘speedy decision’”. ‘Speedy decision' is defined as the ability to make a decision ‘in a speedy manner’. “Speedy’ can mean either ‘fast’ or ‘quick’, or “quickly’ depending on the circumstances.” ‘Fast’ means ‘immediate’ and ‘timely.’ ‘Quick’ refers to the time it takes for an outcome to be reached, ‘speed’ is the speed at which the decision is made, and “speedy” is the length of that time.

name: Andrés López Elorza

The Chamber decided, after examining the request of the applicant, that there is no need to relinquish jurisdiction in favour of the Grand chamber under Rule 72 of the Rules of Court. The parties were informed that the examination of the case was suspended, pending the outcome of the proceedings in the case.

The report indicated that according to the US Federal Sentencing Guidelines, the advisory sentencing range was “188 to 235 months incarceration, far less than the possible life sentence provided for under the statutes with which he was charged” The report noted that under section 3553(a) of Title 18 of the US Code, there was a “need to avoid unwarranted sentence disparities” In that regard, the report stated that several of the applicant’s co-conspirators had already been sentenced in a related case before the same judge. The Court of Appeal included a detailed account of the trial, explaining that on several occasions witnesses could not be questioned by the court because they exercised their right not to testify. The court had heard testimony from nine witnesses and was then hearing four further witnesses. In order to establish whether the applicant had committed the crimes of which he had been accused, testimony from Turkish witnesses was of paramount importance. The continuation of his detention was not disproportionate in view of the importance of the subject matter and the considerable punishment to be expected in case of a criminal conviction. The Court of Appeal found it established that the applicant had ordered the assassination of the policemen by telephone from Germany at the end of March 1993. The court primarily based the applicant’s conviction on testimony from witness S.G. The Court of appeal found that the prolongation of the pre-trial detention was not disproportionate, having regard to the importance of the subject matter and to the seriousness of the penalty to be expected in case of a criminal conviction. On 27 September 2011 the Düsseldorf Court. of Appeal convicted the applicant of two counts of murder and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The appeal has been adjourned until February 2013. The Federal Court of Justice quashed the judgment of the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal and remitted the case to another Chamber of that court. The specific circumstances of the instant case did not allow for an earlier termination of the proceedings. Apart from two counts of murder, of which he had been convicted, the applicant had been accused of holding a leading role in a foreign terrorist organisation. The case-file consisted of approximately 130 large volumes. The reading out of the applicant’s last word alone took four days. The appeal proceedings against the applicant were dismissed on 29 November 2012 and the case was remitted to another chamber of the court. Düsseldorf Court of Appeal (no. III‑6 STS 3/12) ordered the applicant’s continued detention. The detention was justified because the applicant was under strong suspicion of having committed a serious crime. The potential contradictions in the statements made by witness S.G. had to be examined in the new main proceedings. The fact that the Federal Court of Justice had quashed the judgment did not lead to a violation of the obligation to expedite the proceedings, as there was no obvious procedural error. The contradiction in testimony did not concern the core content of his statement, which remained unchanged. The main hearing is expected to begin by the end of April or the beginning of May 2013. The Federal Court of Justice finally considered that the length of detention (almost six years) was not disproportionate. According to that court the applicant remained firmly suspected of having ordered the attack of 1 April 1993, in which two policemen were killed. The Court of Appeal considered that to prolong the detention would be disproportionate. In cases involving pre-trial detention, the criminal courts were under a constitutional obligation to expedite the proceedings (Beschleunigungsgebot). This principle had to be applied even more strictly given the long duration of the applicant’s detention. The applicant was released on that same day. The court considered that it could not foresee when it would hear witness testimony from S.G., who was the primary witness. In August 2014, the criminal proceedings were still pending before the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal. The Court of appeal noted that the statements made by witness G.G. to the Turkish Authorities in 1993 could not be used because it could not been ruled out that they had been obtained by torture. The fact that detention had already lasted almost seven years was also cited as a reason for not using the witness' statements. The court ruled in favor of the witness and he was released from detention in September 2013. The case continues to be heard at the court of appeal in DüSseldorfer Strausberg, Germany.

eval_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 68919/10) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented by Mr C. Lenz, a lawyer practising in Stuttgart. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr H.-J. Behrens, Ministerialrat, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. On 3 June 2013 the applicant’s complaint concerning the length of proceedings before the Federal Constitutional Court and the lack of an effective remedy was communicated to the Government. On the same day the President of the Section sitting in a single-judge formation declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The remaining leapfrog appeal on points of law (Sprungrevision) was dismissed on 13 December 2005 by the Federal Social Court. On 20 January 2006 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint (no. 1 BvR 170/06) with the Federal Constitutional Court. The complaint did not raise a pressing constitutional question as the relevant provision of the social security legislation had meanwhile been amended. The Government informed the Court that in response to the pilot judgment in Rumpf v. Germany ( no. 46344/06, 2 September 2010) an Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations was to be introduced. The application was denied. In December 2011 the Court informed the applicant of the enactment of the new domestic remedy and drew his attention to the transitional provision of that Act. On 6 February 2012 the applicant filed a complaint under the new Act, claiming compensation in respect of pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. He complained that constitutional court proceedings that lasted four years, six months and one day were excessively long, even taking the position and function of the Federal Constitutional Court into account. The judge rapporteur conceded that the applicant’s submissions were sufficiently substantiated for his constitutional complaint to indeed have been dealt with earlier on the basis of the actual reasoning given. On 1 October 2012 the complaints panel of the Federal Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint. The court noted that the actual duration of the proceedings – four and a half years – was unusually long, but not excessive. Unlike the ordinary courts, the capacity and structure of a Constitutional Court were laid down in the Constitution and it served further purposes beyond the administration of individual justice. The scope for adaptation and for the acceleration of proceedings was therefore limited. The decisions and judgments of the Federal Constitutional Court had binding inter omnes legal effect and for this reason had to be drafted with the utmost diligence, the court said. However, the two cases shared sufficient similarities to justify the decision of the former judge rapporteur. The Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations was published in the Federal Law Gazette – Part I, 2011, pp. 2302 et seq. – on 2 December 2011 and entered into force the next day. The Remedy Act introduced general provisions instituting a remedy against any kind of protracted court proceedings. Section 1 applied to criminal and civil proceedings – for details see Taron v. Germany (dec.), no. 53126/07, §§ 19 et seq., 29 May 2012. Section 97b (1) A decision on compensation and reparation shall be rendered by the Federal Constitutional Court. Such compensation shall amount to €1,200 for every year of delay. Complaint of undue delay must be lodged in writing. Complaint must set out circumstances purported to establish the unreasonableness of the length of the proceedings. In the event of a tie the complaint of unduedelay shall be dismissed. The complaints panel shall render its decision without an oral hearing. Reasons need not be given. The decision is not subject to appeal.’2. Transitional provisions under section 23 of the Remedy Act (see for details Taron, § 27, and Garcia Cancio, § 36, both cited above), stipulated that, in the case of terminated proceedings whose length might still become or had already become the subject of a complaint before that court, it was not necessary to raise a complaint.

name: Christopher Ian Scott
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 18 September 1995. It originated in an application (no. 21335/93) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a British national, Mr Christopher Ian Scott, on 2 September 1992. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Government of the United Kingdom, having been informed by the Registrar of their right to intervene (Article 48 (b) of the Convention), did not indicate any intention of so doing.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 18 September 1995. It originated in an application (no. 21335/93) against the Kingdom of Spain lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a British national, Mr Christopher Ian Scott, on 2 September 1992. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 5 paras. 1 and 3 of the Convention. The Government of the United Kingdom, having been informed by the Registrar of their right to intervene, did not indicate any intention of so doing. Mr Scott is a British citizen born in 1958. He is currently detained in Her Majesty’s Prison, Leicester. A Finnish national, Ms T., made a statement to the police in Puerto de la Cruz, Tenerife, Canary Islands, in which she alleged that the applicant had raped her the night before. Ms T. underwent a medical examination and on 9 March 1990 flew back to Finland. Mr Scott was arrested on 8 March 1990, again assisted by a lawyer and an interpreter, and denied the rape allegations. He had escaped from Sudbury Prison, West Midlands, on 22 December 1989. An international warrant for his arrest for the murder of his father had been issued against him on 31 January 1990 by a judge at Birmingham Crown Court. The applicant denied the rape allegations before investigating judge no. 1 in Puerto de la Cruz. A formal request for extradition was filed on 27 April 1990. The British Embassy in Madrid wrote to the Audiencia Nacional that in the applicant’s case the sentence actually served upon conviction for murder was not likely to be more than ten years. Guarantees were requested from the United Kingdom authorities to the effect that, should the extradition be granted and the applicant be convicted in England, the final sentence would not exceed 30 years’ imprisonment (the maximum term of imprisonment under Spanish legislation) The applicant denies the murder allegations and resisted extradition. In May 1991 Mr Scott wrote to the Audiencia Nacional that he was willing to be extradited in order to get medical treatment in the United Kingdom. On 28 June 1991 the Cabinet (Consejo de Ministros) decided not to exercise its discretion not to execute the extradition order. The applicant lodged an appeal (recurso de súplica) with the full court of the Criminal Division of theAudienciaNacional. He was, however, kept in detention under orders made in the extradition proceedings. On 17 March 1992, taking 23 March 1990 as the date of the beginning of the applicant’s detention for rape for the rape case, he was arrested and detained for the murder of his father. In the meantime, on 7 March 1991, the investigating judge in Puerto de la Cruz had decided to extend his detention pending trial. The applicant was detained under Article 504 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and section 10 (3) of the Extradition Act for a period not exceeding two years, that is until 23 March 1994. The applicant lodged an appeal (recurso de súplica) against this decision but on 18 June 1992 a full court of the Criminal Division of the Audiencia Nacional dismissed the appeal on the ground that he had been detained in the extradition case on 23 March 1990, independently of his earlier detention for a different matter. The appeal was rejected after summary proceedings in a decision (auto) of 6 May 1993. The applicant was charged with rape and forgery of documents. A statement taken at a court hearing in Tuusula, Finland, on 14 December 1992 confirmed Ms T’s original allegations. The medical certificates showed that Ms T. had received prolonged psychiatric treatment after her return from Tenerife. In a judgment of 21 March 1994 the Audiencia Provincial acquitted the applicant on the rape charge. With respect to the forgery offence the applicant was convicted and sentenced as charged. The applicant was handed over to the United Kingdom authorities, pursuant to the international arrest warrant and theAudiencia Nacional's decision of 22 February 1991 allowing extradition. On 9 November 1995, following a trial at Birmingham Crown Court, Mr Scott was convicted of the murder of his father. He was sentenced to life imprisonment. -nine days under the different orders for detention pending trial on the rape charge and exactly four years in connection with the extradition proceedings. The trial judge recommended a “tariff period’ (see paragraph 43 below) of 12 years for Mr Scott to serve his sentence for the murder. Mr Scott has now served more than eight years of his life sentence. He has been released on bail pending the outcome of his extradition proceedings to face charges of rape and murder in the UK.

name: Henryk Kreuz

The applicant alleged in particular that his case had not been heard within a reasonable time in breach of Article 6 of the Convention. This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court. By a decision of 14 January 2003 the Court declared the application admissible. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) within that Section. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 46245/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged in particular that his case had not been heard within a reasonable time in breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. The Court declared the application admissible on 14 January 2003. The case was heard by the European Court of Human rights (“the Commission’s” Human Rights Committee) and the hearing was adjourned until 9 March 2012. The decision was returned to the Commission for reconsideration. Unirol Ltd. took the case to the Płock Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki) On 18 November 1994 the Regional Court exempted Unirol Ltd from court fees. On 16 December 1994 the court held the first hearing. On 4 November 1996 the trial court dismissed the applicant’s challenge of the presiding judge. On 5 March 1997 the court decided that it would not deliver the final decision. On 9 June 1999 the court ordered the parties to specify their claims. On 15 October 1999 the hearing listed for 10 July 1998 was cancelled. On 27 August 1998 the Regional court ordered that the lost case-file be reconstituted. Unirol Ltd. asked the court to appoint another expert. On 8 November 2000 the court held a hearing and heard evidence from the expert. The Płock Regional Court delivered a judgment. Both parties appealed. On 27 June 2003 the Supreme Court dismissed both cassation appeals. Unirol Ltd.'s appeal to the Polish Court of Appeal was dismissed in August 2003. The appeal was dismissed by the Polish Supreme Court in October 2007. The case was settled in a settlement of over £1.3 million ($3 million) between Unirol and its former owner, the Polish government. The settlement was reached in September 1999. The parties were able to claim damages and compensation.

name: Yiannis Kyriakou
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18407/91) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the Turkish occupation of the northern part of Cyprus had deprived him of his home and properties. In September 1999 the applicant’s heirs informed the Court that they wished to pursue the application on behalf of the deceased. By a decision of 8 June 1999 the Court declared the application admissible. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The Government of Cyprus, which had exercised its right to intervene, also filed observations on the merits.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18407/91) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the Turkish occupation of the northern part of Cyprus had deprived him of his home and properties. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. In September 1999 the applicant’s heirs informed the Court that they wished to pursue the application on behalf of the deceased. By a decision of 8 June 1999 the Court declared the application admissible. The case was referred to the European Court of Human rights. The applicant's mother, Mrs Maria Yianni, had been the owner of two twelfths of plot no. 20. In 1956 Mr Elias Kyriakou, who had emigrated to Australia, had given all his shares to the applicant. However, no official transfer of ownership had been entered in the land register. The applicant had lived until his death in a small house located in a housing scheme for displaced persons. Since 1974 the applicant had been unable to return to his home and property in the northern part of Cyprus. The case was adjourned until next year, when the judge will rule on whether to order the confiscation of the land. The applicant took part in a car convoy organised by persons from three villages in Kyrenia and from Trypimeni wishing to return to their homes in the north peacefully. The participants in the convoy had informed the commander of the United Nations (UN) forces in Cyprus of their intention to return home. They drove to the ‘buffer zone’ checkpoint on the main road linking Nicosia and Famagusta. There they stopped and asked the UN officer on duty to be allowed to return. They requested him to transmit their demand to the Turkish military authorities. The Turkish authorities refused their request to drive through the checkpoint and enter the northern part of Cyprus.

name: Cengiz Polat
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40593/04) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. eval_texts: The applicant was arrested and placed in police custody on suspicion of involvement in the activities of an illegal armed organisation. On 15 May 2001 the Court of Cassation quashed the applicant's conviction for procedural reasons. He is currently detained in the Edirne F-type Prison. The case originated in an application (no. 40593/04) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 15 October 2004. name: Aziz Canpolat

eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1950 and was detained in the Hilvan prison, in Şanlıurfa at the time of the application. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 31 May 2005 the Court decided to give notice to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the convention, it decided to examine the merits of the applicant's application at the same time as its admissibility. Diyarbakır State Security Court convicted the applicant and his co-accused and sentenced them to six years and three months' imprisonment. Court of Cassation quashed the first-instance court's judgment, holding that the applicant's defence rights had not been respect as they were not informed about the date of the hearing. It also ordered their release from detention having regard to the time that they had spent in prison. They were released from detention on May 25, 2000. They are currently serving a six-year and three-month sentence in a Turkish prison. The application for asylum in the U.S. is still pending.

name: Ian Le Petit
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35574/97) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The case was heard by the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27): the Court ruled in favour of the applicant.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35574/97) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that his naval court-martial did not constitute a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court. By decision dated 5 December 2000, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Government filed observations on the merits. The applicant made admissions at his first interview and gave investigators access to his bank accounts. On 27 November 1995 he was interviewed for a second time and then charged with six charges. All charges related to the making of false representations about travel allowances. The court-martial took place on 8-10 July 1996. Once the applicant’s preliminary objections were rejected (he contested the admission of evidence from his interviews) he pleaded guilty as charged. On 10 July 1996 he was sentenced to three months’ imprisonment. It was considered that his admissions in interview were not the result of oppression and that, given the seriousness of the offences, his sentence was neither manifestly excessive nor wrong in principle.

name: Hasan Dikici

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 18308/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants' son, Ercan Dikici, who was an electrician, had an occupational accident and died from an electric shock. Three persons were charged with involuntary manslaughter under Article 455 of the Criminal Code. On 4 July 1996 the accused persons were acquitted of the charges against them. On 12 May 1997 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the Aliağa Criminal Court. The employers were found guilty of involuntary manslaughter and sentenced to six months' imprisonment. Their sentence was converted into a fine. The applicants were awarded TRL 600,000,000 in respect of non-pecuniary damage. On 5 July 2001 the Court of Cassation decided that the amount of compensation should be increased. This decision was served on the applicants on 22 August 2001. The same day, the defendant party paid TRL 2,677,533,000 to the applicants (approximately USD 1,850). The application was rejected by the İzmir Labour Court on 6 May 2002. The court ordered further expert reports and heard evidence from witnesses. The case was adjourned pending the outcome of the criminal proceedings. It was decided on 24 May 2001 that the applicants had not been in any way financially dependent on their deceased son and therefore rejected their claim.

name: Sabriye Akıncıbaşı

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 13146/02) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. name: Roy H.W. Johnston
train_texts: The present case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 21 May 1985. The case originated in an application (no. 9697/82) against Ireland lodged with the Commission in 1982 under Article 25 (art. 25) by Roy H.W. Johnston, an Irish citizen, Janice Williams-Johnston, a British citizen, and their daughter Nessa. The Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, having been informed by the Registrar of their right to intervene, did not indicate any intention of so doing. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. B. Walsh, the elected judge of Irish nationality.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 9697/82) against Ireland lodged with the Commission in 1982. The request sought a decision from the Court as to the existence of violations of Articles 8, 9, 12 and 13. The Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, having been informed by the Registrar of their right to intervene, did not indicate any intention of so doing. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. B. Walsh, the elected judge of Irish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr. R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The hearing was held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 and 24 June 1986. The Court heard addresses by Mr. Gleeson and Mr. O’Reilly for the Government, by. Gaukur Jörundsson for the Commission and by Senator M. Robinson and Dr. Duncan for the applicants. There appeared before the Court: Mrs. Liddy, Deputy Legal Adviser, Department of Foreign Affairs, Agent, Mr. Lagergren, F. Gölcüklü and R. Macdonald (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 § 4) (art. 43). The first applicant married a Miss M in 1952 in a Church of Ireland ceremony. Three children were born of this marriage, in 1956, 1959 and 1965. On 19 September 1982, he concluded a formal separation agreement with his wife. In 1978, the second applicant, with whom Roy Johnston had been living since 1971, gave birth to Nessa. He consented to his name being included in the Register of Births as the father. Under the Constitution of Ireland, the first applicant is unable to obtain, in Ireland, a dissolution of his marriage to enable him to marry the second applicants. His London solicitors advised that, in the absence of residence within the jurisdiction of the English courts, he would not be able to do so in England, and the matter has therefore not been pursued. The third applicant has, under Irish law, the legal situation of an illegitimate child. Her parents are concerned at the lack of any means by which she can, even with their consent, be recognised as their child. They are also concerned about the possibility of a stigma attaching to her by virtue of her legal situation, especially when she is attending school. She has adopted the first applicant’s surname, which she uses amongst friends and neighbours, but for business purposes continues to use the name Williams. According to her, she has felt inhibited about telling employers of her domestic circumstances. She would like to become an Irish citizen by naturalisation, but she has been reluctant to make an application, not wishing to put those circumstances in issue.

name: Ilyas Elmi Hode
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 22341/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. eval_texts: The case was brought by a Somali national living in the UK and a British citizen living in Djibouti. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal in London on 2 June 2009. The judge ruled in favour of the Somali national, who was granted five years leave to remain in the United Kingdom. The British citizen was granted indefinite leave to stay in the country. The UK Government decided the case was not in the public interest and rejected the application. The U.K. government said the case should be thrown out because it did not meet the criteria for an indefinite stay. The decision was upheld by the Supreme Court on 8 June 2009 and the case continues. The first applicant's leave to remain in the United Kingdom expired on 16 March 2011. He was subsequently granted Indefinite Leave to Remain. The second applicant gave birth to a son on 17 February 2008. The first applicant was named as the father on the birth certificate. The Immigration Judge accepted that the applicants were married and that the first applicant had sufficient funds to accommodate and maintain his wife and child. In April 2011 the Immigration Rules were amended to permit refugees to be joined in the U.K. by post-flight spouses during their initial period of leave to. remain, provided certain other conditions were met. This case has been referred to as ‘the Djibouti case’.

name: Aziz Aydın Arslan

eval_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) Mr Aziz Aydın Arslan (‘the applicant’), was recruited by Türkiye Emlak Bankası A.Ş., a state-owned bank. Court terminated the criminal proceedings against the Director since they were time-barred. The director was acquitted of the charges against him.

name: Wayne Thomas Black
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56745/00) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained under Article 6. 1 about his adjudication proceedings pointing to the role of the Governor and the. lack of a public pronouncement of the decision. He also invoked Article. 3(c) as regards the lack of legal representation. By a decision of 27 September 2005, a Chamber of the Fourth Section of the Court declared the application partly admissible. eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr S. Creighton, a lawyer practising in London. The United Kingdom Government (the Government) were represented by their Agents, Mr C.A. Whomersley and, subsequently, Mr J. Grainger, both of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. A decision of 27 September 2005, a Chamber of the Fourth Section of the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant’s defence was that the item was a suppository. Evidence was adduced that no suppository had been prescribed to the applicant in the 2 years prior to the incident. He was found guilty as charged and awarded 5 additional days’ detention together with exclusion from work and forfeiture of privileges for 10 days. The High Court rejected the application finding, inter alia, that, depending as it does on the circumstances of the case, an order to a prisoner to remove an item from his anus would not necessarily be unlawful. The applicant did not appeal the decision of the Governor. A hearing took place in the High Court on 21 June 1999.

name: J.M. Burden
train_texts: The applicants complained under Article 14 of the Convention taken in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that, when the first of them died, the survivor would be required to pay inheritance tax on the dead sister’s share of the family home. The survivor of a married couple or a homosexual relationship registered under the Civil Partnership Act 2004 would be exempt from paying inheritance tax in these circumstances. The application was allocated to a Chamber within the Fourth Section of the Court. On 12 December 2006 the Chamber unanimously declared the application admissible and delivered a judgment in which it held, by four votes to three, that there had been no violation of Article 14.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 13378/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained that, when the first of them died, the survivor would be required to pay inheritance tax on the dead sister’s share of the family home. The survivor of a married couple or a homosexual relationship registered under the Civil Partnership Act 2004 would be exempt from paying inheritance tax in these circumstances. On 12 December 2006 the Chamber unanimously declared the application admissible and delivered a judgment in which it held, by four votes to three, that there had been no violation of Article 14. The applicants are unmarried sisters, born on 26 May 1918 and 2 December 1925 respectively. They have lived together, in a stable, committed and mutually supportive relationship, all their lives. The house is owned by the applicants in their joint names. According to an expert valuation dated 12 January 2006, the property was worth 425,000 pounds sterling (GBP), or GBP 550,000 if sold together with the adjoining land. The sisters also jointly own two other properties, worth GBP 325,000 in total. In addition, each sister owns in her sole name shares and other investments worth approximately GBP 150,000. Each has made a will leaving all her property to the other.

name: Tor Fredrik Vejdeland
train_texts: The application was made under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights. It was made on 6 July 2006, and the case was heard on 1 February 2011. The case was decided by the Third Section of the Court of Appeal, which ruled in favour of the application on 27 November 2007. The application was brought by four Swedish citizens, who said that the application was a violation of their right to freedom of speech. The decision was made to continue the case until a decision was reached by the Fifth Section. The court of appeal ruled in favor of the applicants on 27 February 2011, but the case continued to be heard by the Fourth Section. In the end, the appeal was dismissed on 28 February 2012.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1813/07) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that the Supreme Court judgment of 6 July 2006 constituted a violation of their freedom of expression. The application was later transferred to the Fifth Section of the Court, following the re-composition of the court’s sections on 1 February 2011. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The case was decided by the President of the Third Section on 27 November 2008. Anti-Swedish teachers know very well that homosexuality has a morally destructive effect on the substance of society (folkkroppen) The applicants disputed that the text in the leaflets expressed contempt for homosexuals. They stated that the purpose of their activity had been to start a debate about the lack of objectivity in the education dispensed in Swedish schools. The Court of Appeal, referring to the Supreme Court’s judgment of 29 November 2005 in the case NJA 2005 p. 805 (see below under “Relevant domestic law and practice”), rejected the charges against the applicants on the ground that a conviction would amount to an aggravated crime. The handing out of the leaflets was not in violation of the right to freedom of expression. The leaflets were not intended to be offensive to any group of people. They were intended to raise awareness of a question of public interest. The issue was whether the leaflets should be handed out in such a way as to not violate the rights of a group of persons. The majority of the court agreed that the leaflets were in no way offensive to the group. The case was adjourned until next week to consider the implications of the ruling. The court will now decide whether to bring the case back to the Court of Appeal for reconsideration. The first three applicants were given suspended sentences combined with fines ranging from SEK 1,800 (approximately 200 euros (EUR) to SEK 19,000 (approximately EUR 2,000) and the fourth applicant was sentenced to probation. The minority wanted to acquit the applicants but gave separate reasons for this conclusion, at least in part. One of them was of the view that the prosecution was not formulated in such a way that the Supreme Court could take into consideration that the leaflets had been distributed at a school and addressed to the pupils. The other agreed with the majority that an overall assessment of the circumstances had to be made.

name: Ivan Hooper

The case was decided by the Court on 9 November 2003, and the case was dismissed on 11 November 2003.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that neither he nor his legal representative were given the opportunity to address the magistrates' court prior to the imposition of a binding over order. By a decision of 21 October 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merit of the case. The applicant was “bound over” in his own recognisance of 50 pounds sterling (GBP) together with a surety of GBP 250. The precise terms of the order were found by the Divisional Court (in the later judicial review proceedings) to be unclear. The applicant was granted leave to apply for judicial review of the decision to impose the binding over order on 2 June 1997. The application was granted on 20 January 1998. The judges agreed that the order had been procedurally irregular and granted a declaration to that effect. The judge ruled that the magistrate had not given any opportunity for the applicant or his representative to make submissions before the order was imposed. Mr Justice Mance quoted headnote of case of R. v. Central Criminal Court ex parte Boulding [1984] 1 QB 813. The position where there was a requirement for a surety was even clearer. A surety required the separate approval of the court as to his suitability. This was outside the control of the person to be bound over. The High Court accepted that the applicant's representative was effectively presented with a ‘fait accompli’ of a nature which she had not come across before. The magistrate did not expressly invite or give opportunity for any submissions, or indeed any discussion, about the proposed terms of the binding over order before he imposed it. Mr Justice Mance said that had the applicant or his representative been able to make submissions about the proposed order the magistrate might have been persuaded to impose different terms. Mr Burnett submitted that it cannot be shown that it would have made any difference if the magistrate had given to the applicant [and his counsel] an opportunity to make representations. However, it seems to me certainly not beyond the bounds of possibility, that if a proper opportunity had been given to [the applicant's counsel] to consider and address the matter. This is all, of course, speculative, but speculation though it may be, the reason why it is speculation is that the magistrate failed, in my judgment, to give the applicant proper time or a proper opportunities.”

name: Stephen Arthur Perry

eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that the police covertly videotaped him for identification purposes and used the material in the prosecution against him. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 26 September 2002, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant is currently detained in HM Prison Brixton. An important part of the prosecution's case rested almost entirely on the ability of the witnesses to visually identify the perpetrator. Permission to covertly video the applicant for identification purposes was sought from the Deputy Chief Constable for the West Midlands Police Force under the Home Office Guidelines on the Use of Equipment in Police Surveillance Operations 1984. A compilation tape was prepared in which eleven volunteers imitated the actions of the applicant as captured on the covert video. This video was shown to various witnesses of the armed robberies, of whom two positively identified the applicant. The applicant was acquitted on this count on 1 August 1997 and later acquitted on another count. The trial lasted 17 days, the applicant and 31 witnesses giving live evidence. Neither the applicant nor his solicitor were informed that a tape had been made or used for identification parade purposes or given an opportunity to view it prior to its use. The judge concluded that there had been no unfairness arising from the use of the video. Eleven persons had been filmed for comparison purposes rather than the required eight and were all within comparative height, age and appearance. Even though the applicant's solicitor was not present to verify the procedures adopted when the witnesses were shown the videos, the entire process had been recorded on video and this had been shown to the court. In his summing-up to the jury, the trial judge warned the jury at considerable length about the ‘special need for caution’ before convicting any defendant. The jury convicted the applicant of three counts of robbery and acquitted him of two others. The judge sentenced him to five years' imprisonment. The jury were made aware of the complaints about the honesty and fairness of his treatment by the police and the alleged breaches of the code of practice relating to identification parades. The Court of Appeal rejected his appeal on 3 April 2000. The solicitors claimed that they were informed on 7 July 2000 that the jury had been told that the video evidence was admissible. The House of Lords rejected the appeal on 14 April 2000, and the case was quashed. The trial judge said he had been entitled to reach the conclusion that the evidence wasAdmissible and that he had directed the jury to give the evidence little or no weight.

name: Rupert John Massey
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 14399/02) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleges that the criminal proceedings brought against him exceeded a reasonable time. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) On 8 April 2003, the Chamber invited the respondent Government to make observations on the applicant's complaints about the length of proceedings. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The Court declared the remainder of the application admissible on 6 January 2004.
eval_texts: The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing was required. The Court declared the remainder of the application admissible in January 2004. The case was settled in favour of the applicant in March 2003. The UK Government was represented by their Agent, Mr Derek Walton of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London. The appeal was dismissed by the Court on 8 April 2003, and the case was dismissed again on 11 April 2004. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of indecent assaults on GL and DM. He was interviewed by the police on 21 March 1997 and was subsequently released on police bail. In October 1997, the police fingerprinted and took DNA swabs from the applicant. On 5 December 1997, he was interviewed with respect to allegations of indecent assault made by a fourth person, MC. On 4 September 1998, the applicant was committed for trial on 20 counts relating to three different victims. On 30 March 1999, the trial was delayed because the. applicant was suffering from depression and memory loss. On 22 November 1999 the trial judge refused another application by the applicant for the proceedings to be stayed as an abuse of process. The applicant was convicted of 16 counts of indecent assault and acquitted of four counts of buggery. He was sentenced to a total of six years' imprisonment and was made subject to the registration requirements of the Sex Offenders Act 1997 for an indefinite period. The applicant sought leave to appeal against conviction and sentence on various grounds including that the trial judge should have stayed the proceedings as an abuse of process. On 5 February 2000, the applicant's counsel requested an extension of time to perfect the grounds of appeal. In May 2001, the case was stayed pending the judgment of the Court of Appeal in an Attorney-General reference case which also concerned issues of delay and abuse. Court of Appeal ruled stay of proceedings could only be granted in exceptional circumstances and only if the defendant showed that a fair trial was impossible. The court considered that Article 6 of the Convention was inapplicable because the applicant had been convicted before the Human Rights Act 1998 came into force. It considered that, on the limited documentary material before him, the judge could not have come to any other conclusion than that afair trial was possible. Court further deemed that there was no basis to conclude that the judge was wrong to refuse the application for a stay made at the end of the prosecution case. It was not the police delay, but GL's ignoring of the police warning that led to discussion between potential witnesses.

name: Husenatu Bah

eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that she had been a victim of a violation of Article 14. On 1 December 2009 the Acting President of the Chamber decided to give notice of the application to the Government. No hearing on the merits was required and the parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. The Equality and Human Rights Commission was given leave to intervene in the written procedure. The respondent Government replied to those comments (Rule 44 § 6). The Court rules in favour of the applicant and the case continues. The applicant applied to the London Borough of Southwark Council for assistance on 9 February 2007, on the basis that she had become unintentionally homeless. An unintentionally homeless person with a minor child would ordinarily qualify as being in priority need pursuant to section 189 of the Housing Act 1996. In the case of the applicant, however, as her son was subject to immigration control, he was disregarded by the Council. As the applicant’s son was not eligible, the applicant did not have a priority need. The Council assisted the applicant to find a private-sector tenancy in September 2007, which she accepted. The applicant and her son were not therefore at any point actually homeless. The applicant had remained on the waiting list for social housing in the Borough of Southwark. She obtained an offer of a social tenancy of a one-bedroom flat in March 2009. She and her son therefore moved back to Southwark and moved into the flat. The applicant had been spending. four hours a day travelling to and from school. for the previous two years. She had also been spending four hours each day on the bus to get her son to school for the past two years for the purpose of travelling back and forth to the home. of her husband in Southwark, which she had moved to in 2008. The application was denied by the council and is now being appealed.

The applicant was taken into custody within the context of a police operation carried out against an illegal organisation, namely the TKP/ML – TIKKO (the Turkish Communist Party-Marxist Leninist - Turkish Workers and Peasants’ Liberation Army). On 17 November 1992 the applicant was placed in detention on remand. The Istanbul Assize Court found the applicant guilty of the alleged offence and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment for having erred in its assessment of the facts. The case was remitted to the Istanbul Assizes Court for re-trial. The proceedings are currently pending before the Court ofCassation. The applicant appealed the conviction and the case is still pending. The application is being heard by the Istanbul High Court of Justice. The trial of the applicant was held between 12 May 2006 and 30 May 2007. The judge convicted the applicant and thirteen other co-accused for actively participating in the illegal activities of the TKP/ML – TIKKO with a view to undermining the constitutional order of the State.

The applicant appealed to the Military Court of Cassation (askeri yargıtay) The case file was transmitted to the military court on 26 December 1994. On 27 December 1995 the Court ofCassation upheld the above judgment. The case was referred to the International Court of Justice. The application was brought by the Government on behalf of the applicant. The Government filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The applicant and the Government each filed observations.

name: Albert Thompson

name: Radosław Antonicelli

eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) by a Polish national, Mr Radosław Antonicelli, on 11 January 2005.
