The only course of action left to the applicant was to request the Ombudsman to lodge an appeal on his behalf. This letter was served on the applicant on 29 March 2005. The Court of Appeal ruled in favour of the lawyer and the appeal was dismissed.

name: Cahit Yetkinsekerci

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 71841/01) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged on 14 May 1998 with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant was released after having served approximately one half of the 12 year sentence, and deported to Turkey. The appeal upon the sentence will be successful to that extent, the court said. The sentence was reduced from 14 years imposed to one of 12 years’ imprisonment, and the applicant was freed after serving approximately one-and-a-half years of his sentence. The court said that, absent any reason for reduction of an unusual kind, had this importation been an importation of diamorphine, a sentence of 18 years could have been expected.

name: David Hood
train_texts: The case was brought to the Court of Appeal under Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) The case was to decide the amount of compensation to be paid to the victims of the attack. The result was that the case was dismissed by the Court. The court ruled in favour of the victims, and the appeal was rejected. The case has been heard by the European Court of Human Rights. The appeal was dismissed on October 17, 2013. The judge ruled that the government had made a fair and just use of the case and that the matter was referred to the ECHR. The ruling was overturned on October 23, 2013, and an appeal was made again by the defendant.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court, as established under former Article 19 of the Convention, by the Government of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (“the Government”) on 14 August 1998. It originated in an application (no. 27267/95) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights by a British national, Mr David Hood, on 18 April 1995. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (former Rule 30). The Grand Chamber included ex officio Sir Nicolas Bratza, the judge elected in respect of the U.K., Mr Wildhaber, the President of the Court and Mrs Palm. The applicant, David Hood, is a British national born in 1970. He was a soldier with the regular forces of the British army. The applicant went absent without leave from his unit in Germany three times. Prior to his third absence, he had been remanded for trial by court martial on an assault charge (later abandoned), he remained absent for almost two and a half years and he gave himself up to the civilian police in December 1993. The Court heard addresses by Mr Mackenzie and Mr Havers. The hearing in this case and in the case of Cable and Others v the United Kingdom took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 9 December 1998. The applicant did not return after two weeks’ leave (his fourth absence without leave) on 11 May 1994. On 27 November 1994 he was arrested at his home by the civilian police. He was taken by army escort to Brompton Barracks. On 4 January 1995 the applicant appeared before the unit adjutant and was given the abstract of evidence. The applicant was then remanded for trial by court martial by his commanding officer and he applied for legal aid from the military authorities. The court martial took place on 3 and 4 April 1995 and the applicant, who was legally represented, pleaded not guilty. During the hearing, the applicant’s solicitor challenged the admission into evidence of the statements of his girlfriend. The applicant was convicted on two charges of absence without leave and on one of the charges of desertion. He was sentenced to be imprisoned for eight months and to be dismissed from the service. The judge advocate (having heard evidence from the unit adjutant and the applicant’s representative) found that Rule 10 of the Rules of Procedure (Army) 1972 had been followed. After confirmation and promulgation of the conviction and sentence, the applicant petitioned the Army. His leave application to the single judge of the Courts-Martial Appeal Court was rejected on 13 September 1995 and his further appeal to the full Courts-martial appeal Court was also refused on 18 March 1996. High Court rejected the application. Court found, inter alia, that the delay report had been properly completed in a timely fashion. It noted that the expressed reason for the applicant’s continued detention was to prevent his absconding and found that ‘perfectly understandable’ given the charges against him. The application was rejected by the High Court. The court found that the Delay Report was properly completed and that the applicant's detention was justified. The High Court found that it was justified given the charge against him and that his detention was proportionate to his actions. The case was dismissed on grounds of the absence of evidence.

name: Çetin İpek
train_texts: The case originated in two applications (nos. 17019/02 and 30070/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were represented by Mr M.S. Tanrıkulu, a lawyer practising in Diyarbakır. The Turkish Government (“the Government’s Agent”) was represented by their Agent. eval_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. They were accused of offences falling within the jurisdiction of the State Security Courts. Since they were accused, they could not benefit from the assistance of a lawyer despite their age. The applicants were released pending trial on 5 February 2002. The charges were brought under Articles 168 and 169 of the Turkish Criminal Code respectively. They have never been convicted of any offence. They are currently being held in the Diyarbakır State Security Court (hereinafter the SSC). They are accused of membership of an illegal organisation and of aiding and abetting that organisation. The second applicant and the other applicants were taken for a medical examination at a medical clinic.

name: Laleş Çeliker

The death penalty was commuted to a life sentence of imprisonment. On 24 January 2001 the Court ofCassation's decision was pronounced in the absence of the applicant's representative.

name: Wendy Costello-Roberts
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 7 December 1991. eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 7 December 1991. It originated in an application (no. 13134/87) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 17 January 1986. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3, 8 and 13. Following a friendly settlement, the case of Y was struck out of the list by a judgment dated 29 October 1992 (Series A no. 247-A) The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 September 1992. The Court heard addresses by Mr Bratza for the Government, by Sir Basil Hall for the Commission, and by Ms Beale for the applicant. The school had approximately 180 pupils, none of whose fees were paid out of public funds, and received no direct financial support from the Government. In September 1985 Mrs Costello-Roberts sent the applicant, who was then aged seven, to an independent boarding preparatory school in Barnstaple, Devon. In the school’s prospectus it was stated that a high standard of discipline was maintained, but no mention was made of this. The school in question operated a system whereby such punishment was administered upon acquisition of five demerit marks. On 3 October 1985 the applicant received his fifth mark for talking in the corridor and for being a little late for bed. The headmaster decided that the only answer to the lack of discipline was to give him three “whacks’ on the bottom through his shorts with a rubber-soled gym shoe. In a letter to his mother he wrote “come and picke me up I have had the wacke’. The school initially denied that he had been punished, but this was denied by the Government. On 5 November, the headmaster wrote to the Governors of the school to express his “grave concern’ about the use of corporal punishment. The applicant's mother complained to the police some time between 4 and 16 November 1985, but was told that there was no action they could take without any visible bruising on the child’s buttocks. A complaint by her to the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children received a similar response. The headmaster was of the opinion that the applicant “strung his parents along“, taking home stories about bullying and the like “which he has clearly made up but which equally clearly his parents believe’. It was argued in Strasbourg, on behalf of the applicant, that he had been extremely disturbed by the slippering, which turned him from a confident, outgoing seven-year-old into a nervous and unsociable child.

name: Mahir Göktaş

name: Janusz Krawczak

name: Eric Oldham

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36273/97) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant was a discretionary life prisoner who had been released on licence and recalled to prison. He complained that he had been denied a fair hearing before the Parole Board on 8 November 1996 and, secondly, that he hadn't had his detention reviewed until just over two years later. The Government of the United Kingdom were represented by their Agent, Mr H. Llewellyn, of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) and declared admissible on 7 March 2000. On 1 July 1996 the police were called to the home of the applicant's partner, M., who is a deaf mute. She was taken to hospital where she received treatment for injuries to her face and back. The applicant's licence was revoked on the grounds that the applicant had caused M.'s injuries after drinking at least eight cans of lager. The case was referred to the Parole Board which confirmed the revocation of the licence on 12 July 1996. In its written decision of 12 November 1996 the DLP stated that it had accepted the evidence which indicated that the. applicant had been responsible for M.’s injuries, rather than the account put forward on behalf of. the applicant. The DLP were granted an extension on their appeal to the British Court of Appeal on 7 December 1998. The appeal had been adjourned to give the DLP more time to consider the case. The DLP's appeal was eventually dismissed on 17 December 1998 and they were allowed to continue their appeal on 1 January 1999. The decision was made to end the appeal on 18 December 1998, but not before the appeal was heard by the Court of Appeals again. The judge ruled that the appeal against the appeal should be allowed to stand. The legal review was rejected and the case was returned to the court of appeal for a new appeal. The case was dismissed on 23 December 1998 with the judge ruling that the case had been decided.

name: Mark Wilkinson

It originated in an application (no. 22299/93) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 7 July 1993. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 and 14 of the Convention. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality and Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court. The applicant, who is black, is a British citizen born in 1966 and currently living in Manchester, England. He was tried for robbery at Manchester Crown Court between 26 and 28 November 1991. The trial ended on the final day of the trial, at 10.46 a.m., the jury retired to consider their verdict. An hour and three quarters later a note was passed by the jury to the judge. It read: “JURY SHOWING RACIAL OVERTONES 1 MEMBER TO BE EXCUSED.” The applicant was legally represented at the trial. The Court heard addresses by Mr Ress, Mr Mansfield and Mr Garnham. Judge showed the note to counsel for the prosecution and defence and consulted them on the appropriate response to it. Prosecution counsel recalls that defence counsel did not raise strong objections to the approach which the judge indicated he intended to pursue. However, defence counsel seems to recall that he did in fact ask the trial judge to discharge the jury in the circumstances, but his application was refused. Defence counsel based his recollection on the grounds of appeal and advice on appeal which he drafted shortly after the trial on 10 December 1991. Neither of these documents suggests that defence. counsel made an express request to the judge to discharged the jury. Judge's recollection is that both counsel agreed to his proposed course of action (see paragraph 11 above). The jury, being unable to reach a unanimous verdict, were recalled by the judge. He informed them that the time had come when he could accept a verdict of at least a majority of ten. At 4.06 p.m. the jury returned and delivered a ten to two majority verdict finding the applicant guilty. The applicant was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment. The appeal proceedings were heard at the Court of Appeal in London. The judge ruled that the trial judge had wrongly failed to make any enquiry into the note with a view to determining whether one of the members of the jury should be discharged on the grounds of racial prejudice and that this failure gave rise to the appeal. Leave to appeal was refused by the single judge on 28 February 1992. The applicant renewed his application to the full Court of Appeal. On 19 January 1993 the application was dismissed. The court continued: “Matters of this kind raise delicate issues. The jury system does require an element of give and take after proper directions from the judge. In our judgment His Honour Judge Hammond dealt with this matter sensitively, sensibly and correctly, and cannot be faulted for a conclusion that the jury should continue the deliberations which they had given their oath to undertake. We, therefore, find no ground for complaint and we dismiss this application’

name: Alison Halford
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 28 May 1996. It originated in an application (no. 20605/92) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Ms Alison Halford, a British citizen, on 22 April 1992. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8, 10, 13 and 14 of the Convention. The applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent her (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’s) on 28 May 1996. It originated in an application (no. 20605/92) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Ms Alison Halford, a British citizen, on 22 April 1992. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent her. On 10 June 1996, in the presence of the Registrar, the President of the Court, Mr R. Ryssdal, drew by lot the names of the other seven members. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 17 March 1997. The Court heard addresses by Mrs Liddy, Mr Makin, Mr Duffy and Mr Eadie. The applicant, Ms Alison Halford, was born in 1940 and lives in the Wirral. From 1962 until her retirement in 1992 she worked in the police service. Ms Halford was appointed to the rank of Assistant Chief Constable with the Merseyside police in May 1983. As such she became the most senior-ranking female police officer in the United Kingdom. She applied unsuccessfully on eight occasions during the following seven years to be appointed as Deputy Chief Constable, in response to vacancies arising. Ms Halford alleges that certain members of the Merseyside Police Authority launched a “campaign’ against her in response to her complaint to the Industrial Tribunal. This took the form, inter alia, of leaks to the press, interception of her telephone calls and the decision to bring disciplinary proceedings against her. Mr Justice MacPherson found that the Chairman and Vice-Chairman of the Police Authority had acted ultra vires and, without imputing ill-motive to them, held that there had been an element of unfairness. Ms Halford was given an ex gratia payment of 10,000 pounds sterling (GBP) by the Chief Constable. As Assistant Chief Constable, Ms Halford was provided with her own office and two telephones, one of which was for private use. She alleges that calls made from her home and her office telephones were intercepted for the purposes of obtaining information to use against her in the discrimination proceedings. It was agreed that she would retire from the police force on medical grounds (arising out of an injury to her knee in 1989). In addition, the Home Office agreed to implement various proposals put by the Equal Opportunities Commission, inter alia to update and review selection procedures for senior posts within the force. The Government accepted that the applicant had adduced sufficient material to establish a reasonable likelihood that calls were intercepted. On 6 December 1991 Ms Halford applied to the Interception of Communications Tribunal (“the Tribunal’) for an investigation under section 7 of the 1985 Act. In a letter dated 21 February 1992, the Tribunal informed her that its investigation had satisfied it that there had been no contravention of sections 2 to 5 of the 1984 Act in her case. The Tribunal confirmed that it could not specify whether any interception had in fact taken place (see paragraph 32 below). The Home Secretary explained that her complaint regarding the interception of calls made from her office telephones “[did] not fall within [his] responsibilities as Home Secretary nor within the terms of the [1985] Act“.

name: John Iselsten
train_texts: The case was brought against the Kingdom of Sweden. The application was made under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’s” Convention) The case was heard by the Court of Appeal on 4 January 2007. The Court found the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the length of the proceedings and the lack of an oral hearing to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). The Court ruled that the application was not inadmissible and that the decision was not to be appealed.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 11320/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 11 March 2005. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr P.-O. Nordh, a lawyer practising in Vallentuna. The Swedish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent, Mr B. Sjöberg, of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the length of the proceedings and the lack of an oral hearing to the Government. The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen), seeking leave to invoke the alleged breach of contract. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. The proceedings were then re-initiated before the District Court, which, in June 1999, issued a summons to the State, represented by the National Tax Board (Riksskatteverket). The State disputed the claims and the applicant was given the opportunity to comment on the State’s submissions. The court called the parties to a preparatory meeting to be held on 18 January 2000. The main hearing was eventually scheduled for 23 and 24 January 2001. During the hearing, four witnesses were heard and extensive written evidence was produced. Court of Appeal upheld the lower court’s judgment in full, noting that the parties had essentially invoked and developed the circumstances on which their claims were based in the same manner as before the District Court. The State consented to the case being decided upon without a main hearing, whereas the applicant opposed it. The Court of Appeal found no reason to depart from the evaluation of the case made by the lower Court. In August 2004 he submitted his supplementary pleadings and, on 14 September 2004, the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. On 20 July 2004 he asked for, and was granted, an extension of the time-limit to supplement his appeal.

name: Kudlip S. Sander
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 34129/96) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained that his case had not been heard by an impartial tribunal because, allegedly, the jury had been racially prejudiced. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 29 June 1999, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Government of the United UK were represented by their Agent, Ms S. Langrish, of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 34129/96) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained that his case had not been heard by an impartial tribunal because, allegedly, the jury had been racially prejudiced. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) In a decision of 29 June 1999, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Government of the United Kingdom was represented by their Agent, Ms S. Langrish, of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The judge discussed the case and ordered the juror who had written the complaint not to join the other jurors. The judge received two letters from the jury the next day. The first letter was signed by all the jurors including the juror who had sent the complaint. The second letter, which the judge commended, was written by a Juror who appeared to have thought himself to have been making the jokes. The juror in question explained at length that he might have done so, that he was sorry if he had given any offence, and that he he was not the one who had made the joke. The case was adjourned and the judge listened to submissions in open court. The defence asked the judge to dismiss the jury on the ground that there was a real danger of bias. The judge decided to call the jury back into court. The jury found the applicant guilty, but acquitted G.C., who was also Asian. On 20 April 1995 the judge imposed on the applicant a sentence of five years' imprisonment. The applicant was given leave to appeal against conviction. In his appeal he raised, inter alia, the following ground: The judge should have reacted to the juror's complaint by dismissing the jury. The juror who had written the complaint should not have been segregated from the other members of the jury in the early stages. The judge was right to confront the jury with the problem and ask them to consider it. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal. The court found that the judge did not err in reaching the conclusion that there was no real risk of bias. The judge dealt with the possibility of tensions among the jurors perfectly sensibly in the direction he gave to them. However, it would be unrealistic to suppose that the jury would not have wanted to know who the author of the complaint was. Other members of the jury, as this led to his identification, were also asked to give evidence in the trial. The jury's decision will be returned in a few weeks' time and the case will be heard in front of a panel of judges and jury members. The trial is expected to last at least three more days before it is adjourned until the jury's verdicts are returned. The verdicts will then be returned to the jury.

name: Peter Brannigan
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 21 February 1992. It originated in two applications against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (nos. 14553-14554/89) both lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 19 January 1989 by Irish citizens, Mr Peter Brannigan and Mr Patrick McBride. For reasons of convenience Mr McBride will continue to be referred to in this judgment as the applicant. The Irish Government, having been informed by the Registrar of its right to intervene in the proceedings (Article 48, sub-paragraph (b), of the Convention), did not indicate any intention of so doing.

The first applicant, Mr Peter Brannigan, was born in 1964. He was arrested at his home by police officers on 9 January 1989 at 6.30 a.m. pursuant to section 12 (1) (b) of the Prevention of Terrorism (Temporary Provisions) Act 1984. Mr Patrick McBride was born in 1951. He was arrested at his home by police officers on 5 January 1989 at 5.05 a.m. pursuant to section 12 (1) (b) of the 1984 Act. During his detention he was interrogated on twenty-two occasions and was subject to the same regime as Mr Brannigan (see paragraph 10 above) He received two visits from his solicitor on 5 and 7 January 1989 and was seen by a medical practitioner on eight occasions during police custody. Mr Mc Bride was shot dead on 4 February 1992 by a policeman who had run amok and attacked Sinn Fein Headquarters in Belfast.

name: Olubukunola Obasa
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 50034/99) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention. name: Henrik Mønsted Jensen

name: William Shannon
train_texts: An Irish national alleged that his conviction and fine for failing to reply to questions from financial investigators violated Article 6 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. The parties did not file observations on the merits. The Court declared the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merit of the application was required. The case was decided on 23 November 2004, and the fine was reduced from £5,000 to £2,000. The matter was referred to the Court of Appeal for the benefit of the applicant, Mr William Shannon (“the applicant’s” case).
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his conviction and fine for failing to reply to questions about specific offences, where he had already been charged with the self-same offences, violated Article 6 of the convention. The parties did not file observations on the merits. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merit of the case was required. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27) was constituted as provided in Rule 26: 1. The applicant was required to attend at Woodbourne Police Station on 26 June 1998. The interview did not take place. On 25 February 1999, the applicant was convicted of this offence in the Magistrates' Court and fined the sum of GBP 200. The Belfast County Court allowed the applicant's appeal against conviction, finding that the prosecution had not proved the absence of a reasonable excuse. The judge noted that the Northern Ireland Court of Appeal had dealt with a similar case (Clinton v. Bradley [2000] NI 196) which related to the same legislation and the same investigation. The appeal was dismissed on 5 July 2002, with the judge noting that the judge had also dealt with the similar case in 2000. The applicant had refused to answer questions at an interview, and he had not been interviewed by the police, or charged with any offence. In Clinton v. Bradley, the Northern Ireland Court of Appeal had held that as Parliament had put in place certain express limitations on the use of information obtained by investigators, it could not have intended that the person concerned could put forward the risk of self-incrimination as a “reasonable excuse”. Lord Justice Carswell, giving judgment, considered, in the light of R. v. Hertfordshire County Council, ex parte Green Environmental Industries Ltd, that Article 6 § 1 of the Convention is directed towards the fairness of the trial itself. The appeal was upheld, and the applicant's conviction confirmed. He was asked by the office of the Director of Public Prosecutions to state a case for the Court of Appeal. But he died before having prepared the stated case. He was asked to prepare a case but died before he had time to do so. He died in 2006, before he could prepare the case for a court of appeal hearing. The case was never heard in court because he was already dead by the time it was due to be heard. He is buried with his wife, mother-of-one, and two other children in Harrow, Hertfordshire. name: Frank Henworth
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 515/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the criminal proceedings, concerning his trial for murder, exceeded a reasonable length of time. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. The Court declared part of the application inadmissible and invited the respondent Government to submit observations on the remaining complaints. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant and the Government each filed observations on their own merits.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the criminal proceedings, concerning his trial for murder, exceeded a reasonable length of time. He was convicted on 26 July 1996 and on 26 September 1996 appealed against the conviction. On 26 February 1998, the conviction was quashed by the Court of Appeal on the basis that the judge had misdirected the jury. A retrial was ordered which took place between 20 July and 5 August 1998, when the jury was unable to reach a verdict and was discharged. The Court declared the remainder of the application partly admissible on 6 September 2003. The applicant was found guilty by a majority of 10 to 2 in a retrial on 21 September 1999. He was sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed against the conviction, arguing it was an abuse of process. The Court of Appeal ruled that there was no reason to conclude that the practice was applicable in the particular circumstances of the applicant's case. The court noted that there. was a practice but not a rule of law for the prosecution not to offer evidence where two juries. have disagreed and found no general principle existed barring further retrial. where the prosecution had failed twice to secure a conviction. It said: “25. ...Where a serious crime has been committed and it is shown that there is a case to answer as far as a defendant is concerned, there. is a clear public interest in having a jury decide positively one" The Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords, but certified two questions of law of general public importance. The court asked whether a defendant having been tried twice without a safe verdict being returned it is oppressive to try him a third time and hence an abuse of the court's process. The Lords refused the petition for leave on 17 June 2001. The appeal was thrown out of court on 28 June 2001, and the appeal against the conviction was upheld by the Supreme Court on 16 July 2001. It was the first time in the UK that an appeal against a conviction for a murder conviction had been rejected by the Appeals Court. The case was decided in favour of the applicant, who was sentenced to life imprisonment.

name: Vernon John Davies

name: Julie Beet

The remainder of the applicants’ complaints were declared inadmissible. On 1 November 2004 these cases were assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section.

name: Christine Goodwin

The applicant remains obliged to pay the higher motor insurance premiums applicable to men. She has received letters from the. name: Per Krohn Rasmussen
train_texts: The present case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on 12 October 1983. The case originated in an application (no. 8777/79) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Commission on 21 May 1979 under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr. Per Krohn Rasmussen, a Danish national. The Commission's request referred to Articles 44 and 48 of the Convention and to the declaration whereby Denmark recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Art. 46) The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 14.

Hearings were held in public on 26 June 1984 at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg. The Court heard. views of the Agent of the Danish Government, the Delegate of the Commission and the. representative of the applicant regarding the necessity for a written procedure (Rule 37 para. 1). The applicant, Mr. Per Krohn Rasmussen, is a Danish citizen, born in 1945. He currently works as a clerk and resides in Nyborg. The Government's and the applicant's memorials were received at the registry on 19 March. On 30 May, the Registrar, acting on the instructions of the President, requested the Commission. and the Government to produce certain documents, which were received on 7, 12 and 15 June. Mr. Rasmussen was married in 1966. Two children were born, a boy in 1966 and a girl, Pernille, on 20 January 1971. The applicant had grounds, even before the latter's birth, for assuming that another man might be the father; however, in order to save the marriage, he took no steps to have paternity determined. Mr. Rasmussen and his wife applied for a separation (separation ved bevilling), which they obtained on 9 August 1973. In accordance with their agreement, Mrs. Rasmussen retained custody of the children and the competent authority issued a decision to the effect that he should pay maintenance for them from 1 September 1973. Rasmussen applied to the Ministry of Justice for leave to appeal out of time to the Supreme Court (Højesteret), but this was refused. His former wife opposed the application, on the ground that such proceedings would have a detrimental effect on the child. The Court of Appeal refused the application for the reason that the applicant had not brought the action contesting paternity within the time-limits provided for in section 5(2) of the 1960 Act on the Legal Status of Children (“the 1960 Act’ - Lov nr. 200 af 18.5.1960 om børns retsstilling; see paragraph 19 below)

Widows' benefits are based on the assumption that women are more likely than men to have been financially dependent on their spouse's earnings. The benefits themselves are concentrated on those widows who are perceived to have the greatest problems. Women on average earn less than men, so even for women who have been working, the financial loss on widowhood is likely to be significantly more than for men. Most widowers of working age will have been in employment before the death of their wives. eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the administrative courts had failed to hold an oral hearing in proceedings relating to his request for life annuity. The application was communicated to the Government on 2 February 2011. The Government responded to the application with a letter of support to the applicant. The Court has now ruled that the application is a case of discrimination. The case was heard by a panel of three judges, the first of whom heard the case on 17 February 2012. The decision was handed down by the Court of Appeal on 17 March 2012. The applicant had a right to a life annuity since his illnesses had been work-related. The court found that the applicant had been exposed to stress in his work but that the causal link between this fact and the applicant’s medical condition could not be established with a sufficiently high degree of probability. The interaction between various risk factors was complex but, in general, the more risk factors were present, the higher the risk of suffering a heart attack or developing vascular disorders. The applicant requested that the Administrative Court of Appeal hold an oral hearing in the case without, however, giving any reasons for his request. He repeated the request on 14 June 2005 and specified that he wanted Dr C-G.E., Dr E.H. and Dr C.E. to testify. The applicant requested an oral hearing to deal with his case as a whole, including the question of leave to appeal. He also wanted to be heard himself about his work situation and the stressful environment. The court asked the applicant to complete his written submissions. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten), reiterating the grounds of appeal already presented before the lower instances. He again invoked Article 6 of the Convention in relation to his right to an Oral hearing. The Supreme Administrative court rejected the request on 29 October 2007. The case was referred back to the Administrative Court of Appeal for an Oral Hearing or to hold an oral Hearing itself. Supreme Administrative Court refused the applicant leave to appeal. The applicant was requested to complete his written submissions. for an oral hearing as it found no reason to hold one in order to decide on the question of leave to appealed. It noted that leave to Appeal was granted if the case was a precedent case or if serious material or procedural mistakes were involved. As this was not so in the present case, the court found no reasons to try the case on its merits. The case was decided in favour of the applicant on a majority of votes. The appeal was dismissed on a vote of 3 to 2, with the decision to be appealed to the Supreme Court.

The applicant complained that civil proceedings instituted by him had not been heard within a reasonable time. On 22 June 1999, the Court declared the application admissible. The Court examined the case in accordance with the provisions of Article 5 of the Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant is a Danish citizen, born in 1966, who resides in Skanderborg, Denmark. He was severely injured in a car accident in 1986 and is now partly disabled. He instituted proceedings against three insurance companies in the City Court ofSkanderborg on 26 February 1988. The applicant claimed that the defendant companies should be held liable to pay, jointly and severally, a specified amount in compensation for permanent disablement and loss of working capacity. On 11 May 1988 the case was adjourned pending the outcome of the applicant’s request to the National Board of Industrial Injuries (Arbejdsskadestyrelsen, hereinafter called the NBI), to give an opinion on the degree of disablement. By letter of 8 February 1991, the Board maintained its opinion. The applicant appealed against the decision to adjourn the case to the High Court of Western Denmark (Vestre Landsret) which, however, upheld the decision on 1 October 1992. The case was heard by the City Court on 25 January 1995. By judgment of 15 February 1995 the defendant companies were held liable to pay 950,803.60 DKK plus interest to the applicant. The defendants appealed against the judgment to the High Court of Western Denmark. The High Court fixed the trial to commence on 1 August 1996. It was later rescheduled to commenced on 5 September 1996. The judgment has become final. The applicant was accordingly examined again by medical experts following which the NBI submitted its opinion as to the. applicant’s degree of disablement and working capacity on 30 June 1994. The NBI then concluded that the applicant was fit to stand trial.

name: Norman Scarth
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 4 December 1998. On 1 June 1999 the Chamber decided not to hold a hearing in the case and agreed to waive the right to the presence of an ad hoc judge.
eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 4 December 1998. It originated in an application (no. 33745/96) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under former Article 25. The applicant requested permission to present his own case (Rule 36 § 4 (b) on 1 March 1999. On 11 May 1999 the Government conceded that there had been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention in the circumstances of the case. The Chamber ultimately constituted within the Section included Mr A. Pastor Rudruejo, Mr L. Caflisch, Mr J. Makarczyk, Mr I. Cabral Barreto and Mrs S. Botoucharova. The case was heard by way of arbitration under Order 19, rule 7, of the County Court Rules. Mr Scarth made an application for the main hearing to be in public and for evidence to be given on oath. The reasons for the refusal were not recorded formally, but in a note of 21 July 1997 prepared in the context of the Convention proceedings, District Judge Elliott made the following comments: “At this stage I can only say that it is likely that I took the view that the [applicant's] reasons as set out in his application were not in my view good Reasons for the private nature of arbitration proceedings to be dispensed with” Mr Scarth applied for leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal alleging a lack of public hearing, misconduct by the judge and an overall unfairness of the proceedings. Mr Scarth was heard in open court and leave was refused on 9 November 1995. Lord Justice Morritt noted that the “European Convention on Human Rights is not part of our law in the way the European Community law is“. He further found that the judge could not be said to have been guilty of any misconduct. He refused the application on 9 May 1995 and made a costs order against MrScarth. These costs were subsequently assessed at GBP 1,032.76. Under the Civil Procedure Rules, which came into force on 26 April 1999, hearings, including those in small claims cases, are to be held in public. There is a discretion for the court to hold a hearing in private where: (a) publicity would defeat the object of the hearing; (b) it involves matters relating to national security; (c) it is confidential information (including information relating to personal financial matters) and publicity would damage that confidentiality; (d) a private hearing is necessary to protect the interests of any child or person suffering from mental incapacity. The Government conceded that there had been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention in the circumstances of this application.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28291/95) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court decided that the application against Turkey was not valid. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) He was then taken to Ankara for questioning in relation to his activities in the organisation. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. In a judgment of 19 July 1989 the Martial Law Court convicted the applicant of membership. It sentenced the applicant to 15 years’ imprisonment, permanently debarred him from employment in the civil service and placed him under judicial guardianship. On 27 December 1995 the Court of Cassation quashed the applicant’s conviction on the ground that he should have been convicted of the offence.

name: Thomas John Crompton

eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The parties requested an oral hearing. However, the Chamber decided not to hold a hearing in the case. The applicant, Mr Thomas John Crompton, is a British national who was born in 1954 and lives in Stalybridge, Cheshire. His discharge from the Army, dated 18 February 1994, was formally made, incorrectly, on the basis that his services were no longer required. He later discovered that his former duties were being carried out by an untrained civilian, while the technical store-man post remained vacant. The applicant complained about his redundancy to the Industrial Tribunal, but his claim was rejected because the Tribunal did not have jurisdiction over military personnel. The matter was then placed before the Army Board. The Army Board met to reach a determination on 11 April 2001. It issued its decision on 16 July 2001, ordering that the applicant be offered compensation in respect of the failure to offer him alternative employment within the Army. The sum was made up of three parts: loss of salary (minus the applicant's actual earnings during the relevant period); a redundancy payment estimated on the basis of the Army Act 1955; and a further offer of settlement. On 10 August 2001, an award of compensation was notified to the applicant but he disputed the calculation of the compensation. The offer of £15,000 was denied on two grounds. The third was that it did not cover the cost of the alleged delay in payment. The claim was eventually dismissed. The case was heard in the High Court again in 2004 but the case was not settled. The award was later reduced to £10,000. The appeal against the decision was dismissed in May 2007. The compensation is now being paid out in full, after a seven-year delay. The court is waiting to hear the outcome of the appeal. The matter was adjourned until the end of the year, when it will be heard again by the judge who made the decision. The applicant received compensation of GBP 153,864.47. The Army Board issued its decision awarding the applicant compensation on 24 May 2005. The applicant's application for judicial review was refused on 24 June 2005 on the ground that the Army Board's decision had brought the finality which the applicant had been seeking. The application was refused again on 22 September 2005. Following the applicant's renewed application and an oral hearing, permission was finally refused on 14 November 2005. eval_texts: Two Turkish nationals, Mr Sait Uysal and Mr İskan Osal (“the applicants”), made an application under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. eval_texts: The case was brought before the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’s) on 13 March 1986. It originated in an application (no. 10426/83) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission on 30 March 1983 under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Swedish citizen, Mr. Bengt Pudas. The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 § 1 and 13 (Art. 6-1, art. 13). The applicant expressed his wish to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The hearing was held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The applicant, Mr. Bengt Pudas, is a Swedish citizen born in 1959. On 1 February 1980, the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen) of Norrbotten granted him a taxi traffic licence, and, on 20 May, a licence to carry passengers and their goods on specified interurban routes (linjetrafik). The licences were expressed in written form. The Court heard addresses by Mr. Corell for the Government, by Mr Gaukur Jörundsson for the Commission and by Mr Ravnsborg for the applicant. The County Traffic Company of Norrbotten applied for a licence to provide interurban transport on routes covered by Mr. Pudas’ second licence. The Company at the same time requested that this licence be revoked, as well as a licence held since 1973 by a certain Mr. Wälimaa. In support of its application, the Company submitted that two traffic services in two different regions were to be united into one regular service with a single time-table. The applicant opposed the revocation of his licence. On 17 August 1981, the County Administrative Board granted the Company a licence, valid as from 1 September 1981, to provideinterurban transport of passengers and goods. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Board of Transport (transportrådet), in which he alleged, inter alia, the following. The County Traffic Company’s application for a licence for the routes covered by his licence had been motivated not by any public interest in improving the transport service. Only very serious reasons, such as misconduct of the licence-holder, could justify revocation. When revoking his licence, the County Administrative Board had failed to take due account of his interests. The transport service on the routes concerned was not likely to be improved simply by being carried out by Mr. Wälimaa and others instead of by himself.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 24874/04) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the refusal of the national courts to lift a confiscation order for a number of books published by his company violated his right to freedom of expression within the meaning of Article 10. He was convicted and served a total period of one year, five months and twenty days in prison and paid the equivalent of 5,121 euros (EUR) in fines. The President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government on 10 March 2009. The Second Chamber of the Ankara State Security Court lifted the confiscation orders in respect of a number of the books. The applicant appealed against the decision of 22 November 2005. The contents of those books amounted not only to “separatist propaganda” but were also unlawful “under various laws”.

name: Gerard O’Halloran

eval_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applications were joined and on 25 October 2005 they were declared admissible by a Chamber of that Section. On 11 April 2006 the Chamber relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber, none of the parties having objected to relinquishment. Luzius Wildhaber and Matti Pellonpää continued to sit following the expiry of their terms of office, in accordance with Article 23 § 7 of the convention and Rule 24 of the Rules of Court. Jean-Paul Costa succeeded him in that capacity and took over the presidency of the grand chamber. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 27 September 2006. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits. The Court heard addresses by Mr Emmerson and Mr Perry and their answers to questions put by judges. Mr O’Halloran (application no. 15809/02) was the registered keeper of a vehicle caught on a speed camera driving at 69 miles per hour (mph) on the M11 motorway. He was asked to furnish the full name and address of the driver of the vehicle on the relevant occasion or to supply other information that was in his power to give and which would lead to the driver’s identification. The applicant was convicted and fined 100 pounds sterling (GBP) for driving in excess of the speed limit. The applicant sought to exclude the confession made in response to the Notice of Intended Prosecution, relying on sections 76 and 78 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 read in conjunction with Article 6 of the Convention. His application was refused in the light of the decision of the Privy Council in Brown v. Stott [2001] 2 WLR 817. Thereafter the prosecution relied upon the photograph of the speeding vehicle and the admission obtained as a result of the section 172 demand. The application for judicial review of the magistrates’ decision was refused. The applicant was summoned to the Magistrates’ Court for failing to comply with section 172(3) of the Road Traffic Act 1988. He was convicted and fined GBP 750 with GBP 250 costs and three penalty points. He states that the fine was substantially heavier than that which would have been imposed if he had pleaded guilty to the speeding offence. The Court of Appeal ruled that the applicant’s right to remain silent and privilege against self-incrimination had not been infringed. The applicant wrote to the Court on 15 November 2001, relying on Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the Convention. On 8 February 2002, the Court cancelled the postponement and fixed the trial for 15 April 2002, on which date the applicant was convicted.

name: Paul Matthew Coyne

eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 16 September 1996. It originated in an application (no. 25942/94) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 on 23 November 1994. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal. The Government offered to settle the case on the basis of the payment of the applicant’s reasonable legal costs and expenses. This offer was rejected by the applicant on 6 May 1997. On 28 May 1997, the Court decided that it would be necessary to hold an oral hearing, limited to issues under Article 50 of the Convention. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 June 1997. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr M.R. Eaton, Deputy Legal Adviser, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr J. Eadie, Counsel, and for the applicant Mr G. Blades. Mr Coyne was charged with various offences of forgery and deception. The charges were connected to a false application for a bank loan. The court martial took place at the RAF Station, Brüggen on 26‑28 January 1994. Mr Coyne pleaded not guilty to all the charges against him. He was sentenced to nine months’ detention, dismissal from the air force and reduction to the ranks. On 31 January 1994 he presented a petition against conviction and sentence to the confirming officer. He claimed that the judge advocate had erred in his summing up of the case, that he had been wrongly convicted and dismissed. The Court of Appeal for the Republic of Ireland rejected the appeal against the conviction. The court found that the sentence was excessive. The decision was made on the basis that the charge was not proven. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that it was not proved. The case was referred to the Court of Appeals again, this time for review. The Court of appeal was allowed to hear the case again, and the conviction was overturned. The Appeal was returned to the Courts of Appeal, who then upheld the conviction, as was the decision to dismiss the appeal. The conviction was upheld by the Appeals Court again, on the same grounds as the original.

name: Bernard Fox

eval_texts: The case was brought before the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 13 July 1989. It originated in three applications (nos. 12244/86, 12245/86 and 12383/86) lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) of the Convention. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them. The object of the request was to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 5 and 13 ( art. 5, art. 13) ofthe Convention. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Buildings, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr Kerr for the Government, by Mr Rozakis for the Commission and by Mr Weir for the applicants, as well as their replies to its questions. The first and second applicants, Mr Bernard Fox and Ms Maire Campbell, are husband and wife but separated. Both reside in Belfast, Northern Ireland. On 5 February 1986 they were stopped by the police in Belfast and brought to Woodbourne Royal Ulster Constabulary (“RUC”) station, where a full search of the vehicle in which they were travelling was carried out. Twenty-five minutes after their arrival at the police station, at 3.40 p.m., they were formally arrested under section 11 (1) of the Northern Ireland law. Mr Fox and Ms Campbell were questioned about their suspected involvement in intelligence gathering and courier work for the Provisional Irish Republican Army. They were not brought before a judge or given any opportunity to apply for release on bail. No charges were brought against either applicant. The first applicant was released at 11.40 a.m. on 7 February 1986 and the second applicant five minutes later. Excluding the time taken to bring them to the police station, the first applicant had thus been detained for 44 hours. The third applicant, Mr Samuel Hartley, was arrested at his home, in his parents’ presence, on 18 August 1986. He was informed at the time of his arrest that he was being arrested under section 11 (1) of the 1978 Act as he was suspected of being a terrorist. Mr Hartley was suspected of involvement in a kidnapping incident in Ballymena. Those involved in the kidnapping were thought to have connections with the Provisional IRA. The motive behind the kidnapping was believed to have been an attempt to force the young woman to retract an allegation of rape made the previous year as a result of which a person had been convicted and sentenced to 3 years’ imprisonment. He was released on 19 August 1986 at 2.10 p.m. after 30 hours and 15 minutes in detention. No charges were brought against him. He brought no proceedings in connection with his arrest or detention. He has not contradicted the Government’s assertion that he was asked about it.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 19859/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1952 and lives in Glasgow. He is an advocate by profession. He owned a flat in a tenement building in Edinburgh. A fire occurred in the building which damaged part of the applicant’s flat. While the applicant was living elsewhere, the commercial property company instructed repair work. When the applicant refused to pay the council for his share of the repair costs, the council brought proceedings in the Sheriff Court (the civil court of general jurisdiction) The applicant claimed that both sets of repairs constituted trespass to his property. The applicant brought proceedings against the commercial property company (‘the first defenders’) and the city council (“the second defenders”) in the Outer House of the Court of Session. He alleged that the statutory notices were invalid on grounds of fraud and illegal conspiracy. The Lord Ordinary granted the first defenders leave to reclaim (appeal) to the Inner House against the interlocutor of 22 September 1998 in so far as it related to the disclosure of documents. By judgments of 17 February 1999, the Sheriff Court rejected the applicant’s claims. The applicant was then informed by the court that he was required to intimate a copy of the closed record to the relevant sheriff clerk. The court gave him leave to do so on 26 February 1998. The first defenders failed to apply for a hearing on their grounds of appeal. The Lord Ordinary found the applicant’s claims to be unfounded and unspecified. The appeal was heard on 21 June 2002. The case was dismissed on 4 September 2002 by the Outer House. The applicant appealed to the Inner House and the appeal was listed for 18 and 19 November 2003. However, on 13 November, it allowed him to abandon his appeal against the second defenders and proceed only against the first defenders. In a written judgment, the LordOrdinary. found the application’S claims to have been unfounded, unspecified and unfounded. The application was dismissed and the case was remitted back to theLord Ordinary. The applicant was found liable for the first defenders’ costs on 18 December 2003. The appeal was unanimously dismissed on 11 December 2003, the court finding that the applicant’s pleadings lacked specification. Complaints made in relation to the solicitors and advocates representing the council were dismissed by their respective professional bodies and then by the Scottish Legal Services Ombudsman on 13 November 2001 and 4 July 2003, respectively. on 18 and 19 November 2003. On 25 July 2002, the applicant petitioned the Court of Session for leave to proceed without the signature of a solicitor. Leave was refused on the papers on 26 July 2002. The applicant also sought to bring proceedings in the Court  in June 2002 against the solicitor acting for the council in the Sheriff Court proceedings.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1176/10) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that in criminal proceedings leading to his conviction he had not been afforded a fair hearing by an impartial tribunal. On 17 July 2013 the application was communicated to the Government. By a judgment of 5 the High Court ruled in favour of the applicant and the Norwegian Government. The case was heard at the Oslo Court of Appeal on 21 March 2013. The judge described the case as ‘a case of alleged sexual assault’ and ruled that it was a case of attempted rape. In February 2009, the Borgarting High Court (lagmannsrett), hearing the applicant’s appeal with a jury, convicted him on the attempted rape charge and sentenced him to one year's imprisonment. It ordered him to pay 60,000 Norwegian kroner (NOK) (approximately 7,500 euros at that time) in compensation to Ms A for non-pecuniary damage. The High Court also noted that Mr B had testified that he had not noticed anything conspicuous about Ms A; she had been cheerful and friendly and her clothes had not been in disorder. However, this did not suggest, in the High Court's view, that she had not was exposed to sexual abuse causing a great burden on her. Counsel for the defence requested that J be disqualified from taking part in the further proceedings on grounds of lack of impartiality. The public prosecutor expressed understanding for the motion without taking a stance. The High Court observed that “the jury member had formed a picture [bilde] of the victim from many years ago where she at the time had experienced her as a quiet and calm person” It decided that a member might be disqualified if the person in question had particular reasons for identifying himself or herself with the victim or if there were any other circumstances to the effect that he or she had a prejudging attitude. However, that was not the situation in the present case. Juror J took part in the entire trial before the High Court, including the jury’s deliberations and vote on the charge of attempted rape. High Court had special regard to the fact that the parties to the case had requested that J recuse herself, but it found the absence of partiality so clear in this case that this could not be decisive. By a judgment of 26 June 2009 the Supreme Court, by three votes to two, rejected the applicant's appeal. The majority did not consider that the juror's knowledge of the victim from her attendance at birthday parties and class outings with the victim in itself indicated an identification with the Victim or weakened in any other way the confidence in her impartiality. J's information about Ms A had emerged after she had given evidence to the High Court for one hour. At that point, the jury, including J, had a good opportunity to form an independent and updated picture of the victim as a person. That defence counsel and the assistant advocate had requested that J withdraw could not be decisive. There were no particular circumstances capable of calling into doubt J’s impartiality for the purposes of section 108 of the Administration of Courts Act, as interpreted in the light of Article 6 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child. The minority considered that the case concerned a serious and stigmatising accusation against the defendant. There was no basis for such a conclusion and there was in any event no reason for attaching weight to such a possibility. It was correct to add that she had experienced the victim as a “quiet and calm person”. The timing of J’s affirmation could easily have given the impression that J expressed a positive assessment of the victim. That J had expressed a view on how she had perceived her “at the time”, was of secondary importance. Under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, “the standpoint of the accused [was] important but not decisive” in this case the “fear” of lack of impartiality by the applicant had been “objectively justified” (see Ferrantelli and Santangelo v. Italy, 7 August 1996, § 58, Reports of Judgments and Decisions 1996‑III).

The applicants, a married couple of Iraqi origin, were born in 1957 and 1963 respectively. They have three children, who are now eighteen, sixteen and eight years of age. From 1 November 1999 they rented a flat in Rinkeby, a suburb of Stockholm. It appears that when the applicants moved in, there was a satellite dish mounted on the façade, next to one of the windows of the flat. The applicants made use of this in order to receive television programmes in Arabic and Farsi. In October 2003 the applicants' landlord changed. The new landlord, a real-estate company, demanded that the satellite dish be dismantled and, by letter of 2 April 2004, the company gave the applicants notice of termination of the tenancy agreement.

The applicants, a married couple of Iraqi origin, were born in 1957 and 1963 respectively and live in Västerås. They rented a flat in Rinkeby, a suburb of Stockholm, from 1 November 1999. Rule 13 of the special provisions of the tenancy agreement stipulated the following: “The tenant undertakes not to erect, without specific permission, placards, signs, sunblinds, outdoor aerials and such like on the house” The agreement further stipulated, as a general condition, that the tenants were obliged to take proper care of the flat and to maintain good sanitary conditions, order and good practice in the house.

The applicants' landlord demanded that the satellite dish be dismantled. The applicants did not comply and, by letter of 2 April 2004, the company gave the applicants notice of termination of the tenancy agreement with effect from 31 July 2004. The landlords claimed that the applicants' satellite installation violated the express ban in Rule 13 of the tenants' tenancy agreement. The couple, of Iraqi origin, have three children, who are now eighteen, sixteen and eight years of age. The case was heard by the Rent Review Board (hyresnämnden) in Stockholm. The verdict was returned in favour of the applicants and the tenants are suing the landlord for damages.

Tenants' Association wanted to use satellite dishes in their homes. Landlord claimed they were exercising their right to receive information. Tenant's appeal to Landlord Review Board found in favour of tenant's right to access TV channels. But judge also found that the installation did not breach the tenancy agreement. The Board found that it was not a breach of the Landlord's obligations to protect the tenants' interests in using a satellite dish. The appeal was dismissed on appeal on 21 October 2004, with the Board's decision to be appealed again on 6 October 2005, with a new order to be issued to the landlord. The original decision was made on 26 August 2004, and the appeal was rejected on 18 October 2005.

Tenants' Association found the installation was stable but recommended that a steel wire be fixed between the dish and the stand. The Board found that the fact that the new satellite installation extended through a window did not involve a breach of Rule 13 of the tenancy agreement. With regard to the general obligation to maintain good sanitary conditions, order and good practice in the house, the Board considered that the actual installation did not and could not damage the house. Also, the liability for damage to persons and property could not reasonably be incurred unless it were able to prevent it. The new installation was, they claimed, in conformity with the rules of the tenants' agreement.

The Tenants' Association, an engineer, examined the installation on 26 August 2004. He found that it was very stable but recommended that, for safety reasons, a steel wire be fixed between the dish and the stand. The applicants, as well as the other tenants, contested the landlord's claims. The Board found that the fact that the new satellite installation extended through a window did not involve a breach of Rule 13 of the tenancy agreement. With regard to the general obligation to maintain good sanitary conditions, order and good practice in the house, the Board considered that the actualinstallation did not and could not damage the house.

The family moved to Västerås, 110 km west of Stockholm, after the court ordered them to remove the satellite dish. The family's three children had to change nursery and school and leave friends because of the move. The court ruled that the dish did not pose a real safety threat, but was in the landlord's interests to comply with the court's order. The judge said the family had not shown that removing the dish was in their best interests or that it would be of any benefit to them to do so. The decision was made to move the family to a new house, which they moved on 1 June 2006.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 23883/06) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that their eviction from their flat following their refusal to remove a satellite dish resulted in violations of Articles 8 and 10. The application was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicants, a married couple of Iraqi origin, were born in 1957 and 1963 respectively and live in Västerås. They have three children, who are now eighteen, sixteen and eight years of age. Landlord sought execution of the notice of termination, claiming that the applicants' satellite installation violated the express ban in Rule 13 of the tenancy agreement. Landlord claimed that the installations a) risked causing injuries to persons and property for which the landlord would be held responsible, b) damaged the house physically and aesthetically and c) obstructed rescue workers' and the landlord's access to the flat. The applicants, as well as the other tenants summoned, contested the landlord’s claims before the Rent Review Board. They stated that, by mounting satellite dishes for the reception of television programmes, some of which were broadcast in their mother tongues, they were exercising their freedom to receive information. Landlord said he was working on the possibility of installing broadband and internet access in the house, which would allegedly give access to the desired television channels. Rent Review Board gave a decision on 21 October 2004 finding in their favour. Landlord appealed to the Svea Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt). The court held an oral hearing at which, inter alia, Mr Tornefelt gave evidence. It also made an inspection of the applicants' satellite installation. By a final decision of 20 December 2005, the court found that the applicants had disregarded their obligations as tenants, under the tenancy agreement and Chapter 12, section 25 of the Land Code. The court found that the landlord had made a reasonable distinction between acceptable and unacceptable satellite installations. They were given a respite until 31 March 2006 to move from the flat. They have stated that, largely because of the scarcity of flats for rent in the Stockholm area but also due to there being a court eviction order against them, they were forced to move to Västerås, approximately 110 km west of Stockholm. In assessing the seriousness of this breach of contract, the court first concluded, with reference to Mr Tornefelt's testimony, that the satellite installation met the reasonable requirements of stability and safety. They did not agree to do this, however, and instead moved on 1 June 2006.

The first applicant, Mr Abdisamad Adow Sufi, is a Somali national who was born in 1987. He is currently in detention in an Immigration Detention Centre in West Drayton. On 3 October 2003 he claimed asylum on the ground that as a member of the Reer-Hamar, a sub-clan of the minority Ahansi clan, he had been subjected to persecution by Hawiye militia. On 15 April 2005 the Secretary of State for the Home Department refused the first applicant’s asylum application, finding that the fact he had remained in Somalia until 2003 undermined his claim to be a minority clan. On 29 June 2005 both the asylum appeal and the human rights appeal were dismissed by an Adjudicator who found that his account of what had happened to him in Somalia was not credible. He was later sentenced to three months’ imprisonment following a conviction for indecent exposure in October 2007.

The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section of the Court. The first applicant, Mr Patrick Benjamin, was sentenced to life imprisonment for rape in 1983. The second applicant, Mr Hueth Wilson, was sentenced to life imprisonment for buggery of a young girl in 1977. The court had before it psychiatric evidence to the effect that he suffered from mental illness. Expert psychiatric evidence recommended that he should be made subject to a hospital order coupled with a restriction order without limit of time. Due to an absence of any beds in hospitals providing the level of security that the trial judge considered necessary, the judge felt unable to make the orders and passed, instead, a discretionary life sentence. His tariff period (the minimum period of detention satisfying the requirements of retribution and deterrence) was set at six years and expired in April 1989. On 9 January 2001, the MHR Tribunal recommended his discharge. The applicants had appealed against their treatment in hospital for mental illness. Their case was reviewed by the MHR Tribunal on 13 June 2000. The Tribunal did not recommend discharge of the second applicant. The applicants were not eligible for review by the discretionary lifer panels empowered by section 34 of the Criminal Justice Act 1991 to order their release on licence. The right to a hearing under the 1991 Act was conferred only on persons who were solely subject to that Act, and not on those who were mental patients. The Court of Appeal reversed the High Court's decision in part in 1994. The House of Lords refused leave to appeal against the decision in 1995.

Police were escorting a post office van carrying significant sums of money on its way to Adare village, Co. Limerick. When the two vehicles arrived at the post office in Adare, the police car was rammed from behind by a stolen vehicle and immediately surrounded by five heavily armed and masked individuals dressed in paramilitary style uniforms. One of the five opened fire at point blank range on the police officers and one of those officers died instantly and the other was seriously wounded. The police suspected a local unit of the Irish Republican Army (an unlawful paramilitary organisation known as the IRA) and the IRA later claimed responsibility for the murder. It was also suspected by the police that the stolen vehicle together with all firearms and ammunition used in the attempted robbery had been stored in a safe house in Patrickswell. The applicant was asked to account for his movements during certain periods of time on 6 and 7 June 1996 immediately before, during and after the incident in Adare. He was charged, pursuant to section 52 of the 1939 Act, on three counts of refusing to give an account of his movements. On 15 May 1997 the District Court dismissed one charge, he was convicted on the second charge (a section 52 request made on 21 July 1996) and was sentenced to six months’ imprisonment. The applicant appealed against conviction and sentence to the Circuit Court and was released on bail pending the appeal. In February 1999 the applicant’s brother pleaded guilty to the charge of conspiracy to commit robbery and the remaining charges were not proceeded with.

He sought a declaration that this provision was incompatible with the European Convention on Human Rights. His application was heard before the Divisional Court on 21 and 22 March 2001, together with the application for judicial review of two other prisoners, Mr Pearson and Mr Feal-Martinez, who had applied for registration as electors and were refused by the Registration Officer. Lord Justice Kennedy concluded that in Europe only eight countries, including the United Kingdom, did not give convicted prisoners a vote.

In October 1991 they had contacted the Social Council and expressed concern about his learning difficulties and his general state of health. Following this, the Council commenced an investigation which, with Mrs Andersson's agreement, led to the placement of her son in the therapeutic school. The applicant, Mrs Anne-Marie Andersson, was a Swedish citizen. She was born in 1943 and died in 1996. She lived in Göteborg, where she worked as a taxi driver. Schäder, Director-General of Legal Affairs. For the applicant Mrs S. Westerberg, Counsel, Mrs C. Bokelund, Lawyer, Mr M. Eliasson, Attorney, Mrs R. Harrold-Claesson, Counsel. Anne-Marie Andersson contacted a psychiatric clinic in Göteborg in order to receive a medical certificate which would enable her to claim sickness benefit from the Health Insurance Office. From 20 August 1991 the applicant was treated by the chief psychiatrist who drew her attention to the possible detrimental effect her situation might have on her son. The psychiatrist informed Mrs Andersson that since the child's health might be at risk, she had an obligation under Swedish law to contact the social authorities. She telephoned a social-welfare officer at the Social Council (socialnämnden) and informed her of the applicant's health problems. At the request of that officer the psychiatrist submitted the following written statement on 16 January 1992: “I do not find that, from a psychiatric point of view, we can do more for the patient, who does not consider herself to be mentally ill.” The psychiatrist's concern for the applicant's son was shared by the headmaster and a teacher at the school he attended. In October 1991 they had contacted the Social Council and expressed concern about his learning difficulties and his general state of health. Following this, the Council commenced an investigation which, with Mrs Andersson's agreement, led to the placement of her son in a non-residential therapeutic school on 2 March 1992. The psychiatrist wrote to the applicant the same day to inform her of the information imparted to the Council. He also wrote to her to say that he had referred her to the district medical officer and she will, thus, have no further contact with me.
